title: Stablecoin Review Tribunal
summary: This is FSTB's short webpage on the Stablecoin Review Tribunal. This appeal body was created under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) to hear challenges to certain HKMA decisions on stablecoin issuer licensing. It names the current chairman and six members. Their term runs from 1 November 2025 to 31 October 2028. The page explains that a person who disagrees with a decision has 30 days to ask the Tribunal to review it. This confirms the ordinance and its appeal mechanism are already operating, not merely proposed.

key_points.point: The Tribunal reviews specified HKMA decisions made under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656).
A person unhappy with a qualifying HKMA decision has 30 days to ask the Tribunal to review it, or longer if the Tribunal allows.
The Tribunal only convenes when needed, not on a fixed schedule.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this confirms the Stablecoins Ordinance appeal mechanism is live, with a sitting Tribunal. This matters if the bank itself becomes a licensed FRS (fiat-referenced stablecoin) issuer, or needs to understand a stablecoin counterparty's recourse against an adverse HKMA decision.
reading_guide: The whole page is short (under 40 lines); read it in full.
flags: This page's existence confirms the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) is already in force with an active appeal body, which is useful corroboration when reading the still-proposal-stage consultation documents in this batch.

counterparty_due_diligence: If a stablecoin issuer counterparty discloses a licence refusal, condition, suspension or revocation, note it can be challenged before this Tribunal within 30 days — relevant to assessing whether a counterparty's licensing status is final or still contested.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: None needed unless the bank itself is party to an HKMA decision under the Stablecoins Ordinance.

title: Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau (CSTCB) — HKPF
summary: This is a short page describing the Hong Kong Police Force's Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau (CSTCB). CSTCB investigates cyber and technology crime, carries out computer forensics, and coordinates with other agencies. It contains no digital-asset-specific policy content.

key_points.point: CSTCB has treated combating technology crime as an operational priority since 2012, covering public awareness, inter-agency cooperation, and proactive investigation.

numbers_and_dates.item: technology crime made an Operational Priority

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the police unit that would investigate crypto-related fraud or hacking affecting the bank's customers; it is background context rather than a source of obligations.
reading_guide: Whole page is short; no skipping needed.

notifications_reporting: Know CSTCB as the referral point if the bank needs to report crypto-related cybercrime or fraud affecting customers
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: None.

title: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers in Hong Kong
summary: This is FSTB's webpage index for the joint FSTB/HKMA public consultation on licensing fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) issuers. It links to the December 2023 consultation paper and the July 2024 consultation conclusions paper. Both linked documents are analysed as separate registry entries below. The underlying consultation fed into the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656), which has since come into force, so this consultation stage is now historical.

key_points.point: The page is purely a links index to the two substantive PDFs; it carries no independent regulatory content.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Use this only as a pointer; the compliance-relevant content sits in the two attached documents in this package.
reading_guide: No independent content to read; go straight to the consultation paper and conclusions paper.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: See the two package entries for board-relevant content on the stablecoin issuer licensing regime.

title: HKEX Virtual Asset Index Series
summary: This is HKEX's own webpage for its Virtual Asset Index Series. It covers the same Bitcoin/Ether reference index and daily reference rate as the companion brochure in this batch. It adds an FAQ on how constituent exchanges are chosen, based on ratings, licensing, and USD trading pairs, plus details of the semi-annual constituent review and the Index Oversight Committee. It names CCData as the index administrator. It is exchange product/marketing content, not a regulatory publication.

key_points.point: Constituent exchanges must be rated 'AA' or 'A' in the latest two Exchange Benchmark Reports, be licensed and regulated, and offer USD direct trading pairs to be eligible.
key_points.locator: FAQ, 'How is a constituent exchange selected'

key_points.point: The top five eligible exchanges by rating become constituents, reviewed every six months (June and December), with an extra quarterly review in March and September if fewer than five qualify.
key_points.locator: FAQ, 'How is a constituent exchange selected'

key_points.point: An Index Oversight Committee, including HKEX and the index administrator, oversees index maintenance and must endorse any methodology changes.
CCData, described as a UK-registered benchmark administrator, calculates and administers the index series for HKEX.

numbers_and_dates.value: up to 5, reviewed semi-annually (Jun/Dec), with extra reviews Mar/Sep if below 5

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this explains the governance behind HKEX's crypto reference prices: how constituent exchanges are vetted, and the oversight committee. A bank would want to understand this before relying on the index for product settlement. It is product literature, though, not an SFC-recognised benchmark standard in itself.
reading_guide: Read the 'About the Index Series' and FAQ sections; skip the long HKEX site-navigation menu that makes up most of the fetched page.
flags: Most of the fetched page content is HKEX website navigation menus, not substantive text; only a small middle section (About the Index Series, Methodology Overview, FAQ) is relevant.

counterparty_due_diligence: If the bank relies on this index for valuing or settling a product, note the constituent-exchange eligibility rules (AA/A rating, licensed and regulated, USD pairs) as a due-diligence reference point on data-source quality.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: None; product-awareness material only.

title: MPFA — no dedicated virtual-asset statement located
summary: This is the Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority's homepage, captured in Chinese, showing routine MPF administration news items (fund prices, savings rates, chairman's blog). It contains no virtual-asset, stablecoin or tokenisation content.

key_points.point: The page is general MPF scheme administration content and mentions no digital-asset topic.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Confirms the MPFA currently has no published digital-asset-specific guidance for the bank's retirement-scheme business to track; nothing to action here.
reading_guide: No action needed; this page has no digital-asset content.
flags: No virtual-asset/stablecoin/tokenisation content found on this page as fetched.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: None.

title: IRD: Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework page
summary: This IRD webpage explains Hong Kong's plan to adopt the OECD's Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF), a global tax-transparency standard for crypto-asset transactions. It sets out who counts as a Reporting Crypto-Asset Service Provider (RCASP), what must be reported, and the timeline for new legislation. It links the enabling bill and OECD guidance material as attachments.

key_points.point: Hong Kong plans its first automatic exchange of CARF tax data with partner jurisdictions in 2028, conditional on the domestic law being ready by 2026.
The enabling bill was gazetted 22 May 2026 and had its First Reading in LegCo on 3 June 2026.

Subject to the Bill's passage, CARF duties (registration, due diligence, reporting) are due to start on 1 January 2027, for firms meeting Hong Kong's nexus tests. The related, amended Common Reporting Standard duties are due to start on 1 January 2028. As of this review, the Bill has had only its First Reading and is not yet enacted.

A business counts as an RCASP if it runs exchange services between crypto and fiat, between different crypto-assets, or operates a trading platform for customers, including as principal or intermediary.
key_points.locator: 'Individuals and entities subject to...' section, p.2

key_points.point: An entity can be caught by HK's nexus rules through tax residence, incorporation, place of management, or having a branch or regular place of business in HK.

Under the proposed Amendment Bill, RCASPs caught by the nexus rules would need to sign up for an account on the future CARF Portal. They would need to do this by 31 January of the year after they first satisfy a nexus test, whether or not they have anything to report that year.
key_points.locator: 'Reporting portal and mandatory registration' section, p.4

key_points.point: The proposed Amendment Bill would require RCASPs to retain due-diligence and reporting records for six years from the date the related CARF return was due. This record-keeping duty continues even after the entity dissolves, falling on whoever was a director at the time.

In the Amendment Bill, the Government proposes penalties for RCASP offences, including an administrative (civil) penalty track as an alternative to prosecution, with a right of appeal to the Board of Review.

numbers_and_dates.value: 31 January of the year after first meeting nexus test

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, if it or an affiliate deals in crypto-asset exchange or transfer services for customers, it may itself become an RCASP (Reporting Crypto-Asset Service Provider). That would bring new registration, due-diligence, and 6-year record-keeping duties from 2027. Compliance should also flag this framework when assessing crypto-asset-linked counterparties and clients.
reading_guide: Read the Overview and 'Individuals and entities subject to...' sections first to check RCASP status; skip the multilingual navigation boilerplate at the top.

obligations: Assess whether the bank or group entities providing crypto exchange/transfer services meet the RCASP nexus tests, locator: 'Nexus rules', p.3

If caught, register on the CARF Portal by 31 January of the following year and run due diligence/self-certification on crypto-asset users, locator: 'Reporting portal', p.4 and 'Due diligence requirements', p.3-4
controls_and_monitoring: Build a 6-year record-retention control for CARF due-diligence and reporting evidence, locator: 'Record keeping requirements', p.4
notifications_reporting: Annual CARF return to IRD once obligations start 1 Jan 2027 (amended CRS from 1 Jan 2028); portal registration deadline 31 January, locator: 'Reporting requirements' and 'Reporting portal' sections, p.3-4
counterparty_due_diligence: Consider whether VATP or custody counterparties are themselves RCASPs and how that affects data-sharing expectations
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told whether the bank group has any RCASP exposure and the 2027 registration deadline, given criminal and proposed civil penalties for non-compliance.

title: Hong Kong Police Force — Press Release listing (JPEX case updates, incl. 16 charged Nov 2025)
summary: This is the Hong Kong Police Force's general press-release index page (a year/month archive of all police press releases, crime, traffic, missing persons, etc). The fetched page shows only navigation and archive controls, not the substantive text of any specific JPEX release.

key_points.point: The page is an archive index of police press releases by month/year, not a single press release with substantive content.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, the JPEX collapse remains a live enforcement matter. Compliance should track the individual charge announcements on this index (not captured here) for AML or fraud red flags relevant to counterparty due diligence. But this listing page itself carries no facts to summarise.
reading_guide: Not useful as fetched; a specific JPEX press release URL would need to be fetched separately for substance.
flags: text_unavailable — only the index/navigation shell was captured, not any specific press release text.

controls_and_monitoring: Monitor named JPEX defendants against customer/counterparty screening lists once specific press releases are available
counterparty_due_diligence: Treat any HK-licensed or applicant VATP with links to JPEX individuals as elevated due-diligence risk
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be aware the JPEX prosecution is ongoing (per src note, 16 charged Nov 2025) as the leading local case study for unlicensed VATP enforcement.

title: Risks associated with virtual commodities
summary: The HKMA's Banking Regulatory Document Repository (BRDR) catalogue page for a short letter sent to all banks in January 2014 about Bitcoin-type virtual commodities. The letter warns banks to be careful about money-laundering risk when dealing with firms that run virtual-commodity schemes. It tells banks to check that such customers have solid anti-money-laundering controls before opening or keeping an account for them. It also says a bank must tell the HKMA before launching any product linked to a virtual commodity. This circular was later replaced by a 2019 letter on virtual assets.

key_points.point: Banks must step up vigilance before starting or continuing a relationship with a customer that runs a virtual-commodity exchange, brokerage or transfer service.
Banks should weigh whether the operator of a virtual-commodity scheme already has real anti-money-laundering controls when judging the money-laundering risk of that customer.
Before offering any new product tied to a virtual commodity, a bank should notify and discuss it with the HKMA.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the founding document in Hong Kong's crypto oversight of banks. It set the first prior-notification expectation, and the customer due-diligence mindset, that every later HKMA virtual-asset circular builds on. This circular has since been superseded.

quote.text: notify and discuss with the HKMA

reading_guide: Read the one-page attachment in full; the catalogue page itself is navigation boilerplate.

obligations: Notify and discuss with HKMA before offering any product linked to a virtual commodity (expected, not stated as a strict legal 'must'), p.1-2
controls_and_monitoring: Escalated vigilance and risk assessment of customers operating virtual-commodity schemes, p.1
notifications_reporting: Prior notification to HKMA before product launch, p.1-2
counterparty_due_diligence: Check whether an operator-customer has effective anti-money-laundering controls, p.1
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Historical baseline only; superseded by later VA circulars, so no current board action needed beyond noting the regulatory lineage.

title: Risks Associated with Virtual Commodities
summary: A short follow-up letter to banks after press reports of more virtual-commodity exchanges appearing in Hong Kong. It repeats the January 2014 warning and reminds banks that filing a suspicious-transaction report with the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit applies equally to virtual-commodity-related dealings. It also points banks to a government public warning on virtual commodities issued in March 2014, and gives named HKMA contacts for questions.

key_points.point: Banks should keep using stronger due diligence for customers linked to virtual-commodity businesses. A customer's full activity may only become clear after the account is already open.
The statutory duty to report suspected money laundering or terrorist financing to the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit applies just as much to virtual-commodity dealings as to any other business.
Banks should stay on top of official warnings and news about virtual commodities, including the government's March 2014 public alert.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this shows the HKMA reinforcing its January 2014 controls only months later. Banks were meant to apply those controls continuously, not just at onboarding. It also shows that statutory suspicious-transaction reporting already covered crypto-linked activity, a decade before licensing regimes existed.

quote.text: statutory requirement to make a disclosure to the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit

reading_guide: One-page follow-up; read in full, skip nothing.

obligations: Continue enhanced vigilance for virtual-commodity operator customers throughout the relationship, not only at onboarding, p.1
controls_and_monitoring: Ongoing transaction monitoring and periodic review of customer risk profiles, p.1
notifications_reporting: File suspicious-transaction reports to the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit where knowledge or suspicion of ML/TF arises, p.2
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Historical; superseded by later guidance, retained for lineage only.

title: Whitepaper On Distributed Ledger Technology
summary: This is HKMA's first whitepaper on distributed ledger technology (DLT), issued 11 November 2016 at HKMA Fintech Day. It introduces DLT's technical building blocks. It then walks through operational, identity-theft and conduct risks, plus early regulatory-compliance questions. It also covers security, privacy, legal issues, and two bank-led pilots on mortgage-loan applications and trade finance. At the time, the HKMA said DLT's compliance with regulatory requirements remained largely unexplored. It treated the paper as a starting point for further study, not as settled guidance. As of this review it is historical background: it predates Hong Kong's virtual-asset and stablecoin licensing regimes.

key_points.point: DLT platforms could be misused for money laundering, illegal-goods payments or receiving ransom payments if a platform lacks Know-Your-Client (KYC) checks and transaction monitoring.

Owners of DLT-recorded assets are responsible for safeguarding their own private keys; HKMA notes that 'cold storage' (keeping keys offline, for example, on a hardware security token) gives better protection than online key storage.

HKMA states that, at the time of writing, regulators had issued little formal guidance on DLT. It remained unclear whether a traditional regulatory approach could adequately address DLT's risks and legal issues.

In permissioned DLT networks, member identities can be kept private from other members through pseudonymous transaction credentials, with only authorised auditors able to link a credential back to a real identity.

Under Hong Kong's Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance, personal data placed on a DLT ledger must still be properly notified to customers, and consented to by them, and kept no longer than necessary. This is hard to reconcile with DLT's immutability (its records cannot be changed or erased). The paper suggests deleting an encryption key, rather than the record itself, as a workaround.
key_points.locator: sec 10, 'Legal implications in relation to data privacy', p.55-56

key_points.point: An unpermissioned DLT network has no central administrator. Because of this, HKMA flags that it may be hard for a harmed participant to identify anyone legally accountable for a loss caused by a coding defect.

A five-bank working group ran a trade-finance DLT pilot. The group included Bank of China Hong Kong, Bank of East Asia, Hang Seng Bank, HSBC, and Standard Chartered. It tested whether DLT could cut duplicate-financing fraud in trade finance.
key_points.locator: Annex, trade finance PoC intro (also summarised at sec 11.2)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the founding document behind the HKMA's later DLT and custody-related expectations — cold storage of keys, AML/KYC on DLT platforms, and data-privacy handling. It is useful only as background, since the HKMA's 2024 circular and 2025 study now state its own current expectations.
reading_guide: Read section 8 (Risk Management and Regulatory Compliance, pp.44-47) and section 10 (Legal considerations, pp.54-57) for the compliance content. The technology chapters (sections 4 and 6) are a generic 2016-era primer and can be skipped.
flags: Text_unavailable not applicable, but note: predates Hong Kong's current VA/stablecoin licensing regimes by several years; treat all compliance statements as historical, superseded in substance by HKMA's 2024 DLT circular and 2025 study.

controls_and_monitoring: Use cold (offline) storage for private keys rather than online storage, an early statement of an expectation HKMA later formalised (sec 8.2, p.45).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Historical background only; no current board action required from this document alone.

title: LCQ16: Application of blockchain technology
summary: This is a 2017 Legislative Council written reply. It describes the government's early, exploratory stance on blockchain: possible public-service uses and an HKMA proof-of-concept study. It also confirms Hong Kong then had no targeted rules for 'virtual commodities' like Bitcoin. It also confirms an early-stage HKMA study into a wholesale central bank digital currency.

key_points.point: The government said Hong Kong had no rules specifically for virtual commodities, treating them as unbacked and not legal tender.
The HKMA had begun a first-phase study, with three note-issuing banks and others, into central bank digital currency for wholesale interbank and securities settlement use.
No government department had a concrete plan to use blockchain for public services like tax filing or land registration at that time.

numbers_and_dates.locator: Reply, para on FSTB/HKMA study, p.1

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is a historical marker showing how far the regime has moved since 2017; useful only for understanding the starting point of HK's digital-asset policy trajectory, not for any current obligation.

quote.text: virtual commodities

reading_guide: Read reply part (3) only, which is the crypto/CBDC-relevant answer; parts (1),(2),(4),(5) concern general e-government blockchain use and are not digital-asset regulatory content.
flags: Historical (2017) document; regulatory stance described has since been superseded by SFC/HKMA regimes.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: None; historical context only.

title: Statement on initial coin offerings
summary: This is the SFC's founding statement on initial coin offerings (ICOs). It establishes that digital tokens issued in an ICO can be 'securities' under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO), depending on their features. For example, tokens can count as securities if they carry share-like, debt-like, or collective-investment-scheme-like rights. Anyone dealing in, advising on, or managing funds in such tokens needs an SFC licence, regardless of location, if they target the Hong Kong public.

key_points.point: Tokens giving shareholder-like rights (dividends, surplus on winding up) may be treated as 'shares' under the SFO.
Tokens acknowledging a debt with fixed repayment or interest may be treated as a 'debenture'.
Pooled token proceeds invested for a share of returns may be treated as an interest in a 'collective investment scheme', also a form of security.
Dealing in, advising on, or marketing a fund in tokens that are securities needs an SFC licence. This applies wherever the firm is based, if it targets the Hong Kong public.
The SFC flags that ICO tokens' anonymity creates inherent money-laundering and terrorist-financing risk and points licensed firms back to its 2014 AML circular on virtual commodities.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this remains the foundational test for deciding whether a token is a 'security' under Hong Kong law. That decision in turn decides whether dealing, advising, or fund activity around the token needs an SFC licence.

quote.text: securities as defined in the Securities and Futures Ordinance

reading_guide: Read the whole (short) statement; the footnotes give the exact SFO definitions used for 'shares', 'debenture' and 'collective investment scheme'.

obligations: Classify any token the bank deals in, advises on, or funds against the share/debenture/CIS tests before treating it as unregulated, locator: 'Offering of securities' section, p.1
controls_and_monitoring: Apply enhanced AML/CFT controls to ICO-token activity given the SFC's stated concern about anonymity, locator: 'Cautionary statement', p.2
counterparty_due_diligence: Check whether an ICO issuer or token the bank is asked to support has features (dividends, fixed repayment, pooled returns) that would make it a security requiring the counterparty to be SFC-licensed
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should know this classification test still underlies day-to-day token/security determinations even though it predates the full VATP licensing regime.

title: Whitepaper 2.0 on Distributed Ledger Technology
summary: This is a technical annex to the HKMA's second DLT whitepaper, made up of seven contributed papers from banks, consultants, a research institute and lawyers rather than from the HKMA itself. It records the outcome of five 2017 proof-of-concept projects on trade finance and digital identity, done with five banks. It also covers a live mortgage-valuation platform BOCHK built afterwards. It adds think pieces on blockchain governance, network security, Hong Kong data-privacy law, and legal liability on a shared ledger. It is descriptive and educational, aimed at helping banks weigh up DLT adoption; it sets no rules and creates no obligations. Much of the technical detail (choice of protocol, consensus thresholds, cloud hosting) is now dated.

key_points.point: Five Hong Kong banks and Deloitte ran a proof-of-concept trade-finance DLT platform, built on a private fork of Ethereum. It let them share purchase-order, shipment and invoice status data, and cut duplicate-financing fraud.
The pilot's own estimate was that banks could cut trade-finance operating costs by roughly 15% to 60% by removing manual reconciliation and forged-document risk.

Deloitte set out three possible ways to govern a shared bank DLT network: an informal working group, a jointly funded private company, or a hybrid body with government involvement. Each option trades off speed of decisions against IP ownership.

ASTRI's digital-identity pilot let a client be onboarded once, by one bank. Only cryptographic hashes of the KYC (know-your-customer) documents, not the documents themselves, were shared on the ledger. This let a second bank confirm authenticity without collecting the paperwork again.

BOCHK's live mortgage-valuation platform, built on the earlier pilot, treats the network as workable once at least two-thirds of its nodes are online. It relies on a rolling node-to-node backup, instead of a separate disaster-recovery site.

BOCHK found that day-to-day governance needed a designated central coordinator, even though the ledger itself has no single owner. This covers patching, onboarding new members, and agreeing who is obliged to act as another node's backup.

Deloitte's control-principles paper frames DLT adoption around three linked themes banks should address together: choice of governance model, the legal/regulatory environment (including whether smart contracts are enforceable), and technical standards.

Writing to a blockchain requires a transaction signed with a private key. Because of this, the paper flags Hardware Security Modules as a necessary control for key generation and storage, alongside the usual network credentials for read access.

Deloitte recommends keeping personal or commercially sensitive data off-chain, and putting only a minimal, permissioned set of fields on the ledger itself. It also recommends building in data-retention and key-destruction plans from the start.

The Law Society's contribution concludes that Hong Kong's Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance still applies to DLT data, even when only a hash is stored. This is true if the transaction details let someone work out who the parties are.
key_points.locator: Annex F, Data protection s.1, p.74-75

key_points.point: It also flags that moving data outside Hong Kong over a DLT network engages the Ordinance's cross-border transfer restriction, which had not yet commenced at the time. Written consent from the data subject is the most workable way to comply.

The academic liability paper (Zetzsche, Buckley, Arner), not PwC, cites well-known losses on public crypto networks: the Mt.Gox and Bitfinex exchange thefts, and the Parity wallet bug. It uses these as evidence that distributed ledgers do not, by themselves, remove custody and legal risk.

The academic liability paper argues that participants in a shared ledger can still be sued in tort by other participants, for losses caused by the network, even without a direct contract. It also argues that node operators cannot dodge AML/CFT duties simply by pointing to the network's decentralised design.

The whitepaper repeatedly notes that most DLT protocols in 2017 (Ethereum, Hyperledger, Corda) could not interoperate with each other, which it treats as a live constraint on any bank choosing a platform.

numbers_and_dates.item: Trade-finance PoC operating cost saving (working group estimate)
Minimum live-node threshold used for BOCHK's production platform
Bitfinex hack loss cited as a custody-risk example

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is HKMA-hosted but externally written background reading, not supervisory guidance, so it creates no obligations. Its main value today is the still-relevant reasoning on DLT governance models, key-management risk, exposure under the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance (PDPO), and third-party liability. Later HKMA custody and tokenisation expectations build on this reasoning.
reading_guide: Skip the diagrams and vendor-specific architecture detail. Read Annex A s.3.4-3.5 for governance options, and Annex D s.1-2 for control principles and key management. Annex F and G, on data privacy and liability, are also still useful for today's custody and governance thinking.
flags: This is a compilation of seven externally-authored contributions (Deloitte, ASTRI, BOCHK, PwC, the Law Society, and three law academics), not the HKMA's own regulatory position -- treat each annex as that author's view.

Content is almost entirely about enterprise/trade-finance DLT infrastructure rather than virtual-asset trading, custody-for-clients, or stablecoins; only Annex G touches crypto-asset custody risk directly.
Technology and vendor references (Ethereum Parity, MEANS stack, 2017-era protocol comparisons) are outdated and should not be read as current HKMA technology preference.

controls_and_monitoring: Where a bank participates in any shared-ledger network, ensure private keys are generated and stored in Hardware Security Modules and that on-chain data is limited to hashes/minimal fields rather than raw personal or client data (Annex D).
counterparty_due_diligence: When assessing a DLT platform operator or consortium, check which governance model it uses (informal working group vs. incorporated entity vs. hybrid), since that determines who is legally accountable if the platform fails (Annex D/G).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No action needed on this document alone; it is useful board background on why later, binding HKMA guidance on custody, key management and DLT governance exists.

title: Whitepaper 2.0 on Distributed Ledger Technology - Annex
summary: This is an annex to HKMA's 2017 whitepaper 2.0 on distributed ledger technology (DLT). It holds seven contributions from outside firms and academics, not from HKMA itself. Topics include trade-finance and digital-identity pilots, a mortgage-loan case study, a governance framework, a security paper, a legal note, and an academic paper on blockchain liability. It is background reference material only, and predates Hong Kong's current virtual-asset and stablecoin regimes.

key_points.point: Deloitte names governance, law and regulation, and technical standards as the three factors that most affect banks adopting private DLT platforms.
It compares three ways banks could govern a shared DLT network: an informal consortium, a joint-venture company, or a government-run statutory body.
Deloitte cites a 2016 Goldman Sachs estimate of about $2 billion in savings for banks from blockchain use in transaction monitoring and account onboarding.
PwC's security paper flags confidentiality, network scalability and availability, and key security as the main technical risks DLT must manage to meet accepted security standards.
The Law Society of Hong Kong asks whether personal data should sit on a DLT ledger directly, or only as an off-ledger hash. Ledger data is hard to delete once written.

An academic paper by Zetzsche, Buckley and Arner warns that courts could treat a multi-bank DLT project as a joint venture. This spreads legal liability across every owner and operator of the ledger, in the authors' view.

Bank of China (Hong Kong)'s mortgage-loan pilot shows how a bank, valuers and the Land Registry could share one DLT platform. It covered property valuation, ownership checks and mortgage-count checks.

numbers_and_dates.item: Estimated banking-sector operational savings from blockchain (Goldman Sachs 2016 estimate cited by Deloitte)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is useful mainly as background, not as HKMA's own rule. It explains the governance choices a bank faces when joining a shared DLT platform with other firms: a consortium, a joint venture, or a statutory body.
reading_guide: If time is limited, read Annex D (governance models, pp.38-56) and skim Annex F and G for legal framing. The trade finance, digital identity and mortgage loan case-study annexes (A-C) are illustrative examples, not compliance guidance.
flags: Third-party (non-HKMA) contributions; disclaimed as not constituting legal advice; predates Hong Kong's current VA/stablecoin licensing regimes.

counterparty_due_diligence: When considering a joint bank DLT consortium, weigh the consortium/joint-venture/statutory-organisation choice against how costs, IP, and liability will be shared and whether courts might treat the consortium as a joint venture for liability purposes (Annex D sec 1.1; Annex G abstract).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Historical background only; no current board action required.

title: Whitepaper 2.0 on Distributed Ledger Technology
summary: This is HKMA's second whitepaper on distributed ledger technology (DLT), following its 2016 whitepaper, and was released around HKMA Fintech Day in October 2017. It updates the earlier technology overview, then works through compliance issues (AML/CFT, systemic risk, technology risk, reporting, governance and legal issues) that a bank should think about when deploying DLT. As of this review, it carries only historical or reference value. It predates Hong Kong's virtual-asset licensing regime, its stablecoin regime, and the HKMA's later DLT circular. But its governance and key-management principles were echoed almost unchanged in the 2025 study.

key_points.point: AML/CFT rules are not disapplied for DLT. A bank using a permissioned DLT platform must still design customer-onboarding and transaction-monitoring controls that satisfy its existing AML/CFT obligations. This includes obligations under the AML Ordinance for Hong Kong financial institutions.

Using an unpermissioned (public, anonymous-participant) DLT platform for mainstream banking is flagged as carrying substantial money-laundering/terrorist-financing risk because participant anonymity is unresolved.

Deploying DLT for outsourced or cloud-based functions triggers HKMA's existing Supervisory Policy Manual modules. These include Outsourcing (SA-2), General Principles for Technology Risk Management (TM-G-1), and Business Continuity Planning (TM-G-2).

Regulators or auditors could in principle be given direct, near-real-time access to DLT ledger data through a 'supervisory node'; institutions should consider this possibility in solution design and related agreements.

Three governance models are set out for permissioned DLT platforms shared between banks: a consortium, a joint venture, and a statutory organisation, each with different cost, flexibility and control trade-offs.

New members joining a shared DLT platform should go through AML-aligned due diligence and a cybersecurity/internal-control check, and sign a binding end-user agreement. Ongoing monitoring and re-certification follow after onboarding.

Key management (authentication and access control) and smart contracts are singled out as the two areas needing the most further work, recommending hardware security modules, multiple signatures, and key revocation/recovery agents.

Concentrating on a small number of third-party DLT service providers raises outsourcing concentration risk. This risk could become systemic if a widely-used provider fails, so banks should prepare contingency and recovery plans with their providers.

The Hong Kong Electronic Transactions Ordinance gives digital signatures the same legal status as handwritten ones, for most purposes. But it excludes certain categories, such as assignments and mortgages. A bank should check this before relying on DLT signatures for those document types.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this whitepaper is now superseded by the HKMA's later DLT circular and 2025 study. But it is the origin of governance and key-management expectations — hardware security modules (HSM), multiple signatures, and key-recovery agents — that the HKMA continued to apply. It is useful background for understanding why those expectations exist.
reading_guide: Read Chapter 5 (Compliance Issues, pp.25-29) and Chapter 6 (Governance and Control, pp.29-40) for the compliance content; skip Chapter 4's technology-platform survey (Hyperledger, Corda, Bitcoin, Ethereum comparisons).
flags: Pre-dates Hong Kong's virtual-asset trading platform licensing regime and stablecoin ordinance; its compliance content should be read as background rather than current expectation.

obligations: Deploying DLT for outsourced/cloud functions should trigger review against SA-2 (Outsourcing), TM-G-1 (Technology Risk) and TM-G-2 (Business Continuity Planning) (sec 5.4, p.28).
controls_and_monitoring: Key management controls (HSM, multi-signature, key revocation/recovery agents) for any DLT platform holding private keys (sec 6.9, p.40).
AML-aligned onboarding due diligence and ongoing re-certification for members of a shared DLT platform (sec 6.2.2, p.31).
counterparty_due_diligence: Consider governance model (consortium/JV/statutory body) and its dispute-resolution and cost/liability-sharing terms before joining a shared DLT platform with other banks (sec 6.2.1, p.30).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Historical background only; no current board action required from this document alone.

title: LCQ15: Regulation of offering and trading of digital tokens
summary: This is a 2017 LegCo written reply restating the SFC's newly issued ICO statement, and the government's early position. Digital tokens are not currencies, ICO regulation varies globally, and existing AML/CFT laws apply to virtual-commodity businesses even without a dedicated crypto regime. It also states that virtual commodities were not seen as posing a systemic risk to Hong Kong at that time.

key_points.point: The government reiterated that digital tokens are a type of virtual commodity, not currency, and are not guaranteed by any issuer.
AML/CFT statutory customer due-diligence and record-keeping duties applied to financial institutions dealing with virtual-commodity operators even without crypto-specific rules.
At the time, virtual commodities were judged unlikely to pose a systemic risk to Hong Kong's financial system given their limited circulation as a means of payment.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Historical confirmation that AML/CFT duties toward virtual-commodity counterparties predate and are separate from the later VATP licensing regime; useful only as background trajectory context now.

quote.text: virtual commodities do not have any backing

reading_guide: Read the reply's middle paragraphs on AML/CFT and systemic-risk assessment; skip the preamble restating the question.
flags: Historical (2017); systemic-risk assessment and regulatory landscape described have both since changed materially.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: None; historical context only.

title: SFC issues reminder on cryptocurrency-related products and derivatives
summary: This press release announces the SFC's circular of 11 December 2017. It cautions investors about Bitcoin futures and other crypto-linked investment products, and reminds financial service providers of licensing rules when targeting Hong Kong customers. It quotes SFC officials warning that unlicensed order routing may be a criminal offence and that risks of volatility and illiquidity may be magnified by leverage. It restates the licensing categories (Types 1, 2, 5, 9) triggered by various Bitcoin futures activities.

key_points.point: Dealing in or routing orders for Bitcoin futures contracts for Hong Kong investors requires an SFC licence regardless of where the business is located.
SFC quotes: parties routing orders without a licence may be committing a criminal offence.
Client assets have in the past been taken through theft or misappropriation from crypto exchanges, some of which later failed.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Public-facing companion to the same-day circular; shows the SFC's early public messaging tone on crypto derivatives that set the stage for later formal guidance.

quote.text: may be committing a criminal offence

reading_guide: Short press release; read in full alongside circular 17EC79 issued same day.

title: Circular to Licensed Corporations and Registered Institutions on Bitcoin futures contracts and cryptocurrency-related investment products
summary: This circular reminds SFC licensees and registered institutions of the legal and regulatory requirements applicable to Bitcoin futures and other crypto-linked investment products. It explains that Bitcoin futures traded on regulated exchanges are 'futures contracts' under the SFO. Dealing, advising, or fund marketing and management activities linked to them trigger Type 1, 2, 5 or 9 licensing requirements. It also notes some cryptocurrency products may separately be 'securities'. It closes with a warning to investors about risks of unregulated exchanges.

key_points.point: Bitcoin futures traded on SFC-authorised exchanges are 'futures contracts' under the SFO even though the underlying asset is unregulated.
Dealing in Bitcoin futures, including relaying/routing orders, requires a Type 2 licence unless exempt.
The SFC expects intermediaries to strictly observe the suitability requirement (Code of Conduct para 5.2) and the conduct requirements under paras 5.1A and 5.3.
Marketing a fund investing in Bitcoin futures is normally Type 1; managing such a fund may be Type 9; advising may be Type 5.
A party providing regulated-activity services relating to Bitcoin futures needs a licence regardless of location, so long as it targets the Hong Kong public.
Other cryptocurrency-related products (options, swaps, CFDs) may be 'securities' under the SFO, triggering licensing, conduct and authorisation requirements.
Engaging in these activities without a licence/authorisation may be a criminal offence under the SFO.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank acting as a Registered Institution (RI), it must map any Bitcoin-futures-linked dealing, advisory or fund activity onto the correct SFO licence category. It must also apply the right suitability rules before offering it to clients. It must not route client orders to SFC-unauthorised exchanges.

quote.text: may be committing a criminal offence under the SFO

reading_guide: Read the full 2-page circular; footnotes provide detail on regulated activity definitions but are optional.
flags: Historical/superseded in practice by later, more comprehensive SFC virtual asset frameworks (Nov 2018 statement and subsequent VATP regime), though not explicitly marked superseded in this document.

obligations: If the bank's RI arm deals in, advises on or markets funds/derivatives referencing Bitcoin futures, it must hold the corresponding SFO licence/registration (Type 1/2/5/9) (p.1)
Observe suitability (Code para 5.2) and derivative-product conduct requirements (Code paras 5.1A, 5.3) for any such services (p.1)
controls_and_monitoring: Confirm which SFO regulated activity each Bitcoin-futures-linked service falls under before launch, given both futures-contract and possible securities characterisation (p.1-2)
counterparty_due_diligence: Check that any exchange whose Bitcoin futures the bank relays orders to is SFC-authorised under Part III SFO (p.1, fn.1)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should note this is the SFC's earliest (2017) statement that crypto-derivatives can trigger existing SFO licensing categories -- the doctrinal root of all later VA guidance.

title: Public education campaign on risks associated with initial coin offerings and "cryptocurrencies" jointly launched by FSTB and Investor Education Centre (with photo)
summary: This announces a joint public-education campaign by FSTB and the Investor Education Centre (a subsidiary of the SFC). It warns retail investors about ICO and 'cryptocurrency' risks, using MTR ads, TV and radio spots, and the Chin Family investor-education website.

key_points.point: The campaign's core message is that cryptocurrencies are volatile, unbacked virtual commodities, not real currencies, and unsuitable for everyone.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is retail investor education, not a rule. Regulators expect firms to reinforce, not undercut, this risk messaging when marketing crypto-linked products to retail clients.

quote.text: high-risk products that are not suitable for everyone

reading_guide: Short release; read in full.
flags: Historical (2018) press release; no ongoing legal obligation attaches to it.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: None.

title: SFC warns of cryptocurrency risks
summary: This press release reports that the SFC sent warning letters to seven cryptocurrency exchanges connected to Hong Kong. It advised them not to trade cryptocurrencies that are 'securities' without a licence, and separately wrote to seven ICO issuers. Most recipients confirmed compliance or ceased relevant activities. The SFC restates that it may lack jurisdiction where there is no Hong Kong nexus, or where products are not 'securities' or 'futures contracts'. But it can refer fraud cases to the police. It warns investors of volatility, hacking and fraud risk.

key_points.point: SFC sent letters to seven cryptocurrency exchanges in or connected to Hong Kong warning against trading 'securities'-type cryptocurrencies without a licence.
Most exchanges confirmed no trading of such cryptocurrencies or took rectification measures (for example, delisting).
SFC also wrote to seven ICO issuers; most confirmed compliance or ceased offering tokens to HK investors.
SFC may lack jurisdiction over exchanges/issuers with no Hong Kong nexus or not dealing in 'securities'/'futures contracts'.
Where fraud is suspected, the SFC may refer cases to the Police.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is background only. It shows the jurisdictional gap that the 2023 VATP licensing regime was later built to close, and is not itself a source of any current bank obligation.

quote.text: we will continue to police the market and enforce when necessary

reading_guide: Read in full; short release; the notes at the end explain the jurisdictional nexus limitation.
flags: Confirms that pre-VATP-regime SFC had no jurisdiction over exchanges dealing only in non-'securities' tokens absent a Hong Kong nexus -- a gap later closed by the licensing regime under AMLO Part 5B.

counterparty_due_diligence: Confirms the SFC could not act against exchanges/ICO issuers outside its 'securities' jurisdiction or without a HK nexus (para 8, p.1) -- a historical reminder that pre-2023 licensing checks alone were not sufficient counterparty comfort.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Historical case showing the pre-VATP-regime enforcement gap; no current action required, useful only as background when briefing the board on why licensing was introduced.

title: Circular on BCBS Sound Practices Implications of Fintech Developments for Banks and Bank Supervisors
summary: The HKMA forwards a February 2018 Basel Committee paper on how fintech may reshape banking, without adding Hong Kong-specific rules. It flags that new technologies such as artificial intelligence, distributed ledger technology and open banking-style interfaces could create new strategic, operational, cyber and compliance risks. Senior management is expected to assess this strategic risk and, for locally incorporated banks, bring the assessment to the board. The HKMA says it had already begun talking to major banks' senior management about their fintech plans.

key_points.point: Distributed ledger technology and other fintech tools may create new strategic, operational, cyber and compliance risks for banks, alongside opportunities.
Bank senior management is expected to assess the strategic risk fintech poses to their institution and build a monitoring plan.
For locally incorporated banks, that strategic-risk assessment should go to the board of directors.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is background policy tone-setting, not a rule. But it is the document that first put fintech (including DLT) strategic-risk assessment on the board's agenda, a theme that later hardened into specific HKMA supervisory expectations.

quote.text: difficult to maintain their current operating models

reading_guide: Two-page letter; read fully, it is short.

obligations: Assess strategic risk from fintech (including DLT) and develop a monitoring plan, p.2
controls_and_monitoring: Ongoing monitoring of technology-related strategic risk by senior management, p.2
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Locally incorporated banks' boards should receive and deliberate the strategic-risk assessment for fintech developments.

title: Crypto product alleged to be launched by the HKMA
summary: The HKMA responds to a public query about a rumoured crypto investment product supposedly launched by the regulator itself. It states plainly that it has never started, and will never start, such a scheme, and that crypto investment products sit outside its supervisory scope. Anyone who thinks they have been defrauded is told to report to the police.

key_points.point: HKMA denies ever launching or planning to launch a crypto investment product for the public.
HKMA says such crypto products are not something it regulates or supervises.
Suspected fraud victims are directed to the police's Commercial Crime Bureau.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: A minor early data point that impersonation of the HKMA for crypto scams is a recurring problem long before the VA regime existed.
reading_guide: One short paragraph; read in full, nothing to skip.

title: A Golden Opportunity for Hong Kong’s Bond Market
summary: This is a 2018 HKMA Insight article by the then Deputy Chief Executive. It argues that Hong Kong should keep developing its conventional bond market, alongside its equity and loan markets. It covers the government's new Pilot Bond Grant Scheme, tax incentives, the CMU settlement system, Bond Connect, and a planned government green-bond programme. It contains no mention of virtual assets, tokenisation, stablecoins or DLT. It is commentary, not a rule or supervisory statement.

key_points.point: The piece describes a new grant scheme and expanded tax exemptions announced in the 2018-19 Budget meant to attract more corporate bond issuance to Hong Kong.
It explains that the Central Moneymarkets Unit, the HKMA's clearing and settlement utility for debt securities, held about HK$2 trillion of securities and had around 200 members at the time.
It announces a planned Green Bond Issuance Programme with a HK$100 billion government borrowing ceiling, with the HKMA running the offering and promotion.

numbers_and_dates.item: Proposed government Green Bond Programme ceiling

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This has no digital-asset content and creates no obligation; a compliance head can treat it purely as historical policy background on conventional bond-market development, unrelated to the digital-asset mandate.
reading_guide: Not essential reading for a digital-assets compliance function; skip unless researching the HKMA's general capital-markets-development history.
flags: Document has no virtual-asset, stablecoin, tokenisation or DLT content; included in this batch only because it was fetched under the HKMA insight feed.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No board action needed; not digital-asset relevant.

title: LCQ5: Issuance of cryptocurrency
summary: This is a 2018 LegCo (Legislative Council) written reply. It summarises the SFC's ICO and crypto enforcement actions to date, including letters to exchanges and issuers, and a Bitcoin-futures licensing reminder. It reconfirms the September 2017 ICO securities test. It also states that the HKMA had no plan to issue a retail central bank digital currency (CBDC) at that time, given Hong Kong's already efficient payments infrastructure.

key_points.point: In February 2018 the SFC sent letters to cryptocurrency exchanges and ICO issuers connected to Hong Kong, warning against trading unlicensed securities-type tokens. Most complied, by delisting tokens or ceasing Hong Kong offers.

The SFC's December 2017 reminder treated dealing in, or relaying/routing orders for, Bitcoin futures contracts as a regulated activity requiring an SFC licence, regardless of where the business is based.

The HKMA stated it had no plan at that stage to issue a central bank digital currency, given Hong Kong's already efficient payment infrastructure, but would keep monitoring international developments.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is historical confirmation of the SFC's early enforcement approach and its reasoning against a retail CBDC. It is largely superseded by e-HKD work since, but is useful background on how the regime moved from warnings toward licensing.

quote.text: no plan to issue CBDC at this stage

reading_guide: Read replies (1) and (3); reply (2) on offshore digital-currency hub ambitions is less relevant to compliance.
flags: Historical (2018); HKMA's CBDC stance has since evolved materially (e-HKD pilot work postdates this reply).

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: None; historical context only.

title: Speech by FS at "Innovative Blockchain-based Remittance Solution to Enhance Financial Inclusion" press conference (English only) (with photo/video)
summary: These are the Financial Secretary's remarks launching a blockchain-based Alipay remittance pilot to the Philippines. They showcase the HKMA's Fintech Supervisory Sandbox, and the growth of the stored value facility (SVF) e-wallet market since the 2015 Payment Systems and Stored Value Facilities Ordinance.

key_points.point: The HKMA's Fintech Supervisory Sandbox had, by mid-2018, supported 22 new technology products/services through to market launch over two years.
SVF account numbers rose 15.4% year-on-year to 46.7 million by end-2017, with transaction value up 27.7% to over HK$38 billion.
The Faster Payment System (FPS), launching September 2018, would connect banks and SVF operators for real-time transfers.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Background only: shows how HKMA used the sandbox mechanism for blockchain-based payments/remittance before any dedicated virtual-asset licensing regime existed; not a source of current obligations.
reading_guide: Skim; mostly promotional remarks with a few statistics of historical interest.
flags: Historical (2018) promotional speech, not a rule or guidance document.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: None.

title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Keynote Speech at Treasury Markets Summit 2018: “Crypto-assets and Money”
summary: In this 2018 keynote, the then Deputy Chief Executive set out the HKMA's early public position on crypto-assets. Bitcoin-style crypto-assets fail all three classic tests of money — medium of exchange, store of value, and unit of account. The HKMA said they should therefore be called crypto-assets, not crypto-currencies. The speech also covers the Financial Stability Board's early view that crypto-assets were not yet a systemic risk, but needed monitoring. It flags money-laundering and investor-protection gaps on unregulated trading platforms. It also references a 2014 HKMA circular that reminded banks to apply KYC and AML controls when dealing with crypto-assets. It closes by noting HKMA research into DLT-based trade finance, and an early, cautious look at central bank digital currency (CBDC).

key_points.point: The speech concludes that Bitcoin-style crypto-assets do not meet the tests of money: medium of exchange, store of value, or unit of account. The main reasons are slow, costly transactions and extreme price volatility.

It reports the Financial Stability Board's contemporaneous assessment that crypto-assets were not yet a material threat to global financial stability given their small size, but that ongoing monitoring was warranted.

It says anonymous, cross-border transfers of crypto-assets make it hard for banks and regulated firms to meet KYC and source-of-funds rules. It recalls that the HKMA issued a circular in 2014 telling banks to apply KYC and AML controls to crypto-asset dealings.
It flags that most crypto-asset trading happens on unregulated platforms, creating gaps in investor protection and exposure to market manipulation and platform security failures.
The speech confirms the HKMA and Hong Kong banks were about to launch a DLT-based digital trade finance platform, plus a bilateral DLT link with Singapore.
It discloses that the HKMA was studying the technical feasibility of a wholesale central bank digital currency, describing the work as still early-stage.

numbers_and_dates.item: Earlier HKMA circular reminding banks of KYC/AML duties on crypto-assets

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the HKMA's earliest public statement that it does not treat crypto-assets as money. It also reminds banks that ordinary KYC and AML duties apply whenever the bank deals with crypto-assets, or with clients connected to them. This remains the baseline expectation behind all later, more detailed guidance.

quote.text: crypto-currencies are not qualified to become money

reading_guide: Read the three-part money-attributes analysis and the three risk categories (financial stability, illicit activity, investor protection); the DLT and CBDC closing remarks are brief context and can be skimmed.
flags: Speech references a 2014 HKMA circular on crypto-asset KYC/AML but does not name or link it, so it cannot itself be treated as the binding source.

The HKMA-published web page bundles an unrelated attachment (a 2026-dated slide deck on AI governance and tokenisation) that has nothing to do with this 2018 speech's topic or date -- likely a feed/fetch artifact, not a genuine document package; see attachment entry a50e9dc16dc7.

obligations: Apply standard KYC and AML/source-of-funds checks whenever a client relationship touches crypto-assets, per the HKMA's 2014 circular referenced here.
controls_and_monitoring: Treat crypto-asset volatility and lack of intrinsic value as a red flag in product-risk classification and client suitability screening.
counterparty_due_diligence: Where a client trades on an unregulated crypto-asset platform, factor in the platform's own security/manipulation track record when assessing the relationship's risk.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should note that the HKMA's foundational stance has long been that crypto-assets are not money and that ordinary AML/KYC duties fully apply to any related dealings.

title: False News Report Claiming HKMA’s Investment in Crypto Products
summary: A fabricated news item, attributed to an international news agency, claimed the HKMA had put money into crypto products through a dedicated trading venue. The HKMA rejects this and says it has no holdings and no intention to acquire any. It again points victims of any related fraud to the police.

key_points.point: HKMA denies the claim that it invested in crypto products via a trading platform.
HKMA says it has no current plans to invest in crypto or related assets.
Members of the public who believe they were scammed should contact the police.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Shows fake HKMA-endorsement scams using crypto as bait predate the licensing regime; a recurring pattern a bank should recognise when advising customers.
reading_guide: Short; read in full.

title: Circular to intermediaries Distribution of virtual asset funds
summary: This circular sets expected standards for SFC-licensed intermediaries (Type 1/Type 9) distributing virtual asset funds. It confirms distribution of a fund investing in virtual assets triggers Type 1 licensing regardless of whether the underlying assets are 'securities'. For funds not authorised by the SFC with more than 10% of gross asset value (GAV) in virtual assets, it imposes selling restrictions. These include limiting sales to professional investors, a client knowledge assessment, and concentration limits. It also requires due diligence on the fund, its manager and counterparties, plus mandatory client risk disclosures. The document itself states it was superseded and updated by a circular dated 28 January 2022.

key_points.point: Distribution of a virtual asset fund in Hong Kong requires Type 1 licensing/registration regardless of whether the virtual assets are 'securities' or 'futures contracts'.
For unauthorised virtual asset funds with stated VA objective or >10% GAV in virtual assets, intermediaries should only target professional investors and assess client knowledge unless institutional.
Intermediaries should ensure aggregate client investment in unauthorised virtual asset funds is reasonable relative to net worth, to avoid concentration risk.
Intermediaries should conduct due diligence on the fund manager, the fund, and counterparties (custodians/exchanges) before distribution.
Custody arrangement of fund assets across exchanges/custodians/hot/cold storage should be understood as part of due diligence.

Intermediaries should provide prominent warning statements to clients on volatility, manipulation, lack of secondary markets, unregulated custodians, counterparty risk, hot-wallet loss risk, and cyber risk.
Failure to comply may affect fitness and properness and result in disciplinary action.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this circular is now superseded, but it is the direct ancestor of today's virtual-asset (VA) fund distribution controls. Those controls cover professional-investor-only sales, a knowledge test, concentration limits, and counterparty due diligence. Compliance can use this mainly to check which of those requirements have since been tightened or replaced.

quote.text: this circular was superseded and updated by the circular dated 28 January 2022

reading_guide: Read the banner notice on p.1 first (supersession), then sections (A)-(C); skip footnote definitions unless needed for precision.
flags: EXPLICIT SUPERSESSION: this circular carries an added banner stating it was superseded and updated by an SFC circular dated 28 January 2022 -- the current live requirements are in that later circular, not this one.

obligations: Only market unauthorised VA funds (stated VA objective, or >10% GAV in VA) to professional investors after a client knowledge assessment, unless the client is institutional ((A)(1), p.2)
Conduct due diligence on the fund manager, the fund itself, and its custodian/exchange counterparties before distribution ((B)(3), p.2-3)
controls_and_monitoring: Monitor aggregate client exposure to unauthorised VA funds against net worth to avoid concentration risk ((A)(2), p.2)
Review the fund's custody split across exchanges/custodians/hot-cold storage as part of ongoing due diligence ((b)(iv), p.4)
counterparty_due_diligence: Assess fund manager track record, fund structure and custodian/exchange counterparties before onboarding a VA fund for distribution ((B)(3), p.2-3)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told this 2018 standard was itself superseded by the 28 January 2022 circular and is retained only as a historical baseline, not the current rulebook.

title: SFC sets out new regulatory approach for virtual assets
summary: This press release announces the same-day Statement on regulatory framework for virtual asset portfolio managers, fund distributors and trading platform operators. It explains that firms managing or distributing virtual asset funds will face new licensing conditions from the SFC. It also explains that the SFC will use its Regulatory Sandbox to test whether platform operators can be brought under supervision and eventual licensing. It quotes CEO Ashley Alder on investor protection goals and the sandbox pathway.

key_points.point: SFC will impose licensing conditions on firms managing or intending to manage portfolios investing in virtual assets, regardless of whether the assets are 'securities' or 'futures contracts'.
Within the SFC Regulatory Sandbox, the SFC will test whether trading platforms dealing in virtual assets could be brought under a licensing regime.
If found appropriate, the SFC would grant a licence and place platform operators under close supervision. Alternatively, it could decide no licence should be granted.
Many virtual assets do not meet the SFO definition of 'securities'/'futures contracts', so managing funds solely investing in such assets is not itself a regulated activity.

numbers_and_dates.item: GAV threshold triggering portfolio manager oversight

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the SFC's founding 2018 policy statement. It does not bind the bank directly, but it explains the professional-investor-only starting point and the sandbox concept. Both later hardened into the licensing regimes that the bank's counterparties operate under today.

quote.text: encourage the responsible use of new technologies

reading_guide: Short release; read in full, then cross-reference the full Statement circular for operative detail.
flags: Confirms as of Nov 2018 the SFC's platform-operator regulation was still exploratory/conceptual, not a licensing regime -- statutory VATP licensing came later.

counterparty_due_diligence: A VA fund manager or trading-platform operator the bank deals with may be operating under an SFC sandbox/portfolio-licensing arrangement rather than a full licence -- check status before treating it as fully regulated (paras on Sandbox and portfolio licensing)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told this 2018 statement is the origin of the professional-investors-only stance and sandbox approach that shaped every later SFC VA framework.

title: Fintech: Meeting the regulatory challenges - Keynote speech at Hong Kong FinTech Week 2018
summary: In this speech, the SFC's then-CEO previewed the SFC's first structured virtual-asset framework. This included new conduct standards for fund managers and distributors dealing in crypto assets, and an opt-in sandbox pathway for exploring regulation of virtual-asset trading platforms. It explains the SFC's reasoning for why it could only reach parts of the crypto market given the legal definition of 'securities'.

key_points.point: SFC-supervised managers putting more than 10% of a mixed portfolio into virtual assets would need to meet new standards, initially limited to professional investors only.
key_points.locator: 'Virtual asset portfolio managers and distributers' section, p.5

key_points.point: Firms distributing funds with crypto exposure, already required to be SFC-registered/licensed brokers, would face new specific guidance on distribution standards for such funds.
key_points.locator: 'Virtual asset portfolio managers and distributers' section, p.5

key_points.point: VATP regulation would start as an opt-in sandbox: interested platforms would explore a conceptual framework with the SFC, with no formal licence granted during that sandbox stage.
key_points.locator: 'Exploring regulation of platform operators' section, p.5-6

key_points.point: The SFC's jurisdiction is legally limited to virtual assets that qualify as 'securities' or 'futures contracts' under the SFO. Assets and platforms outside that definition fell outside its regulatory perimeter at the time.
key_points.locator: 'The regulatory regime for virtual assets' section, p.4

key_points.point: Sandbox-stage platforms would be expected to serve professional investors only and meet standards at least as high as existing automated trading services the SFC already supervises.
key_points.locator: 'Exploring regulation of platform operators' section, p.6

numbers_and_dates.item: portfolio threshold triggering new fund-manager standards
numbers_and_dates.value: more than 10% of a mixed portfolio in virtual assets

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this speech is the origin point for the fund-manager and distributor conduct standards, and for the VATP sandbox-to-licensing pathway that later hardened into today's SFC regime. It helps compliance understand why certain thresholds exist, such as the 10% portfolio trigger, and why the regime started with professional investors only.

quote.text: an opt-in approach for platform operators
quote.locator: 'Exploring regulation of platform operators' section, p.6

reading_guide: Read 'The regulatory regime for virtual assets' through 'Exploring regulation of platform operators' (p.4-6). The opening remarks on general Fintech regulation (p.1-3) are less relevant to digital assets specifically.
flags: Historical (2018) speech previewing what became the SFC's later formal circulars; the sandbox-only, professional-investor-only starting point has since evolved into the full VATP licensing regime and retail access rules.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Useful board context on how far today's VATP licensing regime has progressed since this 2018 sandbox-only starting point, but creates no current obligation itself.

title: Circular to intermediaries Statement on regulatory framework for virtual asset portfolios managers, fund distributors and trading platform operators
summary: This SFC circular, dated 1 November 2018, sends out an attached Policy Statement to intermediaries. The Statement sets Hong Kong's first regulatory approach for firms that manage or distribute virtual asset (VA) portfolios and funds. It also proposes a voluntary, opt-in idea to test in the SFC's Regulatory Sandbox: whether VA trading platforms might one day be regulated. It lists core rules the SFC might apply to a future licensed platform operator, such as a single company, professional investors only, and 98% cold storage (assets kept offline).

key_points.point: A Type 9 or Type 1 licensed firm managing a portfolio aimed at virtual assets must be licensed and follow SFC terms and conditions. This also covers firms investing 10% or more of gross asset value (GAV) in virtual assets.
Only professional investors, as defined in the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO), may invest in these virtual asset portfolios.
key_points.locator: Statement, 'Type of investors and disclosure', p.5

key_points.point: A licensed firm holding non-securities virtual assets for managed portfolios must keep at least HK$3 million in liquid capital, or more if a higher amount applies.
A future licensed Platform Operator should run all its virtual-asset trading business through one single SFC-licensed company.
A Platform Operator should serve only professional investors.
A Platform Operator should only allow ICO tokens to trade from 12 months after the ICO ends, or once the project turns a profit, whichever comes first.
Clients must fully fund each trade in advance; a Platform Operator should not offer margin financing, leverage, or virtual-asset futures or derivatives.
A Platform Operator is expected to keep most client virtual assets not needed at short notice, for example 98%, in cold storage (kept offline).
A Platform Operator should insure client assets fully in hot storage (kept online) and substantially, for example 95%, in cold storage.
The SFC's approach was an opt-in Sandbox exploratory stage: no licence would be granted at first, and the SFC could still decide not to regulate platforms at all.
At this exploratory stage, the SFC would not consider licensing platform operators trading virtual assets that are 'futures contracts' or 'structured products'.

numbers_and_dates.item: GAV de minimis threshold for portfolio manager oversight
Minimum required liquid capital if holding non-SF virtual assets
Cold storage expectation for Platform Operators
numbers_and_dates.value: 98% of client virtual assets not immediately needed
12 months after ICO completion (or when profitable, if earlier)

numbers_and_dates.item: Minimum Sandbox period before exit application

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a compliance head, this 2018 circular is historical background. It shows where today's virtual asset trading platform (VATP) custody and professional-investor rules first came from, but it does not itself bind the bank (status: historical, superseded).

quote.text: explore in earnest whether and if so, how it could regulate virtual asset trading platforms

reading_guide: Read the Statement (pages 1-7) in full for the policy framework. Then read Appendix 1 (portfolio manager terms) and Appendix 2 (platform operator core principles, pages 3-4) closely.
flags: The 98% cold-storage figure and the professional-investors-only restriction, often assumed to originate from the 2019 VATP Guidelines, actually first appear here in November 2018 as proposed (not yet binding) Sandbox terms.

The opt-in Sandbox framework for trading platforms described here was an EXPLORATORY, non-mandatory stage -- it predates and was superseded by the mandatory SFC-licensing VATP approach announced in November 2019 (see id ed4205697ab5) and later the statutory regime under AMLO Part 5B; at this 2018 stage the SFC explicitly could not license platforms trading only non-'securities' tokens.

This statement explicitly says platforms trading only virtual assets that are not 'securities' remain outside SFC's jurisdiction at this stage -- a key limitation later addressed by the opt-in-to-mandatory shift and eventually statutory VATP licensing.

counterparty_due_diligence: Origin of standards (98% cold storage, professional-investor-only, no leverage -- Appendix 2, Core principles, p.4) that later became binding VATP conditions, useful when assessing how long a VATP counterparty's controls have been in place.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Historical/superseded document; note only that today's VATP custody and PI-only expectations trace back to this 2018 proposal, not to the 2023 regime alone.

title: Statement on regulatory framework for virtual asset portfolios managers, fund distributors and trading platform operators
summary: The SFC, Hong Kong's securities regulator, set out how it would bring virtual asset (VA) fund managers and fund distributors under its licensing rules. Most VAs are not legally 'securities' or 'futures contracts', so the SFC used licensing conditions instead of new law. It listed investor-protection risks in VAs, such as valuation, custody, market integrity, money laundering, and fraud, and set standard licensing terms for managers running VA portfolios. It also opened a non-binding sandbox exploration of whether VA trading platforms could one day be licensed.

key_points.point: A firm distributing a fund that invests in virtual assets in Hong Kong needs a Type 1 dealing licence and must follow existing suitability rules.
A licensed asset manager whose portfolio puts 10% or more of gross asset value (GAV) into non-security virtual assets is treated as running a VA portfolio and gets extra licensing conditions.
Firms already managing, or planning to manage, any VA portfolio must tell the SFC, even below the 10% threshold.
If a firm will not accept the SFC's proposed terms and conditions, the SFC refuses its licence application, or the firm must wind down any existing VA portfolio.
VA portfolios may only be sold to professional investors, with a small-amount exception (de minimis carve-out).
The SFC will use its Regulatory Sandbox to watch selected VA trading platform operators run live before deciding whether platforms can be licensed at all.

numbers_and_dates.item: de minimis VA exposure threshold for asset managers
minimum sandbox period before a platform can seek to exit

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the founding document of Hong Kong's opt-in VA regime. It explains why, before 2023, most VA trading platforms a bank might deal with were unregulated by design.

quote.text: significant investor protection risks

reading_guide: Read Section I in full for the manager and distributor rules. Section II is superseded by the 2019 position paper, so skim it for background only.
flags: superseded for platforms by the 2019 SFC position paper (5cd068fcfeb8) and for managers largely folded into later VATP/VA intermediary circulars

controls_and_monitoring: establish a threshold check for whether any managed portfolio has ever crossed 10% VA exposure
notifications_reporting: notify SFC before managing/distributing any VA portfolio, per Section I(a)(iii)
counterparty_due_diligence: when dealing with a VA fund manager, check whether it disclosed its VA exposure to the SFC and accepted the standard terms and conditions
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Historical note only: shows how far VA regulation has moved since 2018; not itself a live obligation for a bank today.

title: BCBS Statement on Crypto-Assets
summary: The HKMA passes on a March 2019 statement from the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), setting out risk expectations for banks' crypto-asset exposures. It says crypto-assets do not reliably act as money, are not legal tender, and are not backed by any government. It warns that growth in crypto trading platforms could raise financial-stability and bank-risk concerns. The HKMA tells banks planning crypto-related activities to discuss this with the HKMA first and show they have proper systems and controls.

key_points.point: Crypto-assets do not reliably work as money, the Basel Committee says, and no government or public authority stands behind them.
A bank planning crypto-asset activities should discuss this with the HKMA in advance and show it has adequate systems and controls to manage the risks.
