why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is an early, direct statement that the HKMA expects prior discussion before the bank takes on any crypto-asset exposure, if it does plan such activities. This same expectation repeats in every later HKMA virtual-asset circular.

quote.text: unsafe to rely on as a medium of exchange

reading_guide: Two-page circular; read in full.

obligations: Discuss any planned crypto-asset activity with the HKMA in advance and show adequate systems and controls, p.1
controls_and_monitoring: Systems and controls to identify and manage crypto-asset risk before engaging in related activities, p.1
notifications_reporting: Prior engagement with HKMA before crypto-asset business activity, p.1
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told that any crypto-asset exposure plan requires prior HKMA discussion and demonstrable risk controls.

title: Statement on Security Token Offerings
summary: The SFC reminded firms that security token offerings (STOs) are almost always 'securities' under Hong Kong law. These are digital tokens structured like traditional securities and backed by real assets or revenue rights. Anyone marketing or distributing them needs a Type 1 dealing licence and must treat them as complex products. They must also check the issuer and the token's backing before offering them, normally only to professional investors. A November 2023 circular later superseded this statement.

key_points.point: Security tokens are likely to count as securities under Hong Kong law, so distributing them needs a Type 1 licence.
Firms distributing security tokens must apply existing suitability rules and treat the tokens as complex products, adding extra investor-protection steps.
Firms must check the issuer's and management's soundness and the rights attached to the backing assets, including reading the whitepaper closely.
Firms are expected to talk to the SFC before starting any STO-related activity.
key_points.locator: para (footnote 5 / final para under selling restrictions)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this sets the baseline: most tokenised-asset offerings a bank might distribute or facilitate count as securities, needing full licensing and suitability compliance, not a lighter VA-specific regime.

quote.text: security tokens are likely to be

reading_guide: Short document; read in full. It was formally superseded by a 2 November 2023 circular, so treat it as background, not current guidance.
flags: explicitly states it was superseded and updated by a circular dated 2 November 2023

obligations: treat security tokens as complex products requiring enhanced suitability disclosures before distribution
controls_and_monitoring: due diligence process on token issuer, management and backing assets before onboarding a security token for distribution
notifications_reporting: discuss STO-related activity with the SFC before engaging in it
counterparty_due_diligence: review the token issuer's whitepaper and the legal basis of the rights the token represents
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Superseded guidance; board should be told the bank's STO procedures must map to the 2023 circular, not this 2019 statement.

title: Circular to intermediaries Statement on Security Token Offerings
summary: This circular sends out the SFC's 28 March 2019 Statement on Security Token Offerings (STOs), reminding firms of the legal rules for STOs. It confirms security tokens are likely 'securities' under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO), so marketing or distributing them needs a Type 1 licence. From July 2019, the Code of Conduct treats security tokens as 'complex products', triggering extra investor-protection steps. It also sets selling limits, due-diligence duties, and client-disclosure rules, similar to the November 2018 rules for virtual asset funds. It tells firms to talk to the SFC first.

key_points.point: Security Tokens are likely to be 'securities' under the SFO, so Hong Kong securities laws apply to them.
Marketing or distributing Security Tokens needs a Type 1 (dealing in securities) licence unless an exemption applies; unlicensed activity is a criminal offence.
From July 2019, the Code of Conduct (para 5.5) treats Security Tokens as 'complex products', adding extra investor-protection steps.
Firms marketing or distributing Security Tokens must hold a Type 1 licence and should only offer them to professional investors.
Firms should check the STO issuer's background and financial soundness, and the rights attached to backing assets, and read whitepapers and marketing materials closely.
Firms are told to consult the SFC before starting any STO-related activity.

numbers_and_dates.item: Code of Conduct para 5.5 complex-product effective date

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this 2019 circular binds SFC-licensed corporations, not the bank itself as an authorized institution (AI). It matters for counterparty due diligence if security tokens are distributed through a group licensed corporation (LC).

quote.text: Security Tokens would be regarded as 'complex products'

reading_guide: Read the 2-page attached Statement in full; the transmitting circular itself is a 1-line cover note.
flags: Confirms early (2019) that tokenised securities/STOs are automatically classified as 'complex products' under SFC rules, a classification that persists in later SFC tokenisation guidance.

This 29 March 2019 circular and the Statement it transmits are explicitly superseded by the SFC's 2 November 2023 circular on tokenised securities-related activities (id a9aa06fbcc12), which lists this document by name as one it replaces.

counterparty_due_diligence: If security tokens are distributed via a group licensed corporation, confirm it treats STOs as complex products under Code of Conduct para 5.5 and markets them only to professional investors (p.1)
Check the distributing LC discussed the STO activity with the SFC beforehand, as the SFC expected (p.2, footnote 5)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told this circular binds SFC-licensed corporations (Type 1), not the bank directly as an AI; it is relevant only if STO distribution runs through a group LC.

title: LCQ20: Regulation of virtual asset investment activities
summary: This is a Legislative Council (LegCo) written question-and-answer from the government, covering virtual assets (VAs). It gives police enforcement statistics on VA fraud and money laundering, and asks whether VA goods like mining rigs count as trade description law. It also covers how profits tax applies to VA transactions, and the government's plan to keep monitoring VA regulation. The government confirmed VA transactions are already taxable under ordinary profits-tax rules, and that police handled hundreds of VA-related crime reports in 2018.

key_points.point: Police recorded 324 virtual-asset-related crime reports in 2018, up from 50 in 2016 and 67 in 2017 (Bitcoin-only figures for those years).
Existing profits tax rules apply equally to virtual-asset transactions; there is no VA-specific tax regime.
The government said the SFC and the HKMA would keep studying whether to increase regulation of virtual-asset activities.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this shows that as of 2019 Hong Kong still had no dedicated VA licensing law; taxation and enforcement relied on general statutes. It is useful context for how far the regime has since moved.
reading_guide: Skim; mainly of historical/statistical interest, no compliance obligations for banks.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: None; background only.

title: LCQ15: Application of blockchain technology
summary: This is a Legislative Council (LegCo) written reply describing early government use of blockchain technology. It covers the bank-consortium trade-finance platform eTradeConnect, a planned cross-border link with Singapore, and blockchain pilots in four government departments. It reports that the Innovation and Technology Fund backed 18 blockchain and distributed ledger technology (DLT) research projects. It has no virtual-asset regulatory content; the focus is public-sector blockchain adoption, not virtual assets.

key_points.point: eTradeConnect, a 12-bank blockchain trade-finance platform helped by the HKMA, was still at an early operational stage in mid-2019.
The HKMA and the Monetary Authority of Singapore were working to connect eTradeConnect with Singapore's trade platform through a 'Global Trade Connectivity Network'.
The Innovation and Technology Fund had backed 18 blockchain and DLT projects worth about HK$67.2 million over the prior three years.

numbers_and_dates.item: ITF blockchain/DLT project funding, 3 years to 2019

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is background on eTradeConnect, the trade-finance DLT platform some banks already use. It does not itself drive any compliance action.
reading_guide: Skim only; general blockchain-in-government background, not virtual-asset regulation.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: None; background only.

title: Terms and Conditions for Licensed Corporations which Manage Portfolios that Invest in Virtual Assets
summary: This short SFC circular announces that the standard Terms and Conditions for 'Virtual Asset Fund Managers' are now published on the SFC website. 'Virtual Asset Fund Managers' are licensed corporations that manage, or plan to manage, portfolios with a stated virtual asset investment goal. This also covers firms that plan to invest 10% or more of gross asset value (GAV) in virtual assets, as first announced in the SFC's 1 November 2018 Statement. The SFC will impose these terms as licensing conditions on all such managers, subject to minor firm-specific changes.

key_points.point: The standard Terms and Conditions for Virtual Asset Fund Managers, referenced in the 1 November 2018 Statement, are now published on the SFC website.
The SFC will apply these terms as a standard licensing condition on every Virtual Asset Fund Manager, subject only to minor firm-specific changes.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this confirms the November 2018 virtual asset portfolio manager framework became real, published terms. These are the legal text a bank's Type 9-licensed asset management arm would follow if it manages virtual asset portfolios.

quote.text: the proforma set of terms and conditions is now available on the SFC's website

reading_guide: One-page announcement. The full terms and conditions sit in a separate linked document not captured in this record's text.
flags: The actual detailed Terms and Conditions text is in a separate linked document (VA_Portfolio_Managers_Terms_and_Conditions) not captured in this circular's own text -- flag text_unavailable for the substantive terms themselves.
text_unavailable

title: Position paper: Regulation of virtual asset trading platforms
summary: In this 2019 position paper, the SFC set up a voluntary licence path (Types 1 and 7) for a centralised platform that trades at least one security token. Licensed platforms sit in the SFC's regulatory sandbox for close oversight. The SFC said it had no legal power over platforms trading only non-security tokens, so many venues could stay unregulated. Still, it judged that regulating this smaller group served the public good while broader legislation was pending. Appendix 1 gives the full terms and conditions for platform operators, covering custody and know-your-customer (KYC) checks. It also covers anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing (AML/CFT) controls, market monitoring, accounting, risk management, and conflicts of interest.

key_points.point: Under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO), only 'securities' or 'futures contracts' fall under SFC authority, so the SFC cannot license or supervise a platform that trades only non-security tokens.
To fall under SFC rules and need a Type 1 and Type 7 licence, an operator must run a centralised online trading platform based in Hong Kong. It must also list at least one security token.
The SFC will not license platforms that only provide a direct peer-to-peer marketplace, or that just route client orders without running automated trading services themselves.
Every virtual-asset trading activity marketed to, or carried out in, Hong Kong must sit under a single SFC-licensed company.

Client virtual assets should be held on trust by an Associated Entity that is incorporated in Hong Kong, holds a Trust or Company Service Provider (TCSP) licence under Cap. 615, and is wholly owned by the licensee.
At least 98% of client virtual assets must sit in cold wallets (kept offline), capping hot-wallet holdings at 2%.
Insurance must cover custody losses: full coverage for assets in hot wallets, and substantial coverage, around 95%, for assets in cold storage.
Licensed operators must hire an independent professional firm to review them each year, with the first report due within 18 months of getting the licence.
From 6 November 2019, operators running a centralised platform that plans to list at least one security token can apply for a licence, though approval may take longer than usual.

numbers_and_dates.item: Estimated global virtual asset market cap (2019)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this paper set the original custody and insurance benchmarks, such as 98% cold storage and insured, trust-held client assets. Compliance can still use these to check how well a virtual-asset platform counterparty protects client assets, even though the paper is now superseded.

quote.text: it is manifestly in the public interest to act now

reading_guide: Read Part I (paras 1-12) for the regulatory approach, and Part III (paras 30-81) for the licensing, custody, KYC and AML standards. The appendix duplicates content already covered in the standalone Terms and Conditions document (id 9c2042fde962), so it can be skipped.
flags: Confirms the SFC's licensing power was jurisdictionally limited to platforms offering at least one security token -- a limitation later closed by the AMLO Part 5B mandatory VASP regime covering all VA exchanges regardless of token type.
Notes explicit legal uncertainty (as of 2019) over whether a virtual asset is 'property' under HK law, affecting insolvency treatment of client assets -- a caveat still often overlooked.

controls_and_monitoring: Use the custody, KYC/AML, market-monitoring and 98% cold-storage benchmarks from this paper when checking how a virtual-asset platform counterparty protects client assets (paras 47, 50, 53, p.10-11)
counterparty_due_diligence: Check that any virtual-asset trading platform the bank deals with, directly or through clients, holds an SFC licence under this framework, keeps client assets in trust through a TCSP-licensed Associated Entity, stores at least 98% of assets in cold wallets, and carries custody insurance (paras 47, 50, 53, p.10-11)

Remember the SFC's original licensing power only covered platforms trading at least one security token -- a gap since closed by the mandatory VASP licensing regime under the Anti-Money Laundering Ordinance (para 4, p.1-2)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board should understand this 2019 paper laid the historical groundwork for virtual-asset custody standards, still used today as a benchmark when checking counterparty platforms, even though the mandatory AMLO licensing regime has since replaced it.

title: SFC issues warnings on virtual asset futures contracts
summary: The SFC warned that virtual-asset futures contracts, for example on Bitcoin, are high-risk. The underlying assets are volatile, hard to value, and traded on largely unregulated venues, some of which have changed trading rules mid-contract or halted trades to investors' harm. A Hong Kong platform offering such futures without a licence may breach the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO). Such contracts could also count as unlawful gambling under the Gambling Ordinance unless expressly authorised. The SFC said it had not licensed any such platform, and said it would be unlikely to do so, though it excluded certain already-authorised US-regulated Bitcoin futures from this warning.

key_points.point: Offering VA futures trading in Hong Kong without a licence or authorisation under the SFO may itself be an offence.
key_points.locator: para beginning 'In Hong Kong, any trading platforms or persons...'

key_points.point: Depending on structure, VA futures contracts can also count as contracts for differences, making them potentially unlawful gambling unless separately authorised.
As of this warning, the SFC had not licensed or authorised anyone to offer or trade VA futures contracts in Hong Kong, and said a grant was unlikely given the risk profile.

US-regulated Bitcoin futures already authorised for automated trading services (ATS) and covered by a 2017 circular to licensed corporations and registered institutions are excluded from this warning.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this confirms unlicensed VA-futures venues carry both SFO licensing risk and a possible illegal-gambling risk in Hong Kong. It is a useful screening flag if customers reference such platforms, or the bank considers a product linked to VA derivatives.

quote.text: extremely risky as they are largely unregulated and highly leveraged

reading_guide: Read the two risk paragraphs and the SFO/Gambling Ordinance paragraphs; skip the footnote detail on the 2017 ATS exclusion unless relevant to a specific product.
flags: Pre-dates the AMLO Part 5B VATP licensing regime introduced June 2023; still cited as background on the SFC's historical stance toward VA derivatives.

controls_and_monitoring: Flag any customer activity referencing VA futures/derivatives platforms for enhanced review given the dual SFO/gambling risk noted by the SFC.
counterparty_due_diligence: Treat any VA-derivatives venue as unlicensed unless it can show a specific SFC authorisation, since none had been granted as of this warning.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Note as background risk context if the bank explores any VA-derivative-linked product or referral relationship.

title: Position paper: Regulation of virtual asset trading platforms
supersedes_or_amends: Statement on regulatory framework for virtual asset portfolios managers, fund distributors and trading platform operators (1 Nov 2018)
summary: The SFC finalised its opt-in licensing framework for centralised virtual asset trading platforms. A platform only falls under SFC jurisdiction once it lists at least one security-type token. Once caught, all its virtual-asset business, security and non-security tokens alike, must sit in one SFC-licensed company holding Type 1 (dealing) and Type 7 (automated trading services) licences. The attached Terms and Conditions set detailed, legally binding rules covering custody (98% cold storage, key management, insurance) and know-your-customer (KYC) checks. They also cover suitability, anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing (AML/CFT) controls, market surveillance, conflicts of interest, record-keeping, and SFC notification duties. Services are restricted to professional investors only, and this framework was the direct forerunner of Hong Kong's later mandatory VATP licensing regime.

key_points.point: A platform only becomes subject to SFC licensing once it offers at least one security-type token; a platform trading only non-security tokens stays outside SFC jurisdiction entirely.
All of a licensed platform's virtual-asset trading activity marketed to, or run in, Hong Kong must sit under one licensed company, so the SFC can oversee the whole business.
Client virtual assets must be held on trust through a separate, wholly-owned Associated Entity, with 98% kept in cold storage and no more than 2% in hot wallets.

Seeds and private keys for client assets must be created and stored in Hong Kong, with backups kept in different places. Strict internal access controls must stop any single person controlling a full key.
An insurance policy must cover client virtual assets in hot storage in full, and in cold storage substantially (the SFC's benchmark example is 95%), at all times.
Platform operators must only serve professional investors, and must assess and record each client's virtual-asset knowledge before onboarding, or provide training first.

Platform operators must run written AML/CFT systems and apply extra checks to tainted wallet addresses, mixing services, and high-anonymity assets. They must unmask or reject clients using masked IP addresses (for example, VPNs) where needed.
Operators must tell the SFC about serious non-compliance, system failures, and various operational changes, usually within seven business days or immediately, and file monthly business reports.

A licensed platform operator should not trade for its own account or make markets on a proprietary basis, and must have written policies restricting and monitoring staff's personal virtual-asset dealing.
Platform operators cannot offer clients financing to buy virtual assets, and cannot offer or trade virtual asset futures or related derivatives at all.

numbers_and_dates.item: minimum cold storage of client virtual assets
maximum hot wallet holding of client virtual assets
insurance coverage example for cold-stored client assets
insurance coverage for hot-stored client assets
minimum liquid own-asset buffer for a licensee

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the core rulebook to benchmark any Hong Kong virtual asset trading platform (VATP) counterparty against for custody, AML, KYC and governance standards. A mandatory regime later replaced it.

quote.text: it is manifestly in the public interest to act now

reading_guide: Read Part I (paras 1-12) for the policy summary. Then read the Terms and Conditions on Custody (Part VII), Dealing with Clients (Part VI) and AML/CFT (Part XIII) for the operative rules.
flags: formally an opt-in regime - platforms trading only non-security tokens remain outside SFC's jurisdiction entirely under this framework, a major carve-out later closed by mandatory AMLO licensing

controls_and_monitoring: use these Terms and Conditions (custody, insurance, AML, market surveillance, record-keeping standards) as the due-diligence checklist when assessing any VATP counterparty licensed under this or a successor regime
counterparty_due_diligence: confirm a VATP counterparty stores at least 98% of client assets in cold storage with keys generated and held in Hong Kong
confirm insurance coverage is full for hot-stored assets and substantial (e.g. 95%) for cold-stored assets
confirm the platform restricts services to professional investors and runs the required AML/CFT and market-surveillance controls
check whether the platform is a genuinely licensed single legal entity covering all its Hong Kong-facing VA business, not a fragmented group structure
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told this is the foundational custody and conduct benchmark (98% cold storage, insurance levels, professional-investor-only) against which the bank assesses any VATP relationship, while noting it was an opt-in regime with a significant unregulated-platform carve-out until later legislation closed it.

title: Keynote Speech at Hong Kong Fintech Week 2019
summary: This 2019 Fintech Week keynote by the then HKMA Deputy Chief Executive reviews three years of the HKMA's Fintech Facilitation Office. It covers the Faster Payment System, virtual bank licensing, open APIs, and a blockchain-based trade finance platform, and previews upcoming AI-governance circulars. Virtual-asset content is minimal. It mentions a joint HKMA and Bank of Thailand blockchain-based central bank digital currency (CBDC) research project, and a trial trade-finance link with the we.trade platform. It is a motivational conference address, not a supervisory or policy document.

key_points.point: The speech confirms the HKMA and the Bank of Thailand had a joint research project exploring blockchain-based central bank digital currency (CBDC) for cross-border payments.

It states the HKMA had recently issued two circulars on banks' use of artificial intelligence (AI): one on risk-management principles, one on consumer protection. Both were deliberately non-prescriptive given how new the area was.

numbers_and_dates.item: FPS registrations reported at time of speech

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, the virtual-asset content here is minimal and non-binding. Its only relevance is as early context for the HKMA's blockchain-based CBDC research, which later grew into the e-HKD and mBridge work streams.
reading_guide: Only the short passage on the Bank of Thailand CBDC research and the we.trade blockchain pilot is relevant to digital assets; skim the rest for context only.
flags: Speech has almost no virtual-asset/crypto content; included here mainly for its brief CBDC reference.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No action needed; background only on early CBDC research.

title: Fintech: a regulatory strategy for a dynamic industry - Keynote speech at Hong Kong FinTech Week 2019 (Ashley Alder)
summary: SFC Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Ashley Alder announced, in this speech, the launch of the SFC's new opt-in licensing framework for virtual asset trading platforms. The SFC issued a separate investor-warning statement on VA futures the same day. He explained the 'same business, same risks, same rules' principle, and why the SFC chose an opt-in route rather than waiting for new legislation. He also noted the framework's built-in limit: it only catches a platform once it lists one security-type token, so platforms trading only non-security tokens stay unregulated. He discussed rising international concern about stablecoins after Facebook's Libra proposal.

key_points.point: A platform is only caught by the new framework once it offers at least one token that is legally a security; once caught, all its operations become subject to SFC rules.
Licensed platforms must hold insurance against loss or theft of virtual assets.
Licensed platforms may only serve professional investors who can show enough virtual-asset investment knowledge.
A platform that keeps all its traded tokens outside the legal definition of securities can simply stay unregulated.
The SFC issued a separate statement the same day warning that offering virtual-asset futures to the public may be illegal under securities or gambling law.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this explains, in the regulator's own words, why pre-2023 VA platforms in Hong Kong were mostly unlicensed by design. It is a key fact when checking the regulatory history of a long-established platform counterparty.

quote.text: same business, same risks, same rules

reading_guide: Read pages 4-6 for the VATP framework announcement; pages 2-3 (stablecoin/Libra commentary) are useful context but not action items.

counterparty_due_diligence: check whether a VA platform counterparty is SFC-licensed under the opt-in regime, and if not, understand it may legally avoid licensing simply by excluding security tokens
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should understand that pre-2023 platform licensing was voluntary and partial, which affects historical due-diligence conclusions about long-standing platform relationships.

title: SFC adopts new approach to virtual asset trading platforms
supersedes_or_amends: Statement on regulatory framework for virtual asset portfolios managers, fund distributors and trading platform operators (1 November 2018) -- Part II (conceptual/opt-in Sandbox framework for trading platforms)
summary: This press release announces the SFC's 6 November 2019 Position Paper, 'Regulation of virtual asset trading platforms', moving from the conceptual November 2018 framework to an actual licensing regime. Platforms operating in Hong Kong that trade at least one security token can now apply for an SFC licence (Types 1 and 7). Licence conditions require serving professional investors only and checking that clients know enough about virtual assets. They also set strict rules on which virtual assets a platform can admit, and place the platform in the SFC Regulatory Sandbox for close supervision. The SFC still has no power to license or supervise platforms trading only non-security tokens, and a companion statement warns investors about unregulated virtual asset futures contracts.

key_points.point: Platforms operating in Hong Kong that trade at least one security token can now apply for an SFC licence (Types 1 and 7 regulated activities).
A Platform Operator must run all group virtual-asset trading business (Relevant Activities) under one company licensed by the SFC.
Licence conditions require the licensee to serve only professional investors and follow the attached Terms and Conditions.
A Platform Operator and its Associated Entity must hold 98% of clients' virtual assets in offline (cold) storage.
Insurance must fully cover virtual assets held in hot storage, and cover most of those in cold storage (for example, 95%) at all times.
Seeds and private keys for client virtual assets must be kept physically in Hong Kong.
A Platform Operator must hold liquid financial resources equal to at least 12 months of operating expenses.
The SFC has no power to license or supervise a platform that trades only non-security virtual assets, since those do not count as 'securities' or 'futures contracts' under the SFO.

A Platform Operator must not trade on its own account or make markets for itself. It must not offer leverage for clients to buy virtual assets, and must not trade virtual asset futures or derivatives.
Only security tokens backed by assets, approved or registered with comparable regulators, and with a 12-month track record after issuance, should be allowed for trading.
Licensed Platform Operators sit in the SFC Regulatory Sandbox for close, intensive supervision, including monthly reporting.

numbers_and_dates.item: Security token post-issuance track record required for admission

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the historical bridge from the 2018 conceptual framework to actual VATP licensing. A compliance head mainly needs it to understand where today's custody and liquidity rules came from, since this Position Paper itself has since been superseded.

quote.text: the SFC has no power to grant a licence to or supervise a platform

reading_guide: Read the press release for the headline shift, then Position Paper Parts I and III (paras 1-12, 30-44) for the rationale and licensing regime.
flags: MAJOR SHIFT: This 2019 Position Paper supersedes the Part II conceptual/opt-in Sandbox framework from the Nov 2018 Statement with an operative SFC licensing regime (Types 1 and 7) -- this is the origin of the mandatory (not merely proposed) 98% cold storage and other custody/insurance requirements, not the Nov 2018 statement where they were only proposed.

The SFC explicitly states it still has NO power to license platforms trading only non-security tokens as of Nov 2019 -- a jurisdictional gap that persisted until the later AMLO Part 5B statutory licensing regime covering all VATPs regardless of token classification.
Seeds/private keys for client virtual assets must be stored physically in Hong Kong (para 7.6(e)) -- an operational constraint easily missed by groups planning offshore key custody.

counterparty_due_diligence: This is the historical source of the 98% cold-storage rule and the 12-months' operating-expense liquidity rule, both still useful benchmarks when checking a VATP's custody and financial strength, even though this Position Paper has since been replaced by the statutory AMLO Part 5B regime.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Background only: this confirms the 2019 shift from an opt-in Sandbox to an actual SFC licence for VATPs trading security tokens — the direct ancestor of today's VATP licensing rules.

title: Hong Kong Fintech Week spotlights digital asset regulation, virtual banking, future technologies and FintechHK Global Competition final (with photos)
summary: This is a general recap press release for Hong Kong FinTech Week 2019, covering virtual banking, blockchain trade finance, and other fintech themes. It briefly notes that the SFC's Chief Executive Officer (CEO) used the event to announce new rules letting virtual-asset trading platforms apply for an operating licence. The new rules are restricted to professional investors and call for insurance against loss or theft of client assets. Most of the release covers unrelated fintech topics: virtual bank licensing numbers, the Faster Payment System, and a China-Hong Kong trade-finance blockchain pilot.

key_points.point: The SFC announced new rules letting virtual asset trading platforms apply for an operating licence, restricted to professional investors and requiring insurance for lost or stolen assets.

numbers_and_dates.item: virtual bank licences granted by HKMA (as of event)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is a media recap of marginal value. The substantive rule content is fully covered by the SFC's own position paper and speech from the same week.
reading_guide: Skim only for the SFC paragraph; rest is general fintech-week publicity, not regulatory content.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: None; superseded in substance by the SFC's own position paper the same week.

title: Managing ML/TF Risks Associated with Virtual Assets (VAs) and Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs)
supersedes_or_amends: Risks associated with virtual commodities (9 January 2014)
Risks Associated with Virtual Commodities (30 April 2014)
summary: This circular formally replaces the HKMA's 2014 virtual-commodity letters, updating guidance to match the Financial Action Task Force's (FATF) 2019 rules on virtual assets (VAs) and virtual asset service providers (VASPs). It tells banks to apply a risk-based approach when banking VASPs, doing extra due diligence in proportion to risk. This includes understanding the VASP's business, checking if it is licensed or registered, and assessing its anti-money-laundering controls. It also says banks must run a money-laundering risk assessment before launching any new VA-linked product.

key_points.point: Banks should assess and differentiate the money-laundering risk of each VASP customer individually rather than applying one blanket approach, since VASP business models vary widely.
Extra due diligence on a VASP customer should include understanding its business, checking its licensing or registration status, and assessing its own anti-money-laundering controls.
Before launching any new banking or investment product linked to virtual assets, a bank should carry out a money-laundering risk assessment and put in place measures to manage the risks found.
This circular replaces the two 2014 letters on virtual commodities.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this circular is the direct predecessor of the AML/CFT due-diligence checklist still used today for onboarding and monitoring VASP customers.

quote.text: no 'one-size-fits-all'

reading_guide: Two-page circular; read in full, note the supersession line on p.2.

obligations: Conduct ML/TF risk assessment before launching any new VA-linked product or service, p.2
controls_and_monitoring: Risk-based, VASP-specific due diligence including collection of business information and AML/CFT control assessment, p.2
counterparty_due_diligence: Check whether the VASP is licensed/registered and assess its AML/CFT controls before or during the banking relationship, p.2
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told that VASP banking relationships now require documented, risk-differentiated due diligence rather than a uniform policy.

title: Managing ML/TF risks associated with virtual assets (VAs) and virtual asset service providers (VASPs)
summary: This circular is addressed to all Stored Value Facility (SVF) licensees. It passes on the Financial Action Task Force's (FATF) June 2019 update to Recommendation 15 and its risk-based guidance on virtual assets (VAs) and virtual asset service providers (VASPs). It tells SVF licensees to apply extra, risk-based due diligence before starting a business relationship with a VASP. This includes checking whether the VASP is licensed or registered and AML/CFT-supervised. It also means running a money-laundering risk assessment (per para 2.11 of the AML/CFT Guideline) before launching any new VA-related product. It signals that more VASPs would become licensed in Hong Kong and elsewhere as FATF-aligned regimes took hold.

key_points.point: SVF licensees must apply a risk-based approach when starting or keeping a relationship with a VASP, tailoring due diligence to that VASP's own risk rather than one fixed check.

Due diligence on a VASP counterparty should cover understanding its business and checking, from public information, whether it is licensed and AML/CFT-supervised. It should also assess the VASP's AML/CFT controls, scaled to the risk found.
Before rolling out any new VA-related product, an SVF licensee must first carry out a money-laundering risk assessment and put in place measures to manage the risks found.
SVF licensees are expected to keep watching international and local VASP developments and keep applying a risk-based approach on an ongoing basis, not just at onboarding.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is an early, direct HKMA instruction. Any bank-affiliated SVF licensee must treat VASP counterparties as a distinct AML/CFT due-diligence category, the template later intermediary and custody guidance builds on.
reading_guide: The whole two-page circular is short enough to read in full; the FATF Guidance it references is external and not part of this text.
flags: Circular predates Hong Kong's own VASP/VATP licensing regime under AMLO Part 5B (2023), so its VASP due-diligence expectations should now be read alongside that regime's licensing status checks, not as a standalone final word.

obligations: If the bank group holds an SVF licence, apply risk-based due diligence before establishing any relationship with a VASP, and run an ML/TF risk assessment before launching any VA-related product (p.1-2).
controls_and_monitoring: Scale the depth of VASP due diligence to the assessed ML/TF risk rather than applying a fixed checklist; keep it under ongoing review as VASP regulatory status changes.
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm from public sources whether a VASP counterparty is licensed/registered and AML/CFT-supervised, and assess the adequacy of its AML/CFT controls before onboarding it.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told that VASP relationships are treated as a distinct, elevated AML/CFT risk category requiring documented risk assessment, not ordinary counterparty onboarding.

title: Inthanon-LionRock: Leveraging Distributed Ledger Technology to Increase Efficiency in Cross-Border Payments
summary: This is the joint report by the HKMA and the Bank of Thailand on the first phase of their shared blockchain experiment for cross-border payments, published January 2020. It describes a working prototype, built with technology partner R3. The prototype lets participating Thai and Hong Kong banks move funds and make foreign-exchange (FX) deals directly with each other, rather than through a chain of correspondent banks. The prototype cut settlement layers and supported same-time payment-and-FX settlement, while also trying to build in local regulatory compliance checks. It closes by naming unresolved legal, regulatory and operational gaps that would need further work; this is the earliest, now-superseded phase of a project family that later grew into mBridge.

key_points.point: The prototype linked Thailand's and Hong Kong's own blockchain payment networks, so participating banks could transfer funds and swap currencies directly, cutting out extra middle banks.
Ten commercial banks took part in total, eight based in Thailand and two in Hong Kong, working alongside the two central banks and blockchain vendor R3.
The prototype let a currency swap and its matching payment settle together, so neither side of the trade completes without the other.
The design tried to build local rulebook checks into the payment flow itself, alongside features to help banks manage their foreign-currency liquidity across the two markets.
The report flags that legal, regulatory, operational and technology limits were not yet resolved, and were left for the next phase of the project.
The authors suggest the next step is to reshape the model to fit each jurisdiction's existing rules and match international standards before real use.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this superseded, proof-of-concept-stage report creates no obligation today. It is useful background on the origins of mBridge and Ensemble, and shows regulators flagged AML and legal-certainty gaps as open problems from the start, a theme continuing in later reports.

quote.text: legal and regulations, operational issues, and technical limitations

reading_guide: Read the Executive Summary (p.9) and the Conclusion (p.58). Skip the 60-page technical walkthrough of liquidity mechanics.
flags: Superseded: this is Phase 1; the project was later renamed mBridge and moved well beyond this prototype.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Historical background only; no current obligation. No board escalation needed.

title: Statements issued by the Financial Action Task Force
summary: This is a routine HKMA relay of the latest Financial Action Task Force (FATF) high-risk and increased-monitoring jurisdiction lists and plenary outcomes. It tells banks to keep applying enhanced due diligence to Iran and North Korea, and to note the updated monitored-jurisdictions list. It also notes that the FATF reviewed how well its virtual-asset and VASP standards are being followed, and published an AML/CFT stablecoins report to the G20 on 7 July 2020.

key_points.point: Banks should keep applying enhanced due diligence and countermeasures to business with Iran and North Korea.
Banks should note the FATF's updated list of jurisdictions under increased monitoring, published on the FATF website.
The FATF reviewed how well countries have put its virtual-asset and VASP rules into practice, and separately reported to the G20 on money-laundering risks in stablecoins.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is a routine sanctions-list relay. It matters to the AML programme generally, but is not crypto-specific except for the FATF virtual-asset workstream it flags.

quote.text: analysis of AML/CFT issues relating to stablecoins

reading_guide: Skim; the substantive content is the same FATF list update each cycle, only the VA/VASP-specific paragraph (where present) is new.

obligations: Apply enhanced due diligence/countermeasures to Iran and DPRK-linked business, p.1
controls_and_monitoring: Update sanctions/high-risk-jurisdiction screening lists per the FATF statement, p.1
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No board escalation needed for a routine list relay unless a new jurisdiction directly affects the bank's book.

title: Keynote Speech at the Hong Kong FinTech Week 2020
summary: This 2020 Fintech Week keynote by the then HKMA Chief Executive launches the Commercial Data Interchange (CDI), a consent-based data-sharing platform to help banks, especially with SME lending. It also gives an update on the HKMA and Bank of Thailand blockchain-based central bank digital currency (CBDC) research. This describes a working proof-of-concept for real-time cross-border peer-to-peer transfers, with plans to explore a multi-CBDC platform. It is a policy-launch speech, not a rule, and has no other virtual-asset content.

key_points.point: The HKMA announced the Commercial Data Interchange (CDI), a consent-based platform letting bank customers authorise data providers to share their data with banks through one connection instead of many separate links.

The HKMA and Bank of Thailand blockchain CBDC project had moved from proof-of-concept to testing cross-border trade settlement and capital-market uses. It also had plans to grow into a multi-CBDC platform.

numbers_and_dates.item: Number of incumbent and virtual banks referenced as operating in Hong Kong

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is background on the origins of the HKMA's cross-border wholesale CBDC work, which later fed into the mBridge and e-HKD initiatives. It creates no obligation on banks.
reading_guide: Read only the CBDC section under 'Addressing pain points in cross-border payments'; the CDI/data-strategy content is not digital-asset relevant.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No action needed; background only on early cross-border CBDC research and the CDI data-sharing initiative.

title: Fintech: the regulatory response to evolving challenges - Keynote address at Hong Kong FinTech Week 2020 (Ashley Alder)
summary: SFC Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Ashley Alder announced that the government had that day proposed a new mandatory licensing regime under anti-money laundering law for all virtual asset trading platforms. This closes the gap left by the 2019 opt-in framework, which only caught platforms that chose to list at least one security-type token. Going forward, all Hong Kong VA platforms would fall under either the existing opt-in regime or the new mandatory regime, with the same standards. He also confirmed that security tokens already fall under existing securities law for both primary distribution and secondary trading.

key_points.point: The government proposed a new mandatory licensing regime under the AML Ordinance, covering any virtual asset trading platform operating in or targeting Hong Kong, whether or not it lists security tokens.
Operating without the new licence, once enacted, would be an offence.
Under the new regime, licensed platforms would at first be restricted to professional investors only.
A secondary market operator trading at least one security token must hold both a Type 1 dealing licence and a Type 7 automated trading services licence, serving professional investors only.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this marks the policy pivot from voluntary to mandatory VATP licensing in Hong Kong, the direct ancestor of the licensing regime a bank must check counterparties against today.

quote.text: same business, same risks, same rules

reading_guide: Read the 'Virtual asset trading platforms' and 'Regulation of security tokens' sections (pages 1-3) in full; skip the closing general Fintech commentary.

counterparty_due_diligence: from late 2020 onward, expect any VA platform serving Hong Kong to eventually need either an opt-in SFC licence or the incoming mandatory AMLO licence; treat lack of either as a red flag once the new regime takes effect
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told mandatory VATP licensing was first announced in Nov 2020, which set the clock running toward the regime banks must check counterparties against today.

title: A New Trend for Fintech - Cross-border Payment
summary: This 2020 HKMA Insight article by the then Chief Executive discusses cross-border payment inefficiencies and Hong Kong's initiatives to fix them. It covers the Faster Payment System and the joint blockchain-based central bank digital currency (CBDC) research with the Bank of Thailand. It also covers early technical talks with the People's Bank of China on piloting cross-border use of e-CNY (digital renminbi). It is commentary, not a rule.

key_points.point: The HKMA and Bank of Thailand's blockchain CBDC research had entered a second stage, exploring specific business uses and growing the platform to three or more participating CBDCs.

The HKMA and the People's Bank of China's Digital Currency Institute were discussing and preparing a technical pilot to use e-CNY for cross-border payments between Hong Kong and the Mainland. No launch date was yet set.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this documents the earliest public signal of a Hong Kong and e-CNY cross-border pilot. It is useful background for CBDC-related product and payments planning, though it creates no compliance obligation.
reading_guide: Short article; read the last two paragraphs on the Bank of Thailand CBDC project and the e-CNY pilot discussions, skip the general FPS background.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No action needed; useful only as background on how early e-CNY cross-border discussions began.

title: Terms and Conditions for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators
summary: This SFC document sets out detailed, binding Terms and Conditions. The SFC imposes them as a licensing condition on virtual asset trading platform (VATP) operators licensed under the voluntary opt-in regime (Types 1 and 7). It covers financial soundness, token admission checks, market manipulation prevention, and client dealing (know-your-customer (KYC) checks, suitability, disclosure, contract notes). It also covers custody of client assets (trust structure through an Associated Entity, cold storage, private key management, insurance). It further covers risk management, cybersecurity, conflicts of interest, record keeping, auditors, AML/CFT, and ongoing reporting. It applies only to platforms serving professional investors and offering at least one security token.

key_points.point: A Platform Operator should hold liquid own assets in Hong Kong at all times, worth at least a year's actual running costs. These can be cash, deposits, treasury bills or certificates of deposit, but not virtual assets.
A Platform Operator and its Associated Entity are expected to hold client assets so that at least 98% sit in cold storage, capping hot-wallet holdings at 2%.
Under the Platform Operator's key-management controls, cryptographic seeds and private keys for client assets are kept within Hong Kong.
An insurance policy should cover client virtual assets in hot storage (full coverage) and cold storage (substantial coverage, for example 95%).
A Platform Operator should not offer clients any financial help, such as margin, to buy virtual assets.
A Platform Operator should not trade for its own account or make markets on a proprietary basis.
A client counts as having enough knowledge of virtual assets once they have made five or more virtual-asset transactions in the past three years.

Records should generally be kept for at least seven years. Some records, such as contract notes, receipts and audit logs, need only two years, and system design papers two years after the system retires.
A Platform Operator is expected to tell the SFC within seven business days of a planned change to its scope of services, controlling persons, or authorisation status.

A token that qualifies as a 'security' can only be admitted for trading if it is backed by assets and approved or registered with a comparable overseas regulator. It should also have a track record of at least 12 months since issuance.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this document does not bind the bank directly. But its 98% cold-storage and Hong Kong-key-storage rules are the origin of the custody standard a compliance head should still expect any VATP counterparty to be measured against.

quote.text: store 98% of client virtual assets in cold storage

reading_guide: Focus on Part IV (token admission), Part VI (KYC, suitability, disclosure), Part VII (custody, including the 98% cold storage and key management rules), and Part XIII (AML/CFT).
flags: A common misconception is that 98% cold storage is a Hong Kong statutory rule of general application; it is in fact a licensing-condition requirement specific to this voluntary opt-in VATP regime (2019-2023), later carried forward in substance into the mandatory VASP regime.
This voluntary regime predates and was superseded by the mandatory AMLO Part 5B VASP licensing regime; the document itself is now largely of historical/reference value for the original T&C baseline.

counterparty_due_diligence: When assessing a VATP counterparty (own group affiliate or third party), check whether custody still meets the 98% cold-storage / Hong Kong-based key-storage baseline this T&C originally set (para 7.5(c), 7.6(e), p.20-22)

Treat the historical insurance benchmark (full coverage hot storage, ~95% cold) as a reference point only, since later rules replaced it with a flexible SFC-approved compensation arrangement (para 7.17, p.25)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told this T&C is superseded historical material; current VATP custody standards must be checked against the live VATP Guidelines, not this 2020 baseline.

title: SFC licenses first virtual asset trading platform
summary: The SFC announced that Hong Kong now has its first SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform (VATP), granted under a voluntary opt-in scheme. The licence covers two regulated activities: dealing in securities (Type 1) and running automated trading services (Type 7). Only professional investors may use the platform, and it must follow the Terms and Conditions written for VATP Operators, echoing rules already used for securities brokers and trading venues. This grant follows the SFC's Position Paper of 6 November 2019. The release separately notes a November 2020 government consultation proposing SFC oversight of every centralised virtual-asset exchange, even non-security-token ones.

key_points.point: The licensed platform may serve professional investors only, matching the definition used in the SFO's Professional Investor Rules.
The platform is licensed for two regulated activities under the SFO: dealing in securities (Type 1) and providing automated trading services (Type 7).
As a licence condition, the platform must follow the Terms and Conditions written for VATP Operators.
At this point, SFC rules reach only platforms that trade at least one security token; platforms dealing solely in non-security tokens stay outside SFC jurisdiction.

The government, in a November 2020 consultation, proposed new legislation letting the SFC oversee every centralised virtual-asset exchange, even non-security-token ones; feedback was due by 31 January 2021.

numbers_and_dates.item: Position Paper date establishing the framework

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this marks the first working SFC-licensed VATP. When checking whether a trading-platform counterparty is properly licensed, compliance can confirm it holds Type 1 and Type 7 licences and follows the professional-investor-only limit.

quote.text: investors in Hong Kong will be able to easily distinguish between platforms

reading_guide: Read the main body (paras 1-4) for the licensing announcement; skim the Notes only for cross-references to the Position Paper and T&Cs, both read in full as separate attachments.
flags: This 2020 voluntary opt-in licence was professional-investor-only -- a common misconception is that HK VATP licensing has always allowed retail access; retail access came later under the mandatory 2023 regime.
The AMLO consultation referenced here (Nov 2020) is the precursor to the eventual VASP mandatory licensing regime, not yet enacted at this date.

counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm that a VATP counterparty holds Type 1 and Type 7 licences and serves only professional investors, where that restriction applies to the platform in question.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board should note this is the first SFC-licensed VATP milestone, showing the regime is operational and that licensed platforms now exist to use as counterparties.

title: Joint statement on Multiple Central Bank Digital Currency (m-CBDC) Bridge Project
summary: The HKMA announced two new members for a joint central bank digital currency (CBDC) project with Hong Kong and Thailand. The new members are the UAE central bank and the People's Bank of China's Digital Currency Institute. The project was renamed the Multiple CBDC (m-CBDC) Bridge. It is supported by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Innovation Hub in Hong Kong. It would build a proof-of-concept using distributed ledger technology (DLT) to let central banks settle real-time cross-border foreign-exchange payments around the clock. The aim is to cut cost and complexity in cross-border transfers.

key_points.point: Four central banks and monetary authorities (HKMA, Bank of Thailand, Central Bank of the UAE, PBoC's Digital Currency Institute) joined the renamed m-CBDC Bridge project.
The project's proof-of-concept targets real-time, 24/7 cross-border foreign-exchange payment settlement using DLT.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is an early-stage wholesale CBDC infrastructure project, not yet operational for banks, but worth tracking as a possible future cross-border settlement rail.
reading_guide: Short; read in full. No action items for banks at this stage.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Informational: wholesale CBDC infrastructure project banks may eventually connect to, no current action needed.

title: Joint statement on the Multiple Central Bank Digital Currency (m-CBDC) Bridge Project
summary: The HKMA and the Bank of Thailand announced that two new members were joining the second phase of Project Inthanon-LionRock. The new members are the Central Bank of the UAE (CBUAE) and the Digital Currency Institute of the People's Bank of China (PBC DCI). The initiative was renamed the 'm-CBDC Bridge' (later mBridge). The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre supports the project. It will build a proof-of-concept prototype for real-time, 24/7 cross-border foreign-exchange (FX) settlement using distributed ledger technology (DLT) across several jurisdictions. It explores both domestic and foreign currency uses.

key_points.point: The CBUAE and PBC DCI joined the second phase of Project Inthanon-LionRock, renamed the m-CBDC Bridge project.
Using a DLT-based proof-of-concept, the project seeks round-the-clock, real-time settlement of foreign-exchange trades across several jurisdictions.
Central banks in the project intend to use the prototype's results to judge whether the approach could work for cross-border payments, trade settlement, and capital-market deals.
Project Inthanon-LionRock started as a joint HKMA-Bank of Thailand (BOT) research project in Q4 2019.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is pure market and infrastructure context. It records the founding of the mBridge multi-CBDC project, with no obligations, controls, or reporting duties for the bank at this stage.

quote.text: strongly supported by the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Hub

reading_guide: Short press release; read in full (4 short paragraphs).

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No action needed now; note as a market-infrastructure development to watch for future cross-border settlement rail options.

title: Hong Kong’s Under-rated Bond Market
summary: This 2021 HKMA Insight article by the then Chief Executive argues Hong Kong's conventional bond-arranging market is under-appreciated, citing International Capital Market Association (ICMA) data on Asian bond issuance. It also covers Bond Connect and the government's green-bond programme. It has no virtual-asset, tokenisation, stablecoin or distributed ledger technology (DLT) content.

key_points.point: The article cites ICMA figures showing Hong Kong arranged 34% of Asian international bond issuance in 2020, the largest share in the region, ahead of the US, UK and Singapore.
It confirms the HKSAR Government planned to double its Green Bond Programme borrowing ceiling to HK$200 billion.

numbers_and_dates.item: Hong Kong's share of Asian international bond arranging (2020)
Proposed doubled Green Bond Programme ceiling

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this has no digital-asset content and creates no obligation. It is purely background on conventional bond-market positioning, not tokenised bonds.
reading_guide: Not essential for a digital-assets compliance function; skip unless researching conventional bond-market policy history.
flags: Document has no virtual-asset, tokenisation or DLT content.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No action needed; not digital-asset relevant.

title: LCQ19: Virtual asset trading platforms
summary: This is a Legislative Council (LegCo) written reply summarising how the SFC's 2018-2019 opt-in virtual asset trading platform (VATP) licensing regime had worked in practice. It confirms the regime only applies to platforms offering at least one securities-type token. It describes the fit-and-proper vetting criteria: custody, cybersecurity, AML, market-abuse controls, and product due diligence. It states that the SFC had by then received four formal licence applications and granted its first VATP licence in December 2020.

key_points.point: Licensed VATP operators may only serve professional investors and must set strict criteria for which tokens they admit for trading.

In vetting applicants, the SFC checks custody arrangements, cybersecurity, customer due diligence, anti-money laundering controls, market manipulation prevention and product due diligence, alongside the general fit-and-proper test.
A VATP licence under the opt-in regime has no fixed term and stays valid until revoked.

numbers_and_dates.item: formal VATP licence applications received under opt-in regime (as of Mar 2021)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this gives the concrete vetting criteria a bank should mirror when doing due diligence on a licensed VATP counterparty. It also confirms how few platforms were licensed as of early 2021.
reading_guide: Read the reply paragraph in full; question text is background only.

counterparty_due_diligence: when assessing a VATP counterparty licensed under the opt-in regime, confirm SFC vetted its custody, cybersecurity, AML/CTF, market-abuse and product due-diligence controls, and that it restricts services to professional investors
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should know that as of March 2021 only one VATP had ever been licensed in Hong Kong, illustrating how nascent the regime still was.

title: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposals to Enhance Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Regulation in Hong Kong – Consultation Conclusions
summary: Published by the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB) in May 2021, this paper concludes a late-2020/early-2021 consultation. It confirms the government would proceed with a licensing regime for virtual asset service providers (VASPs, essentially exchanges) under the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance. It also confirms a separate registration regime for dealers in precious metals and stones. It set the design later enacted: the SFC as licensing authority, professional-investor-only trading, a 180-day transition window, and specific criminal and civil penalties. This regime has since taken effect and been expanded by SFC guidelines, so this paper is now historical background rather than a current rulebook.

key_points.point: Anyone operating a virtual asset exchange in Hong Kong would need an SFC licence as a VASP. The exchange definition catches any platform that takes custody or control of client money or virtual assets at any point.
Peer-to-peer platforms that only post buy/sell listings without ever holding client funds or assets fall outside the VASP licensing definition.
A licensed VASP could at first only serve professional investors, despite over 40% of respondents wanting retail access; the government kept the restriction given the sector's risk and volatility.

VASPs would need to be incorporated in Hong Kong, or hold Companies Ordinance registration as a non-Hong-Kong company here. They must also keep a permanent local place of business, giving the SFC a local entity to supervise.
Applicants and at least two designated responsible officers must pass a fit-and-proper test covering past convictions, compliance history, experience and financial integrity.
A 180-day transition period was set after the regime started, letting existing operators keep running while their licence application was processed.
Marketing a virtual asset trading service to the Hong Kong public without a VASP licence, from Hong Kong or elsewhere, would be banned.

Maximum proposed criminal penalties included a HK$5 million fine and 7 years' imprisonment for operating unlicensed. Lower fines and 2-year terms applied to false statements, AML/CFT non-compliance, or fraud to induce a trade.

numbers_and_dates.item: Maximum fine for unlicensed VASP activity
numbers_and_dates.value: HKD 5,000,000 plus imprisonment up to 7 years, plus HKD 100,000/day for continuing offence

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the design document behind today's VASP/VATP licensing regime that any exchange the bank deals with, for custody, trading, or referral, must hold. It is a useful reference for why VATPs are currently professional-investor-only by default.
reading_guide: Read Chapter 2 (VASP proposals, pp.4-15) in full; Chapter 3 covers precious-metals dealers and can be skipped. Chapter 5 (Conclusions, p.27) gives the implementation timeline.
flags: This 2021 conclusions paper describes the original design of the VASP regime; the regime it describes has since come into force (per other documents in this corpus) and been refined by SFC VATP Guidelines — treat this as historical origin, not the current rulebook.
Chapter 3 on precious-metals/stones dealers is unrelated to digital assets and was not analysed in detail here.

counterparty_due_diligence: When onboarding or assessing a VA exchange counterparty, confirm it is SFC-licensed, Hong Kong-incorporated or locally registered, and restricted to professional investors as originally designed, then check current SFC VATP guidelines for any changes since this 2021 design paper (paras 2.5, 2.10-2.11, 2.15-2.17).
Check whether a VA exchange counterparty's responsible officers have passed the fit-and-proper standard the regime requires (para 2.12, p.8).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should understand that Hong Kong's VASP regime originated as professional-investor-only with strict local-presence and fit-and-proper requirements, framing why the bank's VATP counterparties are currently limited in retail reach.

title: Fintech 2025
summary: This is the HKMA's 2021 Fintech 2025 strategy overview, built around five focus areas. These are an 'all banks go fintech' push, future-proofing for central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), and next-generation data infrastructure. The other two are a fintech-skilled workforce, and growing the fintech ecosystem through funding and policy. Most of the extracted text renders as unreadable glyph codes rather than words. Only headings and a few legible fragments could be read, so the bullet-level detail behind each focus area could not be recovered from this copy.

key_points.point: One of the five stated focus areas is future-proofing for central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), aimed at getting the sector ready at both wholesale and retail levels.
Another focus area, 'All banks go fintech', works to drive fintech adoption across the whole banking sector, not just a subset of innovators.
A third focus area is building next-generation data infrastructure, referencing the Commercial Data Interchange as an enabler.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this names CBDC readiness as one of five pillars of the HKMA's mid-2020s fintech strategy. Because the source text is largely unreadable here, a compliance head should treat this summary as a heading-level index only, not a full account.
reading_guide: This extracted copy is not usable for detailed reading; if full content is needed, re-fetch the source PDF with proper font/glyph mapping rather than relying on this text.
flags: text_unavailable

Most of the extracted text consists of unmapped PDF glyph codes (e.g. '/gid00039...') rather than actual words; only slide/section headings and a few standalone lines were legible. Key points and importance here are a best-effort guess from those legible fragments only.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told this strategy names CBDC readiness as a standing HKMA priority, but that a fuller, legible copy of the document should be sourced before relying on any bullet-level detail.

title: HKMA unveils "Fintech 2025" strategy
summary: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), which supervises banks, launched Fintech 2025. This is a five-year plan pushing banks toward full digital adoption. It covers five areas. First, every bank should use financial technology (fintech) everywhere, checked by a new Tech Baseline Assessment. Second, Hong Kong will prepare for central bank digital currencies, including a study on e-HKD, a possible digital Hong Kong dollar. Third, the HKMA will build shared data systems, such as a Commercial Data Interchange and a credit-data platform using distributed ledger technology (DLT). Fourth, the plan aims to grow fintech skills. Fifth, it gives funding and policy support, including a bigger Fintech Supervisory Sandbox for testing new ideas.

key_points.point: HKMA will run a Tech Baseline Assessment of banks' current and planned fintech adoption to identify gaps needing supervisory support.
HKMA will begin a study of e-HKD, a retail central bank digital currency, covering use cases, benefits and risks.
HKMA will build a DLT-based credit data sharing platform and a Commercial Data Interchange to enable consent-based data sharing.
HKMA will enhance its Fintech Supervisory Sandbox and explore funding support for qualifying fintech projects.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this sets the HKMA's five-year direction for fintech, including work on e-HKD and DLT-based data sharing. That work later produced supervisory guidance banks must follow.
reading_guide: Read all five focus-area sections; each is short.

controls_and_monitoring: expect a Tech Baseline Assessment questionnaire/review from HKMA on the bank's fintech adoption
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be briefed that HKMA has set a 2025 target for comprehensive fintech adoption across the sector, with e-HKD and data-sharing infrastructure as named work streams.

title: The HKMA Unveils "Fintech 2025" Strategy
supersedes_or_amends: Smart Banking Era Strategy (2017)
summary: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) unveiled its 'Fintech 2025' strategy, aiming to get Hong Kong's financial sector to broadly adopt financial technology (fintech) by 2025. It has five focus areas. Focus area 1: getting all banks into fintech, including a Tech Baseline Assessment of how far banks have already adopted it. Focus area 2: preparing Hong Kong for central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), including starting a study on e-HKD and continuing wholesale CBDC and e-CNY cross-border testing. Focus area 3: building next-generation data infrastructure, such as a Commercial Data Interchange, digital corporate identity, and credit-data sharing based on distributed ledger technology (DLT). Focus area 4: growing the fintech-skilled workforce. Focus area 5: nurturing the wider ecosystem through a new Fintech Cross-Agency Coordination Group and an upgraded Fintech Supervisory Sandbox.

key_points.point: The HKMA will run a Tech Baseline Assessment to gauge how far banks have adopted fintech and spot areas that need HKMA support.
The HKMA started a study on e-HKD, covering its uses, benefits and risks, alongside CBDC research and cross-border e-CNY testing with the People's Bank of China.
The HKMA will build next-generation data infrastructure, including a Commercial Data Interchange, digital corporate identity, and a DLT-based platform for consent-based credit data sharing.
A new Fintech Cross-Agency Coordination Group will bring together key industry players to shape supportive fintech policy.
The Industry Project Masters Network scheme will pilot in September 2021, giving postgraduate students internships on banks' fintech projects, including federated learning and AI work.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this policy sets the HKMA's expectation that it fully embraces fintech. That includes a future Tech Baseline Assessment, plus CBDC and data-infrastructure work that later shapes the bank's digital-asset plans directly.

quote.text: All banks go fintech

reading_guide: Read in full; short press release covering all five focus areas.
flags: This is the origin point of the e-HKD study referenced in many later HKMA documents -- useful as the earliest dated source for that initiative.

obligations: Take part in the HKMA's Tech Baseline Assessment of the bank's fintech adoption once it is rolled out (Focus area 1, p.1)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Brief the board that the HKMA expects all banks to embrace fintech by 2025, and that this strategy is where the e-HKD study and digital-infrastructure work the bank will be asked to join first began.

title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Opening remarks at HKAB Fintech Seminar: Next Phase of Hong Kong's Fintech Journey – 'Fintech 2025'
summary: This speech by an HKMA Deputy Chief Executive launched the Fintech 2025 strategy. It is a four-part plan to push banks toward full digitalisation, build data infrastructure, grow fintech talent, and expand sandbox funding. One strand covers central bank digital currency (CBDC) work. This includes continuing wholesale CBDC research with the Bank of Thailand, and starting a new study into a retail CBDC for Hong Kong, later named e-HKD. No virtual-asset or stablecoin rules are announced here; the speech is a strategy launch, not a binding instrument.

key_points.point: The HKMA will ask banks to submit a Three-Year technology-adoption Plan within the fourth quarter of 2021, benchmarked against overseas peers.
key_points.locator: para on 'All Banks Go Fintech', untitled

key_points.point: A Regtech Adoption Practice Guides series was announced covering cloud computing, blockchain and anti-money-laundering surveillance.
The HKMA's wholesale CBDC research with the Bank of Thailand had just been expanded to more participating jurisdictions ahead of what later became mBridge.
The HKMA announced it would start a retail CBDC study, working with the BIS Innovation Hub on 'Project Aurum', and aimed to share initial thinking within twelve months.
A Commercial Data Interchange (CDI) was announced to let banks access corporate data with consent, reducing the need for bespoke data-sharing arrangements.

numbers_and_dates.item: Three Year technology Plan submission window
target for initial retail CBDC view

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is a strategy announcement, not a rule, so it creates no direct obligation. It is useful background because it dates the origin of the HKMA's CBDC and e-HKD work, and the Regtech blockchain guidance the bank may later need to reference.
reading_guide: Read the CBDC paragraphs only; skip the fintech-talent and funding sections, which have no digital-asset content.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No action needed; note only that this speech is the origin point of the HKMA's e-HKD and Regtech-blockchain workstreams the board may hear about later.

title: Warning statement on unregulated virtual asset platforms
summary: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) flags that Binance is offering so-called stock tokens elsewhere and worries these could reach Hong Kong investors. No Binance entity holds an SFC licence. The SFC's view is that these tokens are likely to count as securities under Hong Kong law. They track the price of real overseas shares in fractional form. So selling or promoting them here would need a licence or an exemption. It warns that unregulated platforms may not verify that the tokens are genuinely backed, and that investors could struggle to recover money if the platform fails.

key_points.point: No Binance group entity is licensed to carry out any regulated activity in Hong Kong.
Stock tokens track overseas listed share prices and let investors buy fractional exposure.
SFC's view is these tokens are likely securities under the Securities and Futures Ordinance, bringing them under SFC oversight.
Marketing or distributing such tokens toward Hong Kong investors needs an SFC licence unless an exemption applies.
Offering the tokens to the Hong Kong public without SFC authorisation may itself be a criminal offence.
Buyer protections such as voting or dividend rights tied to the underlying share may not be fully explained on unregulated platforms.
Firms planning to offer virtual-asset financial services are told to approach the SFC early to avoid problems later.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this warns that no Binance entity is SFC-licensed. Unlicensed 'stock token' platforms may be operating illegally in Hong Kong. This is relevant mainly as a name to screen out of any client referral, custody or counterparty relationship.

quote.text: no entity in the Binance group is licensed or registered

reading_guide: Read paragraphs 1-5 for the securities-law reasoning; the remaining paragraphs repeat generic investor-caution language.
flags: Early precedent for treating fractional tokenised equities as SFO securities, relevant well beyond this specific platform.

counterparty_due_diligence: Do not treat any Binance-group entity as licensed or registered to conduct regulated activity in Hong Kong; verify licensing status of any platform offering 'stock tokens' before referring clients or transacting (Notes 1-2)
If the bank's RI arm intends to provide any VA-related financial service, notify and discuss with the SFC early per the 1 June 2018 circular referenced here (final para, Note 4)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be alerted that stock-token platforms marketed to Hong Kong investors may be operating illegally, posing reputational/referral risk if the bank's distribution channels touch them.

title: Inthanon-LionRock to mBridge: Building a multi CBDC platform for international payments
supersedes_or_amends: Inthanon-LionRock: Leveraging Distributed Ledger Technology to Increase Efficiency in Cross-Border Payments
summary: This September 2021 report covers the second phase of a joint central bank blockchain project. The project was rebuilt on new technology and expanded beyond the original Thailand-Hong Kong pairing. It records the point when mainland China and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) joined, and the project was renamed mBridge. The upgraded prototype cut cross-border transfer times from days to seconds. It could also lower several cost components tied to using correspondent banks. The group adopted three guiding principles going forward: do no harm to other currencies; comply with each jurisdiction's laws, including anti-money-laundering rules; and stay interoperable with existing systems. The report also describes a new governance structure, with a steering committee and four specialist subcommittees. One subcommittee is dedicated to legal issues and is chaired by the Hong Kong authority. It lists a work plan of legal, policy and technical gaps still to be closed.

key_points.point: The prototype moved from days-long settlement to a matter of seconds and pointed to potential cost savings compared with routing payments through a chain of correspondent banks.
