Mainland China's central bank digital currency institute and the UAE's central bank joined in February 2021. The project was then renamed from Inthanon-LionRock to mBridge and entered a third phase.

The group adopted three guiding principles: not undermining other currencies' monetary control, complying with each jurisdiction's laws (including anti-money-laundering rules), and staying compatible with existing payment systems.
A legal subcommittee, chaired by the Hong Kong authority, coordinates the project's legal paperwork and examines legal and regulatory issues tied to each proposed use case.
The report lists unresolved gaps. These include synchronising currency exchanges across the platform, scaling it up for real transaction volumes, and writing detailed risk-governance procedures.
key_points.locator: s.5 Conclusion and next steps, p.58

key_points.point: The forward work plan explicitly includes building features so the platform meets each jurisdiction's own regulatory and reporting rules, and designing the legal contracts that will govern participation.

numbers_and_dates.value: February 2021 (PBoC's Digital Currency Institute, Central Bank of the UAE)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this report is where the project commits to following local anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing (AML/CFT) law, and sets up a dedicated legal workstream. This is the clearest early sign that a bank later connecting to mBridge would face jurisdiction-specific AML/CFT and legal-certainty requirements, not just a technical integration. It remains background, not a current instrument, since the platform has since moved on to the pilot and later stages covered in later reports.

quote.text: comply with the regulations and laws of the jurisdictions concerned

reading_guide: Read the Executive Summary (p.6-9) and section 4 on governance and roadmap (p.52-58). Skip the detailed technical design chapters on consensus and privacy architecture (roughly p.15-45).
flags: Superseded by the later 2022 pilot report and 2023 update brochure, which describe a more advanced stage of the same project.

counterparty_due_diligence: Note that the project's own legal subcommittee, not just its technology team, was tasked with clearing each jurisdiction's regulatory requirements before go-live, a useful diligence question for any bank later asked to connect.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Historical/background; no current obligation, but worth noting the project's early, explicit AML/CFT compliance commitment if mBridge participation is raised with the board later.

title: Joint research on multiple central bank digital currency (CBDC) shows potential for speeding up cross-border payments and reducing costs
summary: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) published a report on the mBridge project. Partners in the report include the BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre, the Bank of Thailand, mainland China's Digital Currency Institute, and the Central Bank of the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The report, 'Inthanon-LionRock to mBridge: Building a multi CBDC platform for international payments', presents interim findings. The enhanced prototype can manage central bank digital currency (CBDC) liquidity, monitor flows and balances, enhance transaction privacy, and automate compliance functions. It has the potential to substantially speed up cross-border transfers and cut their cost, compared with using correspondent banks.

key_points.point: The report presents interim findings of the mBridge project, building on the prior cross-border corridor network prototype to support more currencies and interface with domestic payment systems.
The enhanced prototype can manage CBDC liquidity, monitor CBDC flows/balances, enhance transaction privacy, and automate certain compliance functions for participating central banks.
The prototype, compared with today's correspondent banking model, has the potential to cut cross-border transfer times sharply and lower their cost.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Informational for a compliance head tracking the mBridge cross-border CBDC initiative; it reports interim technical findings and creates no bank obligation, control requirement, or filing duty.

quote.text: substantially speed up cross-border transfers and reduce their costs

reading_guide: Short press release; read in full, then see the attached full report for detail.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No action needed; informational update on mBridge's technical progress for awareness only.

title: e-HKD: A technical perspective – Request for Comments
summary: This is a technical discussion paper, prepared with the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Innovation Hub. It explores possible designs for a Hong Kong retail central bank digital currency (e-HKD). The paper is part of a wider e-HKD feasibility study, alongside a separate legal and policy study. It proposes a two-tier model: the central bank issues and redeems e-HKD at a wholesale layer, while commercial banks distribute it at a retail layer. It also sets out seven open research problems: privacy, interoperability, performance, cybersecurity, compliance, operational resilience, and technology-enabled features. The paper states the design is not a blueprint or a decision on e-HKD, only a basis for further dialogue. It invited written comments by 31 December 2021.

key_points.point: The HKMA's CBDC research runs on two tracks: wholesale CBDC work that became Project mBridge, and this separate retail CBDC (e-HKD) track begun in June 2021.

The paper proposes a two-tier architecture. A wholesale system is where the central bank issues and redeems e-HKD. A retail system is where commercial banks distribute and circulate it, or a CBDC-backed e-money form.
The design is explicitly not a blueprint for e-HKD and does not represent a decision on which distribution model will be used.

Seven open problem statements are listed for public comment: privacy, interoperability, performance/scalability, cybersecurity, compliance, operational resilience, and technology-enabled functional capabilities.
Comments on the proposed architecture, including security modelling and new use-case ideas, were invited by email by 31 December 2021.
The compliance problem statement specifically calls for exploring how computing methods can support AML/CFT regulatory compliance goals within an e-HKD system.

The paper's safety design principles state that a CBDC system should be compliance-friendly. This means supporting compliance with anti-money-laundering, counter-terrorist-financing (AML/CFT) and sanctions rules, though full technology-enforced traceability is not a fixed requirement.
Onboarding of retail e-HKD users would need to fulfil KYC/AML rules, and pre-registration is described as desirable to support that compliance.
The paper builds on the BIS Innovation Hub's Project Aurum, which is separately developing a basic prototype implementing parts of the architecture described here.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is a non-binding, now-superseded technical research paper. It shows the HKMA's early thinking that any future e-HKD design would still require banks to run standard KYC/AML onboarding. It would also preserve some transaction traceability for compliance purposes. This is relevant background if the bank's payments or treasury teams engage with later e-HKD pilots.

quote.text: not a blueprint for e-HKD

reading_guide: Read the Executive Summary (p.1-4) and Table 1's seven problem statements in full. The detailed architecture sections (5.1-5.7, p.20-38) and preliminary technical analysis (s.6, p.38-42) can be skimmed unless doing deep technical due diligence.
flags: This 2021 discussion paper has been superseded by later, more concrete HKMA e-HKD work (e.g. the e-HKD Pilot Programme, id 977029967c18); it is retained here as historical/technical background, not current policy

controls_and_monitoring: Note that any future e-HKD retail distribution model considered here would require banks, as retail-layer distributors, to run KYC/AML onboarding and support some transaction traceability (p.18, p.27).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No current action; this is superseded research, useful only as background if e-HKD reaches a later concrete design stage.

title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Technical Whitepaper on Retail Central Bank Digital Currency
summary: This short press release announces publication of the HKMA's first technical whitepaper on a possible retail central bank digital currency (e-HKD), prepared jointly with the BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre. It describes the whitepaper as exploring technical design options, including a privacy-preserving traceability approach. It also invites comment from academia and industry. It sets a target of an initial HKMA view on e-HKD feasibility by mid-2022. The full technical content is in the attached whitepaper, summarised separately.

key_points.point: The whitepaper is described as the first of its kind among central banks to include a technical design allowing transaction traceability while preserving user privacy.
The HKMA aims to form an initial view on the feasibility of issuing e-HKD by around mid-2022.
The HKMA invites academia and industry to comment on unresolved problem statements identified in the whitepaper.

numbers_and_dates.item: target date for HKMA's initial e-HKD feasibility view

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is only an announcement of a research paper open for comment, not a rule. It flags that e-HKD design work was already under way from October 2021. This work could eventually affect the retail payment infrastructure the bank relies on.
reading_guide: This press release is a two-paragraph summary; read the attached whitepaper (id 59a20457a2fc) for substance.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No board action needed for this announcement alone.

title: Statements issued by the Financial Action Task Force
summary: This is a routine HKMA relay of the latest Financial Action Task Force (FATF) lists of high-risk and increased-monitoring jurisdictions, and plenary outcomes. It tells banks to keep applying enhanced due diligence to Iran and North Korea, and to note the updated monitored-jurisdictions list. It also flags that in October 2021 the FATF issued revised risk-based guidance on virtual assets (VA) and virtual asset service providers (VASPs). This guidance covers how the FATF's rules apply to banks engaging in VA activity.

key_points.point: Banks should keep applying enhanced due diligence and countermeasures to business with Iran and North Korea.
Banks should note the FATF's updated list of jurisdictions under increased monitoring, published on the FATF website.
The FATF issued an updated risk-based-approach guidance for virtual assets and VASPs that also applies to banks engaging in VA activity.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Routine sanctions-list relay; relevant to the AML programme generally but not crypto-specific except where it flags a VA/VASP-related FATF workstream, noted below.

quote.text: Updated Guidance for a Risk-Based Approach to Virtual Assets

reading_guide: Skim; the substantive content is the same FATF list update each cycle, only the VA/VASP-specific paragraph (where present) is new.

obligations: Apply enhanced due diligence/countermeasures to Iran and DPRK-linked business, p.1
controls_and_monitoring: Update sanctions/high-risk-jurisdiction screening lists per the FATF statement, p.1
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No board escalation needed for a routine list relay unless a new jurisdiction directly affects the bank's book.

title: Fintech: Metamorphosis of the financial industry - Keynote address at Hong Kong FinTech Week 2021 (Julia Leung)
summary: SFC Deputy CEO Julia Leung reviewed three years of the Securities and Futures Commission's (SFC's) virtual-asset regulatory journey and previewed change. She confirmed the government had by then decided to amend anti-money laundering law to make licensing mandatory for all centralised virtual-asset (VA) trading platforms. She described growing bank and broker interest in offering virtual assets to private-bank and professional-investor clients. This interest often came via introducing-agent or omnibus arrangements. She said the SFC was reviewing its VA regime with the HKMA, expecting to issue a joint circular. She flagged unresolved questions on whether platform-style obligations, like knowledge assessments, should extend to intermediaries who merely introduce clients to VA platforms.

key_points.point: The SFC and HKMA were jointly reviewing the VA regulatory regime and expected to issue a joint circular.

The SFC was considering whether firms using introducing-agent or omnibus-account arrangements to give clients access to VA platforms should face similar obligations to licensed VA trading platforms. This includes client knowledge assessments.
The mandatory AMLO-based VATP licensing regime the government had proposed in late 2020 was confirmed as the direction of travel.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this speech directly foreshadows the joint SFC/HKMA circular on intermediaries' VA-related activities that followed in January 2022. It flags that using an omnibus or introducing-agent structure to access VA platforms does not automatically avoid platform-style compliance obligations.

quote.text: same business, same risks and same rules

reading_guide: Read pages 3-5 (from 'The changing regulatory landscape' onward) for substantive content; the opening butterfly metaphor (pages 1-2) can be skipped.

controls_and_monitoring: anticipate that introducing-agent or omnibus-account access to VA platforms may attract platform-style obligations, including client knowledge assessment requirements
counterparty_due_diligence: for any VA platform accessed via omnibus/introducing-agent arrangement, check whether the platform itself is SFC-licensed
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told a joint SFC/HKMA circular on banks' and brokers' VA-related activities was imminent as of Nov 2021 (issued Jan 2022) and may change omnibus/introducing-agent practice.

title: mBridge - Building a multi CBDC platform for international payments
summary: This is a brochure describing the mBridge project. It is a multi-jurisdiction wholesale central bank digital currency (CBDC) platform. It involves the central banks of Hong Kong, mainland China, Thailand and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), supported by the BIS Innovation Hub. It lists 15 private-sector business use cases identified with 22 participating financial institutions, spanning trade settlement, tokenised bond issuance, foreign-exchange (FX) transactions, and wealth-connect settlement. It reports early trial figures on international trade settlement testing. It also sets out a step-by-step roadmap from pilot toward a production-ready platform from 2022 onward.

key_points.point: mBridge is a collaboration among the central banks of Hong Kong, mainland China, Thailand and the UAE, supported by the BIS Innovation Hub. It tests whether CBDCs can speed up cross-border payments and cut their cost.

Twenty-two private-sector participants across the four jurisdictions -- 19 financial institutions, two banking associations and one exchange -- identified 15 potential business use cases for the platform.

Named participants proposing use cases included Bank of China (Hong Kong), DBS Bank (Hong Kong), Goldman Sachs (Asia), HKEX, HSBC, Societe Generale-FORGE, Standard Chartered, and UBS. Their use cases covered tokenised bond settlement, programmable trade finance, and FX derivatives settlement.

Test transactions on the trial platform for international trade settlement covered four jurisdictions and 11 industries. The combined tested value included 10 billion Thai baht, 1 billion RMB, 2 billion Hong Kong dollars (HKD) and 2 billion UAE dirhams (AED).

The roadmap moves from the 2019 Inthanon-LionRock proof-of-concept, through the Q4 2021 mBridge trial platform. It then moves to a pilot minimum viable product and a production-ready system from 2022 onward.
Implementation considerations flagged for the next phase include a minimum viable legal framework, legal governance, and policy and regulatory compliance requirements.

numbers_and_dates.value: 22 private-sector participants (19 FIs, 2 banking associations, 1 exchange)
mBridge Trial Platform, moving to pilot MVP then production-ready from 2022 onward

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, several major banks it may compete with or partner with were early mBridge participants. This brochure gives useful context on cross-border CBDC settlement infrastructure. That infrastructure could eventually intersect with the bank's own payments and trade-finance business, though nothing here creates an obligation.
reading_guide: Read pages 2-3 for the platform overview and page 7 for the roadmap. The use-case list on pages 4-5 can be skimmed for named participants only.

counterparty_due_diligence: If considering participation in mBridge-linked use cases, check which banks are already involved (p.4-5) and what legal/regulatory compliance framework the next roadmap phase requires (p.7).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Background only; note for the board that peer banks are already testing mBridge use cases in tokenised settlement and trade finance.

title: Enhanced Competency Framework on Fintech | Enclosure: Guide to Enhanced Competency Framework on Fintech
summary: The HKMA's catalogue entry for its Enhanced Competency Framework (ECF) on Fintech, a training and qualification standard for bank staff working in fintech roles. The attached guide sets learning outcomes across professional tracks, including a specialist Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) stream that covers DLT architecture, digital tokens, smart contracts and DLT security and oversight. It is a workforce-competency scheme, not a product or risk-management rule.

key_points.point: The ECF on Fintech includes a specialist Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) track. It covers DLT architecture and design, digital tokens and smart contracts, and DLT security and oversight.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Not a compliance obligation for the bank itself, but useful for planning staff training and assessing whether crypto-facing teams hold the recognised DLT competency qualification.
reading_guide: Skip most of the document (general competency tracks unrelated to crypto); the only DLT-relevant section is Module 7 at p.35.

title: Discussion Paper on Crypto-assets and Stablecoins
summary: The HKMA set out its early thinking on regulating crypto-assets, in particular payment-related stablecoins, and invited industry feedback by 31 March 2022. Payment-related stablecoins are pegged to a fiat currency and likely to be used for payments. The paper explained why these pose distinct monetary, financial-stability, settlement and user-protection risks compared with other crypto-assets. It proposed that any entity carrying out core stablecoin functions be licensed by the HKMA. Core functions include issuance and redemption, reserve management, key custody, transaction validation, or fund transmission. A licensed entity would need to be incorporated in Hong Kong; a branch would not qualify. It would also need to meet prudential, governance, anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing (AML/CFT) and disclosure requirements. The HKMA targeted introducing the new regime no later than 2023/24. It confirmed it would issue separate guidance to banks on their crypto-asset customer interface, separately from this paper. This paper is the direct forerunner of Hong Kong's stablecoin issuer licensing regime under the Stablecoins Ordinance.

key_points.point: HKMA proposed to prioritise regulating payment-related, asset-linked stablecoins pegged to a single fiat currency, over algorithm-based stablecoins, at the initial stage. It planned to keep flexibility to expand scope later.

Seven categories of stablecoin-related activity were proposed for licensing: issuing/destroying stablecoins, managing backing reserves, validating transactions, storing private keys, facilitating redemption, transmitting funds, and executing transactions.

Any entity carrying out a licensable stablecoin activity in or targeting Hong Kong must be a Hong Kong-incorporated entity holding an HKMA licence. A mere branch or office of a foreign company would not qualify.

Proposed requirements for licensed stablecoin arrangements include authorisation, prudential capital and liquidity rules, and fit-and-proper checks on controllers and management. They also include reserve adequacy, legal clarity of holder claims, sound risk management (including anti-money-laundering controls), redemption robustness, and disclosure to regulators and users.

The existing proposed VASP licensing regime for VA exchanges does not cover most core stablecoin functions, like issuance, redemption, custody and reserve management. This leaves a regulatory gap that this paper aims to fill.
HKMA aimed to introduce the new stablecoin licensing regime no later than 2023/24.

Banks distributing VA funds not authorised by the SFC should target only professional investors, assess client VA knowledge, ensure suitability, and give prominent risk warnings. This follows the SFC's November 2018 circular referenced here.
AIs intending to provide VA-related investment services must notify HKMA and SFC in advance.

title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Eddie Yue on Crypto-assets and stablecoins
summary: In this article, the HKMA's Chief Executive sets out the HKMA's three-pronged approach to crypto-assets. The three prongs are: regulating payment-related stablecoins, protecting investors dealing in crypto-assets, and managing how Authorized Institutions (AIs, meaning banks) interface with crypto-asset service providers. The article announces same-day publication of a Discussion Paper on Crypto-assets and Stablecoins, open for comment until 31 March 2022, targeting a new stablecoin regime no later than 2023/24. It also flags that the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) are jointly developing supervisory expectations on AIs' crypto-related intermediary services. A circular giving detailed guidance on AIs' crypto exposure will follow.

key_points.point: The HKMA adopts a 'same risk, same regulation' principle: entities and activities are regulated based on the function performed and risk posed, not the technology label used.
A Discussion Paper on Crypto-assets and Stablecoins was issued the same day. It invited stakeholder feedback by 31 March 2022, targeting a new payment-related stablecoin regime no later than 2023/24.

The HKMA is reviewing whether to adjust the existing regulatory framework, including the Payment Systems and Stored Value Facilities Ordinance. The goal is to capture payment-related stablecoins and their wallets, which can function similarly to stored value facilities.
The HKMA and the SFC are jointly working on supervisory expectations for AIs' provision of intermediary services related to crypto-assets, aimed at investor protection.

The HKMA states it will soon issue a circular giving detailed guidance on AIs' business interface with crypto-assets. This will cover user protection, credit, market, operational, financial-crime and prudential risk.

title: Regulatory approaches to Authorized Institutions' interface with Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers
summary: This is the HKMA's core policy circular on banks' interface with virtual assets (VAs) and virtual asset service providers (VASPs). It is organised around three pillars: prudential supervision, anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing (AML/CFT) and financial crime, and investor protection. The HKMA says it does not currently intend to stop banks taking financial exposure to VAs, provided risk controls and senior-management oversight are adequate. But it expects proper due diligence, prudent exposure limits, conservative loan-to-value ratios on VA collateral, and capital set aside for residual risk. It requires banks to discuss any VA activity with the HKMA and get feedback on their risk controls before launch. It also references the same-day joint circular on intermediaries' VA-related activities for investor-protection detail.

key_points.point: The HKMA does not currently plan to stop banks taking financial exposure to virtual assets. This is conditional on banks having adequate risk-management controls and senior-management oversight.
Banks should carry out proper due diligence on any virtual asset they gain exposure to. This includes its legal and technical structure, and the background of the parties running it.
Banks should set prudent limits on their overall virtual-asset exposure and use conservative loan-to-value ratios when accepting virtual assets as loan collateral.
Where residual risk remains after mitigation, banks should hold sufficient capital against their virtual-asset exposures.

Banks should watch for customers who transfer funds frequently to or from virtual-asset platforms. They should lodge a report with the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit whenever the pattern looks suspicious.

When banking a VASP, banks should assess the risk of that specific VASP. This includes its business model, licensing status and AML/CFT controls. Banks should apply due diligence like that used for correspondent banking relationships.
Investment products linked to virtual assets are considered complex products because retail investors are unlikely to understand their risks, and additional investor-protection measures apply.
A bank intending to engage in any virtual-asset activity should discuss it with the HKMA first. It should get feedback on the adequacy of its risk controls before launching the product or service.

title: Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
supersedes_or_amends: Circular to intermediaries on the distribution of virtual asset funds (1 November 2018)
summary: This is the joint SFC/HKMA circular updating investor-protection rules for intermediaries distributing virtual-asset (VA) products, offering VA dealing services, or giving VA advice. VA-related products are treated as complex products and generally restricted to professional investors. Other clients need a mandatory virtual-asset knowledge test, except for a narrow set of exchange-traded VA derivatives on specified exchanges in designated jurisdictions. Intermediaries providing VA dealing services may only partner with SFC-licensed VA trading platforms. They must keep client fiat currency and virtual-asset holdings segregated, and must not offer any financing to buy virtual assets. A six-month transition period applied from the circular's date. Intermediaries must notify the SFC, and the HKMA where relevant, before starting VA-related activities.

key_points.point: VA-related products are normally complex products and, other than a limited set of exchange-traded derivatives, should only be sold to professional investors.

Before letting most clients trade a VA-related product, an intermediary should first check the client understands virtual assets. It should offer training if the client doesn't already have that knowledge.
An intermediary should be cautious about lending money to clients to invest in virtual-asset products. It must be satisfied the client can meet the obligations even in a worst case.
Intermediaries providing virtual-asset dealing services may only partner with SFC-licensed virtual-asset trading platforms and must serve professional investors only.
Clients may only deposit or withdraw fiat currency, never virtual assets directly, from accounts used for VA dealing services.
An intermediary offering discretionary account management that intends to invest 10% or more of a portfolio in virtual assets must follow the additional RA9 terms and conditions.
Intermediaries already doing VA-related business get a six-month transition period to update systems and controls before the new requirements fully apply.
An intermediary must tell the SFC (and the HKMA where relevant) in advance if it intends to start VA-related activities.

title: Appendix 1 - 6 to the Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
summary: These are the six technical appendices to the joint SFC/HKMA circular on intermediaries' virtual-asset activities. Appendix 1 covers criteria for judging whether a client has virtual-asset knowledge. Appendix 2 lists designated jurisdictions for exchange-traded VA derivative funds. Appendix 3 is a decision flowchart for whether a VA product counts as complex. Appendix 4 is an extra due-diligence checklist for unauthorised VA funds. Appendix 5 gives example client warning statements. Appendix 6 sets full licensing and registration terms and conditions for VA dealing (omnibus account) and VA advisory services. It covers client agreements, disclosure, custody of client assets, record-keeping, auditors, AML/CFT and ongoing reporting.

key_points.point: A client counts as having virtual-asset knowledge if they have executed five or more virtual-asset transactions in the past three years, or have relevant training or work experience.

The professional-investor-only rule does not apply to VA derivative funds that are exchange-traded and dealt on specified exchanges. These funds must also be authorised in one of twelve listed jurisdictions, including the UK, US and Switzerland.

Distributing an unauthorised virtual-asset fund requires extra due diligence on the fund manager, the fund itself, and the fund's counterparties. This includes checking cold/hot storage allocation policy and counterparties' insurance coverage.

An intermediary offering VA dealing services under an omnibus account must hold client virtual assets on trust, in a segregated account with the SFC-licensed platform. It must restrict access to authorised personnel only.
An intermediary must maintain at least 12 months of operating expenses in excess liquid capital in Hong Kong, on a rolling basis, to provide VA dealing services.
An intermediary must not provide financial accommodation for clients to acquire virtual assets and should try to ensure no group company does so either.
An intermediary must not run virtual-asset market-making activity on the same SFC-licensed platform it uses to serve its own VA dealing clients.
Records related to VA dealing activities generally must be kept for at least seven years, with some records (contract notes, receipts, order records) kept for at least two years.
Records related to VA dealing activities generally must be kept for at least seven years. Some records, such as contract notes, receipts and order records, must be kept for at least two years.
The intermediary must fully disclose to clients that virtual assets are not protected by the Investor Compensation Fund and that transactions may be irreversible.

title: Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
supersedes_or_amends: Circular to intermediaries on the distribution of virtual asset funds, 1 November 2018
summary: This joint SFC/HKMA circular updates guidance for intermediaries wishing to distribute virtual asset (VA)-related products, or provide VA dealing or advisory services. It replaces the 2018 professional-investors-only restriction with a more detailed regime. Most VA-related products remain restricted to professional investors as complex products. So may authorised exchange-traded funds (ETFs) in designated jurisdictions, subject to a VA-knowledge test and derivative-product requirements. It also sets conduct requirements for VA dealing services, which are only via SFC-licensed platforms and for Type 1 clients only. The same applies to VA advisory services, for Type 1/Type 4 clients who are professional investors only. A six-month transition period applied. Appendix 6 sets detailed licensing and registration terms and conditions.

A client is deemed to have VA knowledge if they have executed five or more VA transactions in the past three years.

title: LCQ10: Trading of digital assets
summary: This is a Legislative Council written reply covering NFTs and virtual-asset crime trends. It confirms government plans for a mandatory virtual-asset service provider (VASP) licensing regime under the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (AMLO). This was targeted for introduction to LegCo in Q2 2022. It reports sharply rising police-recorded VA-related crime: 360 cases in 2019, 494 in 2020, and 1,397 in 2021. It confirms the HKMA's January 2022 discussion paper on stablecoins. It also explains that NFTs are not separately defined, but are assessed case-by-case against the FATF's functional virtual-asset definition.

HKMA issued a discussion paper on crypto-currencies and payment-related stablecoins in January 2022 inviting industry and public views.

Whether a given NFT falls under the proposed VASP licensing definition of virtual asset depends on its specific terms and characteristics. It applies the FATF's functional test rather than a blanket rule.
Closed-loop, non-transferable tokens such as airline miles or credit-card rewards, and central bank digital currency, are proposed to be excluded from the VA definition.

title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Eddie Yue on Four essential Q&As for e-HKD
summary: This article, by the HKMA's Chief Executive, explains in question-and-answer form why the HKMA is studying a retail central bank digital currency (e-HKD), beyond the earlier technical whitepaper. title: e-HKD: A Policy and Design Perspective
summary: This HKMA discussion paper sets out the policy and design issues in introducing e-HKD, a retail central bank digital currency. It weighs benefits, such as more usable central bank money and readiness against stablecoins, against challenges such as bank funding disintermediation, cyber risk, and reliance on power and networks. It sets out design choices, including issuance mechanism, interoperability, privacy and legal treatment. It states three possible issuance routes, with the HKMA leaning toward a 'Coins approach' run through agent banks. It stresses that no decision has yet been made on whether or when to launch e-HKD, and lists twelve questions for public and industry comment.

key_points.point: e-HKD would be fully backed by USD assets in the Exchange Fund under the Currency Board system, just like existing Hong Kong dollar cash.

If deposits shift into e-HKD at scale, banks could face higher funding costs or reduced lending capacity. But the HKMA judges the bank-run risk from e-HKD to be very low, given the Deposit Protection Scheme and prudential oversight.
Safeguards such as maximum e-HKD account balances and daily conversion or transaction limits are being considered to manage the risk of deposits moving out of banks.

HKMA favours the 'Coins approach'. Designated agent banks submit USD to HKMA in exchange for e-HKD, then distribute it to customers. This is favoured over a banknote-style or Aggregate-Balance-based issuance route.
e-HKD needs to meet the requirements of the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance. Complete anonymity is not an option, since e-HKD has to support AML/CFT compliance.
HKMA envisages a tiered wallet design giving more anonymity to low-value holdings and more traceability to higher-value ones, similar to other central banks' approaches.
Financial institutions distributing e-HKD would likely be tasked with customer due diligence and record-keeping under a two-tier distribution structure.
A review of existing ordinances, including the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance, would be needed. This would give e-HKD a clear legal-tender and AML footing.

Smart-contract programmability of e-HKD is being considered, but carries risks from coding bugs and unreliable external data feeds (oracles). HKMA leans toward building programmability into wallets, rather than into e-HKD itself.
No cybersecurity study of the e-HKD distribution infrastructure had been done as of this paper. HKMA says a rigorous assessment, for example using the STRIDE framework, would be needed.
HKMA had not yet decided whether or when to introduce e-HKD; comments on twelve discussion questions were invited by 27 May 2022

title: SFC reminds investors of risks associated with non-fungible tokens
summary: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) warned investors about non-fungible token (NFT) risks. NFTs can be hard to sell, prices can swing wildly, pricing is often unclear, and there is a risk of hacking and fraud. The SFC says an ordinary collectible NFT usually falls outside its rules. But an NFT split into tradeable pieces that acts like a security, or that gives investors a stake in a collective investment scheme (CIS), can trigger SFC licensing and authorisation duties.

key_points.point: A genuine collectible NFT -- one representing a unique image, artwork, song or video -- generally falls outside SFC rules.
NFTs split into tradable fungible pieces resembling securities, or that give investors a stake in a CIS, can bring the marketing or sale of them under SFC licensing rules.
Offering Hong Kong's public a chance to invest in a CIS through an NFT structure may need SFC authorisation under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO).

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this sets the SFC's test for when an NFT-linked product it might sell or design counts as a regulated security. Is it a genuine collectible, or does it act like a security or a CIS stake?

summary: This is the full SFC report behind its 31 August 2022 circular on online brokerage, distribution and advisory platforms. Among the gaps, it names one licensed corporation that sold virtual asset (VA)-related products, traded on overseas over-the-counter (OTC) markets, to retail investors through its online platform. It did this without meeting the required investor-protection safeguards: the selling limits and the VA-knowledge check set out in the 2022 joint VA circular.

Firms distributing VA-related products must apply the extra investor-protection measures set out in the joint VA circular. These include selling restrictions and a knowledge test, because retail investors are unlikely to understand VA risks.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is a documented SFC finding that shows exactly how a firm breached the VA Circular's retail-selling restriction in practice: an overseas OTC venue, with no knowledge test. It is a concrete negative example for the bank's own control-testing scripts.

reading_guide: The report is long and covers many product types. The only VA-specific passage is paragraph 19 on page 16 (a failure to follow selling restrictions and other regulatory requirements). Skim the rest for general online-platform context.
flags: Concrete finding of a retail-facing VA product sold without required investor-protection safeguards — useful precedent for what NOT to replicate.

controls_and_monitoring: Test that any VA-related product distribution complies with the VA Circular's selling restrictions and knowledge-test requirement before allowing retail access, even via overseas OTC-linked products, para 19
counterparty_due_diligence: When products reference overseas OTC virtual-asset markets, verify the offering complies with Hong Kong selling restrictions before distribution, para 19
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Flag this finding as a control-testing benchmark: the bank should confirm its own platforms cannot expose retail clients to VA-related products via overseas OTC venues without the mandated safeguards.

title: e-HKD - Charting the Next Steps
summary: This is the full HKMA position paper following two rounds of e-HKD market consultation (75 responses in total). It sums up the feedback (Annexes 1-2) and sets out the HKMA's three-track plan for getting ready in case e-HKD is eventually launched. Rail 1 builds the technology, starting with the wholesale layer, and identifies which legal changes are required for legal-tender status. Rail 2 runs deep-dive research and pilots, including Project Sela, e-wallet access pilots, and settling tokenised securities. Rail 3 covers an eventual launch, timed to how Rails 1 and 2 progress. The HKMA says e-HKD's usual reasons, such as financial inclusion, competition and resilience, matter less for Hong Kong. Its payment market is already diverse, unlike places that have launched a retail CBDC (Bahamas, Nigeria) or piloted one (China, Eastern Caribbean).

key_points.point: Rail 1 will first build the wholesale interbank layer, expected to take at least 2-3 years to reach production grade, subject to resources. The retail layer design comes after, since it may change based on further deliberation.
Early legal analysis found the current laws would not give enough certainty to support issuing a digital version of legal tender; changing the legislation would be needed.
The HKMA is inclined to give e-HKD legal tender status. By law this would make it valid for paying a debt unless otherwise agreed, but merchants could not be forced to accept it, just as with cash.

Of the retail CBDCs launched worldwide so far, only the Bahamas' Sand Dollar and Nigeria's eNaira were actually up and running. Mainland China's e-CNY and the Eastern Caribbean's DCash remained at pilot stage.

Consultation respondents generally favoured a two-tier distribution model, an unremunerated e-HKD, offline payment support, and cross-border interoperability (including potential e-HKD/e-CNY convertibility).
Rail 2 pipeline includes Project Sela (cybersecurity), e-wallet app access pilots, DvP settlement of tokenised securities, and studying CBDC as an on/off-ramp for DeFi.
A tiered-account structure (different transaction/holding limits and anonymity levels based on KYC level) was broadly supported by respondents to balance privacy and AML/CFT compliance.

numbers_and_dates.value: 75 (36 to technical whitepaper, 39 to policy discussion paper)
at least 2-3 years to production grade

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, no binding rule attaches yet. But a compliance head should track this roadmap for early sight of possible bank participation, such as Project Sela or settlement pilots. It should also track the legislative-amendment step that will eventually create e-HKD-specific duties.

quote.text: necessary to at least start paving the way for possible future implementation of e-HKD

reading_guide: Read 'Charting the next steps' (p.8-12) in full for the three-rail plan. Skim Annexes 1-2 (consultation feedback tables) for stakeholder positions relevant to the bank's own submission strategy.
flags: Correction to assumption: HKMA explicitly states rCBDC drivers common elsewhere (financial inclusion, competition, resilience) are assessed as less relevant to Hong Kong -- this is not a straightforward 'me-too' CBDC project.
Notes existing HK legislation is NOT adequate for issuing legal-tender digital currency -- legislative change is a prerequisite, not just a technical build.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should hear that e-HKD is a multi-year, wholesale-first roadmap (2-3 years to a production-grade wholesale layer) still awaiting legislative amendment, so no near-term compliance obligation attaches, though Rail 2 pilots may invite bank participation (Rail 1-2 sections, p.9,11).

title: HKMA's policy stance on e-HKD

title: Project mBridge: Connecting economies through CBDC
supersedes_or_amends: Inthanon-LionRock to mBridge: Building a multi CBDC platform for international payments
summary: This BIS-authored report, dated October 2022, covers the first real-value pilot of mBridge, a shared blockchain platform letting four central banks issue their own digital currencies for cross-border settlement. Twenty commercial banks from Hong Kong, mainland China, Thailand and the UAE took part over six weeks in mid-2022. They moved over US$12 million of digital currency and settled more than 160 payment and foreign-exchange trades for corporate clients. The report explains how the platform keeps transaction details private, except to the two counterparties and their central banks. It describes the legal contracts used to give the pilot legal certainty, and sets out where each participant's own bank ran its anti-money-laundering and sanctions checks. A dedicated section covers unresolved legal questions, including how to classify the digital currency itself and who should run the platform, based on external legal advice the project team got.

key_points.point: In a six-week live pilot from mid-August to late September 2022, twenty commercial banks issued over US$12 million of digital currency onto the platform. They settled more than 160 payment and foreign-exchange trades worth over US$22 million for their corporate clients.

Before the pilot, participants signed three sets of legal documents. One covered each central bank's role, one set platform-wide rules, including when a payment counts as final, and one covered each digital currency's own terms of use.

Every payment on the platform required each bank to carry out its own anti-money-laundering, counter-terrorist-financing and sanctions screening before sending or confirming a transaction. The platform itself does not run these checks.

Sensitive transaction details, such as the identities of payer and payee and the amount, are visible only to the two transacting banks and their own central banks. Other participating central banks or banks cannot see them.

The pilot deliberately excluded certain transaction types, such as domestic payments in a foreign digital currency. This was because of the risk that a jurisdiction's own currency could be displaced, or its monetary-policy control weakened.
key_points.locator: s.7.1.2 Foreign and domestic use of CBDC, p.32

key_points.point: External legal counsel reviewed over 200 pages of analysis across four jurisdictions on unresolved questions. These include whether the digital currency should count as currency, a claim on the central bank, or a form of debt.
key_points.locator: s.7.2 Legal and regulatory considerations, p.34

key_points.point: Only banks that are domestically licensed in a given jurisdiction may request new issuance or redemption of that jurisdiction's digital currency. Foreign banks can hold and transact in it, but not create or redeem it directly.
key_points.locator: s.7.1.1 Measures to preserve monetary sovereignty, p.31-32

key_points.point: Fewer currency-exchange trades took place than simple one-way payments during the pilot, partly because pricing for currency exchange happened off the platform beforehand, adding time and complexity to each trade.

The pilot ran on a single, centralised cloud environment hosted in Hong Kong for simplicity. The project team flagged this as a data-privacy and governance point still to be revisited before wider rollout.
key_points.locator: s.7.1.3 Data privacy and governance, p.33

numbers_and_dates.value: 20, from Hong Kong, Mainland China, Thailand, UAE

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the clearest evidence that mBridge, even at pilot stage, put screening duties on each bank itself, not on the platform. This covers anti-money-laundering (AML), counter-terrorist-financing (CTF) and sanctions screening. That is exactly the control gap a bank's compliance function would need to confirm and own before any live use. If the bank is ever asked to connect to mBridge or a successor platform, this report is the primary source for what to expect. It covers the legal paperwork, screening duties and data-visibility limits.

quote.text: conducts the appropriate off-bridge compliance checks, including AML/CTF/sanctions checks

reading_guide: Read the Executive Summary (p.4-5), section 5.4 Key lessons (p.22) and all of section 7, Policy, legal and regulatory considerations (p.31-34). The technical chapters on consensus algorithms (p.24-30) can be skimmed.
flags: AML/CTF and sanctions checks are performed off-platform by each bank, not built into the platform itself — a point compliance teams should not assume is otherwise.

controls_and_monitoring: Any bank connecting to mBridge or a similar multi-CBDC platform would need to run its own AML/CTF and sanctions screening before every payment, since the platform performs none of this itself (s.6.5.2, p.30).
Confirm which counterparties and central banks can see a given transaction's payer/payee identity and amount before assuming confidentiality of client information (s.6.4, p.28).
counterparty_due_diligence: Check whether a prospective platform participant has signed equivalent platform operating terms and issuance/redemption terms to those used in the mBridge pilot, since these establish when a payment is legally final (s.5.1, p.16).

Ask what legal categorisation (currency, claim, debt-like instrument) a jurisdiction has given its digital currency, as this affects how the bank should book and risk-weight any holding (s.7.2, p.34).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board should hear that multi-CBDC platforms like mBridge push AML/CFT and sanctions screening obligations onto each participating bank rather than the platform, so joining one is a compliance resourcing decision, not just a technology one.

title: The Chief Executive's 2022 Policy Address
summary: The 2022 Policy Address is the Chief Executive's annual wide-ranging policy statement. Only one paragraph, in the International Financial Centre section, deals with digital assets. It confirms the Government had already tabled a bill to bring virtual asset service providers under a legally binding licensing regime. It also confirms the HKMA was reviewing market feedback on stablecoin regulation, aiming to align the eventual regime with international standards and local conditions. Separately, it confirms the HKMA had begun preparatory work on issuing e-HKD, and was working with Mainland institutions on cross-boundary testing of e-CNY. This paragraph is a high-level government commitment, not a technical rulebook.

key_points.point: The Government had tabled a bill that would bring virtual asset service providers under a legally binding licensing system.
The HKMA was examining market feedback on stablecoin regulation and intended to align the eventual regime with international recommendations and Hong Kong's local context.
The HKMA had begun preparatory work on issuing e-HKD and was working with Mainland institutions to expand cross-boundary testing of e-CNY in Hong Kong.

It gives compliance functions an official basis to start planning for both regimes ahead of their formal launch.

quote.text: examining market feedback on the regulation of stablecoins

title: Project mBridge: Successful CBDC project for real-value cross-border payment and foreign exchange transactions
summary: The HKMA published 'Project mBridge: Connecting economies through CBDC', together with the BIS Innovation Hub (BISIH) Hong Kong Centre. Other partners were the Bank of Thailand, the People's Bank of China's (PBoC) Digital Currency Institute, and the Central Bank of the UAE. It reports on a six-week trial moving real value across borders using central bank digital currencies (CBDCs). Twenty banks across four jurisdictions ran more than 160 payment and foreign-exchange (FX) trades, worth over HK$171 million (US$22.1 million), the biggest cross-border CBDC trial so far. The project will keep building toward a Minimum Viable Product and, eventually, a system ready for production use.

key_points.point: 20 banks across four jurisdictions -- Hong Kong, Mainland China, the UAE, and Thailand -- ran more than 160 payment and foreign-exchange (FX) trades, settled payment-versus-payment (PvP). These totalled over US$22.1 million during a six-week trial.
This project was among the earliest multi-CBDC efforts to complete actual cross-border payments for corporate clients.
HKMA and the project team will keep building the mBridge platform toward a Minimum Viable Product and, eventually, a system ready for production.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is useful context: it shows a working real-value cross-border CBDC trial. It is worth watching as a possible future alternative to correspondent banking settlement, but it requires no action from the bank today.

quote.text: the largest cross-border Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) pilot to date

reading_guide: Read the press release in full. See the full report (947fa49606ab) for pilot statistics, key lessons, and legal and policy analysis.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No action is needed. Note the trial's scale -- 20 banks, over US$22.1 million -- as a sign mBridge is heading toward a production system worth checking on periodically.

title: Opening Keynote at the Hong Kong FinTech Week 2022
summary: In this keynote, the HKMA Chief Executive looks back at Hong Kong's fintech journey and addresses crypto, stablecoins, decentralised finance (DeFi) and non-fungible tokens (NFTs) directly. He says the HKMA is building a proportionate rulebook, sized to risk, for payment-related stablecoins. He says the SFC is putting together rules to bring digital-asset trading venues under licensing. He adds that the HKMA has already told banks what to watch for if they offer crypto- or DeFi-related account-opening or custody services. He also mentions a first tokenised green bond concept, tested with the BIS Innovation Hub.

key_points.point: The HKMA confirms it is building a proportionate, risk-calibrated rulebook aimed specifically at stablecoins used for payments, applying the idea that comparable activities should face comparable oversight.
The securities regulator (SFC) is separately building rules to bring virtual-asset trading venues under a licensing framework.

The HKMA says banks have already been given pointers on what to check before entering crypto- or DeFi-linked business. This covers both opening accounts for such customers and holding assets in custody for them.

A tokenised green bond, concept-tested with the BIS Innovation Hub, is described as being adopted for an actual issuance later in 2022. This later became the world's first tokenised government green bond.

For mBridge to progress, the speech names three non-technical challenges: building anti-money-laundering requirements into the platform, ensuring on-chain FX liquidity, and developing a shared legal framework.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this speech confirms that HKMA guidance to banks on crypto and DeFi account-opening and custody services already existed by October 2022. The compliance head should find and check the underlying circular, since it directly covers the bank's own crypto-facing controls.

quote.text: same activity, same risks, same regulation

reading_guide: Read the 'Radical Open-Mindedness' section for the regulatory statements. The 'More is More' and 'Beyond Tech' sections are mostly about payment-network effects and can be skimmed, except for the mBridge AML point.
flags: This speech references an already-issued HKMA circular giving banks guidance on crypto/DeFi account-opening and custodial services, which is not itself in this batch and should be located and read directly

obligations: Locate and follow the HKMA's existing guidance (referenced but not reproduced here) that sets out what to check before taking on crypto- or DeFi-linked customers or holding such assets in custody (section 'Radical Open-Mindedness').
controls_and_monitoring: Track development of the SFC's virtual-asset trading platform framework and the HKMA's payment-related stablecoin regime, both under way as of this speech.
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm mBridge-linked counterparties or platforms meet the AML and legal-framework requirements the speech identifies as still under development.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Inform the board that the HKMA has confirmed a forthcoming payment-stablecoin regime and an SFC virtual-asset trading platform framework, and that bank-facing guidance on crypto/DeFi account and custody services already exists and should be reviewed.

title: Embracing Innovation, Regulation and the Future of Finance — Keynote address at Hong Kong FinTech Week 2022
summary: In this keynote, SFC Deputy CEO Julia Leung reviews the SFC's approach to virtual assets after the 2022 'crypto winter' (the collapse of Luna/Terra, Three Arrows, and crypto lenders freezing withdrawals). She explains that since 2018 the SFC has regulated virtual asset trading platforms and fund managers under a 'same business, same risks, same rules' principle. She cites a January 2022 joint circular with the HKMA that lets banks and brokers offer virtual asset dealing if they partner with an SFC-licensed exchange. She announces plans to review the professional-investor-only restriction, and previews a same-day circular authorising Bitcoin and Ether futures exchange-traded funds (ETFs). She explains that tokenised securities will generally be treated like their traditional equivalents, with due diligence and smart-contract audits expected. She confirms a coming VASP licensing consultation once the enabling Bill passes.

key_points.point: The SFC has regulated virtual asset trading platforms and fund managers since 2018 under a 'same business, same risks, same rules' principle, combining investor protection and market integrity requirements with AML controls.

Under the January 2022 SFC-HKMA joint circular, banks and securities brokers can only offer clients virtual asset dealing services if they team up with an SFC-licensed exchange. They also need to satisfy other regulatory conditions.

As of the speech, the SFC had approved 8 virtual asset fund managers and 1 virtual asset exchange, with another approved in principle. It had also approved 2 brokers to trade virtual assets for clients under omnibus account arrangements.

The SFC intends to consult on relaxing the 'professional investor only' restriction for SFC-licensed platforms, STOs and virtual asset funds, given four years of market maturing since the 2018 framework.

The SFC would issue a circular that day authorising virtual asset futures ETFs for public offering. At first this is limited to funds tracking Bitcoin and Ether futures dealt on the CME (Chicago Mercantile Exchange).

Tokenised plain-vanilla securities, such as a tokenised bond, will generally be treated as 'non-complex products' under existing distribution rules. But tokens with novel or complex features and no legal wrapper will likely be treated as 'complex products', restricted to professional investors.
Licensed firms distributing security tokens are expected to carry out sensible due diligence and have the smart contracts audited before offering the tokens to clients.
Following passage of the AML/CTF Amendment Bill (then before LegCo), the SFC will consult publicly on detailed VASP licensing requirements, including whether retail access should be permitted.

numbers_and_dates.value: fell from about US$3 trillion to about US$1 trillion over the prior year

numbers_and_dates.item: Virtual asset fund purchases via overseas platforms by HK investors

title: Circular on Virtual Asset Futures Exchange Traded Funds
summary: This SFC circular sets out when the SFC will authorise exchange-traded funds (ETFs) that get virtual-asset exposure mainly through futures contracts (VA Futures ETFs). Once authorised, they can be sold to the public in Hong Kong under sections 104-105 of the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO). It allows, for the first time, VA Futures ETFs to be authorised, at first limited to those tracking Bitcoin futures and Ether futures traded on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange. It sets track-record rules for the manager, limits on investment strategy and net derivative exposure, and disclosure duties. It also confirms that distribution must follow the Code of Conduct and the January 2022 Joint Circular, including the VA-knowledge test.

key_points.point: SFC is willing, for the first time, to accept applications to authorise VA Futures ETFs for public sale in Hong Kong.
At first, only Bitcoin and Ether futures dealt on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange qualify as underlying futures.
A VA Futures ETF's manager must have a good compliance track record and at least three years of proven ETF-management experience.
A VA Futures ETF's net derivative exposure must not go above 100% of the fund's total net asset value.
The product key facts statement must clearly disclose upfront the large roll costs and operational risks -- such as margin risk -- specific to VA futures.
Selling VA Futures ETFs must follow the Code of Conduct and the Joint Circular, including the mandatory VA-knowledge test, even when the sale isn't a solicitation or recommendation.

numbers_and_dates.item: Minimum management company ETF track record

numbers_and_dates.value: Bitcoin and Ether futures on CME only

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this circular has now been replaced. But it set the original distribution gate, the VA-knowledge test and complex-product disclosure, that a bank's distribution desk had to apply to VA Futures ETFs. A compliance head must check current controls now point to the successor circular.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Tell the board this circular has itself been replaced (refNo 23EC65). Confirm the bank's VA Futures ETF distribution controls point to the current version, not this older text.

title: Government issues Policy Statement on development of Virtual Assets in Hong Kong
summary: This press release announces that the Government has published a Policy Statement on the development of virtual assets (VA) in Hong Kong. It sums up the statement's four themes. First, a facilitating regulatory vision for VA. Second, moves toward a VA service provider licensing regime and an SFC consultation on retail investor access and VA exchange-traded funds (ETFs). Third, openness to reviewing property rights for tokenised assets. Fourth, pilot projects on NFTs, green bond tokenisation and e-HKD. It notes a coming HKMA announcement on stablecoin regulation next steps. The full statement is attached as an annex and is captured as a separate registry entry.

key_points.point: The Government is preparing a licensing regime for VA service providers and will invite global VA exchanges to establish in Hong Kong.
The SFC will consult on how much access retail investors should have to VA, and Hong Kong is open to VA exchange-traded funds.
The Government is open to reviewing property rights for tokenised assets and the legal status of smart contracts.
The HKMA will announce consultation outcome and next steps on stablecoin regulation in due course.
The named pilots are: tokenising a green bond, testing the e-HKD, and issuing NFTs for Fintech Week 2022.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the Government's first combined statement of intent across VASP licensing, stablecoins and tokenisation. It gives compliance a single reference point for the direction of travel that later concrete rules, the AMLO Part 5B licensing regime and the stablecoin ordinance, would follow.

quote.text: same activity, same risks, same regulation

reading_guide: Short press summary; read it in full, then read the attached Policy Statement (id f587b828e3fa) for the substantive detail.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Brief the board that Government has signalled forthcoming VASP licensing and stablecoin regimes, and that a bank due-diligence framework for VA counterparties should be readied.

title: Policy Statement on Development of Virtual Assets in Hong Kong
summary: This is the Government's founding policy statement setting Hong Kong's regulatory direction for virtual assets (VA). It commits to a 'same activity, same risks, same regulation' principle, and confirms an opt-in VA exchange licensing regime already exists. It also confirms guidance had already gone to banks and financial institutions on distributing, dealing in, or advising on VA. It announces work on a mandatory VA service provider licensing regime, plus an SFC consultation on retail access and VA exchange-traded funds (ETFs). It flags stablecoins as a priority, given their growing links to mainstream finance, references an earlier HKMA discussion paper, and says outcomes would follow. It also opens the door to reviewing property-rights law for tokenised assets and smart contracts. It describes three pilot projects: NFT issuance, green bond tokenisation, and e-HKD, describing e-HKD as a bridge between legal tender and virtual assets.

key_points.point: The Government commits to a 'same activity, same risks, same regulation' principle for regulating virtual asset activities.

A licensing regime for VA exchanges already existed on an opt-in basis, and guidance had already gone to banks and financial institutions. It covered distributing VA-related products, and dealing in or advising on VA.

The Government is preparing a new mandatory licensing regime for VA service providers, which would align VA exchanges' AML/CTF and investor-protection requirements with those applied to traditional financial institutions.
Once licensed, VA exchanges would be able to partner with banks and financial intermediaries offering VA dealing services to clients, subject to meeting regulatory conditions.
The SFC would consult on how much retail investors should be allowed to access VA once the new licensing regime is in place. It would also separately publish a circular on VA exchange-traded funds.
The Government is open to reviewing Hong Kong property-rights law to better cover tokenised assets, and the legal status of smart contracts.

Stablecoins were flagged as a priority, given growing links with traditional finance and payment systems. The HKMA had already issued a discussion paper before the 2022 'Crypto Winter' and would announce next steps in due course.

Three named pilot projects were: NFT issuance for Fintech Week 2022, tokenisation of a Government green bond for institutional investors, and e-HKD. e-HKD is described as a potential price-stable bridge supporting future security token offerings.
e-HKD work would proceed via a three-rail approach covering technology/legal foundations, use cases and design, then a launch timeline.

numbers_and_dates.item: Hong Kong asset and wealth management market size cited

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this sets the regulatory principle, 'same activity, same risks, same regulation', that later concrete rules for VASPs, stablecoins and VA distribution would follow. It also confirms banks were already expected to follow guidance when distributing or dealing in VA-related products, making this the policy anchor for a bank's whole VA compliance programme.

quote.text: same activity, same risks, same regulation

reading_guide: Read the main body (paras 1-11, p.1-6) in full. The Annex (p.7-9) gives useful pilot-project detail on NFTs, green bond tokenisation and e-HKD, but is lower priority.
flags: States banks/financial institutions had already been given guidance on distributing VA-related products and on dealing in or advising on VA as of October 2022, predating the later formal VASP licensing law -- worth checking against the bank's own guidance inventory

obligations: Follow existing guidance on distribution of VA-related products and on dealing in or advising on VA (para 5, p.2)
controls_and_monitoring: Track SFC consultation outcomes on retail VA access and VA ETFs (para 7, p.3)
Track HKMA stablecoin consultation outcome (para 9, p.4-5)
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm any VA exchange counterparty holds or is pursuing the relevant licence once the new VASP regime is in force (para 6, p.2)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told that Government policy now formally commits to VASP licensing, a stablecoin regime, and reviewed property-rights treatment of tokenised assets, all of which will generate future compliance obligations.

title: SFST's speech at Crypto Leaders Symposium, London Roundtable (English only)
summary: In this video speech to a London crypto industry event, the Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury largely repeats the October 2022 Policy Statement on Development of Virtual Assets. He restates Hong Kong's 'same activity, same risks, same regulation' principle and the coming VASP licensing regime. He also repeats the SFC's retail-access consultation and VA ETF circular, and the three pilot projects (NFTs, green bond tokenisation, e-HKD). No new commitments or requirements are added beyond the Policy Statement.

key_points.point: The speech confirms the Government's 'same activity, same risks, same regulation' approach to virtual assets, first set out in the October 2022 Policy Statement.
It restates that a new licensing regime for VA service providers is being prepared, aligning AML/CTF and investor-protection requirements with those for traditional financial institutions.
It confirms the SFC had by then published its circular on virtual asset exchange-traded funds.

It is useful only to confirm the Government was actively promoting this stance internationally by mid-November 2022, including confirming the VA futures ETF circular had by then been published.

quote.text: same activity, same risks, same regulation

reading_guide: This closely repeats the October 2022 Policy Statement (id f587b828e3fa, already registered). Skim it only to confirm the ETF circular was published by mid-November 2022.

title: An assessment of the volatility spillover from crypto to traditional financial assets: the role of asset-backed stablecoins
summary: This HKMA staff research memo studies whether volatility in crypto-asset markets can spill over into traditional finance through asset-backed stablecoins, focusing on Tether. It finds that when Tether adjusts its reserves, this makes volatility spillover from crypto assets into money-market instruments worse. That creates a channel through which stablecoin reserve fire-sales could hit traditional markets. The authors, writing in a personal capacity, suggest regulators consider standard reserve-asset disclosure rules for asset-backed stablecoins. They also suggest stronger liquidity-management rules, including limits on reserve makeup and clear redemption rights.

key_points.point: The study finds that Tether's reserve adjustments amplify the spillover of crypto-asset volatility into money-market instruments, indicating a channel through which crypto risk can reach the traditional financial system.
In extreme scenarios, stablecoin or crypto-asset failures could trigger large-scale stablecoin redemptions and a fire-sale of reserve assets, materially affecting money markets.
The paper suggests regulators consider requiring standardised, regular disclosure by asset-backed stablecoin issuers of their reserve-asset holdings, to help assess liquidity risk.
The paper suggests strengthening stablecoin liquidity management via restrictions on reserve-asset composition and clearly defined redemption rights.
The authors note the crypto ecosystem remains largely outside regulatory oversight, with data gaps that hamper assessment of spillover risk.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is HKMA staff research, not an official HKMA policy view. But it explains the reserve-disclosure and liquidity-management reasoning that later shaped Hong Kong's stablecoin issuer regime. It is useful for understanding why reserve transparency and redemption terms matter when assessing a stablecoin issuer counterparty.
reading_guide: Read the Key Points on page 1-2 in full. The statistical methods and appendix tables (page 8 onward) can be skipped unless checking the modelling approach.
flags: Explicitly a staff research paper -- views are the authors' own and do not necessarily represent official HKMA views

controls_and_monitoring: Consider reserve-asset transparency and redemption-rights strength as due-diligence factors when assessing any stablecoin the bank might hold, accept, or facilitate for clients.
counterparty_due_diligence: Check whether a given stablecoin issuer discloses reserve composition and has well-defined redemption rights, per the risk factors this research identifies.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Background only; useful if the board asks why reserve disclosure and redemption terms feature so prominently in Hong Kong's later stablecoin issuer requirements.

title: LCQ1: Promoting the development of Hong Kong into an international virtual assets centre
summary: In this LegCo reply, the Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury confirms a key date. Legislative proposals for a virtual asset service provider (VASP) licensing regime were introduced to the Legislative Council in July 2022. This builds on the SFC's existing 2018 regulatory framework and the January 2022 SFC-HKMA joint circular. It describes investor education steps: an IFEC virtual asset portal and an October 2022 public webinar. It also describes industry-support measures, including InvestHK's Global Fast Track VA track. About 80 VA or blockchain companies were at Cyberport, and seven VA-related projects were funded under the Fintech Proof-of-Concept Subsidy Scheme.

Under the proposed regime, licensed exchanges must comply with AML/CTF requirements and investor-protection requirements including proper asset custody, financial soundness, and avoiding conflicts of interest.
The SFC and HKMA jointly issued a circular in early 2022 providing guidelines for intermediaries wanting to engage in virtual asset-related services.
The Investor and Financial Education Council runs a dedicated virtual asset education portal and held a public webinar with FSTB and SFC in October 2022 on VA investment risks.
About 80 virtual asset or blockchain companies were based at Cyberport, and seven VA-related projects had been approved under the Fintech Proof-of-Concept Subsidy Scheme.

VA-related companies under the FinTech Anti-epidemic Scheme for Talent Development

That gives compliance a firm date to anchor a regulatory timeline.

title: An Event Study on the May 2022 Stablecoin Market Crash
summary: This HKMA staff research memo studies the May 2022 collapse of the algorithmic stablecoin TerraUSD (UST), and why some other stablecoins faced less redemption pressure than others. Studying 18 stablecoins that existed at the time, the authors estimate the fair value of each one's reserve assets. They find that stablecoins with stronger reserve backing suffered smaller falls in market value. Crypto-collateralised stablecoins absorbed the biggest shock from the Terra crash. Among those, stricter collateral rules gave more protection against redemption runs.

key_points.point: TerraUSD (UST), an algorithmic stablecoin, failed to maintain its US$1 peg in May 2022, triggering widespread crypto sell-offs across the market.
Looking across 18 stablecoins, the ones with bigger reserve backing saw, on average, smaller drops in market value during the crash.
Crypto-collateralised stablecoins were the primary shock absorbers of the Terra crash, given their role providing leverage within crypto markets, and faced extra redemption pressure as a result.

Among crypto-collateralised stablecoins, the ones with tougher lending terms (that is, needing more collateral per coin) held up better against redemption pressure, showing the benefit of a bigger safety margin.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this staff research explains, with data, why reserve strength and collateral ratios matter for stablecoin resilience. That is directly relevant background if the bank is assessing counterparty or custody risk from any stablecoin exposure, including an algorithmic or crypto-collateralised stablecoin.
reading_guide: Read the Key points on page 1 in full. The option-pricing method and spillover-model detail in the body are optional unless checking the analysis.
flags: Explicitly a staff research paper -- views are the authors' own and do not necessarily represent official HKMA views

Much of the body text extracted as blank/whitespace lines in this batch's fetch, likely a PDF text-extraction artefact around tables and charts; the Key points section on page 1 was intact and used as the basis for this entry, so importance/flags reflect only that reliably-extracted content

controls_and_monitoring: Factor reserve strength and collateralisation ratio into ongoing monitoring of any stablecoin the bank holds or facilitates exposure to.
counterparty_due_diligence: When assessing a stablecoin issuer or a crypto-collateralised stablecoin counterparty, check its collateralisation ratio and reserve composition against the resilience factors this study identifies.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Background only; cite as empirical evidence if the board asks why the bank applies extra scrutiny to algorithmic or thinly-collateralised stablecoins.

title: Capturing the future of virtual assets
summary: This Financial Services Development Council (FSDC) newsroom article reports on a panel discussion held around Hong Kong FinTech Week 2022, shortly after the government's October 2022 policy statement on virtual assets. Industry panellists welcomed the policy statement. They discussed a coming SFC retail-access consultation, a future VASP licensing regime, and pilot projects such as an NFT issuance, a green bond tokenisation, and e-HKD. It is secondary media commentary, not a regulator document, and includes named market commentators' opinions.

It notes the SFC was expected to consult on how retail investors might access virtual assets, possibly through ETFs.
It references a planned licensing system, still to come, that would bring virtual asset service providers under formal oversight.
It lists pilot projects underway at the time: an NFT issuance for FinTech Week, a green bond tokenisation, and the e-HKD project.

reading_guide: Skim the six body paragraphs; skip the repeated cookie-notice block that follows the article.
