title: LCQ4: Promoting development of virtual assets market
summary: This is a reply the Acting Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury gave in the Legislative Council (LegCo), days after a major overseas virtual asset (VA) exchange collapsed. It sets out planned investor-protection safeguards for Hong Kong's coming licence regime for virtual asset service providers (VASPs), to be overseen by the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC). These include segregated client assets, a one-year expense buffer, a ban on proprietary market-making, and audited accounts sent to the SFC. SFC powers to inspect and direct exchanges are also proposed, and the reply confirms the VASP Bill reached LegCo in July 2022.

key_points.point: A licensed VA exchange must keep client assets in a separate account, inside its own wholly owned subsidiary, apart from its own assets.
A licensed VA exchange must meet financial-resources rules and keep on hand enough funds to cover a full year of its actual running costs.
A licensed VA exchange must avoid conflicts of interest, including not taking part in proprietary market-making activities.
Licensed VA exchanges must regularly submit audited accounts and financial statements, including for their wholly owned subsidiaries, to the SFC.
The SFC will be able to enter a licensed VA exchange's premises, inspect and investigate it, demand records, and direct how it runs its business.
The VASP Bill reached the Legislative Council in July 2022. Anyone running a VA exchange business must apply to the SFC for a licence.
The SFC plans to issue a circular updating its policy on security token offerings given growing interest in tokenising traditional financial instruments.

title: Passage of Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Bill 2022
summary: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) tells banks that the Legislative Council passed the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Bill 2022 on 7 December 2022. The amended law brings virtual-asset service providers (VASPs) under a licensing regime and sets up a two-tier registration system for dealers in precious metals and stones. It also updates several rules to match Financial Action Task Force (FATF) standards, including a new definition of politically exposed person (PEP) and a risk-based approach to former PEPs. It also lets banks use recognised digital ID systems for customer checks, and widens who counts as a beneficial owner of a trust. The changes take effect on 1 June 2023, and the HKMA says it will consult banks on related changes to its AML/CFT guideline.

key_points.point: The amended ordinance brings virtual-asset service providers under a licensing system.
The changes take effect on 1 June 2023, giving the industry time to get ready.
A recognised digital ID system can now be used for customer due diligence, including when a customer isn't physically present.
The HKMA said it would consult banks on related updates to its AML/CFT guideline. It also plans to give specific guidance on key issues before the changes take effect.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this law is the legal basis for the mandatory VASP licensing regime: from the effective date only licensed VASPs should count as compliant counterparties. It also updated the AML/CFT Guideline that the bank's own anti-money-laundering (AML) programme follows.

quote.text: a licensing regime for virtual asset service providers

reading_guide: Two-page circular; read in full.

obligations: Get ready to assess VASP counterparties against the new licensing regime once it takes effect, p.1
controls_and_monitoring: Update customer due diligence steps to allow recognised digital ID systems, p.1
Widen beneficial-ownership checks for trusts to cover trustees, beneficiaries and anyone with a vested interest, p.1

title: Statement on virtual asset arrangements claiming to offer returns to investors
summary: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) warns investors about virtual asset (VA) platforms offering 'deposit', 'savings', 'earnings' or 'staking' products. These products are unregulated, are not the same as a bank deposit, and can carry a big risk of loss, as recent VA platform collapses showed. The SFC reminds firms that such products may count as an unauthorised collective investment scheme (CIS). Under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO), advertising or distributing one to Hong Kong investors without authorisation is an offence.

key_points.point: VA 'deposit', 'savings' and 'staking' arrangements sit outside regulation and work nothing like a bank deposit; investors get no protection.
Such VA products may count as an unauthorised CIS if investors lack day-to-day control and their VA is pooled and managed together for returns.
Inviting people in Hong Kong to join an unauthorised CIS is an offence under SFO section 103. The maximum penalty is a HK$500,000 fine and 3 years in prison.

Promoting or selling a CIS to Hong Kong, or targeting the Hong Kong market, without an SFC licence is an offence under SFO section 114. The maximum penalty is a HK$5,000,000 fine and 7 years in prison.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this shows how the SFC may treat VA yield or staking products as an unauthorised CIS, after major 2022 VA platform collapses. It matters if the bank refers clients to, or partners with, a third-party VA yield platform.

quote.text: they are not regulated and are not the same as bank deposits

reading_guide: Read in full; short warning statement.
flags: Issued in the immediate aftermath of major VA platform collapses (implicitly referencing events like FTX) -- context matters for why the SFC issued this reminder despite having warned before.

title: Statement on virtual asset arrangements claiming to offer returns to investors
summary: The SFC warns the public about platforms offering virtual asset (VA) "deposit", "savings" or "staking" products that promise high or fixed returns. It explains these arrangements are unregulated, carry no protection like a bank deposit, and can fail if the platform or its lending counterparties collapse or are hacked. The SFC notes such arrangements may count as an unauthorised collective investment scheme (CIS) under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO). Promoting or distributing one in Hong Kong without authorisation or a licence is a criminal offence.

key_points.point: Platforms offering VA "deposits" or staking with guaranteed or fixed returns are flagged as high risk and largely unregulated.
VA "deposit" or "savings" products are not bank deposits and carry no depositor protection.
An arrangement can be an unauthorised CIS if investors pool their VA and lack day-to-day control. Promoting or distributing it without authorisation or a licence is an SFO offence.
Unlicensed promotion of an unauthorised CIS to the Hong Kong public can bring a fine up to HK$500,000 and three years' imprisonment.
Marketing or distributing CIS interests in Hong Kong as a business, without an SFC licence, can bring a fine of up to HK$5,000,000 and seven years in prison.

max fine, unlicensed CIS marketing/distribution offence

title: SFST's speech at Listing Ceremony of Asia's First Crypto Futures Exchange Traded Funds (English only)
summary: The Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury (SFST), Christopher Hui, speaks at the Hong Kong Stock Exchange listing of Asia's first crypto futures ETFs. He links the listing to the Government's October 2022 Policy Statement on virtual assets and a related SFC circular authorising VA futures ETFs for public offering. He frames the listing as the start of a new phase of regulated VA products in Hong Kong. He invites more quality VA products and service providers into the market.

key_points.point: The listing follows the Government's October 2022 Policy Statement on VA development. A related SFC circular already allowed VA futures ETFs to be offered to the public.
The speech frames this as Hong Kong's entry into well-regulated, retail-accessible VA products via the securities market.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this confirms official government backing for retail, exchange-listed VA-linked products. It is useful context when assessing demand for the bank to distribute such ETFs, but it adds no new compliance duty.
reading_guide: Short speech; read in full, skip nothing.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: None required; background/political signalling only.

title: Prudential treatment of cryptoasset exposures
summary: The HKMA relays the Basel Committee's final global standard on the prudential (capital) treatment of banks' cryptoasset exposures, issued 16 December 2022. Cryptoassets are split into two groups. Group 1 (qualifying tokenised traditional assets and stablecoins) generally gets the existing Basel risk-based capital treatment. Group 2 (everything that fails the Group 1 tests) gets more conservative treatment, with limited hedging recognition and an exposure limit as a guardrail. The standard adds an infrastructure risk add-on for Group 1 assets and a redemption-risk test for stablecoins to qualify for Group 1. The Basel Committee set a global deadline of 1 January 2025 for banks to apply the standard. The HKMA said it intends to implement it locally on that timetable, and will consult the industry on local details.

key_points.point: Group 1 cryptoassets (qualifying tokenised assets and stablecoins) generally receive the existing risk-based Basel capital treatment.

Group 2 cryptoassets (everything that does not meet the Group 1 conditions) get more conservative capital treatment. Only limited hedging is recognised, and an exposure limit caps how large Group 2 holdings can grow in a bank's portfolio.
Only stablecoins issued by supervised, regulated entities with robust redemption rights and proper governance can pass the redemption-risk test needed for Group 1 qualification.
The Basel Committee's global deadline is 1 January 2025. The HKMA intends to implement the standard locally on that timetable, and will consult the industry on local details in due course.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the capital-charge framework it must plan for on any cryptoasset exposure. It shows which exposures could qualify for lower-capital Group 1 treatment via the redemption-risk test for stablecoins. Other exposures get the stricter Group 2 treatment, ahead of local HKMA implementation.

quote.text: provide a global baseline framework

reading_guide: Two-page circular; read in full.
flags: This December 2022 circular only relayed the Basel Committee's global standard and the HKMA's intention to implement locally by 1 January 2025; that timetable slipped, and local implementation (SPM modules CA-G-1/CA-G-5/CR-G-8/CR-G-9/CR-L-5/LM-1/MR-1/MR-2, the Banking (Exposure Limits) Code, and related Banking (Capital) Rules amendments) only came into force from late 2025, so this circular's proposed treatment is now superseded by the actual local Cryptoassets Standard rather than a still-pending future-effective item.

obligations: Track local HKMA implementation of the Basel standard and prepare for the global 1 January 2025 deadline, p.2
controls_and_monitoring: Classify existing/planned cryptoasset exposures into Group 1 vs Group 2 categories to anticipate capital impact, p.1
counterparty_due_diligence: Assess whether any stablecoin exposure could meet the redemption-risk test (issuer supervision, redemption rights, governance) for Group 1 treatment, p.2
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be briefed on the capital implications of current or planned cryptoasset exposure ahead of local implementation, and on the forthcoming HKMA consultation.

title: Web 3.0 in Hong Kong – from crypto to blockchain
summary: This FSDC newsroom piece reports on a London panel discussion about Hong Kong's virtual asset regulation, held shortly after the 2022 crypto market turmoil. Panellists described Hong Kong moving from a voluntary 2019 licensing option for exchanges to a mandatory licence requirement restricted to professional investors, and discussed tokenisation trends among banks. It is a secondary media summary of speaker opinions, not a regulator statement.

key_points.point: The article recaps that Hong Kong's 2019 regime let virtual asset exchanges opt in to SFC licensing voluntarily, and only one exchange did so.
It describes the then-upcoming mandatory licence requirement covering all virtual asset exchanges, limited to professional investors with no retail offering.
A panellist noted banks and other intermediaries would be able to work with licensed exchanges to offer dealing services.
Another speaker described a growing trend of large banks exploring tokenisation of bonds, equities and real estate.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is useful only as historical colour on how the mandatory VASP licensing regime (which later took effect in June 2023) was described publicly before it existed. It is not a source to cite for current rules.
reading_guide: Read paragraphs 4-11 for the regulatory-history narrative; skip the closing FinTech-tag list and cookie notice.
flags: Secondary source; speaker quotes are opinions, not regulatory text, and must not be cited as if from the SFC or HKMA.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: None; background only.

title: Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Authorized Institutions) (Consultation January 2023)
supersedes_or_amends: Proposed amendments to the October 2018 AML/CFT Guideline (For Authorized Institutions)
summary: This is the draft of the revised AML/CFT Guideline sent to banks for consultation in January 2023, shown as tracked changes against the October 2018 text. It already proposed the HK$8,000 CDD trigger for occasional VA transfers, the s.13A cross-reference and correspondent-type measures for overseas VASPs. Unlike the final text, its footnote 1 did not yet point registered institutions (RIs) to the SFC's virtual asset chapter. The footnote excluding AMLO-defined institutions from the VASP extension was not yet there either. It was replaced by the May 2023 final Guideline.

key_points.point: Draft added a CDD trigger before occasional virtual asset transfers of HK$8,000 or more, linked to s.13A of Schedule 2.
Draft added VA transfers to the HK$8,000 linked-transaction watch and to the five-year record rule for occasional transactions.
Draft para 11.23 already extended correspondent-banking measures to overseas VASPs (using the FATF definition, footnote 74). Paras 11.24-11.25 extended this to own-use versus client-use accounts.
Draft footnote 1 referred RIs only to the SFC guideline for licensed corporations, without the later reference to its virtual asset chapter.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Superseded; useful only to show that the VA provisions were proposed from the outset and that the SFC VA chapter reference for RIs was added after consultation.
reading_guide: Skip unless tracing drafting history; use the final May 2023 Guideline.
flags: Superseded by the May 2023 Guideline (7bfdad704174).

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: None; superseded draft.

The page links to the May 2023 conclusions and marked-up annex.

key_points.point: Consultation opened 18 January 2023 and closed 8 March 2023; status shown as closed.
The draft Guideline enclosure holds the proposed VA transfer threshold and overseas VASP correspondent measures.

title: Conclusion of discussion paper on crypto-assets and stablecoins
supersedes_or_amends: HKMA Discussion Paper on Crypto-assets and Stablecoins (12 January 2022)
summary: The HKMA published its conclusion to the January 2022 discussion paper on crypto-assets and stablecoins, summarising 58 submissions received and its response. It confirmed it will bring certain stablecoin-related activities into a mandatory licensing regime, starting with fiat-referenced stablecoins, with flexibility to scope in other structures later. Key regulated activities are governance, issuance, stabilisation/reserve management, and wallets. Both Authorized Institutions (AIs) and non-AIs may be licensed to issue stablecoins. The HKMA targeted implementation of the regime in 2023/24, with a more detailed consultation to follow.

key_points.point: Certain stablecoin-related activities will fall under a new mandatory licensing regime run by the HKMA. It starts with stablecoins that claim to track one or more fiat currencies.

Four categories of key regulated activities: governance, issuance (issuing/creating/destroying), stabilisation/reserve management, and wallets (custody of cryptographic keys enabling access to stablecoin holdings).

A licence is required for an entity that conducts a regulated activity in Hong Kong, or actively markets one to the Hong Kong public. It is also required for anyone dealing in a HKD-referenced stablecoin, wherever they are based, or where the HKMA decides regulation is needed in the public interest.

Reserve assets must fully back outstanding stablecoins at all times, and must be high quality and highly liquid. Holders should be able to redeem at par within a reasonable period, and algorithm- or arbitrage-based stabilisation will not be accepted.

Both Authorized Institutions (AIs) and non-AIs may be licensed to issue stablecoins, under a 'same risk, same regulation' rule that fits requirements to the issuer type. The HKMA rejected a rule limiting issuance to AIs only.

A 'principal business' rule applies to licensees -- for example, wallet operators must not engage in lending. This rule does not apply to an in-scope AI, because AIs already face similar or stricter deposit-taking rules.

Tokenised deposits of AIs, closed-loop limited-purpose stablecoins, and possibly central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) or settlement tokens, are candidates to be excluded from scope. Separately, the HKMA will work out how tokenised deposits should be regulated, as a distinct question from stablecoin issuance.

The HKMA sees local incorporation as a strong aid to effective supervision and enforcement, such as segregating and seizing assets to protect users. But the HKMA said it would look further at other measures respondents raised instead.

The HKMA flagged possible overlap between its proposed stablecoin regime, the SFC's VASP licensing regime, and the stored value facility (SVF) regime. It said it will work with other regulators to avoid arbitrage and close any gaps.

The target date to start the stablecoin regime is 2023/24. A more detailed consultation will follow, including whether to use new stand-alone legislation or amend existing laws, before any draft bill.

Draft legislation is expected to define which structures and activities are regulated or excluded, and to give the HKMA powers to run the regime and set key requirements. It would also give the HKMA a way, using published 'guiding factors', to bring more stablecoin structures or activities into scope later.

Discussion Paper feedback period end date
Target implementation date for the stablecoin regulatory regime
AMLO amendment bill (VASP/SFC licensing) passage and commencement
numbers_and_dates.value: passed 7 December 2022; regime takes effect 1 June 2023

numbers_and_dates.item: FSB target to finalise revised GSC high-level recommendations

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this signals the HKMA's intent to bring stablecoin issuance under regulation, with implementation expected in 2023/24. Treat it as an early-warning marker for the licensing regime that later took shape, not as a source of present-day duties.

quote.text: a stablecoin should not rely on arbitrage activities to maintain a stable value

reading_guide: Read the Executive Summary (paragraphs 1.1-1.8, pages 3-6) and the HKMA's answers under each heading Q1-Q8 in Chapter 4 (pages 13-26) for the main policy positions. Skim Chapter 3 and Annexes 1-3; they are mostly background.
flags: This conclusion is a policy-direction document only, not yet the licensing regime itself -- the actual regime materialised later as the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656); readers should not treat this as current law.

Contrary to a common assumption that HK would require stablecoin issuers to be licensed banks (as some respondents proposed by analogy to the US President's Working Group report), the HKMA explicitly rejected an AI-only issuance requirement and will allow non-AI issuers subject to calibrated requirements.
Tokenised deposits are explicitly treated as a separate question from stablecoin issuer regulation, to be assessed under the Banking Ordinance framework -- a distinction a HoDA should not blur.

The document explicitly leaves open whether new stand-alone legislation or amendment of the PSSVFO would be used, and whether local incorporation will be an absolute requirement or subject to alternative mitigation measures -- these were unresolved at this stage despite being central compliance questions.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should note the HKMA signalled a stablecoin regulatory regime targeted for 2023/24 -- the direction that later became the Stablecoins Ordinance (see 6c3f349e4f90) -- but no rules existed yet at this point.

title: Conclusion of Discussion Paper on Crypto-assets and Stablecoins
summary: This paper closes out the HKMA's January 2022 discussion paper on crypto-assets and stablecoins, after 58 submissions. It sets firmer proposed terms for the coming stablecoin licensing regime, shaped by the 2022 collapse of TerraUSD and the FTX bankruptcy. It commits to a risk-based regime starting with fiat-referenced stablecoins. Governance, issuance, stabilisation/reserve management and wallet custody are named as the core licensable activities. Key principles are full backing, redemption at par, and a 'principal business' restriction, which is waived for Authorized Institutions (AIs). It also records Hong Kong's parallel move to bring virtual asset exchanges under an SFC licensing regime from June 2023. It notes the government's October 2022 Policy Statement on virtual asset development.

key_points.point: HKMA confirmed it will prioritise regulating fiat-referenced stablecoins first, while building in flexibility to bring other stablecoin structures into scope later.

Four activities were named as core to the coming licensing regime. They are governance of the stablecoin arrangement's rules, issuance (minting or burning), stabilisation and reserve management, and wallet custody of users' cryptographic keys.

A licence would be required for an entity conducting a regulated activity in Hong Kong, or actively marketing one to the Hong Kong public. It would also be required for stablecoins referencing the Hong Kong dollar, or where the HKMA decides regulation is needed in the public interest.

Core proposed principles were full backing and redemption at par at all times, and ruling out algorithm- or arbitrage-based stabilisation. A 'principal business' restriction would stop regulated entities straying outside their licensed activity -- wallet operators, for example, could not lend. This restriction is waived for Authorized Institutions, given their existing prudential rules.
The target implementation date for the regime was reaffirmed as 2023/24, and HKMA was still weighing new standalone legislation against amending existing law.

The May 2022 depegging of TerraUSD, then the largest algorithmic stablecoin, and Tether's brief drop to USD 0.95, were cited as evidence of weak governance, stabilisation and disclosure. The November 2022 FTX collapse was cited too, reinforcing the case for regulation.

Separately, Hong Kong's Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (AMLO) was amended in December 2022 to require an SFC licence for operating a virtual asset exchange, from 1 June 2023. This is a parallel but separate regime from the stablecoin issuer licensing later created by the Stablecoins Ordinance.

Consultation respondents were divided on whether stablecoin licensees should have to incorporate locally. This foreshadowed the requirement that later appeared in the Stablecoins Ordinance for non-bank issuers.

numbers_and_dates.item: Submissions received on the Discussion Paper

numbers_and_dates.value: fell to USD 0.95 before recovering to USD 1.00

numbers_and_dates.item: AMLO amendment for VA exchange licensing takes effect
Target implementation date (as of this paper)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this shows how the TerraUSD and FTX failures shaped the full-backing, par-redemption and 'principal business' rules it now operates under. It also confirms why Authorized Institutions get lighter treatment on some points, which is useful context for explaining the current rules to internal stakeholders.
reading_guide: Read the executive summary table (para 1.4) for the proposed regime terms, and paras 3.2-3.3 for the TerraUSD/FTX context. You can skim the question-by-question summary in Chapter 4, since the later ordinance is the authoritative source.
flags: This 2023 conclusions paper is now superseded by the enacted Stablecoins Ordinance and its 2025 guidelines; treat its 'proposed' parameters as historical drafting context, not current rules.
The paper's original 2023/24 implementation target slipped materially - the regime did not actually commence until 1 August 2025.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Context only - useful if the board asks why the regime requires full backing, par redemption and a principal-business restriction; the TerraUSD/FTX failures are the cited rationale.

title: LCQ11: Tokenised green bonds
summary: In a Legislative Council written reply, Hong Kong's Acting Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury confirms the HKMA plans a pilot tokenised green bond under the Government Green Bond Programme. It is aimed at institutional investors, and is meant to test Hong Kong's legal and market systems for tokenised issuance. The reply explains that tokenisation may cut issuance cost and settlement time. The HKMA will publish a project report afterwards to guide future issuers, and the government will explore using blockchain to track green-project data for bondholders.

key_points.point: The tokenised green bond pilot is for institutional investors only and is expected to be smaller in scale than prior green bond issuances.
HKMA will publish a report on the pilot after issuance to guide future issuers on the process, including issuance, settlement, coupon payment and redemption.
Government will separately explore blockchain-based tracking of green project performance for green bond reporting.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is an early signal that the HKMA intends to pilot tokenised bond infrastructure that its markets or custody teams may later be asked to support. No current duties arise from this reply.
reading_guide: Short LegCo Q&A; read in full.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: None; watch for the HKMA's post-issuance report as a future input to tokenised-bond product review.

title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Eddie Yue on Tokenised Bond: Huge Potential to be Unlocked
summary: This article by the HKMA's Chief Executive marks the world's first tokenised green bond issued by a government. The Hong Kong Government issued it using distributed ledger technology (DLT). It explains that HKD cash tokens, similar to a wholesale central bank digital currency (CBDC), were minted by the HKMA so banks could settle the deal on-platform. This cut settlement time from five business days to one. It flags that custody arrangements will need to be upgraded so custodians can hold digital securities on investors' behalf. The HKMA will publish a white paper on lessons learned, to guide future issuers.

key_points.point: The Hong Kong Government's tokenised green bond is described as the world's first tokenised bond issued by a government, using distributed ledger technology (DLT).

HKD cash tokens, similar to a wholesale CBDC, were created by the HKMA when banks handed over fiat cash. They were used to settle the primary issuance, secondary trading, coupon payment and maturity redemption on-platform.
Settlement time was cut from the conventional five business days (T+5) to one day, using tokenisation instead of separate bond and cash settlement channels.
Existing custody arrangements may need to be upgraded so custodians can hold digital securities for investors. Banks acting as agents may take on new on-platform tasks.

The HKMA states it is writing a white paper on lessons from this issuance, to guide future tokenised issuers. It will also set out its thinking on legal certainty for digital securities created natively on DLT.

The tokenisation approach builds on Project Genesis, a 2021 proof-of-concept co-sponsored with the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Innovation Hub. It also draws on the cash-token mechanism built for the mBridge cross-border CBDC platform.
key_points.locator: paras on Project Genesis and mBridge synergy

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the HKMA's own account of a landmark tokenised bond deal, which points to future custody expectations for digital securities. Compliance should track the promised white paper, since it will likely set out legal-certainty and custody-upgrade expectations for any digital-bond custody or agency role the bank takes on.

quote.text: the world's first tokenised green bond issued by a government

reading_guide: Read the full article; it is short and entirely on-topic for tokenisation, with the custody and legal-certainty paragraphs near the end being the most compliance-relevant.

controls_and_monitoring: Track publication of the HKMA's promised white paper on lessons from this tokenised bond issuance, since it may set expectations for custody and legal-certainty arrangements the bank would need to follow in future tokenised-bond agency or custody roles.
counterparty_due_diligence: If engaging a custodian for digital securities, confirm the custodian has uplifted its arrangements to hold tokens on a DLT platform on investors' behalf, as flagged as a prerequisite here.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Tell the board this is a landmark HKMA-facilitated transaction signalling that tokenised bond infrastructure, cash tokens and digital-custody uplift are moving from pilot to real transactions.

title: HKSAR Government's Inaugural Tokenised Green Bond Offering
summary: The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) Government offered a HK$800 million, one-year tokenised bond, as green debt under the Government Green Bond Programme. It is billed as the first tokenised green bond issued by any government worldwide. A four-bank syndicate distributed the bond. It was cleared and settled through the HKMA's Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU), using Goldman Sachs' GS DAP tokenisation platform. The initial issuance settled delivery-versus-payment, swapping security tokens for HKMA-issued cash tokens on a private blockchain. The HKMA said records on that private blockchain would be the legally final record of ownership, and that CMU settlement enjoys statutory finality under Hong Kong law. The HKMA also said it would publish a paper summarising lessons learned and offering a blueprint for future tokenised bond issuance in Hong Kong.

key_points.point: The tokenised green bond -- HK$800 million, in Hong Kong dollars, one-year term -- is the first tokenised bond any government has issued anywhere. It is also the first one governed by Hong Kong law.

Settlement ran delivery-versus-payment: security tokens stood for a beneficial interest in the bond. These were swapped for cash tokens standing for a claim on Hong Kong dollars owed by the HKMA, completed one business day later (T+1) on a private blockchain network.

The bond clears and settles through the HKMA's CMU, which under Hong Kong law carries statutory finality for settlement. The HKMA describes records on the private blockchain as the legally final record of ownership.
This offering was one of the pilot projects flagged in the Government's October 2022 policy paper on developing virtual assets in Hong Kong.
key_points.locator: quote from Secretary Christopher Hui, p.1

key_points.point: As the Government's representative under the Green Bond Programme, the HKMA said it will publish a paper on lessons learned and next steps. This paper will act as a blueprint for future tokenised bond issuance in Hong Kong.
The deal builds on Project Genesis, a joint effort the HKMA finished with the BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre in 2021.

The bond paid a 4.05% coupon, settled on 16 February 2023 (T+1), and was rated A-1+/F1+ by S&P and Fitch. Bank of China (Hong Kong), Credit Agricole CIB, Goldman Sachs and HSBC acted as joint global coordinators, lead managers and bookrunners.
key_points.locator: Summary terms and conditions table, p.2

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is a market precedent, not a rulebook: it shows a real Hong Kong-law tokenised bond settling on-chain through the CMU with statutory finality. It is relevant if the bank later joins a similar deal, but creates no ongoing compliance duty.

quote.text: the first tokenised bond governed by Hong Kong law

reading_guide: Read the first five paragraphs and the summary terms table (pages 1-2) for the main facts. You can skim the quotes from officials and bank executives (paras 6-13) and the US securities-law disclaimer at the end; these are largely promotional.
flags: The press release states on-chain records on the private blockchain network are 'the legally definitive and final records of ownership' -- a notable legal characterisation of DLT records that a HoDA should distinguish from CMU's traditional register, since here the two are stated to coincide by design.

This is a single pilot issuance, not a standing programme or regulatory instrument; no ongoing legal/regulatory framework is created by this press release itself beyond the stated intention to issue a future whitepaper/blueprint.

counterparty_due_diligence: Useful precedent for later assessing a bank's own role -- as syndicate member, custodian or settlement participant -- in a Hong Kong-law tokenised bond: on-chain records here are described as the legally final record of ownership, a characterisation worth checking against any future deal's documents (para 4, p.1).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: This is a one-off pilot deal, not an ongoing programme -- flag it to the board only as a precedent for future digital-bond mandates, not as a source of continuing obligations.

title: Consultation Paper on the Proposed Regulatory Requirements for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators Licensed by the Securities and Futures Commission
supersedes_or_amends: Terms and Conditions for VA Trading Platform Operators (VATP Terms and Conditions), issued 10 Dec 2020
summary: This SFC consultation paper (20 Feb 2023) proposed the regulatory requirements for VA trading platforms ahead of the AMLO VASP licensing regime commencing 1 June 2023. This sits alongside the pre-existing SFO regime for platforms trading security tokens. It set out a draft version of Guidelines for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators (below, VATP Guidelines), plus a new AML/CFT Chapter 12 for platform operators. It also proposed Disciplinary Fining Guidelines, and transitional arrangements (deeming and non-contravention periods) for pre-existing platforms. Central proposals included allowing retail investor access for the first time, subject to knowledge assessment, suitability, and token admission safeguards. Other proposals were a token due-diligence and 'eligible large-cap virtual asset' framework for retail-available tokens, and 98% cold storage with detailed custody/key-management controls. A flexible compensation-arrangement requirement would replace the old insurance mandate. Licence applicants would also need a two-phase external assessor report. The paper also proposed removing several prior SFO licensing-condition requirements (for example, the 'security token' admission criterion, mandatory voting-rights facilitation, legal opinion for all tokens) as the regime evolved. Comments were due 31 March 2023. The finalised VATP Guidelines were later issued, dated June 2023 per the draft appendix cover. This consultation paper is now a superseded, historical proposal document. But it remains the primary explanatory source for the final Guidelines' rationale and numbering.

key_points.point: The AMLO VASP regime (non-security-token VA trading platforms) commenced 1 June 2023. It runs alongside the existing SFO regime, which already covers platforms offering at least one security token. Dual licensing is required if a platform's token mix spans both.

The SFC proposed for the first time to allow retail investor access to licensed VA trading platforms, subject to robust investor protection measures (knowledge assessment, suitability, exposure limits).

Under the proposed rule, a platform operator, together with its Associated Entity, should keep 98% of client virtual assets in cold wallets, with only limited, SFC-approved exceptions. That is a stricter bar than the roughly 95% cold-storage benchmark cited elsewhere in the same paper for existing SFO licensees.

Seeds and private keys must be stored in Hong Kong, generated in a non-deterministic or random manner. No single person may hold the entirety of seeds, keys or backup passphrases, and distributed backups must mitigate single points of failure.

The prior mandatory insurance requirement (full coverage for hot storage, substantial for example, 95% coverage for cold storage 'at all times') is replaced by a flexible SFC-approved compensation arrangement that may combine third-party insurance and/or trust-segregated own funds.
key_points.locator: Appendix A, para 10.22; main body para 53-55

key_points.point: 'Eligible large-cap virtual assets' for retail trading must be included in at least two 'acceptable indices' from independent index providers. At least one index provider must be experienced in traditional (non-VA) financial markets.

Licensed platform operators must maintain minimum paid-up share capital of HK$5,000,000. They must also hold required liquid capital of the higher of HK$3,000,000 or the Financial Resources Rules basic amount, plus 12 months of operating expenses in liquid HK assets.
Platform operators are barred from offering, trading in, or dealing with virtual-asset futures or related derivative contracts, and from providing algorithmic trading services to clients.

Virtual asset transfers of HK$8,000 or more trigger mandatory Travel Rule originator/recipient information collection. The ordering institution must obtain and record originator and recipient details -- name, account or wallet, and address or ID number -- before executing the transfer. A reduced dataset applies below that threshold.

Transfers to or from unhosted wallets require the financial institution (FI) to obtain and record originator and recipient information from its own customer, since the counterparty institution cannot be relied upon. Risk-based mitigating measures, such as enhanced monitoring or transaction limits, must also apply.

Pre-existing VA trading platforms -- those already operating in Hong Kong with a meaningful, substantial presence before 1 June 2023 -- had until 29 February 2024 to submit a licence application. This let them qualify for the deeming arrangement. They could continue operating penalty-free under a non-contravention arrangement until 31 May 2024. Any platform not licensed or deemed licensed by 1 June 2024 is in breach and subject to enforcement.
key_points.locator: Part IV, para 74, 79(b), 82; Appendix E timeline

key_points.point: The SFC proposed to publish four public lists: licensed, deemed-licensed, closing-down, and unlicensed VA trading platforms. It explicitly warned that appearance on the 'deemed licensed' list does not mean the SFC has vetted the platform's fitness and properness.

The SFC's disciplinary fining power under the AMLO VASP regime caps a pecuniary penalty at HK$10 million or three times the profit gained/loss avoided, whichever is greater, per instance of misconduct.

Licence applicants must engage independent external assessors to produce two reports. A Phase 1 report on design effectiveness is due at application. A Phase 2 report on implementation effectiveness, including penetration and vulnerability testing, is due after approval-in-principle. Both cover governance, token admission, custody, know-your-customer checks, anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing controls, market surveillance, risk management, and cybersecurity.

numbers_and_dates.locator: Appendix A, para 10.6(c); Appendix F Part C(ii)(a)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this consultation paper binds virtual asset trading platforms and SFC-licensed intermediaries, not the bank as an AI. Its lasting value for a compliance head is as the source of the custody, cold-storage and Travel Rule benchmarks to test any VATP counterparty against. The bank's own AML/travel-rule duties are governed separately, by the HKMA AML/CFT Guideline for AIs.

quote.text: the more stringent requirement should prevail

reading_guide: Read the Part I Executive Summary (p.6) and Part III retail-access/custody/insurance sections (p.10-24) first, for the policy rationale. Then read Appendix A Chapters VI, VII, X and XII (Financial Soundness, Operations, Custody, Cybersecurity, p.64-109), for the operative requirements. You can skim the generic AML/CFT boilerplate in Appendix B outside Chapter 12. The same goes for the fitness-and-properness and competence chapters in Appendix A Parts II-IV, which largely restate standard SFC licensing conditions.
flags: The 98% cold-storage figure in the proposed VATP Guidelines (Appendix A para 10.6(c)) is a tightening from the commonly cited 95% cold-storage insurance-coverage benchmark referenced for the prior SFO regime in the same paper (para 53) — these are two different metrics (98% storage location requirement vs. an older ~95% insurance-coverage example) and should not be conflated.

This is a CONSULTATION paper (comments closed 31 March 2023), not the final rule; the appended draft VATP Guidelines are dated June 2023 and were subsequently finalised — readers should verify current requirements against the final published VATP Guidelines and AML Guideline rather than treating this document's Appendix A/B text as currently binding, even though it is the clearest available explanatory source for the numbering and rationale.

The paper explicitly proposes REMOVING several pre-existing SFO licensing-condition requirements — the 'security token' 12-month-track-record admission criterion, mandatory facilitation of token voting rights (reduced to a disclosure-only obligation), and mandatory legal opinions for all traded tokens (narrowed to retail-available tokens only) — a correction to the assumption that the new regime is uniformly stricter than the old one; some obligations were relaxed.

Platform operators are categorically barred from offering VA derivatives/futures and algorithmic trading, and from providing any financial accommodation (margin/credit) for clients to acquire virtual assets — a common misconception is that licensed HK VATPs can offer leveraged or derivative crypto products; they cannot under this framework (a separate future review was floated for institutional VA derivatives).

The Travel Rule $8,000 threshold and the AML CDD $8,000 occasional-transaction threshold are two related but textually distinct triggers (para 12.3.1-12.3.2 vs 12.11.5-12.11.6) — care is needed not to treat them as a single uniform rule.

controls_and_monitoring: Note the Travel Rule HK$8,000 originator/recipient-information threshold and unhosted-wallet handling in Appendix B Chapter 12 are VATP/LC obligations under the SFC AML Guideline, not the bank's own; the bank's AI travel-rule duties are set separately by the HKMA AML/CFT Guideline for AIs (Appendix B, Ch.12, paras 12.11.5-12.11.6, 12.14.1-12.14.3)
counterparty_due_diligence: Check whether a VATP counterparty stores 98% of client VA in cold storage in Hong Kong and keeps seeds/keys HK-based with no single point of failure, as proposed for the VATP regime (Appendix A paras 10.6(c), 10.8(a)-(e))
Check a VATP's compensation arrangement (insurance and/or trust-segregated funds) rather than assuming a single fixed insurance percentage (Appendix A para 10.22)
Confirm a VATP is licensed or 'deemed licensed' and check it against SFC's public VATP lists, since deemed status is not SFC vetting of fitness and properness (Part IV paras 74, 79(b), 86-87)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told this is a 2023 CONSULTATION (superseded by the final VATP Guidelines) whose custody and AML requirements bind VATPs and SFC-licensed LCs/VASPs, not the bank as an AI directly; the bank's own AML/travel-rule obligations sit in the HKMA AML/CFT Guideline for AIs, which should be checked separately.

title: SFC consults on proposals to regulate virtual asset trading platforms
summary: The SFC launched a consultation on proposed requirements for operators of centralised virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs), ahead of a new licensing regime taking effect 1 June 2023. The proposals are based on the SFC's existing 2019 regulatory framework for VATPs trading at least one security token. They are benchmarked to the standards already applied to licensed securities brokers and to automated trading venues. A central question is whether licensed VATPs should be permitted to serve retail investors, and if so what additional investor-protection measures (suitability, token admission) would apply. Pre-existing platforms were told to start preparing to comply; those not intending to apply should prepare for orderly closure. Comments were due 31 March 2023.

key_points.point: A new licensing regime for centralised VATPs carrying on business in or actively marketing to Hong Kong was to take effect 1 June 2023.

Proposed requirements are benchmarked to the existing SFO rules that apply to licensed securities brokers and to automated trading venues, following the SFC's 'same business, same risks, same rules' principle.

The SFC specifically sought views on whether to allow licensed VATPs to serve retail investors, and what extra protections (for example, suitability in onboarding and token admission) should apply if so.
Pre-existing platforms intending to apply for a licence should begin reviewing and revising systems and controls; those not applying should prepare for orderly closure of their Hong Kong business.
A platform counts as 'pre-existing' if it already had a real and substantial footprint operating in Hong Kong before 1 June 2023.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this consultation previews the mandatory VATP licensing regime taking effect 1 June 2023. It creates no bank obligations directly. But it flags that any VA-trading-platform counterparty needed to prepare for licensing or wind down.

quote.text: same business, same risks, same rules
quote.locator: main text, quote from Julia Leung

reading_guide: Read the main release in full (short); skip the boilerplate Notes 1-6 except Note 6 (pre-existing definition). The attached 2019 Position Paper gives full background on custody/insurance benchmarks referenced by this consultation.
flags: This 2023 consultation proposed opening VATP access to retail investors for the first time — a correction to the common assumption (based on the still-referenced 2019 regime) that Hong Kong VATPs are restricted to professional investors only.

Its attachment, the SFC's 6 November 2019 Position Paper, is itself a historical/superseded regime (professional-investor-only, no retail access) but is the direct technical ancestor of the 2023 VATP Guidelines; it specifies the 98% cold-storage / max 2% hot-wallet rule, insurance (full hot-storage, ~95% cold-storage coverage), and the associated-entity trust-structure requirement that HoDA should recognize as the origin of the still-current custody benchmarks.

counterparty_due_diligence: Note pre-existing VA platform operators (including any the bank deals with) were expected to begin reviewing systems and controls for the incoming licensing regime commencing 1 June 2023 (para on 'Operators...should begin to review')
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should note the SFC's mandatory VATP licensing regime was set to begin 1 June 2023, following a consultation seeking views on retail access.

He states the government will review the potential for wider use of tokenisation in the capital market. supersedes_or_amends: Consultation on Proposed Amendments to Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Authorized Institutions) (18 Jan 2023)
summary: The HKMA sets out what banks said about its draft AML/CFT Guideline changes and how it responded. The changes implement the 2022 AMLO amendments, which introduced VASP licensing and updated CDD definitions. On virtual assets, the HKMA confirms banks stay under its own Guideline rather than the SFC's, with RIs referred to the SFC text via footnote 1. It also states banks may carry out VA transfers for customers if the statutory s.13A conditions are met. Other responses cover digital ID, trust beneficiaries, former PEPs, bearer shares and applying new rules to existing customers.

key_points.point: Following the AMLO amendments gazetted on 16 December 2022, the HKMA consulted banks from 18 January to 8 March 2023. It received comments from four industry associations.

The SFC's AML guideline, with its new virtual asset chapter, covers SFC licensees and SFC-licensed VASPs. Banks, including Registered Institutions (RIs), keep following the HKMA Guideline instead. Footnote 1 was updated so RIs and AI associated entities take into account the SFC text.

The HKMA states the AMLO does not bar banks from carrying out VA transfers for customers, provided section 13A of Schedule 2 is met. Banks should keep following HKMA circulars of 28 January 2022 and 27 April 2023 and may raise questions with the AML & Financial Crime Risk Division.

Private-sector remote-onboarding tools are not 'recognised digital identification systems' under Schedule 2; iAM Smart is. Existing remote onboarding practice under earlier HKMA circulars continues to apply.

For trusts, where beneficiaries are a class, banks may gather enough information to identify them at payout. A new para 4.4.13 lets banks verify beneficiaries using trustee-provided information on a risk basis.
Senior management approval is no longer required to stop applying EDD to a former PEP, but banks need sound internal controls and oversight for that decision.
Updated CDD rules can be applied to existing customers through normal periodic or trigger reviews. High-risk ones, such as non-Hong Kong PEPs, should be updated at or before their next review.
The revised Guideline was to be gazetted on 25 May 2023 and take effect on 1 June 2023.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: It is the HKMA's clearest statement that a bank may execute VA transfers for customers if s.13A of Schedule 2 is satisfied. It also confirms the bank answers to the HKMA Guideline, with SFC Chapter 12 relevant only through footnote 1.

quote.text: the AMLO does not prohibit AIs from carrying out virtual asset transfers

reading_guide: Read Part II section 4 (p.7) first, then 6.3 (p.9) and Part III (p.10); sections 1-3 and 5 are background for non-VA changes.
flags: Refers to HKMA VA circulars of 28 Jan 2022 and 27 Apr 2023, which are not in this batch; their text should be checked for bank VA-transfer expectations.

obligations: Meet s.13A Sch.2 AMLO before carrying out VA transfers for customers (Part II para 4.3)
Follow HKMA VA circulars of 28 Jan 2022 and 27 Apr 2023 (para 4.3)

controls_and_monitoring: Controls and oversight for disapplying EDD to former PEPs (para 3.2)
notifications_reporting: Questions on VA transfers can go to HKMA AML & Financial Crime Risk Division (para 4.3)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The HKMA permits bank VA transfers for customers subject to s.13A Sch.2; the board should know which HKMA circulars and statutory conditions govern them.

title: SFC concludes consultation on regulation of virtual asset trading platforms
supersedes_or_amends: SFC consults on proposals to regulate virtual asset trading platforms (23PR5, 20 Feb 2023)
summary: The SFC released Consultation Conclusions on the Proposed Regulatory Requirements for VATP Operators, following 152 written submissions. A significant majority of respondents supported allowing licensed VATPs to serve retail investors, subject to robust protections (suitability onboarding, governance, enhanced token due diligence, admission criteria, disclosures). The resulting Guidelines for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators took effect 1 June 2023, alongside related AML/CFT guidelines and Disciplinary Fining Guidelines gazetted 25 May 2023. The SFC noted that, as of commencement, it had not yet approved any VATP to serve retail investors, and most platforms accessible to the public remained unregulated.

key_points.point: 152 written submissions were received; a significant majority supported allowing licensed VATPs to serve retail investors.

The VATP Guidelines -- formally titled Guidelines for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators -- became effective 1 June 2023. They cover keeping client assets safe in custody, keeping client assets segregated, avoiding conflicts of interest, and cybersecurity.
Despite the regime starting on 1 June 2023, the SFC had not yet approved any VATP to serve retail investors. Most VATPs open to the public remained unregulated by the SFC.

On 25 May 2023 the SFC gazetted the VATP Guidelines, the AML/CFT Guideline for LCs and SFC-licensed VASPs, and the Prevention of ML/TF Guideline for Associated Entities. It also gazetted the Disciplinary Fining Guidelines.
Operators unwilling to meet SFC standards should proceed to orderly closure of their Hong Kong business.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: The retail-access decision and 1 June 2023 commencement date here bind VATPs, not the bank directly. A compliance head needs it mainly to confirm which VATP-facing instrument set (VATP Guidelines plus AML/CFT Guideline) now governs any VATP the bank refers clients to or partners with.

quote.text: same business, same risks, same rules
quote.locator: main text, quote from Julia Leung

reading_guide: Read main text in full; Notes give the exact list of gazetted instruments and dates, useful as a citation index.
flags: Retail access was approved in principle here, but the SFC explicitly states no VATP had yet been approved to serve retail investors as of commencement — retail access was not automatic or immediate upon regime start.

counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm any VATP counterparty operates under the VATP Guidelines effective 1 June 2023 (custody, segregation, conflicts, cybersecurity) and check it against SFC's published lists (main text para 4-5)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should note that, as of regime commencement, the SFC had approved no VATP for retail access, so any bank retail referral to a VATP needed separate verification of that platform's specific approvals.

title: Consultation Conclusions on the Proposed Regulatory Requirements for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators Licensed by the Securities and Futures Commission
supersedes_or_amends: Terms and Conditions for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators (VATP Terms and Conditions)
summary: The SFC finalises the rulebook for platforms it licenses to trade virtual assets, after a public consultation that drew 152 submissions. It allows retail investors onto licensed platforms, subject to knowledge and risk checks, exposure limits, and a narrow list of large, index-listed tokens eligible for retail trading. It sets custody, insurance, financial soundness and cybersecurity standards for platform operators. It also folds virtual-asset anti-money-laundering rules, including a Travel Rule for virtual-asset transfers, into the SFC's AML Guideline. The finalised texts, annexed as appendices, took effect on 1 June 2023, with a 12-month transition for firms already licensed.

key_points.point: Licensed platforms may serve retail clients, but only after assessing each client's virtual-asset knowledge, risk tolerance and personal exposure limit. A client is treated as knowledgeable once they have made five or more virtual-asset trades in the past three years.
Stablecoins cannot be offered to retail investors until Hong Kong's own stablecoin regime is in place. The SFC sees unresolved run and redemption risk in unregulated stablecoins.

A retail-eligible token needs a track record of at least 12 months, except for security tokens. It must appear in at least two independent large-cap indices, one of which follows IOSCO benchmark standards. The SFC will not publish its own eligible-token list.

Every platform must run a token admission and review committee, drawn from senior managers for the core business, compliance, risk and IT lines. This committee sets and enforces listing and delisting rules, and reports to the board at least monthly.

Before listing any token, the platform must complete due diligence covering the team, regulatory status, liquidity, technical security, governance and legal risk. For retail-eligible tokens, it must also confirm the token is not a security under the Securities and Futures Ordinance.

The SFC dropped its original plan to require platforms to file a lawyer's written opinion confirming a token is not a security, citing cost. Platforms still have to satisfy themselves of this before retail listing.
Token listings need an independent smart-contract audit for security flaws. The platform may rely on an audit the token issuer itself commissioned, rather than always ordering its own.

Client virtual assets must be split 98% cold storage and up to 2% hot or other storage. They must be held through a dedicated, wholly owned custody subsidiary, called the Associated Entity, with keys generated and kept in Hong Kong.

Platforms need a compensation arrangement -- insurance, ring-fenced funds, virtual assets, or a bank guarantee, alone or combined. It must cover 50% of cold-storage client holdings and 100% of hot or other-storage holdings, checked daily against the actual value held.

Proprietary trading in virtual assets by the platform itself stays banned. But the SFC relaxed the original blanket ban, so other group companies (affiliates) may trade or market-make, as long as it does not go through the licensed platform.
Platforms may not offer deposit-taking, lending, borrowing or yield/earn-type products alongside their trading service; their role is limited to matching client orders.

A platform must keep a minimum paid-up share capital of HK$5 million at all times. It must also hold liquid capital of at least HK$3 million, or the Financial Resources Rules basic amount if higher. On top of that, it needs 12 months of operating costs in liquid, non-virtual-asset form, held in Hong Kong.
A platform must notify the SFC within one business day if liquid capital falls below 120% of the required minimum, or below half of the last reported figure. Other solvency triggers apply too.

Platforms need a responsible officer accountable for cybersecurity governance. They must also commission an independent technology audit at least once a year, covering the trading and custody systems.

The Travel Rule requires an ordering platform to get and pass on originator and recipient details to the receiving institution, for virtual-asset transfers of HK$8,000 or more. A shorter dataset applies below that threshold. The SFC allowed submission 'as soon as practicable', rather than strictly immediately, as an interim concession until 1 January 2024.

Transfers to or from wallets not hosted by a regulated institution require extra risk-based checks, including regularly reconfirming who owns or controls the wallet, not just a one-off check. Platforms may only whitelist wallets they assess as reliable.
Occasional (one-off, non-account) transactions are not permitted; every customer must go through full onboarding and a business relationship before trading.

The SFC can fine a regulated VA trading platform up to HK$10 million, or three times the profit made or loss avoided, whichever is higher. This applies for misconduct or for no longer being fit and proper.

key_points.point: A platform that wants to trade both non-security and security tokens is expected to hold both an SFO licence and an AMLO virtual-asset-service-provider licence. One person can act as responsible officer under both regimes, rather than needing four separate officers.

The finalised VATP Guidelines, AML Guideline amendments and Disciplinary Fining Guidelines took effect on 1 June 2023. Already-licensed platforms get a 12-month transition period before their old Terms and Conditions licensing condition is withdrawn.

If the group's platform serves retail clients, it must run the token-admission-and-review committee, knowledge/risk onboarding and index-eligibility screening described in Appendix A paras 7.1-7.8 and 9.4-9.7.
controls_and_monitoring: Daily monitoring of the compensation arrangement's adequacy against actual custodied client virtual-asset value (Appendix A para 10.23).
At least annual independent technology/cybersecurity audit of trading and custody systems (Appendix A para 12.7).
Ongoing due diligence and periodic re-review of every listed token against admission criteria, with a documented delisting process (Appendix A para 7.11).

Notification to the SFC within one business day of specified financial-soundness triggers, e.g. liquid capital falling below 120% of the required minimum (Appendix A para 6.9).
Immediate notification to the SFC of material system failures, breaches of the Guidelines, or disciplinary action by another regulator (Appendix A para 16.7).

Check the counterparty's cold/hot storage split and whether its compensation arrangement (insurance, ring-fenced funds, or bank guarantee) meets the 50%/100% coverage standard.
Check the counterparty's Travel Rule compliance posture for virtual-asset transfers, including its handling of unhosted-wallet transfers.
Check for any SFC disciplinary or fining history, since findings are made public.

summary: The HKMA sets out what banks said about its draft changes to the AML/CFT Guideline, and how it responded. The changes carry out the 2022 amendments to the Anti-Money Laundering Ordinance (AMLO), which brought in VASP licensing and updated customer-checking (CDD) definitions. On virtual assets, the HKMA confirms banks stay under its own Guideline rather than the SFC's, with registered institutions (RIs) pointed to the SFC text via footnote 1. It also states banks may carry out VA transfers for customers if the statutory section 13A conditions are met. Other responses cover digital ID, trust beneficiaries, former politically exposed persons (PEPs), bearer shares, and applying new rules to existing customers.

key_points.point: Following the AMLO amendments gazetted on 16 December 2022, the HKMA consulted banks from 18 January to 8 March 2023 and received comments from four industry associations.

The SFC's AML guideline, with its new virtual asset chapter, covers SFC licensees and SFC-licensed VASPs. Banks, including RIs, keep following the HKMA Guideline; footnote 1 was updated so RIs and AI associated entities have regard to the SFC text.

The HKMA states the AMLO does not bar banks from carrying out VA transfers for customers, provided section 13A of Schedule 2 is met. Banks should keep following HKMA circulars of 28 January 2022 and 27 April 2023, and may raise questions with the AML & Financial Crime Risk Division.

Private-sector remote-onboarding tools are not 'recognised digital identification systems' under Schedule 2; iAM Smart is. Existing remote onboarding practice under earlier HKMA circulars continues to apply.

For trusts, where beneficiaries are a class, banks may gather enough information to identify them at payout. A new para 4.4.13 lets banks verify beneficiaries using trustee-provided information on a risk basis.
Senior management approval is no longer required to stop applying EDD to a former PEP, but banks need sound internal controls and oversight for that decision.
Updated CDD rules can be applied to existing customers through normal periodic or trigger reviews. High-risk ones, such as non-Hong Kong PEPs, should be updated at or before their next review.
The revised Guideline was to be gazetted on 25 May 2023 and take effect on 1 June 2023.

Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Authorized Institutions) (Revised May 2023)
supersedes_or_amends: Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Authorized Institutions), Revised October 2018 (SPM AML-2 Oct-2018)
summary: This is the HKMA's binding AML/CFT rulebook for all banks (authorized institutions), including those registered with the SFC. The May 2023 revision came into force on 1 June 2023, alongside the 2022 AMLO amendments that created the VASP licensing regime. Its virtual-asset content is thin and targeted. It has a HK$8,000 trigger for customer checks (CDD) on occasional VA transfers, matching record-keeping, and a cross-reference to section 13A of Schedule 2. It also has correspondent-style due diligence for overseas VASPs, and a footnote pointing RIs to the SFC guideline's VA chapter. Everything else a digital-asset business line touches, such as risk assessment, new-product assessment, CDD, monitoring, sanctions screening, suspicious-transaction reports and records, is governed by the generic chapters. It has nothing specific on stablecoins, unhosted wallets or VA red flags.

key_points.point: The Guideline is the HKMA's AML/CFT rulebook for every Authorized Institution (AI), including AIs that are also SFC Registered Institutions (RIs). It is issued under the AML/CFT Ordinance (AMLO, Cap 615) and the Banking Ordinance; breaches can lead to disciplinary or other action under either law.
Both 'must' and 'should' in this Guideline denote a mandatory requirement, so 'should' is not optional wording for an AI.

Virtual-asset (VA) cross-reference: RIs, and AIs that are associated entities of SFC licensees, must additionally have regard to the SFC's AML/CFT Guideline for Licensed Corporations and SFC-licensed VASPs. This includes its Chapter 12 on virtual assets. This reaches only AIs acting as RIs or associated entities; it does not import SFC Chapter 12 for a bank's general banking business.

Non-compliance can count against the Seventh Schedule authorization criteria under the Banking Ordinance, on adequate systems of control. Courts and the HKMA take the Guideline into account when judging Schedule 2 breaches.

Penalties: an AI that knowingly breaches a specified AMLO provision faces up to 2 years' jail and a HK$1m fine, or 7 years if intent to defraud. Staff and managers who cause a breach face the same. The HKMA can also impose a pecuniary penalty up to HK$10m, or three times the profit gained or cost avoided, whichever is higher.

Each AI should run a documented institution-wide ML/TF risk assessment covering customers, customer and operating jurisdictions, and products, services, transactions and delivery channels. Senior management approves the results, and it is refreshed at least every two years and on material trigger events.

Before launching a new product, business practice or delivery mechanism, or using a new or developing technology, the bank should first weigh the ML/TF risks involved and put mitigants in place. This is the hook for assessing any VA, tokenisation or stablecoin-related service before launch.

The board, or a delegated committee, and senior management must understand the bank's ML/TF risks and receive timely management information. Senior management appoints a management-level Compliance Officer (CO) and a senior Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO), normally based in Hong Kong and independent of business lines as far as size allows.

A Hong Kong-incorporated AI should apply these standards group-wide to overseas branches and subsidiaries doing financial-institution business, and apply the higher of home or host rules. It should tell the HKMA if host law blocks compliance.

The four core customer due diligence (CDD) steps are: identify and verify the customer, and identify the beneficial owner and take reasonable steps to verify them, including understanding ownership and control. The other two steps are: understand the purpose of the relationship, and verify anyone acting for the customer and their authority.

VA transfer threshold: for a walk-in (occasional) customer, an AI must complete CDD before executing a virtual asset transfer of HK$8,000 or more. This applies whether done in one go or split into operations that appear linked. The same trigger applies to wire transfers, while other occasional transactions use HK$120,000.

Footnote 15 points AIs to section 13A of Schedule 2 to the AMLO for virtual asset transfers. The Guideline itself gives no further VA transfer (travel rule) detail, so the statutory text of s.13A is the operative source for a bank's VA transfer obligations.

AIs should watch for a series of small occasional transactions that together reach the HK$8,000 threshold for wire or VA transfers. Linkage is judged by pattern, such as the same payee or regular transfers, and timeframe. CDD applies once the threshold is met.

High-risk relationships need enhanced due diligence (EDD): senior management approval to open or continue, and enhanced ongoing monitoring. Listed higher-risk indicators include anonymous transactions and frequent payments from unknown or unconnected third parties; the Guideline does not name VAs or VASPs as an automatic high-risk category.

Possible EDD steps include more customer information, source of wealth and source of funds, and reasons for transactions. Another possible step is requiring the first payment from an account in the customer's own name at a bank with similar CDD standards.

For customers onboarded without being physically present, such as online, the AI should apply at least one additional safeguard. This can be extra identity verification, supplementary checks, or a first payment routed through an account in the customer's name at a comparably regulated institution.
An AI must not open or keep anonymous or fictitious-name accounts; numbered accounts get the same CDD as any other account.
Ongoing monitoring has two parts: keeping CDD records current through periodic and trigger-based reviews, and scrutinising transactions. High-risk customers must be reviewed at least annually.

Transaction monitoring should be sized to the business and product risk, look at relationships across accounts and business lines, and use parameters and thresholds that are documented, regularly reviewed and independently validated.

Where activity does not fit the customer profile, or is complex or unusual with no clear economic or lawful purpose, the AI should enquire and record its findings and rationale in writing. It should file a suspicious transaction report (STR) with the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit (JFIU) if suspicion remains.

Sanctions: the AI keeps, or subscribes to with sample testing, a consolidated designations database. It screens customers and beneficial owners at onboarding and against new listings, and screens all relevant parties to a cross-border wire transfer before sending it. The text does not separately address VA transfers.

Record-keeping: CDD and account records are kept for the life of the relationship plus at least five years. Records for occasional wire or VA transfers of HK$8,000 or more are kept for five years after the transaction; transaction records must allow reconstruction and are kept five years after completion.

The wire-transfer chapter covers originator and recipient information for ordering, intermediary and beneficiary institutions, the HK$8,000 threshold, and missing-information handling, and is written for electronic transfers of money. It does not mention virtual assets, so it should not be read as the bank's VA travel-rule text.

Correspondent-type services to VASPs: an AI may provide correspondent-like services to a virtual asset service provider, as FATF defines them, or to another financial institution outside Hong Kong. It should then apply the cross-border correspondent banking measures in paras 11.6 and, where relevant, 11.13. This applies even though the AMLO strictly requires them only for respondent banks. Footnote 79 carves out financial institutions as defined in the AMLO.

For an overseas VASP customer, the AI should establish whether the account is for the VASP's own corporate or settlement use, or to serve the VASP's own clients. If the latter, the paras 11.6/11.13 measures apply. The AI may encourage or require separate accounts for the two uses. Those measures mean understanding the business, checking reputation and supervision, and assessing and being satisfied with AML/CFT controls. They also mean senior management sign-off, documented responsibilities, and no relationship until done.

reading_guide: Read fn 1 (p.3) and paras 2.10-2.11 (p.12) first. Then read 4.2.1-4.2.5 with fn 14-15 (pp.20-21) and 8.4 (p.71). Next read 11.6-11.25 (pp.81-86), then Chapters 5 and 6 for monitoring and screening. Chapter 12 (private banking) and the PEP detail can be skimmed for VA purposes.
flags: No provisions on stablecoins, unhosted/self-hosted wallets, VA-specific red flags or blockchain analytics anywhere in the Guideline.

Chapter 10 (wire transfers) covers money transfers only; the only VA travel-rule hook is footnote 15 pointing to s.13A of Schedule 2 AMLO. Bank VA transfer (travel rule) obligations must be read from the statute (and any separate HKMA circulars), not from this Guideline.
Footnote 1 applies SFC AML Guideline Chapter 12 (VA) only to RIs and AI associated entities, and only as 'have regard to'. Corrects the assumption that SFC Chapter 12 binds a bank's whole business.

Para 11.23 extends correspondent-banking measures to VASPs located OUTSIDE Hong Kong; fn 79 excludes AMLO-defined FIs. The Guideline says nothing about how to treat Hong Kong-licensed VATPs as customers beyond normal CDD/EDD.

The HKMA consultation conclusions (para 4.3) confirm the AMLO does not prohibit AIs from carrying out VA transfers for customers if s.13A Sch.2 is met, and direct AIs to HKMA circulars of 28 Jan 2022 and 27 Apr 2023; neither circular is part of this Guideline.

Annual review of high-risk customers and high-risk respondents (paras 5.3, 11.17)

Independent audit review of AML/CFT Systems (paras 3.11-3.12)
notifications_reporting: STRs to JFIU where suspicion arises (paras 5.12, 7.1 ff.)
Inform HKMA if host-country law prevents an overseas branch/subsidiary applying HK standards (para 3.19)
Provide the institutional risk assessment to HKMA on request (para 2.3(e))

Payable-through use: be satisfied the VASP performs CDD and can supply customer data on request (para 11.13)
Consider separate own-account and client-service accounts for overseas VASP customers (para 11.25)
