title: Circular on transitional arrangements of the new licensing regime for virtual asset trading platforms
summary: The SFC set out transition rules under the AMLO for virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs) trading non-security tokens, as the new licensing regime began on 1 June 2023. A 'non-contravention arrangement' lets VATPs already genuinely present in Hong Kong before 1 June 2023 keep operating for 12 months, until 31 May 2024, without breaching licensing rules. A 'deeming arrangement' lets qualifying existing VATPs that file a complete licence application by 29 February 2024 be treated as licensed from 1 June 2024, while the SFC finishes its review. VATPs that were not doing business in Hong Kong before 1 June 2023 get none of this relief and must be licensed before starting up. Platforms trading both security and non-security tokens need licences under both the SFO and the AMLO.

key_points.point: The transition rules apply only to VATPs trading non-security tokens; there is no transition period for meeting SFO (security token) rules.

VATPs genuinely doing business in Hong Kong before 1 June 2023 may keep operating from 1 June 2023 to 31 May 2024. This is a 12-month non-contravention window, and does not breach AMLO licensing rules.

To count as 'genuinely present,' factors include being incorporated in Hong Kong, having a physical office, and running central management from Hong Kong. Other factors are Hong Kong-based key staff, real trading activity, and other supporting evidence. A shell company is not enough.

To qualify for deeming, treated as licensed automatically from 1 June 2024, an existing VATP must file a complete WINGS application between 1 June 2023 and 29 February 2024. It must also meet further conditions on confirmations and evidence.

VATPs with no Hong Kong footprint before 1 June 2023 cannot use these transition rules. They must not start business or actively market to Hong Kong investors until formally licensed; doing so unlicensed is a criminal offence.
An existing VATP must submit at least two Responsible Officer (RO) applications with its licence application. At least one RO must live in Hong Kong, to meet the minimum RO condition for deeming.
Applications filed after 29 February 2024 cannot qualify for deeming, and the SFC cannot extend this statutory deadline.
VATPs trading both security and non-security tokens should apply for licences under both the SFO and the AMLO through one combined application.

numbers_and_dates.item: New criminal VA offences took effect

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this sets the AMLO transition and deeming timetable, which decides whether a VATP counterparty was legitimately operating, deemed-licensed, or required to shut down. That is essential for reviewing any VATP relationship active in 2023-2024.

quote.text: only having 'shell' operations in Hong Kong would not suffice

reading_guide: Read paras 1-20 (eligibility, non-contravention, deeming) and 26-33 (responsible-officer requirements, dual licensing). Skip repeated footnote cross-references to AMLO schedule sections. The Appendix timeline graphic (attachment 273818ad4232) is a useful one-page summary.
flags: Being 'deemed licensed' from 1 June 2024 is not equivalent to being vetted or fit-and-proper-approved by the SFC — it is a conditional, provisional status pending final licence determination, and the SFC can issue a 'no-deeming notice' at any point.

counterparty_due_diligence: When dealing with a VATP counterparty during the transition period, check whether it is (i) a licensed VATP, (ii) an existing VATP that qualifies for the non-contravention or deeming arrangements (application due 29 Feb 2024, deemed licensed from 1 June 2024), or (iii) neither, meaning it was required to close by 31 May 2024.
If a VATP counterparty is dually licensed (trading both security and non-security tokens), confirm it holds approvals under both the SFO and the AMLO.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board should understand that the transition rules created a period lasting into mid-2024 when some VATP counterparties were only 'deemed licensed' pending the SFC's final review, not yet fully vetted.

title: Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism for Licensed Corporations and SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers
supersedes_or_amends: Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism for Licensed Corporations, sixth edition (September 2021)
summary: This is the SFC's seventh-edition AML/CFT rulebook for licensed corporations (LCs) and SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform operators, in force since June 2023. Most of its chapters cover generic bank-style controls: risk-based assessment, customer checks, ongoing monitoring, sanctions screening, suspicious-report filing, record-keeping and staff training. Chapter 12 adds virtual-asset-specific rules binding on LCs and SFC-licensed VASPs, including a Hong Kong version of the international travel rule. This rule requires firms to collect and pass on sender and receiver details for crypto transfers. It also requires counterparty due-diligence duties, and extra checks for transfers to wallets not held by a regulated firm. A bank does not follow this Guideline directly for its banking business, which the HKMA's own AML/CFT Guideline governs. Only a bank's SFC-registered institution (RI) arm must have regard to specific cross-referenced parts of this Guideline. These are the customer definition, the correspondent-relationship provisions, Chapter 12, and the illustrative suspicious-indicator appendix. Otherwise, the bank meets this Guideline only as a due-diligence benchmark for its VATP or LC counterparties.

key_points.point: The guideline is legally grounded in the anti-money-laundering ordinance and the securities law. A firm's failure to follow it can count as misconduct affecting its fitness to hold a licence. It applies to SFC-licensed corporations and SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers. A bank's RI arm is required only to have regard to specific cross-referenced parts, see para 1.6: the customer definition, correspondent-relationship provisions, Chapter 12, and the suspicious-indicator appendix. It need not follow the whole Guideline.

Chapter 12 covers both virtual assets as legally defined and any tokens that count as securities under the securities law. It applies to firms that hold an SFC VASP licence, and to LCs when carrying out VA-related or ML/TF-risk-relevant business.
Before moving crypto worth HK$8,000 or more, the sending firm must capture and record both the sender's and the receiver's identifying details, including an account or wallet reference.
The sending firm has to pass that sender/receiver data on to the receiving platform securely and before or at the same time as the transfer itself.

A firm should vet any platform it transacts with on the other end of a crypto transfer. This covers its licensing status, ownership, and whether its AML controls and data-security practices are adequate.
Deals with a counterparty that is a shell entity with no real presence and no group oversight are banned outright.

For transfers to or from a wallet not controlled by a regulated firm, the firm should still gather comparable sender and receiver information from its own customer. It should also assess whether the wallet looks trustworthy before proceeding.
Firms' screening mechanisms should also cover every party in a crypto transfer against sanctions and watch lists before the transfer goes through.
Sender/receiver data collected for a crypto transfer, and records tied to occasional transactions above the threshold, must be kept for at least five years.
Deposits or withdrawals routed through a third party's crypto wallet get extra scrutiny, and firms are encouraged to pre-approve a whitelist of wallets belonging to clients or vetted third parties.

numbers_and_dates.item: Travel-rule and CDD threshold for virtual asset transfers/occasional transactions
Minimum record retention for CDD documents and virtual asset transfer data

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this Guideline binds its SFC-licensed VATP and LC counterparties directly. Its Chapter 12 travel-rule and counterparty due-diligence content sets the benchmark a compliance head should check any such counterparty against. It does not bind the bank's own banking business directly. For the bank's own AML/CFT programme, the governing text is the HKMA's AML/CFT Guideline. The bank's RI arm need only 'have regard to' the customer-definition, correspondent-relationship, Chapter 12 and suspicious-indicator parts of this Guideline (para 1.6). It need not comply with it as an SFC licensee would.
reading_guide: Go straight to Chapter 12 (p.140-189). Skim Chapters 2-9 only for cross-references Chapter 12 points to, such as paras 4.20 on correspondent relationships. Skip the generic securities-sector CDD detail not tied to virtual assets.
flags: Corrects an earlier over-statement: this Guideline binds SFC-licensed corporations and SFC-licensed VASPs directly (para 12.1.2); it does not bind a bank's own banking business, and a bank's RI arm is only required to 'have regard to' specific cross-referenced parts (para 1.6), not to comply with the whole Guideline as a licensee would. Cite the HKMA's own AML/CFT Guideline (For Authorized Institutions) for the bank's direct obligations, and this Guideline only for counterparty (VATP/LC) due-diligence benchmarks or the bank's own RI 'have regard to' duty.

obligations: As an RI, have regard to Chapter 12 (and the customer-definition, correspondent-relationship and suspicious-indicator parts) of this Guideline for the bank's securities/VA-related RI business (para 1.6); the bank's own primary AML/CFT obligations are set by the HKMA's AML/CFT Guideline
controls_and_monitoring: Where relevant to RI business, risk-based transaction monitoring and blockchain-analytics tooling to trace wallet addresses linked to illicit activity (para 12.7.2-12.7.3)
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm a VATP or LC counterparty's licensing/registration status, AML/CFT control quality, and travel-rule compliance capability, since this Guideline is what the SFC requires that counterparty to meet (para 12.13.6-12.13.9)
For unhosted wallets used by a VATP/LC counterparty's customers, check the counterparty assesses wallet reliability and ownership/control before accepting transfers (para 12.14.2-12.14.3)
Treat a counterparty's dealings with shell VASPs or shell financial institutions as a breach of its own obligations under this Guideline (para 12.13.13)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board/risk committee should understand that this Guideline's Chapter 12 travel-rule and counterparty due-diligence duties bind the bank's SFC-licensed VATP/LC counterparties directly, and bind the bank's own RI arm only as a 'have regard to' duty on specific cross-referenced parts; the bank's own AML/CFT programme is built on the HKMA's Guideline, not this one.

title: SFC Disciplinary Fining Guidelines (for regulated persons under Part 5B of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance)
summary: These guidelines are made under section 53ZSS(1) of AMLO Part 5B. They explain how the SFC decides whether and how much to fine a regulated VATP operator or its staff found guilty of misconduct or unfitness. The maximum fine is HK$10 million, or, if larger, three times the profit gained or the loss avoided, and can be assessed per affected person. The guidelines list general factors that make conduct more or less serious, then detailed specific factors the SFC will weigh. These cover the nature and impact of the conduct, whether it was intentional or negligent, cooperation and self-reporting, remedial steps, prior disciplinary record, and consistency with past cases.

key_points.point: Maximum fine under s.53ZSP(3)(c) is HK$10 million or three times the profit gained/loss avoided, whichever is greater, and may be multiplied by the number of persons affected.
SFC will not impose a fine where facts warrant only a public reprimand, and will publicise all fining decisions as policy.
Intentional or reckless conduct, conduct damaging market integrity, or conduct facilitating money laundering/terrorist financing is treated as more serious.
Timely self-reporting to the SFC, full disclosure, cooperation and remedial action (including client compensation) are mitigating specific considerations.
A fine should not be set so as to place a firm or individual in financial jeopardy, save where financial distress is deliberately engineered to avoid a fine.

numbers_and_dates.value: HK$10 million or 3x profit gained/loss avoided, whichever greater

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this sets out the fining framework its counterparty VATPs, and any bank entity itself licensed under AMLO Part 5B, face for AML/CFT or fitness-and-properness breaches. It is a useful benchmark when assessing the enforcement risk of a VATP relationship.

title: Guidelines for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators
summary: These are the SFC's detailed operating rules for VATP operators licensed under the SFO or the AMLO, or both. They cover fitness-and-properness, competence and training of staff, financial soundness, token admission, client dealing, custody of client assets, governance, cybersecurity, conflicts of interest, record keeping, auditors and ongoing reporting duties. A VATP must hold client assets through a separate Associated Entity, and must keep 98% of those assets in cold storage. Retail clients may only trade large-cap tokens that meet strict listing criteria. The guidelines set the baseline a bank should expect any licensed VATP counterparty in Hong Kong to meet.

key_points.point: A VATP must be either an SFC Type 1/Type 7 licensed corporation or hold an AMLO virtual asset service licence. It should keep client assets on trust for those clients, held through a separate, wholly-owned Associated Entity that does no other business.

Directors, responsible officers and licensed representatives must meet fitness-and-properness and competence tests, including recognised exam papers, minimum industry experience and continuing training hours.

A VATP must at all times maintain HK$5,000,000 minimum paid-up capital and liquid capital above a required threshold. It should keep at least 12 months of operating expenses in liquid non-crypto assets in Hong Kong.

A token admission and review committee, including compliance, risk and IT heads, should set and enforce criteria for listing, suspending and delisting tokens, and report to the board at least monthly.

Before listing any token the platform should run documented due diligence covering the project team, legal status, liquidity, technical design and money-laundering risk, and commission an independent smart-contract audit.
Tokens offered to retail clients should not be securities (unless a prospectus is used) and should be included in at least two independent, IOSCO-aligned large-cap indices.

Platforms should not offer algorithmic trading, virtual asset futures or derivatives, or financial accommodation (margin) to clients to buy tokens, or yield-generating uses of client tokens. They should not engage in proprietary trading or market making on own account.

Clients (other than professional/institutional investors) should be assessed for virtual-asset knowledge, risk profile and a personal exposure limit before trading, and complex products need extra suitability checks and warnings.

At least 98% of client virtual assets should be held in cold storage, such as HSM-based storage. Strict controls apply to private-key generation, multi-person access, and Hong Kong-based storage of seeds and keys.
A VATP should maintain an SFC-approved compensation arrangement (insurance, ring-fenced funds, or bank guarantee) covering 50% of cold-storage and 100% of hot/other-storage client virtual assets.

Client money should be paid into segregated accounts with a Hong Kong authorized institution, or an SFC-agreed overseas bank, within one business day. It may only be used for client-authorised purposes.
The platform should run an independent market-surveillance system from a reputable provider, reviewed at least annually, and notify the SFC promptly of any suspected manipulation.

Cybersecurity requires a responsible officer for the platform, two-factor client login, annual independent cybersecurity assessment (including penetration testing and custody-system source-code review), and a tested contingency plan.
Front-office and back-office functions, and compliance and internal audit, should be segregated with separate reporting lines, and an independent risk-management and compliance function should exist.

Records tied to client assets, KYC, due diligence and suitability should be kept at least 7 years. Order/contract and audit-log records should be kept at least 2 years, and platform design documentation for 2 years after the system is retired.

Employee dealing in virtual assets should go through the platform where practicable, be reported to senior management, and is subject to front-running and insider-dealing controls; client orders always take priority.

Adding or removing a retail-available token needs the SFC's prior written approval; professional-investor-only tokens need advance written notice. Material incidents, system failures and rule breaches should be notified to the SFC.

Platforms should fully disclose to clients the custodial arrangements and standard risk warnings: volatility, irreversibility, no legal-tender status, and no Investor Compensation Fund cover. Clients should understand virtual assets do not enjoy the same statutory protection as securities.

Auditors of the platform and its Associated Entity must report to the SFC any breach they find of the financial soundness, custody or record-keeping parts of the Guidelines. This is a reportable matter under s.53ZSD(4) AMLO.

A single client should not be allowed to hold multiple accounts, other than sub-accounts. Contract notes, monthly statements and receipts should be issued to clients within set timeframes, the 2nd/7th business day rules.

numbers_and_dates.value: 50% of cold-storage assets, 100% of hot/other-storage assets
higher of HK$3,000,000 or basic amount under Financial Resources Rules
by end of 2nd business day after the trade

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the primary rulebook against which it must due-diligence any Hong Kong VATP it partners with, refers clients to, or banks as a customer. The cold-storage, compensation, segregation and reporting thresholds here are the benchmarks compliance should check the VATP actually meets. It also frames the SFC's expectations on suitability and disclosure that a bank distributing or facilitating access to VATP services should mirror.

quote.text: the more stringent requirement should prevail

reading_guide: For a bank compliance head, the core due-diligence checklist for a VATP counterparty has four parts. These are Part X (Custody, p.62), Part VI (Financial Soundness, p.36), Part VII (Token admission, p.40) and Part XVI (Reporting, p.94). The Fitness, Competence and training detail in Parts II-IV (p.7-35), and Schedule 4's application forms, can be skimmed.
flags: Retail access to a token requires two independent large-cap indices from separate providers, effectively excluding most tokens from retail trading on licensed VATPs, which is a stricter retail gate than in many other jurisdictions

controls_and_monitoring: Where a bank refers or onboards clients to a VATP, or accepts a VATP as a banking customer, compliance should periodically confirm the VATP still meets the cold-storage (98%), compensation-arrangement and segregated-account requirements set out here (paras 10.6, 10.11, 10.22).
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm VATP SFC/AMLO licence status and CE number (para 16.1, Schedule 4)
Check the VATP's token admission criteria and whether retail-offered tokens meet the two-index large-cap test (para 7.8)

Confirm client money is held in segregated accounts with an authorized institution (para 10.11)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board/risk committee should be told which VATPs the bank has commercial exposure to (custody banking, referral, or as a client) and whether each currently satisfies the SFC's custody, compensation and financial-soundness requirements.

title: Frequently Asked Questions on streamlined approach for compliance with suitability obligations when dealing with sophisticated professional investors
summary: This is a seven-question FAQ explaining how intermediaries should apply the SFC's streamlined suitability approach for sophisticated professional investors (SPIs). It covers evidencing SPI status, using a representative's investment knowledge, and categorising products, with virtual assets and VA-related products as their own category. It also covers what a Product Category Information Statement should cover, and setting and reviewing a streamlining threshold. Other topics are monitoring that threshold, including via designated sub-accounts, and handling leveraged or margin transactions under the approach.

key_points.point: An SPI's requisite knowledge or experience can be shown by qualifications, work experience, or by having executed at least five transactions in the same product category within the past three years. This includes transactions made via power of attorney or joint accounts.

Intermediaries should create Product Categories such as accumulators/decumulators, insurance-linked-securities funds, loss-absorption debt instruments, virtual assets, and VA-related products, keeping each separate from the others.
An SPI may specify their own streamlining threshold appropriate to their financial situation, and the intermediary is required to keep records of the rationale supporting that threshold.

Intermediaries are not expected to force-unwind a client's exposure just because it later exceeds the streamlining threshold. But they may restrict further top-ups or execute new trades outside the designated account instead.

Intermediaries may execute leveraged or margin trades on behalf of an SPI using the streamlined approach, so long as these stay within the SPI's specified Product Categories and threshold. But they must put in place effective systems and controls that keep the gross leveraged exposure at or below that threshold.

numbers_and_dates.item: Trading-experience threshold for demonstrating VA/product knowledge
numbers_and_dates.value: ≥5 transactions in same category within past 3 years

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this confirms that virtual assets sit in their own ring-fenced Product Category, even for sophisticated clients under the lighter streamlined suitability regime. It sets concrete, auditable criteria, five trades in three years, that the bank's product-categorisation and threshold-monitoring controls must be built around.

quote.text: virtual assets (“VA”) and (v) VA-related products

reading_guide: All three pages are relevant; read in full.

obligations: Maintain records of the rationale for each SPI's streamlining threshold, Q5
Keep virtual assets and VA-related products as distinct Product Categories, Q3
controls_and_monitoring: Systems and controls to monitor gross exposure (including leveraged) against the client-set streamlining threshold, on execution and after top-ups, Q6-Q7
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: None beyond confirming the product-categorisation and threshold-monitoring controls for VA exposure under any streamlined-suitability programme are auditable.

title: Warning: Virtual asset trading platforms engaging in improper practices
summary: The SFC describes patterns of bad behaviour it has seen among unlicensed VATPs during the new licensing regime's transition period. Some falsely claim to have already applied for a licence. Others set up new entities in anticipation of the transitional rules, or keep launching products, such as virtual-asset 'deposits' or 'savings', that the new regime does not allow. The SFC says such conduct will count against a platform's fitness and properness when it does apply for a licence. It repeats that operating in Hong Kong without a licence is a criminal offence.

key_points.point: Some unlicensed VATPs falsely claim to have already applied to the SFC for a licence.
Making a fraudulent or reckless misrepresentation to induce virtual-asset trading is itself an offence.
False licence-application claims will be weighed against the platform when it later seeks an actual licence.
Platforms operating in Hong Kong before 1 June 2023 got a transitional window, but the SFC can still refuse to treat them as 'deemed licensed' if it doubts they can meet requirements.
key_points.locator: heading 'VATPs which do not comply...', para 1

key_points.point: Products like virtual-asset 'deposits', 'savings' or 'earnings' offered to retail clients are not allowed under the new VATP regime.
key_points.locator: heading 'VATPs which do not comply...', para 4

key_points.point: Established unlicensed entities already doing VA business in Hong Kong must apply for a licence or shut down that business.
Operating an unlicensed virtual-asset business in Hong Kong is a criminal offence.

numbers_and_dates.value: fine and up to 7 years' imprisonment

title: Warning: Virtual asset trading platforms engaging in improper practices
summary: The SFC warned that some unlicensed VATPs were falsely claiming to have applied for an SFC licence. It said this is itself a criminal misrepresentation offence under AMLO section 53ZRG, and will count against future fitness-and-properness assessments. It also flagged VATPs setting up new entities, or continuing under existing ones, to launch products the new licensing regime does not allow. These include retail-facing VA deposits, savings or earnings arrangements. The SFC said any past non-compliant conduct, and whether it could reasonably have been avoided or is being genuinely unwound, will feed into licence decisions. It reminded the public that most currently accessible VATPs are unlicensed, and that trading on them carries a risk of total loss with limited recourse.

key_points.point: Falsely claiming to have submitted an SFC licence application is a criminal misrepresentation offence and will be weighed in any later fitness-and-properness assessment.
key_points.locator: para on 'Falsely claiming to have submitted an application', Note 1

key_points.point: VA 'deposit', 'savings' or 'earnings' arrangements offered to retail clients are not permitted under the new VATP regime.
key_points.locator: para 'For example, they may... launch certain virtual assets... virtual asset deposits, savings or earnings'

key_points.point: The SFC will consider whether past non-compliant activity could reasonably have been avoided, and whether the firm shows genuine intent to unwind it, when assessing licence applications.
key_points.locator: para beginning 'Where there have been past non-compliant activities'

key_points.point: Established entities of unlicensed VATPs already operating in Hong Kong must either apply for a licence or close their Hong Kong business; unlicensed operation is a criminal offence.
key_points.locator: para 'Unlicensed VATPs' established entities operating in Hong Kong'

key_points.point: Firms that were providing VA services before 1 June 2023 could continue without breaching the licensing requirement only during the 1 Jun 2023 to 31 May 2024 non-contravention window.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this gives concrete red flags for VATP counterparty due diligence. Unverified licence-application claims, and any retail VA 'savings' or 'earnings' style products, signal a platform the bank should treat as materially higher risk or non-compliant.
reading_guide: Read the 'falsely claiming' and 'VATPs which do not comply' sections in full; the closing 'warning to investors' section repeats the SFC's standard risk language and can be skimmed.

controls_and_monitoring: Treat a counterparty VATP's claim of a pending SFC licence application as unverified until confirmed directly with the SFC or via its published applicant list.
counterparty_due_diligence: Check whether a VATP counterparty offers retail VA 'deposit', 'savings' or 'earnings' products — a strong signal of non-compliance with the licensing regime.

title: Bond Tokenisation in Hong Kong
summary: This is a detailed HKMA report documenting the design, legal and technology choices made in Project Evergreen's inaugural tokenised government green bond. It is meant as a reference for market participants considering their own digital bond issuances. It covers the technology platform: private permissioned blockchains, node-hosting versus API access, and data visibility choices. It also covers deal-structuring questions and forward-looking priorities. The deal-structuring questions cover whether Hong Kong securities and companies law require any particular legal form for a bond, and 'native' versus 'non-native' tokenisation. They also cover on-chain versus off-chain payment, investor access via self-custody or custodians, and credit rating considerations. The forward-looking priorities include cross-platform interoperability, using digital bonds as repo collateral, and extending tokenised bonds to retail investors.

key_points.point: Project Evergreen used a 'non-native' issuance: the bonds existed first as conventional book entries in the CMU's securities database. Beneficial interests were then recorded on the digital platform in tokenised securities accounts, rather than being created directly on-chain.

Neither the Securities and Futures Ordinance nor the Companies Ordinance, nor the Payment Systems and Stored Value Facilities Ordinance, prescribes a particular physical or paper form for debt securities. So a distributed ledger entry can satisfy existing Hong Kong law without new legislation for this kind of issuance.

For a Hong Kong-incorporated corporate issuer, digital bonds are treated as 'debentures' under the Companies Ordinance. This still requires a Debenture Holders Register that can be printed out in hard copy, even if kept electronically.

The Notes were distributed only to 'professional investors' under the SFO. The existing SFO licensing regime for regulated activities, such as dealing, advising and automated trading services, applies to digital bond issuance in the same way as to conventional bonds. So do the securities offering rules.

Investors can hold digital bonds either by self-custody, directly controlling their own digital wallet and, where applicable, private keys, or through a custodian. Self-custody gives more control but exposes the investor to the risk of losing keys or suffering a security breach, with full responsibility on the investor.

Where investors are on-boarded directly to the DLT platform, the platform operator, and any custodian, is expected to carry out know-your-customer checks and enable AML/CFT compliance. Where investors instead access the bond only through a custodian, KYC is the custodian's responsibility.

In Project Evergreen, only custodians that are CMU participants and are on-boarded to the digital platform can open tokenised securities and cash-token accounts. Non-participant investors instead hold their interest through an off-platform custody relationship, recorded in the custodian's own books and records. This is structurally similar to indirect participation in a conventional clearing system like Euroclear or Clearstream.

The Notes were credit-rated on par with the Government's conventional green bonds. The report flags that digital bond ratings should factor in additional risks from largely untested DLT platform technology. It recommends a documented business continuity plan covering platform disruption, cyberattack, and database migration to an alternative platform.

The digital platform used two private, permissioned blockchains, Hyperledger Besu as Layer 1 and Canton as Layer 2, with Daml smart contracts, rather than a public blockchain. This prioritised security and data privacy over the openness of a public chain.

Participants can access a DLT platform either by node-hosting, running their own copy of the ledger, or via a standard API/user interface, a lower technical burden. Node-hosting costs more and carries higher operational and cyber-risk exposure. Project Evergreen participants used a graphical user interface.

Payments in Project Evergreen were made on-platform using 'Cash Tokens' minted by the CMU, each representing a claim on the HKMA equal to one Hong Kong dollar. These settled atomically with the transfer of tokenised securities balances, meaning a delivery-versus-payment transaction either completes fully or not at all.

Other digital bond transactions may instead use payment tokens not issued by a central bank. The report flags these as carrying higher counterparty, credit, operational, volatility and liquidity risk than central-bank-backed cash tokens.

A 'native' issuance is a bond created directly on a DLT platform, without a conventional central securities depository. It can reduce reliance on intermediaries and lower transaction costs and operational risk, compared with the 'non-native' approach Project Evergreen used. But it raises unresolved legal questions, for example how a bearer bond could be 'possessed' and 'delivered' in purely digital form.

The report identifies fragmented, non-interoperable DLT platforms as a key barrier to scaling bond tokenisation. It lists cross-platform connectivity, connectivity with conventional systems, and connectivity with central securities depositories as priority areas for further work.
The report recommends exploring digital bonds as repurchase-agreement (repo) collateral and tokenising already-issued conventional bonds to expand the collateral pool, starting with Government bonds.
key_points.locator: section IV, 'Secondary market and collateral mobility', p.20

key_points.point: Extending tokenised bonds to retail investors (tested conceptually in the earlier Project Genesis) is flagged as a goal requiring further legal, technological and operational work before implementation.

numbers_and_dates.item: Global tokenised bond issuance as of end-March 2023

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the HKMA's own working reference on how tokenised bonds map onto existing Hong Kong securities, companies and payment law. It sets out concrete expectations for KYC and custody roles, business-continuity planning and platform-technology risk. A bank should apply these when structuring, custodying, or rating a digital bond, or when assessing a DLT platform provider as a counterparty.
reading_guide: Read Sections I (Overview), III (Deal Structuring Considerations, especially applicability of securities regulations, investor access and custody arrangement, and credit rating) and IV (Unlocking the Potential of DLT) in full. Section II (Technology and Platform Design) can be skimmed for the network-type and participation-model choices, unless the reader needs the technical architecture detail.
flags: The report's date (24 August 2023) is a legacy metadata field carried from the original press-release folder; the document itself was published as part of Project Evergreen's public materials and is still current HKMA reference material as of this review, not a stale or withdrawn document.

obligations: If distributing or arranging a digital bond, apply the same SFO licensing and securities-offering rules (dealing, advising, automated trading services, professional-investor-only safe harbours where relevant) that apply to conventional bonds (para 23-24).

If the bank acts as a Hong Kong-incorporated issuer of digital bonds structured as debentures, maintain a Debenture Holders Register reproducible in hard copy per the Companies Ordinance even where kept electronically (para 28(b)).
controls_and_monitoring: Where the bank on-boards investors directly to a DLT platform, run KYC and AML/CFT screening at on-boarding; where investors instead access via the bank as custodian off-platform, KYC sits with the bank as custodian (para 44).

Maintain a documented business continuity plan for any DLT platform the bank relies on, covering cyberattack, platform failure, and a fallback/migration plan (e.g., an off-chain mirror record), given DLT platforms remain largely untested at scale (para 47).
counterparty_due_diligence: When assessing a DLT platform provider, check whether the platform is public or private/permissioned and what that implies for data visibility, privacy, and the bank's own confidentiality obligations to clients (paras 11-12, 18-20).

When relying on a payment token for on-chain settlement, distinguish a central-bank-backed cash token from a privately issued settlement token, since the latter carries materially higher counterparty, credit, operational, volatility and liquidity risk (para 34).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board/risk committee should be briefed on the custody-model choice (self-custody vs. bank-as-custodian) the bank offers clients for digital bonds, since self-custody shifts key-loss and security-breach risk fully onto the client, while custodial provision shifts KYC/AML and safekeeping obligations onto the bank.

title: A Bridge to the Future: Hong Kong Fintech Promotion Roadmap
summary: The HKMA, working with the SFC and the Insurance Authority, commissioned outside consultants to review how far banks, brokers and insurers have taken up fintech. It set out a forward plan under a four-part framework it calls PACE (Propagate, Assess, Connect, Equip). Distributed ledger technology (DLT) sits alongside artificial intelligence (AI) as one of two cross-cutting technologies, layered onto three business areas the regulators want to see grow. The document restates known milestones, such as virtual bank and VATP licensing, rather than announcing new rules. It closes by flagging that firms still find blockchain hard to explain internally, and lack a clear business case for it. It is strategic background, not a source of new obligations.

key_points.point: The regulators group emerging technology into five priority areas for the industry. Three are business lines: wealth and investment tech, insurance tech, and green tech; two are cross-cutting layers: artificial intelligence and distributed ledger technology.

Blockchain-based tools are described as most promising for cross-border payments, tokenising financial assets, and building a shared, tamper-resistant record shared between institutions rather than a single central database.

The report recaps a short timeline of past regulatory steps: eight virtual bank licences from 2019, and an opt-in regime for security-token trading platforms from 2019. A further licensing regime followed in 2023, covering platforms trading non-security tokens.

The consultants found firms still struggle to separate the technology itself from the digital-asset market associated with it. They cite unclear rules across different countries as a brake on wider blockchain adoption.
High upfront cost and a weak return-on-investment case are named as the leading practical obstacles firms raise for both AI and blockchain projects.
Staff lacking hands-on blockchain expertise is flagged as the single most common technical obstacle firms report when trying to roll out DLT projects.
By 2025 the survey expects firms to be actively trialling blockchain for central bank digital currency work, clearing and settlement, credit scoring, asset tokenisation and trade finance.

title: HKMA publishes joint report on Project Sela
summary: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the Bank of Israel (BOI) and the BIS Innovation Hub (BISIH) Hong Kong Centre jointly published this report on 12 September 2023. It was launched in Tel Aviv. It is a proof-of-concept study of a possible retail central bank digital currency (rCBDC) design, in which the central bank runs settlement directly. A new type of firm, called an "Access Enabler" (AE), handles all contact with customers. It never holds or controls users' rCBDC funds, and needs no balance-sheet liquidity of its own. This design could open the door to a lower regulatory bar and lower entry barriers for non-bank payment firms. The project does not reflect any policy decision by the HKMA on an e-HKD, or by the BOI on a digital shekel.

key_points.point: Project Sela showed it is technically possible for non-bank payment firms ('Access Enablers') to connect directly to the central bank's CBDC ledger.

Access Enablers (AEs) handle all customer-facing rCBDC services. But they never hold or control customers' rCBDC funds, and need no balance-sheet liquidity of their own, since the central bank settles directly.
This design could let AEs meet a lower regulatory bar and face fewer entry barriers than existing payment-ecosystem firms. Other requirements, such as security and governance, could still apply.
The central bank runs the rCBDC platform and ledger, and gives users pseudo-anonymous accounts. End users control their own rCBDC using self-generated private cryptographic keys.
Project Sela does not reflect any HKMA policy decision on a possible e-HKD. Nor does it reflect any Bank of Israel decision on a possible digital shekel.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is horizon-scanning, not a rule. Project Sela shows a possible rCBDC design where non-bank 'Access Enablers' could avoid bank-style regulatory requirements. This is worth tracking as a disintermediation risk. But it creates no HKMA obligation for banks today.

quote.text: an accessible and secure retail CBDC ecosystem

reading_guide: Read the HKMA press release in full. Then read the report's Introduction (Section 1) and Ecosystem design (Section 2) for the core Access Enabler concept. The Technology/PoC implementation in Section 6 is optional, for architecture specialists only.
flags: The 'Access Enabler' concept — non-bank intermediaries accessing central bank rCBDC settlement directly with potentially lower regulatory requirements than banks — is a notable structural departure from a bank-intermediated payments model, worth flagging as a competitive/disintermediation consideration, not merely a technical curiosity.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Flag as a structural watch item: a lighter-touch 'Access Enabler' model for non-bank rCBDC intermediaries (report Section 1, footnote 6) could affect competitive positioning if any future e-HKD design borrows from it -- no action required now, as HKMA confirms no e-HKD policy decision follows from Sela (footnote 5, p.5).

title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Opening Remarks at the Project Sela Report Launch Conference
summary: Howard Lee, Deputy Chief Executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), gave these opening remarks. He announced the completion of Project Sela, a joint research project by the HKMA, the Bank of Israel and the BIS Innovation Hub. It tested a retail central bank digital currency (CBDC) design that can support competition among intermediaries. He confirmed the HKMA has not yet decided whether or when to issue an e-HKD. He said Sela's findings will feed into ongoing exploration and the wider global CBDC debate.

The HKMA has not yet decided whether or when to launch an e-HKD; Sela is exploratory research, not a launch commitment.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this confirms e-HKD remains at the exploratory research stage, with no decision yet to issue it. It matters for medium-term retail-CBDC planning, but it is not an immediate compliance driver.
reading_guide: Short speech; read in full, no technical detail to skip.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No board escalation needed; background context only.

title: Project Sela – An accessible and secure retail CBDC ecosystem
summary: This joint report by the HKMA, the Bank of Israel and the BIS Innovation Hub describes a proof-of-concept (PoC) for a retail central bank digital currency (rCBDC) system. The central bank runs the settlement ledger directly. A new type of firm, called an "Access Enabler" (AE), handles all contact with customers. This includes onboarding, know-your-customer and know-your-business checks (KYC/KYB), anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing (AML/CFT) screening, and payment routing. An AE never holds customer funds or private keys. Existing banks, called "Funding Institutions", keep the job of converting deposits and cash to and from the CBDC. The report argues AEs could face lighter rules than banks, covering systems, governance and operating capital, but not client-money capital rules, since AEs never hold customer funds. A legal analysis, based on UNIDROIT digital-asset principles, concludes that neither the AE nor the central bank legally "controls" the CBDC; the end user does. The report also sets out cyber-security design principles. These include key management using hardware security modules (HSMs) and trusted execution environments (TEEs), and limits on central-ledger programmability. This lets wider access coexist with strong security. The report is exploratory. It states it does not reflect any HKMA or Bank of Israel policy decision on issuing an actual CBDC.

key_points.point: A new type of firm, the Access Enabler (AE), performs all customer-facing rCBDC services: onboarding, KYC/KYB, compliance and payment routing. Unlike a bank, an AE never holds customer funds or private keys.
Funding Institutions, meaning banks, keep the job of managing customer deposit accounts and ATMs, and converting between rCBDC and bank deposits or cash.
The report proposes that AEs handle AML/CFT customer due diligence and transaction screening, freeing the central bank from that role. It leaves detailed rules to individual countries.

Legal analysis under UNIDROIT's digital-asset control test concludes that end users, not AEs or the central bank, legally control their rCBDC. This is because AEs cannot access private keys or move funds.
The report proposes a lighter, tailored regime for AEs, covering systems and controls, governance, and a minimum operating-capital buffer. This replaces client-money capital rules.

The cyber-security design deliberately keeps programmable functions at the AE layer, not on the central ledger. It relies on hardware security modules (HSMs) and trusted execution environments (TEEs) to protect keys.
The project is explicitly exploratory. It does not reflect any policy decision by the HKMA on introducing an e-HKD, or by the Bank of Israel on a digital shekel.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, if Hong Kong ever adopts an Access-Enabler-style rCBDC design, non-bank firms could gain a lighter-touch route into payment services. This would run on the central bank's own ledger. This is a potential competitive and disintermediation risk to a bank's payments and deposit business. Compliance should track it, even though this remains purely exploratory research.

quote.text: Project Sela does not reflect any policy decisions by the HKMA

reading_guide: Read the Introduction and Conclusion (pages 5-11 and 55-56) for the core design and findings. Skim the cyber-technical sections (5.1-6.2, pages 29-53) unless you are assessing implementation detail. The glossary on page 4 is reference only.
flags: Report is a technical PoC/research paper, not a rule; explicitly disclaims any policy commitment by HKMA to issue e-HKD

counterparty_due_diligence: Should HKMA later pilot an Access Enabler-style regime, assess prospective non-bank AE partners' systems/controls and governance since they would sit directly on the central bank ledger
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Brief the board that HKMA is researching an rCBDC architecture that could let non-bank intermediaries provide payment services without holding a banking licence's balance-sheet obligations, a potential long-term competitive threat to bank payments/deposits franchises; still exploratory, no near-term action required.

title: Warning statement on unregulated virtual asset trading platform
summary: This is the SFC's warning on JPEX, a platform that marketed heavily to Hong Kong retail investors. It used social-media promoters and over-the-counter shops. JPEX has never been licensed by, or applied for a licence from, the SFC. This is despite website claims of overseas licences, which the SFC says are untrue. The notice lists suspicious features: unusually high advertised yields, client withdrawal problems, and a claimed tie-up with a listed company. That tie-up had actually already ended, with no money ever invested. The SFC told promoters to stop marketing JPEX. It warns that fraud and misrepresentation offences under the anti-money-laundering ordinance can carry heavy penalties.

key_points.point: JPEX has never been licensed by, and has not applied to, the SFC to run a VATP in Hong Kong.
JPEX's claims of overseas regulatory licences on its site and in ads are, according to the SFC, untrue.
JPEX advertised very high yields on some products, cited as up to 21% APY.
Clients reported being unable to withdraw assets, or found account balances had been altered.
Some JPEX products resemble virtual-asset 'deposit', 'savings' or 'earnings' arrangements, which are not permitted under the VATP rules.
A publicised partnership with a Hong Kong-listed company had actually already been terminated, with no investment made.
The SFC told the promoters involved to stop marketing JPEX and its products.
Fraud or deception in a virtual-asset transaction is an offence under the anti-money-laundering ordinance (AMLO). So is inducing someone by false representation to trade virtual assets.

numbers_and_dates.item: JPEX added to SFC Alert List

numbers_and_dates.value: fine of $10,000,000 and up to 10 years' imprisonment

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, JPEX itself creates no direct duty. But the SFC's documented red flags give compliance a ready-made due-diligence checklist for vetting any unlicensed virtual-asset (VA) platform that clients or partners mention.

quote.text: no entity in the JPEX group is licensed by the SFC

reading_guide: Read the six lettered points (a)-(f) for the substantive allegations; the notes at the end mostly restate statutory penalty detail.
flags: This is the SFC's original JPEX warning notice, a case widely referenced as the catalyst for tighter VA enforcement in Hong Kong.

counterparty_due_diligence: Use the JPEX pattern (false overseas-licence claims, unusually high advertised yields, client withdrawal problems, unauthorised partnership claims) as a due-diligence red-flag template for any unlicensed platform a client or partner references (para 3(a)-(e))
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be briefed on JPEX as the reference incident behind tightened VATP supervision, relevant to reputational and client-complaint risk if the bank's clients were exposed.

title: Warning statement on unregulated virtual asset trading platform
summary: The SFC named the platform JPEX in this warning. JPEX was promoted in Hong Kong through social-media influencers and over-the-counter (OTC) money-changer shops. No entity in the JPEX group was licensed, or had applied for a licence. The SFC said JPEX falsely claimed local and overseas regulatory approval. It offered unusually high yields, up to 21% APY on some products. Users could not withdraw funds, or found altered balances. A claimed partnership with a listed company had already ended, with no investment actually made. The SFC cited offences under the anti-money-laundering ordinance (AMLO) for fraudulent conduct and misrepresentation in virtual-asset (VA) transactions. It said it had told promoters to stop. It repeated that unlicensed platforms carry the risk of total loss, with little recourse, especially where they have no genuine Hong Kong link.

key_points.point: No entity in the JPEX group was licensed by the SFC to operate a VATP in Hong Kong. None had even applied for one.
JPEX claimed savings-product yields as of 12 September 2023 of 21% APY on ETH, 20% on BTC, and 19% on USDT. This level was flagged as a suspicious feature.
Client arrangements like 'deposit', 'savings' or 'earnings' products are not permitted for a platform operator. This is under paragraph 7.26(b) of the VATP Operator Guidelines.
Fraudulent or reckless misrepresentation to induce a VA transaction is an offence under AMLO s.53ZRG, carrying up to 7 years' imprisonment on indictment.
Deceptive schemes or devices in a VA transaction are separately an offence under AMLO s.53ZRF, carrying up to 10 years' imprisonment on indictment.

JPEX added to SFC Alert List

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the SFC's public account of the JPEX case. It is a reference point for red flags, such as unverified licence claims, high fixed yields, and false partnership claims, that counterparty and customer-activity screening should watch for in VA platforms.

quote.text: has stricter regulatory standards and more transparency

reading_guide: Read the numbered suspicious-features list (a)-(f) and the notes on offences; skip the closing general investor-caution paragraph, which repeats standard SFC wording.

controls_and_monitoring: Treat unusually high fixed VA yields, claims of pending licence applications, and claimed partnerships with listed entities as due-diligence red flags to be independently verified, not accepted at face value.
counterparty_due_diligence: Verify any VATP's licensing status directly against the SFC's published licensed-VATP list rather than the platform's own marketing claims.
Check claimed executive or partner affiliations directly with the named individuals/entities, as in this case such claims were fabricated.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Cite as a precedent case if assessing exposure to, or customer activity involving, an unlicensed VATP claiming false credentials.

title: Misrepresentation by crypto firms using word "bank"
summary: The HKMA warned the public that some crypto firms call themselves things like 'crypto bank' or 'digital asset bank'. Some also label client funds as 'deposits' and market 'savings plans'. This may breach the Banking Ordinance. Only HKMA-authorised institutions, meaning licensed banks, restricted-licence banks and deposit-taking companies, may use the word 'bank' or take deposits in Hong Kong. Using the word, or holding out as a bank, without authorisation is a separate criminal offence under sections 97 and 97A. So is deposit-taking without authorisation, under sections 11, 12 and 92. The HKMA reminded the public that unauthorised crypto firms are not HKMA-supervised. Their funds are not covered by the Deposit Protection Scheme. It pointed to the register of authorized institutions (AI) and restricted-licence banks (RLB) for checking a firm's status.

key_points.point: Only HKMA-authorised institutions may use the word 'bank' in their name/description or represent themselves as carrying on banking business in Hong Kong.
Only an authorized institution may carry on banking business or a deposit-taking business in Hong Kong.
Funds placed with unauthorised crypto firms are not protected under the Hong Kong Deposit Protection Scheme.
The public can verify authorisation status via the HKMA's register of authorized institutions and restricted-licence banks.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this confirms the statutory basis, Banking Ordinance sections 11, 12, 92, 97 and 97A, that an authorized institution (AI) can point to. This applies when a non-bank crypto counterparty or brand uses bank-like naming. It is useful for brand-protection and misrepresentation monitoring.
reading_guide: Read the main body paragraphs. The three end notes just restate the statutory sections cited in the body. Skip them if you already know sections 11, 12, 92, 97 and 97A.

controls_and_monitoring: Monitor for third-party misuse of bank-related naming or brand association that could confuse customers about the bank's own products versus unrelated crypto firms.
counterparty_due_diligence: Verify any counterparty or vendor describing itself with 'bank'-related terms against the HKMA's AI/RLB register before treating any such claim as accurate.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Low; informational unless a specific brand-confusion or customer-complaint incident arises.

title: Alert: Misrepresentation by crypto firms using the word “bank”
summary: The HKMA warns that some crypto firms call themselves things like 'crypto bank'. Others describe client funds as 'deposits' and 'savings plans'. This can suggest they are licensed Hong Kong banks. Under the Banking Ordinance, only authorised institutions may use the word 'bank' or take deposits. Doing so without authorisation is an offence. The HKMA reminds the public that unlicensed crypto firms are not under its supervision. Money placed with them has no protection under the Deposit Protection Scheme.

key_points.point: Firms calling themselves 'crypto bank', 'digital asset bank', or describing services as 'banking accounts', may mislead the public. They may look like HKMA-authorised banks.
Only authorized institutions (licensed banks, restricted licence banks, deposit-taking companies) may use the word 'bank' or run deposit-taking business in Hong Kong.
Using the word 'bank' without HKMA consent, or holding oneself out as a bank, is an offence under s.97/97A of the Banking Ordinance.
Funds placed with unlicensed crypto firms are not covered by the Hong Kong Deposit Protection Scheme.
Public can check whether an entity is an authorised institution via the HKMA's online register.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this warns that unlicensed crypto firms use 'bank'/'deposit' language that could mislead the public into confusing them with real banks. It matters mainly for customer-protection messaging, and for verifying any counterparty's authorized-institution status.
reading_guide: Read paras 1-4 for the substance; the notes just quote the relevant statutory sections.
flags: Direct HKMA statement that describing crypto client funds as 'deposits' or using the word 'bank' can itself breach the Banking Ordinance.

controls_and_monitoring: Screen for crypto firms using 'bank'/'deposit'-style branding that could be confused with the bank's own products, to protect customers from being misled (paras 2-3)
counterparty_due_diligence: Verify any entity claiming banking/deposit-taking status against the HKMA register of authorized institutions before referral or relationship (para on register)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be aware of a live consumer-confusion and reputational risk from unlicensed crypto firms using bank-like branding, which could be mistaken for products of licensed banks generally.

title: Statement on JPEX

The SFC says it has referred the matter to the Police, amid suspicion of fraud, with investigations ongoing.

JPEX was added to the SFC's Alert List back in July 2022, after being uncooperative in SFC enquiries dating from March 2022.
JPEX's publication of confidential SFC correspondence breaches secrecy provisions of the SFO and AMLO.
Suspecting fraud, the SFC has passed the matter on to the Police, with investigations ongoing.
The SFC and IFEC had already issued at least nine prior investor alerts before this statement.

prior investor alerts on JPEX before this statement

title: Statement on JPEX
summary: The SFC issued this statement about suspicious practices and false or misleading claims by JPEX, an unregulated platform claiming to trade virtual assets. None of the companies in the JPEX group hold an SFC VATP licence, or have applied for one. None has been in contact with the SFC on licensing matters.

numbers_and_dates.item: Prior investor alerts issued (before naming JPEX)

It also shows the fraud-referral pathway the SFC used. Both are directly useful for the bank's own VA-counterparty screening.

reading_guide: Read in full; short statement, no boilerplate to skip.

title: SFC steps up information dissemination and investor education on VATPs
summary: In direct response to the JPEX incident, the SFC announced measures to strengthen how it shares VATP information and educates investors. It will publish a 'List of licensed VATPs', a 'List of closing-down VATPs', and a 'List of deemed licensed VATPs'. It will also publish a new 'list of VATP applicants', and an enhanced dedicated list of suspicious VATPs. It will also run a public anti-fraud awareness campaign with the Investor and Financial Education Council (IFEC). It will strengthen intelligence gathering and enforcement. It will explore a dedicated information-sharing channel with the Police.

key_points.point: The SFC will publish a 'List of licensed VATPs', a 'List of closing-down VATPs', and a 'List of deemed licensed VATPs' (as of 1 June 2024). In response to public demand, it will also publish a new 'list of VATP applicants'.
The SFC will enhance and give prominence to a dedicated list of suspicious VATPs to help the public identify problematic platforms.
The SFC and IFEC will launch a public anti-fraud awareness campaign and expand investor education via mass media, social media and education talks.
The SFC will explore setting up a dedicated information-sharing channel with the Police on suspicious VATP activity, and continue to investigate the JPEX incident.
Investors are reminded that being on the 'List of deemed licensed VATPs' does not mean the SFC has vetted a platform's fitness and properness. Such platforms may ultimately not be granted a licence.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this sets out the public list architecture compliance must check before any VATP relationship or client referral. It confirms 'deemed licensed' status is not an SFC endorsement of fitness and properness.

quote.text: same business, same risks, same rules

reading_guide: Read in full; directly follow-on context to the JPEX statement (c8dcca119dab, 20 Sep 2023) and precursor to the VATP-lists publication (dddd919625e9, 29 Sep 2023).
flags: 'Deemed licensed' status is explicitly stated by the SFC not to reflect any vetting of fitness and properness — reinforced here as a direct policy response to JPEX-related public confusion about platform legitimacy.

title: SFC publishes lists of virtual asset trading platforms
summary: The SFC formally published the promised suite of VATP lists on its website. These are the List of licensed VATPs, and a new List of VATP applicants. A companion List of removed VATP applicants covers those returned, refused or withdrawn. There is also the List of closing-down VATPs, and the List of deemed licensed VATPs, effective 1 June 2024. Finally, there is an enhanced dedicated list of suspicious VATPs. The SFC stresses that appearing on the applicants list does not mean SFC licensing or compliance. It warns investors risk losing their entire investment on an unregulated VATP, with limited legal recourse.

A companion List of removed VATP applicants shows names removed because applications were returned, refused, or withdrawn, including for substandard/incomplete applications.

title: HKPF and SFC establish joint working group on VATPs
summary: Following a senior-level meeting on 28 September 2023, the SFC and the Hong Kong Police Force (HKPF) set up a joint working group. Its job is to strengthen cooperation on watching for, and investigating, illegal virtual-asset trading platform (VATP) activity. It draws on three HKPF units: the Commercial Crime Bureau, the Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau, and the Financial Intelligence and Investigations Bureau. It also draws on the SFC's Enforcement and Intermediaries Divisions. Together they share intelligence on suspicious activity, assess risk at VATPs, and coordinate investigations.

key_points.point: A dedicated SFC-HKPF working group was set up after a senior meeting on 28 September 2023. Its goal is to strengthen how they cooperate on spotting and investigating illegal trading-platform activity.

The group brings together three HKPF units: the Commercial Crime Bureau, the Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau, and the Financial Intelligence and Investigations Bureau. It also includes the SFC's Enforcement and Intermediaries Divisions.
Its job is to share intelligence on suspicious platform activity and breaches. It will build a way to assess how risky a suspicious platform is, and improve coordination between investigations.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is background only. It confirms formal SFC-Police cooperation exists on investigating trading-platform fraud. This matters when deciding whether and how to escalate a suspicious virtual-asset counterparty, though it creates no direct duty for the bank.
reading_guide: Read in full; brief press release, no boilerplate.
flags: This working group was established as a direct, dated (28 Sep 2023) institutional response to the JPEX case, formalising SFC-Police cooperation that did not previously exist in this structured form.

counterparty_due_diligence: Notes a formal SFC-HKPF channel exists for reporting suspicious trading-platform activity, worth knowing when the bank's own AML/fraud team is deciding whether to escalate concerns about a virtual-asset counterparty.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No bank obligation; inform the board that enhanced law-enforcement/regulator cooperation on trading-platform fraud exists post-JPEX.

title: Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities
supersedes_or_amends: Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities (28 January 2022)
summary: The SFC and HKMA updated their policy on intermediaries carrying out virtual-asset (VA) activities. title: Terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions which manage portfolios that invest in virtual assets
supersedes_or_amends: RA9 Terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions which manage portfolios that invest in virtual assets, 4 October 2019
summary: Known as the RA9 Terms and Conditions, this is the clean October 2023 text of licensing conditions applied to firms whose managed fund or discretionary account invests in virtual assets. It applies once the fund either aims to invest in virtual assets, or holds 10% or more of its value in them. It covers custody of the fund's virtual assets, including standards for self-custody versus an independent custodian. It also covers segregation of client cash, record keeping, and appointment and oversight of an auditor able to verify virtual-asset holdings. It sets counterparty and cybersecurity risk-management standards, and a duty to report material breaches or business changes to the regulators. A separate schedule adds extra rules for firms running discretionary accounts rather than pooled funds.

key_points.point: The extra rules bite once a fund's stated goal is to invest in virtual assets, or once it intends to hold 10% or more of its value in them. A fund is not automatically caught just because price gains alone push it briefly above 10%, as long as the firm takes steps to bring it back down.

Before choosing between self-custody and an independent custodian, a firm must document its reasoning. It must weigh accessibility against the security of key handling, and the custodian's ability to compensate for any loss.

If a firm chooses self-custody, it must keep the custodial function independent from the fund-management function internally. It may formalise this split, for example by placing a legal declaration of trust over the fund's crypto wallet and keys.

Firms must document why they picked a given independent custodian. This covers its track record with virtual assets, regulatory oversight status, segregation of client assets, and insurance cover. Firms should prefer a custodian that is itself subject to regulatory oversight, where possible.

If more than 10% of a fund's assets sit with one custodian, or in self-custody, that concentration and its risks must be disclosed to fund investors. Any significant later changes must also be disclosed.

The fund's independent auditor must understand how it verifies the existence and ownership of virtual-asset holdings, and the reasonableness of their valuation. This information must be made available to fund investors on request.

A firm must tell the SFC, and HKMA for a registered institution, of any significant change to its business. It must give at least 7 business days' notice before that change takes effect, and report any suspected material breach as soon as practicable.

When vetting a virtual-asset trading platform as a counterparty, a firm should weigh its track record, regulatory status, and governance. It should also weigh custodial arrangements, market-surveillance controls, cybersecurity measures, and its financial ability to cover client losses.

title: Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
supersedes_or_amends: 28 January 2022 joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
summary: This joint circular sets updated ground rules for banks and brokers dealing in virtual assets. It covers selling virtual-asset investment products, running dealing, advisory or discretionary asset-management services, and letting clients deposit and withdraw virtual assets. It replaces the January 2022 version, widening retail access under new safeguards rather than tightening the earlier professional-investor-only stance. Most such products must still be treated as complex products, requiring a suitability check and a virtual-asset knowledge test. But a narrow set of exchange-traded derivative products, tracked on approved exchanges, is carved out of the professional-investor restriction. Firms offering dealing services may only route trades through SFC-licensed trading platforms. Any client deposits or withdrawals of virtual assets must run through segregated accounts, held either with those platforms or with banks meeting HKMA's custody standards. A three-month transition period applied from the issue date for firms already serving clients under the old rules.

key_points.point: Firms distributing products that mainly track the value of virtual assets must treat them as complex products. They must apply the SFC's usual suitability checks, unless the product is one of the narrow exchange-traded derivative types carved out.

Before letting a client trade virtual-asset products, a firm must confirm the client understands the risks. A one-off knowledge test is acceptable. The firm must also confirm the client has enough net worth to bear potential losses, unless the client is an institutional or qualified corporate professional investor.

A defined list of overseas venues qualifies as 'designated jurisdictions'. Certain exchange-traded derivative funds tracked there can be offered without the professional-investor-only limit. The full list sits in Appendix 2 (separate entry, id bf255e1026f4).

Firms may only provide virtual-asset dealing services by routing client business through platforms licensed by the SFC. This can be by introducing clients to those platforms directly, or by running a pooled (omnibus) account with them.

Where a firm lets clients deposit or withdraw virtual assets, this can only happen through segregated accounts. These must be held with its partner SFC-licensed platform, or with a bank (or that bank's subsidiary) that meets HKMA's published custody standards.

A firm managing a portfolio is only pulled into the extra virtual-asset rules once the fund's stated goal is to invest in virtual assets. It is also pulled in once it intends to hold 10% or more of its assets in them.

Before recommending any specific virtual asset to a retail client, a firm must check it is highly liquid. This means it is included in at least two recognised market indices. The firm must also check it is actually tradeable by retail clients on the licensed platform.

Firms already offering dealing services to certain professional-investor clients before the circular's issue date get a three-month grace period. This lets them bring their systems and controls up to the new standard. New entrants must comply from day one.

A firm must tell the SFC, and HKMA where relevant, in advance. This applies before starting, or materially changing, any dealing, advisory or asset-management activity involving virtual assets or tokenised securities.

title: Appendices 1-5 to the Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
summary: These five short appendices flesh out the main joint circular. Appendix 1 lists simple, non-exhaustive tests a firm can use to decide if a client already knows enough about virtual assets. Appendix 2 names twelve overseas markets whose exchange-traded virtual-asset derivative funds can be sold without the usual professional-investor-only limit. Appendix 3 is a decision flowchart for classifying a given virtual-asset product as complex or not. Appendix 4 lists the due-diligence checks a firm should run before distributing a virtual-asset fund that the SFC has not itself authorised. Appendix 5 gives model wording for the risk warnings firms must hand clients.

key_points.point: A client can be treated as having virtual-asset knowledge if they have taken relevant training, or have related work experience. This also applies if they have previously traded virtual assets or related products.

Twelve markets qualify as 'designated jurisdictions'. This lets firms offer certain exchange-traded virtual-asset derivative funds there without the professional-investor-only restriction. The markets are Australia, France, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Taiwan (China), Thailand, the UK and the US.

The Appendix 3 flowchart routes a virtual-asset product first by whether it is a derivative, and whether it trades on a specified exchange. It then lands on whether professional-investor-only and suitability rules apply.

Before distributing an SFC-unauthorised virtual-asset fund, a firm should scrutinise the fund manager's background and internal controls. It should also check whether portfolio management, risk, valuation and custody functions are properly segregated.
Fund due diligence should also cover the fund's custody arrangement, including how assets are split between exchanges, custodians, hot storage and cold storage.

Diligence on the fund's counterparties should check their regulatory status for custody or trading of virtual assets, and their track record. It should also check IT and cybersecurity robustness, and financial soundness including insurance cover.

Model risk-disclosure wording for clients must cover legal uncertainty over whether a virtual asset counts as 'property'. title: Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions providing virtual asset dealing services and virtual asset advisory services
supersedes_or_amends: Terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions providing virtual asset dealing services and virtual asset advisory services, January 2022
summary: This is Appendix 6a to the joint circular. It is the full text of the licensing and registration conditions imposed on firms that run virtual-asset dealing or advisory services, shown with tracked changes against the January 2022 version. Part I covers dealing services, split between two models. Under the introducing-agent model, the firm never holds client assets, and simply refers clients to a licensed trading platform. Under the omnibus-account model, the firm pools client trades through its own account with a licensed platform. Part II covers advisory services. Both parts carry detailed rules on know-your-client checks, disclosure, and custody of client virtual assets and money. They also cover record keeping, an independent auditor's opinion, anti-money-laundering controls, conflicts of interest, and a duty to report material breaches to the regulators.

key_points.point: Under the introducing-agent model, the firm must not relay client orders itself, and must not hold any client money or virtual assets at all. A written client agreement must spell out that the firm provides no dealing, financing, settlement or custody service.

Under the omnibus-account model, a firm may only trade client virtual assets through an account it holds with an SFC-licensed platform. Retail clients may only be given access to virtual assets that platform itself makes available to retail investors.

A firm must never let clients withdraw or transfer virtual assets from its own account. Clients may only deposit and withdraw fiat currency through their segregated account, never virtual assets directly.
A firm must not offer any financing to help a client buy virtual assets. It should also try to stop other companies in its own group from doing so.

Firms must hold client virtual assets on trust in a segregated account. This must be kept either with the SFC-licensed platform itself, or with a bank meeting HKMA's custody standards. Access to move those assets must be tightly restricted to authorised staff.

Firms must tell clients up front how they would be compensated if the licensed platform or its affiliate were hacked, or otherwise caused a loss of client virtual assets. They must also notify clients promptly of events like hard forks or airdrops affecting their holdings.

A licensed corporation's yearly audit must include the auditor's opinion on whether its systems adequately ensured compliance with the custody and record-keeping requirements. It must also state whether the firm met the minimum liquid-capital rule.

Firms must build anti-money-laundering controls specifically for virtual-asset dealing. This includes reviewing red-flag indicators against Financial Action Task Force (FATF) guidance before launching new products or technologies.
A firm may not run virtual-asset market-making activity on the same licensed platform through which it services its own clients' dealing business. This is to avoid a conflict of interest.
Any actual or suspected material breach of these conditions must be reported to the SFC. For a registered institution, it must also be reported to the HKMA, as soon as practicable.

For advisory services, a firm must confirm a client's virtual-asset knowledge and risk tolerance before advising them. When recommending a virtual asset to a retail client, it must confirm the asset is highly liquid, listed on two independent indices, and actually tradeable on a licensed platform.
