title: Experimenting with a multi-CBDC platform for cross-border payments (Project mBridge Update)
summary: This is a joint update from the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Innovation Hub, the HKMA, and three other central banks on Project mBridge. mBridge is an experimental platform letting several central banks' digital currencies (CBDCs) settle wholesale cross-border payments. Its goal is to shorten correspondent-banking chains by letting banks settle directly with each other in central bank money. The platform runs on a custom, permissioned distributed ledger called the 'mBridge Ledger'. It is built to work like Ethereum and uses its own Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus method to agree on transactions. It protects privacy with masked addresses and encrypted transaction details. Governance runs through a Steering Committee and four subcommittees: compliance, technology, legal, and policy. The platform remains experimental only, with no live, production use of real money, and the report outlines a roadmap toward a Minimum Viable Product.

key_points.point: Project mBridge aims to let central banks and commercial banks settle cross-border payments directly in central bank money (CBDC), bypassing multi-hop correspondent banking chains.

Each central bank stays the only body that can issue or redeem its own CBDC on the platform. Only domestic commercial banks may request issuance or redemption of their local CBDC, which preserves currency sovereignty.
The platform is built on a custom permissioned, EVM-compatible DLT ('mBL') using the Dashing Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus protocol and ISO 20022-based APIs for interoperability.

Privacy is protected by masked ('pseudonymous') addresses and encrypted payment details. Only four parties can decrypt those details: the two commercial banks in the transaction, each bank's own central bank, and the central bank that issues the CBDC being used.
Governance runs through a Steering Committee plus four subcommittees (Compliance, Technology, Legal, Policy); banks remain responsible for KYC/AML/CFT compliance off-platform ('off-bridge').

The mBridge Platform Terms form a single contract binding the administrator, each central bank, and each central bank's own commercial-bank participants. Separate, jurisdiction-specific Issuance and Redemption terms, plus a Platform CBDC Instrument, sit alongside this main contract.

At the time of the report, four central banks had founded the project, and more than 25 further members were observing it. The next stage aims to build a Minimum Viable Product, but the platform stays explicitly experimental, with no live-value transactions yet.

Customer checks and anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing (AML/CFT) compliance stay with participating commercial banks, handled off the platform -- the key point for a compliance head to note now.

title: e-HKD Pilot Programme • Phase 1 Report
summary: This is the HKMA's detailed writeup of the first round of its e-HKD Pilot Programme. It launched in late 2022 as part of a three-rail plan toward a possible retail central bank digital currency. Sixteen firms ran 14 pilots across six use-case areas. These included ordinary retail payments, conditional or smart-contract payments, and payments made without a network connection. They also included bank deposits represented as digital tokens, using e-HKD to settle transactions in the Web3/crypto space, and settling other digitally-represented assets. The report walks through case studies and survey feedback, and a table contrasting e-HKD against stablecoins, stored-value wallets, and digital deposit tokens. That table compares who issues them, what backs them, how transferable they are, whether they carry deposit insurance, and how they can be redeemed. It repeats that no call has been made on issuing e-HKD, and describes plans for a further pilot round.

key_points.point: Sixteen firms ran 14 pilots across six use cases: fully-fledged payments, programmable payments, and offline payments. The other three use cases were tokenised deposits, settling Web3 transactions, and settling tokenised assets.

The HKMA identifies three areas where e-HKD could bring something new. These are programmability (payments that carry conditions), tokenisation (representing assets digitally), and atomic settlement (settling transactions instantly and simultaneously).
Hang Seng Bank, HSBC and Visa piloted tokenised deposits with wholesale-CBDC settlement, testing on-us and cross-chain payment atomicity.

A comparison table sets out that digital deposit tokens sit on a commercial bank's own balance sheet. They are generally covered by the Deposit Protection Scheme unless excluded, and are repayable in ordinary currency. This is unlike e-HKD, which is backed by the central bank's statutory authority. It is also unlike stablecoins, which the table describes as generally backed by assets and issued by largely unregulated private entities.
The report cautions that, at the time of writing, neither stablecoins nor digital deposit tokens sat within a settled legal or regulatory framework in Hong Kong.
The HKMA says no call has yet been made on whether, or when, an e-HKD might actually be issued.
The report flags that a DLT is not a prerequisite for a CBDC, and the HKMA remains open to both DLT and non-DLT designs.
Fubon Bank and Ripple piloted using tokenised real-estate liens as collateral for a home equity line of credit settled in hypothetical e-HKD.

title: Circular on intermediaries engaging in tokenised securities-related activities
supersedes_or_amends: SFC Statement on Security Token Offerings (29 March 2019)
summary: The SFC sets out guidance for intermediaries engaging in Tokenised Securities-related activities. It applies a 'same business, same risks, same rules' approach. Tokenised securities stay subject to existing securities law, but intermediaries must also manage new ownership and technology risks from using DLT (distributed ledger technology). Tokenisation itself does not change a security's complex-product classification; the SFC uses a 'see-through' approach based on the underlying security. The circular also lifts the prior mandatory professional-investor-only restriction from the 2019 Statement, for tokenised securities that are fundamentally traditional securities. It formally supersedes the 2019 Security Token Offerings Statement, and distinguishes 'Tokenised Securities' from broader, more bespoke 'Digital Securities' (which remain presumptively complex products).

key_points.point: This circular formally supersedes the SFC's 29 March 2019 Statement on Security Token Offerings.
Whether a Tokenised Security counts as a 'complex product' is assessed by looking through to the underlying traditional security's complexity, not the tokenisation wrapper itself.

The 2019 Statement's mandatory professional-investor-only restriction on security tokens no longer applies. Tokenised Securities are, at their core, ordinary securities carrying a tokenisation wrapper.

Publicly offering Tokenised Securities still requires compliance with the prospectus regime. This sits under the Companies (Winding Up and Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance (C(WUMP)O), and the Part IV Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO) offers-of-investments regime. Otherwise, the offer must be restricted to professional investors, or an exemption must apply.
Intermediaries that issue, or are substantially involved in issuing, Tokenised Securities remain responsible for the tokenisation arrangement even if they outsource it to third-party vendors.

A separate rule, the 'de minimis threshold', applies only to virtual assets under AMLO s.53ZRA. This is the small-amount test for when a fund manager must follow the VA fund manager Terms and Conditions. It does not apply to Tokenised Securities, unless the portfolio also separately meets that VA threshold.

Virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs) must maintain an SFC-approved compensation arrangement for security tokens under Guidelines paragraph 10.22. They may apply, case by case, to exclude certain Tokenised Securities from that required coverage if loss risk is otherwise mitigated.
Digital Securities that are not Tokenised Securities (more bespoke/novel structures) will likely be treated as complex products given heightened legal uncertainty.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This circular directly binds the bank as a Registered Institution. It sets the classification test, and the disclosure and prospectus obligations, for any tokenised bond or fund the bank deals in, advises on, or distributes. It also confirms the outdated 2019 professional-investor-only mandate no longer applies.

reading_guide: Read the full 7-page circular. The Appendix (Parts A and B) gives detailed due-diligence and custody factors; it is useful reference but can be skimmed once you grasp the main body's classification logic.
flags: Common misconception correction: tokenisation does NOT automatically make a security a 'complex product' or trigger a professional-investor-only restriction — this reverses the SFC's 2019 stance and is easy to get wrong if relying on the older Statement.

Distinguishes 'Tokenised Securities' (traditional securities with a tokenisation wrapper) from broader 'Digital Securities' (bespoke/novel structures, presumptively complex) — a taxonomy not obvious from the term 'tokenised securities' alone.

obligations: As a Registered Institution engaging in tokenised securities-related activities, apply the 'same business, same risks, same rules' approach and assess complexity via the see-through test based on the underlying traditional security, not the tokenisation wrapper (para 24, p.5).
If issuing or substantially involved in issuing Tokenised Securities, the bank remains responsible for the tokenisation arrangement even where outsourced to a third-party vendor (para 13, p.3).

Public offers of Tokenised Securities must still meet the prospectus regime (C(WUMP)O) and Part IV SFO offers-of-investments regime, or be restricted to professional investors / an exemption applied (para 27, p.6).
controls_and_monitoring: Apply the see-through complexity classification and distinguish 'Tokenised Securities' from more bespoke 'Digital Securities' (presumptively complex, para 33, p.7) in product governance and suitability processes.
notifications_reporting: Registered institutions must notify the SFC and HKMA of Tokenised Securities activities and provide information the HKMA requests (footnotes 8-9).
counterparty_due_diligence: When distributing via a VATP, confirm required SFC-approved compensation arrangement coverage for security tokens under VATP Guidelines para 10.22, noting case-by-case exclusions are possible (paras 30-31, p.6).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told the SFC lifted the 2019 professional-investor-only mandate for Tokenised Securities and now applies a see-through complexity test -- product committees relying on the old 2019 rule are out of date.

title: Keynote at the Hong Kong FinTech Week 2023
summary: Eddie Yue's keynote reflects on the HKMA's seven-plus years of fintech policy. He uses the Faster Payment System's slow-burn adoption as a case study for long-term commitment, then argues fintech is inherently interdisciplinary and needs collaboration. On virtual assets, he notes the HKMA has worked with the SFC to roll out investor-protection measures, so intermediaries, including banks, understand their responsibilities when distributing digital asset products. He previews a cross-border FPS-PromptPay QR link with Thailand, launching 4 December 2023. He also flags tokenisation, stablecoins, and tokenised deposits as accelerating trends, alongside open questions on how tokenised securities will be defined and whether delivery-versus-payment can be achieved on-chain.

key_points.point: The HKMA and SFC have jointly rolled out investor-protection measures. This helps intermediaries, including banks, understand their responsibilities when distributing or offering virtual asset products and services to clients.

Yue expects accelerating tokenisation of assets and wider use of blockchain-based ways to pay, including stablecoins and tokenised deposits. He flags unresolved questions on the legal definition of tokenised securities and on-chain delivery-versus-payment.
A new FPS x PromptPay QR payment link with Thailand's central bank was announced, to launch on 4 December 2023. It lets Hong Kong FPS users pay at PromptPay merchants without pre-converting currency.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This signals that the HKMA expects banks distributing virtual asset products to be clear on their investor-protection responsibilities, working from SFC/HKMA joint guidance. It also flags tokenised deposits and stablecoins as near-term growth areas a bank's digital-asset strategy should track.
reading_guide: Short speech; read in full, no technical detail to skip.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No board escalation needed; background context only.

title: Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products
summary: The SFC sets out requirements under which it would consider allowing tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products offered to the public in Hong Kong. It permits primary dealing -- subscription and redemption -- of tokenised authorised products, where the underlying product meets all existing authorisation requirements plus additional tokenisation safeguards. Secondary trading of such tokenised products is treated with more caution and remains under SFC review. Product Providers must retain full responsibility for the tokenisation arrangement, avoid unrestricted public-permissionless blockchains, and satisfy disclosure, staff competence, and prior consultation/approval requirements.

key_points.point: Primary dealing (subscription/redemption) of tokenised SFC-authorised products is permitted if the underlying product meets all applicable authorisation requirements plus additional tokenisation safeguards.
Secondary trading of tokenised SFC-authorised products is not yet generally permitted; the SFC will continue to engage with the market on appropriate safeguards.
Product Providers must not rely on public, permissionless blockchain networks unless extra controls are added, for example, imposing a permissioned token.
Product Providers remain fully responsible for the tokenisation arrangement's management and operational soundness despite any outsourcing.
Prior consultation with the SFC is required for new products with tokenisation features seeking authorisation, and for tokenising existing authorised products (which may also require prior approval).
Products should not be issued in bearer form; distributors must be regulated intermediaries complying with existing suitability/onboarding rules.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank distributing or considering issuing tokenised authorised funds or bonds, this sets the gating condition: primary dealing is permitted, but secondary trading is not yet. It directly shapes product launch timing, and requires prior SFC consultation before tokenising any existing fund.

quote.text: secondary trading of tokenised SFC-authorised investment products would warrant more caution

reading_guide: Short 4-page circular; read in full, noting it explicitly cross-references and should be read together with the Tokenised Securities Circular (23EC52).
flags: The document's first page carries a banner stating: 'This circular has been replaced by an updated version' pointing to https://apps.sfc.hk/edistributionWeb/gateway/EN/circular/doc?refNo=26EC22 — so this November 2023 circular is no longer the current version as of the 2026-09-25 status date.

As of this circular, secondary trading of tokenised SFC-authorised products was explicitly NOT yet permitted — only primary dealing (subscription/redemption) — a distinction often glossed over in casual references to 'SFC tokenisation rules'.

obligations: As distributor, only distribute tokenised SFC-authorised products via regulated intermediaries meeting existing suitability/onboarding rules (para 18; footnote 2 to para 11)
notifications_reporting: As Product Provider, prior-consult the SFC (and potentially seek prior approval) before tokenising an existing authorised product or launching a new tokenised one (paras 20-21)
counterparty_due_diligence: Check that a tokenised product's Product Provider avoids unrestricted public-permissionless blockchains and retains full responsibility for the arrangement despite any outsourcing (paras 10, 13)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should note this circular has been replaced by refNo 26EC22 (April 2026), and that as of this version secondary trading of tokenised authorised products was not yet permitted.

title: Hong Kong's vibrant fintech ecosystem attracts Canadian fintech technopreneur setting up Asian headquarters in Hong Kong to facilitate security token offering business
summary: InvestHK announces it helped a Canadian fintech founder set up CoinstreetPRO's Asian headquarters in Hong Kong. A group company, CSpro (Hong Kong) Limited, is described as the first SFC-licensed corporation specialising solely in operating a security token offering (STO) platform. It carries out Type 1 (dealing in securities) regulated activity for professional investors. The release is promotional in tone, quoting InvestHK and CSpro executives on Hong Kong's regulatory and market advantages, with no new rule or requirement announced.

key_points.point: CSpro (Hong Kong) Limited is stated to be the first SFC-licensed corporation specialising exclusively in running a security token offering platform. It handles the platform's primary issuance, distribution, and subscription.
CSpro holds an SFC Type 1 (dealing in securities) licence and serves professional investors only, as defined by Hong Kong law.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is an investment-promotion story about a named private STO platform operator, not a regulatory development. It is useful only as a market-landscape data point: a new SFC-licensed STO distribution venue. A bank that encounters it as a counterparty should still perform its own due diligence.

quote.text: first licensed corporation specialising exclusively in security token offering

reading_guide: Short press release; read in full (under 500 words), no sections to skip.
flags: Named-entity content (CoinstreetPRO/CSpro/named individuals) reported here only as stated in the primary source, with no endorsement or commentary.

counterparty_due_diligence: If CSpro or similar SFC-licensed STO platforms become counterparties, verify their SFC licence and permitted regulated activities (Type 1) directly via the SFC public register rather than relying on this press release.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No escalation needed; informational market development only.

title: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism (1) FATF Statement on High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action (2) FATF Statement on Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring (3) Outcomes from the FATF Plenary, 25-27 October 2023
summary: This is a routine SFC relay of the FATF's October 2023 statements on high-risk jurisdictions and jurisdictions under increased monitoring. Iran and DPRK remain subject to countermeasures, and Myanmar is subject to enhanced due diligence. Bulgaria was added to the increased-monitoring list; Albania, Cayman Islands, Jordan, and Panama were removed. It also summarises other FATF Plenary outcomes from 25-27 October 2023. These include revisions on non-profit organisation terrorist-financing risk, a report on crowdfunding for terrorism financing, and a report titled Illicit Financial Flows from Cyber-Enabled Fraud. There was also consultation on beneficial-ownership guidance.

key_points.point: FATF continues to call for countermeasures against Iran and DPRK, and enhanced due diligence for Myanmar.
Jurisdictions under increased monitoring updated: Bulgaria added; Albania, Cayman Islands, Jordan and Panama removed.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Routine compliance relay for AML/CFT risk-jurisdiction screening; not substantively new policy for VA activities.

quote.text: apply enhanced due diligence, and, in the most serious cases, apply countermeasures

reading_guide: Skim only; this is a routine FATF list relay with no VA-specific new requirements.
flags: Routine FATF relay circular — low substantive value beyond current jurisdiction risk list snapshot.

counterparty_due_diligence: Screen counterparties/customers against the updated FATF high-risk and increased-monitoring jurisdiction lists as part of ongoing AML/CFT due diligence.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No escalation needed; routine FATF jurisdiction-list relay.

title: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism Updated AML/CFT Self-Assessment Checklist
supersedes_or_amends: Previous AML/CFT Self-Assessment Checklist
summary: The SFC published an updated AML/CFT (anti-money laundering / counter-financing of terrorism) Self-Assessment Checklist. It reflects the current AML/CFT Guideline effective 1 June 2023, and refines checklist questions for clarity. Firms are told to use it as part of regular AML/CFT compliance reviews. Senior management must ensure deficiencies are rectified in a timely manner, and the SFC may request documentary evidence of reviews performed.

key_points.point: Updated AML/CFT Self-Assessment Checklist posted, reflecting the AML/CFT Guideline effective 1 June 2023.

Certain travel-rule requirements take effect later, on 1 January 2024. These cover the immediate submission of required information to the beneficiary institution, under paragraphs 12.11.13 and 12.11.10 of the AML/CFT Guideline.
Senior management must ensure compliance deficiencies identified in self-assessment reviews are rectified in a timely manner and may need to provide documentary evidence to the SFC.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Flags a concrete forward deadline (1 January 2024) for the travel-rule 'immediate submission' requirement under the AML/CFT Guideline, relevant to a bank's VA transaction screening build.

quote.text: any compliance deficiencies identified during the regular reviews are rectified in a timely manner

reading_guide: One page; read in full, noting footnote 1's forward-looking 1 January 2024 travel-rule deadline.
flags: Contains a specific forward deadline (1 Jan 2024) for travel-rule immediate-submission requirements under Chapter 12.11 of the AML/CFT Guideline — easy to miss since it's buried in a footnote of what looks like an administrative checklist circular.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No board escalation needed; this SFC checklist is addressed to LCs/SFC-licensed VATPs/associated entities, not to the bank directly. A bank's own AML/CFT self-assessment runs off the HKMA AML/CFT Guideline (per corrections_for_synthesis.md item 1), though the 1 January 2024 travel-rule deadline referenced here is a useful cross-check date.

title: AN ASSESSMENT ON THE BENEFITS OF BOND TOKENISATION
summary: This is a staff research memorandum, not a policy or supervisory document. It empirically studies whether tokenised bonds deliver measurable benefits versus conventional bonds. The authors use data on 28 tokenised bonds issued globally since 2018 (total US$3.9bn by March 2023, about 70% from Asian issuers), matched against similar conventional bonds from the same issuers. They find tokenisation is associated with lower underwriting fees, lower yield spreads, tighter bid-ask spreads, and improved liquidity in the matched conventional bonds too. The paper states the views are the authors' own, not HKMA policy, and cautions the sample is still small.

key_points.point: By end-March 2023 total global tokenised bond issuance reached US$3.9 billion across 28 deals from 23 issuers since 2018, about 70% issued by Asian institutions.
Tokenised bonds in the sample had underwriting fees averaging 0.22 percentage points of par value lower than matched conventional bonds, a 25.8% relative reduction.

Tokenised bonds had yield spreads averaging 0.78 percentage points lower than matched conventional bonds, a 23.9% relative reduction, that is, investors accepted lower compensation for tokenised issuance.
Tokenised bonds showed bid-ask spreads 5.3% tighter than matched conventional bonds on average. This rose to 10.8% tighter when the tokenised bond was open to retail investors.
After an issuer's tokenised bond launch, that issuer's comparable conventional bonds also saw bid-ask spreads tighten by about 8.5%, suggesting a price-discovery spillover effect.
The paper explicitly disclaims that findings represent HKMA views and flags the sample as still small, so results should be read with caution.

numbers_and_dates.item: Total global tokenised bond issuance to end-March 2023
Bid-ask spread reduction, retail-accessible tokenised bonds

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is HKMA staff research, not supervisory guidance, but it is the empirical basis regulators and market participants cite for tokenisation's cost and liquidity case. It is useful background if the bank is weighing participation in tokenised bond issuance, underwriting, or custody, but it creates no obligations.

quote.text: The views and analysis expressed in this paper are those of the authors

reading_guide: Read the Key Points box (p.1) and Section 3 findings (p.7-10); the Annex regression methodology (p.14-17) can be skipped by a compliance reader.
flags: Explicitly a staff research paper with a disclaimer that it does not represent HKMA views or policy -- should not be cited as regulatory guidance

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No escalation needed; useful only as background data if the board is asked to evaluate a tokenised-bond business case.

title: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism Webinar Materials
summary: This is an administrative SFC circular. It notifies that presentation materials from the AML/CFT Webinar held 15-16 November 2023 have been posted on the SFC website for reference and internal training. Speakers came from the SFC and the Commerce and Economic Development Bureau. Also speaking were officers from the Commercial Crime Bureau and, from the Hong Kong Police, its Financial Intelligence and Investigation Bureau.

key_points.point: AML/CFT webinar training materials from the 15-16 November 2023 sessions are posted on the SFC website for reference and internal training.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Purely administrative notice pointing to training materials; no new regulatory requirement.

quote.text: for reference and internal training as appropriate

reading_guide: One-page administrative notice; skim only.
flags: Purely administrative/routine — no substantive regulatory content, just a pointer to training slide decks.

title: SFC warns public of HongKongDAO and BitCuped for involvement in suspected virtual asset-related frauds
summary: The SFC warned about two entities, HongKongDAO and BitCuped, suspected of virtual-asset fraud. It said it had asked police to block their websites, and it issued cease-and-desist letters. HongKongDAO issued a token and was accused of falsely claiming SFC licences and a stake in the government's planned digital-currency exchange licence. BitCuped was accused of falsely naming two senior Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) figures as its chairman and CEO, with no actual affiliation. The SFC repeated its general caution about social-media-driven investment scams and unlicensed promoters.

key_points.point: HongKongDAO's claims of holding Type 4 and Type 9 SFC licences were stated by the SFC to be untrue. So was its claim of applying for a licence in July 2022.
BitCuped falsely named two HKEX senior figures as its chairman and CEO on its website; neither has any affiliation with the firm.
Both entities already appeared, before this warning, on the SFC's list of suspicious virtual-asset trading platforms (HongKongDAO 24 Nov 2023, BitCuped 10 Nov 2023).

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: A routine named-fraud alert; useful only as a specific negative screening reference if a customer or counterparty is connected to either name.
reading_guide: One-page notice; read in full, it is short.

counterparty_due_diligence: Screen any counterparty or customer reference to HongKongDAO/HKD token or BitCuped against this warning.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: None warranted; routine fraud alert.

title: SFC warns public of HongKongDAO and BitCuped for involvement in suspected virtual asset-related frauds
summary: The SFC warns of two suspected scam operations, HongKongDAO and BitCuped. HongKongDAO sells a token and is accused of spreading false claims about holding SFC licences, and about bidding for a 'Hong Kong Digital Currency Exchange Licence' that does not exist. BitCuped falsely named two real, senior Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) executives as its chairman and CEO. Police blocked both groups' websites at the SFC's request, and the SFC repeats its standard caution about too-good-to-be-true social-media investment pitches.

key_points.point: HongKongDAO is accused of falsely claiming SFC licences and involvement in a non-existent 'Hong Kong Digital Currency Exchange Licence'.
BitCuped falsely listed two real HKEX executives as its own chairman and CEO.
Police blocked both entities' websites at the SFC's request.
Both entities were placed on the SFC's Suspicious Virtual Asset Trading Platforms Alert List in November 2023.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Routine scam alert; note only that it shows fraudsters impersonating named real executives of a major HK market institution.
reading_guide: Skim; standard scam-warning template.

title: SFC warns public of LonShiX and Bitbank (Global) Financial Holding Group for suspected virtual asset-related fraud
summary: Routine SFC scam alert about two schemes. LonShiX used a fake Hong Kong address and social-media 'advisors' posing as bank-authorised professionals to lure investors. Bitbank (Global) Financial Holding Group copied the name of a genuine Japanese exchange and falsely claimed SFC licences plus a pending VA service provider application. Both were blocked by police at the SFC's request and listed on the SFC's alert list.

key_points.point: LonShiX gave a fake Hong Kong address and used fake 'bank-authorised' advisors on social media to recruit investors.
Bitbank (Global) copied the name of an unrelated Japanese crypto exchange and falsely claimed SFC licences and a pending VA licence application.
Both entities' websites and related social accounts were blocked at the SFC's request.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Routine; note the recurring pattern of scammers falsely claiming bank-authorised staff status, relevant to customer-education messaging.
reading_guide: Skim; standard template.

title: Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities | Appendices: Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities
supersedes_or_amends: Appendix 6 dealing/advisory terms and conditions, 20 October 2023 (id 8401e273511f)
Proforma RA9 terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions which manage portfolios that invest in virtual assets, 4 October 2019
summary: This is the full appendix set behind the 22 December 2023 joint circular. It gives the client-knowledge test criteria, and the list of jurisdictions whose regulator-approved crypto funds qualify for lighter treatment. It also gives a decision flowchart for classifying crypto-linked products, and a fund due-diligence checklist. It gives model risk-disclosure wording too, plus the current dealing/advisory licence conditions, with a redline against the earlier version. It also gives a separate, standalone set of conditions for firms managing crypto-invested funds or mandates. That last piece, Appendix 7, is effectively its own rulebook for crypto fund managers, covering custody, capital, valuation, record keeping, and reporting -- distinct from the dealing and advisory conditions covered elsewhere.

key_points.point: A firm counts as a knowledgeable client if it has had crypto training, has worked with crypto, or has traded crypto before. Any one of the three is enough.
Twelve named jurisdictions' regulator-approved retail crypto derivative funds and exchanges qualify for the lighter selling regime; anything else defaults to the stricter complex-product path.

A fund counts as a 'Virtual Asset Fund Manager', bound by the Appendix 7 conditions, if it is meant to invest in crypto. It also counts if its manager intends to put 10% or more of its value into crypto.

A licensed corporation acting as such a fund manager, and holding crypto for its funds, must at all times keep liquid capital of at least HK$3 million. It must instead hold its variable required liquid capital if that figure is higher.

The fund manager should use a custodian independent of itself. If it self-custodies, it should show the crypto is legally ring-fenced from its own assets -- for example, by a declared trust over the wallet and keys -- and carry adequate insurance.

Choosing a third-party custodian calls for documented diligence on its crypto track record, regulatory status, asset segregation practices, and financial and insurance strength. The manager should also think about spreading assets across more than one custodian.

The fund manager should tell the SFC, and the HKMA if it is a registered institution, at least 7 business days before any significant change to its business. It should report material non-compliance as soon as practicable.
Fund investors should be told the fund's key crypto risks up front. For example, most trading venues and custodians are still unregulated, and self-custody and hot-wallet use carry loss risk.

Appendix 6 restates the dealing/advisory licence conditions current as of this circular. Appendix 6a marks up exactly what changed from the earlier version, mainly the retail exposure-limit and knowledge-test wording.
Appendix 3's flowchart is the reference tool for working out whether a given crypto-linked product is a complex product and which selling rule therefore applies.

numbers_and_dates.item: Minimum liquid capital for a licensed-corporation crypto fund manager holding fund crypto
numbers_and_dates.value: the higher of HK$3,000,000 or its variable required liquid capital

numbers_and_dates.item: Advance notice required for a significant change in a fund manager's business
Record retention for most Appendix 7 records
numbers_and_dates.value: not less than 7 years (2 years for VA order records)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, Appendix 7 is the key rulebook if its asset-management arm ever runs a mandate meant to hold crypto, or one that could cross the 10% threshold. It sets a hard capital floor, custody and insurance expectations, and a fast notification clock the bank must be able to meet. The rest of the appendices supply the working detail -- the due-diligence checklist, risk wording, and product-classification flowchart -- behind the main December 2023 circular.

quote.text: intention of a fund is to invest 10% or more of its gross asset value

reading_guide: Read Appendix 7 (crypto fund-manager conditions, especially custody in section IV and reporting in section VII) closely if the bank runs, or is considering, any crypto-invested mandate. Appendices 1, 2, and 5 are short reference lists that can be skimmed. Appendix 6/6a largely duplicates id 8401e273511f/bc97c16bac5e's dealing conditions, plus a redline.
flags: Appendix 7 (RA9 terms and conditions for Virtual Asset Fund Managers) is a genuinely separate, substantive instrument bundled inside this one PDF; it has no attachment id of its own in the source metadata, so it is documented here rather than as a separate registry line.
Note: the second listed attachment ca1d1a146f72 is a broken PDF-viewer link with no retrievable content and was excluded (this does not affect the primary document, whose text was fully available).

obligations: Determine whether any bank-managed or bank-distributed fund crosses the 10%-of-GAV or stated-objective threshold that triggers Appendix 7 fund-manager status - Interpretation, p.76
If self-custodying fund crypto, put in place a documented trust/segregation arrangement and adequate insurance - Appendix 7 para 4.4-4.6, p.79
Maintain the HK$3 million (or higher variable) liquid capital floor if holding fund crypto as a licensed corporation - Appendix 7 para 3.1, p.78
controls_and_monitoring: Documented custodian due-diligence and selection file, refreshed on an ongoing basis - Appendix 7 para 4.7, p.80
Use the Appendix 3 flowchart in product governance to classify new crypto-linked products - Appendix 3, p.3
notifications_reporting: Give SFC/HKMA at least 7 business days' notice before any significant change to fund-manager business activities - Appendix 7 para 7.2, p.84
Report material non-compliance with Appendix 7 as soon as practicable - Appendix 7 para 7.1, p.84
counterparty_due_diligence: Vet any third-party crypto custodian used for fund assets on track record, regulatory status, segregation practice and insurance before appointment - Appendix 7 para 4.7 note, pp.80-81
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should hear whether any current or planned fund/mandate triggers Appendix 7 fund-manager status, and if so, confirm the capital floor, custody arrangement and 7-day notification process are all in place.

title: Circular on SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets
supersedes_or_amends: Circular on Virtual Asset Futures Exchange Traded Funds issued on 31 October 2022
summary: This SFC circular sets out the conditions under which the SFC will authorise investment funds with more than 10% of net asset value exposed to virtual assets (VA). Such funds can then be publicly offered in Hong Kong under sections 104-105 of the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO). It covers eligible underlying VA, investment strategy limits, transaction and custody channels, custody standards (cold storage, key management), valuation, disclosure, and prior-consultation requirements. It supersedes the October 2022 VA futures ETF circular, and cross-refers to the companion Joint Circular on intermediaries.

key_points.point: SFC-authorised VA Funds may invest more than 10% of NAV in virtual assets, directly (spot) and/or indirectly (for example, futures, other exchange-traded products).
This circular supersedes the 31 October 2022 circular on Virtual Asset Futures ETFs.
Underlying VA must be limited to tokens the Hong Kong public can already access for trading on SFC-licensed VATPs.
SFC-authorised VA Funds must not carry leveraged VA exposure at the level of the fund itself.
Spot VA transactions/acquisitions must go through SFC-licensed VATPs or HKMA-compliant AIs (or subsidiaries of locally incorporated AIs).
Custodian may only delegate VA custody to an SFC-licensed VATP or an AI meeting HKMA's expected VA custody standards.

Custody standard: most VA holdings must be stored in cold wallets, with hot-wallet amounts and duration kept to what is needed for subscriptions and redemptions. Seeds and private keys must be stored in Hong Kong, with access tightly restricted and resistant to speculation or collusion. This can be done, for example, using multi-signature approval or key sharding, and copies must be backed up.
Valuation of spot VA must use an indexing approach based on trade volume across major VA trading platforms (a benchmark index from a reputable provider).
Funds seeking VA exposure above 10% of NAV (whether new or existing) require the SFC's prior consultation and sign-off.

numbers_and_dates.item: VA exposure threshold triggering this regime

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: If the bank's Registered Institution (RI) arm manages, distributes, or provides custody for SFC-authorised funds with virtual-asset exposure, this circular sets binding requirements. These cover custody segregation, cold storage, key management, disclosure, and prior SFC consultation before exceeding the 10% NAV threshold.

quote.text: store most of the VA holdings in the cold wallet

reading_guide: Read paras 1-2 (scope/supersession) and the custody section (paras 19-20) first; skim footnotes and the disclosure/service-provider paragraphs (22-27).
flags: This circular is itself now superseded — page 1 carries an active banner stating it 'has been replaced by an updated version' (refNo 25EC21); the text captured here is the superseded 2023 version, not the current rules
Common-assumption correction: SFC-authorised VA funds are not limited to futures-based ETFs — direct spot VA investment is expressly permitted, subject to eligibility and custody conditions

obligations: Where the bank (as RI) acts as a management company of an SFC-authorised VA fund, it must have a good compliance track record and at least one competent staff member experienced in VA/related products (para 8)
Spot VA transactions/acquisitions for such funds must go through SFC-licensed VATPs or AIs (or subsidiaries of locally-incorporated AIs) complying with HKMA requirements (para 16)
controls_and_monitoring: If acting as trustee/custodian or delegate for VA holdings, segregate VA holdings from own/other client assets, keep most holdings in cold wallets, and secure seeds/private keys in Hong Kong with multi-signature/key-sharding and backup (paras 19-20)
Disclose VA exposure risks (price, custody, cyber, fork, roll cost) upfront in offering documents/KFS (paras 23-24)
notifications_reporting: Prior consultation with and approval of the SFC required before a fund seeks >10% NAV VA exposure or an existing fund increases VA exposure above that threshold (para 29)
counterparty_due_diligence: As custodian delegate, confirm any AI or subsidiary of a locally-incorporated AI used for VA custody meets HKMA-issued custody standards (para 19)
Confirm participating dealers are SFC-licensed corporations or registered institutions before relying on them for spot VA acquisition/disposal (para 18)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told that if the bank manages, distributes or custodies SFC-authorised VA funds, it takes on specific custody-segregation, cold-storage and disclosure obligations, plus a prior-consultation gate for material VA exposure.

title: Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
supersedes_or_amends: Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities issued on 20 October 2023
Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities issued on 28 January 2022
summary: This joint SFC/HKMA circular updates the conduct rules for intermediaries doing virtual asset (VA) related distribution, dealing, advisory, and asset-management work. It treats most VA-related products as complex products that can only be sold to professional investors, after a suitability check. A VA-knowledge test is also required. It carves out exceptions for exchange-traded derivatives and SFC-authorised funds. It also limits VA dealing to omnibus accounts held with SFC-licensed VATPs (virtual asset trading platforms), and applies RA9 (Type 9, asset management) terms and conditions to VA fund managers. It replaces the October 2023 and January 2022 joint circulars.

key_points.point: VA-related products are 'very likely' complex products, so -- with limited exceptions -- they should go through a suitability check and be sold only to professional investors.

Apart from institutional and qualified corporate professional investors, intermediaries should check a client's VA knowledge before any VA-related transaction (a one-off check is acceptable). If a client lacks that knowledge, the intermediary may proceed only after providing adequate training.

VA futures or derivative funds traded on specified exchanges, or authorised in listed jurisdictions, skip the professional-investor-only and suitability rules if there is no solicitation. The same applies to SFC-authorised VA funds traded on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong (SEHK). They still need the VA-knowledge test.

The SFC and HKMA see a clear need for intermediaries to deal only with SFC-licensed VA trading platforms for VA dealing, using an omnibus account or introducing-agent model. Intermediaries should provide such dealing services only to clients approved for Type 1 regulated activity.

Under the omnibus-account terms and conditions, a licensed corporation must keep excess liquid capital in Hong Kong equal to at least 12 months of actual running costs, on a rolling basis. This is on top of the SF(FR) Rules requirements.

Client virtual assets should be held on trust in separate VA Segregated Accounts, either at an SFC-licensed platform or an HKMA-compliant authorized institution. The intermediary should not give clients financial accommodation (margin or leverage) to acquire virtual assets.

title: Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers in Hong Kong – Consultation Paper
summary: The FSTB and HKMA jointly issued this paper in December 2023. It set out the proposed licensing regime for issuers of fiat-referenced stablecoins (FRS) -- tokens that try to hold a steady value against one or more currencies. It proposed that anyone issuing an FRS in Hong Kong, issuing an HKD-pegged stablecoin, or actively marketing FRS to the Hong Kong public would need an HKMA licence. It set out detailed licensing conditions covering reserve backing, redemption rights, capital, governance, and AML controls, plus who could offer FRS to the public, and the HKMA's supervisory, investigation, and enforcement powers. This proposal was later enacted; the analysis below reflects the original proposal stage, some of which was refined in the July 2024 conclusions paper.

key_points.point: Any company issuing an FRS in Hong Kong, issuing an HKD-referenced stablecoin, or actively marketing FRS issuance to the Hong Kong public would need an HKMA licence.
A licensed FRS issuer must keep reserve assets worth at least the full value of coins in circulation, at all times. Coins backed only by algorithms or arbitrage would not qualify for a licence.

Reserve assets must be held separately from the issuer's own assets. They would normally sit with a licensed bank or an HKMA-approved custodian, under a trust structure that protects holders if the issuer becomes insolvent.

Issuers must let holders redeem coins at face value in the referenced currency, promptly and without unreasonable conditions or fees. They must also keep a contingency plan for orderly redemption if the issuer runs into trouble.

A minimum paid-up capital was proposed at whichever is higher: HK$25 million, or 2% of the coins in circulation. This, and three other criteria, would not apply to issuers that are already authorized institutions (that is, banks).

Only licensed FRS issuers, banks, licensed securities dealers, and licensed virtual asset trading platforms would be allowed to offer FRS to the Hong Kong public. Unlicensed-issuer coins could only be offered to professional investors, and must be clearly labelled as such.
HKMA would get powers to intervene in a struggling issuer's management, gather information, conduct on-site inspections, investigate suspected offences, and apply for search warrants.

Proposed criminal penalties for unlicensed issuance reached a HK$10 million pecuniary penalty, or three times the profit or loss avoided, whichever is higher. Lower fines, and up to seven-figure fines with prison terms, applied for specific offences under the wider financial-crime framework the paper draws on.

Pre-existing stablecoin issuers with a real Hong Kong presence would get a 6-month grace period to keep operating. This was conditional on applying for a licence within the first 3 months after the regime starts; those who did not apply in time would have to wind down by month 4.

6 months, with licence application due within first 3 months

It shows which licensing conditions apply differently to banks (as authorized institutions) versus non-bank issuers, and it sets the baseline for due-diligence questions to any stablecoin issuer counterparty.

title: Legislative Proposal to Implement the Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers in Hong Kong (Consultation Paper)
summary: In this joint consultation paper, the FSTB and HKMA set out a detailed legislative plan for licensing fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) issuers. It builds on the HKMA's January 2022 discussion paper and its January 2023 conclusions. It proposed a new stand-alone ordinance. Under it, the Monetary Authority (MA) would licence anyone who issues an FRS from Hong Kong, or issues any stablecoin pegged to the Hong Kong dollar. The same would apply to anyone who actively promotes FRS issuance to people in Hong Kong. Licensing criteria covered full reserve backing, par-value redemption rights, restricted business scope, and Hong Kong incorporation and management presence. They also covered minimum capital, disclosure (a 'white paper'), governance, risk management, audit, and AML/CFT controls. It proposed that only licensed FRS issuers, authorized institutions, licensed corporations, and licensed VATPs may offer FRS in Hong Kong, with unlicensed-issuer FRS restricted to professional investors. This 2023 consultation was the direct precursor to what became Hong Kong's Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656). By 2026 the regime it proposed has been substantially enacted, so this paper itself is superseded as a proposal, though historically important.

key_points.point: A company would need a Monetary Authority licence if it issues an FRS in Hong Kong, or issues a stablecoin pegged to the Hong Kong dollar. The same applies if it actively promotes FRS issuance to the Hong Kong public.

An FRS issuer must ensure reserve assets are at all times at least equal in value to the par value of FRS in circulation ('full backing'). Algorithmic or arbitrage-only stabilisation would not be licensable.

Reserve assets must be high-quality, highly liquid, and generally held in the referenced currency. They must be segregated, through an effective trust arrangement, in accounts with licensed banks or MA-approved custodians, protected against theft, fraud, and misappropriation.
FRS issuers may not pay their FRS users any interest; income or losses on reserve assets belong to the issuer, not the holder.

FRS users have a right to redeem at par value without undue cost or unreasonable conditions. This includes direct redemption from the issuer if an intermediary channel becomes unavailable, backed by a contingency redemption plan.

FRS issuers may only conduct FRS issuance and closely ancillary activities (for example, wallet services for their own FRS); lending, financial intermediation and other regulated activities (SFO, MPF, insurance) are off-limits.

Non-bank FRS issuers must be Hong Kong-incorporated with a registered office. Their chief executive, senior management, and key personnel -- heads of operations, IT, finance, risk, compliance, and internal audit -- must be based in Hong Kong. This requirement, plus restricted business scope and minimum capital, does not apply to issuers that are already authorized institutions.
Proposed minimum paid-up share capital for a non-bank issuer is the higher of HK$25,000,000 or 2% of the par value of FRS in circulation.
Issuers must publish an MA-notified white paper disclosing the stabilisation mechanism, reserves management, technology and risks, and must disclose redemption policy, fees and timeframe.

Total FRS in circulation and reserve asset value must be disclosed at least daily, and reserve composition at least weekly. An independent auditor must attest to reserve adequacy and issuer compliance at least monthly.

Only licensed FRS issuers, authorized institutions, licensed corporations (holding a Type 1 licence permitted to deal in virtual assets), and licensed VATPs may offer FRS in Hong Kong. FRS from unlicensed issuers may only be offered to professional investors by these entities, and must be clearly labelled as not issued by a licensed issuer.

People who control, direct, or run an FRS issuer as chief executive must meet fit-and-proper standards. The MA's prior consent is needed for any change in ownership, controllers, or senior management.
Issuers must have adequate risk management (security, fraud monitoring, technology risk, contingency arrangements) and perform a risk assessment at least annually.
AML/CFT controls are required covering customer due diligence on issuance and redemption, transaction monitoring, and travel-rule wire-transfer requirements aligned with FATF standards and the AMLO.

The MA would have powers to intervene in a failing or at-risk licensee, such as restricting its business or requiring an MA-appointed advisor or manager. It could also gather information, conduct on-site examinations, issue directions and guidelines, and make regulations.
The MA would have investigation powers including compelling evidence, requiring attendance to answer questions, and applying for search warrants where an offence is reasonably suspected.

Proposed civil and supervisory sanctions include caution, reprimand, and licence suspension or revocation. They also include a pecuniary penalty of up to HK$10,000,000 or 3 times the profit gained or loss avoided, whichever is higher. Criminal offences would cover unlicensed issuance and giving false information to the MA.

A proposed appeal tribunal would hear challenges to MA decisions, such as licence refusal, condition attachment, and revocation or suspension. A further appeal would go to the Court of Appeal on a point of law.

A transitional grace period of 6 months (the paper calls this a 'non-contravention' period) was proposed for pre-existing FRS issuers with a meaningful Hong Kong presence. This was conditional on filing a licence application within the regime's first 3 months of starting; issuers not applying in time would have to wind down by month 4.

The proposed regime would sit in a new stand-alone ordinance, not amendments to the AMLO (Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance) or the Stored Value Facilities Ordinance. It would exclude FRS issuance by a licensee from overlapping securities and SVF regimes, to avoid double regulation.

title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Eddie Yue on Stablecoins – Regulating issuers to accord protection to users
summary: This is Eddie Yue's public explainer, published the same day as the FSTB/HKMA joint public consultation paper on a legislative proposal for regulating fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) issuers. It explains what stablecoins are, and why unregulated stablecoin failure risks harm to users and financial stability. It summarises the proposed regime at a high level. This covers an HKMA licence requirement for FRS issuers, local incorporation and management presence, and financial resources rules. It also covers an effective par-value redemption mechanism backed by high-quality liquid reserves held in proper custody, AML/CFT compliance, and a planned supervisory sandbox. It states only licensed issuers' stablecoins may be offered to retail investors. The full technical proposal is in the attached consultation paper (id 41a8fe3f0ec7).

key_points.point: The HKMA proposes that any entity issuing a fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) in Hong Kong must hold an HKMA licence. It must also be locally incorporated, with local management presence, and meet financial resources requirements.
Only stablecoins issued by HKMA-licensed issuers may be offered to retail investors; unlicensed-issuer stablecoins are implicitly restricted to non-retail channels.

Licensed issuers must maintain an effective stabilisation mechanism. This is generally a pool of high-quality, highly liquid reserve assets in matching currencies, with proper custody, so users can redeem at par.
The HKMA plans to launch a supervisory sandbox to communicate expectations to firms interested in issuing stablecoins in Hong Kong, with details to follow separately.

title: Consultation on legislative proposal to implement regulatory regime for stablecoin issuers and announcement on introduction of sandbox arrangement
summary: The FSTB and HKMA jointly launched a public consultation, running 27 December 2023 to 29 February 2024. It covered a proposed licensing regime for issuers of fiat-referenced stablecoins (FRS) in Hong Kong, to be administered by the Monetary Authority (MA). The consultation paper proposes a new standalone ordinance requiring FRS issuers to be licensed. It sets licensing criteria: full backing, segregation, redemption at par, no interest payment, minimum capital, physical presence, and disclosure. It also restricts who may offer FRS, and proposes MA supervisory and investigation powers, offences, and a transitional arrangement. A parallel sandbox arrangement was announced for prospective issuers.

key_points.point: Any entity issuing an FRS in Hong Kong, or issuing an HKD-referenced stablecoin, would need an FRS issuer licence from the Monetary Authority. The same would apply to any entity actively marketing FRS issuance to the Hong Kong public.
FRS reserve assets must at all times be at least equal in value to the par value of FRS in circulation (full backing). Issuers deriving value from arbitrage or algorithms would not be licensed.
FRS issuers may not pay their FRS users interest earned on reserve assets.
Proposed minimum paid-up share capital: the higher of HKD 25,000,000 or 2% of the par value of FRS in circulation.

The FRS issuer must be Hong Kong-incorporated with a registered office, with key personnel based in Hong Kong. This, and the business-restriction/financial-resources criteria, do not apply to authorized institutions.

Only licensed FRS issuers and authorized institutions may offer FRS in Hong Kong or market it to the Hong Kong public. Licensed corporations (with a Type 1 licence permitted to deal in VA) and licensed VATPs may do so too. Non-MA-licensed FRS may only be offered to professional investors.
Proposed maximum pecuniary penalty: HKD 10,000,000 or 3x the profit gained/loss avoided, whichever is higher, plus criminal offences for unlicensed issuance/marketing.

Proposed transitional arrangement: the regime would start 1 month after gazettal. Pre-existing FRS issuers with a meaningful Hong Kong presence would get a 6-month grace period (a 'non-contravention period'). This is conditional on lodging an application with the MA during the regime's first three months.
Consultation period ran from 27 December 2023 to 29 February 2024, alongside a new HKMA sandbox for prospective FRS issuers.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told this is a PROPOSAL, not yet law, but that AIs would be exempt from several licensing criteria (business restriction, physical presence, financial resources) if the bank pursues FRS issuance (paras 6.2.14, 6.3.2).

title: Tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products (Investment Products Division presentation, 10 January 2024)
summary: This SFC presentation explains its 'see-through' approach to tokenised SFC-authorised investment products. It treats them as fundamentally traditional products, wrapped in tokenisation technology. It sets out extra safeguards product providers must apply for primary dealing, flags secondary trading as needing more caution, and requires prior SFC consultation for new or changed tokenised products.

key_points.point: The SFC treats tokenised products as traditional products with a technology wrapper, applying existing product rules plus extra safeguards for the new risks.
Secondary trading of tokenised fund units needs more caution than primary dealing because of 24/7 trading and market-infrastructure readiness challenges.
Product providers/fund managers must remain ultimately responsible for the tokenisation arrangement and ownership record-keeping, even if a technology provider is engaged.
Products should not use public-permissionless blockchains without extra controls, such as a permissioned token layer.

Offering documents must clearly disclose token ownership rights, and whether settlement is on-chain or off-chain and final. They must also disclose transfer limits, smart-contract audit status, and associated cybersecurity and legal risks.

Distributors of tokenised funds must be SFC-licensed for Type 1 regulated activity, and follow suitability and onboarding rules. They must also choose a custodial arrangement suited to the product's ownership and technology risks.

Prior consultation with the SFC is required both for new tokenised products seeking authorisation, and for adding tokenisation to an existing authorised fund. Adding a further, substantially similar tokenised share class to the same fund does not need fresh prior approval.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: If the bank distributes or manufactures tokenised SFC-authorised funds, this sets the disclosure, custody, staff-competence, and prior-consultation checklist compliance must apply before launch. It also clarifies that outsourcing tokenisation technology does not shift legal responsibility away from the manager or distributor.

quote.text: traditional products with a tokenisation wrapper

reading_guide: Read pages 10-16 (SFC guidance section); the introduction and global-adoption comparison (pages 3-8) are useful context but not obligations.

obligations: If distributing tokenised SFC-authorised funds, hold a Type 1 SFC licence, run standard onboarding/suitability checks, and pick a custody model fit for the product's tech and ownership risks, locator: p.15
If the bank or an affiliate manages a tokenised product, keep ultimate responsibility for the tokenisation arrangement even where a tech provider is engaged, locator: p.13
controls_and_monitoring: Confirm at least one staff member has relevant expertise to operate or supervise the tokenisation arrangement, locator: p.15
Check offering documents disclose ownership, settlement finality, transfer limits, and smart-contract audit status before distribution, locator: p.14
notifications_reporting: Prior SFC consultation before launching a new tokenised product or adding tokenisation to an existing fund, locator: p.16
counterparty_due_diligence: Assess the fund manager/issuer's tokenisation infrastructure, key-management, and business continuity arrangements before distributing a tokenised fund, locator: p.11 and p.13
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told that tokenised fund distribution triggers licensing, custody, and disclosure duties equivalent to (plus extra to) a normal fund, and that SFC prior consultation is mandatory before launch.

title: SFC and Police warn public of Aramex and DIFX for suspected virtual asset-related frauds
summary: Joint SFC/Police alert on two schemes, Aramex and DIFX, both named after unrelated real companies. Both lured victims via social-media chat groups offering free advice, then directed them to deposit money into bank accounts for crypto investment, after which withdrawals stopped working. The case came via the joint SFC-Police working group set up to tackle illegal VATP activity.

key_points.point: Both Aramex and DIFX copied the names of unrelated legitimate companies.
Victims were drawn in through free-advice chat groups and told to deposit funds into designated bank accounts.
After depositing, victims could not withdraw their funds.
SFC and Police shared intelligence through a dedicated joint working group monitoring VATP-related crime.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Routine; illustrates the recurring 'deposit-into-a-bank-account-then-blocked' fraud pattern banks' fraud teams may need to recognise.
reading_guide: Skim; standard template.

title: SFC warns public of suspicious crypto-related products “Floki Staking Program” and “TokenFi Staking Program”
summary: The SFC flags two staking products advertising annualised returns of 30% to over 100%. Neither is authorised for sale to Hong Kong's public, and neither is backed by any explanation the SFC found satisfactory for how such returns could be earned. The SFC reiterates that VA staking arrangements can amount to unauthorised collective investment schemes, leaving investors with little to no protection.

key_points.point: Two staking products advertised returns of 30% to over 100% a year.
Neither product is authorised by the SFC for sale to the Hong Kong public.
The operator could not satisfactorily explain to the SFC how the advertised returns would be generated.
VA staking arrangements can amount to unauthorised collective investment schemes, which offer investors little to no legal protection.

numbers_and_dates.item: added to Suspicious Investment Products Alert List

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Reiterates the SFC's stance that VA staking programmes may be unauthorised collective investment schemes, relevant if a bank considers offering or distributing staking-linked products.
reading_guide: Skim; standard template, notes restate CIS offence provisions already covered elsewhere.

title: Disciplinary Proceedings at a Glance (for regulated persons under Part 5B of AMLO)
summary: This SFC guide explains, in plain terms, how the SFC disciplines regulated persons under Part 5B of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (AMLO). These are virtual asset trading platform (VATP) licensees, their responsible officers, and managers. It sets out the criteria the SFC weighs before taking action and setting sanction levels. It also lists the available sanctions, up to licence revocation and fines up to HK$10 million or three times profit gained or loss avoided. It also sets out the step-by-step process, from investigation through to a Notice of Proposed Disciplinary Action, representations, and a decision notice. It ends with rights of review before the Review Tribunal, and appeal to the Court of Appeal.

key_points.point: The SFC can only discipline 'regulated persons': licensed VATP operators, their licensed representatives, responsible officers, and individuals involved in management. This includes directors and those serving as Managers-in-Charge of Core Functions.

Factors the SFC weighs include the nature and seriousness of conduct, and the impact on market integrity or Hong Kong's reputation. They also include losses caused, whether conduct was intentional or negligent, prior SFC guidance on the conduct, and the degree of cooperation shown.

Available sanctions include licence revocation or suspension, and prohibition from applying for a licence or to be a responsible officer. They also include a fine of up to HK$10 million or three times the gain made or loss avoided, whichever is larger, plus reprimand and remedial action orders.
Except for a private reprimand, all SFC sanctions are announced publicly by press release.
A regulated person that receives a Notice of Proposed Disciplinary Action is normally given 30 days to make representations, extendable on reasonable request.

If the person does not apply for a review, the SFC's decision takes effect once the 21-day review-application window, from service of the decision notice, expires. An application for review suspends the decision until the Review Tribunal rules.
A person dissatisfied with the Review Tribunal's determination may ask for leave to bring the matter before the Court of Appeal. This must be done within a 14-day window from that determination.

numbers_and_dates.value: HK$10 million or 3x profit gained/loss avoided, whichever higher

numbers_and_dates.item: deadline to apply for Review Tribunal review
deadline to seek leave to appeal to Court of Appeal

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For counterparty due diligence on VATPs, this is the SFC's own roadmap of what triggers enforcement, what sanctions can follow, and how public the outcome will be. A bank should treat a VATP's history of Notices of Proposed Disciplinary Action (NPDAs), decision notices, or public reprimands as material to its ongoing due diligence and monitoring of that platform.

quote.text: Summary only, not legal advice

reading_guide: Read pages 3-9 (English) in full; the Chinese-language section from page 10 onward duplicates the same content and can be skipped for an English-reading audience.

controls_and_monitoring: Monitor SFC enforcement news and decision notices for any VATP counterparty, since only private reprimands are kept confidential.
counterparty_due_diligence: Check whether a prospective or existing VATP counterparty has received any NPDA, decision notice, or public sanction (revocation, suspension, reprimand, fine) as part of onboarding and periodic review.
Treat SFC disciplinary history as a factor in assessing a VATP's fitness and properness before referring or servicing clients through it.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be made aware of the sanction ceiling (HK$10m or 3x profit/loss) and public-disclosure norm, so that any VATP counterparty's disciplinary record is escalated promptly if discovered.

title: A new phase in virtual asset regulation
summary: In this blog post, the Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury restates that Hong Kong's approach to virtual assets (VA) is risk-based. It follows the principle 'same activity, same risk, same regulation'. It recaps the VASP (virtual asset service provider) licensing system that began operating on 1 June 2023, and notes two licensed platforms could then offer Bitcoin and Ethereum trading to retail investors. It sets out the transitional-arrangement deadlines for VASPs operating before licensing began. These VASPs had a 29 February 2024 deadline to apply for a licence. Those not treated as licensed must wind down by 31 May 2024, or within three months of a 'No-deeming notice' (a notice that a VASP will not be treated as licensed). It also flags an imminent consultation on regulating OTC virtual asset venues, and reminds the public that the stablecoin issuer consultation with the HKMA was closing that same month.

key_points.point: Existing VA service providers operating before the licensing regime must have submitted a licence application by 29 February 2024, to be considered for treatment as a licensed provider ('deemed-licensed' status).
The SFC will issue a 'No-deeming notice' to applicants it considers unable to meet the transitional arrangement's requirements.
Existing service providers that miss the 29 February 2024 deadline, or receive a No-deeming notice, must cease operations by 31 May 2024, or within three months of the notice -- whichever applies.
The public should only use SFC-licensed platforms for VA transactions; the SFC will keep an online list of licensed platforms updated.

The government intends to bring OTC (over-the-counter) virtual asset venues -- physical shops and online platforms -- under regulation, and will launch a public consultation on this shortly. This is partly because OTC venues played a role in some fraud cases involving unlicensed VA platforms.

A joint HKMA/FSTB public consultation on a legislative proposal for a stablecoin-issuer licensing regime was due to close at the end of February 2024. It covered all qualified fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) issuers.
The HKMA intends to introduce a 'sandbox' arrangement to give regulatory expectations and compliance guidance to prospective FRS issuers ahead of the formal regime.

numbers_and_dates.item: deadline to cease operations if not deemed licensed
numbers_and_dates.value: 31 May 2024, or 3 months from No-deeming notice

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This blog is a useful contemporaneous regulator statement of the VASP transitional deadlines, and of the pipeline for OTC-venue and stablecoin-issuer regulation. Both are directly relevant to how a bank should screen VA counterparties and anticipate upcoming regimes. The specific 2024 deadlines are now historical, though, and should be checked against the final rules that followed.

reading_guide: Read paragraphs 3-7 in full for the transitional-deadline mechanics and forthcoming consultations; the opening two paragraphs are scene-setting context that can be skimmed.

controls_and_monitoring: Track the SFC's online list of licensed VA trading platforms referenced here as the authoritative source for which platforms are licensed at any given time.
counterparty_due_diligence: Before onboarding or continuing to deal with a VA trading platform, confirm whether it applied for a licence by 29 February 2024, was deemed licensed, or received a No-deeming notice, since unlicensed operation after the transitional deadlines was flagged as a compliance and fraud risk.
Note the forthcoming OTC-venue consultation and stablecoin-issuer consultation as upcoming regimes likely to create new due-diligence categories for OTC counterparties and stablecoin issuers.

title: SFC urges investors to check regulatory status of virtual asset trading platforms as transition period will end soon
summary: The SFC reminded investors to check whether a virtual asset trading platform (VATP) operating in Hong Kong is on its licensed list or applicant list. This was ahead of the 29 February 2024 licence-application deadline. VATPs that had not submitted a licence application by 29 February 2024 were required to close their Hong Kong business by 31 May 2024. This was under the AMLO Schedule 3G transitional arrangements. Unlicensed post-deadline operation is a criminal offence. Applicant-listed VATPs were not yet licensed, and might ultimately be refused.

key_points.point: VATPs operating in Hong Kong before 1 June 2023 had to get a licence application in front of the SFC by 29 February 2024. This let them keep operating on or after 1 June 2024.
VATPs not on the licensed list or the applicant list by 29 February 2024 had to close down, or transfer clients to SFC-licensed VATPs, before 31 May 2024.

Being on the 'List of virtual asset trading platform applicants' does not mean a VATP is licensed or SFC-regulated. Applications may be refused, and the platform may later appear on the 'List of closing-down virtual asset trading platforms'.

Operating in Hong Kong without a licence on or after 1 June 2023, for a platform not grandfathered, is a criminal offence under the AMLO. So is continuing to operate after 1 June 2024 without having applied by 29 February 2024.
