title: Cryptoasset Exposures — Consultation Paper CP 24.01
summary: The HKMA proposes to bring the Basel Committee's December 2022 global standard on banks' cryptoasset exposures into Hong Kong's capital, liquidity, leverage and large-exposure rules. It targets an effective date no earlier than 1 July 2025. Cryptoassets are split into Group 1 (tokenised traditional assets and stablecoins meeting four strict conditions) and Group 2 (everything else). Group 2 gets far more punitive treatment. This includes a 1,250% risk weight and, for systemically important banks, a hard cap of 1-2% of Tier 1 capital. Banks must self-classify every cryptoasset they hold on an ongoing basis, document the assessment, and tell the HKMA before acquiring a new type. The HKMA can overrule the bank's classification. The paper also sets out liquidity, leverage, large-exposure, operational-risk, disclosure and risk-governance expectations. A 2025 letter to the industry shows the HKMA has since moved to a soft consultation on draft rule text. So this paper is the original blueprint, not the current in-force wording.

key_points.point: The HKMA does not plan to bring the new capital rules into effect any earlier than 1 July 2025. Rule-gazetting and Legislative Council tabling are expected in Q2 2025.

Banks must continuously assess whether each cryptoasset they are exposed to meets the four classification conditions. They must keep full documentation available to the HKMA on request, and must tell the HKMA before acquiring a new type of cryptoasset.
The HKMA can override a bank's own classification of a cryptoasset if it disagrees with the bank's assessment.

Cryptoassets fall into two broad groups. Group 1, tokenised traditional assets and cryptoassets with an effective stabilisation mechanism such as certain stablecoins, gets treatment close to the underlying traditional asset. Group 2, everything failing those tests, gets much harsher capital treatment.

To qualify as Group 1, a cryptoasset must pass four cumulative tests on an ongoing basis. It must confer the same legal rights as the traditional asset, or have an effective peg. All rights must be clearly and legally enforceable, and transfers final. The token's network and functions must not create material added risk. And every entity performing key functions, such as redemption, custody or settlement, must be regulated or subject to appropriate risk standards.

A stablecoin only meets condition 1 if its reserve assets equal or exceed the aggregate redemption value at all times, including under stress; where risky, it must overcollateralise. Reserves must be of minimal market or credit risk, held in matching currencies, and independently audited at least annually, with daily value and weekly composition disclosure.
A cryptoasset arrangement only meets condition 2 if full redemption can happen within a five-calendar-day window from the time it is requested, at all times.

A bank adopting the basic approach must risk-weight almost all Group 1a and Group 1b cryptoassets at 1,250%, meaning it must hold capital equal to the exposure. It cannot use them as collateral, unless they are issued by the HKSAR Government or a designated public sector entity.

Systemically important banks (G-SIBs and D-SIBs) must cap their total Group 2 cryptoasset exposure at no more than 1% of Tier 1 capital as a normal ceiling. They must never exceed 2%. Breaching 1% requires prompt notification to the HKMA and rapid rectification. Any exposure above the limit is treated at the harsher Group 2b rate in the meantime.

A Group 2 cryptoasset defaults to the harshest (Group 2b) capital treatment. This applies unless the bank proves to the HKMA's satisfaction that it meets the Group 2a hedging-recognition tests. These tests are: a regulated derivative or ETF exists, the asset is highly liquid, and sufficient price and volume data exists.

Banks must maintain a monitoring framework to verify at all times that a stablecoin's peg-stabilisation mechanism is actually working. They must document the evidence used, including for newly launched coins where data is thin.

Operational risk from cryptoasset activity must be captured through the standard operational-risk framework (Business Indicator and Internal Loss Multiplier). If that is insufficient, the HKMA will act through the supervisory review process.

A cryptoasset cannot count as a High-Quality Liquid Asset under the LCR/NSFR liquidity regime. The exception is a Group 1a token of an asset already eligible as HQLA, if it meets all the same characteristic and operational requirements as the underlying asset.

Stablecoins that a bank issues must generally be treated as 100% cash outflow under the LCR, if redeemable within 30 days. The exception is stablecoins backed by HQLA held outside the bank's own eligible HQLA pool, where a reduced outflow may apply.

Boards and senior management must formally set the AI's risk appetite for holding cryptoassets or servicing cryptoasset operators. This must be consistent with senior management's own assessment of the bank's risk-management capability, particularly for market, counterparty, liquidity and operational risk.

Banks must tell the HKMA about their cryptoasset policies, assessment results and actual or planned exposures in a timely manner. They must demonstrate they have fully assessed the permissibility and risks of the activity.
The HKMA may impose extra capital charges, require provisioning, or set internal exposure limits where it judges a bank's cryptoasset risk management or capital coverage to be inadequate.

Banks must disclose, on a regular basis, qualitative information on their cryptoasset business and risk management. They must also disclose quantitative exposure, capital-requirement and accounting-classification data for each Group 1a/1b/2a/2b cryptoasset type, following the same five guiding principles used for other disclosures.

A bank must specifically weigh several risks in its cryptoasset risk management. These include DLT network stability and consensus design, and key-loss or cyberattack exposure. They also include node-operator trustworthiness, legal uncertainty around ownership and settlement finality, and AML/CFT exposure from banking VASPs or VASP customers.
The prudential treatment does not cover central bank digital currencies, which sit outside this framework entirely

title: SFC warns public of suspicious crypto-related product “Hong Kong International Financial Centre Token”
summary: The SFC warns about a product called the Hong Kong International Financial Centre Token. The scheme also bundles node-pledging, a metaverse offering, and references to digital offshore RMB and a digital Hong Kong dollar.

title: HKSAR Government’s Digital Green Bonds Offering
summary: The HKSAR Government announced the successful offering of roughly HK$6 billion in multi-currency Digital Green Bonds (HKD, RMB, USD, EUR) under the Government Green Bond Programme. This is its second digital bond issuance, after the February 2023 inaugural tokenised green bond. The bonds were digitally native, with no prior traditional-CSD issuance. They were cleared and settled through the HKMA's Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU), with HSBC Orion serving as the digital assets platform. They were linked to Euroclear and Clearstream for broader investor access. The issuance adopted ICMA's Bond Data Taxonomy, a first for this bond category, and integrated green bond disclosures on the digital assets platform. It builds on the HKMA's 2021 Project Genesis proof of concept.

key_points.point: Government issued ~HK$6bn multi-currency Digital Green Bonds (HKD, RMB, USD, EUR tranches), a two-year tenor, priced across four currencies.
This is the world's first multi-currency digital bond offering and Hong Kong's first digitally native bond issuance.
Settlement is via CMU (operated by HKMA) with statutory settlement finality under Hong Kong law; HSBC Orion is the digital assets platform.
International investors can access the bonds via Euroclear or Clearstream accounts, broadening the investor base. This could help interoperability across digital-asset platforms and traditional CSDs.
The issuance adopted ICMA's Bond Data Taxonomy (BDT), the first such adoption by this issuer category and the first green bond to use BDT.
Direct Participants on the platform hold legal title to the bonds; non-Direct-Participants hold beneficial interests via CMU, Euroclear, Clearstream or custodian arrangements.

It shows the settlement/custody model, where Direct Participants hold legal title, that a bank's digital assets business may need to interoperate with.

title: Cryptoasset Exposures - Consultation paper | CP 24.01
summary: The HKMA sets out how it plans to apply the Basel Committee's global capital rules for banks' cryptoasset holdings in Hong Kong. It sorts cryptoassets into Group 1 (tokenised traditional assets and well-backed stablecoins that pass strict tests) and Group 2 (everything else, including most crypto). Each group gets very different capital, liquidity and large-exposure treatment. It also caps how much of a systemically important bank's capital can sit in Group 2 cryptoassets. The paper invited comments by 6 May 2024 and targeted an effective date no earlier than 1 July 2025.

key_points.point: Cryptoassets fall into Group 1 (tokenised assets or stablecoins that meet four strict tests) or Group 2 (everything else). Only Group 1 gets treatment close to the underlying traditional asset.

A stablecoin's stabilisation mechanism only meets classification condition 1 if its reserve assets equal or exceed the peg value at all times. They must also be minimal-risk and currency-matched, and externally audited at least annually, with value disclosed daily and composition disclosed weekly. A separate condition (condition 2) requires full redeemability within five calendar days.
Banks must assess and document classification of every cryptoasset on an ongoing basis, and tell the HKMA in advance before acquiring a new type. The HKMA can override a bank's own classification.
Group 2 cryptoassets that fail hedging tests get a punitive 1,250% risk weight, meaning a bank must hold capital equal to the full value of the position.

A cryptoasset can only count as a high-quality liquid asset if it is a Group 1a tokenised version of an asset that already qualifies. The tokenised and traditional forms must both meet the same eligibility tests.

Only systemically important banks (G-SIBs/D-SIBs) face a formal ceiling. Group 2 cryptoasset exposure should generally stay under 1% of Tier 1 capital, and must never exceed 2%. Breaches must be reported to the HKMA as soon as practicable.

Banks must fold cryptoasset risk into existing risk-management frameworks: board-approved risk appetite, and operational resilience per SPM OR-1/OR-2. They must tell the HKMA about their actual and planned cryptoasset activities.
Banks must give qualitative and quantitative public disclosures on cryptoasset business activities, risk management and exposures, following the SPM CA-D-1 disclosure principles.
Planned local timeline: preliminary consultation in H2 2024, draft rule consultation in Q1 2025, gazetting in Q2 2025, with revised rules taking effect no earlier than 1 July 2025.

title: Government launches consultation on legislative proposals to regulate over-the-counter trading of virtual assets
summary: The government announced a two-month public consultation on a new licensing regime for over-the-counter (OTC) trading of virtual assets. This would be run by the Commissioner of Customs and Excise, rather than a financial regulator. The proposal responds to fraud cases linked to unlicensed VA OTC shops. It applies the same anti-money-laundering standard already used for licensed VA trading platforms. The full legislative proposals are set out in the attached consultation paper.

key_points.point: Any person doing business as a VA-for-money OTC trader in Hong Kong would need a licence from the Commissioner of Customs and Excise (CCE).
The regime would cover both physical shops and digital platforms, but exclude licensed VA trading platforms, which are already regulated separately.
Consultation ran for two months, closing 12 April 2024.

The bank's AML monitoring and transaction-pattern rules for retail flows to VA OTC counterparties may need updating once this regime is enacted.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Inform the board that a new licensing gap (VA OTC shops) linked to fraud cases is being closed, relevant to AML typology reviews.

title: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposals to Regulate Over-the-Counter Trading of Virtual Assets
summary: This paper proposes a new licensing regime for businesses that buy and sell virtual assets for cash over the counter (OTC), including physical shops and digital platforms. It would be run by the Commissioner of Customs and Excise (CCE), rather than the SFC or HKMA. Licensees would only be able to trade VA-for-money, and transfer coins to wallets the customer can prove they own. They could only offer tokens already tradable by retail investors on an SFC-licensed platform, or stablecoins issued by an HKMA-licensed issuer. Authorized institutions, licensed corporations and licensed VA trading platforms providing such services would be exempt from the new regime, because they are already regulated. The paper proposes fines up to HK$1 million and up to two years' imprisonment for operating without a licence.

key_points.point: A VA OTC licence would be required for anyone conducting spot VA-for-money trading as a business, whether through a physical outlet, ATM, or digital platform.
Licensees could not offer VA-to-VA conversion trades; customers wanting that would need to use a licensed VA trading platform instead.
Licensees could only offer tokens that retail investors can already access via an SFC-licensed VA trading platform, or stablecoins from an HKMA-licensed issuer.
Authorized institutions (banks), licensed corporations and licensed VA trading platforms providing OTC services would be exempt from the new regime, since they are already regulated by the HKMA/SFC.
Operating an unlicensed VA OTC business would be an offence carrying a fine of HK$1 million and up to two years' imprisonment.

CCE would gain powers to inspect premises, investigate, arrest, and impose sanctions including licence suspension or revocation, plus a proposed power to block websites of unlicensed or fraudulent operators.
Proposed transitional period is six months, during which pre-existing operators must apply for a licence within the first three months to keep operating.

But its retail and private-banking teams should know that, once enacted, sending client funds to an unlicensed OTC shop becomes a criminal offence for the counterparty. This is relevant to fraud-typology monitoring and customer education.

title: Provision of Custodial Services for Digital Assets
summary: This cover letter introduces the HKMA's expected standards, set out in the accompanying Annex, for banks that safekeep clients' digital assets. This applies whether as part of virtual-asset intermediary activity, tokenised-product distribution, or standalone custody. It applies to banks and to subsidiaries of locally incorporated banks. It covers 'digital assets' broadly: virtual assets, tokenised securities, other tokenised assets, and the private keys used to access them. It requires banks already offering such custody to confirm compliance with the Annex's standards within six months.

key_points.point: The circular applies to 'digital assets' broadly: virtual assets as defined under the AML ordinance, tokenised securities, and other tokenised assets. It expressly extends to the means of accessing them, meaning private keys, seeds and their backups.
The circular does not apply to custody of a bank's own proprietary digital assets that are not held on behalf of clients.
Banks should apply the expected standards whether the digital assets are received while acting as a virtual-asset intermediary, distributing tokenised products, or providing standalone custody.
A bank planning to launch digital asset custody should talk to the HKMA before doing so, and satisfy the HKMA that it meets the expected standards.

Banks already providing digital asset custody should review and, if necessary, revise their systems and controls. They should notify the HKMA confirming compliance with the Annex within six months of the circular's date.

title: Guidance on Expected Standards on Provision of Custodial Services for Digital Assets by Authorized Institutions
summary: This Annex sets the HKMA's detailed, numbered expected standards for a bank's custody of client digital assets. It covers governance, segregation, safeguarding of keys, delegation/outsourcing, disclosure, record-keeping, AML/CFT and ongoing monitoring. Core requirements include client-asset segregation from the bank's own assets, and board-level risk oversight before launch. They include a written key-management policy covering generation through destruction, a numeric cold-storage floor, and insurance/compensation floors for virtual assets specifically. They also include strict limits on who a bank may delegate custody to. The standards are risk-based for most digital assets, but become prescriptive, effectively mandatory, minimums for virtual assets.

key_points.point: Before launching digital asset custody, a bank must complete a comprehensive risk assessment, and put in place policies and controls. The board and senior management must exercise effective oversight, both before launch and on an ongoing basis.

A bank must allocate adequate resourcing and expertise to custody activities. It must ensure staff and control-function personnel have the necessary knowledge and skills, kept current through ongoing training given the pace of change.

A bank must have clear accountability, roles, responsibilities and reporting lines for custody. It must have adequate policies to identify, manage and mitigate conflicts of interest, for example between the bank's own activities and its affiliates.
A bank must hold client digital assets in accounts, including wallet addresses, segregated from its own assets. This protects them from the bank's creditors on insolvency or resolution.

A bank must not transfer, lend, pledge, re-pledge or encumber client digital assets. Exceptions are to settle transactions or fees owed by the client, with the client's prior written consent, or as required by law. The bank must have controls to stop client assets being used for its own account.

A bank must have effective controls that cut the chance of client digital assets being lost to theft, fraud, negligence or misappropriation. These controls must also stop access being delayed or lost.

A bank may take a risk-based approach to safeguarding controls generally. But where client digital assets are virtual assets, the detailed controls in paragraph 11 are 'generally required', not merely risk-based options.

Required key-management controls include generating and storing seeds and private keys, and backups, in tamper-resistant environments such as a hardware security module (HSM), ideally offline. They include generating, storing and backing them up in Hong Kong. They include strict need-to-know access with multi-factor authentication and audit trails. And they include splitting keys among multiple authorised personnel (key sharding) to avoid a single point of failure.
For client virtual assets under custody, a bank should keep 98% of the total safely offline in storage with no internet connection. This applies unless there is good reason to do otherwise.

For client virtual assets under custody, a bank should maintain compensation or insurance covering at least 50% of the virtual assets held in cold storage. It should cover 100% of those in hot or other storage.

Deposits and withdrawals of client digital assets should only be allowed through wallet addresses confirmed to belong to the client. This can be verified, for example, by message signing or a micropayment test, and the addresses whitelisted.
As a general rule, for virtual assets a bank can hand its custody role only to another authorized institution, or its subsidiary, or an SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform.

Before appointing any custody delegate or service provider, a bank must perform due diligence on its financial soundness, reputation, technical capability and ability to meet the Annex's standards. It must document the assessment, and monitor the delegate's performance on an ongoing basis.
A bank stays fully answerable and on the hook for any custody work it hands off to a delegate or outsourced provider.

A bank must give clients full and fair disclosure of the custody arrangement. This includes their ownership rights on the bank's insolvency, how assets are segregated, fees, and any insurance or compensation cover. It also includes whether assets are commingled with other clients', and the treatment of forks, airdrops and voting rights.

A bank must keep client-by-client books and records tracking ownership and asset movements. It must perform regular, frequent reconciliation covering both on-chain and off-chain records, escalating discrepancies to senior management promptly.
A bank must keep and safeguard all custody-related records and provide them to the HKMA on request in a timely manner.

AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls must effectively manage money-laundering and terrorist-financing risk arising from digital asset custody. This applies the HKMA's AML/CFT guideline and any custody-specific AML/CFT guidance.
A bank must regularly review its custody policies and procedures and conduct independent audits of its systems, controls and compliance.

Where a non-virtual-asset digital asset sits on an open, permission-free distributed ledger with no gatekeeper, a bank must take extra care. It must closely assess whether handing off custody makes sense at all.

title: Sale and distribution of tokenised products
summary: The HKMA sets out its expectation for when a bank sells a 'tokenised product' to customers. A tokenised product is a digital wrapper around a real-world asset, excluding securities-law-regulated tokens and stablecoins. The same consumer-protection rules that already apply to the underlying non-tokenised product apply equally to its tokenised form. Banks are expected to do enhanced due diligence on issuers and technology vendors, and disclose tokenisation-specific risks to customers. They must put proper risk-management and custodial controls in place before launching such sales. The circular does not create a new licensing regime; it layers tokenisation-specific expectations on top of existing product rules.

key_points.point: The circular covers tokenised digital representations of real-world assets, such as structured investment products and precious metals. It does not apply to instruments already regulated under the Securities and Futures Ordinance, or to stablecoins.

As a general rule, the existing supervisory and investor-protection requirements for a traditional product also apply to its tokenised version. This is because the tokenised form carries the same terms, features and risks as the underlying asset, apart from tokenisation-specific risk.

Tokenisation can change a product's substance; for example, fractionalised tokenised interests may become a collective investment scheme. Because of this, banks should independently evaluate the terms, features and risk of each tokenised product, and use professional judgment on which legal regime applies, seeking outside advice if unsure.
Before selling a tokenised product, banks should have adequate systems, controls and additional internal controls addressing the product's specific tokenisation risks.

Banks should perform ongoing due diligence on the tokenised product itself, on its issuer, and on any third-party technology vendor, such as the tokenisation platform. This includes their track record and systems for managing ownership and technology risk.

Due diligence should specifically cover private-key management, safeguards against theft, fraud or hacking, and technology audits, including smart-contract audits where used. It should also cover contingency plans for DLT network failure or loss of private keys.

Before offering a tokenised product, banks should disclose tokenisation-specific risks to customers, in plain, non-technical language. These include DLT network risk, cybersecurity vulnerability, transfer restrictions, smart-contract risk, legal uncertainty on ownership or settlement finality, and custodial risk.

A bank issuing a tokenised product itself should apply the same due-diligence expectations to its own issuance. It should consider the most appropriate custodial arrangement, with extra care for permissionless public tokens.
Banks providing custody of tokenised products should separately meet the HKMA's expected standards on digital asset custody (the companion custody circular).
Banks intending to engage in tokenised-product activities should discuss their plans with the HKMA in advance of launch

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this confirms that selling a tokenised product does not escape existing suitability, disclosure and conduct rules. Compliance must extend, not replace, its existing product-governance and disclosure controls to cover tokenisation-specific risks. It must also pre-clear new tokenised offerings with the HKMA.

title: The 2024-25 Budget
summary: In the digital finance and Web3.0 sections of the 2024-25 Budget speech, the Financial Secretary reported on the HKMA's e-HKD pilot. It had wrapped up the first phase and was moving into the second. He said Project mBridge cross-border central bank digital currency settlement was progressing. He announced expansion of the e-CNY pilot in Hong Kong. He confirmed the government had issued a second, larger multi-currency batch of tokenised government green bonds. He said the government had consulted on a stablecoin issuer licensing regime, and that the HKMA would soon launch a stablecoin issuer sandbox. He also referenced the SFC's existing VA trading platform licensing regime and the new OTC trading consultation.

key_points.point: The HKMA wrapped up the first phase of its e-HKD pilot, which explored programmable payments, offline payments and tokenised deposits. A second phase would explore further use cases.
Project mBridge's Phase 1 service, expected to launch in 2024, would be among the first projects globally to settle cross-border corporate transactions using central bank digital currencies.
Hong Kong would expand e-CNY pilot testing, letting residents set up e-CNY wallets and top them up via the Faster Payment System.

A second batch of tokenised government green bonds worth HK$6 billion, denominated in four currencies, was issued in early 2024. It was described as the world's first multi-currency tokenised bond issuance.

Following the 2023 consultation on stablecoin issuer regulation, the HKMA would launch a sandbox for prospective stablecoin issuers to trial their issuance process and risk management under supervision.

The SFC's VA trading platform licensing regime, running since June 2023, was cited as putting Hong Kong ahead of many major jurisdictions on VA trading regulation. A new OTC trading consultation had also been launched.

title: SFC reminds public VATP application period has ended under transitional arrangements
summary: The SFC reminded the public that the 29 February 2024 deadline for virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs) operating in Hong Kong to submit licence applications had passed. This was under the AMLO Schedule 3G transitional arrangements. VATPs that did not apply by that deadline must close their Hong Kong business by 31 May 2024. Continuing to operate unlicensed is a criminal offence. Investors were urged to check the SFC's lists of licensed VATPs and VATP applicants, and to close accounts with, or transfer away from, platforms not on either list.

key_points.point: VATPs operating pre-1 June 2023 that missed the 29 February 2024 licence-application deadline must close down their Hong Kong business by 31 May 2024 under AMLO Schedule 3G transitional arrangements.
Carrying on unlicensed VATP activity in Hong Kong is a criminal offence.
Applications on the 'List of virtual asset trading platform applicants' are still being processed and may or may not be approved. Trading on these platforms carries risk.
Investors are strongly urged to confine their virtual asset trading to SFC-licensed VATPs.
VATP applicants ultimately refused a licence may be required to close down and be placed on the 'List of closing-down virtual asset trading platforms'.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is a counterparty-due-diligence checkpoint, not a bank obligation. After the cutover date, compliance must verify any HK VATP counterparty is licensed or a listed applicant, since operating unlicensed is now a criminal offence for that platform.

quote.text: It is a criminal offence to carry on any unlicensed activity.

reading_guide: Short document; read in full (under 2 minutes).

counterparty_due_diligence: Before dealing with any HK VATP counterparty, verify it appears on the SFC's licensed or applicant list, since the 29 February 2024 application deadline has passed and non-applicants had to close by 31 May 2024 (para 1-2, Note 1, p.1).
Treat 'applicant' status as unresolved risk: applications on the applicant list are still being processed and may be refused (para 6-7, p.1).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should know that using an unlicensed HK VATP counterparty after this cutover is now a criminal-offence risk for that counterparty (para 2, p.1), heightening the bar for the bank's own onboarding checks.

key_points.point: BitForex claims a Hong Kong head office but has never been licensed by or applied to the SFC.
Victims faced growing withdrawal difficulties blamed on 'wallet and website maintenance', then the site shut down entirely.
Police blocked BitForex's websites and social-media pages at the SFC's request.

summary: SFC warning about fake websites copying two genuine licensed VATPs, Hash Blockchain Limited and OSL Digital Securities Limited. Victims reported withdrawal problems and demands to pay large 'fees and taxes'. Police blocked the sites still accessible at the SFC's request. Victims reported withdrawal problems and were asked to pay large 'fees and taxes' to get funds out.
Public is urged to check the SFC's Public Register and licensed VATP list before transacting.

title: HKMA unveils Project Ensemble to support development of Hong Kong tokenisation market
summary: The HKMA announced Project Ensemble: a wholesale central bank digital currency (wCBDC) programme meant to back interbank settlement of tokenised money. The initial focus is tokenised deposits issued by commercial banks. These would use the wCBDC as a settlement foundation for tokenised asset transactions, such as green bonds, carbon credits and trade documents. A wCBDC Sandbox and an industry Architecture Community, including banks and technology firms, were planned to test use cases and set standards.

key_points.point: Project Ensemble is a wholesale CBDC initiative to enable interbank settlement of tokenised money, initially focused on bank-issued tokenised deposits.
A wCBDC Sandbox would test tokenisation use cases including settlement of green bonds, carbon credits, aircraft, EV charging stations, e-bills of lading and treasury management.
An Architecture Community of banks, digital asset firms and tech companies would help set industry standards for the project.
The HKMA said it may conduct a live issuance of the wCBDC later if the sandbox draws sufficient industry interest.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, tokenised deposits are a bank-issued product. So if the bank's treasury or digital-asset unit wants to participate, compliance should track evolving expectations on tokenised deposit issuance and custody arising from this initiative from the start.

quote.text: reinforce our forefront position in tokenised money and assets

reading_guide: Read the full short press release; it is the founding announcement for Project Ensemble, later expanded in the Architecture Community (9ccf297cfe6c) and Sandbox launch (373d764e8ed3) releases.

controls_and_monitoring: If participating, ensure tokenised deposit issuance is governed by the same controls as existing deposit-taking (KYC, ledger reconciliation)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Advise the board this is a voluntary HKMA-led pilot; participation decision should weigh strategic positioning against operational/resourcing cost.

title: HKMA unveils Project Ensemble to support the development of the Hong Kong tokenisation market
summary: The HKMA announced Project Ensemble: a wholesale central bank digital currency (wCBDC) effort meant to back Hong Kong's tokenisation market. It will initially focus on tokenised deposits (a digital representation of commercial bank deposits) as the settlement asset for tokenised real-world-asset transactions (for example, green bonds, carbon credits, aircraft, EV charging stations, e-bills of lading, treasury management). A wCBDC Sandbox is planned to launch later that year, supported by a wCBDC Architecture Community of banks, digital-asset firms, tech companies and the CBDC Expert Group. The HKMA said it may conduct a 'live' wCBDC issuance later if the sandbox garners sufficient industry interest.

key_points.point: Project Ensemble will explore new financial market infrastructure enabling interbank settlement of tokenised money via a wholesale CBDC (wCBDC).
Initial focus is tokenised deposits — a digital form of the deposits that commercial banks issue and offer to the public.
A wCBDC Sandbox will be launched in 2024 to test tokenisation use cases including settlement of tokenised real-world assets.

The HKMA will form a wCBDC Architecture Community. This will include local and multinational banks, digital-asset industry players, tech companies and the CBDC Expert Group, to set industry standards.
If the Sandbox garners sufficient industry interest, HKMA will conduct a 'live' issuance of the wCBDC at an appropriate time.
Project Ensemble builds on prior HKMA tokenisation work. This includes e-HKD, mBridge, Dynamo, Genesis, and 2023 tokenised-deposit experiments with HSBC, Hang Seng Bank and Ant Group.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, no compliance obligation attaches yet. But a compliance head should track Project Ensemble as the origin of the tokenised-deposit infrastructure the bank may be asked to connect to. This carries governance and control implications once real transactions begin.

quote.text: Project Ensemble will provide fresh impetus to our vibrant financial industry

reading_guide: Read in full; short. Treat as background/superseded by later Ensemble Sandbox and Architecture Community announcements in this batch.
flags: Status marked superseded because later documents in this batch (Architecture Community establishment, Sandbox launch) update/operationalise this initial announcement.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be briefed that HKMA's tokenised-deposit infrastructure initiative (Project Ensemble) is now underway and may invite the bank's participation in the forthcoming Sandbox (para 3, p.1).

title: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism (1) FATF Statement on High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action (2) FATF Statement on Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring (3) Outcomes from the FATF Plenary, 21-23 February 2024

Myanmar remains subject to a call for enhanced due diligence. The Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring list added Kenya and Namibia, and removed Barbados, Gibraltar, Uganda and the UAE. It also relays FATF Plenary outcomes. These are finalised guidance on Recommendation 25 (beneficial ownership of legal arrangements), and an agreed publication on VASP regulation/supervision steps by major jurisdictions. They also include proposed amendments to Recommendation 16 (payment messaging), open for public consultation until 3 May 2024.

FATF continues to call for enhanced due diligence proportionate to risk from Myanmar due to continued lack of progress on its action plan.
Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring list updated: Kenya and Namibia added; Barbados, Gibraltar, Uganda and the UAE removed.
FATF finalised updated Risk-Based Guidance for Recommendation 25 on beneficial ownership of legal arrangements (trusts etc.).
FATF agreed to publish an overview of steps taken by major virtual-asset jurisdictions to regulate/supervise VASPs, to encourage full implementation of Recommendation 15.
FATF released proposed amendments to Recommendation 16 (payment messaging) for public consultation, closing 3 May 2024.

title: Stablecoin Issuer Sandbox
summary: The HKMA announced the launch of a sandbox for firms planning to launch stablecoins pegged to fiat currencies in Hong Kong. This follows a December 2023 consultation paper on a future licensing regime. The sandbox lets the HKMA communicate supervisory expectations and gather feedback from participants testing stablecoin business models, in a limited, risk-controlled way. Admission requires a genuine plan to issue stablecoins, a concrete testing plan, and a reasonable prospect of meeting future rules. Sandbox status is not a licence, and does not guarantee a future licence. The HKMA warned the public to watch for scams using the sandbox's name.

key_points.point: Applicants must show genuine interest in, and a workable plan for, launching fiat-referenced stablecoins from Hong Kong. They must also have a concrete sandbox participation plan, and a reasonable prospect of eventually complying with the proposed rules.
key_points.locator: section 'Eligibility for accessing the sandbox', para 11

key_points.point: Sandbox testing will run on a limited scale, and will not use members of the public's money at the initial stage. The HKMA can adjust the scope as testing goes on.
Sandbox participants who break the terms can have their participation ended by the HKMA.
Being admitted to the sandbox does not mean the HKMA or any other regulator endorses or regulates the firm. A separate licence application will still be needed once the regime is in force.
Sandbox applicants should not reveal their application before admission. Admitted participants should seek the HKMA's agreement before making public announcements about their status.
key_points.locator: section 'Staying alert to virtual asset scams', para 21

key_points.point: The HKMA will post the names of sandbox participants online and update the page regularly so the public can check claims.

numbers_and_dates.item: Consultation responses received on the December 2023 stablecoin proposal

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this marks the start of direct HKMA engagement with prospective stablecoin issuers, ahead of the eventual Stablecoins Ordinance. A bank considering issuing or partnering with a sandbox participant should check the published participant list, rather than rely on a counterparty's own claims.

quote.text: successful admission as a sandbox participant does not imply

reading_guide: Read the whole announcement; it is short and each paragraph carries a distinct eligibility or conduct rule.

controls_and_monitoring: Before treating any counterparty as a legitimate stablecoin issuer or sandbox participant, check the HKMA's published sandbox participant list rather than relying on the counterparty's own representation.
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm sandbox status (and any public statements about it) against the HKMA's official list; sandbox status is not a licence and carries no HKMA endorsement.
Note that participants must obtain HKMA agreement before making public sandbox-related announcements — an unauthorised claim is a red flag.

title: HKMA launches stablecoin issuer sandbox arrangement

title: HKMA launches the stablecoin issuer sandbox arrangement
summary: The HKMA launched a sandbox arrangement for parties with a genuine interest in launching fiat-referenced stablecoins from Hong Kong. It is tied to the ongoing consultation on the proposed stablecoin issuer regulatory regime. The sandbox lets the HKMA communicate supervisory expectations and gather industry feedback before the regime is finalised. Per the attached Annex, applicants register interest via a dedicated HKMA email. Admission is not an endorsement or a guarantee of eventual licensing. Participants must seek HKMA agreement before making public statements about their participation, and can be withdrawn for non-adherence or voluntary exit.

key_points.point: The sandbox is intended to support virtual-asset ecosystem development, communicate supervisory expectations, gather feedback on proposed requirements, and develop good practices (reserves management, governance, user protection, AML/CFT, data transparency).
Admission to the sandbox does not mean HKMA endorsement or that the participant is qualified for future regulation.
Sandbox participants wishing to apply for a licence after the regime is implemented must submit a separate application to the licensing authority.
Applicants should demonstrate genuine interest, a reasonable stablecoin issuance plan, a concrete sandbox participation plan, and a reasonable prospect of complying with proposed requirements.
Before admission, no applicant should make announcements about application status. After admission, any announcement about sandbox participation should first get HKMA agreement.
A participant is deemed withdrawn if HKMA finds it fails to adhere to its anticipated operation, or if it voluntarily exits with advance notice.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this establishes the sandbox through which prospective stablecoin issuers, including banks, could engage with the HKMA before the licensing regime was finalised. It is relevant mainly if the bank is or becomes a sandbox participant or issuer applicant.

quote.text: does not mean that such sandbox participant is in any way endorsed by the HKMA

reading_guide: Read the press release plus the full Annex (2 pages) — the Annex contains the operative rules.
flags: Sandbox participation is explicitly NOT an endorsement and does NOT guarantee future licensing — a common misconception to correct.

title: HKMA launches Phase 2 of the e-HKD Pilot Programme
summary: The HKMA announced Phase 2 of the e-HKD Pilot Programme. This builds on Phase 1, completed October 2023, which studied domestic retail use cases such as programmable payments, tokenised-asset settlement and offline payments. Phase 2 will go deeper into selected Phase 1 pilots, such as programmability, tokenisation and atomic settlement, plus new use cases. It is supported by an enhanced e-HKD sandbox built on the wCBDC sandbox under Project Ensemble. Applications to participate were due by 17 May 2024.

key_points.point: The e-HKD Pilot Programme's first phase wrapped up in October 2023, covering programmable payments, tokenised-asset settlement, and offline payments.
Phase 2 will explore selected Phase 1 pilots more deeply (programmability, tokenisation, atomic settlement) plus new use cases.
An enhanced e-HKD sandbox, leveraging the wCBDC sandbox under Project Ensemble, will support Phase 2. It will study interoperability and interbank settlement between e-HKD and other tokenised money.
Organisations interested in Phase 2 should submit applications by 17 May 2024.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a compliance head, this is informational. It confirms e-HKD pilot infrastructure and Project Ensemble's tokenised-deposit sandbox are technically converging. This is useful context for the bank's digital-asset roadmap, but not a source of any obligation.
reading_guide: Short; read in full.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No action needed; note the technical convergence of the e-HKD sandbox with Project Ensemble's tokenised-deposit sandbox for awareness of shared infrastructure.

title: HKMA launches Phase 2 of e-HKD Pilot Programme

title: SFC warns public against unlicensed virtual asset trading platform Bybit
summary: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) warns that Bybit is not licensed for any regulated activity in Hong Kong. Bybit offers many derivative-like and yield crypto products across global markets, and these can count as futures contracts or securities under Hong Kong law. So marketing or dealing in them to Hong Kong investors needs a licence, unless an exemption applies. A similarly named Hong Kong firm, Spark Fintech Limited, which runs a '.com.hk' website, is not related to Bybit's products.

key_points.point: No entity in the Bybit group holds an SFC licence or SFC registration for any regulated activity in Hong Kong.
Bybit's products listed include futures, options, leveraged tokens, dual-asset products, liquid staking, lending and wealth management.
These products may be futures contracts or securities under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO), so dealing or marketing them needs a Hong Kong licence.
Issuing related advertisements to the Hong Kong public without SFC authorisation is also an offence.
A separate, similarly-named Hong Kong-incorporated company (Spark Fintech Limited, bybit.com.hk) is not involved in offering these products.

numbers_and_dates.item: added to Alert List (platform and products)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this warning shows that crypto derivatives, staking and lending products can count as futures or securities under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO). A compliance head should apply that classification check to any platform a client mentions.
reading_guide: Read paras 1-5; notes mainly define statutory terms already used elsewhere.

counterparty_due_diligence: Treat unlicensed derivative/staking/lending crypto platforms referenced by clients as needing SFC Alert List and licensing-status verification before any dealings (para 3-4)

title: SFC warns public against unlicensed virtual asset trading platform MEXC
summary: This notice targets the real MEXC exchange, not the earlier fraud case using the same name from 9 February 2024. MEXC actively marketed to Hong Kong investors, including sign-up bonuses, without ever being licensed by or applying to the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC). The SFC treats this as unlicensed operation and marketing under the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (AMLO).

key_points.point: MEXC has neither been licensed nor applied for a licence to run a virtual asset trading platform (VATP) in Hong Kong.
Operating a virtual-asset exchange, or actively marketing one, to Hong Kong investors without a licence is an offence under the AMLO.
MEXC ran a Hong Kong-targeted campaign: 20 USDT for finishing know-your-client (KYC) checks within seven days, and 10 MX for referrals hitting set trading volumes.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this confirms that even a widely used international exchange was treated as unlicensed in Hong Kong, showing the reach of SFC enforcement against large platforms.
reading_guide: Skim; template plus a note distinguishing it from the earlier fraud-only MEXC notice.
flags: Confirms two separate SFC notices concern different 'MEXC' matters: a fraud impersonation case (9 Feb 2024) and the genuine exchange operating unlicensed (this notice, 15 Mar 2024).

title: Realising the Potential of Blockchain in Advancing Hong Kong's Financial Services Industry
summary: This is a report from the Financial Services Development Council (FSDC), a government-funded advisory body. It argues Hong Kong should keep encouraging blockchain use in business-to-business finance, separate from crypto trading. A dedicated FSDC working group looked at how policy and regulation can help this happen. It links blockchain adoption to national technology strategy goals, and it is advocacy and commentary, not a rulebook, creating no obligations.

key_points.point: The paper is produced by an FSDC-appointed working group of industry people, not a regulator, so it carries no legal force.
Its main angle is enterprise blockchain use outside cryptocurrency, such as data sharing and identity verification between businesses.
It ties Hong Kong's blockchain push to the Mainland's 14th Five-Year Plan tech goals.
It calls for closer government-industry cooperation to grow blockchain-based Web3 activity in the city.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is industry commentary, not a regulator statement, so it carries no direct compliance duty. It points to the policy direction regulators like the FSTB and the HKMA are likely to keep following on enterprise blockchain.
reading_guide: Read only the summary text on the landing page (paras 1-4); the rest of the fetched page is site navigation and cookie-consent boilerplate.

title: Keynote speech at the ICMA “The Chinese and Asian Cross-border Bond Markets – Innovations and Opportunities” Event
summary: A senior Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) official reviewed the Asian and Mainland cross-border bond market in 2023-24, covering Bond Connect, green finance, and technology. The speech also referenced adoption of a market bond-data taxonomy to make bond information machine-readable.

title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - New Fintech Promotion Roadmap: Opening Remarks at the Seminar on Distributed Ledger Technology - Unlocking the Potential of DLT in Financial Services
summary: Opening remarks at a Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) seminar on distributed ledger technology (DLT), part of the new Fintech Promotion Roadmap. The speaker set out the HKMA's stance on DLT: risk-based, technology-neutral, and guided by 'same activity, same risk, same regulation'. Its key forward-looking announcement is that the HKMA planned to issue non-binding guidelines within weeks, setting out considerations for reviewing banks' DLT applications.

key_points.point: The HKMA's supervisory approach to DLT is risk-based and technology-neutral, applying the principle of 'same activity, same risk, same regulation'.
The HKMA said it planned to issue guidelines within weeks setting out the considerations it takes into account when reviewing banks' DLT applications.
The planned guidelines were described as non-exhaustive and non-binding on banks, intended as a benchmark rather than a rulebook.
Regulators were running other DLT-adoption support activities alongside the guidelines, including sandboxes, research projects and training sessions with the SFC, Insurance Authority and MPFA.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, forthcoming HKMA guidance on DLT applications would not be binding, but would work as the real supervisory benchmark. Compliance should track the guidance once issued and align internal DLT project reviews to it.

quote.text: same activity, same risk, same regulation

reading_guide: Short speech; read paragraphs 6-11 for the supervisory-approach and forthcoming-guidelines content, skip the introductory remarks on DLT use cases generally.
flags: Announces forthcoming non-binding DLT guidelines; confirm separately whether/when the HKMA actually published these (not evidenced in this document).

obligations: Design and review DLT-based banking initiatives against the equivalence principle 'same activity, same risk, same regulation' rather than assuming DLT projects sit outside existing prudential and conduct rules.
controls_and_monitoring: Track publication of the announced (non-binding) HKMA DLT application-review guidelines and incorporate them into internal DLT project governance once issued.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Inform the board/risk committee that the HKMA is moving toward a published benchmark for reviewing bank DLT applications, which will shape internal approval processes for DLT initiatives.

title: SFC warns public against unlicensed virtual asset trading platform Sure X
summary: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) warns of Sure X, which posed as a blockchain education and training provider. Sure X may have sold unlicensed virtual asset trading platform (VATP) services to people in Hong Kong under that cover. Even after its main sites went offline, the SFC notes Hong Kong investors could still reach the platform through other means.

Even with its listed websites inaccessible, users could still reach the platform through other internet routes.

reading_guide: Short; read in full.

title: Keynote Speech at the International Conference on Central Bank Digital Currencies and Payment Systems
summary: A senior Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) official outlined a 'digital money framework' with three possible parts: retail central bank digital currency (CBDC), stablecoins, and tokenised deposits. The speech reviewed the HKMA's CBDC projects (mBridge, the e-HKD Pilot, and Aurum) and confirmed a completed stablecoin issuer consultation requiring full, high-quality liquid reserve backing. It also announced a wholesale CBDC sandbox under the new Project Ensemble, to test interbank settlement between banks' own tokenised-asset ledgers.

key_points.point: The HKMA set out a digital money framework built around three components: retail CBDC, regulated stablecoins, and tokenised bank deposits.
A retail CBDC decision remained open; the HKMA planned a use-case-driven approach given Hong Kong's already efficient payments system.
The HKMA had just completed its stablecoin issuer licensing consultation, which would require full backing by high-quality, highly liquid reserve assets.
Tokenised deposits were described as a natural evolution of ordinary bank deposits, representing the same claim on the issuing bank once converted to token form.
The HKMA announced a wholesale CBDC sandbox under Project Ensemble, to test interbank settlement in central bank money between institutions' own tokenised-asset ledgers.
A CBDC-backed 'reserve-backed token' under Project Aurum was called a close cousin of a stablecoin, differing mainly in who issues it: a central bank or a commercial bank.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this gives the clearest early view of how the HKMA expects stablecoins, tokenised deposits and CBDCs to fit together. This should shape the bank's own tokenised-deposit and digital-asset strategy relative to the regulator's roadmap.

quote.text: A dollar is a dollar, regardless of who is issuing the money

reading_guide: Read the 'Digital Money Framework', 'Stablecoins', 'Tokenised Deposits' and 'A wholesale CBDC' sections (roughly paragraphs 43-85) in full; the historical CBDC background at the start can be skimmed.

controls_and_monitoring: Monitor how the announced full-backing, high-quality/high-liquidity reserve requirement for stablecoin issuers develops, as banks partnering with or holding exposure to issuers will need to assess this in due diligence.
counterparty_due_diligence: When assessing a stablecoin issuer counterparty, check whether its reserve backing and asset quality claims match the direction set out here (full backing, high-quality and highly liquid reserves).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Brief the board that HKMA policy is converging on three parallel forms of digital money (retail CBDC, stablecoins, tokenised deposits) any of which could affect the bank's own product and settlement strategy.

title: SFC warns public of TCAME and BitCloud for suspected virtual asset-related fraud
summary: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) warns of TCAME and BitCloud, both accused of falsely claiming foreign regulatory licences that were not genuine. Investors reported having to make extra 'deposits' to process withdrawals, and some accounts were frozen.

key_points.point: TCAME falsely claimed licences from regulators in St Vincent, Canada and the Philippines, none of which appeared genuine.
BitCloud falsely claimed certificates from US regulators, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) and the National Futures Association (NFA).
Investors were asked to make additional 'deposits' to process withdrawals, and some accounts were frozen.

reading_guide: Short; read in full.

title: Risk management considerations related to the use of DLT
summary: This Annex lists ten non-binding considerations the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) applies when reviewing a bank's distributed ledger technology (DLT) projects. They are grouped under governance, application design and development, and ongoing maintenance and monitoring. Key themes include board-level ownership of DLT risk, careful choice of network type, smart-contract governance and audit, and legal-risk awareness around settlement finality. Other themes are third-party and node-operator due diligence, interoperability, cybersecurity matching traditional systems, secure private-key management, data-privacy compliance on unchangeable ledgers, and DLT-specific contingency planning.

key_points.point: A bank's board and senior management are fully responsible for adopting DLT and managing its risks. This includes updating risk, continuity and outsourcing policies, and ensuring enough in-house DLT expertise and staff training.
Where a DLT solution is customer-facing, the bank should review whether DLT-specific consumer education, dispute handling, redress and compensation mechanisms are needed.

DLT network-type choice (permissionless, private- or public-permissioned) affects security, stability, scalability and resilience. The HKMA expects the bank to justify its choice against the risk profile, with compensating controls for higher-risk designs.
Permissionless networks are not always the best fit for moving sensitive data. But they need not be ruled out if the bank shows mitigations like zero-knowledge proofs or hybrid on/off-chain designs.

Where smart contracts are used, the bank must manage the operational, third-party and legal risks, with governance covering suitability assessment, due diligence, design controls, upgrades, and audits before deployment.

Because settlement finality and legal standing under DLT can be less clear than under traditional systems, banks should identify these grey areas, seek professional advice where needed, and build in mitigations.

Banks must assess whether a DLT network's node operators are trustworthy, reliable and diverse enough. They should avoid permissionless networks, where node operators may be pseudonymous, for critical functions unless adequate controls exist.

Banks should design DLT systems to work with traditional and other DLT systems where practicable. That way a tokenised deposit is not confined to the issuing bank's own network, while interbank links stay secure.

DLT applications must have cybersecurity as strong as traditional systems. This covers DLT-specific threats such as 51% attacks and common threats such as DDoS, with response plans updated for risks like quantum computing.

Banks acting as custodian of client digital assets should apply stricter private-key security: secure generation, storage, backup, access controls and cold storage, cross-referencing the HKMA's separate custody circular.

Banks must keep complying with data privacy rules whether data sits on a centralised system or a DLT ledger. This means addressing issues like data retention on an unchangeable ledger, confidentiality on transparent ledgers, and data localisation.
For DLT used in critical functions, business continuity plans should include DLT-specific test scenarios -- common cyberattacks, key loss or theft, forking -- and backup options for DLT outages.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the HKMA's working checklist for any DLT proposal -- tokenised deposits, custody platforms, settlement systems. Technology and compliance teams should map each planned DLT initiative against these considerations before HKMA submission, since supervisors will actually probe them.
reading_guide: Read all ten considerations (pp.2–6); each is short and none is boilerplate.
flags: Explicitly non-binding guidance rather than a rule — there is no fixed compliance deadline or numeric threshold, unlike the custody circular's 98% cold-storage figure

obligations: Update technology risk management, BCP and outsourcing policies to reflect DLT-specific factors before deployment (item 1)
Justify DLT network-type choice against application risk and put in place compensating controls for higher-risk designs (item 2)
Maintain a smart-contract governance framework covering due diligence, design controls and upgrade procedures (item 3)
Comply with data privacy/protection requirements notwithstanding DLT's immutability and transparency (item 9)
controls_and_monitoring: DLT-specific cybersecurity controls for both DLT-specific and common threats, kept current with emerging technology (item 7)
Rigorous private-key security procedures where the bank acts as custodian (item 8)
DLT-specific BCP testing scenarios and backup options (item 10)
notifications_reporting: Take these considerations into account when preparing DLT-related submissions to the HKMA (cover letter, p.2)
counterparty_due_diligence: Assess trustworthiness, reliability and diversity of node operators validating any DLT network the bank relies on (item 5)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should see how each active DLT initiative (e.g. tokenised deposits) has been assessed against network-choice, smart-contract, legal, third-party, interoperability, cybersecurity, key-management, data-privacy and contingency-planning considerations.

title: Risk management considerations related to the use of distributed ledger technology
summary: This cover letter explains why the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) is publishing non-binding risk-management considerations for banks exploring distributed ledger technology (DLT) in traditional finance. The considerations, in the attached Annex, focus particularly on tokenised deposits. It confirms the HKMA's risk-based, technology-neutral supervisory stance. The HKMA will assess whether a bank has adequate systems and controls for the extra risks DLT introduces, rather than approving or banning specific technologies outright.

key_points.point: The considerations set out in the Annex are non-binding and non-exhaustive, and will keep evolving as the market and technology develop.

The HKMA's review of a bank's DLT proposal checks whether the bank has adequate systems and controls for DLT's extra risks. It uses a risk-based, technology-neutral approach rather than a fixed checklist.
The HKMA has specifically been encouraging banks to explore issuing tokenised deposits and wants the considerations to help banks design those and similar DLT solutions.
Banks are advised to take the considerations into account when preparing DLT-related supervisory submissions to the HKMA.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, every DLT pilot or tokenised-deposit project runs subject to case-by-case HKMA review against these considerations. Early engagement with the HKMA before launch, not just after, is the expected practice.

quote.text: non-binding, non-exhaustive

title: HKMA establishes the Project Ensemble Architecture Community
summary: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) set up the Project Ensemble Architecture Community, an industry group that will build shared standards. These standards will help wholesale CBDC, tokenised money, and tokenised assets work together, starting with bank-to-bank settlement of tokenised deposits using wholesale CBDC. The group will also help build and run the Project Ensemble Sandbox, a test environment once aimed at a mid-2024 start. Founding members include the HKMA, the SFC, the CBDC Expert Group, the BIS Innovation Hub, and seven private firms -- four banks and three technology companies.

key_points.point: This Community will build shared industry rules so wholesale CBDC, tokenised money, and tokenised assets can work with each other.
The first goal is a way for banks to settle tokenised deposits between each other using wholesale CBDC whenever tokenised assets are traded.
The Community will help build and run the Project Ensemble Sandbox, a test environment once aimed at a mid-2024 start.

Founders include HKMA, SFC, CBDC Expert Group, BIS Innovation Hub, HashKey Group, Ant Digital Technologies, Microsoft Hong Kong, HSBC, Hang Seng Bank, Standard Chartered Hong Kong, and Bank of China (Hong Kong).

It creates no duty for the bank yet, but shows where wholesale CBDC and tokenised-deposit infrastructure is heading, which the bank may need to follow later.

title: SB-1 Supervision of Regulated Activities of SFC-Registered Authorized Institutions (V.3)
summary: This is the HKMA's Supervisory Policy Manual module on how it oversees banks that are also SFC-Registered Institutions (RIs), covering activities like dealing, advising, or asset management. It is not crypto-specific: it covers registration, executive-officer appointment, HKMA-SFC cooperation, supervision, an escalation model for deficiencies, and conduct requirements such as KYC, suitability, and product due diligence. Its one direct link to this batch's subject is a reference in the product-due-diligence section. That reference points to the HKMA-SFC joint circular on intermediaries' virtual-asset-related activities.

key_points.point: The HKMA is the day-to-day 'front line supervisor' of SFC-registered banks, while the SFC keeps ultimate responsibility. The two regulators may rely on each other's supervision under a Memorandum of Understanding.
Every RI must appoint at least two executive officers per regulated activity, with one available to supervise it at all times; these officers need the HKMA's written consent.

The HKMA applies a three-level, risk-based escalation model: encouraging good practice, then requiring corrective action for control gaps, then enforcement action where there is a clear case for discipline.

The module's product-due-diligence guidance lists the HKMA-SFC 'Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities' (22 Dec 2023). That circular covers distribution of VA-exposed products, VA dealing, VA asset management, and VA advisory services.

title: Expanding the cross-boundary e-CNY pilot in Hong Kong
summary: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and the People's Bank of China (PBoC) widened the cross-border e-CNY trial in Hong Kong. Hong Kong residents can now open e-CNY wallets with just a local mobile number and top them up through the Faster Payment System (FPS) at 17 participating retail banks. The HKMA called this the world's first link between a real-time payment system and a central bank digital currency (CBDC). e-CNY wallets support cross-border retail spending but not transfers between individuals, and now also work in mainland pilot zones beyond the Greater Bay Area.

key_points.point: Hong Kong residents can open a personal (tier-4) e-CNY wallet at one of four wallet operators using only a Hong Kong mobile number.
Retail customers can top up e-CNY wallets through FPS at 17 Hong Kong banks; some of these let users convert HKD to RMB directly.
The HKMA describes this as the world's first pairing of a real-time payment network with a CBDC system.
e-CNY wallets can only be used for retail purchases -- transfers between individuals are not permitted.
Tier-4 personal wallets cap balances at RMB10,000, transactions at RMB2,000, daily totals at RMB5,000, and yearly totals at RMB50,000, though operators can set tighter limits.
Customers can cash out their e-CNY wallet balances at designated Hong Kong branches of the four wallet operators.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this shows a cross-border e-CNY and FPS link that some retail banks already support as a top-up channel. It creates no new duty for the bank itself.

quote.text: the first linkage of a faster payment system with a central bank digital currency system

reading_guide: Read main release plus Annex 2 (user guide/limits); Annex 1 is just the bank list.
flags: e-CNY wallets explicitly disallow person-to-person transfers — a common misconception given e-CNY is often assumed to work like a general-purpose digital wallet.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: If the bank is one of the 17 banks offering FPS top-up (Annex 1, p.1), check operational readiness for e-CNY top-up volumes; otherwise this is background information only.

title: SFC statement on the end of non-contravention period for virtual asset trading platforms
summary: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) said the grace period under the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (AMLO) for virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs) ends on 1 June 2024. From that date, every VATP in Hong Kong must be SFC-licensed or a 'deemed-to-be-licensed' applicant, since unlicensed operation is a criminal offence. A deemed-to-be-licensed applicant is NOT formally licensed, must not market to or onboard new retail clients before showing effective controls, and must keep Mainland Chinese residents from accessing services. The SFC will run on-site inspections focused on client-asset safeguarding and know-your-client (KYC) checks, and will swiftly refuse licences where key investor-protection rules are breached.

key_points.point: From 1 June 2024, all VATPs in Hong Kong must be SFC-licensed or deemed-to-be-licensed applicants under the AMLO; unlicensed operation is a criminal offence.
Firms on the deemed-to-be-licensed applicant list do not hold an actual SFC licence, and the SFC may still turn down their applications.
The SFC does not expect deemed-to-be-licensed applicants to market services or onboard new retail clients before showing effective controls and becoming formally licensed.
VATPs and their ultimate owners must stop Mainland Chinese residents from accessing virtual-asset services, and ensure related parties do the same.
Any non-compliance with key investor-protection regulatory requirements by a deemed-to-be-licensed applicant will result in swift refusal of its licence application.
The SFC will run on-site inspections of deemed-to-be-licensed applicants, focused on client-asset safeguards and KYC processes, feeding into licence decisions.
Deemed-to-be-licensed applicants must hire a qualified external assessor to check how well their controls have actually been implemented, under the scope the SFC set out in June 2023.

title: Consultation conclusions for legislative proposal to implement regulatory regime for stablecoin issuers in Hong Kong released
supersedes_or_amends: Consultation paper on legislative proposal to implement the regulatory regime for stablecoin issuers in Hong Kong (27 December 2023)
summary: The Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB) and the HKMA jointly released their conclusions on the proposed licensing regime for stablecoin issuers. This followed 108 submissions during the December 2023-February 2024 consultation. Fiat-referenced stablecoins (FRS) in circulation must always be fully backed by reserve assets, with no break at any time. Reserves must generally match the referenced currency, though HKD issuers may hold USD reserves with the Monetary Authority's (MA's) flexibility. Reserve assets must be kept separate and safeguarded through trust or custodian arrangements, usually with licensed Hong Kong banks, and redemption must happen within one business day at par. Paying interest to FRS users is banned, though marketing incentives are not. Minimum paid-up capital is HK$25 million or 1% of FRS in circulation, whichever is higher, down from the 2% first proposed. Non-Hong Kong incorporated issuers, other than authorized institutions, must set up a Hong Kong subsidiary, and only a specified group of licensed entities may offer FRS to the public. A six-month grace period was set, and the bill was to go to the Legislative Council (LegCo) later in 2024.

key_points.point: The full value of FRS in circulation must be matched by reserve assets without exception, at every point in time. Issuers must show the MA that steps such as over-collateralisation are in place to meet this.

Reserve assets must generally be held in the same currency the FRS references; MA prior approval is required for a currency mismatch. HKD-referenced FRS issuers may hold USD-denominated reserves with MA flexibility.

Reserve assets must be kept separate from the issuer's own assets, and safeguarded through an effective trust arrangement, generally safekept with licensed Hong Kong banks. A draft trust deed and independent legal opinion must go to the HKMA for review.
A qualified independent auditor must attest to reserve assets monthly, no matter how large the FRS in circulation is.
FRS issuers must not pay interest to FRS users, whether directly or through a third party. Marketing incentives stay allowed if they do not amount to interest.

Redemption requests must be met within one business day in normal circumstances, at par value in the referenced currency, without undue cost. MA prior approval is needed if an issuer expects difficulty meeting this timeframe.
FRS issuers are banned from lending or financial intermediation. Only activities that support FRS issuance, such as wallet services for their own FRS, are allowed.

Non-Hong Kong incorporated companies, other than authorized institutions incorporated outside Hong Kong, must set up a Hong Kong subsidiary to apply for a licence. Key management, the chief executive and alternate, must be based in Hong Kong.
The minimum paid-up share capital was set at whichever is greater of HK$25 million or 1% of FRS's circulating par value, down from the 2% floor first proposed.

The public may only be offered FRS by a specified licensed entity: an FRS issuer holding an HKMA licence, an authorized institution, a licensed corporation, or a licensed VATP. None needs a separate MA licence to offer FRS, but each must meet its own regime's rules.
A six-month grace period was set for FRS issuers that already existed before the regime started.
The FSTB and HKMA planned to introduce a bill to the Legislative Council later in 2024, with licensing and supervisory guidelines to follow.
