title: Alert: Misrepresentation and misuse of the word “bank” in Hong Kong by crypto firms
supersedes_or_amends: Alert: Misrepresentation by crypto firms using the word “bank” (15 September 2023)
summary: This is a follow-up HKMA alert citing two specific incidents. An overseas crypto firm hosting an event in Hong Kong reportedly called itself a 'bank'. Another firm marketed a 'bank card' product on its website. Neither is a licensed Hong Kong bank. The HKMA repeats that only authorized institutions may use the word 'bank' or carry on banking/deposit business, and that such misuse breaches the Banking Ordinance.

key_points.point: At a Hong Kong-hosted event, an overseas non-bank crypto firm was reported to have described itself as a 'bank'.
A second overseas crypto firm marketed a 'bank card' product on its website despite not being a licensed bank.
Only licensed banks, restricted licence banks and deposit-taking companies may use the word 'bank' or run banking/deposit business in Hong Kong.
Products or services carrying the word 'bank' are not necessarily provided by a licensed Hong Kong bank.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is a second HKMA alert (after fcbcbb5d9d99) on overseas crypto firms misusing 'bank' branding at Hong Kong events. It is relevant for customer-protection messaging and verifying counterparty authorized-institution status, not as a direct bank obligation.
reading_guide: Read paras 1-4; the note restates the statutory sections already covered by the September 2023 alert.
flags: Second HKMA alert on crypto firms' misuse of the word 'bank', roughly a year after the first (Sept 2023), showing the issue persists.

controls_and_monitoring: Screen for crypto firms using 'bank'/'bank card' branding at HK-hosted events that could be confused with the bank's own products or licensed-bank status (paras 1-3)
counterparty_due_diligence: Verify any entity representing itself as a bank against the HKMA register of authorized institutions before any relationship or referral (para on register)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be aware of a recurring reputational/confusion risk from overseas crypto firms using 'bank' branding in Hong Kong, potentially affecting trust in licensed banks generally.

title: Misrepresentation and misuse of the word "bank" in Hong Kong by crypto firms
summary: The HKMA repeated its earlier caution (from its September 2023 notice on the same theme) about overseas crypto firms describing themselves as 'banks' or their products as 'bank cards' in Hong Kong. It said it had observed two specific instances at Hong Kong-hosted events: one firm representing itself as a bank, another describing a card product as a 'bank card'. It restated that only HKMA-authorised institutions may use 'bank' in their name or hold themselves out as such, under Banking Ordinance sections 97 and 97A. It again pointed the public to the authorized institution / restricted licence bank (AI/RLB) register for verification.

key_points.point: The HKMA observed two specific Hong Kong-hosted-event instances of overseas crypto firms making bank-related representations without authorisation.

Only a licensed bank in Hong Kong may use the word 'bank', or its letters in sequence, in its business description. The same applies to holding itself out as a bank, under Banking Ordinance sections 97 and 97A.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is a second, near-identical caution to the one issued in September 2023. It is useful mainly to confirm the concern is recurring rather than a one-off, for brand-protection monitoring purposes.
reading_guide: Skim; content substantially repeats the September 2023 HKMA notice on the same topic.
flags: Near-duplicate in substance of the HKMA's 15 September 2023 notice on the same 'bank' misrepresentation theme (different instances cited, same statutory basis).

controls_and_monitoring: Monitor recurrence of bank-related brand misuse by non-bank crypto firms at HK-hosted events the bank or its staff may attend.
counterparty_due_diligence: Verify any counterparty or vendor using bank-related terms against the HKMA's AI/RLB register.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Low; informational unless a specific incident directly touches the bank's own brand.

title: Guideline on the Digital Bond Grant Scheme
summary: This guideline sets the eligibility and application rules for the Digital Bond Grant Scheme (DBGS), a subsidy announced in the 2024 Policy Address to encourage tokenised bond issuance in Hong Kong. It reimburses 50% of eligible expenses per issuance. This is up to HK$1.25 million (Half Grant, basic requirements only) or HK$2.5 million (Full Grant, basic plus additional requirements), capped at two issuances per issuer group. Eligibility hinges on a Hong Kong nexus (lead arranger or DLT team presence, or issuance on the CMU's DLT platform). For the Full Grant, it also needs independence of the DLT platform provider, and a HK$1 billion minimum issuance size. It further needs at least five unrelated investors, and listing on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong (SEHK) or an SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform (VATP).

key_points.point: The DBGS reimburses 50% of Eligible Expenses per digital bond issuance, up to HK$1.25 million (Half Grant) or HK$2.5 million (Full Grant).
An issuer group, counting its associates as one, can draw DBGS support for no more than two digital bond deals.

To qualify at all, the issuance must be half-or-more arranged by Hong Kong-recognised lead arrangers. It must also either have a substantial Hong Kong DLT team, or be issued using the CMU's own DLT platform.

For the Full Grant, the digital bond must also use a DLT platform provider unrelated to the issuer, and be at least HK$1 billion equivalent in size. It must also be issued to five or more unrelated investors, and be listed on SEHK or a licensed VATP.
Eligible expenses include fees to unrelated DLT platform providers, Hong Kong-based arrangers, legal advisers, auditors/accountants/rating agencies, listing fees, and CMU lodging/clearing fees.

For green, social, sustainability or transition digital bonds, the issuer must pick one source for general issuance costs. It is either DBGS or GSF Grant Scheme Track I, capped at HK$2.5 million, not both. The external sustainability review sits separately under Track II, capped at HK$800,000.
Applicants may seek an optional pre-application consultation, then must submit a formal application within three months of the bond's issuance.
The scheme opened for applications on 28 November 2024 for an initial three-year period, and covers bonds issued on or after the 16 October 2024 Policy Address announcement.
The HKMA keeps full discretion over whether eligibility requirements are met and over the amount of any subsidy granted, and may adjust the scheme's design over time.

numbers_and_dates.item: Minimum issuance size for Full Grant

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this gives a concrete cost-recovery incentive and eligibility checklist. Its treasury, debt capital markets (DCM) or digital-assets team should use this when structuring or arranging a Hong Kong digital bond issuance. It explicitly recognises listing on SFC-licensed VATPs as a qualifying route.
reading_guide: Read the whole guideline (six pages); it is short and every section (Overview, Basic/Additional Requirements, Eligible Expenses, Application Process) is operationally relevant.

obligations: If claiming the DBGS grant, ensure the digital bond issuance actually meets the stated Basic (and, if claiming Full Grant, Additional) Requirements before applying (s.2-3).
controls_and_monitoring: Track the HK$1 billion Full Grant minimum size, the 2-issuance-per-issuer cap, and the 3-month post-issuance application deadline as controls in any digital bond issuance project plan.
notifications_reporting: Optional pre-application consultation with the HKMA via dbgs@hkma.gov.hk before formal application (s.5).
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm a DLT platform provider's independence from the issuer if targeting the Full Grant, since a related-party platform provider disqualifies the issuance from the Full Grant (s.3(a)).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Worth flagging to treasury/finance as an available subsidy (up to HK$2.5m) that materially offsets DLT platform, arranger, legal and listing costs for a qualifying issuance.

title: HKMA launches Digital Bond Grant Scheme
summary: The HKMA launched the Digital Bond Grant Scheme (DBGS), announced in the 2024 Policy Address. It aims to grow Hong Kong's digital securities market and support wider take-up of tokenisation using distributed ledger technology (DLT). Per the attached Guideline, DBGS covers 50% of eligible expenses per digital bond issuance, up to HK$1.25 million (Half Grant) or HK$2.5 million (Full Grant). Each issuer, including associates, may claim for a maximum of two issuances. Basic Requirements include Hong Kong issuance/arranger presence, plus either substantial Hong Kong digital-team presence or issuance on a CMU-operated DLT platform. Additional Requirements for the Full Grant include an independent DLT platform provider, minimum HK$1 billion issuance size, five or more independent investors, and listing on SEHK or an SFC-licensed VATP. Applications opened 28 November 2024 for an initial three-year period, covering bonds issued on or after 16 October 2024.

key_points.point: Maximum grant per eligible digital bond issuance is HK$2.5 million (Full Grant); Half Grant caps at HK$1.25 million, covering 50% of Eligible Expenses.
Each issuer, together with its associates, can draw DBGS subsidies for at most two digital bond issuances.

Basic Requirements: the bond must be issued in Hong Kong, with half or more of lead arrangers being recognised arrangers. It must also have either a substantial Hong Kong digital team, or issuance on a CMU-operated DLT platform.

Additional Requirements for the Full Grant: the DLT platform provider must not be an associate of the issuer, and minimum issuance size is HK$1 billion equivalent. It must also be issued to five or more unrelated investors, and listed on SEHK or a licensed VATP.
Eligible expenses include DLT platform provider fees, Hong Kong-based arranger/legal/audit/rating fees, listing fees, and CMU lodging/clearing fees.

A green/social/sustainability bond that is also a digital bond cannot claim general issuance costs under both DBGS and GSF Track I. It can claim under only one, up to HK$2.5 million. External sustainability review costs are separately covered by GSF Track II, up to HK$800,000.
Formal application must reach the HKMA no later than three months after the bond is issued; an optional pre-application consultation with HKMA is available.
DBGS applications opened 28 November 2024 for an initial three-year period, eligible for bonds issued on or after 16 October 2024, the Policy Address announcement date.

numbers_and_dates.item: Minimum issuance size for Full Grant
GSF Track II sustainability review cap

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this directly matters as a prospective digital-bond issuer: it sets concrete eligibility conditions and a 3-month post-issuance filing deadline. The bank's treasury/DCM and compliance functions must plan around these to capture the HK$1.25m/2.5m grant.

quote.text: encourage broader adoption of tokenisation technology in capital market transactions

reading_guide: Read the press release plus the Guideline sections 1-5 (6 pages) in full — all are operative eligibility/process rules.
flags: Full Grant explicitly requires the DLT platform provider NOT be an associate of the issuer — a bank cannot self-deal via its own captive DLT platform and still get the Full Grant.

obligations: To claim the Digital Bond Grant Scheme, meet the Basic Requirements: HK issuance/arranger presence and either substantial HK digital-team presence or issuance on a CMU-operated DLT platform (Guideline s.2, p.3).

For the Full Grant, additionally meet the Additional Requirements: independent (non-associate) DLT platform provider, minimum HK$1 billion issuance, 5+ independent investors, and listing on SEHK or an SFC-licensed VATP (Guideline s.3, p.4).
notifications_reporting: Submit the formal DBGS application within three months of the bond's issuance; an optional pre-application consultation with HKMA is available (Guideline s.5, p.6).
counterparty_due_diligence: If seeking the Full Grant, ensure the DLT platform provider is not an associate of the issuer (Guideline s.3, p.4) -- the bank cannot use its own captive platform and still qualify for the Full Grant.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should weigh the grant economics (up to HK$2.5m, capped at 2 issuances per issuer group, Guideline s.1, p.2) against the 3-month post-issuance filing deadline before committing to a digital bond issuance.

title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Eddie Yue on Project Evergreen: From concept to application
summary: The HKMA Chief Executive reviewed Project Evergreen's progress on bond tokenisation after two successful tokenised government green bond issuances. He announced the launch of the Digital Bond Grant Scheme (DBGS), offering up to HK$2.5 million per eligible digital bond issuance. The article also describes 'EvergreenHub', a new knowledge repository on digital bonds. It sets out forward priorities too: interoperability between DLT platforms and conventional infrastructure, expanding secondary-market and repo use of digital bonds as collateral, and eventually extending tokenised bonds to retail investors. It notes the first-ever repo transaction in Hong Kong using a digital government bond as collateral.

key_points.point: The Digital Bond Grant Scheme, offering up to HK$2.5 million per eligible digital bond issuance, began accepting applications the same day.
The second Project Evergreen tokenised bond issuance was roughly seven times the size of the first, and helped attract more institutional investors and secondary-market activity.
Earlier in 2024, two banks executed the first repo transaction in Hong Kong using the Government's digital bond as collateral.
The HKMA launched 'EvergreenHub', a single online resource pulling together material on digital bond transactions, and will keep adding to its content.

Forward priorities include interoperability between digital platforms and conventional infrastructure, mobilising digital bonds as repo collateral, and eventually extending tokenised bonds to retail investors.
Project Evergreen (bond tokenisation) and Project Ensemble (broader tokenisation market infrastructure) are described as complementary and intersecting initiatives.

numbers_and_dates.item: Global market value of tokenised bonds issued in past decade

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this sets out the HKMA's stated future direction for bond tokenisation, covering collateral mobility, interoperability, and retail access. This shapes what its markets, custody and collateral-management functions should plan for. It also flags a live grant scheme worth using for any qualifying digital bond issuance.
reading_guide: Read in full; short article with each paragraph covering a distinct initiative. The DBGS eligibility detail is in the companion guideline (package item), not here.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Flag the Digital Bond Grant Scheme to the board/treasury function as a funding incentive if the bank is considering any digital bond issuance in Hong Kong.

title: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism Webinar Materials
summary: This is an administrative SFC circular noting that presentation materials from an AML/CFT webinar have been posted on the SFC website. The webinar was held 25-26 November 2024, with SFC staff and Hong Kong Police Force Financial Intelligence and Investigation Bureau speakers. Licensed corporations, virtual asset service providers (VASPs) and associated entities can download them for reference and internal training.

key_points.point: Webinar materials from the 25-26 November 2024 AML/CFT Webinar (SFC and Hong Kong Police Force speakers) were posted on the SFC website.
The SFC encourages licensed corporations, VASPs and associated entities to obtain these materials and use them internally for training and reference purposes.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is an administrative pointer only. It shows Hong Kong Police Force's Financial Intelligence and Investigation Bureau is actively collaborating in SFC's AML/CFT training for VASP-related firms.
reading_guide: One page; read in full.
flags: No substantive regulatory content — purely a pointer to externally hosted training materials not included in this text.

title: Gazettal of Stablecoins Bill
summary: The government gazetted the Stablecoins Bill. It creates a licensing regime run by the Monetary Authority. The regime covers anyone issuing fiat-referenced stablecoins in Hong Kong, issuing stablecoins pegged to the Hong Kong dollar, or actively marketing such stablecoins to the Hong Kong public. The Bill also gives the Monetary Authority supervision, investigation, and enforcement powers over licensees. Officials say it fulfils Hong Kong's Financial Stability Board commitments and applies a same-activity, same-risk, same-regulation approach. The Bill had its first Legislative Council (LegCo) reading on 18 December 2024, and was later enacted as the Stablecoins Ordinance, so this gazettal announcement is now superseded by the enacted law.

key_points.point: A person must be licensed by the Monetary Authority to issue fiat-referenced stablecoins in Hong Kong. A licence is also needed to issue stablecoins pegged to the Hong Kong dollar, or to actively market such stablecoins to the Hong Kong public.
The Bill gives the Monetary Authority supervisory, investigatory, and enforcement powers to run the licensing regime.
The Bill had its first reading in the Legislative Council on 18 December 2024.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the origin point of Hong Kong's fiat-referenced stablecoin licensing regime. A bank that issues, markets, or partners with issuers of HKD-pegged or Hong Kong-marketed stablecoins needs to track this Bill through to the enacted ordinance.

quote.text: put in place a regulatory regime for issuers of fiat-referenced stablecoins

reading_guide: Short press release; read in full for the licensing trigger activities in paragraph 2.
flags: Bill later enacted as the Stablecoins Ordinance; this gazettal entry is now historical and superseded by the enacted law and its subsidiary guidance

obligations: If the bank or a group entity issues or actively markets fiat-referenced stablecoins in Hong Kong or pegged to HKD, it will need a Monetary Authority licence once the regime commences (locator: para 2).
counterparty_due_diligence: Check whether any stablecoin counterparty or partner the bank deals with is licensed under the eventual regime once it commences.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told a licensing regime for fiat-referenced stablecoins is being legislated, with direct relevance if the bank has or is considering stablecoin issuance or distribution plans.

title: LCQ15: Policy on digital assets
summary: In a written Legislative Council (LegCo) reply, the Acting Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury set out the government's digital-asset policy. The reply was given in response to questions about a dedicated crypto commissioner and bitcoin as a strategic reserve asset. It describes the government's existing approach: the Task Force on Promoting Web3 Development, the 2022 Policy Statement's same-activity-same-risk-same-regulation principle, and the virtual asset service provider licensing regime. It does not state whether a new department or commissioner will be created. It confirms plans to introduce the stablecoin bill within December 2024, run a second over-the-counter (OTC) trading consultation in 2025, and introduce a virtual asset custodian licensing regime in 2025. It also states the Exchange Fund does not target crypto-assets, though external managers may hold small amounts, and that the Linked Exchange Rate System is unaffected by virtual asset developments.

key_points.point: The government amended the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (AMLO) to introduce the existing licensing regime for virtual asset trading platforms.
The Treasury bureau will introduce the fiat-referenced stablecoin issuer licensing bill to the Legislative Council within December 2024.
A second public consultation on regulating over-the-counter virtual asset trading is planned for the following year, and a virtual asset custodian licensing regime will also be introduced that year.
The Exchange Fund does not target crypto-assets as an investment class, though its external managers may hold small amounts as part of diversified mandates.
The Linked Exchange Rate System is described as unaffected by virtual asset market developments, and remains the cornerstone of Hong Kong's monetary stability.

In November 2023 the SFC issued two circulars: one on intermediaries' tokenised-securities-related activities, the other on how SFC-authorised investment products are tokenised. Both aim to make the regulator's investor-protection expectations clearer.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this confirms the government's official policy stance and legislative timetable for digital assets in one statement. It is useful for briefing senior management on the current regulatory approach and how the Exchange Fund and currency peg relate to virtual assets. It does not say whether a dedicated crypto commissioner will be created.

quote.text: same activities, same risks, same regulations

reading_guide: Read the numbered reply paragraphs (1)-(4); skip the original Legislative Council question, which is speculative framing rather than government policy.

counterparty_due_diligence: Note the two referenced SFC circulars (tokenised securities activities; tokenisation of SFC-authorised products) as the source of current SFC expectations on tokenisation intermediaries should check counterparties against.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be briefed on the confirmed legislative calendar (stablecoin bill, VA OTC consultation, custodian regime) so the bank can plan resourcing ahead of each stage.

title: Hong Kong commits to implementing Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework
summary: The government told the OECD's Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information that Hong Kong will implement the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF). CARF is an OECD standard for automatic exchange of crypto-asset account and transaction information between tax authorities, extending the existing Common Reporting Standard model to crypto-assets. The government's initial plan is to have the local legislative amendments in place by 2026. It also aims to start the first automatic exchanges with partner jurisdictions from 2028, on a reciprocal basis with jurisdictions that meet data confidentiality standards.

key_points.point: Hong Kong committed to the OECD's Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, an annual automatic exchange mechanism. It covers account and transaction information on crypto-assets, shared between jurisdictions where the account holder is tax resident.

The government's initial plan targets the necessary local legislative amendments by 2026, and the first automatic exchanges under CARF from 2028, run reciprocally with partners meeting data confidentiality and security standards.

numbers_and_dates.item: Target for first automatic exchanges under CARF

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank offering or facilitating crypto-asset services in Hong Kong. This signals it should anticipate future CARF-driven reporting and client due-diligence duties once the local legislative amendments are enacted. Likely feeding into existing tax-reporting and Common Reporting Standard (CRS) processes.
reading_guide: Short press release; read in full for the two dated commitments.

obligations: Once local CARF legislation is enacted (targeted for 2026), a bank with crypto-asset activities may need to collect and report account holder tax residency and transaction data, similar to existing CRS processes.
controls_and_monitoring: Track the CARF implementing legislation as it moves through the Legislative Council so client onboarding and tax-reporting systems can be updated in time.
notifications_reporting: First automatic exchanges under CARF targeted from 2028, contingent on reciprocal partner jurisdictions being in place.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/tax and compliance functions should be told CARF is coming with a 2026 legislative target and 2028 exchange start, so systems and client documentation processes can be planned ahead of time.

title: Circular to virtual asset trading platforms on licensing process and revamped Second-phase Assessment
summary: The SFC set out its virtual asset trading platform (VATP) licensing roadmap and a revamped Second-phase Assessment. After on-site inspections, deemed applicants get a conditional licence that requires completing a rectification plan. They must also pass a satisfactory independent penetration test and vulnerability assessment before operating on a restricted scope of business. VATPs must then engage an External Assessor (EA) under a tripartite agreement with the SFC for the Second-phase Assessment. This is a direct assurance engagement, signed off by a practising accountant (CPA) under standards like HKSAE3000. It checks whether the VATP's policies, procedures, systems and controls are suitably designed and implemented against the VATP Guidelines and AML/CFT Guideline. Once this is done satisfactorily, the SFC lifts the business-scope restriction.

key_points.point: Deemed applicants get a conditional licence after agreeing a rectification plan with the SFC. As a licensing condition, they must complete rectifications and pass an independent penetration test and vulnerability assessment before operating on a restricted scope of business.

The vulnerability assessment should include analysis of the custody system's compiled code, including supply-chain libraries, to check production code matches the reviewed version, plus external and internal vulnerability scans.

Penetration testing should check firewalls, servers, databases, wallets, network devices and customer-facing applications (desktop, web, mobile). Tests must cover both the application layer and the network layer.
The VATP must engage an External Assessor (EA) under a tripartite agreement with the SFC to conduct the Second-phase Assessment.

The Second-phase Assessment must be a direct assurance engagement, for example under HKSAE3000, signed off by a practising certified public accountant. It assesses whether revised policies, procedures, systems and controls comply with the VATP Guidelines and AML/CFT Guideline.

As soon as practically possible, the VATP must tell the SFC and EA of any material change to its policies and procedures. It must also promptly report any material breaches or failures found during the assessment.
Once the Second-phase Assessment is completed to its satisfaction, the SFC will lift the licensing condition restricting the VATP's scope of business.
The SFC will pay HK$1 toward the Second-phase Assessment fees; the VATP pays the balance of total fees, disbursements and expenses.

numbers_and_dates.item: SFC's contribution to Second-phase Assessment fees

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this binds VATPs, not the bank directly. But it sets the exact assurance bar: penetration test, custody-system analysis and tripartite external assessment. A compliance head should require evidence of these before relying on a VATP's custody and security controls.

quote.text: Binary analysis of the custody system should be performed

reading_guide: Read the full 3-page circular plus the 1-page Appendix flowchart, which shows the licensing and assessment sequence.
flags: The SFC pays only a nominal HK$1 toward Second-phase Assessment costs — the VATP bears essentially the entire cost despite SFC's active tripartite supervisory role.

counterparty_due_diligence: Before relying on any VATP's (including a bank-affiliated one's) custody and security controls, confirm it has passed its independent penetration test/vulnerability assessment, including binary analysis of the custody system, and the tripartite Second-phase Assessment (paras 5-6, 13; Vulnerability assessment box, p.2)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: If the bank sponsors or is affiliated with a VATP applicant, board should be told the VATP bears nearly the full cost of the tripartite Second-phase Assessment despite the SFC's active supervisory role (footnote 4, p.2).

title: SFC licenses virtual asset trading platforms under swift licensing process
summary: The SFC granted licences to four virtual asset trading platform (VATP) applicants: Accumulus GBA Technology (Hongkong), DFX Labs Company, Hong Kong Digital Asset EX, and Thousand Whales Technology (BVI). This followed the SFC's swift licensing process for deemed applicants, after it finished risk-based on-site inspections of all deemed applicants. They may operate on a limited scope of business until they finish rectification work, plus a satisfactory independent vulnerability assessment and penetration test. The SFC published a matching circular on the licensing process and second-phase assessment the same day.

key_points.point: Four VATP applicants were licensed under the swift licensing process: Accumulus GBA Technology (Hongkong) Co. Limited, DFX Labs Company Limited, Hong Kong Digital Asset EX Limited, and Thousand Whales Technology (BVI) Limited.

As a licence condition, they may operate on a limited scope of business after finishing rectification work from on-site inspection feedback, plus a satisfactory independent vulnerability assessment and penetration test.
The SFC will oversee the whole second-phase assessment through three-way engagement with the VATPs and their outside assessors, and will lift business-scope limits once satisfied the work is done.
Remaining deemed-applicant applications keep being reviewed under the same swift licensing process. Further guidance for new, non-deemed VATP applicants was expected in early 2025.

numbers_and_dates.item: Number of VATPs licensed in this release

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this confirms four VATPs were licensed through a fast process only after on-site inspection and remedial work. They also operate with only a limited business scope until second-phase assessment finishes. This is useful for scoping what a newly licensed VATP counterparty can and cannot yet do.
reading_guide: Short; read in full plus companion circular 6fc7dd34c485 for the licensing-process detail.

counterparty_due_diligence: Note that a VATP counterparty granted a swift-process licence starts out on a limited business scope, pending finished rectification work and a second-phase outside assessment. Check scope limits before relying on services outside them.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board should note the SFC found inspection-driven gaps needing fixes at deemed applicants before licensing them — useful context when judging the maturity of any VATP counterparty licensed through this swift process.

title: HKMA launches Supervisory Incubator to foster responsible adoption of distributed ledger technology
summary: The HKMA launched the Supervisory Incubator for Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT). A new supervisory arrangement to help banks responsibly adopt DLT and manage its risks, with tokenised deposits as a core initial focus. For an individual bank, it offers a one-stop platform to reaffirm risk-management adequacy before fully launching a DLT initiative. Access to a dedicated HKMA team, and the option of live trials. At the industry level it promotes best practices through supervisory guidance, sharing sessions and research. It was announced at FiNETech4, an event with over 300 professionals from banking, securities, insurance, the Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) sector and technology. Part of the FiNETech series launched in April 2024 and backed by the HKMA, SFC, Insurance Authority (IA) and MPFA.

key_points.point: The Supervisory Incubator is a new HKMA supervisory arrangement to help banks manage the risks of DLT adoption. With a particular focus on risks arising as banks bring services such as deposits and loans into production across DLT-based and legacy infrastructure.
Tokenised deposits are a core focus of the Incubator upon inception.

At the individual bank level, the Incubator offers a one-stop platform for banks to reaffirm risk-management adequacy before full DLT-initiative launch. With access to a dedicated HKMA team and optional live trials.
At the industry level, the Incubator promotes DLT risk-management best practices through supervisory guidance, industry sharing sessions and research projects.

The Incubator was announced at FiNETech4, part of the FiNETech series established in April 2024. It is backed by the HKMA, SFC, Insurance Authority and MPFA, industry associations such as HKAB and the FinTech Association of HK, Cyberport and HKSTP.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is a direct, bank-facing HKMA supervisory arrangement. A compliance head should treat pre-launch engagement with the Supervisory Incubator as the expected first step before productionising any DLT-based banking service, particularly tokenised deposits.

quote.text: help banks responsibly unlock the transformative potential of distributed ledger technology

reading_guide: Read in full; short.

obligations: Before full launch of a DLT-based banking initiative (e.g. tokenised deposits), the bank may use the Supervisory Incubator to reaffirm its risk-management adequacy with the HKMA (para 3, p.1).
controls_and_monitoring: Incubator engagement is framed around managing risks as a bank productionises services spanning DLT-based and legacy infrastructure (para 2, p.1) -- use it to pressure-test controls before go-live.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told this is HKMA's expected pre-production engagement channel for DLT initiatives, with tokenised deposits as an initial focus (para 2, p.1); treat non-engagement before launch as a supervisory-expectations gap.

title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Opening Remarks at FiNETech4 on “Charting the New Frontiers of Finance with DLT”
summary: These are opening remarks at the FiNETech4 event announcing the launch of the Supervisory Incubator for Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT). A new HKMA arrangement to help banks bring DLT-based banking products and services into production carefully, with risk kept under control. The speech frames DLT's potential across tokenised assets, tokenised money (including tokenised deposits) and tokenised information or data, while flagging legal, technical and regulatory adaptation challenges. It references an earlier Shenzhen-Hong Kong cross-boundary data-verification pilot using blockchain. It signals the Incubator's early focus on products that span DLT-based and legacy banking infrastructure, with tokenised deposits cited as a prime example.

key_points.point: The HKMA launched the Supervisory Incubator for DLT, a one-stop supervisory arrangement offering a dedicated team. Socialisation of DLT-based proposals, supervisory feedback, and live risk-controlled trials for banks.
The Incubator will also provide supervisory guidance, sharing sessions, and forward-looking research to build the banking sector's DLT risk-management understanding and best practices.

Any bank can bring any DLT-related idea to the Incubator. Though the HKMA flagged it would concentrate at first on offerings that bridge DLT-based and legacy banking systems, with tokenised deposits as the leading example.

The HKMA said adopting DLT would need a period of adjustment covering technical, legal and regulatory issues. Banks should not have to carry that adjustment burden alone; the HKMA stands ready to help.

The speech points to the Shenzhen-Hong Kong cross-boundary data verification platform pilot, run jointly with mainland authorities, as an example. It uses blockchain and data coding to confirm documents are genuine without moving or storing the original paper copies.

numbers_and_dates.item: Estimated global annual clearing/settlement cost savings from DLT (cited GFMA report)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this establishes a formal, named supervisory channel, the Supervisory Incubator for DLT. That a bank can use to get early HKMA feedback before productionising a DLT-based product. It signals tokenised deposits as the near-term priority area for supervisory engagement.

quote.text: the onus to navigate these challenges should not be on the private sector alone

reading_guide: Focus on the paragraphs where the HKMA head introduces the new Incubator and notes it welcomes proposals from every bank, roughly paragraphs 19-23. The long sailing metaphor earlier can be skimmed, though it has substantive points on tokenised assets, money and information.

controls_and_monitoring: Consider routing any planned DLT-based product (especially one spanning DLT and legacy infrastructure, e.g. tokenised deposits) through the Supervisory Incubator for early risk-management feedback before go-live.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Inform the board that a dedicated HKMA supervisory channel now exists for DLT product development, which can de-risk the approval pathway for the bank's own DLT initiatives, with tokenised deposits flagged as the near-term supervisory priority.

title: HKMA launches Supervisory Incubator to foster responsible adoption of distributed ledger technology (with photos)
summary: The Monetary Authority launched a Supervisory Incubator for Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT). A new supervisory arrangement to help banks manage the risks of adopting DLT for banking services such as deposits and loans. It gives participating banks access to a dedicated Monetary Authority team for supervisory feedback. Banks also get the option to run live trials to check risk-management controls before fully launching a DLT-based service. Tokenised deposits are named as a core initial focus. The Incubator also runs industry-wide initiatives, such as supervisory guidance and sharing sessions, to raise sector-wide DLT risk-management readiness.

key_points.point: The Supervisory Incubator for Distributed Ledger Technology is a new HKMA supervisory arrangement to help banks manage risk when adopting DLT-based services. Particularly where those services cut across DLT-based and legacy banking infrastructure.
Tokenised deposits are the core initial focus of the Incubator, given strong industry interest in bringing them into production.

Through the Incubator, banks can check their risk-management safeguards are adequate before rolling out a DLT-based initiative in full. Drawing on a dedicated HKMA team and, if they wish, running live trials.
The Incubator will also run industry-wide initiatives, including supervisory guidance, sharing sessions and research, to raise sector-wide DLT risk-management readiness.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank planning a tokenised deposit or other DLT-based service, this shows it should engage the Incubator before launch to pre-validate risk controls with the Monetary Authority. This is now the practical supervisory on-ramp for DLT initiatives.
reading_guide: Read paragraphs 2-4 for what the Incubator offers and its tokenised-deposits focus; skip the FiNETech4 event background in the later paragraphs.

controls_and_monitoring: Before launching a DLT-based banking service, particularly tokenised deposits, the bank should be prepared to validate its risk-management controls through the Incubator's one-stop supervisory platform.
notifications_reporting: Engaging the Incubator ahead of a DLT-based product launch functions as a form of prior supervisory consultation, though not described as mandatory in this release.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should know that the Monetary Authority now offers a dedicated supervisory pathway for DLT adoption, and that tokenised deposits are its initial priority, relevant to any bank considering such products.

title: Supervisory Incubator for Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT)
summary: The HKMA announces a new 'Supervisory Incubator', giving banks a dedicated supervisory contact point and the option to run live trials of DLT risk-management approaches, under a hands-on, iterative process. Banks accessing the Incubator may be offered a degree of supervisory flexibility, assessed case by case, similar in spirit to the existing Fintech Supervisory Sandbox. This is on the understanding they are actively working to manage the risks involved. Where existing rules do not fit distributed ledger technology (DLT) well and the mismatch is inadvertent, the HKMA says it will consider regulatory adaptations consistent with 'same activity, same risk, same regulation'.

key_points.point: The Incubator gives banks access to a dedicated HKMA team for supervisory feedback on DLT proposals, and the option of live trials, run in a hands-on, iterative and phased manner.

Banks accessing the Incubator may be offered supervisory flexibility, for example on certain supervisory requirements, assessed case by case. This is based on factors similar to those used for the Fintech Supervisory Sandbox: boundary setting, customer protection, risk controls, readiness, and monitoring.
Supervisory flexibility is offered on the understanding that the bank will work to manage the risks of its trial in a way that matches the trial's scale, scope and nature.

Existing regulatory or legal rules may sometimes be inadvertently incompatible with DLT adoption, conflicting with 'same activity, same risk, same regulation'. Where that happens, the HKMA will consider whether regulatory adaptation or flexibility is warranted, taking account of international standards.

Longer term, the Incubator will run broader industry initiatives building on successful pilots, including further supervisory guidance, industry sharing sessions and forward-looking research on emerging DLT risk areas.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this offers a formal, lower-friction route to pilot DLT projects, including limited supervisory flexibility, in exchange for close HKMA engagement and demonstrated risk management. Compliance should treat Incubator access as a supervised trial, not a compliance exemption.

quote.text: same activity, same risk, same regulation

reading_guide: Short 2-page circular; read in full.
flags: This is a pilot supervisory-engagement mechanism, not a change to substantive rules; any flexibility offered is discretionary and case-by-case, not a blanket exemption

obligations: If accessing the Incubator, endeavour to manage risks commensurate with the trial's scale, scope and nature as a condition of any supervisory flexibility (p.1)
controls_and_monitoring: Apply the same operating principles used for HKMA Fintech Supervisory Sandbox trials (boundary setting, customer protection, risk management controls, readiness, monitoring) (p.1, footnote 2)
notifications_reporting: Contact the HKMA's dedicated Incubator team to apply for access and report on trial progress
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should know whether any DLT pilot is being run inside or outside the Incubator, and what supervisory flexibility, if any, has been granted and under what conditions.
