title: Annex 2: Disclosure Requirements in Relation to Cryptoasset Exposures
summary: This document proposes new public disclosure duties for banks holding cryptoassets, added to the Banking (Disclosure) Rules from 1 January 2026 to match the Basel Committee's cryptoasset disclosure standard. It introduces four new disclosure items. First, yearly qualitative disclosure of crypto activities and how the bank applied the classification rules. Second, twice-yearly disclosure of crypto exposures and their risk-weighted amounts. Third, twice-yearly disclosure of how crypto holdings and liabilities are treated in the accounts. Fourth, twice-yearly disclosure of how crypto positions feed into liquidity ratios, for banks that must meet those ratios. It also creates a new defined term, 'cryptoliability', for digital liabilities tied to a cryptoasset.

key_points.point: A new term, 'cryptoliability', is added, meaning a digital liability tied to a cryptoasset. It covers a bank's own token issuance liabilities and other digital liabilities linked to cryptoassets.

Each year, a bank with cryptoasset or cryptoliability exposures must publicly disclose an overview of its crypto-related business. The risks involved, its risk-management policies, and how it decided whether each Group 1 cryptoasset it holds meets the classification conditions.

Twice a year, a bank must disclose an overview of its cryptoasset exposures broken down by regulatory bucket (Group 1a, 1b, 2a, 2b) and the related risk-weighted amounts. It must also disclose its operational-risk policies for crypto, and the market value and types of crypto it holds in custody for clients. It must explain any material change during the period.

The twice-yearly exposure disclosure must break out material individual holdings of Group 1b, Group 2a and Group 2b cryptoassets separately, not just totals; tokenised traditional assets are excluded from this breakdown.
Twice a year, a bank must disclose how it classifies and measures its cryptoasset and cryptoliability holdings for accounting purposes, with a breakdown of carrying values by regulatory bucket.

A bank that is a category 1 institution is subject to the full liquidity coverage ratio and net stable funding ratio rules. Twice a year, it must disclose how its cryptoasset and cryptoliability exposures feed into those liquidity ratio calculations.

Banks incorporated outside Hong Kong face a lighter version of these rules. Limited to an overview of crypto activities that create liquidity risk and, for category 1 institutions, the classification-conditions disclosure.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this sets the public reporting cadence compliance must run once the bank has any cryptoasset exposure. It means annual qualitative disclosure of activities and classification methodology, plus semi-annual quantitative disclosures on exposures, accounting treatment and, for larger banks, liquidity impact.

quote.text: digital liability which is tied to a cryptoasset

reading_guide: Read the four new disclosure sections (16ZQH-16ZQK, pages 5-9) in full. The amendments to existing sections 2, 11 and 91-105 (pages 2-4, 10-14) are mostly consequential cross-referencing and can be skimmed.
flags: This is a soft consultation draft; new section numbers are still bracketed as proposals.

obligations: Prepare an annual qualitative disclosure of crypto activities, risks and classification methodology for each Group 1 cryptoasset held, per new s.16ZQH, p.5-6.

Prepare semi-annual quantitative disclosures: exposure breakdown by regulatory bucket and risk-weighted amounts (s.16ZQI, p.6-7), accounting classification and carrying values (s.16ZQJ, p.8), and, if a category 1 institution, liquidity-ratio impact (s.16ZQK, p.9).
controls_and_monitoring: Set up a process to track material individual holdings of Group 1b, Group 2a and Group 2b cryptoassets separately for disclosure purposes, per s.16ZQI(2), p.7.
Coordinate with finance/accounting to keep the crypto carrying-value breakdown aligned with the regulatory bucket classification used for capital, per s.16ZQJ, p.8.
notifications_reporting: Semi-annual and annual public disclosure deadlines to be tracked once the rules commence (targeted 1 January 2026), per p.1 and new ss.16ZQH-16ZQK.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board/risk committee should be told that public disclosure of crypto exposures, risk-weighted amounts and custody holdings will become a recurring reporting obligation from 1 January 2026, requiring coordination between risk, finance and disclosure-committee processes.

title: Annex 1: Prudential Treatment of Cryptoasset Exposures
summary: This document sets out the HKMA's proposed line-by-line changes to the Banking (Capital) Rules. These bring in a dedicated capital regime for banks' cryptoasset exposures, copying the Basel Committee's December 2022 standard and its July 2024 amendments, targeted for 1 January 2026. It defines a cryptoasset and a cryptoasset exposure, and sorts cryptoassets into four buckets with different capital treatment. It also adds new rules for classifying them, and assigning them to the banking or trading book. These rules cover working out risk-weighted amounts, and capping how much of a bank's capital can sit in the riskiest bucket. A bank must itself decide the bucket for each cryptoasset it holds, based on conditions it must document, and that the HKMA can override.

key_points.point: A cryptoasset is a digital token representing value that can be used for payment, investment, or to access a good or service. It is built mainly using cryptography together with distributed-ledger or comparable technology. A cryptoasset exposure is any on- or off-balance-sheet exposure to one that carries credit, market, valuation-adjustment, operational or liquidity risk.

Cryptoassets fall into four buckets. Group 1a is a tokenised version of a traditional asset. Group 1b is a token with an effective mechanism pegging it to a traditional asset or basket, such as a stablecoin-type instrument. Group 2a is a liquid token with an approved derivative, ETF or ETN referencing it; Group 2b is everything else, treated as the riskiest bucket.

Tokens that run on a fully open, permissionless blockchain cannot qualify for Group 1a or Group 1b. This is because the HKMA judges that risk controls for such networks are not yet proven under stress.

A bank decides which bucket each cryptoasset belongs in, on an ongoing basis, against conditions the HKMA sets. It must keep records showing how it met those conditions and hand them to the HKMA on request.

The first time a bank takes on exposure to a cryptoasset it has never held before, it must tell the HKMA immediately. It must also treat that cryptoasset as the riskiest bucket, Group 2b, until the HKMA is satisfied a better bucket applies.
The HKMA can overrule a bank's own bucket decision for any cryptoasset if it judges that prudent.

Group 1a and Group 1b tokens go in the banking or trading book depending on how the equivalent traditional asset would be booked. Group 2a tokens always go in the trading book; Group 2b tokens always go in the banking book.

For each riskiest-bucket, Group 2b, cryptoasset, a bank must work out both the total of its long positions and the total of its short positions in that token. It then applies a 1,250% risk weight to whichever total is bigger. This one number stands in for credit, market and valuation-adjustment risk together, so none of those are calculated separately for that token.

A bank must work out a Group 2 cryptoasset exposure ratio, its combined exposure to Group 2a and Group 2b tokens, divided by Tier 1 capital. A globally or domestically systemically important bank must keep this at or below 1% at all times, or below 2% if it only occasionally goes over 1%.

If a systemically important bank's Group 2 exposure ratio goes over 1%, it must tell the HKMA in writing. It must also add extra capital using a set formula, and act quickly to get back under the 1% line. Going over 2% forces the bank to hold capital as if every Group 2 token were in the riskiest bucket.

For a derivative contract on a riskiest-bucket cryptoasset, the exposure used in the capital calculation is the fair value of the underlying token grossed up for leverage. This is capped at the most the bank could possibly lose on the contract.

The HKMA can order a bank in writing to hold extra capital. This applies if the bank has sizeable short positions in riskiest-bucket tokens that could lose more than the standard risk weight already covers.

numbers_and_dates.item: Risk weight for Group 2b (riskiest-bucket) cryptoasset exposures
Group 2 cryptoasset exposure ratio soft limit (G-SIB/D-SIB)
Group 2 cryptoasset exposure ratio hard limit (G-SIB/D-SIB)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the draft capital rulebook it must build systems and governance against before 1 January 2026. It fixes how every cryptoasset position gets bucketed, which bucket triggers a punitive 1,250% risk weight, and a hard portfolio limit that forces board-level notification and remediation if breached.

quote.text: the institution has never held an exposure before

reading_guide: Read Item 1, definitions (pages 2-8), and Item 13.3-13.4, classification and book assignment (pages 56-63). Also read Items 18.4 and 20, risk weight and exposure ratio (pages 97-103), closely. Skim the technical market-risk formula sections in Item 18.1-18.3 (pages 89-97) unless building the trading-book model itself.
flags: This is a soft (industry) consultation draft, not final rules; item, section and part numbers are still bracketed as proposals and may change before enactment.

The proposed capital treatment is deliberately punitive for the default (Group 2b) bucket, which will capture most crypto that is not a recognised tokenised traditional asset, an effective stablecoin, or backed by an approved derivative/ETF/ETN.

obligations: Build and document a cryptoasset classification process (Group 1a/1b/2a/2b) with evidence retained for HKMA review on request, per Item 13.3(1) and (7), p.56 and p.61-62.
Notify the HKMA immediately on first taking any exposure to a cryptoasset type not previously held, and treat it as Group 2b until the HKMA confirms otherwise, per Item 13.3(5), p.58-60.
Assign cryptoasset exposures to the correct book (banking vs trading) per the fixed rules in Item 13.4, p.62-63.

Where the bank is a G-SIB or D-SIB, monitor and cap the Group 2 cryptoasset exposure ratio at 1%/2% of Tier 1 capital and notify the HKMA in writing if either threshold is breached, per Item 20.2, p.100-103.
controls_and_monitoring: Build risk systems capable of applying a 1,250% risk weight to Group 2b positions and of running the Group 2 exposure ratio calculation continuously, per Item 18.4 and Item 20.1, p.97-101.
Maintain evidence trails for each cryptoasset's classification conditions in case of automatic fallback to Group 2b or an HKMA challenge, per Item 13.3(6)-(7), p.61-62.
notifications_reporting: First-exposure notification to HKMA for any newly held cryptoasset type, per Item 13.3(5), p.58-60.
Written notice to HKMA if the Group 2 exposure ratio exceeds 1% (and separately if it exceeds 2%), with rapid rectification expected, per Item 20.2(2)-(3), p.101-103.
counterparty_due_diligence: For any tokenised-traditional-asset or stablecoin-type product offered by a counterparty, check whether it would meet the Group 1a/1b conditions (permissioned network, clear legal enforceability, regulated redemption/reserve entities), since these drive the bank's own capital cost of holding it, per Item 13.3(2)-(3), p.56-57.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board/risk committee should be told that a new, capital-intensive cryptoasset regime is proposed for 1 January 2026, that any material crypto exposure not meeting the favourable-bucket conditions will attract a 1,250% risk weight, and that G-SIB/D-SIB status brings a hard portfolio cap requiring notification on breach.

title: Letter to HKAB: Soft consultation on prudential treatment of cryptoasset exposures
summary: Following up on CP 24.01, the HKMA sends the Hong Kong Association of Banks, and separately the DTC Association, draft amendments to the Banking (Capital) Rules and Banking (Disclosure) Rules. These would implement cryptoasset prudential treatment, plus a proposed new Part of the Capital Rules dedicated to cryptoasset capital requirements. It asks for comments by 20 February 2025, and gives 1 January 2026 as the planned start date, matching the Basel Committee's own schedule. That is later than the 'no earlier than 1 July 2025' target in the original 2024 consultation paper.

key_points.point: The draft amendments cover multiple parts and schedules of the Banking (Capital) Rules and the Banking (Disclosure) Rules, plus a wholly new Part of the Capital Rules dedicated to cryptoasset capital requirements.
The HKMA plans for the new rules to take effect on 1 January 2026, matching the Basel Committee's own implementation schedule.
Industry comments on the draft rule amendments were requested by 20 February 2025.
The HKMA expects to issue supplementary guidance, such as FAQs or Supervisory Policy Manual modules, to help put the amended rules into practice where necessary.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this updates the implementation clock from CP 24.01. Compliance should now plan against a 1 January 2026 target for the cryptoasset capital and disclosure rule amendments becoming binding. Rather than the earlier 'no earlier than 1 July 2025' marker, and should watch for further FAQ or Supervisory Policy Manual (SPM) guidance.

quote.text: in line with the Basel timeline

reading_guide: One page; read in full. The actual annexed draft rule text is not included in this extract.
flags: Confirms the effective date slipped from the original paper's 'no earlier than 1 July 2025' language to a stated target of 1 January 2026

controls_and_monitoring: Track draft Capital/Disclosure Rules amendments and prepare systems, data and capital-calculation changes ahead of the intended 1 January 2026 commencement
notifications_reporting: Industry association comments were due 20 February 2025; individual banks should have fed views through HKAB/DTC Association by that date
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be updated that the cryptoasset capital rule commencement date has moved to 1 January 2026 and that draft legislative text is now in circulation via industry associations.

title: SFC extends swift licensing process to new virtual asset trading platform applicants
summary: The SFC announced that all new, non-deemed, virtual asset trading platform (VATP) applicants can now use its swift licensing process. This means applicants put in place policies, procedures, systems and controls before a single external assessment, with the SFC as a party to the engagement. This extends the approach already used for deemed-to-be-licensed applicants. The SFC also published its on-site inspection findings the same day, to clarify expected regulatory standards.

key_points.point: All new VATP applicants can now seek licences under the swift licensing process. This means putting in place policies and procedures before a single external assessment, with the SFC as a party to the engagement.
This extension follows the effectiveness of the SFC's direct engagement approach, used with deemed applicants during risk-based on-site inspections.
On 18 December 2024, four VATP applicants received licences from the SFC through the original swift licensing process aimed at deemed applicants.
The SFC published its risk-based on-site inspection findings the same day, to provide clarity on expected regulatory standards.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this does not itself bind the bank. But it signals a faster regulatory pathway now available if the bank were to sponsor or invest in a new VATP applicant. It also points to the same-day inspection findings worth reviewing for expected standards.
reading_guide: Short; read alongside companion circular 2f950979195e and findings circular 0c93d9a066e6, both issued the same day.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: If the bank is considering sponsoring a new VATP applicant, board should know the swift licensing pathway (single external assessment with the SFC as a party) is now open to all new applicants, not just deemed ones (para 1-2).

title: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities Findings from inspections on deemed-to-be-licensed virtual asset trading platform applicants and expected standards of conduct for virtual asset trading platform operators
summary: The SFC ran on-site inspections of all deemed-to-be-licensed virtual asset trading platform (VATP) applicants, focused on cybersecurity, safeguarding of client assets, and know-your-client (KYC) checks. It then published two documents. Appendix 1 sets out 22 detailed 'Expected standards of conduct', labelled A-V. These cover cybersecurity, client virtual asset handling and segregation, the 98/2 cold and hot wallet ratio, seed and private key storage, contingency planning, compensation arrangements, client money, and access controls. Appendix 2 lists specific deficiencies found during inspections, mapped to each standard. Examples include weak or outdated cryptographic algorithms such as AES-ECB and MD5, manual-only privileged access controls, and single-staff-member security operations centres. Other examples include mixing of house and client virtual assets, and understated hot-wallet calculations breaching the 98/2 rule. Further examples are multi-signature keys held partly outside Hong Kong, and bank-account signatory authority given to non-operational staff. All Platform Operators are told to review their policies, procedures and systems, and immediately fix deficiencies.

key_points.point: Platform Operators should split their networks so critical systems and sensitive data are kept apart from higher-risk network segments. Inspections found some operators allowed direct internet access to trading or custody systems, or unrestricted firewall access between outer and internal networks.
key_points.locator: Appendix 1 Std A p.1; Appendix 2 paras 1-2, p.1

key_points.point: Platform Operators should deploy centralised control over privileged access at every level (servers, workstations, network edges), with senior management approving each use. Inspections found manual controls, permanent unreviewed access, and one operator where a single staff member held most administrative accounts.
key_points.locator: Appendix 1 Std B p.1; Appendix 2 paras 3-4, p.1-2

key_points.point: Platform Operators should use up-to-date, strong encryption for stored and transmitted data. Inspections found outdated or weak algorithms, such as AES-CBC, AES-ECB and MD5 hashing, and unprotected internal data traffic despite TLS 1.2/1.3 on client-facing channels.
key_points.locator: Appendix 1 Std C p.1-2; Appendix 2 paras 5-6, p.3

key_points.point: Under the 98/2 rule, Platform Operators must keep at least 98% of client virtual assets in cold storage. Inspections found miscalculations, such as wrong wallet classification and excluding pending deposits, that let hot wallets exceed the 2% cap.
key_points.locator: Appendix 1 Std I-K p.3; Appendix 2 paras 17-20, p.7-8

key_points.point: Seeds and private keys should be kept in Hong Kong in a secure environment, such as a certified hardware security module, and cold wallets should not use smart contracts. Inspections found a hot wallet with 2-of-3 multisig keys split across the US, Singapore and Hong Kong, and a cold wallet using a 3-of-4 multisig smart contract.
key_points.locator: Appendix 1 Std L p.3-4; Appendix 2 paras 21-22, p.8

key_points.point: Compensation arrangements should cover 50% of cold-wallet and 100% of hot-wallet client virtual assets, with insurance sufficiency properly analysed, including exclusions and event deductibles. Some operators assumed house funds would cover deductibles without proper assessment.
key_points.locator: Appendix 1 Std R p.5; Appendix 2 paras 33-35, p.12-13

key_points.point: Client money should go directly into the associated entity's segregated bank account, not routed via the Platform Operator's own account first. Bank account signatory authority should be limited to staff involved in day-to-day operations.
key_points.locator: Appendix 1 Std T-U p.5-6; Appendix 2 paras 38-41, p.13-14

key_points.point: Platform Operators should screen and block access from restricted jurisdictions, those under sanctions or banning virtual asset trading. They should also detect attempts to bypass this using VPNs or proxies, with documented checks on screening-tool accuracy.
key_points.locator: Appendix 1 Std V p.6; Appendix 2 paras 42-44, p.15

numbers_and_dates.value: 98% of client virtual assets in cold storage
2% of total client virtual assets under custody
50% of cold-wallet + 100% of hot-wallet client virtual assets
restore services within 12 hours; test contingency plans at least annually

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this publishes SFC inspection findings showing gaps in VATP applicants' cybersecurity, client-asset safeguarding and KYC processes. Compliance should factor these observations into counterparty due diligence on any VATP relationship, though the circular does not bind the bank itself.

quote.text: Platform Operators should keep seeds and private keys in Hong Kong

reading_guide: Read the 1-page cover circular for context, then Appendix 1, 6 pages, standards A-V, as the operative checklist. Then skim Appendix 2, 15 pages, for real deficiency examples under each standard, especially cybersecurity, 98/2 custody, and client-money sections.
flags: Multiple deemed applicants were found holding multisig keys OUTSIDE Hong Kong (US, Singapore) — a direct breach of the 'seeds/keys must be kept in Hong Kong' requirement, correcting any assumption that key geography is a minor technicality.

An operator's use of Ethereum's token-approval mechanism to let a house wallet access client-wallet assets without client signature was found to effectively commingle client and house assets despite assets being nominally in 'separate wallets' — a subtle custody-segregation failure mode.
SFC pays only a nominal $1 toward the external/second-phase assessment costs referenced across these circulars — the applicant bears nearly all cost despite SFC's active tripartite role.

controls_and_monitoring: Use the SFC's inspection findings on VATP cybersecurity, client-asset safeguarding and KYC (Appendix 2) as a reference point when assessing a VATP counterparty's operational maturity
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm a VATP counterparty (including deemed applicants) deploys adequately qualified staff, technology and financial resources per VATP Guidelines paras 11.6, 11.7 and 12.5, and has rectified inspection findings
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should note the SFC found systemic gaps in deemed-applicant VATPs' cybersecurity, client-asset and KYC controls -- a red flag to factor into ongoing VATP counterparty risk assessments.

title: Circular to new virtual asset trading platforms seeking to be licensed – Enhanced licensing process and revamped external assessments
supersedes_or_amends: Scope of External Assessment Reports (SFC, June 2023)
summary: This circular sets the enhanced virtual asset trading platform (VATP) licensing process for new corporations applying for a licence, as distinct from deemed applicants. It applies to applications submitted after 18 December 2024, and replaces the June 2023 Scope of External Assessment Reports. It collapses the previous first-phase and second-phase assessments into a single external assessment. This happens only after the applicant has all systems and controls in place, under a tripartite agreement with the SFC and an External Assessor (EA). This is a direct assurance engagement, under HKSAE 3000 or an equivalent such as ISAE 3000, signed off by a practising accountant (CPA).

key_points.point: Separate first-phase and second-phase assessments are being dropped for VATPs. Going forward, new applicants complete just a single external assessment across the whole licensing process.

Applicants must submit a licensing application bundle via WINGS, including written policies and procedures, documentation showing a suitable External Assessor has been identified, and that assessor's capability statement.

The SFC will assess the applicant's business structure, competence, and fitness of the applicant and its ultimate controllers, owners, substantial shareholders, proposed responsible officers and managers, plus the assessor's capability. It may oppose the assessor or return an incomplete application.

After acceptance, the applicant must put its systems and controls in place, covering market surveillance, AML and KYC tools, and custody solutions. It must also fully adapt its policies and procedures before the external assessment.

The external assessment must be a direct assurance engagement, under HKSAE 3000 or an equivalent standard such as ISAE 3000, signed off by a practising certified public accountant. Its job is to say whether the VATP's policies and procedures were properly designed and put into practice under the VATP Guidelines and AML/CFT Guideline.
The SFC will pay HK$1 toward the external assessment fees; the VATP applicant pays the balance of all fees, disbursements and expenses.
As soon as practicable, the applicant must tell the SFC and the assessor about any later material change to its policies and procedures.
Once the external assessment is done and any remaining issues, such as a capital top-up, are cleared, the SFC will issue a licence provided it considers the applicant fit and proper.

numbers_and_dates.item: Cutoff for applicability of this enhanced process
SFC's contribution to external assessment fees

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this binds new VATP applicants, not the bank directly. But a compliance head sponsoring or partnering with a bank-backed new VATP should understand the revised single-assessment. Post-deployment sequencing when planning that entity's licensing timeline.

quote.text: VATPs will no longer be required to conduct the first-phase and second-phase assessments

reading_guide: Read the full 3-page circular plus the 1-page Appendix flowchart, which shows the sequence from application through external assessment to licence approval.
flags: Supersedes/replaces the June 2023 'Scope of External Assessment Reports' document entirely for new (non-deemed) applicants.

This is a DIFFERENT process from the deemed-applicant Second-phase Assessment circular (6fc7dd34c485, 18 Dec 2024) — the two must not be conflated: deemed applicants get a conditional licence first then complete Second-phase Assessment, while new applicants complete external assessment before any licence is granted.

counterparty_due_diligence: If sponsoring or partnering with a new (non-deemed) VATP applicant, note it now faces a single external assessment performed only after full system deployment (para 7-8, p.2), not the earlier two-phase process -- factor this sequencing into any joint build-then-license project timeline.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No direct bank obligation; flag the revised licensing sequence to the board if the bank is backing a new VATP applicant.

title: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Cybersecurity Webinar
summary: This administrative SFC circular announces two Cybersecurity Webinar sessions, on 17 and 19 February 2025, via Zoom. They will share observations from the 2023/24 thematic cybersecurity review of licensed corporations, and raise awareness of emerging cybersecurity threats in Hong Kong. The sessions are free, offer 2.5 Continuous Professional Training (CPT) hours, and enrolment is limited to two representatives per firm via a linked form, due 7 February 2025.

key_points.point: Two cybersecurity webinar sessions were held on 17 and 19 February 2025, covering the 2023/24 thematic cybersecurity review findings and emerging cybersecurity threats.
Attendance offers 2.5 Continuous Professional Training (CPT) hours for those attending the whole session.
Firms may enrol at most two representatives each. The first-named nominee on each firm's submitted form gets priority, first-come first-served, with entries due by 7 February 2025.
Speakers include the SFC's Suptech Office head and a Hong Kong Police Force Cyber Security and Technology Crime Bureau representative.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is an administrative notice. It signals the SFC's continued focus on cybersecurity for intermediaries broadly, not VATP-specific, including collaboration with the Hong Kong Police Force.
reading_guide: Two pages; skim, mainly logistics.

title: Letter to DTCA: Soft consultation: miscellaneous amendments to the BCR
summary: The HKMA wrote to the Deposit-Taking Companies Association (DTCA) on 11 February 2025, about a second, separate set of Banking (Capital) Rules changes. These are unrelated in subject to the cryptoasset standard, but timed to start alongside it. The main content covers a revised capital treatment for a bank's direct holdings of certain non-capital loss-absorbing-capacity (LAC) liabilities. It also makes clarifying edits to existing definitions to better match the Basel framework. Comments were due by 7 March 2025, with an intended effective date of 1 January 2026, the same date as the cryptoasset capital rules.

key_points.point: The amendments mainly cover a revised capital treatment for a bank's own direct holdings of certain non-capital loss-absorbing capacity (LAC) liabilities.
Other changes are definitional or clarifying edits meant to better line up the Capital Rules with the Basel framework.
The HKMA intends to bring in these changes at the same time as the cryptoasset capital standard, that is, 1 January 2026.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is not itself a crypto rule, but it bundles into the same 1 January 2026 start date as the cryptoasset capital package. So a bank's Basel-implementation project plan for that date needs to track both streams together.
reading_guide: One-page cover letter; the actual amendment text was not part of this attachment set. This is a near-duplicate letter to the one sent the same day to the Hong Kong Association of Banks (id 843b382f9c92).
flags: This letter is about non-capital LAC liability treatment and definitional cleanups, not cryptoasset exposures; included here because it shares the batch and the 1 January 2026 commencement date with the cryptoasset package.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: n/a - administrative cover letter for a non-crypto capital rule change; note only for project-timeline coordination with the crypto package.

title: Letter to HKAB: Soft consultation: miscellaneous amendments to the BCR
summary: This is the HKMA's near-identical 11 February 2025 letter to the Hong Kong Association of Banks (HKAB). It covers the same proposed non-capital loss-absorbing-capacity (LAC) liability treatment as the DTCA version of the letter (id 5fef8ce369b7). It also has the same definitional clean-up amendments to the Banking (Capital) Rules. Both are timed for the same 1 January 2026 start date as the cryptoasset capital package. It is sent in near-identical wording to the parallel DTCA letter.

key_points.point: The amendments mainly cover a revised capital treatment for a bank's own direct holdings of certain non-capital loss-absorbing capacity (LAC) liabilities, plus clarifying definitional edits.
The HKMA intends to bring in these changes at the same time as the cryptoasset capital standard, that is, 1 January 2026.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is a duplicate of the DTCA letter for the Hong Kong Association of Banks channel; the same 1 January 2026 coordination point applies.
reading_guide: Duplicate of id 5fef8ce369b7; no need to read both in full.
flags: Near-duplicate of id 5fef8ce369b7 (same letter sent to a different trade association on the same day); not a cryptoasset-specific document.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: n/a - duplicate administrative cover letter; see id 5fef8ce369b7.

title: SFC convenes inaugural Virtual Asset Consultative Panel meeting
summary: The SFC held the first meeting of its new Virtual Asset Consultative Panel (VACP). It is chaired by Dr Eric Yip, the SFC's Executive Director of Intermediaries, and made up of senior management representatives from every licensed virtual asset trading platform (VATP). The Panel is meant to feed into the SFC's regulatory policy-making and help set priorities for building a sustainable, resilient virtual asset ecosystem.

key_points.point: The VACP is chaired by the SFC's Executive Director of Intermediaries, and comprises all licensed VATPs, represented by their senior management.
The VACP will contribute to the SFC's regulatory policy-making, and help identify policy priorities for market and regulatory development backed by investor safeguards.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this body does not include banks unless they operate a licensed VATP. A compliance head should note it as an indirect policy-influence channel, only available through a bank's own VATP-licensed entity.
reading_guide: Very short; read in full.
flags: VACP membership is limited to licensed VATPs only, not the broader VASP/intermediary population.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should note this consultative panel is limited to licensed VATPs' senior management, so the bank can only influence SFC VA policy through a licensed VATP subsidiary, not directly as an AI (para 2).

title: Keynote Speech at ASIFMA Annual Conference
summary: This speech covers the growing China-ASEAN trade and investment corridor and Hong Kong's role in it, touching on trade finance, the internationalisation of the renminbi (RMB), capital markets, and sustainability. The only content related to virtual assets is one line noting the HKMA is trying out tokenisation use cases in trade and supply-chain finance through the Project Ensemble Sandbox. There is also a brief mention of working with the Bank of Thailand on tokenisation use cases such as trade payments and carbon credits.

key_points.point: The HKMA said it was trying out tokenisation use cases in trade and supply-chain finance through the Project Ensemble Sandbox, as part of digitalisation work supporting the China-ASEAN trade corridor.

The HKMA said last October it was teaming up with the Bank of Thailand on Project Ensemble and Project San. They are looking at tokenisation applications covering both payment-versus-payment and delivery-versus-payment models, for uses such as trade payments and carbon credits.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is a small confirmation that Ensemble Sandbox tokenisation work now covers cross-border trade-finance and carbon-credit use cases with a second central bank, Thailand. It has limited direct relevance to a bank's compliance function.
reading_guide: Skip almost all of this speech, the trade corridor, RMB and sustainability content. Only the two short passages referencing Project Ensemble and Project San are virtual-asset relevant.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No action item here; this is background only.

title: SFC sets out new roadmap to develop Hong Kong as a global virtual asset hub
summary: The SFC laid out 12 major initiatives under a five-pillar 'ASPIRe' roadmap: Access, Safeguards, Products, Infrastructure, Relationships. This aims to boost the security, innovation and growth of Hong Kong's virtual asset market. Planned steps include making it easier to reach global liquidity, building adaptive compliance and product frameworks. Creating new regulatory frameworks for virtual asset (VA) over-the-counter (OTC) trading and VA custodian services, expanding VA products and services. Streamlining virtual asset trading platform (VATP) operating requirements, fighting illicit activity, educating investors, and reaching out proactively to stakeholders, including through the newly formed Virtual Asset Consultative Panel.

key_points.point: The ASPIRe roadmap has five pillars, Access, Safeguards, Products, Infrastructure, Relationships, and covers 12 major initiatives.
New regulatory frameworks will be built for virtual asset over-the-counter (OTC) services and VA custodian services, which were not separately regulated before.
The range of VA products and services on offer will grow, and the operating rules for VA trading platforms will be simplified.
The roadmap also covers fighting illicit activity, educating investors, and reaching out to stakeholders, including through the Virtual Asset Consultative Panel.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this sets out the SFC's five-pillar ASPIRe roadmap. It creates no direct obligation itself, but is the reference plan behind later binding circulars, on staking. Dealing and custodian consultations, cybersecurity, and market-making, and should be tracked as a preview of coming change.

quote.text: a living blueprint, one that invites collective efforts to advance Hong Kong’s vision

reading_guide: Short press release; the referenced Appendix, not fully included in fetched text, would list the 12 initiatives in detail. Treat this record as the headline announcement, not the full initiative list.
flags: Announces forthcoming regulatory frameworks for VA OTC and VA custodian services that did not previously exist as distinct SFC-licensed regimes — a bank should not assume custody/OTC activity is already fully covered under the VATP regime.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Brief the board on the ASPIRe roadmap as the master plan behind later SFC initiatives -- staking, custodian and OTC regimes, leveraged products -- that will affect counterparty VATPs and, in some cases, bind the bank directly.

title: “A-S-P-I-Re” for a brighter future: SFC’s regulatory roadmap for Hong Kong’s virtual asset market
summary: The SFC set out a five-pillar roadmap, named Access, Safeguards, Products, Infrastructure and Relationships (ASPIRe), for developing Hong Kong's virtual asset regulatory regime over the coming years. It opens with market context on institutional versus retail participation, fragmented trading venues, and global regulatory convergence between traditional finance and virtual assets. It then lists twelve forward-looking initiatives. These include new licensing regimes for over-the-counter (OTC) trading and custody, more flexible custody and cold-storage rules, staking and lending for professional investors, and better market surveillance. Most items are described as exploratory or under development rather than final rules, so the roadmap signals direction rather than imposing immediate new obligations. It targets custody legislative preparations for completion by end-2025.

key_points.point: The SFC will support the government's introduction of a dedicated licensing framework for virtual asset OTC trading desks, applying the same rules that already bind licensed trading platforms.

The SFC will build a separate licensing regime for virtual asset custodians, modelled on traditional custodian standards for capital, cybersecurity and asset segregation, with legislative preparation targeted for completion by end-2025.

The SFC will explore moving away from a fixed mandatory cold-storage ratio, toward outcome-based, technology-neutral custody standards backed by real-time monitoring, audits and cybersecurity controls.

The SFC will look at professional-investor-only new token listings and virtual asset derivatives trading, and at aligning margin-trading requirements with securities-market risk safeguards. It will also look at allowing staking, under custody and operational safeguards, and professional-investor-only borrowing and lending services.

The SFC will consider straight-through regulatory reporting for digital-asset information. It will also deploy data-driven surveillance tools such as blockchain intelligence and wallet tracing to detect illicit activity market-wide.
The SFC will strengthen cross-agency collaboration with local regulators and law enforcement, and promote cross-border cooperation with overseas regulators.
The SFC will consider a regulatory framework for financial influencers, to address their growing role in shaping investor decisions about virtual assets.

numbers_and_dates.item: Target completion for virtual asset custodian licensing legislative preparation
Global virtual asset market value cited

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this roadmap previews where SFC rules for VATPs, custodians and OTC desks are heading. Compliance can anticipate new counterparty licensing categories, and start planning for potential custody, staking or product changes among the intermediaries it uses or works with.
reading_guide: Read the Executive Summary for context, then Pillar A, custody and OTC licensing, and Pillar S, custody flexibility, closely, as these most affect bank counterparties. Pillars P, I and Re can be skimmed for direction only, as none commit to firm rules yet.
flags: Most initiatives are exploratory ("will explore", "will consider") rather than committed rules; only the custodian licensing legislative timeline (end-2025) is dated.

Only new token listings, VA derivatives (Initiative 6) and borrowing/lending (Initiative 8) are stated as professional-investor-only; margin trading (Initiative 7) and staking (Initiative 8) are not stated as PI-restricted in the text.

As of 25 Sep 2026 several of this roadmap's initiatives have concrete follow-through in later canon entries: OTC/custodian licensing reached Consultation Conclusions in Dec 2025 (ids 32c47580e27d, f41a543388bc) and updated custody guidance is in force from May 2026 (ids 48603e3bc124, ce05e67bcdce); treat this Feb 2025 roadmap as background context, not the current state of those workstreams.

controls_and_monitoring: Monitor SFC progress on the OTC and custody licensing regimes and on any relaxed cold-storage standards, since these will change the due-diligence baseline for VATP and custodian counterparties.
counterparty_due_diligence: Once the OTC trading and custodian licensing regimes take effect, check that any VA OTC desk or custodian the bank uses holds the relevant new SFC licence, not just the existing VATP licence.
Watch for the outcome of the custody technology and cold-storage-ratio review, which may change what counts as adequate custody controls at a counterparty custodian.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be briefed that the SFC plans new licensing categories (OTC trading, custody) by end-2025 and is reconsidering rigid cold-storage rules, both of which will change counterparty due-diligence criteria.

title: Circular to licensed corporations, SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities Cybersecurity webinar materials
summary: This follow-up circular attaches the slide deck from the SFC's Cybersecurity Webinar held on 17 and 19 February 2025. It covers findings from the SFC's 2023/24 thematic review of cybersecurity, real incident case studies, and new risk areas. The deck, presented by the SFC's Steve Poon and Markus Au Yeung, reports on a review of 50 licensed corporations. This included on-site checks of 7 internet brokers and talks with 6 licensed corporations that operate globally. It covers cloud security, remote access, managing third-party vendors, retiring old, end-of-life, software, and phishing. Two case studies are given. One is a ransomware attack that started from a weak VPN gateway and an exposed remote server. The other is unauthorised trades that followed an attack on an unpatched website using unencrypted data.

key_points.point: The 2023/24 thematic review looked at 50 licensed corporations, with on-site checks at 7 internet brokers and discussions with 6 licensed corporations running global operations.
The review looked at cloud security, controls on remote access, management of third-party vendors, handling of software that is no longer supported, end-of-life, and phishing.
92% of internet brokers rely on trading systems built by outside vendors. The top 5 vendors hold 70% of that market, and the single biggest vendor holds 30%, a concentration risk.
Mobile apps have overtaken desktop computers as the main way clients trade online: 82% used mobile and 65% used desktop in 2023/24, compared with 80% each in 2019/20.

Between 2021 and 2024, 8 serious cybersecurity incidents were reported to the SFC, including ransomware attacks. Others were a vendor network breach that disrupted back-office services, and account takeovers through weaknesses in network security.

Case study 1: attackers used a weak VPN gateway and an exposed remote server to plant ransomware. This disrupted trading, settlement, and back-office systems, and forced a halt to online trading and client-money processing. Missing logs made it hard to find the root cause.

Case study 2: attackers exploited an unpatched website that carried unencrypted data and outdated, end-of-life database software. This let them break into internal servers, alter the client database, and place unauthorised trades.
Lessons for licensed corporations: strengthen network security, apply software patches, control user access rights, monitor client accounts, keep audit logs, and encrypt data.
Cyber Defender and Scameter, both tools from the Hong Kong Police Force, were highlighted as ways to stay informed about cybersecurity threats.

numbers_and_dates.item: Third-party trading system usage among internet brokers
Mobile app share of internet trading channels (2023/24)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, these SFC-documented case studies offer lessons it can apply directly to its own digital-asset or brokerage cyber-risk defences. They cover a ransomware attack through a VPN gateway, and unauthorised trades through an unpatched web app. They also show real concentration risk among third-party trading-system vendors.

quote.text: Some LCs violated most of the baseline requirements and expected standards

reading_guide: Read the 2-page cover circular, then the attached deck's case illustrations (pages 9-12) for the concrete incident lessons. Earlier pages, landscape statistics, are useful context but less operative.
flags: This thematic review covers licensed corporations broadly (internet brokers, leveraged FX firms, fund managers), not VATPs specifically — distinct from the VATP-focused custody/cybersecurity standards in circular 25EC3 (0c93d9a066e6).

title: LegCo Subcommittee on Issues Relating to the Development of Web3 and Virtual Assets visits Consensus Hong Kong (with photos)
summary: A Legislative Council (LegCo) subcommittee on Web3 and virtual assets visited the Consensus Hong Kong industry conference. The first time this cryptocurrency, blockchain and Web3 event was held in the city. Members received a briefing on the event, watched startup and blockchain-solution competitions, and exchanged views on growing the local Web3 ecosystem. The visit is a fact-finding activity with no policy announcement or binding content.

key_points.point: A Legislative Council subcommittee visited the Consensus Hong Kong conference on 20 February 2025, the event's first staging in the city, to learn about the cryptocurrency, blockchain and Web3 industries.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is a routine legislative fact-finding visit with no regulatory content, useful only as background on legislators' continued engagement with the local Web3 industry.
reading_guide: Short press release; read in full, no substantive regulatory content to isolate.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No escalation needed.

title: Keynote Address at Asia Pacific Loan Market Association (APLMA) Global Loan Market Summit
summary: This speech is mainly about the syndicated loan market, Generative AI adoption, including the HKMA's GenAI Sandbox, sustainable finance and infrastructure financing. The virtual-asset content is limited to two points. One is a comment that tokenisation could help solve double-counting problems in carbon-credit trading. The other is confirmation that the Financial Secretary's Budget Speech that morning announced the government would regularise tokenised bond issuance going forward. The HKMA is readying a third tranche, and is still working to encourage privately arranged issuances under the Digital Bond Grant Scheme.

key_points.point: The Financial Secretary's Budget Speech announced that tokenised bond issuance would be regularised going forward. The HKMA said it was preparing a third tranche of tokenised government bonds, and would continue encouraging private digital bond issuances via the Digital Bond Grant Scheme.
Tokenisation technology was cited as a potential solution to double-counting problems in carbon-credit trading, which could unlock new business models for sustainability-linked finance.

title: 2025-26 Budget
summary: The Financial Secretary's annual budget speech contains a short section on digital-asset and fintech plans alongside broader fiscal announcements. It also notes the stablecoin issuer bill had already reached the legislature. Most of the 179-page document covers unrelated fiscal, tax and spending matters.

A second policy statement on virtual assets was flagged as coming soon, aimed at combining traditional finance with new technology.

A bill to license issuers of fiat-referenced stablecoins had already been put before the legislature, and the HKMA would speed up processing licence applications once it passed.

title: Distributed Ledger Technology in the Financial Sector - A Study on the Opportunities and Challenges
summary: This is a lengthy HKMA research report on distributed ledger technology (DLT) in finance. It describes DLT's architecture and core features, then walks through ten real-world adoption cases. These include a hypothetical e-HKD use case, HKEX's Synapse platform and a UBS tokenisation pilot, covering payments, trade settlement and digital identity. It sets out practical adoption challenges such as strategy alignment, novel operational risks and regulatory uncertainty. It also gives good-practice guidance for managing risks including third-party reliance, node concentration, smart contracts, key management, cybersecurity, data privacy and interoperability. It closes with the HKMA's own initiatives, the DLT Supervisory Incubator and financial and talent support, and a comparison of how Hong Kong, Singapore, the US and UK support DLT sandboxes.

key_points.point: The Executive Summary describes the paper's exploration of 10 real-world DLT adoption cases across programmable payments, trade settlement and digital identity. The case studies themselves (Section 3) name platforms such as a hypothetical e-HKD use case, HKEX's Synapse and a UBS tokenisation pilot.

Node concentration risk arises when a party gains control of over half a DLT network's nodes, computing power or staked tokens. Permissioned networks face elevated concentration risk because a fixed, known set of parties already controls validation.

Recommended mitigations for node concentration include diversifying node-hosting providers, robust software review and stress testing, contingency plans for non-DLT fallback, and, for permissionless networks, monitoring validator concentration.
Smart contracts carry coding-vulnerability and oracle-concentration risks, since bugs can be exploited automatically and at speed, and reliance on a single oracle creates a single point of failure.

The paper's practical guidance for banks starting DLT projects (Figure 21) includes developing a firm-wide DLT strategy, and centralising efforts with a dedicated DLT team. It also covers delivering fit-for-purpose training, developing mitigation plans for identified risks, and proactively communicating with regulators.
The HKMA's own DLT support includes the Supervisory Incubator sandbox, alongside comparable sandbox schemes run by the SFC, its Regulatory Sandbox, and the Insurance Authority, its Insurtech Sandbox.

numbers_and_dates.value: control of over 50% of nodes/computing power/staked tokens

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is educational and good-practice material, not a binding rule. It is useful as a risk checklist, covering third-party, node concentration, smart contract, key management, cyber, data privacy and interoperability risk, when a business line proposes a DLT pilot. It also points to the HKMA's own sandbox route for engaging supervisors early.
reading_guide: Read the Executive Summary (page 6) and the risk and mitigation guidance in Section 4 (pages 41-59). Pay special attention to Figure 21 on page 43 and the risk-mitigation list on pages 48-53. The ten case studies (Section 3, pages 17-40) and glossary and appendix (Section 6) can be skimmed or used for reference only.
flags: This is a research/educational paper, not a rule or circular obligation; none of its content is mandatory.

controls_and_monitoring: Use the paper's risk categories (third-party, node concentration, smart contract, immutability, private key, cybersecurity, data privacy, interoperability, scalability) as a checklist when reviewing any proposed DLT pilot, per Section 4.1, p.44-58.
counterparty_due_diligence: For a DLT vendor or platform partner, ask about node diversification, software review/testing practices and contingency arrangements, per Section 4.1 item 1-2, p.44-49.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board/risk committee can be told this is HKMA-published good-practice guidance (not a rule) that the bank uses to structure risk assessment of any DLT initiative, and that the HKMA's Supervisory Incubator is available as a low-friction engagement channel.

title: Distributed Ledger Technology in the Financial Sector: A Study on the Opportunities and Challenges
summary: The HKMA commissioned this study, with input from the SFC, Insurance Authority (IA) and Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) Schemes Authority. It did so after interviewing ten institutions and surveying 113 firms on their DLT projects. It builds on two earlier HKMA circulars: the April 2024 risk-management circular and the January 2025 Supervisory Incubator launch. The paper walks through ten Hong Kong pilot deployments, then sets out adoption barriers and a set of good-practice pointers banks can use when scaling DLT work. It is framed as research and guidance rather than a new binding rule, and it repeats and elaborates several expectations the 2024 circular already set.

key_points.point: Boards and senior management should update governance, technology-risk, business-continuity and outsourcing policies before rolling out a DLT solution. They should also add safeguards such as dispute handling or a loss-compensation approach where customers interact with it directly.

A firm should keep enough in-house DLT expertise, echoing the 2024 circular. The paper suggests a centralised team, for example a Centre of Excellence or hub-and-spoke model, blending technologists and business staff to run this.

For outsourced DLT platforms, a bank should vet vendor reliability, security and regulatory standing at every stage. It should also put performance and data-security terms in the contract, and keep backup vendors or failover plans ready.

Control of over half a network's nodes, computing power or staked tokens can let an attacker corrupt the ledger. Because of this, firms should spread node hosting across providers and locations, and run software review and stress testing to cut shared points of failure.

Smart contracts should not be used for every process; manual override should stay possible. Firms also need a governance framework covering suitability review, testing before go-live, and contingency plans if a contract misbehaves.
Because ledger entries are essentially irreversible, firms should build strong upfront data-validation controls, since correcting an error or fraudulent entry after the fact may not be possible.

A bank holding client private keys as custodian is expected to run tight controls: secure key generation, restricted access, proprietary cold storage, backups and an incident-response plan. The paper flags hardware security modules and multi-party-computation wallets, which split a key into shares, as ways to cut single-key concentration risk.

DLT platforms still need ordinary cyber defences, for example multi-factor authentication against endpoint attacks and phishing. Firms should also track emerging threats such as quantum computing and adjust response plans over time.

Where a ledger's transparency would expose counterparty or transaction details a firm needs to keep confidential, it should use privacy techniques, such as stealth addresses, ring signatures and zero-knowledge proofs. It should also plan for participants who want their data removed from the network.

The paper repeats the principle that new HKMA rules for DLT-based activity will track existing rules for the equivalent traditional activity rather than create a separate regime. Summarised as 'same activity, same risk, same regulation'.

Whether a smart contract counts as a binding legal contract in Hong Kong still has no statutory definition. Enforceability turns on ordinary contract-formation tests, agreement, consideration, certainty, intent and formalities, the same approach the paper says Singapore, the US and the UK currently take.

The HKMA's Supervisory Incubator for DLT, launched January 2025, lets a bank get HKMA feedback and run live trials on its risk controls before fully launching a DLT initiative. The paper also flags the SFC's ASPIRe roadmap, February 2025, 12 initiatives across five pillars, as the parallel securities-side track.

numbers_and_dates.item: Node/stake control threshold for network compromise risk
numbers_and_dates.value: >50% of nodes, computational power or staked tokens

numbers_and_dates.item: Survey respondents citing legal & regulatory uncertainty as a major challenge
Supervisory Incubator for DLT launch date

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, although framed as research, this is the HKMA's fullest current public statement of what it expects banks to have in place. That covers governance, third-party, node and smart-contract, key-custody, cyber and privacy risk when running DLT. It largely restates the April 2024 circular. Compliance should treat sections 4.1-4.2 as the working checklist examiners are likely to benchmark a bank's DLT risk framework against.

quote.text: same activity, same risk, same regulation

reading_guide: Read pages 41-59, adoption challenges and the six practical-guidance sub-sections, especially the risk-mitigation list at pages 48-53 and the regulatory-coordination section at pages 57-59. Pages 7-40, the DLT technology primer and ten case studies, are background and can be skimmed.
flags: Non-binding research/guidance paper, not a new supervisory issuance; most risk-management expectations it states were already set out in HKMA's 16 Apr 2024 circular, which it cites throughout as "the previous HKMA circular".

obligations: Review/refresh governance, technology-risk, BCP and outsourcing policies to cover DLT-specific factors before launch (Section 4.2.1, p.44)
Maintain sufficient in-house DLT expertise, consistent with the 2024 circular (Section 4.2.2, p.44-45)

Identify and document mitigation plans for third-party, node-concentration, smart-contract, immutability, private-key, cybersecurity and data-privacy risks before deploying DLT solutions (Section 4.2.4, p.48-53)
controls_and_monitoring: Diversify node hosting/providers and run stress testing and software review for permissioned or permissionless networks used (p.48-49)
Require code audits and a structured approval process for smart contracts, with manual-override capability preserved (p.49-50)
Apply HSM/MPC key-splitting, secure key generation, cold storage and an incident-response plan wherever the bank holds client private keys as custodian (p.51-53)
Extend MFA and standard cyber controls to DLT infrastructure and monitor emerging threats such as quantum computing (p.53)
notifications_reporting: No mandatory filing created by this paper; engaging HKMA's Supervisory Incubator for DLT before a full launch is offered as a voluntary supervisory-feedback channel (Section 4.2.6, p.59)
counterparty_due_diligence: Vet DLT technology vendors' reliability, security protocols and regulatory standing at each stage of the adoption lifecycle, with contractual SLAs and backup-vendor arrangements (p.48)
Conduct due diligence on consortium partners and their staff for permissioned-network participation (p.50-51)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should see the DLT strategy, business case, budget and milestones, and confirm governance and risk-management controls address the DLT-specific risks above before any solution goes live (p.44).

title: Circular on SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets
supersedes_or_amends: Circular on SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets (22 December 2023)
summary: This circular sets the rules the SFC uses to authorise investment funds that put more than 10% of net asset value (NAV) into virtual assets (VA Funds). These are funds for public sale in Hong Kong under sections 104-105 of the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO). It replaces the 22 December 2023 circular. VA Funds can get direct, spot, or indirect, for example futures or exchange-traded products, exposure to virtual assets. They must only invest in VA tokens that Hong Kong's public can already trade through SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs). They cannot use fund-level leverage. Any spot VA trading or custody must go through an SFC-licensed VATP or an authorized institution (AI) that meets the HKMA's virtual-asset custody standards. Custody rules require segregated holdings, mostly cold-wallet storage, and Hong Kong-based, access-restricted storage of seeds and keys. New under this version, VA Funds may now stake or do other VA-related activities under the ASPIRe roadmap. This is allowed as long as they follow guiding principles. These are fitting the fund's investment strategy, having strong internal controls, doing due diligence on counterparties, and giving specific disclosures in offering documents and reports. Funds wanting more than 10% VA exposure, or wanting to stake, must first consult the SFC and get its approval.

key_points.point: SFC-authorised VA Funds are limited to holding, whether directly or through another vehicle, VA tokens that Hong Kong retail investors can already trade on an SFC-licensed VATP.
At fund level, SFC-authorised VA Funds should carry no leveraged exposure to VA.
Transactions and acquisitions of spot VA should be conducted through an SFC-licensed VATP, or through an AI, or a locally incorporated AI's subsidiary, that meets HKMA's regulatory requirements.

The trustee or custodian should only delegate VA custody to an SFC-licensed VATP or a qualifying AI, or its subsidiary, that meets HKMA's expected VA custody standards. VA holdings should be kept segregated, mostly stored in cold wallets, with seeds and keys kept securely in Hong Kong. Access should be restricted, generated non-deterministically, protected by multi-signature controls, and properly backed up.

A fund's offering documents, including the product key facts statements, must spell out VA exposure limits and the key risks. These are price, custody, cybersecurity and fork risk for spot VA; and roll costs and operational risks for VA futures.

VA Funds may now stake and do other VA-related activities, newly allowed under the ASPIRe roadmap's Pillar P. This is provided the management company follows guiding principles. These are fitting the fund's goals, implementing robust internal controls over risk and conflicts, and proper custody. They also include due diligence on counterparties, disclosing VA amounts used in offering documents, and telling investors about material changes.
Funds wanting VA exposure above 10% of NAV, whether new or existing, or wanting to stake or do VA-related activities, must first consult the SFC and get its approval.

numbers_and_dates.item: VA exposure threshold triggering this circular's requirements

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this rule applies to SFC-authorised fund providers and trustees, not directly to the bank as an authorized institution. It matters because if the bank's AI or a subsidiary provides VA custody to one of these funds, it must meet the HKMA custody standard referenced here. Staking is now also allowed for funds.
reading_guide: Read paragraphs 6-27, the Requirements section, in full; paragraphs 1-5 are background and history.
flags: CRITICAL: the fetched document text itself states at the top: 'This circular has been replaced by an updated version' with a link to refNo=26EC31 — meaning as of the time this text was captured, an even newer version supersedes this one; readers should treat this record's content as historical/superseded and check refNo=26EC31 for current requirements.

This is a REVISED version (marked 'Amended'/'Newly added' inline) of the original 22 December 2023 circular, adding the staking-related provisions in paragraph 27 as new content not in the original 2023 version.

counterparty_due_diligence: Check that any VA fund's custody is handled only by an SFC-licensed VATP or a qualifying AI meeting HKMA's VA-custody standards, with mostly cold-wallet, Hong Kong-based key storage (paras 19-20)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Tell the board this circular has itself been replaced (by refNo 26EC31), and that VA funds are now allowed to stake under guiding principles -- a loosening from the earlier rule (para 27).

title: SFC sets out staking guidance for licensed virtual asset trading platforms and authorised virtual asset funds
summary: The SFC published two linked pieces of staking guidance. A circular lets licensed virtual-asset trading platforms offer staking services under risk-management and disclosure conditions. An updated circular lets SFC-authorised virtual-asset funds stake holdings through licensed platforms and authorised institutions, within a cap meant to manage liquidity risk. The SFC framed staking as part of its ASPIRe roadmap, to widen the range of products and services on offer.

key_points.point: SFC-authorised virtual-asset funds may only stake their holdings through licensed trading platforms and authorised institutions, and only up to a cap set to manage liquidity risk.
The guidance is presented as advancing the 'Products' part of the ASPIRe roadmap, which aims to broaden what platforms can offer.
Trading platforms should maintain measures to prevent errors in staking services, safeguard staked client assets, and ensure proper disclosure of the risks staked assets may carry.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this lets licensed trading platforms and authorised funds offer staking; the bank itself has no direct duty here. But if it distributes such funds or refers clients to platforms offering staking, compliance should confirm those counterparties meet the asset-protection and disclosure standards this guidance sets.

quote.text: the safety of client virtual assets continues to be front and centre

reading_guide: Short summary; read companion circulars 50bf95ba3143 (VATP staking) and 353535602a83 (VA Fund staking) for full operative requirements.

controls_and_monitoring: If the bank's regulated arm relies on a trading platform or authorised fund offering staking, check that measures to prevent errors, protect client assets and disclose risk are actually in place for staked holdings (VATP staking circular)
counterparty_due_diligence: Where the bank distributes SFC-authorised virtual-asset funds that stake holdings, confirm the staking only happens through licensed platforms and authorised institutions, within the liquidity-risk cap (VA Funds staking circular)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Tell the board staking is now a regulator-approved activity for trading platforms and funds, which changes the risk profile of any digital-asset product involving staked holdings that the bank distributes or its clients use.

title: Provision of Staking Services for Virtual Assets from Custodial Services
summary: This 7 April 2025 circular sets the HKMA's expected standards for authorized institutions, and subsidiaries of locally incorporated AIs, that offer staking of virtual assets from their custodial services to clients. Staking here means locking client virtual assets so a validator can take part in a proof-of-stake blockchain, in exchange for rewards distributed back to the client. The circular covers internal controls, required client disclosures, and due diligence over the blockchain protocols and third-party providers used. It also asks banks to discuss implementation with the HKMA in advance.

key_points.point: This circular covers authorized institutions themselves, plus any subsidiary of a locally incorporated AI, when either offers staking as part of its custodial services for clients. The parent AI must make sure such a subsidiary's conduct, practices and controls also comply.
A bank should maintain possession or control of everything needed to unstake client virtual assets, such as withdrawal keys and any pre-signed exit instructions.

A bank should maintain policies to catch errors or misconduct in its staking service. It should also keep staked client assets adequately safeguarded, and have internal controls for operational risk and conflicts of interest.

A bank should disclose to clients which tokens it stakes, any third parties involved, fees, and activation and minimum lock-up periods. It should also disclose how rewards are paid, the unstaking process and its length, uptime performance, what happens during outages, and its custodial arrangements.

A bank should disclose the extra risks clients face from staking, including slashing, a validator penalty that can reduce staked assets, and lock-up risk. It should also disclose blockchain bugs, hacking, validator inactivity, and legal uncertainty over a client's rights in staked assets, and how losses from these would be handled.

Before it offers staking on a given blockchain protocol, a bank needs to carry out thorough due diligence. It must confirm its controls, technology and infrastructure can handle that protocol and manage the associated risks.

Where staking is outsourced to a third-party provider, the bank should perform proper due diligence and ongoing monitoring. This includes checking the provider's track record, technology infrastructure, risk mitigation and security controls.
Before rolling out staking services, AIs should have suitable policies, procedures, systems and controls in place, and should talk to the HKMA about their plans beforehand.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the current, in-force operating standard it must satisfy before or while offering custodial staking to clients. It covers key-control, disclosure and third-party due-diligence expectations, plus a clear signal to talk to the HKMA before launch.

quote.text: committing or locking client VAs for a validator

reading_guide: Read the whole circular, three pages. Sections A-C set the substantive standards; the closing Implementation paragraph sets the expectation of prior HKMA discussion.

obligations: Retain possession/control of withdrawal keys and unstaking mechanisms for all client staked virtual assets, per p.2 section A.
Maintain internal controls addressing operational risk and conflicts of interest for the staking service, per p.2 section A.
Give clients the specified disclosures on fees, lock-up periods, reward arrangements, unstaking process, uptime, outage handling and custodial arrangements, per p.2 section B.
Disclose staking-specific risks (slashing, lock-up, blockchain bugs, hacking, validator inactivity, legal uncertainty) and the loss-allocation approach, per p.2 section B.
Carry out due diligence on each blockchain protocol before offering staking on it, and confirm internal capability to manage its risks, per p.2-3 section C.
Discuss implementation plans with the HKMA in advance of launching staking services, per p.3 Implementation.
controls_and_monitoring: Operational rules governing staking services must be documented and in place, per p.2 section A.
Ongoing monitoring of any third-party staking service provider, per p.3 section C.
notifications_reporting: Prior discussion with the HKMA before launching staking services, per p.3 Implementation.
counterparty_due_diligence: Where staking is outsourced, check the third-party provider's experience and track record, technology infrastructure and risk mitigation measures, and security controls, per p.3 section C.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board/risk committee should be told that offering custodial staking triggers specific key-control, client-disclosure and third-party due-diligence obligations, and that the HKMA expects prior engagement before launch.

title: Circular on staking services provided by virtual asset trading platforms
summary: This circular allows SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs) to provide staking services to clients. This was previously prohibited under VATP Guidelines paragraph 7.26(b), which barred VATPs from generating returns on client virtual assets. It does this by modifying VATP licence conditions, subject to the SFC's prior written approval and detailed 'Terms and conditions for providing staking services' in an attached Appendix. VATPs must maintain possession or control of withdrawal mediums, with no third-party custody of staked assets. They must implement whitelisting and verification controls, and disclose staking terms and risks, such as slashing, lock-up, technical, hacking, inactivity and legal uncertainty risk. They must also conduct due diligence on blockchain protocols and third-party validators, and retain records for at least 7 years. They must get SFC approval before including any protocol for retail clients; notification only is needed for professional-investor-only staking.

key_points.point: A VATP and its associated entities must keep hold of, or control, every means by which a client's staked VAs could be withdrawn. For instance, the withdrawal address's private key and any pre-signed voluntary exit message. They cannot leave that custody to an outside service provider.
key_points.locator: para 6, p.1; Terms and conditions para 4, p.1

key_points.point: VATPs should implement systematic whitelist controls, ensuring staking withdrawal addresses are limited to designated whitelisted addresses managed by the client's cold wallet private key. They should also independently verify staking instructions before broadcast.

VATPs should disclose on their website or app: specific VAs staked, third parties involved, fees, and minimum lock-up periods. They should also disclose the unstaking process and length, outage and business-resumption arrangements, custodial arrangements, and risks, such as slashing, lock-up, technical, hacking, inactivity and legal uncertainty.
key_points.locator: circular para 9-10, p.2; Terms and conditions para 12, p.3-4

key_points.point: Except for institutional or qualified corporate professional investors, VATPs should get a client acknowledgement confirming understanding of staking risks before providing staking services.

VATPs should get the SFC's prior written approval before including any blockchain protocol for retail-client staking, or terminating retail staking services. For professional-investor-only staking, advance written notification to the SFC suffices.
Records relating to staking services, staked assets, validators, wallet addresses, dates, returns, protocol-selection rationale, should be kept for not less than 7 years.

VATPs should exercise due skill, care and diligence selecting blockchain protocols and third-party validators. This includes reviewing smart contract audits, validator track record, security controls, financial soundness, and insurance for slashing risk.

numbers_and_dates.item: Minimum record retention period for staking records

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this circular binds VATPs, not the bank. But a compliance head assessing a VATP partner's staking offering should use it as the checklist. That checklist covers no third-party custody of staked assets, mandatory risk disclosure, and SFC approval before retail-client protocols go live.

quote.text: custody of client virtual assets by third party service provider is not permitted

reading_guide: Read the 3-page cover circular for the policy shift and background, then the 6-page Appendix, Terms and conditions, for the full operative requirements. Both are needed, as the circular incorporates the Appendix by reference.
flags: This circular reverses/modifies the prior blanket ban in VATP Guidelines para 7.26(b) on VATPs generating client returns from client VAs — staking is now expressly permitted subject to conditions, correcting outdated assumptions from the original 2023 VATP Guidelines.
Staking is legally classified as an 'incidental service' under the VATP Guidelines' definition of Relevant Activities, not a separate licensable activity.

counterparty_due_diligence: Before using or referring clients to a VATP's staking service, confirm the VATP maintains possession/control of withdrawal mediums itself and does not delegate custody of staked assets to a third party (Terms and conditions para 4, p.1).
Check the VATP has obtained SFC prior written approval for retail-client staking protocols, or advance notification for professional-investor-only staking (Terms and conditions para 23-24, p.6).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No direct bank obligation; if the bank distributes or advises on VATP staking products, the board should know staking is now permitted subject to strict custody and disclosure conditions, reversing the prior blanket ban.

title: New speech by Christina Choi: Keynote speech at Hong Kong Web3 Festival
summary: This is a short SFC news item. It says the regulator has posted a keynote address by Christina Choi, given at Hong Kong's Web3 Festival, about the growth of the city's Web3 and digital-asset sector. Beyond that pointer, this notice gives no further detail.

key_points.point: A keynote address given by Christina Choi at Hong Kong's Web3 Festival, on the growth of the city's Web3 and digital-asset sector, is now available on the regulator's site.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is only a pointer. There is no regulatory substance in the text fetched here, and the actual speech is not included.
