title: Four main themes and their corresponding use case categories to be tested on the Project Ensemble Sandbox
summary: This is a short fact sheet listing the four broad themes being trialled on the HKMA's Project Ensemble Sandbox, a tokenisation testbed run with the securities regulator and industry. The four themes are fixed income and fund products, liquidity management, green and sustainable finance, and trade and supply chain finance, each broken into two use-case categories. It names the banks and other firms taking part as Architecture Community members or Industry Pioneers for each theme, including several major Hong Kong-licensed banks. The list is presented as provisional and subject to change over time.

key_points.point: The sandbox groups pilot use cases under four themes: fixed income and investment funds, liquidity management, green and sustainable finance, and trade and supply chain finance.
Eight specific use case categories sit under the four themes, spanning bonds, funds, repo, treasury management, carbon credits, EV charging, supply chain finance and trade finance/payments.

Named participating banks include Bank of China (Hong Kong), Hang Seng Bank, HSBC, JPMorgan Chase Bank and Standard Chartered Bank (Hong Kong), alongside asset managers, exchanges and technology firms.
The document states the theme and participant list can change, with updates to be posted by the HKMA over time.

numbers_and_dates.item: Last revision date shown on document

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this names which banks are already active in the HKMA's flagship tokenisation sandbox. Useful for benchmarking a bank's own DLT and tokenisation ambitions and for due diligence on peers or partners already engaged with the HKMA on tokenised assets.

title: Speech by FS at Hong Kong Web3 Festival (English only) (with photos/video)
summary: The Financial Secretary's remarks at Hong Kong's Web3 Festival restate the government's pro-innovation stance and recap existing measures. These are the VATP licensing framework, virtual-asset spot exchange-traded funds (ETFs), the near-final stablecoin legislation, and the planned over-the-counter (OTC) and custodian consultations. He references Project Ensemble as a sandbox for tokenised real-world assets, and previews a second virtual-asset policy statement. The speech is promotional in tone with no new binding rules.

key_points.point: Stablecoin legislation was described as close to passage, with the licensing regime targeted to start within the year.
key_points.locator: speech text, para on stablecoin legislation

key_points.point: The government confirmed plans to consult on licensing for virtual-asset OTC trading and custodian services.
key_points.locator: speech text, para following stablecoin mention

key_points.point: Project Ensemble was cited as the HKMA's sandbox letting firms trial tokenised real-world-asset use cases with early regulator feedback.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is a promotional speech restating known plans. It is useful only as a timeline marker showing the stablecoin bill and dealing and custodian consultation were imminent as of early April 2025.

quote.text: Markets, not mandates, should decide which innovations prevail.
quote.locator: speech text, para beginning 'First, it is the very vision'

title: LegCo Subcommittee on Issues Relating to the Development of Web3 and Virtual Assets visits Hong Kong Web3 Festival (with photos)
summary: A short notice records that members of a Legislative Council subcommittee toured the Hong Kong Web3 Festival and met industry representatives to discuss Web3 development. It names the attending members and the event themes but contains no policy or regulatory content.

key_points.point: LegCo subcommittee members visited the Web3 Festival to hear about blockchain infrastructure, crypto finance, and Web3 security/compliance, and to discuss Web3 development with industry representatives

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is purely a diary item confirming ongoing legislative interest in Web3. It carries no obligations or new facts for compliance.
reading_guide: Read in full; one page, no substantive content.

title: Opening Remarks at MO•MENTS 2025 organised by Ant International on Global Outlook: Unlocking Market Potential through Financial Connectivity
summary: A senior HKMA speaker addresses a payments-industry conference, reviewing Hong Kong's stored value facility and Faster Payment System ecosystems and their cross-border links with mainland China and Thailand. The speech then turns to newer forms of money and value transfer. First, mBridge, a multi-central-bank wholesale central bank digital currency (CBDC) project, reaching minimum viable product stage. Second, Project Ensemble's work on tokenisation standards and its Sandbox launched with the securities regulator. Third, the stablecoin licensing law nearing enactment alongside a running stablecoin issuer sandbox. It closes with remarks on fraud risk, cross-border collaboration and operational resilience in payments.

key_points.point: Project mBridge, a cross-border wholesale central bank digital currency platform co-run by the HKMA and other central banks, reached minimum viable product stage in 2024.

Project Ensemble's Architecture Community is developing common standards so central bank digital currency, tokenised money and tokenised assets can interoperate. Its Sandbox launched in August 2024 with the securities regulator and private sector.

The stablecoin licensing law was, at the time of the speech, close to being passed. The HKMA described it as one part of a wider set of rules covering exchange, trading and custody of crypto assets, meant to support a responsible crypto ecosystem.
A stablecoin sandbox running alongside the legislative process lets prospective issuers test scheme features and controls, and feeds into the HKMA's eventual detailed rules.

numbers_and_dates.item: Deception cases reported in Hong Kong (prior year)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this gives an early, high-level signal, April 2025, of how close the HKMA was to enacting the stablecoin licensing regime. It also signals the tokenisation and CBDC infrastructure, mBridge and Ensemble, that the bank's DLT and payments strategy will need to plug into.
reading_guide: Read the paragraphs on mBridge, Ensemble and stablecoins, roughly the middle third of the speech; the payments-history and fraud sections are background only.
flags: The attached PDF (a50e9dc16dc7) is a generic 'latest speech slides' link that, as fetched, actually contains slides from an unrelated, much later (25 September 2026) HKIB conference speech, not slides from this April 2025 speech; see the separate registry entry for that PDF's actual content.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board awareness only: stablecoin licensing and tokenisation infrastructure (mBridge, Ensemble) are approaching implementation and will need a bank strategy response.

title: SFC’s senior executives visit Abu Dhabi and Dubai to promote collaboration on virtual assets
summary: The SFC's Executive Director of Intermediaries, Dr Eric Yip, and Director of Intermediaries and Head of Fintech, Ms Elizabeth Wong, met regulatory counterparts and Web3 industry stakeholders in Abu Dhabi and Dubai. Both cities are in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Regulators met included the Securities and Commodities Authority of the UAE, the Abu Dhabi Global Market's Financial Services Regulatory Authority, the Dubai Financial Services Authority, and Dubai's Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority. They went to exchange virtual asset (VA) regulatory insights and explore cross-border collaboration, in line with the ASPIRe roadmap.

key_points.point: The SFC held discussions with four UAE regulators. These were the Securities and Commodities Authority (UAE), the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of ADGM, the Dubai Financial Services Authority, and Dubai's Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA).
Discussions centred on evolving VA regulatory approaches and supervisory experience, supporting the SFC's ASPIRe roadmap objective of fit-for-purpose policymaking.
Industry participants said clear, consistent rules were essential for the sector to grow, and called for balanced regulation that supports growth without letting systemic risks build up.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this signals the SFC's active engagement with UAE VA regulators, including VARA, a jurisdiction many banks' digital-asset units already operate under. Relevant context for a bank tracking potential future mutual-recognition or cross-border cooperation arrangements.
reading_guide: Short; read in full.

title: Government welcomes passage of Stablecoins Bill
summary: The Legislative Council passed the Stablecoins Bill, creating a licensing regime under the Monetary Authority. This covers anyone issuing a fiat-referenced stablecoin in Hong Kong, or issuing one pegged to the Hong Kong dollar from anywhere. Licensees must meet requirements on reserve-asset management, client-asset segregation, at-par redemption, anti-money-laundering controls, risk management, disclosure and fitness. Only licensed issuers may offer a stablecoin to retail investors, and only advertisements for licensed issuance are allowed, including during a planned six-month grace period. The press release confirms further consultation on detailed rules, and previews upcoming over-the-counter (OTC) and custodian consultations and the second policy statement.

key_points.point: Anyone issuing a fiat-referenced stablecoin in Hong Kong, or a Hong Kong dollar-pegged one anywhere, will need a licence from the Monetary Authority once the Ordinance takes effect.
Licensees must properly segregate client assets, run a robust price-stabilisation mechanism, and process redemption requests at par value on reasonable terms.
Only specified licensed institutions may offer a fiat-referenced stablecoin in Hong Kong, and only a licensed issuer's stablecoin may be offered to a retail investor.
During the six-month non-contravention, or grace, period, only advertisements for licensed stablecoin issuance are permitted.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this confirms the statutory basis for its later stablecoin obligations: only licensed issuers may reach retail clients. Advertising restrictions also apply from day one, so marketing and product teams must not promote unlicensed stablecoin offerings even during the transition window.
reading_guide: Read in full; short and directly relevant to the licensing timetable and retail-offering restriction.

obligations: Only offer or facilitate access to stablecoins issued by an HKMA-licensed issuer to retail clients once the regime is in force (para 3, p.1)
Do not advertise or distribute materials for any stablecoin issuance that is not licensed, including during the six-month grace period (para 3, p.1)
controls_and_monitoring: Screen any stablecoin product or issuer referenced in marketing or distribution materials against the HKMA's list of licensed issuers before publication
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm a prospective stablecoin issuer counterparty holds or is applying for an HKMA licence before entering into any distribution or referral arrangement
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board/risk committee should be told that offering or advertising an unlicensed stablecoin to Hong Kong retail clients is now a statutory breach, not merely a reputational risk.

title: Government welcomes passage of the Stablecoins Bill
summary: The Legislative Council passed the Stablecoins Bill, creating a licensing regime for fiat-referenced stablecoin (FRS) issuers in Hong Kong. Under the resulting Stablecoins Ordinance, a licence from the Monetary Authority (MA) is needed by anyone issuing an FRS in Hong Kong. A licence is also needed for an FRS claiming to hold a stable value referenced to the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) anywhere in the world. Only specific licensed institutions may offer an FRS, and only a licensed issuer's coin may go to retail investors. At all times, including the six-month transition period, only advertisements for licensed FRS issuance are allowed. The government said it would soon launch consultations on virtual-asset over-the-counter (OTC) and custodian services, and publish a second virtual-asset policy paper.

key_points.point: Under the Ordinance, anyone issuing an FRS in Hong Kong, or an FRS claiming stable value referenced to HKD anywhere in the world, needs a Monetary Authority licence.

Licensees must meet requirements on managing and redeeming reserve assets, keeping them separate, and using a solid stabilisation method. They must also redeem at par value on reasonable terms, and meet AML, risk management, disclosure and audit requirements, and be fit and proper.
Only institutions holding the right licence may issue an FRS here in Hong Kong, and only that licensed issuer's FRS is allowed to reach retail investors.
At all times, even during the six-month transition period, only advertisements for licensed FRS issuance are allowed, aimed at stopping fraud and scams.
The Ordinance was due to take effect later in 2025, with a transition arrangement giving industry time to apply for licences and sort out their business.
The government said it would soon launch consultations on virtual-asset OTC trading and custodian services, and publish a second policy paper on virtual-asset development.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, as the law bringing in Hong Kong's stablecoin regime, this directly obliges compliance to make sure the bank only markets or offers MA-licensed FRS coins. Including HKD-referenced coins issued anywhere in the world, right from the start of the transition period.

quote.text: same activity, same risks, same regulation

reading_guide: Read in full; short but dense with operative rules.
flags: Confirms extraterritorial reach: an FRS purporting to maintain stable value referencing HKD is caught even if issued OUTSIDE Hong Kong — a correction to any assumption that only Hong Kong-incorporated issuers are covered.
Advertising restriction applies even during the six-month non-contravention transitional period — unlicensed FRS cannot be marketed even while transitional arrangements are otherwise in effect.

obligations: Do not advertise or market an FRS unless it is licensed, even during the six-month transition period (para 3)
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm any FRS the bank offers or refers to is issued by an MA-licensed issuer, noting the rules also reach HKD-referenced stablecoins issued outside Hong Kong (para 2)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Tell the board the Stablecoins Ordinance is now in force, reaches beyond Hong Kong for HKD-referenced stablecoins, and that further consultations on virtual-asset OTC and custodian services, plus a second policy paper, are coming soon (para 6).

title: Consultation Paper on the Proposed AML/CFT Requirements for Regulated Stablecoin Activities
summary: The HKMA's consultation paper explains, at a policy level, the proposed anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing (AML/CFT) rules. These will apply to entities it licenses to issue stablecoins under the new Stablecoins Ordinance. It covers customer checks on issuance and redemption, extra controls where customers use unhosted, self-custody wallets, the Travel Rule for stablecoin transfers, and ongoing monitoring of stablecoins once in circulation. It also flags that the HKMA is separately drafting supplementary AML guidance for other digital-asset activities such as custody. This guidance would reference the securities regulator's existing rules to keep requirements consistent across regulators. The detailed rules were to be finalised in a companion draft Guideline; comments closed 30 June 2025.

key_points.point: The paper should be read together with the Stablecoins Ordinance and a parallel draft supervisory Guideline. The Legislative Council enacted the Stablecoins Bill on 21 May 2025.
A licensed issuer must run customer checks before issuing or redeeming stablecoins for any transaction of HK$8,000 or more.

Issuers should work out whether a customer's wallet is custodial or unhosted, and confirm the customer controls it. They should also run due diligence on the institution behind a custodial wallet before issuing stablecoins to it.
Where a customer uses an unhosted wallet, the proposal adds extra controls: closer monitoring of those transfers, sending coins only to wallets assessed as reliable, and possible transaction limits.
The Travel Rule under AMLO Schedule 2 section 13A applies to stablecoin transfers, and an issuer may act as ordering, intermediary or beneficiary institution depending on its business model.
Issuers are expected to keep monitoring stablecoins after they are issued, using blockchain analytics to trace transactions and to blacklist or whitelist wallet addresses as needed.

The HKMA is drafting separate supplementary AML guidance covering other digital-asset activities, such as custody services and stablecoin offering by banks and other licensees. This draws on the securities regulator's existing rules for consistency.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this sets out the AML expectations the HKMA planned to impose on any stablecoin-issuer entity within its group. It also foreshadows a related supplementary guideline on custody and other digital-asset activities that would apply more broadly across the bank. It was largely superseded once the final Guideline was published in August 2025.

quote.text: same activity, same risk, same regulation

reading_guide: Read sections 2 (background and scope) and 3 (proposed requirements) in full; section 5 (next steps) is procedural only.
flags: This is a consultation draft; the finalised requirements were issued as a separate Guideline on AML/CFT for Licensed Stablecoin Issuers in August 2025 (see id 4d98c6a80b4d), so this entry is treated as superseded by that final text.

obligations: If the banking group applies for a stablecoin issuer licence, its issuing entity would need to build CDD, wallet-risk and travel-rule controls along these lines (paras 3.2-3.5).
controls_and_monitoring: Blockchain analytics for tracing and screening stablecoin transactions and wallet addresses (para 3.6.2).
counterparty_due_diligence: Due diligence expectations on custodial wallet providers used by a stablecoin issuer inform what a bank should expect of its own VASP/custodian counterparties (para 3.2.3).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Relevant to the board only if the group is considering, or already holds, a stablecoin issuer licence application.

title: Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Licensed Stablecoin Issuers)
summary: This is a draft AML/CFT guideline the HKMA circulated for consultation in May 2025. Meant for entities that hold a licence under Hong Kong's Stablecoins Ordinance to issue fiat-backed stablecoins. It largely mirrors the structure of existing AML rulebooks: risk assessment, governance and staff training, customer checks on stablecoin holders, ongoing monitoring, sanctions screening, suspicious-transaction reporting and record-keeping. Its distinctive chapter applies a travel-rule-style regime to stablecoin transfers, requiring issuers to capture and pass on sender and receiver details above a threshold. The draft was still unnumbered as a Cap.[-] ordinance at the time of publication, confirming it was published ahead of the underlying law being finalised. It has not yet been confirmed as the final in-force text.

key_points.point: The guideline would bind anyone holding a stablecoin-issuer licence, covering how they manage laundering and terror-financing risk from issuing, redeeming and otherwise handling their stablecoins.
A licensee must appoint both a Compliance Officer and a Money Laundering Reporting Officer, which can be the same person for a smaller issuer.
An independent audit function with a direct line to senior management and the board must review the issuer's AML controls.
Before transferring stablecoins worth HK$8,000 or more, the sending institution must record sender and receiver identity details and pass them to the receiving institution securely and immediately.

A licensee must vet a stablecoin transfer counterparty's money-laundering or terrorist-financing risk before dealing with it, similar to the counterparty checks other AML guidelines apply to crypto exchanges.
Filing a suspicious transaction report does not close the matter. The issuer must still review the relationship and may need to freeze or burn the stablecoins involved.
Records of customer checks and stablecoin transaction data must be retained for at least five years after the transaction, even if the relationship has since ended.

If a licensee sets up branches or subsidiaries outside Hong Kong, it must apply group-wide AML standards and. Where local law blocks the stricter of the two rule sets, tell the HKMA and take extra risk-mitigating steps.

Its travel-rule and counterparty-vetting provisions closely track the SFC's VATP guideline, so a bank can largely reuse existing crypto AML controls when assessing stablecoin-issuer counterparties.

title: Draft Guideline on Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers
summary: This consultation-stage HKMA guideline spells out, in detail, what a licensed stablecoin issuer must do under the Stablecoins Ordinance to keep its licence. It covers how reserve assets are chosen, valued, segregated and disclosed, and how issuance and same-day redemption must work. It also covers minimum capital, and detailed risk-management expectations, including token, wallet and private-key, cybersecurity and third-party controls. It further covers incident, business-continuity and wind-down planning, and corporate-governance and fitness-and-propriety standards for directors and managers. It uses 'must' for statutory duties lifted from the Ordinance, and 'should' for the HKMA's own supervisory expectations layered on top. The consultation closed 30 June 2025; a finalised version was expected to follow.

key_points.point: An issuer must at all times hold reserve assets whose market value is at least equal to the face value of stablecoins in circulation. An extra buffer, over-collateralisation, must be built in to cover market-price swings.

Reserve assets are limited to short-dated bank deposits, and high-quality marketable government or public-sector debt. They also include overnight reverse repos and dedicated investment funds holding those instruments, or other assets the HKMA accepts.

Reserve assets must be held in the same currency the stablecoin references. They must also be segregated from the issuer's own assets and protected from the issuer's other creditors, normally via an independent trustee or trust declaration.
An issuer must not pay interest or interest-like returns to stablecoin holders; any yield on reserve assets belongs to the issuer.
Reserve composition and value must be disclosed daily internally, and normally reported to the HKMA and the public weekly, with regular independent attestation of full backing.
Valid redemption requests must be honoured within one business day without unreasonable fees or conditions, unless the HKMA has given prior written consent to a longer period.

An issuer must get the HKMA's consent before conducting any business beyond its licensed stablecoin activity. It must also show that other business will not put its stablecoin operations or customers at risk; this does not apply to an issuer that is itself an authorized institution.
A non-bank issuer must always hold at least HK$25 million in paid-up capital, or an HKMA-approved equivalent.
Issuers should run three lines of defence, business units, risk and compliance, and internal audit, with the risk function reporting directly to the board.

Detailed technology-risk rules require documenting token standards and smart-contract architecture, and multi-signature or similar controls so no single person can unilaterally mint, burn, freeze or blacklist tokens.

'Significant' private keys, governing contract upgrades, role changes or large mint and burn operations, must be generated and stored offline. This must be in an air-gapped, Hong Kong-based, or HKMA-accepted, environment with elevated physical security.
Smart contracts must be independently audited by a qualified third party at least annually and on every deployment or upgrade.

Material third-party arrangements, such as custody of reserve assets, distribution, and critical IT services, must be pre-notified to the HKMA. Access for the HKMA and auditors must not be blocked even where service providers sit outside Hong Kong.
An issuer must have a business continuity programme and a separate, board-approved business exit plan for orderly wind-down and redemption in the event it must stop operating.
Any plan to delay redemptions beyond the one-day rule as part of an incident or wind-down response needs the HKMA's prior written consent.

At least one-third of the board should be independent non-executive directors. The HKMA's consent is also needed before appointing directors, chief executives or, for bank issuers, the stablecoin manager.
Fitness-and-propriety assessment of directors, controllers and managers weighs prior conduct, regulatory record, criminal history, financial position and conflicts of interest.

Each stablecoin type must have a public white paper covering the issuer, coin details, and reserve management. It must also cover issuance and redemption mechanics, underlying technology and risks; the HKMA must be notified before publication or material changes.
Complaints handling must be accessible, fair and timely, run by staff independent of the matter complained about, with outcomes fed back to the HKMA.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the core prudential and operational rulebook its stablecoin-issuer subsidiary, or an authorized institution issuing directly, would have to meet. It is also the reference standard compliance should use when assessing any third-party stablecoin issuer the bank deals with as a counterparty, custodian or distributor.

title: Stablecoins Ordinance to commence operation on August 1, 2025
summary: The government published a Gazette notice setting 1 August 2025 as the date the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656), which licenses stablecoin activities, takes effect. A second notice, relying on section 9(2)(b)(iii) of the Ordinance, names professional investors as a class who may still be offered a specified stablecoin issued by an unlicensed person. Separately, the HKMA opened a consultation on the detailed regulatory requirements, including anti-money-laundering rules. Both notices were due before the Legislative Council on 11 June for negative vetting.

key_points.point: The Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) commenced operation on 1 August 2025, as fixed by the Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury's commencement notice.
A specified stablecoin issued by a person without a section 15 licence may still be offered to professional investors, as defined under the Securities and Futures Ordinance.
The HKMA launched a consultation on detailed regulatory requirements for the regime, including anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing provisions.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this fixes the exact date the stablecoin licensing regime became binding law. It also confirms an unlicensed issuer's stablecoin can still lawfully reach professional investors, but not retail investors, which matters for the bank's private banking and institutional client segments.
reading_guide: Read in full; short and gives the exact commencement date and the professional-investor carve-out.

obligations: Treat August 1, 2025 as the in-force date for stablecoin licensing obligations and the retail-offering restriction (para 1 and 3, p.1)
controls_and_monitoring: Client-classification controls should distinguish professional investors (who may still be offered an unlicensed issuer's stablecoin) from retail investors (who may not) before any stablecoin-related transaction
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Confirm to the board that the stablecoin licensing regime and its retail-offering restriction are now in force, not merely proposed.

title: Keynote Speech at International Conference on Roads and Railways 2025
summary: A senior HKMA official speaks at an infrastructure-industry conference about how Hong Kong can help fund regional transport projects such as roads and railways. The talk covers debt markets, government bond programmes, public-private partnerships, securitisation and blended finance, with a climate-resilience angle. It says nothing about virtual assets, stablecoins, tokenisation or distributed ledger technology (DLT).

key_points.point: The speaker names three roles for Hong Kong: promoting itself as a financial centre, issuing government bonds, and investing official reserves.
The Hong Kong Government had issued about US$47 billion of green and infrastructure bonds by then, funding projects such as flood prevention and energy-efficient buildings.
The Hong Kong Mortgage Corporation turned infrastructure loans into a separate asset class, issuing about US$820 million in two deals since 2023.

Third, the redemption-risk add-on for stablecoin-linked group 2a trading-book exposures. Fourth, the group 2b risk-weighted amount. The notes describe the same build-up for the output floor in Division B, including separate treatment for trading-book exposures under the standardised (STC) approach.

key_points.point: Item 2.5, the crypto add-on, sums five things. First, the group 1 infrastructure risk add-on for banking-book exposures. Second, the redemption-risk add-on for group 1b trading-book exposures. Third, the redemption-risk add-on for stablecoin-linked group 2a trading-book exposures. Fourth, the group 2b risk-weighted amount. Fifth, the group 2 concentration add-on for globally or domestically important banks (G-SIB/D-SIB).

Item 2.7, the total risk-weighted amount for the CAR calculation, is the sum of items 2.1 through 2.6. So the crypto add-on in item 2.5 directly raises the bank's total RWA and, all else equal, lowers its capital ratio.

For institutions subject to the output floor, item 1(i)(e) of Division B aggregates several STC-approach crypto add-ons. First, the redemption-risk add-ons for trading-book group 1b and stablecoin-linked group 2a exposures. Second, the banking-book group 1 infrastructure add-on. Items 1(ii)(c) and 2(ii)(d) each carry, on their own line, the infrastructure risk add-on for Group 1 crypto exposures held in the trading book. This figure comes from the market-risk return MA(BS)3A Part I.

title: Letter to HKAB: Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return templates
summary: This is the HKMA's cover letter to the Hong Kong Association of Banks. It sends a similarly worded letter to the Deposit-Taking Companies Association. It opens a 13 June to 11 July 2025 industry consultation on revised return templates. It follows an earlier statutory consultation on draft rules applying the Basel cryptoasset prudential standard, plus other minor updates. Seven returns are touched, covering capital, funding and exposure reporting. On capital: the Leverage Ratio return (MA(BS)27) and the Large Exposures return (MA(BS)28). Also on capital: the Capital Adequacy Ratio return (MA(BS)3), and the Market Risk and CVA Risk Capital Charge return (MA(BS)3A). On liquidity and compliance: the Liquidity Position return (MA(BS)1E), the Certificate of Compliance return (MA(BS)1F), and the Stable Funding Position return (MA(BS)26). Where a template's layout stays the same, only explanatory notes or completion instructions are being issued. It asks for feedback by 11 July 2025 and notes the templates are preliminary, meant to help banks start building their systems.

key_points.point: This consultation follows an earlier statutory consultation on draft rules applying the Basel Committee's standard for how banks should treat cryptoasset exposures for prudential purposes, plus other minor updates.

Also on capital: the Capital Adequacy Ratio return (MA(BS)3), and the Market Risk and CVA Risk Capital Charge return (MA(BS)3A). On liquidity and compliance: the Liquidity Position return (MA(BS)1E), the Certificate of Compliance return (MA(BS)1F), and the Stable Funding Position return (MA(BS)26).
Where a return's layout does not change, only explanatory notes or updated completion instructions are given, rather than a whole new template.

summary: This is the draft revised template for Part IIIa of the capital adequacy return MA(BS)3. It covers risk-weighted assets for credit risk under the Basic Approach (BSC). The consultation adds a wholly new Division A2, Risk-weighted Amount for Cryptoasset Exposures, alongside the existing Division A1 for non-crypto exposure classes. The new division splits crypto holdings into group 1a (for example, tokenised traditional assets issued by government or deposit-taking issuers) and group 1b (for example, certain stablecoin-type exposures). It reports the bank's top five individual crypto exposures by risk-weighted amount. It also adds separate lines for crypto derivative contracts and secured-lending exposures involving crypto collateral. It was open for comment from 13 June to 11 July 2025.

Group 1a cryptoasset exposures are split by issuer type into those issued by the HKSAR Government, by deposit-taking supervised entities, and by other issuers.
Group 1b cryptoasset exposures get their own reporting line separate from group 1a.
Banks must identify and report their five largest individual group 1 cryptoassets ranked by risk-weighted amount.

It must also separately capture crypto derivatives and crypto-collateralised financing on the quarterly CAR return, once the rule takes effect.

summary: This is the Annex II-A companion to the MA(BS)3 Part II completion instructions in the same 13 June 2025 package. It is a worked numerical example. It shows how a consolidated bank may recognise minority interests in CET1, Additional Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital, when a subsidiary issues capital instruments partly held by third parties. It has no cryptoasset content -- the example and its figures are unchanged from the prior version. It is included only because it sits under the same Part II completion instructions being reissued.

key_points.point: The annex is a fully worked numeric example of the minority-interest recognition formula. It uses a hypothetical subsidiary, Bank S, issuing CET1, Additional Tier 1 and Tier 2 instruments partly held outside the group.
No cryptoasset-related wording or figures appear anywhere in this annex. It is unchanged material, carried over into the reissued Part II package.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this has no direct crypto relevance. Compliance can treat it as an unchanged reference example, with no need to re-check it for the crypto rule rollout.
reading_guide: Can be skimmed or skipped. It carries no crypto-specific content.
flags: Despite sitting inside the cryptoassets-standard consultation package, this specific attachment has no crypto content.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No board item; unrelated to crypto reporting.

title: Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return templates |  | Explanatory notes : MA(BS)3 Part IIIb
summary: These explanatory notes go with the draft MA(BS)3 Part IIIb template and explain the crypto Division A2 under the Standardised (STC) approach. They give worked examples on tracing a group 1a cryptoasset back to the traditional asset it represents -- for example, a tokenised bond. They cover reporting separately any exposure secured by recognised group 1a crypto collateral. They also explain the redemption-related risk that must be reported for group 1b crypto exposures, where redeemers can ask for traditional assets back.

key_points.point: To classify a group 1a cryptoasset exposure, a bank must look through to the traditional asset it represents -- for example, treating a tokenised debt security like the underlying bond.
Any exposure secured by recognised collateral that is a group 1a cryptoasset must be reported separately, whether or not the underlying exposure is itself a crypto exposure.

Where a group 1b cryptoasset points to a pool of traditional assets, the exposure must be split out by the credit-risk subclass of those reference assets. This uses the IRB framework's mapping, even for a bank on the STC approach.
A separate line captures the risk that arises when the redeemer of a group 1b cryptoasset can demand the underlying cryptoasset itself, rather than cash or traditional assets.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this gives the look-through method that product and risk teams need to apply consistently. It is used when tagging tokenised holdings to their correct crypto group and underlying asset class.

quote.text: Division A2 is a new division added for reporting cryptoasset exposures subject to the STC

reading_guide: Read in full. It is a short document focused entirely on the new crypto division.

obligations: Apply the look-through classification method (tracing what backs each asset) when filling in Division A2 of MA(BS)3 Part IIIb.
controls_and_monitoring: Keep a record of the basis for classifying each tokenised holding as group 1a or 1b, for audit-trail purposes.
notifications_reporting: Feeds into the same quarterly MA(BS)3 Part IIIb submission.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No separate escalation is needed beyond the return template.

title: Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on return templates |  | Return template: MA(BS)3 Part IIIf
summary: Part IIIf is a wholly new part of the MA(BS)3 return, applying regardless of which credit-risk approach a bank uses. It is titled Additional Risk-weighted Amount for Cryptoasset Exposures. It captures two Basel add-ons that sit on top of the ordinary risk-weighting done elsewhere in the return. One is an infrastructure risk add-on for group 1 cryptoasset exposures, reflecting operational and settlement risks of the underlying blockchain. The other, for group 2 (unbacked or algorithmic-type) cryptoasset exposures, has two parts. One is an add-on tied to how much of the bank's exposure is in group 2, relative to a cap. The other is a separate capital charge for group 2b exposures that use intermediaries to perform the redemption function.

key_points.point: Part IIIf is a new part of MA(BS)3 that applies to every credit-risk approach, dedicated entirely to additional cryptoasset risk-weighted amount add-ons.

Division A reports the infrastructure risk add-on for group 1 cryptoasset exposures. It also separately lists the group 1b and group 1 cryptoassets where an intermediary performs the redemption function.
Division B reports group 2 cryptoasset exposures, including a risk-weighted amount for each individual group 2b cryptoasset.

Division C reports the group 2 cryptoasset exposure ratio and the associated add-on. This add-on applies when a bank's group 2 crypto holdings exceed a specified threshold, relative to its Tier 1 capital.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, holding any cryptoasset means completing this new stand-alone Part IIIf, regardless of its credit-risk approach. This is where the additional infrastructure-risk and group-2-exposure-ratio capital add-ons required by the Basel crypto standard actually land on the return.

quote.text: Additional Risk-weighted Amount for Cryptoasset Exposures

reading_guide: This is a short, one-page template. Read it in full, alongside the explanatory notes for the same part.
flags: This new Part IIIf applies to all AIs with cryptoasset exposures irrespective of which credit-risk approach (BSC/STC/IRB) they otherwise use.

obligations: Complete new Part IIIf every reporting period if the bank holds any cryptoasset exposures, covering the infrastructure risk add-on and the group 2 exposure ratio add-on.
controls_and_monitoring: Monitor the group 2 cryptoasset exposure ratio against its threshold on an ongoing basis, not just at quarter-end, since breaching it triggers an additional capital add-on.
notifications_reporting: Quarterly MA(BS)3 return to HKMA once the crypto capital rules commence (targeted 1 Jan 2026).
counterparty_due_diligence: Check whether an intermediary performs the redemption function for any group 1b/2b crypto product the bank holds, since that changes which Division A/B line applies.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told a hard concentration-style ratio (group 2 crypto exposure vs capital) now carries its own capital add-on, which is a new type of limit to monitor.

title: Robust and Sustainable Development of Stablecoins
summary: HKMA's Chief Executive uses this speech to set expectations around the newly-passed Stablecoins Ordinance. He confirms it would take effect on 1 August 2025, after which HKMA would begin accepting licence applications. He describes stablecoins as a payment instrument, not an investment. He signals that only a small number of licences would be granted at first. Use-case viability and operational readiness would be scrutinised heavily. Joining HKMA's stablecoin issuer sandbox does not guarantee a licence. He references the Financial Stability Board's (FSB) 2023 global crypto-asset framework as a basis for Hong Kong's approach. He also notes HKMA's role coordinating the FSB's review of how that framework is being implemented worldwide.

key_points.point: The Stablecoins Ordinance was expected to commence on 1 August 2025, after which HKMA would start accepting stablecoin issuer licence applications.
HKMA describes stablecoins as a payment instrument, not an investment or speculative asset, and groups them with CBDC and tokenised deposits as alternative emerging payment options.

Hong Kong's regulatory approach draws on the Financial Stability Board's 2023 global regulatory framework for crypto-asset activities, and HKMA was coordinating the FSB's review of that framework's global implementation.
HKMA expects to grant only a small number of licences initially, and applicants must demonstrate viable use cases and prudent, sustainable operating capability.

Applicants need to show capability across reserve-asset management, price stabilisation, redemption, technology security, risk management and anti-money laundering (AML) controls. Cross-border applicants must also show their partners hold the necessary regulatory approvals.
Participation in the Stablecoin Issuer Sandbox is not a precondition for, or guarantee of, obtaining a licence.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this confirms the licensing regime's go-live date and signals a deliberately restrictive, high-bar initial licensing approach. Compliance should factor this into any group decision about applying for a stablecoin issuer licence, or partnering with an applicant.

quote.text: same activity, same risks, same regulation

reading_guide: Read in full. It is a short piece with no boilerplate to skip.

counterparty_due_diligence: Confirms HKMA's high licensing bar; useful context when assessing whether a prospective stablecoin-issuer counterparty is likely to be licensed.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should note the confirmed 1 August 2025 commencement date and the restrictive initial licensing stance when weighing any stablecoin business plans.

title: Consultation on revised disclosure templates and tables |  | Annex 1: Standard disclosure templates and tables for making disclosure under the BDR
supersedes_or_amends: Cryptoassets Standard: SPM Modules, Code of Practice, Disclosure Templates and Tables, and Banking Returns - Annex 3/Annex 4 Standard Disclosure Templates and Tables
summary: The HKMA wrote to industry on 25 June 2025 to consult on revised standard Pillar 3 public disclosure templates and tables under the Banking (Disclosure) Rules (BDR). This annex adds a new Part XII, Cryptoasset exposures. It has Table CAEA: qualitative disclosure on an authorized institution's (AI's) cryptoasset activities, risk profile and classification approach. It also has three templates: CAE1 (cryptoasset exposures and risk-weighted assets (RWAs)), CAE2 (accounting classification) and CAE3 (liquidity requirements, category 1 institutions only). CAE1 requires disclosure, by cryptoasset group (1a/1b/2a/2b), of credit-risk exposure/exposure at default (EAD)/RWA and market-risk long/short exposure/RWA. It requires a total row, and rows for AIs whose group 2 cryptoasset exposure ratio breaches the BCR's 1% or 2% thresholds. Group 1 and group 2 cryptoasset exposures must also be folded into the general disclosure templates that cover equivalent traditional-asset exposures elsewhere in the package. Comments were due 25 July 2025.

key_points.point: A new Part XII, Cryptoasset exposures, is added to the standard public disclosure package, comprising Table CAEA and Templates CAE1, CAE2 and CAE3.
key_points.locator: Part XII contents listing, p.9; substantive Part XII section, pp.99-108

key_points.point: Table CAEA requires an AI to describe its cryptoasset-related business activities, how each affects its risk profile, and the scope of its cryptoasset reporting. It must also describe its most significant current and emerging cryptoasset risks, and, for group 1 cryptoassets, how it assesses each of the four BCR section 361 classification conditions.

Template CAE1 requires, for each cryptoasset group (1a, 1b, 2a and 2b), disclosure of total credit-risk exposure, exposure/EAD and RWA, plus market-risk long and short exposure and RWA. It also needs a total row, and separate rows for AIs whose group 2 cryptoasset exposure ratio breaches the BCR's 1% or 2% thresholds.

Beyond the dedicated Part XII templates, an AI must also fold its group 1 and group 2 cryptoasset exposures into the general disclosure templates. These cover equivalent traditional-asset exposures elsewhere in the package. For example, Template OV1's row 5c covers cryptoasset credit-risk RWA under BCR section 376, and row 8a covers RWA for the group 2b cryptoasset derivative-contract method.
key_points.locator: Template CAE1 Points to note item 2, p.103; cross-referenced rows in Template OV1, p.10

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is separate from the internal prudential returns. It is what the bank must publish externally about its crypto exposures, under Pillar 3. Compliance and disclosure teams, not just regulatory reporting, need to build a public-facing crypto disclosure process alongside the internal MA(BS) returns.

quote.text: Cryptoasset exposures and RWAs

reading_guide: Go straight to Part XII, Template CAE1, around p.363-373. The rest of the annex covers unrelated Pillar 3 templates, which can be skipped for crypto purposes.

obligations: Publicly disclose cryptoasset exposures and RWAs via new Template CAE1 in Pillar 3 disclosures if the bank has group 1 or group 2 cryptoasset exposures.
controls_and_monitoring: Establish a disclosure sign-off process linking Template CAE1 figures back to the internal MA(BS)3/3A/IIIf regulatory return figures for consistency.
notifications_reporting: Periodic (per BDR schedule) public Pillar 3 disclosure once the disclosure rules commence.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/disclosure committee should be told the bank's crypto exposure and risk-weighting approach will become publicly disclosed information, not just internal regulatory data.

title: Second policy statement on development of digital assets issued to scale Hong Kong to new heights of global digital asset leadership
summary: The government issued Policy Statement 2.0 on the Development of Digital Assets, building on its October 2022 statement. It sets out the 'LEAP' framework: legal and regulatory streamlining, expanding tokenised products, advancing use cases, and people/partnership development. It confirms the SFC will be the lead licensing authority for digital-asset dealing and custodian service providers. FSTB and HKMA will separately lead a legal review of tokenisation covering bonds and other real-world assets. Full detail, including HKMA's role supervising banks in dealing/custodian activities, is in the attached Annex (package: a29b51bffc6b).

key_points.point: The Policy Statement 2.0 organises initiatives under the LEAP framework: legal streamlining, expanding tokenised products, advancing use cases, and people/partnership development.

The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) will be the lead licensing authority for digital-asset dealing and custodian service providers. FSTB and HKMA will separately lead a legal review to enable tokenisation of real-world assets and financial instruments.
The FSTB and SFC would launch public consultations shortly on licensing regimes for digital-asset dealing and custodian service providers.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this press release is the headline announcement of a framework that leads directly to future dealing and custodian obligations. The substantive detail compliance needs is in the attached Annex.
reading_guide: Read this press release for the headline. Then read the Annex (id a29b51bffc6b) for the substance.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board should be briefed that the government has committed to a comprehensive licensing framework covering dealing and custody, which will bring new obligations for the bank's own digital-asset activities and its counterparty due diligence.

title: Policy Statement 2.0 on the Development of Digital Assets in Hong Kong
supersedes_or_amends: Policy Statement on Development of Virtual Assets in Hong Kong (October 2022)
summary: This is the full annex of Policy Statement 2.0. It replaces the term 'virtual assets' with 'digital assets' in government usage. It sets out the LEAP framework across four areas. First, unifying licensing for digital-asset exchanges, stablecoin issuers, and dealing and custodian providers, under SFC leadership. Second, regularising tokenised government bond issuance and clarifying stamp duty treatment for tokenised ETFs. Third, supporting stablecoin payment use cases, including proposals to test licensed stablecoins in government payments. Fourth, expanding talent and cross-border cooperation. It confirms tax concessions for privately-offered funds will be extended to specified digital assets from the 2025/26 year of assessment.

key_points.point: The government will use 'Digital Assets' instead of 'Virtual Assets' going forward, to better match international usage.
SFC will be the lead authority for licensing digital-asset dealing and custodian service providers, while HKMA will be the frontline regulator supervising banks conducting those activities.
FSTB and HKMA will lead a legal and regulatory review of tokenisation, starting with the bond market and covering settlement, registration and record requirements.
HKMA is exploring an Ensemble Infrastructure to support interbank settlement of tokenised deposits.
Government will clarify that the existing stamp duty waiver for ETFs listed on the stock exchange also applies to tokenised ETFs.
Profits-tax concessions for privately-offered funds and family investment vehicles will be extended to cover specified digital assets, subject to LegCo approval, from the 2025/26 year of assessment.
The stablecoin issuer licensing regime, commencing August 1, 2025, is described as a cornerstone for enabling licensed issuers to pursue payment and cross-border settlement use cases.
Government invited proposals from market participants on how it might test licensed stablecoin usage, including for government payments.

numbers_and_dates.item: Two tokenised government green bond issuances to date
Effective date of extended fund tax concessions for digital assets

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the core policy document compliance should treat as the source of the upcoming licensing structure. It confirms SFC-led licensing, with HKMA as bank supervisor, for both dealing and custody. This frames every later consultation and future obligation for the bank's digital-asset business.

quote.text: same activity, same risks, same regulation

reading_guide: Read the LEAP framework list on pages 2-3 and the regulatory-authority paragraphs (5-6, pages 3-4). The talent/partnership section (pages 8-9) can be skimmed.
flags: Terminology shift: government now uses 'Digital Assets' in place of 'Virtual Assets', though 'virtual asset' remains the legally defined term under the AMLO

obligations: Track the coming SFC dealing/custodian licensing regime, under which the bank as an authorised institution will be supervised on the front line by the HKMA for any dealing or custody activity (para 5-6, p.3-4)
If claiming the extended fund tax concession for digital assets from YA 2025/26, ensure the transaction qualifies once the legislative proposal is enacted (para 15, p.6)
controls_and_monitoring: Monitor FSTB/HKMA legal review outputs on tokenisation of bonds and real-world assets, since settlement and registration practice may change (para 9, p.4)
counterparty_due_diligence: When assessing a digital-asset counterparty, note that stablecoin issuers regulated by HKMA are positioned as the anchor for licensed payment use cases (para 16, p.7)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told the government has set a policy direction placing SFC as sole licensing authority (with HKMA supervising banks) for both digital-asset dealing and custody, directly shaping the bank's future licensing path.

title: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism (1) FATF Statement on High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action (2) FATF Statement on Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring (3) Outcomes from the Joint FATF-MONEYVAL Plenary, 12-13 June 2025
supersedes_or_amends: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - AML/CFT (refNo=25EC15, 7 March 2025)
summary: This is a routine SFC circular passing on the Joint FATF-MONEYVAL Plenary's June 2025 statements. Countermeasures calls against North Korea (DPRK) and Iran continue. Myanmar remains under enhanced due diligence, with countermeasures to be considered if there is no progress by October 2025 -- five years of limited progress have been noted. The Increased Monitoring list added Bolivia and the British Virgin Islands, and removed Croatia, Mali and Tanzania. The circular also relays several Plenary outcomes. FATF approved changes to Recommendation 16 on payment transparency, published 18 June 2025. It updated Recommendation 1 guidance on financial inclusion, published 23 June 2025. It issued a report on complex proliferation-financing and sanctions-evasion schemes, published 20 June 2025. A global terrorist-financing risk report is forthcoming. FATF also published its 6th Targeted Update Report on VA/VASP implementation, plus Best Practices on Travel Rule Supervision, both on 26 June 2025.

key_points.point: FATF countermeasures calls against DPRK and Iran continue (carried forward, Iran's countermeasures suspension remains fully lifted).
Myanmar has shown limited progress over the past five years; FATF will consider countermeasures if no further progress by October 2025.
Increased Monitoring list updated: Bolivia and the Virgin Islands (UK) added; Croatia, Mali and the United Republic of Tanzania removed.
FATF signed off on revisions to Recommendation 16 and its Interpretive Note, aimed at improving payment-transparency and sanctions detection, with the revised text released 18 June 2025.
FATF published its 6th Targeted Update Report on VA/VASP standards implementation, and Best Practices on Travel Rule Supervision, both on 26 June 2025.

numbers_and_dates.item: Deadline for Myanmar progress before countermeasures considered
6th Targeted Update Report / Travel Rule Best Practices publication

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is a routine FATF jurisdiction-list update that supersedes the March 2025 circular. It points to the FATF's newly published 6th Targeted Update Report on VA/VASP implementation and Travel Rule Best Practices -- useful primary sources for benchmarking the bank's own travel-rule compliance.
reading_guide: Skim the jurisdiction-list changes (section 2). Note the two virtual-asset (VA) specific FATF publications in section 3(e) as further-reading sources.
