title: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Dealing in Virtual Assets
supersedes_or_amends: Consultation paper on a licensing regime for VA OTC trading services (February-April 2024 consultation)
summary: The Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB) and the SFC jointly asked for public comment on a revised plan to license providers who deal in virtual assets (VAs). Comments were due 29 August 2025. This replaces the narrower 2024 proposal that only covered VA over-the-counter (OTC) trading. Feedback on the earlier plan showed the industry is far wider than physical coin shops. It includes ATMs, broker-dealers, digital-only platforms, payment firms and card networks, serving both retail and institutional clients. It also flagged a need for custody rules the first proposal lacked. Under the new plan, anyone dealing in VAs as a business -- buying, selling, subscribing, underwriting, or profiting from VA price swings -- would need SFC licensing or registration. This covers everything from simple conversions to complex brokerage, block trading, advice and asset management, whether done in person or online. Banks and stored value facility (SVF) operators would register with the SFC after consulting the HKMA, echoing how banks' securities business is already split between the two regulators. HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers dealing only in their own coin issuance and redemption would be exempt. There is no proposed transition period for existing providers -- the rules would apply fully from day one. So the paper urges firms already in the business to contact the SFC or HKMA early, to avoid having to stop trading.

key_points.point: Anyone dealing in VAs as a business -- buying, selling, subscribing, underwriting, or profiting from price movements -- would need an SFC licence or registration. Banks and SVFs would register with the SFC after consulting the HKMA, which would supervise them day-to-day.
Stablecoin issuers already licensed by the HKMA would not need a separate VA dealing licence for issuing or redeeming their own coins in the primary market.

The plan covers both simple conversions between VAs or between VA and cash, and more complex work such as brokerage, block trades, advice and asset management, done through shops or platforms. Pure peer-to-peer trades with no middleman are excluded.

A VA dealer that lets a third party hold client VAs on its behalf must use a VA custodian licensed or registered in Hong Kong. This is the topic of a separate, related consultation launched the same day.

Applicants other than banks must be incorporated or registered in Hong Kong, and keep a permanent local office suitable for record-keeping. They must also name at least two officers -- SFC-approved for most firms, HKMA-approved for banks -- who are personally responsible for compliance.

Proposed capital rules for non-bank applicants: at least $5 million in paid-up share capital. Up to $3 million in required liquid capital, depending on the business model, plus spare liquid capital equal to at least a year's running costs.

Licences would run indefinitely until cancelled, with no transition period for firms already operating. The rules would bind everyone once in force, so existing providers are urged to reach out to the SFC or HKMA early, rather than risk having to shut down.
Firms already vetted and operating with SFC or HKMA approval -- such as existing licensed corporations, registered institutions, or licensed trading platforms -- would get a faster approval track.
Fees would mirror the existing Type 1 securities-dealing fees. Currently $4,740 to apply and renew for a licensed corporation, and $23,500 to apply plus $35,000 a year for a registered institution.

Proposed penalties include up to seven years in prison and civil fines of up to $10,000,000. This is along with licence suspension or cancellation, reprimands and orders to fix problems -- similar to the existing trading-platform regime.
A tribunal modelled on the existing money-laundering review tribunal is proposed to hear appeals against SFC or HKMA decisions.
By end-June 2025, the SFC had licensed 11 trading platforms, with 10 more applications pending, including four operators treated as already licensed during the transition.

numbers_and_dates.item: First (2024) VA OTC consultation submissions received

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this proposal names banks directly. A bank offering VA dealing services would have to register with the SFC, while the HKMA acts as its day-to-day supervisor, mirroring how bank securities business already works. Compliance should keep watching how this consultation turns into law.

quote.text: we are not inclined to provide a deeming arrangement to the pre-existing VA dealing

reading_guide: Read Chapter 1 (background and scope, pp.1-9) and Chapter 2 (regulatory requirements, pp.10-26) in full. Skip the FATF/DNFBP footnote boilerplate. The 12 consultation questions, listed at the end, map directly to each subsection and work as a structured checklist.
flags: Unlike the VATP regime (2023) and the original VA OTC proposal (2024), this revised dealing-services regime explicitly proposes NO deeming/grace-period arrangement — pre-existing dealers who fail to engage SFC/HKMA before commencement risk forced business cessation, a materially different (harsher) transition than prior VA licensing regimes.

Banks and SVFs are registered (not licensed) with the SFC but IN CONSULTATION WITH HKMA, with HKMA as frontline regulator — mirroring the existing securities-business supervisory split, a nuance a bank's compliance function must not conflate with direct SFC licensing.

This consultation is issued the SAME DAY (27 June 2025) as a separate, related consultation on VA custodian services (referenced in footnote 21) — the two regimes are interdependent and should be read together, not in isolation.

obligations: Under this plan, a bank offering VA dealing services would register with the SFC, with the HKMA consulted (para 1.10)
Registered VA dealing firms would fall under AML/CFT duties in Schedule 2 of the AMLO plus other regulatory requirements (para 1.10)
counterparty_due_diligence: Stablecoin issuers already licensed by the HKMA are proposed to be exempt from this new licensing regime when they issue or redeem their own coins, since the HKMA already supervises them (para 1.10)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Tell the board that under this proposal the HKMA would stay the bank's day-to-day supervisor for VA dealing, matching the securities-business model, and that this is still only a proposal -- comments were due 29 August 2025.

title: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Custodian Services
summary: This paper proposes a new SFC licensing regime for virtual-asset custodian services. It defines custody as safekeeping virtual assets, or the private keys that control them, on a client's behalf. Banks, stored value facilities and subsidiaries of locally incorporated banks providing such services must register with the SFC, with the HKMA supervising banks and SVFs. It proposes incidental exemptions for entities whose safekeeping is merely part of another licensed activity, and a full exemption for a stablecoin issuer custodying only the stablecoins it issues. Financial-resource floors, external-assessment requirements, and sanctions mirroring the VATP regime are also proposed. Licensed or registered entities, including fund managers, would be required to use only SFC-licensed or SFC-registered custodians in Hong Kong to safekeep client assets.

key_points.point: Providing virtual-asset custodian services as a business - safekeeping VAs, or instruments such as private keys enabling their transfer - requires an SFC licence or registration.
SFC is proposed as licensing authority and standard-setter for VA custodians; HKMA would oversee banks and SVFs directly as day-to-day supervisor of their custodian business.

Regulated entities holding client VAs only incidentally to another licensed activity, and not safekeeping private keys, would be exempt. A stablecoin issuer custodying only its own issued stablecoins is fully exempt, even if it holds the private keys.
Licensed or registered entities, including fund managers, would be required to use only SFC-licensed or -registered VA custodians in Hong Kong to safekeep client assets.
Proposed minimum financial resources: HK$10 million paid-up share capital and up to HK$3 million liquid capital, benchmarked against the SFO Type 13 depositary-licence requirements.
Custodians safekeeping private keys must engage an external assessor, with the SFC as a party to that engagement, before being licensed - mirroring the swift VATP licensing process.
No deeming/grace arrangement is proposed; the regime becomes fully effective from the commencement date of the statutory provisions.
Unlicensed provision or active marketing of custodian services carries a fine of HK$5 million and up to seven years' imprisonment on indictment.

numbers_and_dates.item: Minimum paid-up share capital for a VA custodian
Application fee for Type 3 SFO activity used as fee benchmark

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the core reference for its own future custody obligations, if it safekeeps client digital assets or private keys. It also sets the standard the bank must use to vet any external custodian it relies on, since regulated entities will be required to use only SFC-licensed or -registered custodians.

quote.text: same activity, same risks, same regulation

reading_guide: Read Chapter 2 (pages 6-26) in full, especially the definition, exemptions and 'other regulatory requirements' sections. Chapter 1 background can be skimmed.
flags: Custody definition explicitly captures group-entity personnel who help safeguard shared private keys - the paper asks whether each group entity would need its own licence, an open question with real implications for a banking group's shared operations model

obligations: Register with the SFC (via HKMA consultation) before providing digital-asset custody, including safekeeping private keys, once the regime commences (para 2.13, p.10)
Use only SFC-licensed or -registered VA custodians in Hong Kong to safekeep client digital assets, whether acting as custodian or relying on one (para 2.20, p.12)
Engage an SFC-party external assessor of systems and controls before being licensed if the bank will safekeep private keys directly (para 2.42, p.22)
controls_and_monitoring: Implement private-key management, cybersecurity and business-continuity controls consistent with the VATP custody standard once finalised (para 2.38, p.19)
notifications_reporting: Submit and keep current information on wallet addresses and scope of custodian business provided to the SFC/HKMA (para 2.39(f), p.20)
counterparty_due_diligence: Verify any third-party or group-entity custodian's licensing status and its use of key-sharding/MPC arrangements before delegating custody to it (para 2.15, p.10)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told the group's internal operating model for shared key-management across entities may itself require multiple licences under the proposed regime, an unresolved question worth a formal consultation response.

title: FSTB and SFC launch consultation on legislative proposals for regulating digital asset dealing and custodian services
supersedes_or_amends: Public consultation on legislative proposal for regulating VA over-the-counter trading services (February-April 2024)
summary: FSTB and SFC opened a two-month joint public consultation, to 29 August 2025, on revised plans for two new licensing regimes: digital-asset dealing services and digital-asset custodian services. Both would require a licence or registration with the SFC as standard-setter, with the HKMA supervising banks and stored-value-facility (SVF) licensees offering the services. Dealing covers both simple conversions and complex activities like brokerage and block trading. Custody covers safekeeping of assets, or of private keys that enable their transfer. No deeming (automatic grace-licence) arrangement is proposed, meaning the regimes take full effect from their commencement date. Full detail is in the two attached consultation papers.

key_points.point: Consultation on the two licensing regimes runs from June 27 to August 29, 2025.
For both regimes, the SFC will set standards and licence/register providers, while banks and stored-value-facility registrants would be supervised day-to-day by the HKMA.
Dealing licensing would cover both simple conversions and complex activities such as brokerage, block trading, and advisory or asset-management activity.
Custody is proposed to be defined as safekeeping digital assets, or instruments (including private keys) that enable their transfer, on behalf of clients.
Both regimes are proposed to take full effect on commencement, with no deeming/grace arrangement for existing providers.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the direct forerunner to its own future licensing obligations for any dealing or custody activity in digital assets. It also shapes due-diligence expectations for VATP and custodian counterparties. The full substance is in the two linked consultation papers.
reading_guide: Read this press release for the summary, then the two consultation papers (f673ef6dcb63 dealing, 30b60438f017 custody) for the detail.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should note that a live consultation on the bank's own future dealing/custody licensing obligations closes August 29, 2025, and that compliance should consider a formal submission.

title: FSTB and SFC consult on proposed regimes to regulate virtual asset dealers and custodians
summary: This SFC press release announces that the FSTB and SFC jointly launched a public consultation. It introduces licensing regimes for virtual asset (VA) dealing and VA custodian service providers, one day after the Government's Policy Statement 2.0 on Digital Asset Development. It frames the proposals as advancing the 'Access' pillar of the SFC's ASPIRe roadmap, and the 'same business, same risks, same rules' principle. It quotes SFC CEO Julia Leung and FSTB Secretary Christopher Hui, and sets a comment deadline of 29 August 2025.

key_points.point: FSTB and SFC jointly launched a public consultation on licensing regimes for VA dealing and VA custodian service providers.
The consultation was launched the day after the Government released Policy Statement 2.0 on the Development of Digital Assets in Hong Kong (issued 26 June 2025).
The two proposed regimes are positioned as advancing 'Access', one of the five pillars of the SFC's ASPIRe roadmap issued 19 February 2025.
Comments on the consultation are invited by 29 August 2025.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is a consultation announcement, not yet a rule. It signals that VA dealer and custodian licensing regimes are coming, worth tracking for future direct impact on the bank's own VA dealing and custody arrangements. It creates no obligation yet.

quote.text: same business, same risks, same rules

reading_guide: Read this short press release in full, 2-3 minutes, as context for the companion consultation paper (25CP7). Skip nothing.
flags: This is a companion announcement, not the substantive consultation paper itself (ddc173e5aaa2) or the parallel VA dealing consultation, which are the primary sources for requirements.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Flag to the board that new licensing regimes for VA dealing and VA custody are being consulted on (comment deadline 29 August 2025, para 5, p.1) and will likely shape future bank VA-dealing and custody arrangements once finalised.

title: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Custodian Services
summary: This joint FSTB/SFC consultation paper proposes a new licensing or registration regime for providers of virtual asset (VA) custodian services in Hong Kong. It extends the 'same activity, same risks, same regulation' principle already applied to VA trading platforms (VATPs). It defines VA custodian service as safekeeping VAs, or instruments enabling their transfer such as private keys, on behalf of clients, as a business. It proposes the SFC as licensing authority, with the HKMA as frontline regulator for banks and SVFs. It sets eligibility, fit-and-proper, financial resources (HK$10 million paid-up capital), individual licensing, and prohibition and sanctions provisions modelled on the VATP regime. It seeks views via 17 questions, with comments due by 29 August 2025.

key_points.point: VA custodian service is defined as, by way of business, safekeeping VAs or instruments enabling transfer of VAs (including private keys) on behalf of clients; self-custody by the client is excluded.

SFC will be the licensing and registration authority and standard-setter for VA custodians. HKMA is the frontline regulator for banks and SVFs providing VA custody, and VA custodians that are subsidiaries of locally incorporated banks are regulated by the SFC.

Associated entities of SFC-licensed VATPs currently providing custody by safekeeping private keys will need to obtain a separate VA custodian service licence under the new regime if they wish to continue.

A licence or registration will also be needed by banks, by subsidiaries of a locally incorporated bank, and by SVFs. This applies wherever they themselves hold the private keys, or similar instruments, that let client VAs be moved. It applies even where that happens as part of VA dealing, or acting as depositary for a fund.

A stablecoin issuer licensed by the HKMA that only custodies the stablecoins it issues is proposed to be exempted from the VA custodian licensing regime. This holds even though it safekeeps private keys, because it is already subject to HKMA supervision.

An incidental exemption is proposed for SFC/HKMA regulated entities, where safekeeping of client VAs is wholly incidental to their principal licensed or registered business. This applies provided they do not safekeep the private keys themselves.

Except for banks and SVFs, an applicant must either be locally incorporated and physically based in Hong Kong, or be a company formed elsewhere but registered here under the Companies Ordinance. It must also name at least two responsible officers (for the SFC) or executive officers (for the HKMA).

Non-bank licensees would need baseline financial resources. These are proposed at a minimum of HK$10 million in paid-up share capital. They also need minimum liquid capital of up to HK$3 million, depending on the business model, modelled on the existing Type 13 (depositary) requirements.

No grandfathering is planned for firms already providing VA custodian services. The licensing regime is meant to apply in full from the day the relevant statutory provisions commence. So firms are encouraged to approach the SFC or HKMA early, for example before applying, to avoid having to halt their business.

VA custodians safekeeping private keys will be required to engage an external assessor for an assessment of systems and controls before licensing or registration. This mirrors the VATP process, with the SFC party to the engagement.

Unlicensed provision, holding out, or active marketing of VA custodian services is proposed to be a criminal offence. On conviction on indictment, this means a fine of $5 million and imprisonment for 7 years. Knowingly advertising an unlicensed provider's services carries a level 5 fine ($50,000) and 6 months' imprisonment.

Custody technology and security requirements -- private key management, cybersecurity, business continuity, storage ratios -- will be aligned with existing VATP custody requirements. They will be made subject to a further, separate public consultation, alongside SFC exploration of a 'dynamic approach' to custody technologies and storage ratios under the ASPIRe roadmap.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this directly affects its operating model. Any group entity -- the bank itself, a locally incorporated subsidiary, or an associated entity -- that safekeeps client private keys will need a new SFC/HKMA licence, with no automatic transitional relief. This calls for an entity-mapping exercise now.

quote.text: same activity, same risks, same regulation

reading_guide: Read Chapter 1 (background, paras 1.1-1.10), then Chapter 2's Scope of Regulation, Definition and Coverage, Eligibility, and Other Regulatory Requirements sections (paras 2.12-2.44). The 17 consultation questions and footnote cross-references can be skimmed after the matching paragraph.
flags: As of this batch's fetch date (2026-09-25), the meta record for this document notes Consultation Conclusions (ref 25CC6) were already issued on 2025-12-24 — this consultation paper's proposals should be read as provisional/superseded pending review of those conclusions, not as final rules.

No grandfathering/deeming arrangement is proposed for existing VA custodian providers, contrary to a common assumption that incumbents get automatic transitional relief; firms must proactively engage the SFC/HKMA pre-application.

Stablecoin issuers get a narrower custody exemption than other regulated entities: they are exempted even though they safekeep private keys (unlike the general incidental exemption, which requires NOT safekeeping private keys).

The custody technology/security requirements (private key management, storage ratios) are explicitly deferred to a SEPARATE future consultation, so this paper does not itself set technical custody standards — a common misreading risk.

obligations: If the bank or a subsidiary safekeeps private keys for client VAs (including as part of VA dealing or fund depositary work), plan to obtain a VA custodian service licence/registration once enacted, with SFC as licensing authority and HKMA as frontline regulator for banks/SVFs (paras 2.12(a), 2.21(b))
Begin pre-application engagement with the SFC/HKMA early, since no grandfathering/deeming arrangement is proposed for existing custodians (para 2.41)
counterparty_due_diligence: Check whether an associated entity of an SFC-licensed VATP the bank uses for custody will itself need a separate VA custodian licence (para 2.21(a))
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board must be told there is NO grandfathering proposed for existing VA custody arrangements, so any group entity that safekeeps private keys needs an early gap-assessment and pre-application plan before commencement (para 2.41).

title: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Dealing in Virtual Assets
supersedes_or_amends: Public consultation on legislative proposal for regulating VA OTC trading services (Feb-Apr 2024)
summary: This is the full consultation paper on a proposed SFC licensing regime for virtual-asset dealing services. It replaces the narrower 2024 over-the-counter (OTC) shop proposal, after feedback showed dealing activity is far more varied. Banks and stored-value-facility (SVF) licensees must register with the SFC, in consultation with the HKMA, which remains their frontline supervisor. Licensees must hold client virtual assets with a licensed custodian, and meet financial-resource, AML/CFT, risk-management, conduct and record-keeping requirements. Stablecoins from HKMA-licensed issuers are expected to be an eligible traded asset for retail clients. The paper proposes no deeming arrangement, and heavy sanctions, including fines up to HK$10 million and imprisonment up to ten years for fraud-related offences.

key_points.point: Any person carrying on a business of dealing in virtual assets in Hong Kong, including simple conversions and complex brokerage/block-trading/advisory/asset-management activity, needs an SFC licence or registration.
Banks and stored value facilities must register with the SFC for virtual-asset dealing activity, with the HKMA as frontline regulator, similar to the existing model for banks' securities business.

A licensed stablecoin issuer conducting only primary-market offering or redemption of the stablecoins it issues is proposed to be exempt from the dealing licence. This is because it is already supervised by the HKMA.
Licensees or registrants must hold client virtual assets with a licensed or registered virtual-asset custodian in Hong Kong.
For retail clients, tradable virtual assets are expected to broadly follow VATP practice, including large-cap tokens meeting index criteria and stablecoins from HKMA-licensed issuers.
Minimum financial resource requirements proposed: HK$5 million paid-up share capital, up to HK$3 million liquid capital, plus 12 months' operating expenses in excess liquid capital.
No deeming/grace licence is proposed - the regime takes full effect on the commencement date of the statutory provisions.
Operating without a licence while dealing or actively marketing dealing services carries a fine of HK$5 million and up to seven years' imprisonment on indictment.
Fraudulent or deceptive behaviour in virtual-asset transactions carries a fine of HK$10 million and up to ten years' imprisonment on indictment.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this paper sets out in detail how it would become a registered digital-asset dealer under HKMA frontline supervision, including the mandatory-custodian rule and proposed financial-resource floors. It also gives compliance the specific consultation questions worth a formal bank response.

quote.text: same activity, same risks, same regulation

reading_guide: Read Chapter 2 (pages 10-25) in full for the substantive regime. Chapter 1 background (pages 2-9) can be skimmed for context on the prior 2024 consultation.
flags: The regime proposes no deeming arrangement, meaning existing unlicensed VA dealers must cease operating on commencement day unless already licensed

obligations: Register with the SFC (in consultation with the HKMA) before conducting any virtual-asset dealing service, once the regime commences (para 1.10, p.8)
Hold client virtual assets only with an SFC-licensed or -registered custodian in Hong Kong (para 2.13/2.23, p.13/17)

Meet fit-and-proper, financial-resource, AML/CFT and conduct requirements applicable to registrants, and appoint at least two SFC/HKMA-approved responsible/executive officers (para 2.14-2.16, 2.24-2.25, p.14-19)
controls_and_monitoring: Implement risk-based transaction monitoring, including blockchain analytic tools, to trace the origin and destination of client VA transfers (para 2.23, p.17)
For retail clients, restrict tradable tokens to eligible large-cap virtual assets and HKMA-licensed stablecoins per VATP-aligned criteria (para 2.19, p.15-16)
notifications_reporting: Submit and keep current a wide range of information to the SFC/HKMA, including wallet addresses used and the scope of services provided (para 2.25(f), p.19)
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm any VA custodian used to hold client assets is licensed or registered with the SFC in Hong Kong before relying on it (para 2.13, p.13)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told the bank's own future virtual-asset dealing activity will require SFC registration with HKMA as frontline supervisor, mandatory use of a licensed local custodian, and exposes the bank to criminal sanctions (up to 10 years' imprisonment) for fraud-related non-compliance.

title: Appointments to Task Force on Promoting Web3 Development
summary: The government named 20 people, new and returning non-official members, to the Task Force on Promoting Web3 Development. This takes effect 1 July 2025, for a two-year term. The Financial Secretary has chaired the Task Force since it was set up in 2023, and it gives advice on Web3 development. It includes non-official industry members plus regulator and government officials. The notice lists everyone currently on it.

key_points.point: The government named 20 people, as new and returning non-official members, to the Task Force on Promoting Web3 Development, effective 1 July 2025, for a two-year term.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is only a personnel-appointments notice, with no regulatory content. It is useful just to know who currently advises the government on Web3 policy.
reading_guide: Skim the membership list only if tracking who advises the government. There is no substantive content otherwise.

title: Fintech Adoption: Progress and Future Directions
summary: This HKMA report presents the results of a January 2025 Tech Maturity Stock-take, covering 56 submissions from 58 authorized institutions, benchmarked against a 2022 baseline. It measures adoption of Regtech, Wealthtech, Greentech, Insurtech, artificial intelligence and distributed ledger technology (DLT). It finds implementation cost, novel-technology risk and integration are the top adoption challenges. It sets out the HKMA's next-phase promotion plan, built around AI, DLT and high-performance computing, underpinned by data excellence and cyber resilience. DLT-specific detail is limited to adoption statistics and general commentary; this is not a rulebook.

key_points.point: DLT adoption among surveyed authorized institutions rose from 30% in 2022 to 45% in 2025, with many institutions moving from exploratory pilots to operational use.
One financial institution highlighted in the report uses DLT to provide tokenisation, issuance, distribution and custody services across the digital asset lifecycle.

HKMA's next-phase Fintech promotion names DLT as one of three priority technology enablers, along with AI and high-performance computing. It focuses on risk management, resilient operations and systems integration, as tokenisation initiatives are explored.
Top adoption challenges cited by authorized institutions include implementation cost (75%), risk of novel technology (73%) and integration with existing systems (71%).

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this gives sector-wide DLT adoption benchmarks and the HKMA's stated forward priorities -- risk management and systems integration for tokenisation. It is useful for internal business cases, but is not itself a source of obligations.
reading_guide: Skim Key Observations 1-2 (pp.10-14) for DLT/AI adoption figures, and the Way Forward section (pp.19-22) for the HKMA's stated priorities. Detailed Regtech/Wealthtech figures are not digital-asset relevant.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Useful benchmarking data only; no escalation required.

title: Explanatory Note on Licensing of Stablecoin Issuers
summary: This note explains how the HKMA will license stablecoin issuers under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656). It defines a 'stablecoin', a 'specified stablecoin' (currently only fiat-referenced coins), and when issuing or offering one counts as a regulated activity needing a licence. It walks through the minimum licensing criteria in Schedule 2. These cover corporate status, capital, reserve-asset segregation and backing, and redemption rights. They also cover fitness of directors and managers, risk management, AML/CFT, disclosure via a white paper, complaint handling, a ban on paying interest, and recovery or wind-down planning. It also sets out the application process, the HKMA's supervisory powers over a troubled licensee, and the grounds and process for licence revocation or suspension.

key_points.point: A stablecoin is a cryptographically secured digital value token. It acts as a medium of exchange or store of value, is transferable electronically, runs on a distributed ledger, and claims to hold a stable value against one or more assets. Central bank money, securities, SVF float and bank deposits are carved out.
Only 'specified stablecoins' - currently those referencing one or more official currencies (fiat-referenced stablecoins) - fall inside the licensing perimeter for now.

Issuing a specified stablecoin in Hong Kong, or issuing one anywhere that is pegged even partly to the Hong Kong dollar, is a regulated activity requiring a licence. Doing so without one, or holding oneself out as doing so, is an offence.

A licensee may only let a defined list of 'permitted offerors' distribute its coins. These are itself, an authorized institution, an SVF licensee, an SFC-licensed VA trading platform, or an SFC Type 1 licensed corporation.
An applicant must be either a Hong Kong-incorporated company or an authorized institution; other foreign entities must set up a local subsidiary to apply.
Non-bank applicants need at least HKD25 million in paid-up capital or MA-approved equivalent financial resources, which cannot be used for dealings with related parties.

Reserve assets backing each type of coin must be segregated, and held under a trust arrangement backed by independent legal opinion. Their value must never fall below the circulating coins' par value, with a buffer for risk. They must be audited regularly by an independent auditor, and disclosed to the public.
Holders have a right to redeem at par, normally processed within one business day, and licensees must publicly disclose fees, conditions, mechanics and timing of redemption.

Chief executives, directors, the stablecoin manager and controllers must be fit and proper, with relevant knowledge and experience. The HKMA looks for at least a third of the Board to be independent non-executive directors. It generally wants to give consent before they take up post. This is not required for an authorized institution's own appointees.

Licensees must run a full risk management programme covering governance, credit/liquidity/market risk, technology risk, operational risk, reputation risk, and incident/business continuity/exit planning.
Licensees must publish a white paper covering the issuer, the coin, reserve management, issuance/redemption mechanics, technology and risks, before offering coins to the public.
Stablecoins must not carry any interest, return or yield tied to holding period, par value or market value.
A change of registered address must be reported within 7 days, and material changes in circumstances relevant to the minimum criteria must be reported as soon as practicable.

If a licensee becomes, or is likely to become, unable to meet its obligations, the HKMA can act. After consulting the Financial Secretary, it can order immediate action, appoint an advisor, or appoint a statutory manager to take over the licensee's affairs.

HKMA can revoke a licence on 16 listed grounds. These include failing the minimum criteria, insolvency, providing false information, breaching a licence condition, ceasing business, or non-payment of fees. They also include conduct that threatens Hong Kong's standing as an international financial centre, for example involvement in money laundering.

Before revoking, the HKMA must give written notice of intent and grounds. It must allow the licensee to make representations. A licensee can refer a revocation or suspension decision to the Stablecoin Review Tribunal, though referral does not automatically pause the decision.
HKMA can suspend a licence for up to 6 months (renewable) after a revocation ground arises, or use a fast 14-day temporary suspension in urgent cases.

numbers_and_dates.value: within 1 business day of a valid request, unless otherwise approved
within 14 days after licence takes effect, then annually
6 months, extendable by a further 6 months
at least one-third independent non-executive directors

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the master rulebook for anyone it might deal with as a stablecoin issuer. This also applies to the bank itself, if it or an affiliate ever considers issuing a fiat-referenced stablecoin under its own authorized-institution (AI) status. It sets the baseline the bank's due diligence on any stablecoin counterparty should be checked against, especially reserve segregation, redemption rights, and permitted-offeror status.
reading_guide: Read Chapter 2 (definitions and scope) and Chapter 3 (minimum criteria, especially reserve assets 3.4 and redemption 3.5) closely. Chapters 4-7 (process, powers, revocation) can be skimmed except section headings. Annex B's document checklist only matters if the bank itself applies.
flags: Only fiat-referenced stablecoins are currently 'specified stablecoins'; algorithmic or crypto-asset-referenced coins are outside the licensing perimeter for now, which is a narrower scope than the term 'stablecoin' might suggest.

An authorized institution applicant is exempt from several minimum criteria that apply to non-bank applicants (local incorporation, financial resources requirement, HKMA consent for controllers/chief executive/directors, business activities restriction) because it is already prudentially supervised.

obligations: If the bank itself becomes a licensee (as an AI), it must maintain segregated, trust-protected reserve assets at least equal to par value, with independent audit and public disclosure (para 3.4.1-3.4.6, p.11-13).
If licensed, the bank must honour valid redemption requests within 1 business day absent HKMA approval otherwise, and disclose redemption terms publicly (para 3.5.2-3.5.4, p.13-14).
If licensed, the bank must not pay any interest or return on the stablecoin (para 3.13.1, p.19-20).
If distributing another issuer's coin, the bank must itself qualify as a 'permitted offeror' under section 9(5) of the SO (para 2.10.1, p.9-10).
controls_and_monitoring: Full risk management framework covering credit/liquidity/market, technology, operational, reputation, and incident/continuity/exit risk if the bank is a licensee (para 3.7.1, p.15-16).
Fit-and-proper vetting and MA-consent tracking for chief executive, directors, stablecoin manager and controllers (para 3.6.1-3.6.4, p.14-15).
notifications_reporting: Report likely inability to meet obligations, insolvency or suspension of payment to HKMA immediately (para 5.4.1, p.26).
Report change of address within 7 days (para 5.5.2, p.26).
Report material change in circumstances affecting the minimum criteria as soon as practicable (para 5.6.2-5.6.3, p.27).
counterparty_due_diligence: Check that a stablecoin counterparty is a licensed issuer and that whoever distributes its coins to the bank's customers is a permitted offeror under section 9(5) of the SO (para 2.10.1, p.9-10).
Check the counterparty issuer's reserve segregation, trust arrangement and redemption terms are consistent with para 3.4-3.5 before relying on par-value redeemability.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told if the bank contemplates applying for a stablecoin issuer licence, given the capital, reserve-segregation and revocation/suspension powers HKMA would then hold over the business.

title: LCQ5: Promoting development of stablecoins
summary: In a written Legislative Council reply, the Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury describes government plans to grow stablecoin use cases, attract global issuers, and consider offshore renminbi stablecoins. It confirms the HKMA's stablecoin issuer sandbox, opened early 2024, is not a prerequisite for licensing. Applicants with cross-border use cases must show a comprehensive compliance plan and confirm their business partners hold necessary regulatory approvals in relevant jurisdictions. It also notes the licensing regime allows pegs to different fiat currencies, not only the Hong Kong dollar.

key_points.point: Participation in the HKMA's stablecoin issuer sandbox is not a prerequisite for a future licence application.
key_points.locator: reply to Q1, para on sandbox

key_points.point: Stablecoin issuer applicants must show adequate setup across reserve-asset management, price-stabilisation, redemption policy, technology security, risk management and AML capability.

For cross-border use cases, applicants must also show a compliance plan and demonstrate financial strength. They must also confirm their business partners hold necessary approvals and will comply with regulations in Hong Kong and other relevant jurisdictions.
The licensing regime allows an issuer to peg its stablecoin to different fiat currencies, not just the Hong Kong dollar.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this confirms it must expect stablecoin-issuer counterparties, and their partners, to demonstrate cross-border regulatory compliance as part of licensing. This is a useful due-diligence benchmark when the bank assesses potential stablecoin partners.
reading_guide: Read the reply to question 1 in full for licensing expectations. Question 3, on offshore RMB stablecoins, is exploratory and can be skimmed.

counterparty_due_diligence: When assessing a stablecoin issuer or its business partners, confirm they hold necessary regulatory approvals and will comply with applicable rules in Hong Kong and other relevant jurisdictions for cross-border use cases (reply to Q1)

title: Invest Hong Kong strengthens Web3 and fintech ties between Hong Kong and Japan (with photos)
summary: InvestHK describes an outbound delegation of 16 Hong Kong organisations to Japan, to build Web3 and fintech business ties. It references the recently issued Policy Statement 2.0 and its LEAP framework as context. It also highlights a few company case studies, including a family office launching a real-estate tokenisation project in Japan. It contains no new regulatory content.

key_points.point: An InvestHK-led delegation of 16 Hong Kong organisations visited Japan to build Web3 and fintech business ties, with one participating family office launching a real-estate tokenisation initiative there.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is promotional trade-mission news with no regulatory bearing. It is background only.
reading_guide: Skim only. There is no substantive regulatory content.

title: SFC convenes second Digital Asset Consultative Panel meeting
summary: This SFC press release reports on the SFC's second consultative-panel meeting with SFC-licensed VA trading platforms. It covers market and regulatory developments under the ASPIRe roadmap's Access and Products pillars, including the VA dealing and custodian licensing proposals and market accessibility and product offerings. It also notes the forum was renamed from 'Virtual Asset Consultative Panel' to 'Digital Asset Consultative Panel', to align with the terminology of Policy Statement 2.0.

key_points.point: The SFC held its second engagement session with the Digital Asset Consultative Panel (DACP), made up of SFC-licensed VA trading platforms.
The panel was renamed from 'Virtual Asset Consultative Panel' to 'Digital Asset Consultative Panel' to align with terminology used in the Government's Policy Statement 2.0 (issued 26 June 2025).
Topics covered included ASPIRe roadmap Pillars A (Access) and P (Products), including the VA dealing and custodian licensing proposals and market accessibility/product offerings.
The DACP is described as part of the initiative under Pillar Re (Relationships) of the ASPIRe roadmap.

numbers_and_dates.value: reported in SFC press release of 14 February 2025

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is a minor engagement-channel update. It is useful mainly to know the Digital Asset Consultative Panel (DACP), a renamed body, exists as an SFC-VATP forum, and that it discussed the dealer/custodian licensing proposals. It contains no new substantive requirements.

quote.text: constructive and insightful

reading_guide: This is very short; read it in full (1-2 minutes). It is chiefly useful for the naming-history flag: VACP became DACP.
flags: Naming correction: the 'Virtual Asset Consultative Panel' was renamed 'Digital Asset Consultative Panel' (DACP) in mid-2025 to match Policy Statement 2.0 terminology — sources referring to 'VACP' after June 2025 refer to the same body.

title: Opening remarks by Permanent Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury (Financial Services) at Deloitte's Digital Asset Forum (English only) (with photos)
summary: A senior FSTB official's remarks recap the digital-asset policy timeline. This covers the 2022 first policy statement, the June 2023 VATP regime, the Stablecoins Ordinance (effective 1 August 2025), and the LEAP framework from Policy Statement 2.0. They preview details on tokenised bonds and the dealing/custodian consultation. The speech restates already-known facts and figures, with no new binding content.

key_points.point: The second batch of tokenised government green bonds was issued in 2024 across four currencies, worth close to HK$6 billion in total. The government describes it as the first-ever green bond issued natively in digital form across more than one currency.
The SFC has established a consultative panel on market and regulatory issues, which had held its second meeting the day before this speech.

numbers_and_dates.item: Second tranche of tokenised green bonds (2024)
numbers_and_dates.value: about HK$6 billion equivalent, four currencies

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is largely a recap speech. The only new detail is confirmation the SFC has stood up an industry consultative panel on digital-asset regulatory issues, which compliance could seek to engage with.
reading_guide: Skim this. Most content restates facts already in Policy Statement 2.0 and the Budget speech.

title: Gazettal of banking amendment rules to implement Basel cryptoassets standard
supersedes_or_amends: Banking (Capital) Rules (Cap. 155L)
Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules (Cap. 155S)
summary: The government gazetted three sets of amendment rules -- to the Banking (Capital) Rules, Banking (Disclosure) Rules, and Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules -- implementing the Basel Committee's prudential standard on banks' cryptoasset exposures. The rules take effect 1 January 2026, in line with the Basel Committee's global timetable, and also make other alignment amendments informed by industry feedback. They were tabled at the Legislative Council (LegCo) on 16 July 2025.

key_points.point: Three amendment rules sets implement Basel Committee capital, disclosure and exposure-limit standards for banks' cryptoasset exposures.
The amendment rules take effect on January 1, 2026, matching the Basel Committee's implementation timeline.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is a direct, binding prudential obligation as an authorised institution. Capital, disclosure and exposure-limit rules for cryptoasset exposures took effect 1 January 2026 and have applied since then. Risk and finance teams should confirm their calculations and disclosures are already compliant.
reading_guide: Read this in full; it is a short notice, but confirms a hard compliance deadline for the bank's prudential treatment of cryptoasset exposures.

obligations: Apply the new Banking (Capital), (Disclosure) and (Exposure Limits) Amendment Rules 2025 to any cryptoasset exposure from January 1, 2026 (closing para, p.1)
controls_and_monitoring: Risk and finance functions should build capital, exposure-limit and disclosure calculations for cryptoasset exposures ahead of the January 1, 2026 effective date
notifications_reporting: Prepare disclosure reporting on cryptoasset exposures consistent with the amended Banking (Disclosure) Rules from the effective date
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told of the hard January 1, 2026 deadline for new capital, exposure-limit and disclosure requirements on any bank cryptoasset exposure, and asked to confirm readiness.

title: Gazettal of rules: cryptoassets standard and other updates
summary: This HKMA circular tells all authorized institutions that three rules were gazetted on 11 July 2025. These are the Banking (Capital) (Amendment) Rules 2025, the Banking (Disclosure) (Amendment) Rules 2025, and the Banking (Exposure Limits) (Amendment) Rules 2025. These rules put in place the Basel Committee's prudential standard for cryptoasset exposures, plus related changes to disclosure and exposure limits, along with some other minor alignment changes. The Legislative Council (LegCo) was due to receive these rules on 16 July 2025 for negative vetting. Assuming that stage cleared, the rules were expected to start applying on 1 January 2026, in step with the Basel Committee's timeline.

key_points.point: Three amendment rules were gazetted on 11 July 2025: the Banking (Capital) (Amendment) Rules 2025, the Banking (Disclosure) (Amendment) Rules 2025, and the Banking (Exposure Limits) (Amendment) Rules 2025.
The amendments mainly bring in the Basel Committee's capital standard for cryptoasset exposures, along with its related disclosure and exposure-limit requirements.
The rules were scheduled for tabling before LegCo on 16 July 2025, to start the negative-vetting process.
If that vetting process went through, the rules were expected to take effect on 1 January 2026, matching the Basel Committee's timeline.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this marked the formal legal milestone when the crypto capital, disclosure, and exposure-limit rules moved from consultation to gazetted subsidiary legislation. This had a 1 January 2026 start date that has since arrived and passed. The rules are now in force, and banks should already be running the associated reporting and disclosure processes.

quote.text: the prudential treatment of cryptoasset

reading_guide: This is a short, one-page letter; read it in full.

obligations: Track the outcome of negative vetting and get ready for the three amendment rules to take effect.
notifications_reporting: No return needs to be filed for this notice itself; it sets the legal start date for all the crypto reporting changes in the rest of the package.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Tell the board the crypto capital, disclosure, and exposure-limit rules have now been formally gazetted, targeting a 1 January 2026 start date.

title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Eddie Yue on The Steadfast and Sustainable Development of Stablecoins
summary: HKMA's Chief Executive pushes back on what he calls overhyped and speculative market enthusiasm for stablecoins. He notes many prospective applicants he has met lack concrete use cases or technical capability, and reiterates that only a handful of licences will be issued. He confirms the HKMA consulted the market on both the supervision and AML/CFT implementation guidelines. It was refining them for publication by end of July 2025, expecting the final rules to include tighter AML requirements than the consultation drafts. He also announces that an Explanatory Note on the licence application process would follow the next week.

key_points.point: Many of the dozens of institutions that approached HKMA about stablecoin issuance had only conceptual proposals lacking concrete use cases, implementation plans or risk-management competence.
HKMA reiterates that only a handful of stablecoin issuer licences would be granted, meaning most applicants will be disappointed.

The Stablecoins Ordinance commencement on 1 August 2025 would make it illegal to offer any unlicensed fiat-referenced stablecoin to Hong Kong retail investors. It would also be illegal to actively market such an unlicensed coin to the Hong Kong public.

HKMA had consulted the market on both the supervision guideline and the AML/CFT guideline, following passage of the Stablecoins Bill. It was refining them for publication by end of July 2025, expecting the AML requirements in the final version to be stricter than in the consultation draft.
An Explanatory Note on Licensing of Stablecoin Issuers, covering how HKMA would accept and process applications, was announced for release the following week.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this signals that the final AML/CFT and supervision guidelines would be stricter on AML than the May 2025 consultation drafts. It also confirms the exact date from which offering an unlicensed stablecoin to Hong Kong retail investors becomes illegal -- both directly relevant to any group entity distributing or dealing in stablecoins.

quote.text: it is better for regulated stablecoin business

reading_guide: Read this in full; it is a short commentary piece.

obligations: From 1 August 2025, do not offer or actively market any unlicensed fiat-referenced stablecoin to Hong Kong retail investors.
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm any stablecoin a distribution partner offers to Hong Kong retail customers is HKMA-licensed once the Ordinance commences.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/compliance should confirm no marketing or distribution of unlicensed stablecoins to Hong Kong retail clients occurs on or after 1 August 2025.

title: Implementation of regulatory regime for stablecoin issuers
supersedes_or_amends: Draft Guideline on Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers (26 May 2025 consultation draft)
Draft Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Licensed Stablecoin Issuers) (26 May 2025 consultation draft)
summary: The Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) regulatory regime for stablecoin issuers took effect on 1 August 2025. Alongside it, this HKMA press release announces, HKMA published four documents. These are the finalised Guideline on Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers and its consultation conclusions, the finalised AML/CFT Guideline for Licensed Stablecoin Issuers and its consultation conclusions, plus two Explanatory Notes. These notes cover licensing and application procedures, and transitional arrangements for pre-existing issuers. The attached Supervisory Guideline sets detailed ongoing requirements on reserve assets, issuance, redemption and distribution, financial resources, risk management -- including extensive technology and private-key controls -- corporate governance and business conduct. The AML/CFT Guideline sets customer due diligence, wallet risk management, the HK$8,000 Travel Rule threshold, sanctions screening, suspicious transaction reporting (STR) and five-year record-keeping requirements. The Explanatory Notes define scope terms: stablecoin, regulated stablecoin activity, and permitted offeror. They also cover the application process and minimum criteria. They set the three-month, six-month and closing-down transitional timeline for issuers operating before 1 August 2025. As of the press release date, no licence had yet been issued.

key_points.point: The regulatory regime under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) took effect on 1 August 2025. The finalised Guideline on Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers and the AML/CFT Guideline were both gazetted the same day.
Parties interested in applying for a licence were encouraged to contact HKMA by 31 August 2025. Those wanting to be considered early were asked to submit applications by 30 September 2025.
It is an offence under the SO to falsely claim to be a licensee or an applicant. As of the press release date, no licence had been issued.

A licensee must keep the reserve assets' market value at or above the par value of all outstanding specified stablecoins in circulation, at every point in time. This includes any coins that are frozen or blacklisted. Holding some excess collateral as a cushion is expected.

Reserve assets are restricted to a defined 'eligible assets' list: cash, short-term bank deposits, qualifying marketable debt securities, overnight reverse repos, dedicated investment funds, or HKMA-acceptable equivalents. Tokenised representations of eligible assets can qualify, if the licensee demonstrates no added technology or operational risk.

Reserve assets must be held via effective trust arrangements, either an independent trustee or a declaration of trust. They must be segregated from the licensee's own assets, and protected from other creditors, with an independent legal opinion on effectiveness submitted to HKMA.

Valid redemption requests must be honoured, generally within one business day, without unreasonable fees or unduly burdensome conditions. Any delay beyond one business day requires the Monetary Authority's prior written consent.

A licensee must always hold at least HK$25 million in paid-up share capital, or an HKMA-approved equivalent amount of financial resources. This must be reserved solely for its stablecoin business, and is off-limits for transactions with related parties.
key_points.locator: Supervisory Guideline para 5.1.1; Explanatory Note on Licensing para 3.3.2

key_points.point: Significant Seeds/Private Keys are those tied to smart-contract deployment or upgrades, role management, or large-scale minting/burning. For these, the licensee must create, keep and use them inside an air-gapped setup, physically in Hong Kong or another HKMA-acceptable location, never on a system connected to the internet. A cloud-based HSM will not usually meet this bar.
key_points.locator: Supervisory Guideline para 6.5.7(iv), (vii); Consultation Conclusions para 2.6.3

key_points.point: The HKMA generally wants at least a third of the Board to be independent non-executive directors (INEDs). This expectation is waived where the licensee is itself a bank, an authorized institution, which instead follows the Banking Ordinance.

For stablecoin transfers under the Travel Rule, the HK$8,000 threshold determines the scope of required originator and recipient data, and identity verification. Transfers to or from unhosted wallets of non-customer holders are exempt from the transfer-specific data requirements, but still subject to ongoing circulation monitoring.

Unless a licensee can demonstrate to the HKMA's satisfaction that risk-mitigating measures are effective, the identity of every individual stablecoin holder must be verified, including non-customers. This can be done by the licensee, a supervised financial institution (FI) or virtual asset service provider (VASP), or a reliable third party. This is a notably stricter default than typical VA intermediary AML regimes.

Records covering CDD, transactions and stablecoin-transfer (Travel Rule) information need to be retained for a minimum of five years. This is counted from when the business relationship ends, or the particular transaction or transfer is completed.

A 'specified stablecoin' currently only covers fiat-referenced stablecoins. Stablecoins issued by central banks or governments, limited purpose digital tokens, securities or futures contracts, SVF floats or deposits, or bank deposits are excluded from the definition entirely.

Pre-existing issuers, operating in Hong Kong before 1 August 2025, had until 31 October 2025 to submit a licence application, plus a declaration and undertaking. This let them keep operating without a licence until 31 January 2026, under transitional provisions. Missing the deadline, withdrawal, or rejection triggers a closing-down period, normally 1 month and extendable, during which the entity may only act to wind down.
key_points.locator: Explanatory Note on Transitional Provisions paras 3.3-3.5, 4.1-4.6, 5.1-5.3

numbers_and_dates.item: Deadline to contact HKMA to indicate licensing interest
Travel Rule / CDD occasional transaction threshold

numbers_and_dates.value: complaint ack. within 7 calendar days; full response generally within 60 calendar days

numbers_and_dates.locator: Supervisory Guideline para 7.2.7; Explanatory Note Annex A para 18

numbers_and_dates.value: within 14 days of licence taking effect, then annually

numbers_and_dates.locator: Consultation Conclusions on Supervisory Guideline para 1.2; AML Consultation Conclusions para 1.3

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this brings the Stablecoins Ordinance regime into effect and sets the application timetable. It is directly relevant if the bank is a market participant handling, or considering issuing, licensed stablecoins. It also sets the register the bank should check when doing counterparty due diligence on any stablecoin issuer.

quote.text: the identity of each individual stablecoin holder should be verified

reading_guide: Read the main press release in full, it is short, then the Supervisory Guideline sections 1-5 (reserve assets, issuance/redemption, financial resources) and 6.5 (technology/key management) closely. AML/CFT Guideline chapters 4-6 (CDD, wallets, Travel Rule) and 9 (record-keeping) are the operational core. The two Consultation Conclusions documents mainly repeat the finalised Guidelines as annexes -- skim only the Q&A sections (paras 2.x) for the HKMA's interpretive clarifications, not the annexes.
flags: The AML/CFT Guideline's default position (para 5.11) requires identity verification of every individual stablecoin holder, even non-customers with no direct relationship to the licensee, unless the licensee proves its mitigating measures work — a materially stricter starting point than the 'travel rule only above threshold' assumption common in other VA regimes.

Significant private keys must be generated, stored and used in an air-gapped environment physically in Hong Kong (or an HKMA-acceptable location) — correcting any assumption that cloud-based HSM/key-management-as-a-service is acceptable for high-significance keys; HKMA explicitly flagged cloud HSMs as generally non-compliant for this tier (Consultation Conclusions para 2.6.3).

The Explanatory Note on Licensing and both Consultation Conclusions documents are largely restatements/annexed copies of the Supervisory and AML/CFT Guidelines already covered elsewhere in this batch — most incremental value from those two files is in their Q&A (HKMA responses to consultation comments), not the annexed guideline text.

Pre-existing issuers who miss the 31 October 2025 application deadline, are rejected, or withdraw enter a 'closing down period' where continuing to carry on the regulated activity beyond that narrow wind-down purpose is itself a criminal offence under s.8(1) SO — a hard compliance cliff-edge, not merely a licensing failure.
This is a Hong Kong dollar (HK$8,000 / HK$25,000,000) regime; a HoDA should not assume the Travel Rule/CDD thresholds default to a US$ or other-currency equivalent used elsewhere.

obligations: Market participants, including any AI, must observe the Stablecoins Ordinance and its two Guidelines (Supervision, and AML/CFT for Licensed Stablecoin Issuers) once in effect from 1 August 2025 (para 1)
It is an offence under the Stablecoins Ordinance to falsely claim to be a licensee or applicant (para on due caution)
notifications_reporting: A bank interested in applying for a stablecoin issuer licence should contact the HKMA by 31 August 2025, and submit its application by 30 September 2025 if seeking early consideration (paras 5-6)
counterparty_due_diligence: As of the issue date, no HKMA stablecoin issuer licence had yet been granted -- verify any counterparty's claimed licensed/applicant status against the future HKMA register before relying on it (final paras)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told the stablecoin issuer licensing regime is now in force (1 August 2025) and, if the bank is considering issuing a stablecoin itself, the application windows and guideline requirements that would apply.
