title: LCQ10: Promoting virtual asset development
summary: A written Legislative Council reply reviews progress across virtual-asset licensing, tokenisation and AML cooperation, in response to questions about licensing speed and international competition. It confirms 11 VATPs are licensed, with 9 more applications pending, and describes the SFC's swift licensing process, introduced June 2024 and expanded January 2025. It notes SFC circulars from November 2023 on tokenised securities, and the 2024 authorisation of a retail tokenised gold product. It also notes the first-in-Asia-Pacific authorisation of three retail tokenised money market funds in Q1 2025. These had grown to over HK$700 million in assets under management by end-March 2025. It also summarises Hong Kong's FATF standing and international AML cooperation channels.

key_points.point: As of early July 2025, the SFC had licensed 11 digital-asset trading platforms and was processing nine further applications.

The SFC issued a 'Circular on intermediaries engaging in tokenised securities-related activities' and a 'Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products' in November 2023. These guide intermediaries on tokenisation risks.
In 2024 the SFC authorised Hong Kong's first retail tokenised investment product, a gold token offering fractional ownership of physical gold.
In Q1 2025 the SFC authorised three retail tokenised money market funds, the first in the Asia-Pacific region, which held over HK$700 million in assets under management by end-March 2025.
Hong Kong's AML/CFT regime is recognised by FATF as overall compliant and effective, and Hong Kong participates in FATF's Virtual Assets Contact Group.

numbers_and_dates.item: Retail tokenised money market fund AUM (end-March 2025)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this confirms two SFC circulars from November 2023 that already govern intermediaries handling tokenised securities and tokenised SFC-authorised products. This is directly relevant if the bank distributes or advises on tokenised funds or securities today.
reading_guide: Read replies (1) and (2) for licensing progress and tokenisation circulars. Reply (3), on AML cooperation, can be skimmed.

counterparty_due_diligence: If distributing or advising on a tokenised security or tokenised SFC-authorised fund, confirm compliance with the SFC's November 2023 circulars on tokenised securities-related activities and tokenisation of SFC-authorised products (reply (2), para 2)

title: Guideline on Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers
summary: This is the HKMA's detailed operating rulebook for licensed stablecoin issuers under the Stablecoins Ordinance, expanding on the minimum criteria in Schedule 2. It sets detailed expectations across several areas. These are: reserve-asset backing, composition, segregation and disclosure; and issuance, redemption and distribution controls. They also cover financial resources, and a full risk-management stack covering credit, liquidity and market risk, technology risk (including detailed private-key and wallet controls), operational risk and reputation risk. They further cover incident management, business continuity and wind-down planning; corporate governance and fitness-and-propriety; and business conduct, including white papers and complaints handling. It distinguishes statutory 'must' requirements from supervisory 'should' expectations throughout. In several places, it also exempts a licensee that is itself an authorized institution (AI) from requirements that would otherwise apply to it.

key_points.point: A licensee must ensure the market value of reserve assets backing each coin type never falls below the par value of coins in circulation. This uses a prudent valuation approach with reconciliation. Even temporarily frozen or restricted coins must remain fully backed.

Eligible reserve assets are limited to a defined list. This is cash, bank deposits of no more than 3 months, and high-quality marketable debt securities of no more than 1 year residual maturity. It also includes overnight reverse repos collateralised by such securities, dedicated investment funds holding only such assets, or other HKMA-acceptable assets. Tokenised versions of these are allowed if the issuer can show they meet the same quality bar.
Reserve assets must generally be held in the same currency as the coin they back, with cross-currency mismatches allowed only with HKMA's prior written approval.

Reserve assets must be held under a trust arrangement backed by independent legal opinion, safe-kept by a qualified custodian, either a licensed bank or an HKMA-acceptable custodian. The issuer stays primarily accountable for their safekeeping, even if a custodian or investment manager is used.
No interest or interest-like return may be paid on coins based on holding period, par value or market value, though non-interest marketing incentives are allowed.

Issuers must submit daily internal statements on reserve composition and coin circulation to HKMA on request. They must report to HKMA and publish key reserve information weekly. An acceptable independent auditor must attest to full backing at least at period-end and one random business day, filed with HKMA within one month.

Valid redemption requests must be honoured within 1 business day, absent HKMA consent to a longer period, without unreasonable fees or unduly burdensome conditions. An independent legal opinion confirming holders' redemption and pro-rata claim rights must be filed with HKMA.

An issuer that engages third parties to distribute its coins must ensure they are 'permitted offerors' where they offer coins in Hong Kong. It must also due-diligence and risk-assess distributors and secondary-market liquidity providers.

Customer on-boarding and account operations must use effective identity verification and, generally, two-factor authentication. Transfers are restricted to pre-registered, customer-named bank accounts and wallet addresses. Controls must guard against VPN-based location spoofing, to prevent unlawful cross-border offering.

Private and seed key management must cover the full lifecycle: generation, distribution, storage, usage, backup, recovery, destruction. It needs elevated air-gapped, HSM-based controls and multi-party authorisation for 'Significant Seeds/Private Keys' tied to contract deployment, role or minter management, or large-scale minting or burning.
Smart contracts must be independently audited at least annually and whenever redeployed or upgraded, and each coin's token standard, ledger and full contract architecture must be documented.
A licensee needs three independent lines of defence (business units, risk/compliance, internal audit), each with adequate authority, resources and a direct Board or senior-management reporting line.

Material third-party arrangements, including reserve custody, coin distribution and critical IT services, require prompt HKMA notification before they start. Offshore arrangements require the issuer to assess foreign-authority data-access risk, and notify HKMA if foreign authorities seek access.

Issuers must have a business continuity and disaster recovery plan, and a separate wind-down (business exit) plan. This must cover orderly liquidation of reserve assets and honouring redemptions, tested at least annually, with key-personnel contacts filed with HKMA.
Any delay to the 1-business-day redemption deadline triggered by an incident, BCP or exit plan needs HKMA's prior written consent.

At least one-third of the Board should be independent non-executive directors; this is not required for an authorized-institution licensee. Every proposed director appointment, including INEDs, needs advance justification submitted to HKMA.

A white paper covering the issuer, the coin, reserve management, issuance, redemption and distribution mechanics, technology and risks must be published before offering, in plain language where feasible. HKMA must be notified before publication or any material change.
Audited financial statements covering the reserve assets must reach HKMA within four months of financial year-end.

Complaints must be acknowledged within 7 calendar days, and substantively responded to within 30 days, extendable generally to no more than 60 days. Records must be kept at least 2 years, and HKMA notified of complaints that reveal compliance issues or repeat unresolved matters.

numbers_and_dates.value: daily internal statements; weekly public/HKMA reporting

numbers_and_dates.item: Reserve eligible bank deposit tenor cap
Reserve eligible debt security maturity cap
numbers_and_dates.value: no longer than 1 year residual maturity
1 business day, unless HKMA approves otherwise
30 calendar days (interim), generally not exceeding 60 days
at least one-third independent non-executive directors

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the operating-level checklist the HKMA will use to supervise any stablecoin issuer, including a bank that becomes one. It also sets the benchmark compliance should use to assess a third-party stablecoin issuer's reserve, custody and redemption practices, before the bank relies on, distributes, or accepts that coin.
reading_guide: Read section 2 (reserve assets) and section 3 (issuance, redemption, distribution) closely for counterparty due diligence purposes. Read 6.5 (technology and key management) closely if assessing custody quality. Sections 6.6-6.8, 7 and 8 can be skimmed for headings and modal verbs, unless the bank itself is applying for a licence.
flags: The 1-business-day redemption deadline is a supervisory expectation with a statutory backbone (Schedule 2 s.6 requires redemption without undue delay); any deviation needs HKMA's prior written consent, which is a tighter timeline than many crypto-asset redemption practices elsewhere.

Reserve assets may include 'tokenised representations' of eligible assets provided the issuer can demonstrate equivalent quality and liquidity - a detail easy to miss when assuming reserves must be plain cash/bonds.

obligations: If licensed, maintain full reserve backing at all times including for temporarily frozen coins, with prudent valuation and reconciliation (para 2.2.1-2.2.2, p.5-6).
If licensed, only use eligible reserve asset classes, held in the referenced currency absent HKMA approval for mismatch (para 2.3.1, 2.4.1, p.6-7).
If licensed, maintain 3 lines of defence with independent risk, compliance and internal audit functions (para 6.2.3-6.2.4, p.20-21).
If licensed, notify HKMA before starting any material third-party arrangement, including reserve custody or coin distribution (para 6.6.11, p.41).
controls_and_monitoring: Private/seed key lifecycle controls with air-gapped, HSM-based, multi-party authorisation for significant keys (para 6.5.7, p.25-30).
Annual (or on-upgrade) independent smart contract audits (para 6.5.5, p.24-25).
Two-factor customer authentication and pre-registered-account transfer restrictions (para 3.5.1-3.5.3, 6.5.8-6.5.10, p.13-14,30-31).
Quarterly stress testing of the reserve portfolio under credit/liquidity/market stress (para 6.4.6-6.4.7, p.23-24).
notifications_reporting: Weekly reserve composition/backing disclosure to HKMA and the public (para 2.7.2, p.9).
Independent reserve attestation report to HKMA within 1 month of period end (para 2.7.3, p.9).
Audited annual financial statements to HKMA within 4 months of year-end (para 8.2.5, p.57).
Prior HKMA notification before publishing or materially changing a white paper (para 8.2.3, p.56).
HKMA consent required before any redemption delay beyond 1 business day (para 6.8.21, p.47).
counterparty_due_diligence: For any stablecoin issuer counterparty, check reserve composition eligibility, currency matching, trust/custodian arrangement and attestation cadence against sections 2 and 6.6 before treating the coin as reliably par-redeemable.

For any distributor or custodian the bank itself engages for stablecoin activity, apply the same third-party due diligence factors HKMA expects issuers to apply (para 6.6.4, p.40) - cost, quality, financial soundness, reputation, technical capability, audit availability.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be briefed on the full scope of governance, technology and reserve controls HKMA expects before the bank considers becoming a licensed issuer, and on any material incident, de-pegging event or reserve shortfall disclosed by a counterparty issuer the bank deals with.

title: Guideline on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (For Licensed Stablecoin Issuers)
supersedes_or_amends: Consultation Paper on the Proposed AML/CFT Requirements for Regulated Stablecoin Activities (26 May 2025)
summary: This is the HKMA's finalised, binding AML/CFT rulebook for entities licensed under the Stablecoins Ordinance to issue stablecoins, issued jointly under that Ordinance and the Anti-Money Laundering Ordinance (AMLO). It covers institutional risk assessment. It also covers AML governance, including a compliance officer, money laundering reporting officer, independent audit and training. It covers detailed customer due diligence, including on wallets and third-party distributors, and ongoing transaction and secondary-market monitoring. It also sets a full Travel Rule regime for stablecoin transfers between institutions and to or from unhosted wallets. It further covers sanctions and terrorist-financing screening, suspicious transaction reporting, and record-keeping, generally five years. Compliance is enforced through both the Stablecoins Ordinance and the AMLO, and failures can also jeopardise a licensee's ongoing eligibility under the Ordinance's minimum criteria.

key_points.point: A licensee must run an institutional money-laundering/terrorist-financing risk assessment covering customer, country, product/service and delivery-channel risk factors, approved by senior management and kept up to date.
AML/CFT systems must include compliance management with a named Compliance Officer and Money Laundering Reporting Officer, an independent audit function, staff screening and ongoing training.

Customer due diligence is required before establishing a business relationship or before any occasional transaction (for example, issuance/redemption) of HK$8,000 or more, and must identify beneficial owners holding more than 25% control.

Enhanced due diligence, including source of wealth/funds checks and senior management approval, is required for Hong Kong, non-Hong Kong and international-organisation politically exposed persons presenting higher risk.

For customer wallets, the issuer must confirm wallet ownership or control. For custodial wallets, it must run due diligence on the custodian. For higher-risk unhosted wallets, it must screen the wallet address, and may apply enhanced monitoring or transaction limits.

Ongoing monitoring must cover both individual customer transactions and, more broadly, stablecoins already in circulation, using risk-based technology (for example, blockchain analytics) to trace sources/destinations and flag illicit or sanctioned wallet addresses.

A licensee must prove its screening and monitoring controls are effective against illicit use, particularly for peer-to-peer unhosted-wallet transfers. Otherwise, HKMA expects the identity of every stablecoin holder to be verified. This can be done by the licensee, a supervised institution, or a reliable third party.

The Travel Rule requires an ordering institution to obtain, and securely and immediately transmit, originator and recipient information for stablecoin transfers of HK$8,000 or more. A reduced data set applies below that threshold. A licensee must verify the identity of an originator for transfers at or above that threshold.
A licensee is barred from executing stablecoin transfers where the counterparty institution is a shell bank or a shell virtual-asset service provider.

For transfers to or from unhosted wallets of the licensee's own customers, the licensee must still collect originator and recipient details from that customer. Peer-to-peer transfers between unhosted wallets of non-customers are exempt from this specific requirement, though ongoing circulation monitoring still applies.
A licensee must screen customers and beneficial owners against terrorist/sanctions databases at both issuance and redemption, and screen all parties to a stablecoin transfer before executing it.

Suspicious transaction reports must be filed with the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit as soon as reasonably practicable, once knowledge or suspicion arises. 'Tipping off' a customer about a report, even one raised only internally, is a separate offence.

CDD information, transaction records and Travel Rule data must generally be kept for at least five years, after a transaction, transfer or the end of a business relationship. HKMA can direct a longer retention period.

Where a licensee has branches or subsidiaries outside Hong Kong doing the same business, it must apply group-wide AML/CFT systems. Where host-country law is more permissive, it must apply the higher of the two standards. If the host jurisdiction bars this, HKMA must be told and extra mitigation taken.

A licensee may rely on an intermediary to perform parts of CDD, but retains ultimate responsibility. It must be able to obtain underlying CDD records from the intermediary on request, including for at least five years after the relationship ends.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is the binding, in-force AML/CFT rulebook for any bank-affiliated stablecoin issuer. Its Travel Rule, wallet-risk and screening standards are also the benchmark compliance should apply when assessing third-party stablecoin issuers, custodial wallet providers and distribution partners as counterparties.

quote.text: the ultimate responsibility for ensuring that CDD requirements are met remains with the licensee

reading_guide: For a compliance head, focus on Chapter 4 (CDD, especially wallet risk paras 4.33-4.40), Chapter 6 (stablecoin transfers/Travel Rule) and Chapters 7-9 (sanctions, STR, record-keeping). Chapter 3's generic governance content overlaps with standard AML guidelines and can be skimmed.
flags: Finalises and tightens the May 2025 consultation draft (id 0d6e6d0253ff), consistent with HKMA's July 2025 public statement that final AML requirements would be stricter than the consultation version.

obligations: If the group operates a licensed stablecoin issuer: build CDD (para 4.3), wallet-risk (paras 4.36-4.39), Travel Rule (paras 6.5-6.24) and sanctions-screening (para 7.5) controls exactly as set out.
Never transact with shell FIs/VASPs as stablecoin transfer counterparties (para 6.39).
File STRs with the JFIU as soon as reasonably practicable and avoid tipping off (paras 8.1-8.2).
controls_and_monitoring: Blockchain-analytics-based screening of stablecoin transactions and wallet addresses, both at issuance/redemption and for coins already in circulation (paras 5.4, 5.9-5.10).
Group-wide AML/CFT systems across overseas branches/subsidiaries, applying the higher of local and Hong Kong standards where permitted (paras 3.9-3.13).
notifications_reporting: Retain CDD, transaction and Travel Rule records for at least 5 years, longer if HKMA directs (paras 9.3-9.8).
Report suspicious transactions to the JFIU without delay (para 8.5).
counterparty_due_diligence: Apply stablecoin transfer counterparty due diligence (paras 6.28-6.39) and custodial wallet provider due diligence (para 4.37) standards when assessing any VASP, custodian or issuer counterparty.
Confirm a counterparty is not a shell FI/VASP before dealing in its stablecoin transfers (para 6.39).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be briefed on the group's stablecoin AML control framework (if issuing), on Travel Rule compliance costs/technology, and on due diligence standards applied to any stablecoin-related counterparties.

title: Joint statement by HKMA and SFC on stablecoin-related market movements
summary: HKMA and SFC jointly warned about sudden share-price swings linked to companies' stablecoin-related announcements or rumours, some of which referred to contact with regulators. The SFC's surveillance team will act against manipulative or misleading conduct. The statement calls for caution and responsible public communication.

key_points.point: A company saying it has shown interest, applied for a licence, or spoken with HKMA does not mean approval or endorsement -- that's only one step in a longer licensing process.
HKMA takes a careful, high-bar approach and expects to grant only a small number of stablecoin issuer licences at the start.
SFC's market surveillance team will take firm action against manipulative or deceptive trading tied to stablecoin-related rumours.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is a useful flag for markets and communications teams. Treat any public statement suggesting regulatory approval of a stablecoin plan, even from a counterparty, with caution. Unusual trading tied to stablecoin rumours can draw SFC surveillance action.

title: Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Custodian Services
summary: This joint FSTB/SFC consultation document proposes a new statutory licensing regime for providers of virtual asset (VA) custodian services in Hong Kong, applying the 'same activity, same risks, same regulation' principle. It explains the current patchwork of custody requirements: VATP associated entities, and SFC/HKMA rules for intermediaries and funds. It proposes bringing standalone VA custodian services within a dedicated licensing and registration framework, subject to AML/CFT and other regulatory requirements. Comments were invited by 29 August 2025.

key_points.point: Government's October 2022 Policy Statement committed to a comprehensive digital-asset regulatory framework under 'same activity, same risks, same regulation'; a second Policy Statement was promulgated 26 June 2025.
As of end-June 2025, SFC had formally licensed 11 VATPs, with 10 applicants (including 4 deemed-to-be-licensed) pending.

VATPs are currently required to provide custody through wholly-owned associated-entity subsidiaries. SFC-licensed intermediaries dealing in VAs must custody client VAs with SFC-licensed VATPs, banks, or subsidiaries of locally incorporated banks.
Consultation responses were due by 29 August 2025; the FSTB/SFC may reproduce and publish submissions and contributor names unless anonymity is expressly requested.
Growth drivers cited for a dedicated VA custodian licensing regime include the proposed VA dealing (OTC) licensing regime and growth of VA funds such as SFC-authorised spot VA ETFs.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this directly implicates it both as an eligible VA custodian for other intermediaries' clients today. It also implicates it as a prospective SFC registrant, HKMA-supervised, for its own VA custody business under the proposed new licensing regime.

quote.text: same activity, same risks, same regulation

reading_guide: Read Chapter 1 (Introduction/Background, pp.1-5) in full for the policy rationale. The remaining chapters, not captured in this excerpt beyond p.5, set out the detailed licensing proposal and should be read for implementation specifics before drafting any custody licensing strategy.
flags: This is a consultation, not yet enacted law — no VA custodian licence type currently exists; banks/VATPs must still rely on the interim custody arrangements described in paras 1.5-1.6 until legislation passes.
Only the first ~5 pages (Chapter 1) were available in the read excerpt; the substantive licensing proposal chapters were not reached — treat as partial coverage.

obligations: Under the current regime, SFC/HKMA-regulated intermediaries (including banks registered with the SFC) providing VA-related services must custody client VAs only with SFC-licensed VATPs, banks, or subsidiaries of locally-incorporated banks (para 1.6)

Under the proposed new VA custodian licensing regime, a bank providing VA custodian services would need to be registered with the SFC (which will consult the HKMA), with HKMA as day-to-day supervisor -- mirroring the existing securities-business model (paras 2.12(a), 2.13, fn.19)
controls_and_monitoring: If the bank already provides VA custody, apply the governance, risk-management, segregation and record-keeping standards in the HKMA's February 2024 custody guidance (para 2.10)
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm any VA custodian counterparty (VATP, bank, or bank subsidiary) currently used by the bank or its clients meets the existing safekeeping standards referenced here, pending the new licensing regime (paras 1.6, 2.8-2.9)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told that if the bank provides or plans to provide VA custody services, it currently operates under HKMA's February 2024 guidance and would move to SFC registration (HKMA-supervised) under this proposed regime -- still a consultation as of the document date.

title: Circular to licensed virtual asset trading platform operators on custody of virtual assets
summary: This SFC circular sets minimum custody rules that every SFC-licensed virtual-asset trading platform (VATP) operator and its associated entities must follow. It was issued after overseas custody-related cyber incidents and an SFC review that found some Hong Kong operators fell short. It covers who in senior management is responsible, and how cold wallets should be built and run. It also covers use of outside wallet providers, round-the-clock threat monitoring, and staff training, with sample 'good practice' examples. The rules apply immediately, and will also form the baseline for the coming licensed virtual-asset custodian regime.

key_points.point: A platform operator should put someone in charge of custody matters -- a Responsible Officer or Manager-in-Charge -- for everything this circular covers.
Seeds and private keys should, where practical, be created offline and kept in a secure setting such as a certified hardware security module (HSM).
Cold wallets should avoid smart contracts on public blockchains, to cut down online attack routes.
Once a client withdrawal is signed, its destination address cannot be changed before it reaches the blockchain; cold-wallet transfers need whitelist controls.
Seeds and private keys should be created and kept safe on offline (air-gapped) cold-wallet devices.
Blind signing -- approving a transaction without seeing its details -- must be blocked; transaction details must be shown in readable form before anyone signs manually.
key_points.locator: Section III, para 11 and footnote 6, p.4

key_points.point: Operators should set up a security operations centre or similar function that watches for threats around the clock, including holidays.
Before using an outside wallet provider, operators need to vet it, keep reviewing it, run independent code checks, and test its disaster-recovery plans.
These rules apply right away and should feed into operators' annual outside compliance and technology review.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, these are custody rules for trading platforms, not a direct bank duty. But compliance should use them as the checklist for vetting any custody partner. This includes offline key generation in a hardware security module (HSM), blocking blind signing, and round-the-clock monitoring, since they also preview the coming statutory custodian regime.

quote.text: The security of client assets is only as strong as its most vulnerable point.

reading_guide: Read Sections I-VI in full (pp.2-7). The 'Good Practice' boxes (pp.4, 6, 7) are illustrative and can be skimmed after grasping the numbered minimum requirements.
flags: Corrects an assumption that HSM/MPC/Multi-Sig choice alone is sufficient — SFC states vulnerabilities persist 'regardless of the custody solutions used' (p.2), i.e. technology choice does not substitute for process controls.

Standards are described as future core expectations for the separate (not-yet-enacted) Virtual Asset Custodian Services licensing regime (footnote 2), signalling upcoming statutory custody regulation beyond VATP licensees.

counterparty_due_diligence: When checking a custody partner, confirm it names a Responsible Officer or Manager-in-Charge for custody and creates seeds/private keys offline in a certified HSM.

Check the platform blocks blind signing, shows transaction details in readable form before manual signing, and runs round-the-clock security monitoring through a security operations centre or similar.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No direct bank duty, but the board should know these standards preview the future statutory virtual-asset custodian licensing regime, so any bank custody partnership should expect this bar to become law.

title: Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)3A(I): Divisions A to F and L - Market Risk Capital Charge
supersedes_or_amends: HKMA consultation of 13 June 2025 on revised return templates for the Basel cryptoasset exposure standard
summary: This part of the market-risk return covers the sensitivities-based method (Divisions A-F) and the simplified standardized approach (Division L) for trading-book positions. It adds group 2a cryptoasset positions, broadly stablecoin-type, as a new risk bucket. Banks are instructed to report the highest of three correlation-scenario capital charges for that bucket, regardless of charges elsewhere. They should add a separate curvature-risk charge for price moves in those tokens. Under the simplified method, they should report each group 2a token and its hedges on its own line.

key_points.point: Group 2a crypto positions form their own risk bucket. The capital charge reported for it should be the highest of the three prescribed correlation-scenario results, kept separate from charges on other risk types.
A price-curvature-risk capital charge specific to group 2a token price movements should also be calculated and reported, on top of the correlation-scenario charge.
Where a fund (CIS) exposure includes a group 2a crypto slice, that slice's capital requirement should be captured in this same section.
Under the simplified standardized approach (Division L), each group 2a token should be reported on its own line, together with its associated hedging positions.
Cryptoasset exposures more generally should also follow the Part 12 crypto rules of the Banking (Capital) Rules in addition to this form's own instructions.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, this is where its trading-book stablecoin-type exposure turns into a specific, separately-tracked capital charge each month. This is on top of whatever the bank already reports for other market risk.
reading_guide: Read paras 18-19 (bucket treatment), the curvature-risk paragraphs around p.21, and Division L paras on group 2a reporting. Skip the non-crypto risk-class mechanics if pressed for time.

obligations: Ensure the trading system can isolate group 2a crypto positions into their own risk bucket and produce all three correlation-scenario results monthly (para 18).
controls_and_monitoring: Build a monitoring check that the highest-of-three-scenarios rule is being applied consistently, since using the wrong scenario would misstate capital (para 18).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should see the monthly group 2a (stablecoin-type) market-risk capital charge alongside other trading-book risk metrics once live.

summary: This draft splits the credit-risk basic-approach section of the Capital Adequacy Ratio return into two halves. Division A1 covers ordinary exposures, and a brand-new Division A2 is dedicated to crypto holdings. Banks using the basic approach must now separately identify holdings in government-issued, bank-issued and other-issuer group 1a tokens, plus group 1b tokens. They must rank their five largest crypto positions by risk-weighted amount. It also tells banks where to book crypto derivative and repo-style exposures held in the trading book instead. Banks should total up risk-weighted amounts per individual token and list only their five largest group-1 crypto positions by that measure.

Crypto assets held in the trading book for market-risk or repo-style purposes go to the new market-risk return (MA(BS)3A) instead. Any redemption-default risk-weighted amount is routed to the dedicated crypto capital form.

summary: This is the general instructions cover for the whole market-risk-and-CVA return, which has two parts. The crypto-specific detail lives in the Part I and Part II division instructions, registered separately. This introduction sets the reporting basis, frequency and who must file, which apply equally to the new crypto items added elsewhere in the form.

key_points.point: The market-risk part of the return is completed monthly by each locally incorporated authorized institution. Institutions exempted under the de-minimis criteria complete only a reduced annual set of divisions instead.

A footnote records that the standards were rolled out first as a reporting-only requirement, on a quarterly basis no earlier than 1 July 2024. This moved to full monthly reporting no earlier than 1 January 2025 -- a general-standard timeline, not crypto-specific.
Banks exempted from market risk under the de-minimis test still complete Divisions G to K once a year, as at end-December. This is purely for the HKMA to re-check their exemption status.
Part II (CVA) is filed by banks with covered transactions under section 322J of the Banking (Capital) Rules; a bank with none still files a nil return.

numbers_and_dates.item: Annual exemption-status check date for de-minimis banks

flags: The page-footer date stamp is garbled by an apparent tracked-change artifact showing both a 2024 and a 2026 year fragment run together, so the exact draft revision date could not be reliably read from it.

title: Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)3(IIIc) - Return of Capital Adequacy Ratio, Part IIIc - Internal Ratings-based Approach
supersedes_or_amends: HKMA consultation of 13 June 2025 on revised return templates for the Basel cryptoasset exposure standard
summary: This part of the return covers banks that use their own internal models, the IRB approach, to measure credit risk. The draft adds a brand-new memorandum form, IRB_CRYPTO, that pulls out and separately shows the crypto slice of exposures already reported in the bank's other IRB forms. Banking-book group 1a crypto holdings are split further by the type of traditional asset that was tokenised, and group 1b holdings get their own reporting logic. Investment-fund (CIS) exposures that include crypto also get a special risk-weighting rule cross-referenced here.

key_points.point: A new memorandum form, IRB_CRYPTO, should show the crypto share of exposures already captured under the bank's other IRB forms (IRB_CSB, IRB_SLSLOT, IRB_RETAIL, IRB_CIS, IRB_OTHER).
IRB_CRYPTO covers only group 1 crypto exposures held in the banking book under the IRB approach, split into on-balance sheet and off-balance sheet amounts.

Group 1a crypto exposures should be broken down by the kind of traditional asset that was tokenised. They should also be separately flagged if in default, or subject to the 1.25 asset-value-correlation multiplier for financial-institution counterparties.
Where a fund (CIS) investment includes group 1b or group 2 crypto exposures among its underlying assets, a specific risk-weighting method applies to that crypto slice.
Non-crypto trading-book crypto derivatives and repo-style deals are again routed to the market-risk return, matching the other Part III forms.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank on the IRB approach, this needs a new control. This control should feed the memorandum IRB_CRYPTO form correctly from existing IRB systems, since it is an add-on reconciliation rather than a fresh data source.
reading_guide: Read paras 29 and 42-52 (Section C.6) on Form IRB_CRYPTO. Skip the general IRB-class tables, which are largely unchanged.
flags: Draft version stamp only, not finalised as captured.

obligations: Stand up a reconciliation control so the new IRB_CRYPTO memorandum form ties back to crypto amounts already reported in the bank's other IRB forms (para 29).
controls_and_monitoring: Test that group 1a crypto exposures are correctly tagged by underlying tokenised-asset type and by default/correlation-multiplier status (item 1, p.18-19).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: IRB-model banks should confirm to the board that model outputs can already isolate the crypto slice needed for the new memorandum return.

title: Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)28 - Return of Large Exposures
supersedes_or_amends: HKMA consultation of 13 June 2025 on revised return templates for the Basel cryptoasset exposure standard
summary: This return tracks a bank's exposure concentration to a single counterparty, or a group of connected counterparties, under the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules. It is filed quarterly. Its crypto-specific additions are two reporting-column clarifications. Certain crypto-related exposures unconnected to counterparty credit or default risk can be left out of the exempted-exposure figure. Default-risk exposures from crypto derivatives or repo-style deals must be included in the default-risk-exposure column.

key_points.point: AIs report their large-exposure positions as at each quarter-end, with submission due within one month of quarter-end.

Crypto-related exposures that are not tied to counterparty credit or default risk do not have to be counted in the exempted-exposure-before-CRM figure. This is alongside similar carve-outs for commodity and foreign-currency exposures.

The default-risk-exposure column should include default-risk exposures arising from crypto derivative contracts or crypto securities-financing transactions, alongside conventional derivative/SFT exposures.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, large-exposure and single-counterparty-limit monitoring must now correctly fold in crypto derivative and repo-style default-risk exposures. It must also correctly exclude the carved-out crypto amounts, or the reported concentration figure will be wrong.
reading_guide: Read para 12 (exemption carve-out) and para 31/32 (default-risk column). Skip the general large-exposure mechanics, which are unchanged.

obligations: Update large-exposure/counterparty-limit monitoring to include crypto derivative and SFT default-risk exposures in the relevant column (para 32).
controls_and_monitoring: Check that the exempted-exposure carve-out for non-credit-risk crypto amounts is applied correctly so exposures are neither over- nor under-counted (para 12).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No new board obligation beyond ensuring large-exposure/counterparty-limit monitoring correctly reflects crypto positions from the next filing cycle.

title: Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)26 - Return of Stable Funding Position of an Authorized Institution
supersedes_or_amends: HKMA consultation of 13 June 2025 on revised return templates for the Basel cryptoasset exposure standard
summary: This return measures a bank's stable-funding position. Category 1 institutions report the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) at quarter-end, and category 2A institutions report an average Core Funding Ratio (CFR) over the quarter. Both add new memorandum items breaking out cryptoasset-related amounts. These are tokenised customer claims counted as available or core stable funding, and crypto assets counted as required stable funding, cross-referencing a dedicated SPM guidance annex (LM-1, Annex 3).

key_points.point: Category 1 institutions calculate the NSFR on the quarter-end date, and the return as a whole is filed quarterly.

Category 1 institutions should additionally report the total weighted amount of tokenised customer or counterparty claims counted as available stable funding. They should also report cryptoassets counted as required stable funding, in new memorandum items 3(a) and 3(b).
Category 2A institutions report an average Core Funding Ratio calculated over each calendar month of the quarter.
Category 2A institutions should additionally report tokenised-claim and cryptoasset amounts feeding their average core funding ratio, in new memorandum items 4(a) and 4(b).

The completion instructions define 'cryptoasset' by cross-reference to the Banking (Capital) Rules and point banks to a dedicated annex of SPM module LM-1 for the funding treatment of crypto exposures.
AIs must send the HKMA the complete return, including the new crypto memorandum items, once every quarter, no later than one month after that quarter ends.
key_points.locator: para 4 (Reporting frequency and submission timeline), p.2

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: For a bank, treasury and ALM functions get a new quarterly disclosure obligation, isolating how much of the bank's funding position comes from tokenised claims or crypto assets. This is a number the board and regulator can now track separately from the headline ratio.
reading_guide: Read paras 12-15 for the new crypto memorandum items, and the para 46-49 area for filing frequency. The rest of the NSFR/CFR mechanics is largely unchanged.

obligations: Produce the two new crypto-related memorandum figures each quarter for category 1 (items 3(a)/(b)) or category 2A (items 4(a)/(b)) institutions (paras 14-15).
controls_and_monitoring: Reference SPM module LM-1 Annex 3 to confirm which tokenised claims and cryptoassets qualify for the new memorandum items.
notifications_reporting: File this return quarterly, within one month of each quarter-end, including the new crypto memorandum items.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Treasury/ALCO should see the new crypto-related funding memorandum figures each quarter alongside the main NSFR/CFR number.

title: Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)3(IIIf) - Return of Capital Adequacy Ratio, Part IIIf - Additional Risk-weighted Amount for Cryptoasset Exposures
supersedes_or_amends: HKMA consultation of 13 June 2025 on revised return templates for the Basel cryptoasset exposure standard
summary: This is an entirely new form, required of every locally incorporated bank, that gathers extra capital add-ons the other capital forms do not capture. It has four sections: an infrastructure add-on the HKMA can impose on banking-book group 1 crypto by written notice. A charge for the risk that a token's redemption mechanism or its issuer fails, for banking-book group 1b tokens and trading-book group 2a stablecoins. A charge for each individual group 2b (unbacked/high-risk) crypto position. And a bank-wide ratio plus an extra add-on that only applies to globally or domestically systemically important banks.

key_points.point: Every locally incorporated bank should complete this form to work out its extra capital charge for crypto holdings.

The HKMA can separately notify a bank of an infrastructure-risk add-on for banking-book group 1 crypto, and of its size. The bank then reports this add-on under section 380 of the Banking (Capital) Rules.
A capital charge for the risk that a redemption mechanism or intermediary fails applies to banking-book group 1b tokens (section 376) and to trading-book group 2a stablecoins (section 384).
key_points.locator: paras 5-8, Div A.2 and Div B.1, p.1-2

key_points.point: Each group 2b (higher-risk) crypto position gets its own capital charge, including any extra add-on the HKMA sets, under section 385 of the Rules. The crypto-linked slice of a fund holding is captured the same way.
All banks report a bank-wide group-2 crypto exposure ratio (section 387). Only global or domestic systemically important banks also report an extra add-on tied to that ratio (section 388).

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the single clearest new capital-reporting obligation from the whole package. Any bank with crypto exposure now needs a process to produce four separate crypto-specific capital numbers each period, including a systemic-bank-only add-on.
reading_guide: Read the whole form -- it is short (about two pages) and every paragraph is a distinct new reporting item; nothing to skip.
flags: The footer already shows a specific month (March 2026) rather than the 'XX/202X' placeholder used on most sibling forms, suggesting this form was closer to finalised when captured.

obligations: Build the capability to calculate and report all four new crypto capital charges: infrastructure add-on, redemption-default risk-weighted amount, group 2b position charges, and the group-2 exposure ratio (paras 3-12).
controls_and_monitoring: Set up monitoring for any HKMA written notice imposing an infrastructure add-on under section 380, since that add-on is only reportable once notified (para 3).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should see the bank's projected group-2 cryptoasset exposure ratio, and, if the bank is a G-SIB/D-SIB, the extra capital add-on it triggers (Division C).

title: Completion Instructions: Return of Liquidity Position of an Authorized Institution, Form MA(BS)1E
supersedes_or_amends: Completion Instructions for Form MA(BS)1E (prior version, referenced as 01/2025 in the footer)
summary: This draft sets out how authorized institutions (AIs) should fill in Form MA(BS)1E. This monthly return calculates the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) for category 1 institutions and the Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) for category 2 institutions. The new material tells banks how to assign a reporting currency to cryptoassets, and adds dedicated lines for weighted cryptoasset holdings, tokenised customer claims, and stablecoins issued by the bank. It cross-refers repeatedly to a new Annex 3 in the companion SPM module LM-1 for the underlying classification and weighting rules. The rest of the document restates existing general LCR/LMR mechanics (bases of reporting, valuation, currency breakdowns) largely unchanged.

key_points.point: For a cryptoasset pegged to a fiat currency, report it in that currency. For one with no traditional peg, use the currency it was bought in or is managed in. Otherwise use 'other currencies'.

Category 1 institutions must fill in two new memo items. The first is the weighted amount of cryptoassets counted in high-quality liquid assets. The second is the weighted amount of tokenised customer claims treated as deposits or funding.
A cryptoasset cannot be counted as a high-quality liquid asset unless it also meets the extra conditions in Annex 3 of the draft SPM module LM-1.

Tokenised deposits or funding that are a legal claim on the bank may be reported like ordinary deposits, but they never qualify for the lower 3%/5% 'stable deposit' outflow rate. If the bank cannot always identify the token holder, the cash outflow should be reported in item 6(b).

Stablecoins a bank itself issues are generally treated like the bank's own debt securities for outflow purposes. If they are fully backed by qualifying liquid assets, they can instead be reported as secured funding.
Category 2 institutions get matching new memo items for cryptoasset liquefiable assets and cryptoasset-related qualifying liabilities (including issued stablecoins).

numbers_and_dates.item: LCR minimum HKD level-1 asset threshold (rule 37 institutions)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the actual reporting template compliance will have to populate for any cryptoasset, tokenised-deposit or stablecoin exposure on the balance sheet. Getting the currency-attribution and cryptoasset memo items wrong misstates the bank's regulatory LCR/LMR.

quote.text: the term “cryptoasset” has the meaning given by section 2(1)

reading_guide: Read paragraphs 10 and 30-32 (cryptoasset currency attribution, tokenised claims, stablecoins) plus the new memo items in Part 1. Skip the unchanged general LCR/LMR mechanics in paragraphs 4-9 and 15-29.
flags: Draft is a mark-up of the existing form so paragraph numbers appear doubled (e.g. '13.14'); treat the second number as the renumbered version.
Substance depends entirely on Annex 3 of the companion SPM module LM-1, which this document does not reproduce.

obligations: Attribute a reporting currency to every cryptoasset holding using the three-tier test (para 10, p.5).
Populate the new cryptoasset and tokenised-claim memo items in Part 1 for the relevant institution category (paras 13.14 and 14.15, pp.8-9).
Confirm any cryptoasset claimed as HQLA meets the extra Annex 3 conditions in SPM LM-1 before including it (para 15.16, p.10).
controls_and_monitoring: Process to identify, at each reporting date, whether tokenised deposit/funding holders can be identified, since this drives the outflow-rate treatment (para 31, p.14).
Process to test whether issued stablecoins remain fully backed by qualifying liquid assets to keep the more favourable secured-funding treatment (para 32, p.14).
notifications_reporting: Monthly submission of Form MA(BS)1E within 14 days of month-end, per basis of reporting applicable (para 5, p.3).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told that any cryptoasset, tokenised-deposit or stablecoin business line will require new LCR/LMR reporting lines and may affect reported liquidity ratios once the CIs take effect.

title: Letter to HKAB: Cryptoassets standard and other miscellaneous amendments: consultation on revised completion instructions
supersedes_or_amends: HKMA consultation of 13 June 2025 on revised return templates for the Basel cryptoasset exposure standard
summary: This is the HKMA's cover letter to the Hong Kong Association of Banks opening industry consultation on the draft revised completion instructions bundled in this package. It covers six returns: MA(BS)1E (Liquidity Position), MA(BS)1F(a)/(b) (Certificate of Compliance) and MA(BS)3 (Capital Adequacy Ratio). It also covers MA(BS)3A (Market Risk and CVA Risk Capital Charge), MA(BS)26 (Stable Funding Position) and MA(BS)28 (Large Exposures). It sets out a transitional arrangement so banks without any crypto exposure do not have to move to the new templates immediately, and asks for comments within one month. The letter is the master timeline document for the whole consultation package registered in this batch.

key_points.point: This consultation follows an earlier 13 June 2025 consultation on the revised return templates themselves; this round covers only the accompanying completion instructions for the same six returns.

The six returns being updated are Liquidity Position (MA(BS)1E), Certificate of Compliance (MA(BS)1F(a)/(b)) and Capital Adequacy Ratio (MA(BS)3). They also include Market Risk and CVA Risk Capital Charge (MA(BS)3A), Stable Funding Position (MA(BS)26) and Large Exposures (MA(BS)28).
A bank counts as a 'Transition AI' only if it has no cryptoasset exposure as at 1 January 2026. Such banks may keep filing on the old templates for a further six months.
Any bank with cryptoasset exposure as at 1 January 2026 -- and any Transition AI that later acquires exposure -- must use the revised templates from that point onward.
All Transition AIs, regardless of when they acquire crypto exposure, must be on the revised templates by 1 July 2026 at the latest, once the six-month transitional window ends.

Apart from the crypto-related changes, banks must start using the updated instructions for completing Part II of Form MA(BS)3 from 1 January 2026. That part's layout stays the same; the update just covers other, unrelated miscellaneous amendments.
The HKMA asked the Association to send comments on the draft instructions and the proposed transitional arrangement by 3 October 2025.

title: Supervisory Policy Manual LM-1: Regulatory Framework for Supervision of Liquidity Risk (draft V.5)
supersedes_or_amends: SPM module LM-1 'Regulatory Framework for Supervision of Liquidity Risk' (V.4, 13 December 2024)
summary: This is a statutory guideline under section 7(3) of the Banking Ordinance, in draft form. It adds a new section 5.9 and Annex 3 on cryptoassets to the HKMA's existing liquidity-risk supervision module. It tells authorized institutions how cryptoasset exposures should be folded into the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) and Core Funding Ratio (CFR). The default principle is to treat a cryptoasset the same as the traditional asset or liability it economically resembles, unless it carries extra risk from its digital form. The draft sets specific rules for three buckets: tokenised claims that are a legal claim on the bank, stablecoins, and all other cryptoassets. It also reserves the HKMA's right to apply tougher treatment case by case.

key_points.point: As a baseline, cryptoasset exposures should get the same LCR/NSFR/LMR/CFR treatment as an economically equivalent traditional exposure, because of their extra risk and limited track record.

A cryptoasset can only count as a high-quality liquid asset (HQLA) if it is a 'group 1a' tokenised version of an already-eligible traditional asset. Both the token and the underlying asset must meet all the usual HQLA conditions. The token must also meet extra operational conditions, for example living on a well-established ledger with an active, sizable market so it can be sold quickly with little loss of value.

A bank may issue tokens that are a direct, par-value redeemable claim on it, backed one-to-one by a matching pool of assets. It can then treat the resulting liability like ordinary deposits or unsecured funding, but only from the earliest date holders could demand redemption. It only gets the favourable retail/small-business rate if the bank can always identify the token holders.

Stablecoins a bank issues get a 100% LCR outflow rate if redeemable within the LCR window. This does not apply if they are fully backed by HQLA-eligible assets; then the more favourable secured-funding outflow rates may apply instead.

Stablecoins a bank holds, rather than issues, are treated as ordinary non-HQLA debt securities. This generally means a 0% LCR inflow rate and an 85% NSFR required-stable-funding factor. A lower 50% factor can apply if the maturity is short and it will convert to fiat within 12 months.

Any other cryptoasset the bank holds or has borrowed gets the harshest treatment: no LCR inflow recognition and a 100% NSFR funding requirement. It also gets a 100% outflow rate if the bank owes the asset back to a counterparty.

The HKMA can impose stricter LCR/NSFR treatment for a specific cryptoasset if the asset carries extra liquidity risk, or if the bank has contingent exposure from issuing or trading it. For example, the bank might feel pressure to support redemptions to protect its reputation.
The same tokenised-claim, stablecoin and 'other cryptoasset' logic carries over largely unchanged to the Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (for category 2 institutions) and the Core Funding Ratio.

numbers_and_dates.item: Group 2 cryptoasset borrowing LCR outflow rate
Issued stablecoin LCR outflow rate (unbacked case)
Held stablecoin default NSFR RSF factor
numbers_and_dates.value: 85% (or 50% if near-term fiat convertible within 12 months)

Verify any cryptoasset claimed as HQLA against the full Annex 3 test, including ledger and market-liquidity conditions, before counting it (Annex 3 para 1, p.88).

title: Supervisory Policy Manual MR-2: CVA Risk Capital Charge (V.2 - Consultation)
supersedes_or_amends: SPM module MR-2 'CVA Risk Capital Charge' (V.1, 15 March 2024)
summary: This draft statutory guideline adds a new section 4 on cryptoassets to the module covering credit valuation adjustment (CVA) risk capital. CVA is the capital a bank must hold against the risk that a derivative counterparty's credit quality worsens. Derivatives and securities-financing transactions referencing tokenised traditional assets or stablecoins (groups 1a/1b) are generally treated the same as instruments on the underlying traditional asset. A bank must still separately check the token's own liquidity behaviour rather than assuming it matches the original asset. Group 2a cryptoasset derivatives cannot use the more risk-sensitive standardised CVA approach at all. Group 2b exposures are folded into an existing, very conservative flat risk-weight treatment with no extra CVA calculation.

key_points.point: Derivatives and financing trades on group 1a tokenised assets are generally charged CVA capital the same way as trades on the non-tokenised version of the asset.

A bank must independently assess the tokenised asset itself against this module's tests. It cannot simply assume the token qualifies for a treatment just because the underlying traditional asset does, because liquidity behaviour can differ between the two.
If there is not enough data to model how those liquidity differences affect the tokenised asset's value, the standardised CVA approach cannot be used. The basic approach applies instead.
Group 2a cryptoasset derivatives and securities-financing trades must use the basic CVA approach. The standardised approach is not permitted for them.

Group 2b cryptoasset exposures generally need no separate CVA calculation because they already carry the conservative 1,250% risk weight that covers credit, market and CVA risk together. This only changes if a fair-valued, cryptoasset-collateralised transaction's credit risk is calculated some other way, in which case the 1,250% weight is applied specifically for CVA.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Sets the capital a derivatives or securities-financing desk must hold for counterparty credit-quality risk on any cryptoasset-referencing trade. It also confirms less-standard tokens cannot use the more capital-efficient standardised method.

reading_guide: Read section 4 in full (pp.44-46); the rest of the module is unchanged general CVA mechanics.

obligations: Independently test each tokenised or stablecoin-referencing derivative against this module's own criteria rather than inheriting the underlying asset's treatment (para 4.2.2, p.44).
Route group 2a cryptoasset derivatives through the basic CVA approach only (para 4.3.1, p.45).

title: CR-L-5 Major Acquisitions and Investments: BELR Part 3
supersedes_or_amends: CR-L-5 Major Acquisitions and Investments: BELR Part 3 (V.2), 09 Aug 2019
summary: CR-L-5 explains how HKMA exercises its consent power over an AI's major acquisitions of another company's share capital under Part 3 of the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules. The revision adds a footnote clarifying that a cryptoasset counting as equity ownership is treated the same as ordinary share capital for this consent regime.

key_points.point: A locally incorporated AI needs HKMA's written consent before acquiring, in one go or in stages, 5% or more of a company's share capital measured against the AI's Tier 1 capital.
'Share capital' for this purpose is defined to also include a cryptoasset that conveys the same economic substance as equity ownership, so token-based equity stakes now count toward the 5% threshold.
The 5% threshold is measured against how much Tier 1 capital the AI held when it made the acquisition, usually taking the figure from the end of the preceding quarter.
Certain small or deemed-consent acquisitions are exempt from needing prior consent, as set out later in the module.

title: Letter to HKAB: Cryptoassets standard: consultation on new and revised SPM modules and code of practice
summary: This is the HKMA Banking Policy Department's covering letter to the Hong Kong Association of Banks (addressed to its then chairperson). It opens formal industry consultation on a package of cryptoasset-related prudential guidance. This package is a brand-new SPM module, CRP-1, on classifying cryptoassets, plus revisions to eight other modules and one code. The stated purpose is to implement, at the Hong Kong level, the Basel Committee's global standard on how banks should treat cryptoasset exposures for capital purposes. It also covers related amendments to the capital, disclosure and exposure-limit rules. The HKMA asked for comments within about a month and noted it sent an equivalent letter to the DTC Association the same day.

key_points.point: The consultation covers a brand-new module, CRP-1 'Classification of Cryptoassets', plus revisions to eight further items. These are CA-D-1, CA-G-5, CR-G-8, CR-G-9, CR-L-5, LM-1, MR-1, MR-2 and the Banking (Exposure Limits) Code.

The revisions implement, at the local level, the Basel Committee's global standard on prudential treatment of banks' cryptoasset exposures. This runs alongside the Banking (Capital) (Amendment) Rules 2025, the Banking (Disclosure) (Amendment) Rules 2025 and the Banking (Exposure Limits) (Amendment) Rules 2025.
A separate, related revision to module CA-G-1 (overview of the capital adequacy regime) is being consulted on separately, not as part of this package.
Comments were requested by 10 October 2025.

title: CA-G-5 Supervisory Review Process
supersedes_or_amends: CA-G-5 Supervisory Review Process (V.6), 24 Jan 2025
summary: CA-G-5 explains how the HKMA runs its Pillar 2 Supervisory Review Process (SRP) to set a bank-specific capital add-on on top of the Pillar 1 minimum. Crypto activities and their risks are still new and changing. The revision adds an explicit statement that the HKMA may respond to weak crypto risk management with capital add-ons, provisioning requirements, activity limits, or other measures. These are decided case by case.

key_points.point: Cryptoasset activities and their risks are relatively new and still evolving. Because of this, the HKMA's supervisory response to gaps in an AI's crypto capital or risk management can include capital add-ons and provisioning requirements for foreseeable crypto losses. It can also include activity limits or other mitigation steps.
The HKMA's Pillar 2 capital add-on (P2A) is meant to capture material risks not already fully covered by the Pillar 1 minimum requirement.
Before raising or lowering an AI's Pillar 2 capital requirement, HKMA may hold off temporarily to check whether the underlying issue is genuinely resolved or just temporary.
Extra capital is not treated as a substitute for good risk management; HKMA may instead, or in addition, require better systems and controls.
Stress tests (sensitivity tests and scenario analyses) run by the AI feed into how HKMA assesses capital adequacy under the SRP.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the mechanism by which weaknesses in the bank's crypto risk management can translate directly into a higher firm-specific capital requirement or forced activity limits. It links crypto operational risk straight to the capital plan.
reading_guide: Read para 3.6.6 (the new crypto-specific supervisory response) and the surrounding 3.6 sub-section on Pillar 2 capital setting first. The legal-framework sections (2.1-2.2) can be skimmed.

controls_and_monitoring: Maintain the ability to provision for foreseeable and estimable crypto-related losses, since HKMA may require this as a supervisory response to identified gaps (para 3.6.6(ii))
Maintain stress-testing capability covering crypto exposures, since results feed HKMA's Pillar 2 capital assessment (paras 3.7.1-3.7.4)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should understand that weak crypto risk management can directly raise the bank's Pillar 2 capital add-on or trigger HKMA-imposed activity limits.

title: CA-D-1 Guideline on the Application of the Banking (Disclosure) Rules
supersedes_or_amends: CA-D-1 Guideline on the Application of the Banking (Disclosure) Rules (V.43), 16 Aug 2019
summary: CA-D-1 interprets how AIs should meet the Banking (Disclosure) Rules, which implement Hong Kong's Pillar 3 public-disclosure regime. This revision adds two new items tied to the cryptoassets standard. An annual qualitative disclosure of crypto-related business that creates liquidity risk, and, for larger institutions, a semi-annual quantitative disclosure of liquidity requirements tied to crypto exposures. The rest of the module sets out general disclosure timing, review and exemption rules that already applied to AIs.

key_points.point: An AI with any cryptoasset exposure must give an annual, mainly qualitative, disclosure of its crypto-related activities that create liquidity risk, using the standard table the HKMA specifies.

An AI that is a 'category 1 institution' and has cryptoasset exposures must also give a semi-annual disclosure of the liquidity requirements tied to those exposures. This uses a standard template and is mostly quantitative.

Quarterly disclosures are due within 8 weeks of period-end, interim (half-year) disclosures within 3 months, and annual disclosures within 4 months, generally aligned with publication of the related financial statements.
A failure to meet any disclosure requirement is a criminal offence for every director, chief executive and manager of the AI, and can also count against the bank's continuing authorization.

Before publication, the board (or a delegated committee) and senior management must have the disclosures reviewed by staff independent of those who prepared them, to check they are not false or misleading.
Disclosure statements must be lodged with the HKMA before publication and e-mailed to the HKMA's register within 3 working days after publication.

numbers_and_dates.value: quarterly: 8 weeks; interim: 3 months; annual: 4 months after period end

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This creates a standing Pillar 3 reporting obligation about the bank's crypto activities. There is personal criminal liability for directors and managers if it is missed, so compliance needs a dedicated review-and-sign-off workflow.

title: CR-G-8 Large Exposures and Risk Concentrations
summary: CR-G-8 governs how AIs measure and limit large exposures and risk concentrations. This revision inserts a dedicated set of rules, Division 5A, for valuing cryptoasset-related exposures for large-exposure purposes. These are separate from the general rules used for other counterparty-credit-risk and non-counterparty-credit-risk exposures.

key_points.point: Cryptoasset-related exposures are valued for large-exposure purposes under a new, separate set of rules, Division 5A of Part 7 of the BELR. This replaces the general divisions used for other exposures.
Before applying the crypto valuation rules, an AI must first pin down the specific counterparty (or connected group) the exposure relates to.

Which specific rule applies to a given crypto exposure depends on how it's defined under the BELR. It also depends on whether the asset is classed Group 1a/1b/2a/2b, and whether it sits in the banking book or trading book.
For some crypto exposures, the AI must reuse the valuation figure it already calculated under the Capital Rules rather than doing a separate calculation for large-exposure purposes.
Because crypto markets and technology are still evolving, HKMA can give an individual AI written instructions to use a different valuation method for its crypto exposures than the one in the rules.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This determines how much of a client's or counterparty's crypto-linked exposure counts against the bank's concentration limits. That affects how much crypto business the bank can safely do with any one counterparty.
reading_guide: Read paras 2.8.8-2.8.12 (the new crypto valuation division). The surrounding general large-exposure material can be skimmed if already familiar with CR-G-8.

obligations: Value cryptoasset-related large exposures under the new Division 5A rather than the general exposure-valuation divisions (para 2.8.8)
Identify the specific counterparty behind each cryptoasset-related exposure before valuing it for concentration-limit purposes (para 2.8.9)
controls_and_monitoring: A process to tag each crypto exposure by classification group (1a/1b/2a/2b) and book (banking/trading), since this drives the applicable valuation rule (para 2.8.10)
notifications_reporting: Follow any AI-specific valuation methodology HKMA prescribes by written notice for crypto exposures (para 2.8.12)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should know concentration-limit headroom for crypto-heavy counterparties now depends on a distinct, more judgement-based valuation approach.

title: CRP-1 Classification of Cryptoassets
summary: CRP-1 is a new HKMA guideline that sorts a bank's cryptoasset holdings into capital-treatment groups. Group 1 covers tokenised traditional assets and well-backed stablecoins that meet strict conditions, and gets treated like the underlying traditional asset. Group 2 covers everything else and needs much heavier capital backing, with a limited sub-category (Group 2a) recognised for hedging. The module takes effect from 1 January 2026 and sits alongside the Banking (Capital) Rules, which prevail if the two conflict.

key_points.point: Cryptoassets split into Group 1 (meets four classification conditions) and Group 2 (does not). Group 1 splits further into 1a (tokenised traditional assets) and 1b (stablecoins with an effective peg mechanism).
The rules and this module start applying from 1 January 2026.
Any cryptoasset exposure an AI already holds before that date defaults to the most conservative bucket (Group 2b) until the HKMA agrees a different classification.
Before acquiring a brand-new type of cryptoasset, an AI has to tell the HKMA and hold it as Group 2b until the HKMA agrees to a better classification.
If a cryptoasset later stops meeting its group's conditions, the AI has to move it straight back to Group 2b.

For a stablecoin to qualify as Group 1b, its reserve assets must, even in stress, always be worth at least the total amount holders could redeem. Its reserve assets must also be high quality, liquid, currency-matched to the peg, and independently audited at least once a year.
A stablecoin issued under the HKMA's own stablecoin licensing regime is automatically treated as meeting the extra safeguards needed for permissionless-blockchain assets to qualify for Group 1.

To count as Group 2a (limited hedging recognition), a cryptoasset needs deep, liquid markets. It needs an average market capitalisation of at least HKD 78 billion and a 10%-trimmed average daily trading volume of at least HKD 390 million over the prior year.
AIs must keep full records of how they classified each cryptoasset and hand them to the HKMA on request.

numbers_and_dates.item: Effective date of CRP-1 and the cryptoassets standard

numbers_and_dates.value: HKD 390 million (10% trimmed mean daily, previous year)

numbers_and_dates.item: Minimum price observations for Group 2a data sufficiency
numbers_and_dates.value: 100 real price observations over the previous year

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This module decides how much capital the bank must hold against any crypto exposure it books. It forces a conservative default and an HKMA-notification step for anything new — both are matters compliance must build a process around before 1 January 2026.

quote.text: same activity, same risks, same regulation

flags: Central bank digital currencies and centrally-administered dematerialised securities are explicitly carved out of scope (paras 1.2.2-1.2.3)

Existing crypto positions default to the harshest capital bucket on day one of the new regime unless the AI has already secured HKMA agreement on a better classification — a transition trap for banks with legacy exposures (para 1.4.2)

obligations: Classify every cryptoasset exposure into Group 1a/1b/2a/2b on an ongoing basis and document the assessment for HKMA review (para 2.1.1)
Notify HKMA before acquiring a new type of cryptoasset and hold it as Group 2b pending HKMA agreement to a different classification (para 2.1.2)
Reclassify a cryptoasset to Group 2b immediately if it stops meeting its classification conditions (para 2.1.3)
controls_and_monitoring: Maintain an ongoing monitoring framework to check that a stablecoin's peg-stabilisation mechanism is actually working (para 2.2.4)
Obtain a legal review confirming enforceability and settlement finality of each cryptoasset arrangement (para 2.3.1)
notifications_reporting: Notify HKMA ahead of acquiring a new type of cryptoasset exposure (para 2.1.2)
Provide classification-assessment documentation to HKMA on request (para 2.1.1)
counterparty_due_diligence: Check whether a stablecoin issuer is itself supervised under prudential capital/liquidity requirements before relying on Group 1b treatment (para 2.2.4)
Check reserve-asset composition, custody arrangements and independent audit frequency for any stablecoin the bank holds (para 2.2.9)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Flag to the board/risk committee that any material new cryptoasset position starts life under the most capital-intensive treatment until HKMA sign-off, which can materially move capital ratios.

title: Banking (Exposure Limits) Code (draft, consequential and other amendments)
supersedes_or_amends: Banking (Exposure Limits) Code (approved 2 December 2024, effective 1 January 2025)
summary: This is a draft update to the statutory code of practice under the Banking Ordinance. It guides how AIs apply parts of the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules (BELR), covering large-exposure limits, connected-party rules and related concepts. Despite being bundled into the HKMA's cryptoasset prudential-standard consultation, the drafted text itself covers unrelated topics. These include what counts as a reliable third-party market data provider and what security is acceptable to a prudent banker, including life insurance policies. It also covers how to calculate an employee's annual salary for staff-lending limits, self-use land, and when two counterparties are 'economically dependent' for large-exposure grouping. No cryptoasset-specific provision appears in the text supplied.

key_points.point: A bank should judge a third-party market-data provider's reliability by its market standing, financial strength and service capacity, track record, and back-up arrangements. The bank can also weigh any other factor it considers relevant.

A life insurance policy can count as acceptable security if written by a Hong Kong-authorized insurer, the insurer or its parent holds at least a BBB- rating (or equivalent). It is valued at the lower of surrender value or 75% of cash value, or a more conservative internal valuation.

An employee's annual salary for staff-lending-limit purposes should add basic salary, other fixed payments and benefits, and estimated performance-based pay for the year. It should exclude variable bonuses and non-monetary benefits like medical insurance.

Two counterparties are 'economically dependent', and so grouped for large-exposure limits, if 50% or more of one party's income or spending, or of its output, flows to or from the other. They are also grouped if one has guaranteed the other's exposure to a degree that could cause its own default.

numbers_and_dates.value: lower of surrender value or 75% of cash value

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Bundled procedurally with the cryptoasset package but not itself cryptoasset-relevant. Compliance can note it and deprioritise it against the LM-1/MR-1/MR-2/CRP-1 drafts.

flags: Despite the 'Cryptoassets standard' consultation title, this Code's drafted text has no cryptoasset provisions in the material supplied -- likely bundled as a consequential/administrative amendment alongside the crypto package rather than a substantive crypto rule.

obligations: Apply the updated market-data-provider reliability factors when relying on subscribed market data for exposure calculations (para 3(2), p.1).
Apply the revised 'economically dependent' tests when grouping counterparties for large-exposure limits (para 6(4), p.14).
controls_and_monitoring: Periodic review of counterparties for economic-dependence indicators during credit reviews and at new-facility approval (para 6(2), p.13).
counterparty_due_diligence: Request counterparties to disclose economic-dependence indicators as part of standard credit review (para 6(2), p.13).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No cryptoasset-specific escalation needed; general large-exposure-grouping update only.
