title: Supervisory Policy Manual MR-1: Market Risk Capital Charge (V.2 - Consultation)
supersedes_or_amends: SPM module MR-1 'Market Risk Capital Charge' (V.1, 15 March 2024)
summary: This is a draft statutory guideline under section 7(3) of the Banking Ordinance for locally incorporated AIs, adding a new section 6 on cryptoasset exposures to the market-risk capital module. It tells banks how to calculate the market-risk capital charge for cryptoasset positions under each of the three approaches the module already covers. These are the simplified standardised approach, the full standardised approach, and internal models. Tokenised assets that mirror a traditional asset (group 1a) and stablecoins referencing traditional assets (group 1b) are generally mapped onto the same risk factors as the assets they represent. This means netting and hedging against the traditional asset is allowed. A separate, harsher, standalone capital charge applies to less traditional 'group 2a' cryptoassets, and internal models cannot be used for them at all.

key_points.point: A bank should follow CRP-1 (a separate module) to first classify each cryptoasset into group 1a, 1b, 2a or 2b before applying this module's rules.

For the simplified standardised approach, a group 1 cryptoasset is converted to HKD at the current spot price and mapped to the same risk category as the traditional asset it represents. Hedging and netting between a token and its underlying traditional asset is recognised for group 1a, and between a stablecoin and the asset it references for group 1b.

Under the full standardised (sensitivities-based) approach, a tokenised instrument's risk exposure must be mapped onto exactly the risk factors used for the conventional asset it mirrors. The bank must apply matching sensitivities in doing so.
Internal models cannot be used at all for instruments referencing group 2 cryptoassets.

Group 2a cryptoassets (which meet a separate hedging-recognition test in CRP-1) get their own standalone capital charge under modified versions of the simplified or full standardised approach. A bank cannot net or offset a group 2a cryptoasset position across different exchanges.

For each group 2a cryptoasset, a bank works out a net long/short position and applies a capital requirement equal to the full value of that net position. Only 65% of any offsetting long-vs-short amount is recognised.
A bank with any cryptoasset exposure cannot use the small-portfolio, de-minimis exemption from market-risk capital rules that would otherwise be available.

Group 2b cryptoassets are not subject to a market-risk capital charge at all. Instead they get the very conservative combined credit/market/CVA-risk treatment (a 1,250% risk weight) under a different section of the capital rules.

numbers_and_dates.item: Group 2a offset recognition factor between long and short positions

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Determines how much market-risk capital a trading or dealing desk must hold against any cryptoasset position, and confirms that holding cryptoassets removes access to the small-book capital exemption.

quote.text: not qualified for the de-minimis exemption for market risk

reading_guide: Read section 6 in full (pp.152-157); it is the only cryptoasset-specific material -- the rest of the module restates existing non-crypto market-risk mechanics.
flags: Depends on the separate CRP-1 module for the group 1a/1b/2a/2b classification test, which this module does not itself define.
Marked 'V.2 - Consultation' in the header, distinct from the currently effective V.1.

obligations: Classify every cryptoasset exposure via CRP-1 before applying a market-risk capital treatment under this module (footnote 79, p.152).
Exclude cryptoasset holdings from any market-risk de-minimis exemption claim (footnote 80, p.152).
Apply the standalone group 2a capital charge with no cross-exchange netting for such positions (paras 6.2.1-6.2.6, p.155).
controls_and_monitoring: Trading-desk systems need to track cryptoasset positions by group (1a/1b/2a/2b) since each has a different capital methodology.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told that any cryptoasset trading book removes the small-book capital exemption and that less liquid ('group 2a') tokens attract materially higher, standalone capital charges.

title: LCQ10: Regulation of digital assets
summary: A written Legislative Council reply clarifies who may lawfully offer a stablecoin under the Stablecoins Ordinance, in response to concerns that virtual-asset OTC shops were exploiting grey areas. It confirms only five categories of 'permitted offeror' may offer a specified stablecoin. Licensed stablecoin issuers, SFC-licensed virtual-asset service providers, stored-value-facility licensees, SFC Type 1-licensed corporations, and authorised institutions (banks). Virtual-asset OTC trading institutions are not permitted offerors and cannot offer stablecoins to any investor type. It also confirms no stablecoin issuer had yet been licensed as of the reply date. That the licensing timetable for the dealing/custodian regimes would be announced after the consultation (closed August 29, 2025) is digested.

key_points.point: Only five types of 'permitted offeror' may offer a specified stablecoin. Licensed stablecoin issuers, SFC-licensed virtual-asset service providers, stored-value-facility licensees, SFC Type 1-licensed corporations, and authorised institutions.
Permitted offerors may offer a regulated (HKMA-licensed-issuer) stablecoin to both retail and professional investors, but an unregulated stablecoin may only be offered to professional investors.

Because virtual-asset OTC trading institutions do not qualify as permitted offerors, they are barred from selling any specified stablecoin to any investor type, whether or not that stablecoin is itself regulated.
As of this reply, the HKMA had not licensed any stablecoin issuer, so members of the public acquiring any stablecoin currently bear their own risk.
The FSTB and SFC are still formulating details of the dealing/custodian licensing regimes based on consultation feedback and will announce a legislative timetable in due course.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is a core compliance reference. It confirms the bank, as an authorised institution, is itself one of only five categories of entity legally permitted to offer a stablecoin. It also confirms that a range of common counterparties, such as VA OTC shops, are explicitly barred from doing so. The bank should build this fact into its own product-distribution and counterparty-screening rules.
reading_guide: Read reply (1) in full for the permitted-offeror list and OTC-shop exclusion; replies (2) and (3) are shorter status updates.
flags: As of the reply date (2025-09-10) the HKMA had licensed no stablecoin issuer, so all currently circulating stablecoins in Hong Kong were unregulated

obligations: As an authorised institution, the bank is a permitted offeror and may offer a stablecoin from an HKMA-licensed issuer to retail and professional investors, but may only offer an unregulated stablecoin to professional investors (reply (1), para 2)
controls_and_monitoring: Client-facing systems should distinguish HKMA-licensed (regulated) stablecoins, tradable with retail clients, from unregulated ones, restricted to professional investors (reply (1), para 2)
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm any referral partner or platform is a permitted offeror (one of the five listed categories) before relying on it to distribute a stablecoin to a client; note that VA OTC shops are explicitly excluded (reply (1), para 3)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told that no stablecoin issuer was HKMA-licensed as of September 10, 2025, so any current stablecoin exposure or distribution by the bank is necessarily to an unregulated issuer and must be limited to professional investors.

title: SB-1 Supervision of Regulated Activities of SFC-Registered Authorized Institutions
supersedes_or_amends: Circular Depositaries of SFC-authorised Collective Investment Schemes (Type 13 Regulated Activity), 27 Jul 2023
summary: SB-1 sets out how HKMA supervises the day-to-day conduct of an AI's SFC-registered activities once it becomes a Registered Institution (RI). It explains HKMA's role as frontline supervisor working alongside the SFC, the mandatory appointment and registration of executive officers and relevant individuals, and HKMA's tiered response to control deficiencies and misconduct. It also lists the events an RI must proactively report, including any plan to start or change virtual-asset-related activities.

key_points.point: Once an AI is registered by the SFC to carry on a regulated activity, it becomes a Registered Institution (RI). The HKMA acts as the RI's frontline day-to-day supervisor while the SFC keeps overall regulatory responsibility and can rely on HKMA's supervision.

An RI must have a minimum of two executive officers responsible for the direct supervision of each of its regulated activities. Each needs the HKMA's prior written consent, with at least one available at all times per activity.

Every 'relevant individual' who performs a regulated function for an RI must be entered in the HKMA Register before starting that work. Any change to their registered details must be notified within 7 business days.

HKMA uses a three-step, risk-based approach to deficiencies. It first shares good practice, then requires corrective action or an independent review for control weaknesses. Finally, it moves to disciplinary or enforcement action where there is a prima facie case of misconduct or unfitness.
HKMA generally expects an RI to meet the same conduct standards the SFC applies to licensed corporations, and can add extra investor-protection requirements specific to the banking context.

For anti-money-laundering purposes, RIs and their AI associated entities must follow the HKMA's AML/CFT Guideline for Authorized Institutions. They must also take into account specific parts of the SFC's own AML/CFT guideline, including its virtual-asset chapter, for definitions and provisions relevant to securities-sector business.

An RI should tell the SFC and HKMA before it starts any virtual-asset activities, such as dealing, advisory or asset-management services in VA products. It should also tell them before changing how it runs those activities, including changes to the kinds of clients it serves.

An RI must give at least 7 business days' advance notice before ceasing a regulated activity or changing its address for carrying one on. It must also notify certain changes to relevant individuals' backgrounds within 7 business days of becoming aware of them.

Both HKMA and SFC can discipline a relevant individual or executive officer found guilty of misconduct or no longer fit and proper. This can include removing them from the HKMA Register or withdrawing an executive officer's consent, with a right of appeal to the Securities and Futures Appeals Tribunal.

numbers_and_dates.item: Minimum executive officers per regulated activity
numbers_and_dates.value: at least two, at least one available at all times

numbers_and_dates.item: Advance notice before ceasing a regulated activity / changing address

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the core rulebook for how HKMA actually supervises the bank's RI status day to day. It covers who must be appointed, what must be pre-notified before touching virtual assets, and how the bank's people and licence can be disciplined.

Register every relevant individual performing a regulated function in the HKMA Register before they start (paras 4.3.1, 4.3.5)

title: 2025 Policy Address
summary: The Chief Executive's 2025 Policy Address is a wide-ranging annual government speech. Only its digital-asset/fintech passages are captured here (paragraphs 97, 103-104, 110-111 and Annex item 22, on pages 39-43 and 97). It confirms continuation of Project Ensemble, including encouraging banks to issue tokenised deposits and settle tokenised money market funds, plus regularising government tokenised bond issuance. It confirms the government is implementing a stablecoin issuer licensing regime. The government is also drafting legislative proposals for a new licensing regime covering digital asset dealing and custodian service providers, with a bill targeted for the Legislative Council in 2026. It also notes the SFC is exploring wider digital asset products for professional investors, and plans automated reporting and surveillance tools. It also notes a tokenised-gold investment product initiative, and a pilot use of tokenised deposits in commodity trade finance with Brazil's central bank.

key_points.point: The government will support issuers in launching tokenised gold as a new investment vehicle, as part of building Hong Kong into a regional gold trading and storage hub.
The HKMA will keep advancing Project Ensemble, encouraging commercial banks to issue tokenised deposits and to settle tokenised money market fund transactions using tokenised deposits.
The HKMA will help the government regularise (make routine) the issuance of tokenised government bonds, and will encourage banks to strengthen risk management via the supervisory sandbox.

The government is implementing the licensing regime for stablecoin issuers and is separately drafting legislative proposals for new licensing regimes covering digital asset dealing and custodian service providers.

The SFC is looking at whether professional investors could be given access to a broader menu of digital asset products and services, conditional on adequate investor safeguards. The SFC will also bring in automated reporting and data-surveillance tools against digital asset risks.
A pilot with Banco Central do Brazil will test tokenised deposits and electronic bills of lading to support international commodity trade finance.
The government commits to bringing a bill to the Legislative Council in 2026 that would set up licensing for firms dealing in digital assets and providing digital asset custody.

title: Supplemental joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities
supersedes_or_amends: Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities, 22 Dec 2023 (amended, not replaced)
summary: This circular updates the original December 2023 SFC-HKMA Joint Circular on intermediaries' virtual-asset activities, easing several requirements after a market review while keeping investor protection. It lets intermediaries offer staking through segregated accounts, allows VA trades via a licensed platform's off-platform service, and clarifies that VA-funded subscriptions/redemptions are not 'dealing' services. It also drops certain suitability and disclosure steps for institutional and qualified corporate professional investors. Separate guidance on HKMA-licensed stablecoin activities is still to come.

key_points.point: Intermediaries -- licensed corporations and registered institutions -- can now offer staking to existing virtual-asset clients. This is only via segregated accounts held at an SFC-licensed trading platform, at an authorized institution, or at that institution's subsidiary.
Staking is defined as locking up a client's virtual assets in a proof-of-stake blockchain's validation process to earn and pass on rewards.

Intermediaries may now execute client virtual-asset trades through a licensed platform's off-platform trading service, after removing the earlier restriction in clause 4.2 of the Terms and Conditions.

Clients paying for or receiving investment-product subscriptions/redemptions in virtual assets are not treated as using a 'dealing' service. The intermediary must still tell the regulators in advance, hold the assets at a licensed platform or authorized institution, and apply the AML travel-rule chapter to those movements.

The net-worth suitability check for clients of VA-exposed products, and the requirement to give a VA-futures-specific risk warning, no longer apply to institutional and qualified corporate professional investors.

Intermediaries must tell the SFC, and HKMA where relevant, in advance before several changes. These are changing the type of clients they serve, first letting clients deposit or withdraw virtual assets, or first offering staking. They also include first allowing VA-funded subscriptions or redemptions, or making other material changes to their VA activities.
Guidance specific to activities involving stablecoins issued under HKMA's own licensing regime is not yet published and will follow separately.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: As an RI, the bank reaches this circular through HKMA's frontline supervision. It now permits staking and simplifies VA-funded subscriptions for the bank's clients, but only inside tightly controlled, pre-notified arrangements.
reading_guide: Read paras 4-10 in full — they are the in force changes; para 1-3 is background on why the update was made.
flags: Corroborates the corrections note that this reaches banks as RIs via HKMA's frontline-supervisor role, not as a direct SFC-issued rule on the bank.

obligations: Offer staking to VA-dealing clients only via segregated accounts at a licensed platform or authorized institution/subsidiary (paras 4-5)
Give SFC/HKMA advance notice before starting or materially changing any VA-related activity, including staking or VA-funded subscriptions (para 10)
Apply AML Chapter 12 controls when handling client VA deposits/withdrawals tied to subscriptions/redemptions (para 7)
controls_and_monitoring: Segregated-account controls that keep staked client VA separate from firm and other client assets (para 5)
Updated suitability workflow to identify institutional/qualified corporate professional investors exempt from the net-worth and VA-futures disclosure steps (paras 8-9)
notifications_reporting: Advance notice to SFC (and HKMA where applicable) before: first VA deposits/withdrawals, first staking, first VA-funded subscription/redemption, or other material VA-activity changes (para 10)
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm any staking or VA-holding arrangement runs through an SFC-licensed platform or authorized institution/subsidiary, not an unregulated venue (para 5)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should note the bank, as an RI, can now offer staking and streamlined VA-funded subscriptions, but only through tightly controlled, pre-notified arrangements — and that stablecoin-specific guidance is still pending.

title: Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions providing virtual asset dealing services and virtual asset advisory services (Appendix A to the Supplemental Joint Circular)
supersedes_or_amends: Appendix 6 to the Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities (22 December 2023 / October 2023 version)
summary: The full, consolidated Terms and Conditions (September 2025 version, Appendix 6) governing licensed corporations/registered institutions providing VA dealing services (via omnibus account with an SFC-licensed platform) and VA advisory services. Covers interpretation, applicable codes/guidelines, financial soundness (12 months' operating expenses in excess liquid capital), operational controls, market-abuse prevention, and extensive client-facing duties (KYC, suitability, disclosure, contract notes/statements/receipts). It also covers custody of client assets and money, a new Part VIII on staking, record keeping, auditor reporting, conflicts of interest, and ongoing SFC/HKMA reporting obligations.

key_points.point: A licensed corporation must keep, in Hong Kong, liquid capital in excess of its own actual operating expenses for a rolling 12-month period. This is over and above the ordinary Financial Resources Rules requirement.

Client virtual assets must be held on trust in segregated 'VA Segregated Account(s)' with an SFC-licensed platform or a qualifying authorized financial institution. Withdrawals must go directly to the client from that account.
Discretionary account managers may only invest less than 10% of a client's account gross asset value in virtual assets where VA trading authority is ancillary to a securities discretionary mandate.

New Part VIII (Staking): intermediaries may only stake client VAs via an SFC-licensed platform or authorized financial institution ('Staking Service Provider') with the necessary regulatory approval, or after discussion with HKMA. They must disclose staking risks (slashing, lock-up, validator risk) and obtain client acknowledgement.

A licensed corporation should not engage in VA market making on an execution venue, for example an SFC-licensed platform, through which it also provides Relevant VA Dealing services to clients. This is a conflicts-of-interest restriction.

Auditors must report annually on whether adequate custody control systems were in place and whether the firm complied with the Custody and Record Keeping parts and the financial soundness requirement.

Standard mandatory risk disclosures to retail clients include that VAs may not be 'property' under law and are not covered by the Investor Compensation Fund. They also include that VAs are not legal tender, and transactions may be irreversible.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the current master terms and conditions for the bank's VA dealing and advisory activities as a registered institution. It directly sets the capital buffer, segregated-custody and new staking-disclosure obligations a compliance head must have live controls for, not merely track for the future.

title: Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions providing virtual asset dealing services and virtual asset advisory services (Appendix A to the Supplemental Joint Circular, September 2025)
supersedes_or_amends: Appendix 6 (October 2023) to the Joint Circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
summary: This is the September 2025 set of licensing conditions that the SFC and HKMA impose on banks and brokers that deal in or advise on virtual assets. Part I covers two dealing models: acting purely as an introducer to an SFC-licensed trading platform, and running client trades through the firm's own omnibus account at such a platform. Part II covers advisory services. The document sets client-classification, suitability, disclosure, custody, record-keeping and reporting standards, and for the first time gives detailed conditions for staking services offered to clients.

key_points.point: A firm that only introduces clients to an SFC-licensed platform must not hold client money or virtual assets itself and must use a written client agreement describing its limited role.
A firm running an omnibus account must keep at least 12 months of operating expenses as excess liquid capital in Hong Kong, on top of the normal Financial Resources Rules.

Retail clients may only trade virtual assets through an omnibus account at a platform that itself is allowed to serve retail investors. They may only trade in tokens that platform makes available to retail investors.
The firm must not offer clients any financing to buy virtual assets, and should try to stop group companies doing so too.

Recommended virtual assets for retail clients must be liquid enough to appear in at least two independent, IOSCO-consistent market indices. They must also be tradable for retail investors on the platform used.
Client virtual assets must be held on trust in a segregated account at either an SFC-licensed platform or an authorized institution (or its subsidiary) that meets HKMA's expected custody standards.

A firm may stake client virtual assets only via a Staking Service Provider that is either an SFC-licensed platform or an authorized institution. This is only once that provider holds the necessary SFC clearance or has discussed the service with the HKMA.

Clients must be told the risks specific to staking, such as slashing, lock-up delays, validator hacking and legal uncertainty over their interest in staked assets. They must sign an acknowledgement of those risks before staking, unless they are institutional or qualified professional investors.
Records on client virtual assets, money, orders and staking must be kept for at least seven years, with contract notes/receipts kept for at least two years.
Any actual or suspected material breach of these terms must be reported to the SFC, and also to the HKMA if the firm is a registered institution, as soon as practicable.

For advisory services, a firm must assess a client's virtual-asset knowledge and risk tolerance before advising, and train clients lacking knowledge. It may only recommend liquid, index-qualifying tokens to retail clients.

title: Supplemental joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities
supersedes_or_amends: Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities (22 December 2023)
summary: This circular adds to the SFC and HKMA's 22 December 2023 Joint Circular on intermediaries' virtual asset (VA)-related activities, bringing in relaxations after industry feedback. It lets intermediaries offer staking services to clients through SFC-licensed platforms or authorized financial institutions (AIs), and allows trade execution through off-platform virtual asset trading platform (VATP) services. It also clarifies that subscribing to or redeeming investment products using virtual assets is not itself a VA dealing service. It exempts institutional or qualified corporate professional investors from certain net-worth and risk-disclosure rules. Separate guidance on activities involving HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers is promised. Updated Terms and Conditions (Appendix 6) come with this circular.

key_points.point: Intermediaries can now offer clients staking services. This is only via segregated accounts kept at an SFC-licensed trading platform, at an authorized financial institution, or at a subsidiary of a locally incorporated authorized institution.

A licensed corporation or registered institution can now route a client's virtual-asset dealing trade through an SFC-licensed platform's own off-platform trading service. The earlier restriction in clause 4.2 of the prior Terms and Conditions has been dropped as a result.

Clients subscribing to or redeeming investment products using virtual assets, or making in-kind subscriptions or redemptions of VA funds, are not treated as receiving VA dealing services. This applies as long as advance notice and custody conditions are met.
The net-worth rule in paragraph 6.2 of the Joint Circular no longer applies to clients who are institutional professional investors or qualified corporate professional investors.
The requirement to give risk disclosure statements for VA futures contracts (Joint Circular paragraph 13) no longer applies to institutional or qualified corporate professional investors.

Intermediaries must tell the SFC, and the HKMA where relevant, in advance of material changes. These include a client's first deposit or withdrawal, first staking service, or first subscription or redemption using VA.
Separate guidance specific to activities involving HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) will come later.

numbers_and_dates.item: Original Joint Circular date being supplemented

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: As an update to the Joint Circular that reaches the bank through the HKMA, this circular relaxes some rules, such as off-platform trading and staking. It also adds new advance-notice duties for staking, VA-funded subscriptions and redemptions, and other material changes to VA-related activities.
reading_guide: Read the full 3-page body. The Appendices, Appendix A clean T&Cs and Appendix B tracked-changes T&Cs, are the detailed in-force rules. They should be read via the separate T&C attachment records rather than in full duplicate here.
flags: Removes the previous restriction (old clause 4.2) that required off-platform VA trades to go through the VATP's own platform only — intermediaries can now use off-platform VATP execution services directly.
Stablecoin-specific intermediary guidance is explicitly deferred to a future, separate circular — this circular does not yet cover HKMA-licensed stablecoin distribution specifics.

obligations: Intermediaries, including RIs, may now offer staking services to clients, but only through segregated accounts with an SFC-licensed platform or an AI (or AI subsidiary), while meeting information and risk-disclosure rules.

Client subscriptions and redemptions of investment products using virtual assets are not VA dealing services, but relevant intermediaries must give advance notice to the SFC (and HKMA where relevant), hold the VAs in accounts with SFC-licensed platforms or AIs, and follow AML/CFT Guideline Chapter 12 for such deposits and withdrawals.

Give the SFC (and HKMA where relevant) advance notice before making material changes to VA-related activities, including the type of client served, a first-time VA deposit or withdrawal, first-time staking services, or a first-time subscription or redemption using VAs.
controls_and_monitoring: Off-platform (over-the-counter) VA trading through SFC-licensed platforms is now allowed for executing client trades, removing the old clause 4.2 restriction.
notifications_reporting: Give the SFC and HKMA advance notice of the changes listed above, and before starting staking or VA-funded subscription/redemption services for clients.
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm staking only happens through licensed VATPs or AIs/AI subsidiaries that follow HKMA staking guidance.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Tell the board this circular updates and relaxes the 2023 Joint Circular — allowing staking and off-platform trading, and clarifying net-worth and disclosure exceptions for institutional or qualified professional investors.

title: LCQ21: e-CNY wallets
summary: This is a written Legislative Council question-and-answer about digital yuan (e-CNY) wallets in Hong Kong. A lawmaker asked about uptake statistics, merchant acceptance, transaction limits, and cross-border settlement under Project mBridge. The Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury replied that the HKMA does not itself hold e-CNY wallet usage statistics, since Mainland operating institutions run the wallets. He confirmed possible future increases to wallet limits are still under discussion with the People's Bank of China, with no fixed timetable. He also gave an update on mBridge reaching a Minimum Viable Product stage in June 2024.

key_points.point: The HKMA does not compile statistics on how many Hong Kong residents have set up e-CNY wallets or how often they use them, because Mainland institutions operate the wallets.

The Legislator's question states the current e-CNY wallet limits as RMB 2,000 per transaction and RMB 50,000 per year. The Government's reply does not dispute this and says only that a possible relaxation is still being discussed with the People's Bank of China, with no confirmed date.
Project mBridge reached its Minimum Viable Product stage in June 2024 and now forms part of Hong Kong's financial market infrastructure, with participating banks setting their own service fees.

The government plans to keep expanding e-CNY application scenarios, and separately plans to keep expanding mBridge's public- and private-sector participation, but gave no fixed rollout timetable for either.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Confirms there is no official Hong Kong data on e-CNY wallet adoption a bank can rely on for market sizing. That mBridge fee-setting is left to participating banks' own commercial judgement, which matters for any bank already connected to mBridge.

title: LegCo Secretariat releases Policy Pulse on "Latest developments in fintech and digital assets in Hong Kong"
summary: This press release announces a LegCo Secretariat briefing paper summarising Hong Kong's fintech and digital asset developments and related Legislative Council discussion. It notes the Stablecoins Bill was enacted in May 2025, creating a licensing regime for fiat-referenced stablecoin issuers with HKMA investigatory and enforcement powers. It records that the government amended the Bill during passage to let stored value facility licensees, not just the original four types of applicants, offer fiat-referenced stablecoins. It also references Legislative Council members' suggestions, including developing offshore renminbi stablecoins and treating Hong Kong as a stablecoin testing ground, plus unrelated fintech topics like green bond tokenisation.

key_points.point: The Stablecoins Bill was enacted in May 2025, creating a licence-based framework for issuers of fiat-pegged stablecoins and giving the Monetary Authority investigation and enforcement powers.
During the Bill's passage, the government widened the pool of eligible applicants to also cover stored value facility licensees, on top of the four categories first put forward.
Some Legislative Council members suggested Hong Kong should seek support to develop offshore renminbi stablecoins and act as a general testing ground for stablecoin activity.
Hong Kong's green and sustainable bond issuance, some of it tokenised, has reached about US$43 billion and has ranked first in Asia for seven straight years since 2018.

title: Supervisory Policy Manual CA-G-1: Overview of Capital Adequacy Regime for Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions (Version 5 - consultation draft)
supersedes_or_amends: Supervisory Policy Manual CA-G-1, Version 4, 29 November 2024
summary: This draft module explains, at a general level, how the HKMA supervises the capital adequacy of locally incorporated banks. It covers solo and consolidated capital ratios, the leverage ratio, capital buffers and the risk-weighting framework. The version put out for consultation adds a new subsection setting out, in outline, how cryptoasset exposures are folded into the existing credit-risk capital-charge methodology. This subsection references the detailed cryptoasset capital rules set out elsewhere in the Banking (Capital) Rules.

key_points.point: A bank's capital adequacy ratio and leverage ratio must be calculated in line with the Banking (Capital) Rules. The MA can impose bank-specific minimum ratios above the regulatory minimum.
For a tokenised traditional asset (Group 1a cryptoasset) held in the banking book, the bank applies the same capital treatment as it would to the underlying asset.

For a Group 1b cryptoasset, held in the banking book, the bank must separately capitalise the credit risk of the reference asset. For example, a reference-asset-backed token such as certain stablecoins counts as Group 1b. The bank must also capitalise the credit risk of the entity performing redemption.

Where only some token holders can redeem directly with the issuer, a member bank must also capitalise the risk that it may have to buy the token from non-member holders. A non-member bank must instead capitalise its credit risk on the members.
Riskier tokens that do not meet the Group 1 classification tests (Group 2b cryptoassets) get a conservative capital treatment set by a separate Banking (Capital) Rules provision.

Extra capital add-ons apply for Group 1b assets held in the trading book, an infrastructure-risk add-on for Group 1 assets, a further add-on for Group 2a stablecoin exposures. A concentration add-on for global or domestic systemically important banks whose Group 2 cryptoasset exposure exceeds a prescribed limit.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the overview-level anchor for the bank's cryptoasset capital charge. The compliance head needs it to confirm the bank's capital model correctly separates Group 1a, 1b and 2 cryptoasset exposures and applies the right add-ons. The line-by-line formulas sit in the underlying capital rules and CRP-1 classification guideline.
reading_guide: Read section 8.7 (pages 47-49) closely. Sections 1-7 and 9-15 are the pre-existing general capital-adequacy overview and only need a skim for context.
flags: This module cross-refers to specific numbered provisions of the Banking (Capital) Rules (e.g. section 376, 380, 384, 385, 388) for the detailed cryptoasset capital formulas; this module itself only summarises them.

obligations: Classify each cryptoasset exposure into the correct Group (1a, 1b, 2a, 2b) before applying a capital charge, per para 8.7.1-8.7.3, p.47-48
Capitalise both reference-asset credit risk and redeemer credit risk for Group 1b holdings in the banking book, per para 8.7.2(a), p.47-48
controls_and_monitoring: Capital-calculation systems and models should be updated to apply the Group 1/2 cryptoasset add-ons described in para 8.7.4, p.48-49, including the systemic-bank concentration add-on where relevant
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board/risk committee should be told how the bank's Pillar 1 capital charge changes once cryptoasset exposures are classified under this new subsection, particularly for any Group 2 concentration add-on if the bank is a G-SIB or D-SIB.

title: HKMA completes e-HKD Pilot Programme and outlines future direction of e-HKD
summary: The HKMA announced the publication of the 'e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 2 Report,' presenting findings from 11 industry pilot groups and the HKMA's updated policy stance. A key Phase 2 finding: the public sees e-HKD and tokenised deposits in a similar light, given high trust in Hong Kong's banking system.

title: e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 2 Report
summary: The HKMA's full Phase 2 Report on the e-HKD Pilot Programme (part of Project e-HKD+) documents 11 industry pilot groups' work. This work is grouped into three areas: tokenised-asset settlement, programmable-money use cases, and payments while offline. It was carried out after Phase 1 finished in October 2023. The report concludes that e-HKD and tokenised deposits deliver comparable retail benefits, and that commercial banks lean slightly toward tokenised deposits (lower cost of capital, faster time-to-market, customer stickiness). It also sets out key design considerations, such as interoperability, programmability, privacy, identity, convertibility, and reliability/performance, for any future retail e-HKD. The HKMA's resulting policy stance prioritises wholesale e-HKD development, treating retail extension as a longer-term, conditional option.

key_points.point: Commercial banks leaned slightly toward tokenised deposits rather than e-HKD, pointing to a lower cost of capital under fractional banking and more design flexibility with a shorter time-to-market. Commercial banks also cited stronger customer stickiness as a reason to favour tokenised deposits.

A natively 'programmable e-HKD' with explicit spending conditions risks undermining fungibility and the 'singleness of money'. Purpose-bound money (PBM)/programmable payments are preferred alternatives that preserve fungibility.

Privacy-enhancing technologies (ZKPs via Zeto and Anonymous Zether) improved privacy with similar settlement times but increased gas fees up to 320 times versus no PETs. A tiered privacy model (basic for low-value, advanced PETs for high-value/high-risk) is recommended.

Public DLTs such as Ethereum Layer 1 currently manage only roughly 15-30 transactions each second, a throughput limit for high-volume retail e-HKD use. The HKMA does not rule out public DLTs but flags a need for further optimisation.
HKMA will prioritise e-HKD development for financial institutions (wholesale); a sustainable private-sector business model for retail e-HKD has not yet been identified.

Digital identity: pilots tested a digital identity framework using verifiable credentials (VCs) and unique identifiers (UIDs) issued by a trusted authority, cryptographically verified before each signed transaction.

It also flags concrete constraints, such as privacy-cost trade-offs and throughput limits, relevant to any DLT settlement build.

title: e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 2 Report
summary: This HKMA report presents the findings of Phase 2 of the e-HKD Pilot Programme. Eleven industry pilot groups tested e-HKD and tokenised deposits across three areas: settling tokenised assets, programmable-money features, and offline payments. It compares e-HKD against privately-issued digital money, especially tokenised deposits, and finds banks generally prefer tokenised deposits for cost-of-capital and design-flexibility reasons. It concludes that most of the programmability and settlement benefits come from smart contracts rather than from the choice of settlement medium. It also concludes that a viable business case for a retail e-HKD has not yet emerged. The HKMA states it will prioritise e-HKD development for wholesale (interbank) use. It will continue preparatory legal, policy and technical groundwork for a possible retail extension by the first half of 2026, without committing to launch retail e-HKD.

key_points.point: Phase 2 involved eleven groups of firms trialling e-HKD and tokenised-deposit use cases in three areas: settling tokenised assets, programmable-money features, and offline payments.

Commercial banks leaned slightly toward tokenised deposits rather than e-HKD, pointing to a lower cost of capital under fractional banking, greater design flexibility, and stronger customer stickiness.

The HKMA will prioritise developing e-HKD for wholesale (interbank) use. It will keep preparing the policy, legal and technical groundwork to allow a possible retail extension, with that preparatory work targeted for completion in 2026. This is not a decision to launch retail e-HKD.
key_points.locator: Executive Summary p.6 / Section 5 Path Forward, p.34

key_points.point: Gains from programmability (smart contracts) were found to come mainly from the smart-contract layer itself, not from whether the settlement medium is e-HKD or tokenised deposits. So e-HKD offers no unique programmability advantage.

Achieving same-day (T+0) settlement of tokenised funds requires on-chain net asset values calculated close to real time, and wider native on-chain tokenisation rather than mere 'digital twins'. It would need a major redesign of core banking infrastructure, not just a new settlement medium.

Privacy-enhancing technologies (zero-knowledge proofs such as Zeto and Anonymous Zether) improved transaction privacy. They increased gas fees by up to 320 times versus transactions without such technology, creating a cost/privacy trade-off for any future e-HKD design.

About 35% of surveyed respondents in one pilot said they would be less likely to use e-HKD for routine payments. They cited concern about the central bank's potential access to personal and transaction data.

For offline payments, survey data showed limited appetite. 48% of respondents said Hong Kong's existing offline payment options, used by about 98% of the population, already meet their needs. 68% of merchants expected fees in line with current merchant fees, making cost recovery for an offline e-HKD difficult.

The e-HKD Industry Forum, formed December 2024, includes a Programmability Working Group of nine firms, co-led by BOCHK, DBS and HSBC. This group is developing common token standards, due to be published separately by the first half of 2026.
The report recommends an account-based balance model over a UTXO model for any future offline e-HKD, because it needs less local device storage and simpler synchronisation.

Design considerations flagged as critical for any retail e-HKD include interoperability across DLT networks and tiered privacy. Tiered privacy means basic privacy for low-value transactions and stronger privacy-enhancing technology for high-value or high-risk ones. Other design considerations include a digital identity/verifiable-credential framework, and non-interest-bearing design to avoid competing with bank deposits.

The report notes that if e-HKD is extended to retail, holding limits and non-interest-bearing design are being considered. This is to reduce the risk of large-scale deposit outflow from banks during stress.

title: Circular on expansion of products and services of virtual asset trading platforms
summary: Under Pillar P (Products) of the ASPIRe roadmap, this circular widens what SFC-licensed VATPs may offer. (i) drops the 12-month track-record requirement for virtual assets sold to professional investors, and for stablecoins from HKMA-licensed issuers sold to retail investors. That 12-month rule still applies when other virtual assets are offered to retail clients. (ii) lets VATPs sell digital-asset-related products and tokenised securities and hold client assets in trust/client accounts with third-party custodians for that purpose. And (iii) lets VATPs' associated entities custody digital assets not traded on their own platform, subject to conditions.

key_points.point: The 12-month track record requirement no longer applies to virtual assets (including stablecoins) offered to professional investors, nor to stablecoins issued by an HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuer offered to retail investors. It still applies to retail offerings of other virtual assets.
VATPs must still perform reasonable due diligence on all virtual assets before admission and disclose where a professional-investor-only asset has less than a 12-month track record.
The 12-month track-record rule is entirely inapplicable to tokenised securities and other digital securities.

VATPs may apply to amend standard licensing conditions to explicitly permit distribution of digital asset-related products and tokenised securities. They may also apply to open trust/client accounts in the VATP's own name with the custodian of the distributed product.

VATPs (via associated entities) may now apply to provide custody services for digital assets not made available for trading on their own platform -- previously disallowed under existing licensing conditions.

VATPs still awaiting completion of the second-phase assessment may nonetheless be allowed to custody tokenised securities where the SFC agrees individually. They must finish that assessment before they can custody other digital assets not traded on their platform.

title: Circular on shared liquidity by virtual asset trading platforms
summary: Under Pillar A (Access) of the ASPIRe roadmap, this circular lets SFC-licensed VATP operators link their order books with affiliated overseas trading platform operators (OVATPs) through a 'Shared Order Book'. This pools client orders into one combined liquidity pool. It sets rules for eligible OVATPs, trading and settlement risk management, and preventing market misconduct. Settlement risk management includes delivery-versus-payment (DVP) settlement, an Unsettled Trade Limit, a reserve fund, and compensation arrangements. It also requires mandatory prior written SFC approval, with detailed terms and conditions in the appendix (id fda3c03f239d).

key_points.point: An OVATP wanting to join a Shared Order Book should be based somewhere that belongs to the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), or to an FATF-style regional body. Its rules should broadly match FATF and IOSCO recommendations for crypto/digital-asset markets on market abuse and safeguarding client assets.

The Shared Order Book should only take fully pre-funded orders, settled through delivery-versus-payment (DVP), with settlement happening at least once a day and during the day too. This keeps unsettled exposure within a set Unsettled Trade Limit.

Platform Operators must keep a Hong Kong reserve fund, held on trust, sized at no less than the Unsettled Trade Limit, to cover client losses from failed settlements. They must also keep insurance or compensation cover for Settlement Assets no less than required under VATP Guidelines para 10.22.
Retail clients can only use a Shared Order Book if the extra cross-border risks, including possibly weaker client protection overseas, are clearly disclosed and the client chooses to take part.
Platform Operators should obtain prior written SFC approval before running a Shared Order Book, and conditions will be imposed through licence terms.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This binds the affiliated VATP, not the bank directly, but a compliance head overseeing a bank-affiliated VATP group should treat these as the requirements to meet. FATF-aligned overseas affiliate regulation, a funded Hong Kong reserve, and prior SFC approval -- before that VATP shares order-book liquidity.

quote.text: Virtual asset trading is borderless by nature and liquidity is fragmented across liquidity pools

reading_guide: Read the main circular body (pp.1-4) for the policy rationale and headline requirements. The appended Terms and Conditions (id fda3c03f239d) contain the enforceable in force detail and should be read alongside it.
flags: Only permits intra-group/affiliated OVATP integration as a first step, not third-party liquidity pools — SFC states it will separately 'explore the feasibility' of extending to regulated overseas pools within the same group before any further expansion.

Settlement risk is newly introduced by this regime: under current (non-shared) VATP operation, settlement risk is minimal because trades are pre-funded and settled instantly within the Platform Operator.

counterparty_due_diligence: If the bank's affiliated VATP wants to join a Shared Order Book, confirm the overseas affiliate operates in an FATF (or FATF-style regional body) member jurisdiction, with rules substantially matching FATF/IOSCO recommendations (para 7, p.1-2).
Check the VATP keeps a Hong Kong reserve fund on trust, sized at no less than the Unsettled Trade Limit, plus compensation cover no less than VATP Guidelines para 10.22 (paras 16-17, p.3).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: If the bank has an affiliated VATP, tell the board that Shared Order Book access needs prior written SFC approval (paras 26-27, p.4), and brings new settlement risk not present in standalone VATP operation.

title: Terms and conditions for operating a Shared Order Book (Appendix to the Circular on shared liquidity by virtual asset trading platforms)
summary: These are the detailed, licence-imposed terms and conditions supporting the shared-liquidity circular. They define eligibility (the Other Virtual Asset Trading Platform (OVATP) must be a 'related corporation' under section 53ZRC of the AMLO), what Shared Order Book Rules must cover, and trading operations. They also define settlement controls, which cover delivery-versus-payment, netting, and Unsettled Trade Limit factors. They also cover default management, compensation and reserve fund mechanics, and steps to prevent market misconduct. They set a 7-year record-keeping duty, client disclosures, and mandatory reporting of incidents and regulatory changes to the SFC.

key_points.point: The OVATP should be a 'related corporation' of the Platform Operator, as defined in section 53ZRC of the AMLO.

The reserve fund should be kept, in fiat currency unless the SFC agrees otherwise, across one or more segregated accounts at an authorized financial institution. It must be at least as large as the Unsettled Trade Limit.
Records must be retained for at least 7 years, enough detail to rebuild the complete history of every order, trade, settlement, surveillance alert, and incident response.

A Platform Operator should tell the SFC without delay about any actual or suspected serious breach, or any regulatory action taken against the OVATP or its Designated Custodian. It should also report any serious adverse event, or any possible regulatory change that could affect them.
A Platform Operator should keep a contingency plan ready to pause order matching with the OVATP and isolate its own client orders if there is a serious disruption.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This binds VATPs that run shared order books, not the bank directly. It sets the bar for reserve funds, record-keeping, and incident reporting that a compliance head should expect from a bank-affiliated VATP before relying on shared-liquidity arrangements.

title: HKSAR Government’s Third Digital Green Bonds Offering
summary: The HKSAR Government announced pricing of its third digital green bond issuance (~HK$10 billion equivalent across HKD, RMB, USD and EUR tranches) on the HSBC Orion platform, cleared via CMU. It is the first digital bond anywhere to bring tokenised central bank money, e-CNY and e-HKD, into how it settles. It reached a record size for a digital bond with over HK$130 billion in total subscriptions, and stretched its tenor to 5 years. It also used Digital Token Identifiers (DTIs) plus wider ICMA Bond Data Taxonomy coverage. It is the first issuance since the Government's Policy Statement 2.0, which commits to making tokenised Government bond issuance a regular practice.

key_points.point: This is the first digital bond issuance anywhere to bring tokenised central bank money (e-CNY and e-HKD) into its settlement process. This runs alongside the traditional settlement rails, for the HKD and RMB tranches.
The issuance size hit a record HK$10 billion, drawing total subscriptions above HK$130 billion, the biggest digital bond deal seen anywhere so far. Its tenor stretched to as long as 5 years.
Digital Token Identifiers (DTIs, ISO 24165) were obtained for all tranches and linked to ISINs and the issuer's LEI. ICMA Bond Data Taxonomy adoption was expanded versus the second issuance.

This is the first tokenised bond issuance following the Government's Policy Statement 2.0 on Development of Digital Assets in Hong Kong, which commits to regularising issuance of tokenised Government bonds.
Settlement cycle is T+1. Clearing and settlement via CMU (operated by the HKMA) with linkage to Euroclear and Clearstream. Governing law is Hong Kong law. Listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Names the bank, or its peers, as direct participants -- platform provider, joint coordinators, settlement agents -- in a HK$10 billion tokenised bond issuance settling partly via tokenised central bank money. This gives compliance a live template for tokenised-deposit/CBDC settlement operational and counterparty risk.

flags: This confirms actual (not merely piloted) use of tokenised central bank money in a live government bond settlement, ahead of the HKMA's own e-HKD Phase 2 report (same period) which deprioritises retail e-HKD but treats wholesale/tokenisation use as the near-term priority — the two documents are mutually consistent (wholesale-first).

title: HKMA introduces HKEX as strategic shareholder in CMU OmniClear Holdings Limited (with photo)
summary: The HKMA announced a deal under which Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX) is to acquire a 20% stake in CMU OmniClear Holdings Limited. CMU OmniClear Holdings is the holding company the HKMA's Exchange Fund set up in October 2025 to own CMU OmniClear Limited. CMU OmniClear operates the Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU), Hong Kong's central securities depository system, on the HKMA's behalf. After the deal, the Exchange Fund will hold 80% and HKEX 20%. The stated goal is to grow CMU into a broader, multi-asset-class central securities depository, supporting settlement and collateral services across a wider range of asset classes. title: HKMA announces new phase of Project Ensemble to support real-value transactions in tokenised deposits and digital assets
summary: The HKMA launched EnsembleTX, the pilot phase of Project Ensemble, moving from the proof-of-concept Ensemble Sandbox (running since August 2024) to real-value transactions in tokenised deposits and digital assets. Seven named commercial banks will issue tokenised deposits to customers and settle interbank tokenised deposit transactions through EnsembleTX, alongside other named industry pioneers. The pilot's initial focus is tokenised money market fund transactions and real-time liquidity/treasury management. EnsembleTX runs throughout 2026, starting with interbank settlement via the existing HKD Real Time Gross Settlement system, before being upgraded to round-the-clock settlement in tokenised central bank money. The SFC is a partner in the Ensemble Architecture Community.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This pins down exactly which banks are live participants issuing and settling real-value tokenised deposits under Ensemble TX from launch. This is direct competitive and peer-group intelligence for a bank's own tokenised-deposit strategy.
reading_guide: Two short list pages; read in full.

title: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism Detection and prevention of potential layering activities in money laundering
summary: This SFC circular alerts licensed corporations, SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities to an emerging pattern of layering activities in money laundering. This pattern is characterised by frequent, swift fund/VA deposits and withdrawals with little or no trading. It sets out red flags drawn from the AML/CFT Guideline and Hong Kong Police Force intelligence, including scam-related proceeds being converted to VAs and withdrawn to unhosted wallets. It reiterates regulatory expectations that firms implement robust transaction monitoring, screen VA transactions and wallet addresses, and establish bank account/wallet address registration or whitelisting mechanisms. It warns of supervisory and enforcement action, including licence conditions, suspension or revocation, for firms that fail to detect and prevent such activity.

key_points.point: Licensed firms are reminded that strict AML/CFT compliance is both a legal obligation and essential to safeguarding operational and systemic integrity.

Typical layering pattern: frequent, scattered small/odd-amount deposits from multiple bank accounts, later withdrawn to the client's own (sometimes different) bank accounts. There is no or minimal trading, and accounts going inactive afterward.
Scam proceeds are being layered through licensed firms via bank transfers, some converted to VAs and withdrawn to unhosted wallets, to obscure fund flows.

Licensed firms must put in place transaction-monitoring systems that are robust and effective, scaled to their transaction volume and ML/TF risk. They must also apply extra vigilance when handling deposits and withdrawals.

Firms should establish a registration mechanism for client bank accounts and a whitelisting mechanism for VA wallet addresses, verifying ownership (for example, micropayment test, message signing test). They should avoid sole reliance on client-provided documents.

Whenever a registered bank account or whitelisted wallet address is added or replaced, senior management should review and approve it, applying a risk-sensitive approach. This can be the MIC of AML/CFT, the compliance officer, or the MLRO.
Clients may not share bank accounts or wallet addresses with each other. This bar covers ones that were previously removed or replaced too, except where an account is jointly owned.
Firms should consider limiting withdrawals to the accounts/wallets from which funds/VAs were originally deposited and implementing a withdrawal holding period (for example, one to two days).
VA transactions and wallet addresses should be screened using blockchain analytical tools before and, on a risk-sensitive basis, after transactions to identify illicit-linked addresses.

SFC will not hesitate to use powers under the SFO and AMLO against firms and senior management (directors, ROs, MIC, MLRO) for AML/CFT failures. This includes licence conditions, business restrictions, suspension/revocation, fines and reprimands.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This circular's AML/CFT obligations bind licensed corporations and SFC-licensed VA service providers, not the bank directly (the bank's governing text is the HKMA AML/CFT Guideline). Compliance should use its layering red flags as reference indicators for the bank's own monitoring and be alert when client fund flows touch LC/VATP accounts exhibiting these patterns.

quote.text: will not hesitate to exercise its powers under the Securities and Futures Ordinance

reading_guide: Read paras 5-23 (the red flags and expected controls); paras 1-4 and 24-26 are framing/contact boilerplate and can be skimmed.
flags: Explicitly links scam/fraud proceeds to VA conversion and unhosted wallet withdrawal as a specific observed ML typology, correcting an assumption that VA-related AML risk at licensed firms is mainly about crypto-native crime rather than traditional bank-fraud proceeds being laundered through VA conversion.

controls_and_monitoring: Use the red-flag typologies here (structured deposits, rapid deposit-withdrawal with no trading, VA conversion to obscure fund flow, shared IP/device, cross-jurisdiction transfers) as reference indicators when calibrating the bank's own AML/CFT transaction-monitoring thresholds, since the SFC AML/CFT Guideline cited (paras 5.4, 5.7-5.8, 7.20, 7.29, 12.7, 12.16 and Appendix B) binds LCs and SFC-licensed VASPs, not AIs directly (paras 5-11, 15-23)
counterparty_due_diligence: Where the bank's clients also hold accounts with LCs/VATPs, note these firms are expected to register/whitelist client bank accounts and wallet addresses and scrutinise frequent changes -- useful context when reconciling unusual transfer patterns touching the bank's own accounts (paras 19-23)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told this typology addresses layering via LCs and VATPs specifically -- the bank's own governing AML/CFT text is the HKMA's AML/CFT Guideline for Authorized Institutions, not this SFC circular, though the red flags are useful cross-reference for the bank's transaction monitoring.

title: CA-G-5 Supervisory Review Process
supersedes_or_amends: CA-G-5 Supervisory Review Process (V.6, 24.01.2025)
summary: This statutory guideline sets out how the HKMA runs the Pillar 2 supervisory review process, including how it may adjust a bank's individual capital requirement above the regulatory minimum. Version 7 adds a dedicated paragraph on cryptoassets. Because crypto activities and their risks are still new and evolving, the HKMA may respond to capital or risk-management shortcomings tied to crypto. It may use capital add-ons, provisioning requirements, activity limits, or other mitigation measures. Separately, the module's general Pillar 2 governance guidance now lists cryptoasset activity alongside securitisation as an example of a complex activity. The board and senior management must understand this as part of firm-wide risk oversight.

key_points.point: Because crypto risks are new and still developing, the HKMA may use any of four supervisory tools where it sees capital or risk-management gaps tied to a bank's crypto activity. These are extra capital add-ons, requiring provisions for foreseeable and estimable crypto losses, imposing activity limits, or other mitigation measures.

The board and senior management should understand firm-wide risks from complex or new activities. Crypto is now named alongside securitisation and 'originate-to-distribute' lending as an example. They should also set firm-wide prudential limits consistent with the bank's risk appetite.
A dedicated SPM module, CRP-1 Classification of Cryptoassets, is now listed in this module's index of related modules under a new 'Cryptoassets' heading.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Compliance should flag that examiners can now raise Pillar 2 capital or impose activity limits specifically because of crypto risk-management gaps. Any internal audit or risk-management finding on crypto should be remediated before a supervisory review cycle.

quote.text: Cryptoasset activities and associated risks are relatively new and evolving

reading_guide: Read para 3.6.6 (p.52-53) and para 4.2.8 (p.63) for the crypto-specific text. The rest of the module is the general Pillar 2/SRP framework and can be skimmed unless capital planning is in scope.
flags: The cover page date reads 'V.7 - xx.12.2025', an unfilled placeholder date rather than a specific day, even though the HKMA catalogue lists the issue date as 27 Nov 2025 - worth confirming the final gazetted date before citing this version number externally.

obligations: Ensure board/senior management oversight of crypto activity is documented as part of firm-wide risk management, since examiners now look for this explicitly (para 4.2.8, p.63)
controls_and_monitoring: Maintain evidence that crypto-related risks are identified, quantified, and provisioned where losses are foreseeable, to avoid triggering a Pillar 2 capital add-on (para 3.6.6, p.52)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told that a Pillar 2 review can now result in capital add-ons, provisioning demands, or activity limits specifically tied to crypto risk-management weaknesses (para 3.6.6, p.52).

title: CR-G-8 Large Exposures and Risk Concentrations
supersedes_or_amends: CR-G-8 Large Exposures and Risk Concentrations (V.4) dated 13.12.2024
summary: CR-G-8 version 5 is a statutory guideline under Banking Ordinance s.16(10). It explains how locally incorporated AIs apply the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules (BELR) on single-counterparty, equity and land exposures. The crypto change is a new part of section 2.8: cryptoasset-related exposures are valued under a new Division 5A of BELR Part 7. Only crypto exposures that carry a counterparty's default risk count toward large exposure limits; pure holdings without counterparty risk are disregarded. The bank identifies counterparties as it already does for capital purposes. Valuation depends on the exposure type, its Group 1a/1b/2a/2b classification and whether it sits in the banking or trading book. The rest of the module restates existing limits, board oversight and breach notification duties that apply equally to crypto-related counterparty exposures.

key_points.point: The module is a statutory guideline and applies to AIs incorporated in Hong Kong; overseas-incorporated AIs still report large exposures of their Hong Kong operation.
A large exposure is any exposure to one counterparty or linked group equal to or above 10% of Tier 1 capital.
The statutory ceiling on exposure to a single counterparty or linked group is 25% of Tier 1 capital. Local global systemically important banks face a 15% cap toward other such groups.
Crypto-related exposures are valued under BELR Part 7 Division 5A, separately from ordinary exposures in Divisions 4 and 5.

For crypto exposures that carry counterparty default risk, the bank must first identify each counterparty or linked group, reusing the counterparty identification already done for capital, then value each under Division 5A.
Crypto exposures with no counterparty credit or default risk are ignored when measuring large exposures.
Which valuation rule applies depends on the exposure category in the Rule 2(1) definition, the asset's Group 1a/1b/2a/2b classification, and banking versus trading book.
Some crypto exposures borrow Division 5 methods (for example Group 1a banking book items). Others reuse capital-rule figures for credit or default risk or jump-to-default amounts.
Because crypto markets change fast, the Monetary Authority may set a different valuation method for one or more AIs by written notice under BELR Rule 77A(2).
Any breach of statutory or HKMA-set limits should be reported to the HKMA as soon as practicable, with an impact assessment and a rectification plan.
A notifiable breach must be reported in writing with details of the limit, timing, cause and remediation; suspected breaches should be flagged before the investigation ends.
Failing to meet a prescribed notification or remedial action requirement is an offence for the AI and its directors, chief executives and managers.

numbers_and_dates.item: Local G-SIB to G-SIB-linked group limit

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Exposures to crypto counterparties, such as a stablecoin issuer, custodian or derivative counterparty, now count toward the bank's large exposure limits under a dedicated valuation method. Compliance must make sure limit monitoring and breach notification cover these crypto-linked counterparties.
reading_guide: Read paras 2.8.1 and 2.8.8-2.8.12 for the crypto valuation rules, then section 6 on breach notification. The rest restates the existing large exposure framework.
flags: The PDF version header shows 'V.5 - xx.12.2025' with the day left blank; the catalogue issue date is 27 Nov 2025.

Crypto holdings with no counterparty default risk (e.g. unbacked tokens held outright) are disregarded for large exposure limits (footnote 13), so they are controlled through capital rather than this limit.

obligations: Identify each counterparty or linked group behind a crypto-related exposure and value it under BELR Part 7 Division 5A (paras 2.8.8-2.8.9).
Keep counterparty exposures within 25% of Tier 1 capital (para 2.2.1).
controls_and_monitoring: Ensure large exposure systems capture crypto-related counterparty exposures and apply the right method by group and book (para 2.8.10).
Watch for any HKMA written notice setting a different crypto valuation method (para 2.8.12).
notifications_reporting: Report limit breaches to the HKMA as soon as practicable with a rectification plan (para 6.1.1).
Notifiable events must be reported in writing with the listed particulars (paras 6.2.1-6.2.2).
counterparty_due_diligence: Identify stablecoin issuers, custodians and derivative counterparties as exposure counterparties where default risk exists (para 2.8.9).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board should know that crypto counterparty exposures now count toward large exposure limits and that breach notification failures are criminal offences for directors and managers.

title: LM-1 Regulatory Framework for Supervision of Liquidity Risk
supersedes_or_amends: LM-1 Regulatory Framework for Supervision of Liquidity Risk (V.4) dated 13.12.2024
summary: LM-1 version 5 is a statutory guideline on applying the Banking (Liquidity) Rules (BLR). It covers the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR), Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) and Core Funding Ratio (CFR). The crypto additions are section 5.9 and a new Annex 3. Crypto exposures generally follow the treatment of traditional exposures with equivalent economic risk, but Annex 3 sets specific rules. Only Group 1a tokenised versions of eligible assets can count as high-quality liquid assets (HQLA). Bank-issued tokenised claims can be treated as deposits, stablecoins are treated like non-HQLA debt securities, and Group 2 cryptoassets get the harshest treatment. The HKMA may impose stricter treatment for any cryptoasset with extra liquidity risk, and CBDCs are excluded.

key_points.point: Crypto exposures, whether assets, liabilities or contingent items, should generally be treated like traditional exposures with economically equivalent risk across LCR, NSFR, LMR and CFR.
Annex 3 adds crypto-specific rules because of extra risks and thin historical data. CBDCs are outside Annex 3 and are generally treated like the issuing jurisdiction's notes and coins.

A cryptoasset can count as HQLA only if it is a Group 1a token of an eligible asset class, and both the traditional and tokenised forms meet the HQLA criteria. It must also meet operational requirements, for example an established ledger and a deep market.

An issuing bank may treat its tokenised claims (Group 1a, redeemable at par in fiat, backed by the bank's own balance sheet) as deposits or unsecured funding. If the bank cannot identify holders at all times, it must treat them as other unsecured wholesale funding, and they can never count as stable retail deposits.
Tokenised claims used mainly for payment within an operational relationship with wholesale customers follow the operational deposit treatment.

A bank holding tokenised deposits issued by another AI or a regulated bank treats them like unsecured loans to financial institutions. No inflow is recognised if they cannot be redeemed within 30 days.
Stablecoins in this annex are Group 1b coins, plus fully collateralised Group 2 coins that fail only the redemption test because of notice periods or fixed terms.

A bank that issues a stablecoin redeemable within the LCR period must apply a 100% outflow rate, unless the backing assets would qualify as HQLA apart from encumbrance. The segregated backing assets count as pledge under the NSFR.

A bank holding a stablecoin treats it as non-HQLA debt, generally with a 0% LCR inflow and an 85% NSFR required stable funding factor. This falls to 50% if it matures within 12 months into fiat. Issuer redemption options are assumed not exercised.
Group 1a tokens that are not HQLA follow their traditional equivalent. Any extra liquidity risk from the token form, such as delayed cash flows from the infrastructure, must be reflected.

Other Group 2 cryptoassets held get a 100% NSFR required stable funding factor and no LCR inflow. Unsecured crypto borrowings due within the LCR period take a 100% outflow unless covered by the bank's own unencumbered stock, and crypto-denominated funding gets 0% available stable funding.
The HKMA may impose stricter treatment where a cryptoasset carries extra liquidity or contingent risk, for example the need to support redemptions of a stablecoin the bank issues or services.
Crypto derivatives, crypto-collateralised funding, collateral swaps and committed crypto lending lines follow existing treatment for similar transactions.

For smaller category 2 institutions, the LMR and CFR broadly mirror these rules. Only eligible Group 1a tokens can be liquefiable assets, stablecoins redeemable within a month are qualifying liabilities, and Group 2 holdings get no inflow and a 100% required core funding factor.

numbers_and_dates.item: Stablecoin issuer LCR outflow (redeemable in LCR period)

numbers_and_dates.value: 85%; 50% if maturing within 12 months into fiat

numbers_and_dates.item: Group 2 cryptoasset holdings NSFR RSF factor
Unsecured Group 2 crypto borrowings LCR outflow

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: If the bank issues tokenised deposits or a stablecoin, or holds either, Annex 3 sets how they hit the LCR and NSFR. The holder-identification test for tokenised deposits and the 100% outflow for issued stablecoins are the points most likely to affect product design and compliance sign-off.

quote.text: these liabilities must not be treated as stable retail deposits

reading_guide: Go straight to section 5.9 (p.67) and Annex 3 (pp.91-98). The rest of the module is the general liquidity framework and can be skipped for crypto purposes.
flags: Tokenised deposits whose holders the issuing bank cannot identify at all times are treated as wholesale funding under the LCR, a harsh outcome for permissionless or freely transferable deposit tokens (Annex 3, para 4).
Footnote 98 names non-contractual support for stablecoins the bank issues or services as a reason for stricter HKMA treatment.
Version header shows 'V.5 - xx.12.2025' with the day left blank.

obligations: Count crypto as HQLA only if all Annex 3 para 1 conditions are met.
Apply the Annex 3 para 4 holder-identification test to any tokenised deposits the bank issues.
Apply a 100% LCR outflow to issued stablecoins redeemable within the LCR period (Annex 3, para 7).
Apply the Group 2 treatment (100% RSF, no inflows, 0% ASF on crypto funding) (Annex 3, para 8(b)).
controls_and_monitoring: Liquidity reporting systems must tag crypto exposures by type (tokenised claim, stablecoin, other) and group (Annex 3, para 3).
Reflect infrastructure-driven delays in token cash flows in maturity buckets (Annex 3, para 8(a)).
notifications_reporting: Be ready for HKMA-imposed stricter treatment of a specific cryptoasset (Annex 3, para 9).
counterparty_due_diligence: For tokenised deposits held, confirm the issuer is an AI or regulated bank and check redemption timing (Annex 3, para 5).
For stablecoins held, check backing, segregation and contractual maturity or notice terms (Annex 3, paras 6-7).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Issuing tokenised deposits or a stablecoin changes the bank's liquidity ratios; the board should see the Annex 3 impact, including potential non-contractual support risk, before launch.
