title: Code of Practice for the Purposes of Providing Guidance in Respect of the Provisions of Rules 20(4)(b), 37(2) and (3) and 41 of the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules (Chapter 155S)
supersedes_or_amends: Banking (Exposure Limits) Code (prior version)
summary: Known as the Banking (Exposure Limits) Code, this statutory code of practice interprets three specific rules under the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules. It covers how to judge whether a third-party data provider is 'competent and reliable' for valuing collective investment scheme exposures. It also covers what counts as a bank's self-use land, and when two counterparties are 'economically dependent' on each other for large-exposure grouping purposes. It took effect 1 January 2026. Despite being bundled into the November 2025 cryptoassets standard package, the code's own text contains no cryptoasset-specific rule. It appears to be a general large-exposures code amended and reissued alongside the crypto package rather than a crypto-specific instrument.

key_points.point: To decide if a market data provider is competent and reliable for equity-exposure valuation under rule 20(4)(b), a bank should weigh several factors. These are the provider's market standing, financial strength, service capacity, track record, and contingency arrangements.

The code defines when one counterparty is 'economically dependent' on another for grouping purposes under rule 41. It lists seven specific tests, such as 50%+ of receipts coming from the other party or shared reliance on the same funding source.

A bank may rely in good faith on information a counterparty provides about its own economic dependence, as long as it does not conflict with information the bank otherwise holds. The bank should actively request this information during credit reviews and when granting new facilities.

Where Entity A depends economically on Entity B, the bank has to fold Entity A into Entity B's linked-counterparty group. However, that does not automatically mean Entity B belongs in Entity A's group too, unless Entity B independently satisfies the grouping criteria.

numbers_and_dates.item: effective date of this amended code
economic dependence threshold based on shared revenue/output
numbers_and_dates.value: 50% or more of gross receipts, expenditures, or product/output tied to the other entity

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This code governs how the bank groups connected counterparties for its large-exposure limits generally. Compliance should note it is not crypto-specific despite arriving in the crypto package. It does not change how crypto counterparty exposures are treated beyond the ordinary economic-dependence tests.

quote.text: economically dependent on the reference counterparty

reading_guide: Read paras 3 and 6 (pages 4-12) for the two live guidance items. Para 5A on self-use land premises is a narrow, low-relevance point and paras 4, 5 and 7 are repealed and can be skipped.
flags: Despite being Annex 2(j) of the 'Cryptoassets Standard' package, this code contains no cryptoasset-specific text at all - it is a general amendment to the large-exposures code bundled into the same release date; treat it as background, not crypto-specific guidance.

obligations: Apply the five-factor test when assessing a third-party market data provider used for CIS look-through valuation under rule 20(4)(b) (para 3(2), p.4)
Apply the economic-dependence tests when building linked-counterparty (LC) groups for large-exposure limit purposes under rule 41 (para 6(4), p.10)
controls_and_monitoring: Request economic-dependence information from counterparties during regular credit reviews and at new-facility approval, and cross-check it against information already held (para 6(2), p.11)
counterparty_due_diligence: Check whether a counterparty is controlled by, or economically dependent on, other counterparties already on the bank's books, since this determines its LC group membership and exposure limit treatment (para 6(4)-(5), pp.10-11)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Not a board-level matter on its own; relevant to large-exposure limit calculation and monitoring, and this code brings no new crypto-specific board consideration.

title: CR-L-5 Major Acquisitions and Investments: BELR Part 3
supersedes_or_amends: CR-L-5 Major Acquisitions and Investments: BELR Part 3 (V.2) dated 09.08.19
summary: CR-L-5 version 3 is a statutory guideline about acquiring share capital in a company. It explains when a locally incorporated AI needs the Monetary Authority's prior written consent, which is needed once the stake is worth 5% or more of its Tier 1 capital. The crypto change is a footnote: under BELR Rule 21(2), a cryptoasset that carries the economic substance of equity ownership counts as share capital for these rules. The module also covers exemptions (debt recovery, underwriting, insurance business, trading book below a threshold), application content, grounds for refusal, conditions, revocation and a one-month advance notice for other significant acquisitions.

key_points.point: A locally incorporated AI should not acquire shares in a company worth 5% or more of its Tier 1 capital without the Monetary Authority's written consent. This also covers setting up a company.
Tokens that give the economic substance of equity ownership count as share capital for this consent regime.
The 5% test uses book value at acquisition plus any unpaid amount, normally against the previous quarter-end Tier 1 figure.
Exemptions cover debt recovery, underwriting for up to seven working days, insurance business meeting set conditions, and trading book holdings whose assessment amount is below 5% of Tier 1.
The rule applies on a solo and consolidated basis, so acquisitions through a consolidated subsidiary also need consent.
AIs should approach the HKMA early and file a written notice with details such as value, capital impact, funding, business plan and the target's regulation.
Consent may be refused, conditioned or revoked if depositors' interests would be threatened; the AI gets a chance to make representations first.

AIs are expected to give at least one month's notice of other acquisitions with significant effect. Examples include entering a new line of business or cutting the capital ratio by around 0.5% or more.

numbers_and_dates.item: Advance notice for other significant acquisitions

numbers_and_dates.value: around 0.5% or more of capital adequacy ratio

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: A bank taking a stake in a digital asset business, or holding tokens that represent equity, may need prior HKMA consent at the 5% of Tier 1 level. A strategic crypto investment that changes the bank's business line may need a month's advance notice even below that level.
reading_guide: Read para 1.1, footnote 1 on page 3 and paras 2.5 and 2.9; the deemed-consent transition in 2.4 is historical.
flags: Only crypto link is footnote 1 extending 'share capital' to equity-like cryptoassets.
Version header shows 'V.3 - xx.12.2025' with the day left blank.

obligations: Obtain the Monetary Authority's prior written consent before acquiring share capital, including equity-like tokens, of 5% or more of Tier 1 (para 1.1, footnote 1).
controls_and_monitoring: Track aggregate holdings in each company, including tokenised equity, against the 5% Tier 1 threshold on solo and consolidated bases (paras 2.1.3, 2.3.1).
notifications_reporting: Submit a formal written notice seeking consent, with the listed information (para 2.5.1).
Inform the HKMA of major changes between application and completion (para 2.5.3).
Give at least one month's advance notice of other significant acquisitions (para 2.9.1).

title: Cryptoassets standard: SPM modules, code of practice, disclosure templates and tables, and banking returns
summary: This HKMA circular finalises a package of capital, disclosure and reporting changes for Hong Kong's new cryptoasset prudential standard. The changes follow several rounds of industry consultation. It finalises a new module, CRP-1 (classification of cryptoassets), plus revisions to nine other Supervisory Policy Manual (SPM) modules and a code of practice. All of these take effect on 1 January 2026, alongside related Banking (Capital), (Disclosure) and (Exposure Limits) amendment rules. It also issues a revised disclosure package with a new crypto-specific disclosure part, and confirms new banking return templates. A six-month transitional easement lets banks with no cryptoasset exposure on 1 January 2026 keep using the old return templates until 30 June 2026.

key_points.point: Ten SPM modules/code items (listed (a) to (j)) were finalised and take effect on 1 January 2026, implementing three sets of Banking Ordinance amendment rules due to commence the same day.
key_points.locator: p.1, 'SPM modules and code of practice'

key_points.point: Compared with the consultation draft, the HKMA further clarified how central bank digital currencies are treated for prudential purposes. It also eased the process for classifying tokenised traditional assets, both in module CRP-1.
The HKMA clarified that moving a position between books purely because of a cryptoasset reclassification is not treated as a book switch. So it does not trigger the usual capital surcharge in MR-1.
A revised standard disclosure package, including a new Part XII for cryptoasset exposures, takes effect for any reporting period ending after 1 January 2026.
Seven new or revised banking return templates, including capital adequacy, market risk/CVA, liquidity, leverage and large exposures returns, were scheduled for release in December 2025.
Banks with no cryptoasset exposure as of 1 January 2026 may keep using the old return templates for six months, until 30 June 2026, for four of the listed returns.
Even banks using the transitional easement must still apply the revised completion instructions for unrelated miscellaneous changes in the capital adequacy ratio return from 1 January 2026.

A bank that gains cryptoasset exposure after 1 January 2026 may agree a temporary alternative reporting arrangement with the HKMA. The same option is open to a transitional bank not yet ready to switch return formats. The arrangement covers the period 31 January to 30 June 2026.

title: MR-1 Market Risk Capital Charge
supersedes_or_amends: MR-1 "Market Risk Capital Charge" (V.1) dated 15 March 2024
summary: MR-1 is the HKMA's Supervisory Policy Manual module telling locally incorporated banks how to work out the capital charge for market risk. A new section 6, added for the cryptoassets standard, sets out how each of the four cryptoasset categories defined in module CRP-1 must be handled. Group 1a tokens (tokenised traditional assets) and Group 1b tokens (asset-referenced coins such as stablecoins) are mapped onto the risk factors of the asset they represent or reference. So they mostly ride on the existing framework. Group 2a tokens get their own separate risk bucket with no diversification benefit against other assets, and cannot use a bank's internal model. Group 2b tokens fall outside market-risk rules altogether. Instead they pick up the flat, punitive treatment set in the credit-risk rules.

key_points.point: Before applying any market-risk method, a bank must first sort each crypto position into Group 1a, 1b, 2a or 2b using module CRP-1.
A bank holding any cryptoasset exposure loses access to the small-portfolio (de-minimis) exemption from market-risk capital rules, even if the position is tiny.
For Group 1a tokens, hedging and netting against the underlying traditional asset is allowed provided both are mapped to the same risk category.

For Group 1b tokens (for example, stablecoins), the credit risk that the redeemer or an intermediary fails to honour redemption is capitalised separately under the credit-risk rules, not under market risk.
Banks using the internal models approach cannot use it at all for Group 2a tokens; only the two standardised methods are allowed for that group.
For Group 2a tokens, positions in the same coin held on different exchanges cannot be netted against each other; long and short amounts must be kept separate.
The formula for a Group 2a token's net position only lets 65% of the smaller of the long/short side offset the larger side, so full netting is not available.
The capital charge for a Group 2a token's position risk is simply 100% of that net position, added up across all such tokens with no diversification credit.
Options on a Group 2a token must be valued with a scenario (matrix) method. This moves the price and volatility by up to 100% each way; simpler option methods are banned for these tokens.

A footnote confirms that when a bank moves a position between the banking book and trading book purely because of a CRP-1 reclassification, this is not treated as a book-switch. It does not trigger the usual capital surcharge for switching.
key_points.locator: para 6.1.1, footnote 79, p.151; also para 2.1.15 with footnote 13, p.14

numbers_and_dates.item: Offsetting haircut in Group 2a net position formula
numbers_and_dates.value: 35% of the smaller side is disregarded (65% offset factor)

numbers_and_dates.item: Position-risk capital charge for a Group 2a cryptoasset
Scenario-matrix price/volatility shift range for Group 2a options
numbers_and_dates.value: plus/minus 100%, at least seven observation points

title: MR-2 CVA Risk Capital Charge
supersedes_or_amends: MR-2 "CVA Risk Capital Charge" (V.1) dated 15 March 2024
summary: MR-2 tells banks how to compute the capital charge for CVA risk, the risk that a derivative counterparty's credit quality worsens before a trade settles. A new section 4 extends this to crypto derivatives and to securities-financing trades collateralised by cryptoassets. Group 1a and 1b tokens are broadly treated like the traditional asset they represent, though a bank must separately check the tokenised version for extra liquidity mismatch risk. Group 2a tokens can use most CVA methods except the advanced standardised approach. Group 2b tokens skip CVA calculation entirely and instead get the same flat, punitive capital charge used for their credit risk.

key_points.point: Derivatives and securities-financing trades on Group 1a tokens are generally capitalised the same way as trades on the underlying traditional asset.
A bank must assess the tokenised asset in its own right, not simply assume it qualifies for the same treatment as the traditional asset it copies, because liquidity can differ.

If a bank cannot get enough data to model the liquidity difference between a tokenised asset and its traditional counterpart, it must fall back to the simpler basic CVA approach. It cannot use the standardised approach instead.
Derivatives on Group 1b tokens (stablecoin-type instruments) follow the same CVA treatment as trades on non-tokenised assets.
For Group 2a tokens, every CVA method applies except the standardised CVA approach, which is off-limits for these instruments.
Group 2b token exposures do not get a separate CVA calculation; they instead carry the same conservative 1,250% risk weight used for their credit risk.
Securities-financing trades collateralised by Group 2b tokens only attract a CVA charge if the HKMA decides that CVA risk on those trades is material.

numbers_and_dates.item: Conservative risk weight applied to Group 2b cryptoasset CVA/credit exposures

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This module sets how much extra capital a bank's derivatives desk needs to hold against counterparty credit-spread risk on crypto trades. It also flags that the harshest, 1,250% treatment applies automatically to the riskiest token category, with no modelling option.

quote.text: Qualification for a given treatment cannot be derived from the respective traditional

flags: 1,250% risk weight for Group 2b tokens is the same flat treatment used elsewhere in the package for the same category, confirming there is no separate lighter CVA path for it

obligations: Independently assess each tokenised traditional asset for liquidity/basis-risk differences before assuming it can use the standardised CVA approach (para 4.2.2)
Apply the 1,250% conservative treatment to Group 2b token CVA/credit exposures with no separate CVA modelling (para 4.3.2)
controls_and_monitoring: Maintain data sufficient to model liquidity-characteristic differences between a tokenised asset and its traditional equivalent, or default to the basic CVA approach (para 4.2.2)
notifications_reporting: Securities-financing trades collateralised by Group 2b tokens only need a CVA charge if the HKMA determines the risk is material — implies case-by-case HKMA engagement (para 4.3.3)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board/risk committee should know that the most speculative token category (Group 2b) automatically draws the harshest fixed capital treatment across both credit and CVA risk, discouraging exposure to it.

title: Annex 4: Standard Disclosure Templates and Tables
supersedes_or_amends: Implementation of Pillar 3 Disclosure Requirements – Consolidated and Enhanced Framework – Standard Disclosure Templates and Tables (2018)
summary: This is the full set of Pillar 3 public disclosure templates and tables that locally incorporated banks must use, updated to add a new Part XII covering cryptoasset exposures. Part XII adds four items. Table CAEA is a narrative on the bank's crypto activities and risk approach. Template CAE1 covers exposure amounts and risk-weighted assets by cryptoasset group. Template CAE2 covers accounting classification of crypto holdings. Template CAE3 covers liquidity metrics for crypto exposures, for banks designated as category 1 institutions. Crypto exposures must also feed into the ordinary credit-risk, market-risk and liquidity templates elsewhere in the package, not only the dedicated crypto tables. Frequency ranges from annual (Table CAEA) to semi-annual (CAE1-3), and formats are mostly flexible rather than fixed.

key_points.point: Table CAEA requires an annual narrative naming the bank's crypto-related activities. These include holding crypto directly, trading for clients, equity stakes in crypto exchanges or fund managers, or issuing crypto liabilities, and whether the bank acts as a redemption intermediary.
The same narrative must cover how each crypto activity feeds into credit, market, operational and liquidity risk, the mitigation policies applied, and the most significant current and emerging risks.
For group 1 cryptoassets, the bank must explain, using public information only, how it assessed each of the four BCR classification conditions.

Template CAE1 breaks out total exposure, exposure at default, and risk-weighted assets separately for group 1a, 1b, 2a and 2b cryptoassets. It splits these by credit risk and market risk columns, on a semi-annual basis.

A bank must add extra rows for any individual stablecoin or unbacked cryptoasset that is 'material' under the template's own test. Broadly, that means the bank's group 2 exposure ratio is at or above 0.3% and that single asset is over 5% of all group 2 holdings.

Template CAE1 also captures how close a bank is to the group 2 (unbacked/algorithmic) cryptoasset concentration limits. It must show any exposure or RWA once the 1% of Tier 1 capital threshold is crossed, and total RWA once the 2% cap is breached.

The bank must separately state the total market value of client cryptoassets it holds in custody, broken down by tokenised traditional assets, stablecoins, and other crypto, as narrative accompanying CAE1.

Template CAE2 shows how crypto holdings and crypto liabilities are booked on the balance sheet: cash, financial assets by measurement basis, and intangibles. This is split again by the four crypto groups, on a semi-annual basis.

Template CAE3 reports the liquidity-coverage-ratio haircuts, inflow and outflow rates, and net-stable-funding factors applied to each crypto category. It is required semi-annually, only from banks designated as category 1 liquidity institutions with crypto exposure.

Group 1 and group 2 crypto exposures reported in the crypto-specific templates must also be folded into the bank's ordinary templates elsewhere in the package. This includes the credit-risk, market-risk and liquidity disclosure templates. Doing so avoids double-counting confusion.
key_points.locator: Template CAE1, points to note (ii); Template CAE2, point to note (i)

numbers_and_dates.value: bank's group 2 exposure ratio >= 0.3% and that single asset > 5% of total group 2 exposure

title: CR-G-9 Exposures to Connected Parties
supersedes_or_amends: CR-G-9 Exposures to Connected Parties (V.4) dated 13.12.2024
summary: CR-G-9 version 5 is a statutory guideline under Banking Ordinance s.7(3) on how locally incorporated AIs identify, limit and control exposures to connected parties under BELR Part 8. The text does not mention cryptoassets directly. It appears in the package because connected-party exposures are valued the same way as Part 7 large exposures, which now include the new crypto valuation rules. It sets the aggregate and single connected-party limits, arm's-length dealing, board oversight, independent monitoring and breach reporting.

key_points.point: AIs should deal with connected parties at arm's length, and the same impartiality applies to non-lending dealings such as asset sales and service contracts.
Breaching a Rule 87 limit is a notifiable event; the AI must tell the Monetary Authority as soon as practicable after it knows or should know.
Connected parties include directors, credit approvers, controllers and their relatives, plus firms and unlisted companies in which they hold key roles.
The aggregate connected-party exposure ratio must not exceed 15% of Tier 1 capital. Exposure to a single connected natural person is capped at the lower of HK$20 million or 5% of Tier 1.
Connected-party exposures are valued in the same way as Part 7 counterparty exposures, subject to Part 8 adjustments, and only the portion not covered by recognised credit risk mitigation counts.
The board should understand the legal limits, approve a connected-party policy and ensure systems exist to monitor and control these exposures.
A designated independent unit should monitor connected-party exposures, and internal audit should review them regularly.
Figures in the large exposures return, MA(BS)28, and the compliance certificate, MA(BS)1F(a), must be accurate, and limit breaches reported promptly.

numbers_and_dates.value: lower of HK$20m and 5% of Tier 1 capital

title: CRP-1 Classification of Cryptoassets
summary: CRP-1 is a new, non-statutory SPM guidance note (Version 1, dated 1 January 2026). It explains how AIs sort their cryptoasset exposures into prudential groups, under the HKMA's implementation of the Basel cryptoasset standard. A cryptoasset reaches Group 1 only if it passes four classification conditions. Group 1a covers tokenised traditional assets and Group 1b covers stablecoins with an effective stabilisation mechanism, while everything else falls into Group 2. Group 2 is split into Group 2a (limited hedge recognition, if three hedging recognition criteria are met) and Group 2b (no hedge recognition). The module sets extra safeguards for assets on permissionless blockchains, requires HKMA notification and agreement before any new cryptoasset can leave Group 2b, and lets the HKMA override a bank's classification. The Banking (Capital) Rules (BCR), Part 12, carry the legal requirements and prevail over the module in any conflict.

key_points.point: CRP-1 is guidance, not statute: a new non-statutory guidance note that applies to every AI from 1 January 2026.
The legal rules on classification conditions, initial approval and later reclassification sit in BCR Part 12. If CRP-1 and the BCR differ, the BCR wins.

A cryptoasset is a digital store of value that relies mainly on cryptography and distributed ledger technology (DLT). It can be used to pay, invest or access goods and services. Securities issued on DLT are in scope; securities on centrally run electronic registers are not.
Central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) sit outside the standard and are generally treated like the fiat money of the issuing central bank.
Group 1 requires all four classification conditions. Group 1a is tokenised traditional assets; Group 1b is stablecoins with an effective stabilisation mechanism. Anything not in Group 1 is Group 2.

Group 1 assets get the same capital, liquidity and other treatment as the underlying traditional asset. The HKMA may add an infrastructure risk add-on, which starts at zero but can be raised if weaknesses are seen in the underlying technology.

Group 2 covers all unbacked cryptoassets, plus tokenised assets and stablecoins that fail the conditions, and attracts full capitalisation. Hedging recognition criteria split it into Group 2a (some hedging recognised) and Group 2b (none).
Look-through: funds such as Group 2b cryptoasset ETFs, entities whose value derives mainly from Group 2b assets, and equity, derivative or short positions in them are all treated as Group 2b.
The standard and CRP-1 took effect on 1 January 2026. Any cryptoasset exposure held before that date must sit in Group 2b until the HKMA agrees the bank's classification assessment.

Classification is a continuing duty. AIs must have policies, procedures, governance, staff and IT able to assess cryptoasset risk, and must fully document the evidence for each classification and give it to the HKMA on request.

Before acquiring a new type of cryptoasset, an AI must notify the HKMA and hold it as Group 2b until the HKMA agrees any better classification. A first Bitcoin spot or derivative trade triggers notification; Bitcoin futures after existing spot exposure do not.

If an agreed Group 1a, 1b or 2a asset stops meeting its conditions or criteria, the AI must drop it to Group 2b at once until it complies again. Later purchases take the last assessed classification. Moving back up from Group 2b needs HKMA agreement.
The HKMA will override a bank's classification it disagrees with, and will compare and share classification information with overseas supervisors for consistency.

For the same type of tokenised asset issued on the same platform (for example the CMU) with identical infrastructure, one assessment is enough once the HKMA is satisfied. The AI must still watch for material platform changes.

Condition 1 (tokenised assets): the token must carry the same credit and market risk and the same legal rights as the traditional asset. It fails if it must first be redeemed or converted to gain those rights, or if its design adds counterparty credit risk.

Condition 1 (stablecoins): the coin must be redeemable for a fixed amount of reference assets. The AI needs a monitoring framework showing the peg works, must verify reserve ownership, and must run due diligence including a basis risk test, with methods and results available to the HKMA. The issuer must be prudentially supervised for capital and liquidity.

Redemption risk test: reserves, net of other claims, must always cover the total peg value of coins outstanding, even under severe stress, with over-collateralisation if the reserves carry extra risk.

For currency-pegged coins, reserves must be low-risk, short-dated, high-quality and liquid enough for instant redemption. They must be held bankruptcy-remote and in the peg currency (a small-amount exception applies). A bank acting as both custodian and deposit taker need not be bankruptcy-remote from itself if it meets the stated conditions.
Reserve governance: a public reserve mandate; circulation value disclosed every trading day and composition weekly; independent verification at least every six months; external audit at least yearly.
Coins backed by other cryptoassets, or kept stable by algorithmic supply changes, can never meet condition 1.

Condition 2: rights must be legally enforceable wherever the asset is issued and redeemed, with settlement finality. The AI must commission a legal review, and stablecoins must redeem within five calendar days. Issuer documentation must be public; a regulator-approved public offer satisfies this, otherwise an independent legal opinion is needed.

Condition 3: the asset's functions and network must adequately control material risks (credit, market, liquidity, operational, cyber, third-party, AML/CFT), and network design must make every transaction and participant traceable.

Condition 4: every entity that redeems, transfers, stores or settles the asset, or manages reserves, must be regulated and supervised (or meet suitable risk standards) and disclose its governance. Node validators may rely on risk standards instead.

Permissionless blockchains: such assets can still reach Group 1 if issuer-level extra measures cover governance, technology, settlement and AML/CFT risk. HKMA-licensed stablecoins are treated as meeting them; other stablecoins need a regime the HKMA judges comparable to the Stablecoins Ordinance. Tokenised traditional assets need approval by a financial market regulator plus comparable rules; sovereign issues are treated as compliant. The measures include segregation of high-risk operations, advance notice to the supervisor of material outsourcing, annual business continuity tests, holder identity checks and controls on unhosted wallets.

Group 2a needs all three hedging criteria: an eligible exposure, high liquidity, and at least 100 real price observations. An eligible exposure is, for example, spot backed by a single-asset derivative or ETF/ETN traded on a regulated exchange and cleared by a qualifying central counterparty. High liquidity means an average market capitalisation of at least HKD 78 billion and a 10% trimmed mean daily volume of at least HKD 390 million over the past year. The HKMA will adopt any Basel updates to these thresholds.

numbers_and_dates.item: Effective date of standard and CRP-1
Maximum redemption period for full redeemability

numbers_and_dates.value: average at least HKD 78 billion over previous year
10% trimmed mean daily volume at least HKD 390m over previous year
at least 100 real price observations over previous year (BCR s.281)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Every crypto or tokenised exposure the bank takes needs a documented classification, including tokenised deposits, bonds, stablecoins and crypto ETFs. Any new asset type needs an HKMA notification and sits in punitive Group 2b until the HKMA agrees otherwise. Compliance should own the notification and evidence trail, because missing it means full-capital treatment and supervisory override.

quote.text: an AI must immediately reclassify the cryptoasset as a Group 2b cryptoasset

reading_guide: Read sections 1.3-1.4 and 2.1 first (group structure, effective date, notification and reclassification process), then section 2.6 for permissionless chains and section 3 for Group 2a thresholds. Paragraphs 2.2.6-2.2.9 on reserve quality matter mainly when assessing a specific stablecoin.
flags: CRP-1 is a non-statutory guidance note; the binding rules are in BCR Part 12, which prevails (para 1.1.4).
Exposures held before 1 January 2026 default to Group 2b until the HKMA agrees the assessment (para 1.4.2), even if they would otherwise qualify.
Stablecoins licensed by the HKMA are only deemed to meet the permissionless-chain measures (para 2.6.3); they still need to pass classification conditions 1-4.
Footnote 10 carves out a bank that is both custodian and deposit counterparty from the bankruptcy-remoteness test for reserve deposits.
Per corrections_for_synthesis item 4, a later HKMA letter (June 2026) clarifies and loosens para 2.6.4; check that letter before citing para 2.6.4 as current practice.

obligations: Classify every cryptoasset exposure into Group 1a, 1b, 2a or 2b on an ongoing basis (paras 2.1.1, 2.1.8-2.1.10).
Keep pre-2026 holdings in Group 2b until the HKMA agrees the classification assessment (para 1.4.2).
Hold any newly acquired cryptoasset type in Group 2b pending HKMA agreement (para 2.1.2).
Downgrade to Group 2b immediately if an agreed asset stops meeting its conditions or criteria (para 2.1.3).
Apply the last assessed classification to later purchases of the same asset (para 2.1.4).
Run a legal review of each cryptoasset arrangement for condition 2 (para 2.3.1).
For stablecoins, run due diligence and a basis risk test at acquisition and regularly after (para 2.2.4).
controls_and_monitoring: Maintain risk policies, procedures, governance, staffing and IT able to assess cryptoasset risks (para 2.1.1).
Operate a monitoring framework confirming each stablecoin's stabilisation mechanism works as intended (para 2.2.4).
Verify ownership of stablecoin reserve assets independently of the issuer; third-party assessments only if reliable (para 2.2.4).
Monitor material changes to tokenisation platforms covered by a single assessment (para 2.1.11).
Track Group 2a thresholds (HKD 78bn market cap, HKD 390m trimmed volume, 100 price observations) over a rolling year (para 3.1.1).
Fully document classification evidence, reserve assessment, basis-test methods and legal reviews (paras 2.1.1, 2.2.4, 2.3.1).
notifications_reporting: Notify the HKMA before acquiring a new type of cryptoasset (para 2.1.2, footnote 7).
Obtain HKMA agreement for any classification other than Group 2b, and for any reclassification out of Group 2b (paras 1.4.2, 2.1.2, 2.1.5).
Provide classification evidence, basis-test methods and results, and legal reviews to the HKMA on request (paras 2.1.1, 2.2.4, 2.3.1).
counterparty_due_diligence: Stablecoin issuers: prudential supervision, reserve sufficiency and quality, bankruptcy remoteness, public mandate, disclosure frequency, audit and verification (paras 2.2.4-2.2.9).
Legal enforceability and settlement finality in all issue and redemption jurisdictions; redemption within five calendar days (paras 2.3.1-2.3.2).
Regulated status and governance disclosure of transfer/settlement operators, wallet providers, reserve custodians and stabilisation administrators (paras 2.5.1-2.5.2).

For permissionless chains: issuer licensing or comparable regime, or financial-market-regulator approval for tokenised assets; issuer governance, technology, continuity and AML/CFT controls (paras 2.6.3-2.6.7).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board should know that each new crypto or tokenised asset needs an HKMA notification and starts in full-capital Group 2b, that the HKMA can override the bank's classification, and who owns the ongoing classification evidence.

It sets out which of the new crypto disclosures are mandatory only for banks that actually have cryptoasset exposure, and cross-references the standard templates annex for the exact format.

Banks designated as category 1 liquidity institutions with cryptoasset exposure must file the semi-annual liquidity-requirements-for-crypto template (Template CAE3) under section 16ZQK (local banks) or 103AC (overseas-incorporated banks).

A summary table maps each liquidity disclosure item to who must make it, on what frequency, and in what format. The crypto liquidity narrative is annual and flexible in format, while the crypto liquidity template is semi-annual and fixed format.
For the standard templates generally (including the new crypto ones), a bank must follow the associated explanatory notes issued by the HKMA rather than relying on the BDR text alone.
The guideline is interpretive only - if it conflicts with the Banking (Disclosure) Rules themselves, the Rules prevail, and this text is not a substitute for the bank obtaining its own legal advice.

title: Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework: Frequently Asked Questions (Last updated December 2025)
summary: This is the OECD's own FAQ on interpreting CARF, hosted by IRD as background reading rather than a Hong Kong-specific document. It clarifies edge cases such as branch nexus, retail payment reporting thresholds, staking/wrapped-token treatment, NFT exclusions, and how tokenised traditional financial assets are treated.

key_points.point: A retail payment transfer above USD 50,000 made as agent for the customer must be reported as a separate 'Reportable Retail Payment Transaction' category.
Moving crypto into a staking contract and receiving a matching tokenised version back counts as a reportable exchange transaction.

An NFT is excluded from reporting only if it does not represent a financial asset and is not marketed as an investment. It must also not be an AML/KYC (anti-money laundering / know-your-customer) virtual asset under FATF rules. On top of that, it must have low value and trading volume (illustratively, under USD 200 and no meaningful trading).

A tokenised traditional financial asset is NOT treated as a reportable crypto-asset if it can only be held or transferred through custodial accounts at regulated custodians, that is, it is not truly disintermediated.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: These OECD interpretive answers will likely shape how Hong Kong's own CARF rules are applied in practice. Compliance can use them to pressure-test edge cases (staking, tokenised securities, NFTs), even though the document itself is not a Hong Kong legal instrument.

title: Public consultation on implementation of Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and amendments in relation to Common Reporting Standard launched
summary: The government launched a public consultation on implementing the OECD's Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) and related amendments to the Common Reporting Standard (CRS) in Hong Kong. Both will be enacted via changes to the Inland Revenue Ordinance (Cap. 112). CARF, published by the OECD in 2023, lets partner jurisdictions automatically swap tax data on crypto-asset transactions with each other. The government plans to finish the local legislative amendments within the coming year, aiming to start CARF information exchange from 2028 and the newly amended CRS from 2029. Proposed changes also include mandatory registration for relevant financial institutions and higher penalties, partly in response to an OECD peer review of Hong Kong's CRS framework. The consultation runs to 6 February 2026.

key_points.point: The government will amend the Inland Revenue Ordinance (Cap. 112) to implement the OECD's Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and the newly amended Common Reporting Standard.
The government targets completing the legislative amendments within the coming year, starting automatic exchange of crypto-asset tax information from 2028 and the newly amended CRS from 2029.
Proposed amendments include mandatory registration for relevant financial institutions and increased penalty levels, partly to address an ongoing OECD peer review of Hong Kong's CRS administration.
The public consultation covers reporting procedures, record-keeping requirements, and penalties and enforcement, and closes for comments on 6 February 2026.

title: Implementation of Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and Amendments in Relation to Common Reporting Standard in Hong Kong
summary: This joint FSTB/Inland Revenue Department consultation paper sets out legislative proposals for Hong Kong. It would bring the OECD's Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) and an amended Common Reporting Standard (CRS) into the Inland Revenue Ordinance. It defines who counts as a Reporting Crypto-Asset Service Provider (RCASP), what crypto-asset transactions must be reported, and what due diligence RCASPs must run on customers. It also proposes mandatory RCASP registration, record-keeping, enforcement powers, and a tiered penalty regime modelled on existing CRS sanctions. Separately, it proposes amending CRS itself so it also covers certain digital financial products. It excludes CBDCs (central bank digital currencies) and specified electronic money products, which fall under CARF instead. It also proposes strengthening CRS's own administrative framework (mandatory RFI registration, higher penalties) in response to an OECD peer review. It sets a phased implementation timeline running from 2027 through the first CARF information exchange in 2028 and first amended-CRS exchange in 2029, and invites comments by 6 February 2026.

key_points.point: A Reporting Crypto-Asset Service Provider (RCASP) is any business executing crypto-asset exchange transactions or transfers for customers, or making available a trading platform (including certain decentralised platforms). RCASPs will have to register, run customer due diligence and report transaction data to the Inland Revenue Department.

Crypto-assets that cannot be used for payment or investment are outside CARF's reporting scope. So are central bank digital currencies and specified electronic money products, though CBDCs and some e-money products fall under the amended CRS instead.

RCASPs must obtain customer self-certifications to determine tax residency, cross-checked against AML/KYC information. For existing customers, self-certifications must be obtained within twelve months of CARF taking effect in Hong Kong.

All RCASPs with any nexus to Hong Kong must register on the IRD's CARF Portal, whether or not they have information to report. Registration is proposed to run from September 2027 and be completed by end-December 2027 or end-January 2028, depending on when the nexus arose.
key_points.locator: para 2.8 and Chapter 6 timeline, p.20 and p.48

key_points.point: RCASPs must keep due diligence and reporting records for at least six years. They must tell IRD within one month if the business is dissolved or terminated, with the obligation to preserve records falling on former directors if the RCASP is dissolved.

Proposed penalties for RCASP non-compliance range from a HK$10,000 fine for failing to register or file a return. The maximum is a HK$100,000 fine plus three years' imprisonment on indictment for knowingly providing false information with intent to defraud. An administrative-penalty alternative to prosecution is also proposed.

Entities that are both RCASPs and Reporting Financial Institutions (RFIs) will, under the proposed default treatment, have to report the same crypto-asset sale or redemption proceeds twice. They must report under both CARF and the amended CRS, and will not be allowed to report only once.

The government proposes introducing mandatory registration and a stronger penalty regime for CRS-reporting financial institutions generally. This responds to an OECD peer review finding gaps in how Hong Kong identifies reporting financial institutions and enforces the existing CRS regime.

Implementation is phased. RCASP due diligence starts January 2027, and RCASP registration starts from September 2027. First CARF returns are filed by RCASPs in June 2028, with first CARF information exchange with partner jurisdictions in September 2028. Amended-CRS due diligence starts January 2028, with first exchange in September 2029.

numbers_and_dates.item: Maximum penalty for fraudulent RCASP information on indictment
numbers_and_dates.value: HK$100,000 fine or HK$20,000 per user, whichever higher, plus 3 years' imprisonment

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: If the bank or a group entity executes crypto-asset exchange transactions or operates a trading platform for customers, it will likely be an RCASP. It will face new mandatory registration, customer due diligence, and reporting duties from 2027, with real penalties for non-compliance. Banks that are already CRS Reporting Financial Institutions must also plan for dual CARF/CRS reporting on the same crypto-asset disposals under the government's proposed default treatment.

quote.text: no room for deviation

reading_guide: Read the Executive Summary (p.1-4) and Chapter 1 (RCASP scope, transactions, due diligence, p.5-21). Also read the penalty and timeline sections of Chapter 2 (p.23-26) and Chapter 6's implementation table (p.44-45). Chapters 3 and 5's treaty and administrative detail, and Annex C, can be skimmed unless drafting a formal consultation response.
flags: CARF and the amended CRS are described in the paper as internationally finalised standards with 'no room for deviation'; the consultation only invites views on Hong Kong-specific implementation choices (e.g. dual reporting treatment, registration mechanics), not on whether to adopt CARF/CRS at all.

The proposed default treatment requires reporting the same crypto-asset sale/redemption proceeds under both CARF and CRS for dual RCASP/RFI entities -- this is a genuine compliance duplication the government acknowledges but still recommends, to avoid IT complexity from an alternative optional treatment.

obligations: If the bank or an affiliate executes crypto-asset exchange/transfer transactions or operates a trading platform for customers, assess RCASP status against the nexus criteria (tax residency, incorporation, management, or place of business in Hong Kong) (para 1.9-1.13, p.9-11).
Prepare to register on the IRD's CARF Portal from September 2027 if any RCASP nexus criterion is met, regardless of whether there is any information to report (para 2.8, p.20).

Build customer due diligence processes to obtain and validate self-certifications of tax residency for crypto-asset users, cross-checked against existing AML/KYC data, from January 2027, including for pre-existing customers within twelve months of CARF taking effect (para 1.15, p.13).

If the bank is a CRS Reporting Financial Institution as well as an RCASP, prepare to report crypto-asset sale/redemption proceeds under both CARF and the amended CRS, since the government's proposed default treatment does not permit single reporting (para 4.14-4.17, p.35-36).
controls_and_monitoring: Retain due diligence and CARF/CRS reporting records for at least six years, including a defined process for record preservation and IRD notification if any RCASP entity is dissolved or its business terminated (para 2.5-2.7, p.19-20).
Build validation controls for CARF XML data files before submission, since IRD requires test-file validation before self-developed software can be used (para 3.6, p.28-29).
notifications_reporting: File annual CARF Returns via the CARF Portal from June 2028 onward (including nil returns with stated reasons if no reportable crypto-asset information exists) (para 3.5, p.28, and Chapter 6 table, p.44-45).
Notify IRD within one month of any RCASP entity's dissolution or business termination, or change of contact details after termination (para 2.6-2.7, p.19-20).
counterparty_due_diligence: Where the bank deals with third-party RCASPs (e.g. VATPs or crypto exchanges as counterparties or referral partners), check their expected CARF registration and due diligence readiness given the 2027 compliance start date.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board/risk committee should be told that the bank may become subject to a new mandatory crypto-asset tax reporting regime (RCASP registration, due diligence and returns) from 2027, with meaningful penalties for non-compliance, and that if the bank is both an RFI and RCASP it faces duplicated CARF/CRS reporting on the same crypto-asset transactions under the government's current proposal; the 6 February 2026 consultation deadline is the window to raise concerns before the rules are finalised.

title: Supervisory Policy Manual CR-G-8: Large Exposures and Risk Concentrations
supersedes_or_amends: Supervisory Policy Manual CR-G-8, prior version
summary: CR-G-8 is a general SPM module (V.5, effective 19 Dec 2025) explaining how banks value exposures for the statutory large-exposure limits. These limits sit under the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules (BELR) Part 7. Most of it covers ordinary credit, derivative and securities-financing exposures and does not mention cryptoassets. A dedicated set of paragraphs was added covering how cryptoasset-related exposures are valued for large-exposure purposes, cross-referring to the new Banking (Capital) Rules cryptoasset provisions.

key_points.point: For large-exposure valuation, ordinary (non-cryptoasset) exposures are valued under Part 7 Divisions 4 and 5. Cryptoasset-related exposures get their own valuation regime under a new Division 5A.

Division 5A covers both credit-counterparty-risk and non-credit-counterparty-risk cryptoasset exposures. A bank must first identify the counterparty for each exposure, using the same counterparty identification already done for the capital-rules cryptoasset calculation.

How Division 5A applies to a given cryptoasset exposure depends on which definitional limb it falls under. It also depends on whether the underlying is a group 1a, 1b, 2a or 2b cryptoasset, and whether it sits in the banking or trading book.

In some cases a bank must apply the ordinary Division 5 valuation rules to certain non-credit-counterparty-risk cryptoasset exposures. In others it can reuse the valuation it already produced for capital purposes.

Because cryptoassets and their underlying technology and markets are still new and changing, the HKMA can prescribe a different valuation methodology than the standard one in the BELR. It does this by written notice to one or more banks.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Confirms that cryptoasset exposures are not simply folded into existing large-exposure valuation methods. They sit under a separate BELR division, and the HKMA has reserved a case-by-case power to override the standard valuation approach for individual banks.

quote.text: innovative, evolving and dynamic nature of cryptoassets

reading_guide: Read paras 2.8.1 and 2.8.8-2.8.12 (pages 18-21); skip the surrounding general discussion of sovereign concentration risk and standard derivative/SFT valuation.

obligations: Identify counterparties for cryptoasset-related exposures consistently with the identification already performed for capital-rules purposes, before valuing them under Division 5A (para 2.8.9).
Apply the correct valuation limb (Division 5 vs 5A, and group 1a/1b/2a/2b classification) per exposure (para 2.8.10).
controls_and_monitoring: Maintain a mapping/classification process so large-exposure valuation for cryptoassets stays consistent with the CRP-1 classification used for capital purposes.
notifications_reporting: Watch for individual written notices from the HKMA prescribing a bespoke valuation methodology (para 2.8.12); no generic filing obligation stated.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Flag to risk committee that HKMA retains discretion to impose bank-specific valuation methodologies for cryptoasset large exposures.

title: Supervisory Policy Manual CA-G-5: Supervisory Review Process
supersedes_or_amends: Supervisory Policy Manual CA-G-5 Supervisory Review Process, earlier version
summary: CA-G-5 is a large, general SPM module (V.7, effective 19 Dec 2025). It explains how the HKMA's Pillar 2 Supervisory Review Process sets bank-specific capital add-ons on top of the minimum ratio. Most of the module is generic (governance expectations, ICAAP, stress testing) and does not mention cryptoassets. Two passages were added for the cryptoasset standard. One is a paragraph on how the HKMA may respond to capital or risk-management shortfalls tied to cryptoasset activities. The other is a reminder that boards must understand cryptoasset-related risks as part of firm-wide risk oversight. A companion cross-reference lists the new CRP-1 'Classification of Cryptoassets' module.

key_points.point: Because cryptoasset business is new and still developing, the HKMA may respond to related capital or risk-control gaps in several ways. These include temporary capital add-ons, requiring provisions against foreseeable cryptoasset losses, imposing exposure limits, or other mitigation measures.

As part of sound firm-wide risk management, the board and senior management should fully understand risks tied to new or complex activities, giving cryptoasset activities as one worked example alongside securitisation.
The module's own list of related SPM modules confirms a new module, CRP-1 'Classification of Cryptoassets', now sits alongside the credit, liquidity and market-risk modules.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This confirms the HKMA treats cryptoasset activity as a distinct trigger for extra Pillar 2 capital or provisioning if a bank's controls are not yet mature. It expects that judgement to be made at board level, not left to a trading desk.

quote.text: Cryptoasset activities and associated risks are relatively new and evolving.

reading_guide: Read only paras 3.6.6 and 4.2.8 (pages 53 and 63); the rest of this 300-page module is generic Pillar 2/ICAAP/stress-testing guidance unrelated to cryptoassets.
flags: The module is overwhelmingly generic; crypto-specific text is limited to two short paragraphs despite this being one of the eight modules gazetted for the cryptoasset standard.

obligations: Ensure the board and senior management demonstrably understand cryptoasset-related risks as part of the firm-wide risk framework (para 4.2.8).
Be prepared for HKMA-imposed capital add-ons, forced provisioning, or exposure limits if cryptoasset risk management is judged deficient (para 3.6.6).
controls_and_monitoring: Track adequacy of provisioning for foreseeable, estimable cryptoasset losses (para 3.6.6).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told that HKMA views cryptoasset risk management maturity as a live Pillar 2 capital lever, separate from the minimum ratio.

title: Cryptoassets standard: gazettal of revised SPM modules and code of practice
supersedes_or_amends: Cryptoassets standard: consultation on new and revised SPM modules and code of practice
summary: This is the operative HKMA circular (19 Dec 2025, Ref B1/15C etc.) announcing that the Monetary Authority has gazetted eight revised SPM modules and one revised code of practice. These are statutory guidelines or code under the Banking Ordinance. The stated purpose is to implement locally the Basel Committee's standard on the prudential treatment of banks' cryptoasset exposures. This is done via the Banking (Capital) (Amendment) Rules 2025 and consequential changes in the Banking (Exposure Limits) (Amendment) Rules 2025. All nine instruments take effect 1 January 2026.

key_points.point: The Monetary Authority has, by notice in the Gazette, issued eight revised SPM modules as statutory guidelines under sections 7(3) or 16(10) of the Banking Ordinance. It also issued a revised code of practice under section 97M(1). These are CA-G-1, CA-G-5, CR-G-8, CR-G-9, CR-L-5, LM-1, MR-1, MR-2, and the Banking (Exposure Limits) Code.

The revisions primarily implement the Basel Committee's standard on the prudential treatment of banks' cryptoasset exposures. This is given effect through the Banking (Capital) (Amendment) Rules 2025, plus consequential amendments in the Banking (Exposure Limits) (Amendment) Rules 2025.
All the revised modules and the code of practice take effect on 1 January 2026 and are accessible via the HKMA's Banking Regulatory Document Repository or the Supervisory Communication Website.

title: CA-G-1 Overview of Capital Adequacy Regime for Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions
supersedes_or_amends: CA-G-1 "Overview of Capital Adequacy Regime for Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions" (V.4) dated 29 Nov 2024
summary: CA-G-1 is the HKMA's master overview module. It explains how a locally incorporated bank works out its capital adequacy ratio and leverage ratio, covering capital composition, buffers, and the whole risk-weighting framework. This gazetted version (effective from the module's structure, aligned to the 1 January 2026 package) adds cryptoasset exposures throughout. It adds a new section 8.7 on credit risk for tokenised assets and stablecoins, and cross-references to the market-risk and CVA modules for crypto trading positions. It also clarifies that a cryptoasset exposure is never treated as an intangible asset for capital-deduction purposes. It formally replaces the fourth edition of CA-G-1 dated 29 November 2024.

key_points.point: A cryptoasset exposure is not counted as an intangible asset for the purpose of deducting contingent items from a bank's capital base.
A new Part 12 was added to the risk-weighting framework, dedicated to calculating risk-weighted amounts for cryptoasset exposures.
Tokenised traditional assets held in the banking book (Group 1a) are generally risk-weighted the same way as the underlying traditional asset would be.
For stablecoin-type tokens (Group 1b) held in the banking book, a bank must separately calculate the credit risk of the referenced asset and the credit risk that the redeemer defaults.
Where only some holders can redeem a Group 1b token directly, extra credit risk applies. It depends on whether the bank is a redeeming member or must rely on a member to redeem on its behalf.
The riskiest token category, Group 2b, is subject to a fixed conservative capital treatment set in the Banking (Capital) Rules rather than a bespoke risk calculation.
A large or domestic systemically important bank faces an additional capital add-on once its ratio of Group 2 cryptoasset exposures to total capital passes a prescribed limit.
For trading-book market risk, crypto positions must use one of three specified methods, with the internal models approach barred for Group 2a tokens. Detailed rules sit in module MR-1.

For CVA risk, crypto trades generally follow the same rules as trades on non-tokenised assets, except that the standardised CVA approach cannot be used for Group 2a token trades. Detailed rules sit in module MR-2.

numbers_and_dates.item: Version date on this gazetted edition

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the current, citable master reference for how any cryptoasset exposure on the bank's books feeds into its regulatory capital ratio. Compliance should map any crypto product against these classification-driven rules before onboarding it.

quote.text: intangible asset does not include a cryptoasset exposure

reading_guide: Read section 8.7 (paras 8.7.1-8.7.4, pages 47-48) for the core credit-risk treatment. Plus the short crypto cross-references in paras 8.9.13-8.9.14 (page 52) and footnote 17 (page 23) on capital deductions. The rest of the module is general, non-crypto background.
flags: This is textually near-identical to the 27 November 2025 pre-gazettal draft (id cbf7a73d0c18) except that the placeholder date was filled in and minor spacing/formatting fixed

obligations: Calculate separate credit-risk-weighted amounts for the reference asset and the redeemer of any Group 1b (stablecoin-type) token held in the banking book (para 8.7.2)
Apply the fixed conservative capital treatment to Group 2b cryptoasset exposures rather than a bespoke risk-weight calculation (para 8.7.3)
Monitor the Group 2 cryptoasset exposure ratio against the prescribed limit if the bank is a G-SIB or D-SIB, since breaching it triggers a capital add-on (para 8.7.4(d))
controls_and_monitoring: Do not classify cryptoasset exposures as intangible assets when running capital-deduction calculations (para 6.6.1, footnote 17)
Route trading-book crypto positions to the correct market-risk method (STM/IMA/SSTM per token group) per module MR-1 cross-reference (para 8.9.13)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The board/risk committee should be told that stablecoin and tokenised-asset holdings carry layered credit-risk capital charges (reference asset plus redeemer risk), and that systemic banks face an added capital charge if speculative (Group 2) crypto exposure grows too large relative to capital.

title: Supervisory Policy Manual MR-2: CVA Risk Capital Charge
supersedes_or_amends: Supervisory Policy Manual MR-2, prior version
summary: MR-2 is a general SPM module (V.2, effective 19 Dec 2025) on calculating credit valuation adjustment (CVA) risk capital charges for derivatives and securities-financing transactions (SFTs). It adds a dedicated section 4, 'Cryptoasset exposures', applying the CVA framework to derivatives and material fair-valued SFTs referencing group 1a. 1b, 2a and 2b cryptoassets, with different treatment for each group.

key_points.point: Derivatives and SFTs on group 1a (tokenised) cryptoassets generally get the same CVA capital treatment as the equivalent non-tokenised traditional asset would receive.

A bank must independently assess the tokenised asset itself against the module's eligibility criteria (including liquidity characteristics). It cannot simply inherit the treatment of the underlying traditional asset, because differing liquidity between the two can create extra basis risk.

If there is not enough data to model the liquidity-driven basis risk between a tokenised asset and its traditional equivalent, the simpler basic approach (BA-CVA) must be used. This replaces the standardised approach (SA-CVA).
Derivatives on group 1b cryptoassets (stablecoins) get the same CVA capital treatment as derivatives on the traditional assets they reference.
Group 2a cryptoassets follow the module's requirements generally, except that SA-CVA is not permitted for derivatives or fair-valued SFTs referencing them -- only the basic approach applies.

Group 2b cryptoasset CVA risk is generally already captured by the conservative 1,250% risk-weight treatment, so no separate CVA calculation is needed. If credit risk for such an exposure is not already assessed at 1,250%, the bank must instead apply that conservative treatment for CVA risk specifically.
Fair-valued SFTs collateralised by cryptoassets are only brought into the CVA charge if the HKMA determines the resulting CVA risk is material.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This sets out exactly when a crypto derivatives desk can use the more capital-efficient SA-CVA model versus being forced onto the basic approach. Confirms the HKMA treats the least-mature cryptoasset bucket (group 2b) with a blunt, very high risk weight rather than a modelled charge.

quote.text: such tokenised assets are subject to the BA-CVA

reading_guide: Read section 4 in full (pages 43-45, paras 4.1.1-4.3.3); the rest of the module is the general CVA framework for traditional derivatives and SFTs.

obligations: Independently assess each tokenised cryptoasset against MR-2's eligibility criteria before applying a traditional-asset CVA treatment (para 4.2.2).
Apply the basic approach (BA-CVA), not SA-CVA, wherever there is insufficient data on tokenised-vs-traditional basis risk, or for any group 2a exposure (paras 4.2.2, 4.3.1).
Apply the 1,250% conservative treatment to group 2b cryptoasset CVA risk where credit risk is not already captured at that risk weight (paras 4.3.2-4.3.3).
controls_and_monitoring: Maintain data sufficient to model basis risk between tokenised assets and their traditional equivalents, since a data gap forces the less favourable BA-CVA (para 4.2.2).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Treasury/markets risk should confirm whether current CVA models can support SA-CVA for tokenised exposures or will default to the more conservative basic approach.

title: Supervisory Policy Manual LM-1: Regulatory Framework for Supervision of Liquidity Risk
supersedes_or_amends: Supervisory Policy Manual LM-1, prior version
summary: LM-1 is a broad Supervisory Policy Manual (SPM) module (version 5, effective 19 December 2025) covering the HKMA's approach to supervising liquidity risk. This includes the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) and Core Funding Ratio (CFR). It adds a short new section 5.9 and a large new Annex 3 explaining how cryptoasset exposures, tokenised assets, stablecoins and other cryptoassets are treated for liquidity purposes. This splits category 1 and category 2 institutions and leaves central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) out of the annex's scope.

key_points.point: Cryptoasset exposures should generally get the same treatment as traditional exposures carrying the same economic risk, for LCR, NSFR, LMR and CFR purposes.
Because cryptoasset exposures can carry extra risk and there isn't much historical data yet, more detailed liquidity treatment is spelled out separately in Annex 3.
Annex 3's cryptoasset rules do not cover CBDCs. CBDCs are generally treated like physical banknotes and coins of the issuing jurisdiction, subject to each CBDC's own features and legal standing.

A cryptoasset cannot count as a high-quality liquid asset (HQLA), or as a liquefiable asset for category 2 institutions. The only exception is a group 1a cryptoasset that tokenises a traditional asset already eligible as HQLA. Even then, both the token and the underlying asset must meet all the usual eligibility tests.

If a bank has issued group 1a cryptoassets that meet the tokenised-claim conditions, it must treat the resulting liabilities as deposits or unsecured funding. The exact outflow or inflow treatment depends on whether holders can be identified and whether the cryptoasset is mainly used to make payments.

Stablecoins -- defined here as group 1b cryptoassets, plus some group 2 cryptoassets meeting similar stability tests -- are treated like non-HQLA debt securities. An issuing bank must assume full redemption within the LCR window. The exception is when the backing assets independently qualify as HQLA; then the earliest possible redemption date sets the inflow or outflow treatment.
A bank holding a stablecoin must treat it as a non-HQLA debt security and generally apply a 0% inflow rate, adjusted if the stablecoin has a set remaining maturity.

Other cryptoassets split into two kinds. Group 1a cryptoassets that don't qualify as HQLA follow the treatment of whatever traditional asset they represent. Other group 2 cryptoassets get a full 100% run-off or required-collateral treatment under the CFR, and no inflow credit under the LMR.

The HKMA can decide a particular cryptoasset carries extra liquidity risk, say because of its technical design or the bank's role as holder or issuer. It can then demand extra safeguards. These include protecting the bank's own liquidity when it issues, or is a key service provider helping redeem, certain stablecoins.

Derivatives linked to a cryptoasset are explicitly covered by the Annex 3 rules, not carved out. The same is true of secured funding or lending using cryptoassets as collateral, cryptoasset collateral swaps, and committed facilities to lend cryptoassets.

numbers_and_dates.value: redemption treatment differs for stablecoins redeemable within a month vs longer

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the clearest statement yet from the HKMA on how stablecoins and tokenised assets must be modelled in a bank's LCR and NSFR calculations. It puts direct liquidity-outflow consequences on a bank that issues or helps redeem stablecoins. Compliance needs this built into treasury's liquidity models and data feeds.

quote.text: the requirements on cryptoasset exposures set out in Annex 3 do not cover central bank

reading_guide: Read para 5.9 (page 65) for the general principle, then Annex 3 in full (around page 78 onward, paras 1-16+) for the detailed tokenised-claim, stablecoin and other-cryptoasset treatment. Skip the surrounding generic LCR/NSFR calculation mechanics.
flags: The module explicitly carves CBDCs out of the cryptoasset liquidity annex and treats them like cash instead — a distinction easy to miss if only skimming for 'cryptoasset'.

obligations: Sort every cryptoasset exposure -- tokenised claim, stablecoin issued or held, other cryptoasset -- into the right Annex 3 category before working out LCR, NSFR, LMR and CFR.
If the bank issues stablecoins or group 1a tokenised claims, apply the required deposit/unsecured-funding or non-HQLA-debt-security treatment to the resulting liabilities.
controls_and_monitoring: Keep the ability to identify who holds any cryptoassets the bank issues, since the outflow treatment depends on it.
Track whether the backing assets of any stablecoin the bank issues or holds still qualify as HQLA, since this changes the inflow/outflow treatment.
counterparty_due_diligence: Where a stablecoin is issued by another bank or a regulated, supervised entity, confirm its status before applying more favourable inflow treatment.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Treasury and the Asset and Liability Committee (ALCO) should confirm liquidity models and data now separately tag tokenised assets, stablecoins and other cryptoassets, since getting the category wrong directly changes LCR and NSFR results.

title: Supervisory Policy Manual MR-1: Market Risk Capital Charge
supersedes_or_amends: Supervisory Policy Manual MR-1, prior version (15 March 2024)
summary: MR-1 is a large, general SPM module (V.2, effective 19 Dec 2025) on calculating market risk capital charges under the simplified standardised (SSTM). Full standardised (STM) and internal-models (IMA) approaches. It adds a dedicated section 6, 'Cryptoasset exposures', covering how each approach treats group 1 (tokenised assets and stablecoins) and group 2a cryptoassets. Plus a trading-book/banking-book boundary rule for cryptoasset reclassifications and a footnote excluding cryptoasset exposures from the market-risk de-minimis exemption.

key_points.point: A bank with any cryptoasset exposure cannot use the market-risk de-minimis exemption that smaller trading books would otherwise qualify for.

Under SSTM, group 1 cryptoasset positions are converted to HKD at spot price. They are mapped to the same risk category (interest rate, equity, FX or commodities) as the traditional asset they represent or reference. Netting and hedging are recognised between a tokenised or stablecoin instrument and its traditional-asset equivalent.

Under STM, a tokenised instrument (group 1a) or stablecoin (group 1b) is broken down using the same risk factors that apply to the traditional asset it represents or references. Sensitivities are matched inside the existing risk classes.
The IMA may be used for group 1 cryptoassets but is not permitted for instruments referencing group 2 cryptoassets.

Where a group 1b cryptoasset (stablecoin) carries redeemer default risk or redemption-intermediary risk, that risk must be captured under the credit-risk capital framework rather than market risk. This applies across the SSTM, STM and IMA approaches.
Group 2a cryptoassets must sit in the trading book and get a modified, standalone SSTM or STM treatment with limited hedging recognition. The IMA cannot be used for them.
For each group 2a cryptoasset, the position-risk capital requirement is 100% of the net position, calculated with a formula that only gives 65% offset credit between long and short positions.

Group 2b cryptoassets are not subject to this market-risk capital charge at all. Instead they get the conservative treatment (a flat risk weight covering credit and market risk together, including CVA risk) under a separate capital-rules provision.

Book transfers of an instrument can be triggered by a cryptoasset's reclassification under the new CRP-1 classification module (paras 2.1.2-2.1.3 of CRP-1). Such a transfer is not treated as a discretionary trading or banking-book switch. So it escapes the usual capital surcharge for such switches.

numbers_and_dates.value: 0.65 offset between long and short positions

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is where the bulk of a bank's market-risk capital methodology work for any crypto trading book will sit. It dictates classification-dependent decomposition, hedging recognition. A harder capital treatment (100% net position, no IMA) for the riskier group 2a bucket. Plus an explicit ban on the small-book market-risk exemption once any cryptoasset exposure exists.

quote.text: An AI with cryptoasset exposures will not be qualified for the de-minimis exemption

reading_guide: Read section 6 in full (pages 150-155ish, paras 6.1.1-6.2.28) plus footnote 13 on page 14 for the boundary/reclassification carve-out. The rest of this ~300-page module is standard SSTM/STM/IMA mechanics for traditional instruments.

obligations: Classify every cryptoasset trading position by group (1a/1b/2a/2b) using CRP-1 before applying the relevant SSTM/STM/IMA treatment (para 6.1.1, footnote 79).
Do not apply the market-risk de-minimis exemption to any book containing cryptoasset exposures (footnote 80).
Route group 1b stablecoin redeemer/intermediary default risk to the credit-risk framework, not market risk (paras 6.1.2, 6.1.6, 6.1.12).
controls_and_monitoring: Monitor and restrict discretionary book transfers of cryptoasset instruments given the strict switching limits, while correctly exempting CRP-1-driven reclassifications from the surcharge (footnote 13).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Market risk/trading desk heads should confirm systems can classify and decompose cryptoasset positions into the mandated risk factors before any crypto trading book capital is calculated.

title: Supervisory Policy Manual CR-L-5: Major Acquisitions and Investments: BELR Part 3
supersedes_or_amends: Supervisory Policy Manual CR-L-5, prior version
summary: CR-L-5 is a general Supervisory Policy Manual (SPM) module (version 3, effective 19 December 2025). It covers how the HKMA reviews and approves bank consent for major share acquisitions under Part 3 of the Banking (Exposure Limits) Rules (BELR). It is almost entirely about ordinary corporate shareholdings and otherwise says nothing about cryptoassets. One footnote was added, widening the module's definition of 'share' to also capture certain cryptoassets.

key_points.point: For BELR Part 3 and this module, any mention of 'share' or 'share capital' now also covers a cryptoasset that gives the same economic effect as owning equity. This is as defined under BELR rule 2(2).

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: A bank buying a cryptoasset that works economically like equity in another company must put it through the same major-acquisition consent process as an ordinary shareholding. This process is based on the 5% of Tier 1 capital threshold.
