title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Opening Remarks at “Tokenisation: Banking the Future”
summary: Deputy Chief Executive Arthur Yuen's opening remarks (event held 9 March 2026) frame DLT's transformative effect on bank liquidity through three concepts. 'novel', 'smart' and 'trusted' liquidity -- and position banks as trusted intermediaries bridging traditional and digital finance. The speech announces that HKMA is issuing, the same day. A circular that asks banks to review their business models strategically in light of digital transformation (see the separate registry entry for that circular, id 3ec5b269b5dc).

key_points.point: DLT is described as unlocking three new forms of liquidity. 'Novel Liquidity' (tokenising previously illiquid assets like corporate loans, carbon credits and IP), 'Smart Liquidity' (smart-contract automation compressing settlement time). 'Trusted Liquidity' (banks as trusted intermediaries verifying underlying assets and smart contract integrity).

The same day, HKMA is issuing a circular that calls on banks to strategically review their business models in response to digital transformation. Covering product offerings, revenue models, customer engagement, risk management frameworks and operational processes.
The strategic review is meant to steer how banks navigate the next five years as DLT, AI, cloud and high-performance computing reshape business models.

numbers_and_dates.value: 9 March 2026 (per speech note, though webpage publish date is 12 March 2026)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Directly previews the HKMA circular (see 3ec5b269b5dc) requiring the bank's board to endorse a formal digital-transformation strategic business plan within six months. Frames the regulator's rationale for expecting banks to act as trusted intermediaries in tokenisation.

reading_guide: Read in full (short); the circular referenced (footnote 3) is the operative document and is separately registered (id 3ec5b269b5dc).

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told this speech announces the strategic-review circular (id 3ec5b269b5dc) requiring board endorsement of a digital-transformation business plan within six months.

EnsembleTX entered pilot phase in November 2025, enabling real-value transactions in tokenised deposits and digital assets. From 2026, HKMA plans to onboard more banks, add use cases and enhance EnsembleTX. The speech calls on banks to take proactive steps to capture tokenisation opportunities.

EnsembleTX entered its pilot phase in November 2025. Enabling market participants to conduct real-value transactions in tokenised deposits and digital assets for liquidity and investment management.

Starting in 2026, HKMA intends to grow the tokenisation ecosystem, with priorities that include bringing in more banks, developing further use cases, driving wider adoption. Improving EnsembleTX to keep up with market needs.
HKMA urged banks to take proactive steps to capture the opportunities of tokenisation, citing early global adoption of products such as tokenised money market funds.

title: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism (1) FATF Statement on High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action (2) FATF Statement on Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring (3) Outcomes from the FATF Plenary, 11-13 February 2026
supersedes_or_amends: SFC circular issued 12 November 2025 (25EC61) on FATF High-Risk Jurisdictions
summary: This SFC circular relays the FATF's February 2026 statements. These identify DPRK and Iran as jurisdictions subject to a call for countermeasures, and Myanmar as subject to enhanced due diligence (with countermeasures to be considered if no progress by June 2026). The updated list of jurisdictions under increased monitoring adds Kuwait and Papua New Guinea. It also flags three FATF Plenary (11-13 February 2026) outputs of particular relevance to VA-related firms. These are a paper on cyber-enabled fraud (published 24 February 2026) and a report on offshore virtual asset service provider risks (published 11 March 2026). There is also a targeted report on stablecoins and unhosted wallets illicit-finance risks (published 3 March 2026).

key_points.point: FATF reiterates calls for countermeasures against DPRK given continued AML/CFT deficiencies and proliferation financing risks linked to increased DPRK connectivity with the international financial system.
FATF calls for effective countermeasures against Iran, citing non-compliant ratification of the Palermo and TF Conventions and continuing failure to address its action plan since 2016.

Myanmar remains subject to a FATF call for enhanced due diligence proportionate to risk. The FATF says it will weigh countermeasures should this situation still lack meaningful improvement come June 2026.
The FATF's updated list of Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring adds Kuwait and Papua New Guinea.

Among FATF's listed countermeasures, one option is capping or cutting off dealings and money movements, including in virtual assets, with persons or entities tied to the flagged jurisdiction, applied according to risk.

FATF approved publication of a targeted report (3 March 2026) on stablecoins and unhosted wallets. It highlights illicit finance risks from criminals' misuse of stablecoins via peer-to-peer transactions through unhosted wallets, with recommended controls.

FATF approved publication of a report (11 March 2026) on understanding and mitigating risks of offshore virtual asset service providers, examining how regulatory/supervisory gaps are exploited by criminals.

Licensed firms are reminded to exercise extra care and apply special high-risk-situation requirements (per paras 4.9 and 4.13 of the AML/CFT Guideline). This applies to business relationships and transactions with higher-risk jurisdictions generally, beyond the specifically listed ones.

numbers_and_dates.item: Stablecoins and unhosted wallets report published

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: The stablecoin/unhosted-wallet and offshore VASP FATF reports flagged here are directly relevant to a bank's stablecoin and VA AML risk assessments and travel-rule/unhosted-wallet controls. The DPRK/Iran call-for-action list must feed sanctions screening for VA transactions specifically.

quote.text: limiting business relationships or financial transactions, including virtual asset transactions

reading_guide: This is a routine FATF-relay circular. Skim the jurisdiction lists (largely boilerplate) but read part (3) on FATF Plenary outcomes (p.3) closely, as it points to substantive new reports on stablecoins/unhosted wallets and offshore VASPs.
flags: Contains a substantive pointer (not boilerplate): a new FATF targeted report specifically on stablecoins and unhosted wallets illicit-finance risk, published 3 March 2026 - relevant to any bank issuing or transacting in stablecoins.

title: Strategic innovation drives growth of Hong Kong's listing and digital asset markets: SFC Quarterly Report
summary: The SFC's Quarterly Report (covering Q4 2025 / full-year 2025) highlights Hong Kong becoming the world's top IPO venue (over $280 billion raised in 2025) and growth in the digital asset ecosystem. SFC-authorised tokenised retail money market funds' AUM grew to $8.66 billion by December 2025 (up 14% quarter-on-quarter). Hong Kong's 11 listed virtual asset spot ETFs (Asia's first, introduced 2024) reached total market capitalisation of over $5.4 billion, up 142% since launch. It also reports broader capital market metrics (Stock Connect volumes, licence applications, ETF/L&I market cap growth. Fund flows) and investor protection actions, including the SFC's first custodial sentence against an unlicensed finfluencer.

key_points.point: Hong Kong became the world's top IPO venue in 2025, raising over $280 billion. The Technology Enterprises Channel (TECH) received 119 IPO applications (73 biotech, 46 specialist technology) since its May 2025 launch through December.
SFC-authorised tokenised retail money market funds' AUM grew to $8.66 billion as of December 2025, up 14% from a quarter ago.
There are 11 virtual asset spot ETFs listed in Hong Kong (Asia's first, launched in 2024). Their combined market value has jumped 142% since listing, passing $5.4 billion.

Combined market value of SFC-authorised ETFs and leveraged-and-inverse (L&I) products rose 33.7% year-on-year to $618.7 billion by December 2025. The segment drew $9.2 billion in net inflows last quarter and made up 14% of Hong Kong's market turnover.
The SFC received 9,637 licence applications in 2025: 9,338 from individuals and 299 from corporations. This was a 17% increase from 2024.
The SFC won its first case resulting in a jail term for a finfluencer who lacked a licence and offered paid investment tips on social media.

numbers_and_dates.value: over $5.4 billion (+142% since 2024 launch); 11 ETFs listed

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: An SFC quarterly market report giving no bank obligations, but useful board-level context on the scale and growth of Hong Kong's tokenised fund and VA ETF market. On rising SFC licence-application volumes.

quote.text: strategic innovation propelled robust capital formation, an accelerating digital ecosystem

reading_guide: Read paras 1-6 for headline digital-asset and IPO figures; the 'Other highlights' bullet list (Stock Connect, licensing, enforcement, anti-scam outreach) is supplementary context.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be given quarterly market-size context: tokenised money-market fund AUM ($8.66bn) and VA spot ETF market cap ($5.4bn) growth, to calibrate the scale of Hong Kong's digital asset ecosystem the bank operates in.

title: Supervisory Policy Manual CA-G-5 Supervisory Review Process V.78 – 19.12.2025 Consultation
supersedes_or_amends: SPM module CA-G-5 Supervisory Review Process (19 Dec 2025 version)
summary: This is the draft revised text of SPM module CA-G-5 on the Pillar 2 supervisory review process, out for consultation from 19 March to 23 April 2026. It is a broad module on how the HKMA assesses an authorized institution's capital adequacy and risk management. Cryptoasset-specific content is limited to two short passages on supervisory tools for crypto-related risk deficiencies and on board oversight of new/complex activities. A separate existing module, CRP-1, covers cryptoasset classification and is only cross-referenced here, not reproduced.

key_points.point: Where an AI has capital-adequacy or risk-management shortcomings tied to cryptoasset activities, the HKMA can respond with capital add-ons. Provisioning for foreseeable crypto losses, activity limits, or other mitigation, chosen case by case.

Boards and senior management are expected to fully understand firm-wide risks. Cryptoasset activity is named as an example (alongside originate-to-distribute and securitisation) of a new or complex activity they must grasp.

The module's reference list shows a separate, already-existing SPM module, CRP-1 ‘Classification of cryptoassets’. Filed under a dedicated ‘Cryptoassets’ category alongside interest-rate and market-risk modules.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Confirms the HKMA's toolkit for crypto-related capital or risk-management gaps is discretionary and case-by-case. That board-level understanding of crypto activities is an explicit supervisory expectation to be evidenced.

quote.text: capital add-ons

reading_guide: Skip the general Pillar 2 methodology. Read only para 3.6.6 (p.52), para 4.2.8 (p.62), and the module index (p.90) for the cryptoasset-relevant content.
flags: This is a general Pillar 2 module, not a VA-specific instrument; crypto content is two short paragraphs out of a ~90-page module.
CRP-1 (Classification of cryptoassets) is only referenced by title here, not summarised; a separate registry pass would be needed if CRP-1's own text is read.

obligations: Ensure the board/senior management can demonstrate understanding of the bank's cryptoasset-related activities as part of firm-wide risk oversight (para 4.2.8, p.62).
Be prepared for HKMA to impose capital add-ons, provisioning, or activity limits if crypto-related risk management is found deficient (para 3.6.6, p.52).
controls_and_monitoring: Risk appetite framework should explicitly address cryptoasset activity risk (para 4.2.8, p.62).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told that supervisory capital add-ons or activity limits are an explicit, available HKMA response to crypto risk-management gaps, and that board-level crypto risk literacy is itself a supervisory expectation.

title: LCQ18: Development of digital Renminbi and stablecoins
summary: In a written Legislative Council reply, the Financial Secretary's Bureau gave an update on the cross-boundary e-CNY (digital Renminbi) pilot with the People's Bank of China. E-CNY wallet issuance by Mainland institutions has grown to five. 18 local banks now support top-ups via the Faster Payment System, roughly 80,000 wallets were registered as of end-January 2026. Around 5,200 local merchants now accept e-CNY. On stablecoins, the reply confirms the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) took effect 1 August 2025 and reiterates that stablecoins, e-CNY and tokenised deposits are expected to develop with differentiated roles. Determined largely by market forces rather than official design.

key_points.point: By the close of January 2026. Roughly 80,000 e-CNY wallets tied to Hong Kong mobile numbers had been set up in total, per PBoC data.
Local retail merchants taking e-CNY payments have grown in number from about 300 at the pilot's start to roughly 5,200 now.
18 local banks now participate in e-CNY wallet top-ups via the Faster Payment System, up from 17 at the pilot's start.
The government confirms the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) took effect on 1 August 2025, introducing a licensing regime for regulated stablecoin activities.

Officials expect stablecoins, e-CNY and tokenised deposits to develop with differentiated roles based on their distinct characteristics and market forces. Rather than a government-directed allocation.

numbers_and_dates.item: cumulative e-CNY wallets registered (Hong Kong numbers)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This confirms the e-CNY pilot remains small in absolute scale in Hong Kong and that government policy is explicitly leaving stablecoin-versus-CBDC-versus-tokenised-deposit positioning to the market. Is useful context when a bank weighs which of these payment rails to prioritise.
reading_guide: Read the full reply; it is short and entirely on-topic, no boilerplate to skip.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No specific board action; useful data point on e-CNY pilot scale and government's market-led (not directed) stance on stablecoins vs. CBDC vs. tokenised deposits.

title: Robust development of the regulated stablecoin ecosystem in Hong Kong
summary: HKMA announced its first two stablecoin issuer licences under the Stablecoins Ordinance: Anchorpoint Financial Limited — jointly owned by Standard Chartered Bank (Hong Kong), HKT and Animoca Brands — and HSBC. Both will initially issue HKD-referenced stablecoins for cross-border payments, local payments, tokenised asset trading settlement and other programmable use cases. HKMA received 36 first-batch applications by the 30 September 2025 deadline and assessed them mainly on risk-management capability and viable use cases. Licensees must complete technology and risk-management preparatory work before launch, expected mid-to-second-half of 2026, and will face ongoing on-site/off-site supervision. HKMA signalled the overall number of licences will remain very limited given high licensing thresholds.

key_points.point: HKMA granted the first two stablecoin issuer licences under the Stablecoins Ordinance to two firms. One is Anchorpoint Financial Limited, owned jointly by Standard Chartered Bank (Hong Kong), HKT and Animoca Brands. The other is The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited (HSBC).

HKMA received 36 applications in the first batch by the 30 September 2025 deadline. These were assessed chiefly on (1) applicants' risk-management capability and compliance commitment, and (2) their ability to propose distinct, viable use cases.

Both licensees plan to initially issue HKD-referenced stablecoins for cross-border payments, local payments, tokenised asset trading settlement, and other programmable use cases such as conditional payments and supply chain financing.

Licensed issuers must implement robust risk-management measures. These cover fiat reserve asset safekeeping, price stabilisation, redemption arrangements and technology risk mitigation, plus AML controls including blockchain analytics tools and holder identity verification (directly or via reliable third parties).

Prior to launch, licensees must complete preparatory work including technology platform and systems testing and implementation of risk-management measures and HR arrangements. Regulated stablecoins are expected to launch in mid-to-second-half of 2026.
Once the regulated stablecoins launch, HKMA plans continuous oversight -- a mix of site visits, remote reviews, independent assessments, and direct contact with licensees' senior leadership.

HKMA signalled the licensing threshold will remain high and the overall number of licences granted, even if more are approved later, will remain very limited. This reflects stablecoin activity risk, user protection needs and market capacity considerations.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the first concrete market outcome of the Stablecoins Ordinance and directly names one bank counterparty (HSBC) now licensed to issue regulated stablecoins. Relevant for counterparty due diligence on any regulated-stablecoin product, payments partnership, or as a competitive-landscape reference given the very limited number of licences signalled.

quote.text: same activity, same risks, same regulation

reading_guide: Read in full; it is the primary source for the first two HKD stablecoin licensees and their planned use cases and ongoing supervisory approach.
flags: Per the site's editorial neutrality rule, note that Anchorpoint and HSBC are named strictly as stated in this HKMA release with no added commentary on either firm.

controls_and_monitoring: If the bank distributes or accepts a regulated stablecoin, confirm the issuer's AML controls (blockchain analytics, holder identity verification) meet HKMA's stated supervisory expectations.
counterparty_due_diligence: Verify any stablecoin counterparty holds a current HKMA licence via the Register of Licensees (see id 270f1f7324ab) and check its licensed use cases match the intended business relationship.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be informed that HKMA has now issued its first stablecoin issuer licences (to HSBC and Anchorpoint), that the licensing bar will stay high, and that the total number of licensees is expected to remain very limited.

title: Granting of stablecoin issuer licences
summary: The HKMA announced that the Monetary Authority had licensed two firms, Anchorpoint Financial Limited and HSBC, as stablecoin issuers under the Stablecoins Ordinance, with licences effective the same day. Based on their business plans, the licensees intend to finish preparation and launch business in the coming months. The HKMA keeps a public Register of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers and warns the public to only get or use stablecoins through regulated channels. Staying alert for fraud claiming ties to the licensees.

key_points.point: Under the Stablecoins Ordinance, the HKMA licensed two firms -- Anchorpoint Financial Limited and HSBC -- to issue stablecoins, with effect from 10 April 2026.
According to their business plans, the licensees intend to finish the needed preparation and launch business within the coming few months.
The HKMA keeps a public Register of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers, listing licensee names, addresses, email contacts, and other details.
The public is reminded to only acquire or use stablecoins through regulated channels, and to check a licensee's legitimacy through the HKMA's Register.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This licence grant is a direct matter. An Authorized Institution is now a licensed stablecoin issuer under the Stablecoins Ordinance, so its business-plan promises to the HKMA become live commitments. It is also the benchmark precedent for any other bank weighing the same licence.

quote.text: an important milestone for the development of digital assets in Hong Kong

reading_guide: Short press release; read in full.
flags: Confirms that a major international bank (HSBC) is among the very first two entities licensed as a stablecoin issuer in Hong Kong, correcting any assumption that early Hong Kong stablecoin issuance would be dominated by native crypto/fintech firms rather than incumbent banks.

obligations: As one of the first two HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers, the named bank must carry out its business plan's preparation work and launch its business as it told the HKMA it would.
counterparty_due_diligence: Check that counterparties use stablecoins only through issuers listed on the HKMA's Register of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Brief the board on this licence grant strictly as the HKMA stated it, following the named-entity rule, with no commentary on the licensee's prospects.

title: Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products
supersedes_or_amends: earlier version of this circular (revised/amended 20 April 2026, per the 'Amended' markings in the text)
summary: This SFC circular (revised 20 April 2026) sets the rules for turning SFC-authorised investment products. Authorised under Part IV of the SFO for public sale in Hong Kong -- into tokenised form. Using a 'see-through' approach, SFC allows primary dealing (buying and selling units) in tokenised versions of SFC-authorised products. As long as the underlying product still meets every authorisation rule, plus extra safeguards for tokenisation-specific risks. Record-keeping, cybersecurity, avoiding open public blockchains, smart-contract integrity, disclosure, distributor regulation, and staff competence. Secondary trading of these tokenised products on SFC-licensed VATPs is allowed separately, under a companion circular. New tokenised products, or big changes to how tokenisation works, need SFC consultation and approval first.

key_points.point: The SFC will permit subscription and redemption (primary dealing) in tokenised versions of SFC-authorised investment products. This applies provided the underlying product satisfies all standard authorisation rules, along with extra safeguards specific to tokenisation.

Trading tokenised SFC-authorised investment products in the secondary market on an SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform is permitted too. This is provided rules on fair pricing, orderly trading, liquidity and disclosure are met, as detailed in the companion 'Circular on secondary trading of tokenised SFC-authorised investment products'.
Product Providers stay fully responsible for running the tokenisation arrangement soundly and for keeping ownership records, even if parts of the work are outsourced.
Tokenised SFC-authorised investment products are not expected to be issued as bearer instruments.
Product Providers should avoid open, permissionless public blockchain networks unless extra controls -- such as a permissioned token -- are added.

If SFC asks, Product Providers must show their operations are sound. They must get independent audit or verification of the tokenisation setup and smart-contract integrity, and obtain a satisfactory legal opinion to back their application.

Offering documents must clearly explain the tokenisation setup. This includes whether settlement is final off-chain or on-chain, how tokens represent ownership, and the risks involved: cybersecurity, system outages, undiscovered technical flaws, and a changing regulatory landscape.

Anyone distributing tokenised products, including a Product Provider selling its own products, must be a regulated intermediary (an SFC-licensed corporation or registered institution) following existing conduct, onboarding and suitability rules.
Product Providers must confirm at least one staff member has the relevant experience to run or oversee the tokenisation setup and manage the new ownership and technology risks.
New tokenised products need SFC consultation before authorisation. Tokenising an existing product, or making a major change to how tokenisation works, may also need prior approval.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This rule applies to the fund or product-provider entity, not directly to the bank as an authorized institution. But if the bank distributes or structures tokenised SFC-authorised products through its licensed corporation or fund arm, a compliance head must make sure smart-contract audits, staff competence. Blockchain controls are all in place, and that SFC has been consulted beforehand.

quote.text: Product Providers should not use public-permissionless blockchain networks without additional and proper controls

reading_guide: Read Section A (background, paras 2-7) for context, then Section B (paras 8-19) in full as the binding requirements. Section C (paras 20-22) covers the prior consultation/approval process. The document shows 'Amended' markers indicating this is a revised version.
flags: The circular explicitly discourages use of fully public-permissionless blockchains for tokenised SFC-authorised products absent additional controls (e.g. permissioned tokens), correcting an assumption that SFC tokenisation approval is blockchain-agnostic.
The document is marked as revised/amended on 20 April 2026, indicating an earlier version existed; the original issuance date is not stated in the text itself.

notifications_reporting: As a Product Provider, consult SFC in advance for new tokenised products or major changes to tokenisation arrangements, and prior approval may also be needed (paras 20-21)
counterparty_due_diligence: Check that a tokenised product's provider avoids open public blockchains without added controls, has had its smart-contract integrity audited, and has competent staff overseeing the tokenisation setup (paras 13-14, 19)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Tell the board this is the current, in-force tokenisation circular (replacing the 2023 version), and that distribution partners must be regulated intermediaries following existing conduct rules (para 18).

Advancing Hong Kong's Digital Asset Journey', delivered at the Hong Kong Web3 Festival 2026, has been posted on the SFC website. It directs readers to the SFC website's Speeches page (found under Published resources) for the full text and other speeches.

key_points.point: Dr Eric Yip delivered a keynote titled 'ASPIRe in Action. Advancing Hong Kong's Digital Asset Journey' at the Hong Kong Web3 Festival 2026, now posted on the SFC website.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Low-priority pointer notice; the full speech (not included in this batch) may contain useful policy signalling on ASPIRe roadmap progress, but this notice itself carries no substantive content.

quote.text: ASPIRe in Action: Advancing Hong Kong's Digital Asset Journey

reading_guide: One-paragraph pointer notice; read in full (very short); the actual speech text is a separate document not included here.
flags: This is only a pointer notice; the substantive speech content is not captured in this document and would need to be sourced separately.

title: Circular on secondary trading of tokenised SFC-authorised investment products
summary: This SFC circular lays out the conditions for permitting public secondary trading, on SFC-licensed VATPs, of Tokenised Products -- tokenised SFC-authorised investment products, mainly open-ended funds. It should be read together with the Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products and the Circular on intermediaries engaging in tokenised securities-related activities. It covers on-platform trading rules and fair-pricing controls, including a mandatory Price Deviation Alert measured against indicative net asset value (NAV). It also covers liquidity requirements: at least one market maker, with 3 months' notice before ending that role, and appointed SFC-licensed distributors. It also covers detailed disclosure duties in offering documents and Key Facts Statements (KFS). It requires prior SFC consultation or approval for new or existing tokenised products and for major changes to trading arrangements.

key_points.point: Secondary trading of Tokenised Products can be offered to retail investors through on-platform, on-screen auto-matching trading on SFC-licensed VATPs. This follows the existing VATP Guidelines' trading rules and risk controls.

SFC-licensed VATPs must run a Price Deviation Alert that warns investors when the trade price would move significantly away from the product's real-time or near real-time indicative NAV. VATPs must also apply controls such as trading bands and cooling-off periods to guard against sharp price swings and manipulation.
Product Providers should make their best effort to line up at least one market maker per Tokenised Product, and give at least 3 months' notice before ending that arrangement.

Distributors appointed for Tokenised Products need to hold SFC licences (as corporations or registered institutions) and normally take care of creation and redemption requests coming from third-party investors.

Offering documents, including the Key Facts Statement, must clearly disclose the risks of secondary trading: liquidity, price deviation, price differences across trading channels, and reliance on the market maker. They must also disclose how the trading channel works, market-making arrangements and incentives, and any conflicts of interest if a market maker is an affiliated entity.

SFC-licensed VATPs and Connecting Brokers must maintain online tools that display real-time or near-real-time indicative NAV, together with the last NAV. These must refresh no less often than every 15 seconds while trading is underway. They must also obtain client confirmation of understanding the risks before allowing secondary-market trades.

Product Providers must immediately tell SFC and investors if dealing in a Tokenised Product stops or is suspended, or if market-making activity stops, is disrupted, or is suspended. They must include an assessment of the impact and a plan to fix or manage the situation.

New tokenised products need prior SFC consultation before authorisation. Adding tokenisation or secondary-trading features to an existing SFC-authorised product needs both prior consultation and approval.
Registered institutions doing secondary trading of Tokenised Products must also notify HKMA, following the Circular on intermediaries engaging in tokenised securities-related activities.

numbers_and_dates.value: at least every 15 seconds during trading hours

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This directly binds the bank as a Registered Institution if it sells tokenised SFC-authorised funds or connects clients to secondary trading of them on VATPs. It creates Price Deviation Alert, risk-disclosure, and advance-notification duties to both SFC and, at the same time, HKMA.

quote.text: price fragmentation risks (including different trading prices across different trading channels)

reading_guide: Read Section A (background, paras 1-6, p.1) then Section B in full (paras 7-22, p.2-6) as the operative requirements. Section C (paras 23-28, p.5-6) covers the prior consultation process, important for registered institutions needing dual SFC/HKMA notification.
flags: Registered institutions face a dual-notification obligation (SFC and HKMA) not required of licensed corporations - easy to overlook for a bank's RI entity structuring its VATP secondary trading business.

obligations: If the bank's Registered Institution arm acts as a Connecting Broker, routing client secondary-trading orders to SFC-licensed VATPs for Tokenised Products, it must show the Price Deviation Alert and tell investors about the primary-market alternative (paras 13, 20).

As a Product Provider or distributor, make sure eligibility, disclosure (KFS risk disclosures on liquidity, price deviation, and market-maker reliance), and market-maker arrangements match the requirements set out (paras 15, 19).
Registered institutions must notify HKMA under the tokenised-securities circular, at the same time as any SFC prior consultation (para 27, fn.13).
controls_and_monitoring: If acting as a distributor or participating dealer, confirm capital and product holdings are sufficient before carrying out any client trade (para 10).
notifications_reporting: Registered institutions doing secondary trading of Tokenised Products for the first time must notify and discuss it with their SFC case officer (and HKMA, where relevant) beforehand, and again for major changes (paras 27-28).
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm distributors and market makers used for Tokenised Products meet the applicable SFC and other regulatory conduct requirements (para 17).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Tell the board that if the bank connects clients to secondary trading of tokenised SFC-authorised funds via VATPs, it takes on Price Deviation Alert, disclosure, and advance-notification duties, with HKMA notification required at the same time as a Registered Institution.

title: SFC unveils new regulatory framework to allow secondary trading of tokenised SFC-authorised investment products
summary: SFC rolled out a fresh set of rules, in a same-day circular, to pilot secondary trading of tokenised SFC-authorised funds (mainly open-ended funds) on SFC-licensed VATPs. Over-the-counter deals are looked at case by case. It builds on the tokenisation framework SFC first put in place through two circulars dated 2 November 2023. By March 2026, Hong Kong had 13 such tokenised products on the market. Their combined tokenised-class assets under management (AUM) had grown roughly seven times over within a year, reaching $10.7 billion. The plan is to let trading run around the clock, beyond normal market hours, potentially helped along by licensed stablecoins and tokenised deposits. The first products under the scheme are likely to be tokenised money-market funds.

key_points.point: SFC first put its tokenisation framework in place via two circulars dated 2 November 2023. These were the 'Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products' and the 'Circular on intermediaries engaging in tokenised securities-related activities'.
By March 2026, Hong Kong had 13 tokenised products on public sale. Their combined tokenised-class AUM had grown roughly seven times over within a year, reaching $10.7 billion.

The new scheme aims to let tokenised open-ended funds trade around the clock. This may be helped by licensed stablecoins (fiat-referenced stablecoins approved under the Stablecoins Ordinance) and tokenised deposits, to keep liquidity flowing at all hours.
Trading mainly happens on SFC-licensed VATPs under this scheme, though SFC may also weigh up over-the-counter secondary-trading setups on an individual basis.
New safeguards cover fair pricing, orderly trading, liquidity, and disclosure, drawing on lessons from exchange-traded fund (ETF) trading and SFC-licensed VATP systems.
The first products likely to launch under this scheme are tokenised money-market funds. SFC plans to review how things go before widening the range of products covered.
Firms that issue these products, and intermediaries such as SFC-licensed VATPs, are encouraged to consult the SFC or give notice before undertaking work connected to this framework.

numbers_and_dates.value: approximately seven-fold to $10.7 billion over the past year

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This sets out a framework for VATPs and fund issuers, not a direct bank obligation. A compliance head should track it as it shapes how the bank's tokenised fund products could achieve round-the-clock secondary trading through regulated stablecoins and tokenised deposits.

quote.text: supported by the use of regulated stablecoins and tokenised deposits to facilitate round-the-clock

reading_guide: Short press release; read in full; cross-reference the same-day circular 26EC23 for the binding rules.
flags: Explicitly links the new secondary trading framework's round-the-clock settlement vision to future use of regulated (licensed) stablecoins and tokenised deposits - a direct connection between the April 2026 stablecoin issuer licensing and the tokenised fund trading agenda that is easy to miss if these workstreams are tracked separately.

counterparty_due_diligence: If the bank distributes or holds tokenised funds through a VATP under this framework, note that secondary trading is at first limited to SFC-licensed VATPs, with OTC arrangements considered only case by case (para 2, p.1).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Tell the board the first batch of products will focus on tokenised money market funds (para 7, p.1), and that regulated stablecoins and tokenised deposits are expected to support round-the-clock settlement -- relevant to any bank stablecoin or tokenised-deposit strategy tied to fund tokenisation.

title: Speech by FS at Hong Kong Web3 Festival 2026 (English only) (with photos/video)
summary: The Financial Secretary set out Hong Kong's policy approach to the convergence of Web3, tokenisation and AI. Reaffirming 'same activity, same risks, same regulation' and a dual regulatory mandate of prudent oversight plus market facilitation. He confirmed that two stablecoin issuer licences had been granted earlier that month. Described more than US$2 billion in tokenised green and infrastructure bonds issued to date with issuance now regularised. Referenced EnsembleTX (launched the previous November) which lets participants put tokenised deposits to work in money-market-fund dealings and treasury management. He flagged three cross-cutting risks from AI-driven Web3 activity — settlement speed keeping pace with machine-speed transactions, maintaining human control over autonomous AI agents. Keeping regulation and accountability current — and announced a new Committee on AI+ and Industry Development Strategy that will cover the Web3/AI intersection.

key_points.point: Two stablecoin issuer licences had been granted earlier in the month the speech was given (April 2026).
Hong Kong has carried out several rounds of tokenised green and infrastructure bond issuance worth more than US$2 billion in total. This is now a regular programme rather than a one-off effort.
EnsembleTX, launched under Project Ensemble the previous November, lets market participants use tokenised deposits for money-market-fund transactions and real-time liquidity/treasury management.

The Financial Secretary identifies three policy challenges from AI-driven Web3 activity: keeping settlement infrastructure and cross-border standards at machine speed. Ensuring autonomous AI agents remain predictable, traceable and open to human intervention; and keeping regulation/accountability frameworks current as activity spans platforms.
A new Committee on AI+ and Industry Development Strategy, flagged in the 2026-27 Budget. Will treat the Web3/AI intersection as one of its focus areas.

numbers_and_dates.item: stablecoin issuer licences granted by speech date

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is a useful confirmation that only two stablecoin issuer licences existed as of the speech date. It flags coming AI-governance expectations (predictability, traceability, human override) that compliance should anticipate extending to any AI-agent-driven digital-asset activity the bank builds or relies on.
reading_guide: Read the whole speech; it is short. The operative policy content is concentrated in 'The issues to be addressed' and 'Hong Kong's vision and pathway'; the opening and closing remarks are ceremonial.
flags: Confirms only 2 stablecoin issuer licences had been issued as of April 2026, useful for tracking market concentration among licensed issuers a bank might rely on.

counterparty_due_diligence: If the bank plans to distribute or accept a stablecoin, note that only two issuers were licensed as of this speech, narrowing the counterparty pool (section 'Hong Kong's vision and pathway').
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be aware Hong Kong is signalling forthcoming AI-governance expectations (traceability, human override, accountability) that will likely extend to AI-agent-driven digital-asset activity, relevant to any AI tooling the bank deploys in this space.

title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Register of Licensees under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656)
summary: This is HKMA's statutory public register, maintained under section 21 of the Stablecoins Ordinance, of persons licensed under section 15(1) to issue specified stablecoins in Hong Kong. As of the page's last revision, it lists two licensees, Anchorpoint Financial Limited (licence FRS01) and HSBC (licence FRS02), both effective 10 April 2026. It notes that nobody may conduct a regulated stablecoin activity, or represent that they do so, without holding the required licence.

key_points.point: The Register is maintained under section 21 of the Stablecoins Ordinance and published for public inspection under section 21(7).

As of the page's last revision (23 April 2026), two entities are licensed. Anchorpoint Financial Limited (licence number FRS01) and The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited (licence number FRS02). Both with an effective date of 10 April 2026.
Under section 5 of the Stablecoins Ordinance, nobody may conduct, or claim to conduct, a regulated stablecoin activity without being licensed to do so.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the authoritative, primary-source list a bank must check to confirm any stablecoin issuer counterparty is validly licensed under the Stablecoins Ordinance before dealing with or distributing its stablecoin.

quote.text: must not carry on a regulated stablecoin activity

reading_guide: The operative content is the register table itself; the rest of the page is HKMA site navigation boilerplate and can be skipped.

controls_and_monitoring: Check this register (or its successor) before any relevant stablecoin activity is carried on with, or distribution/dealing involving, a purported stablecoin issuer.
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm a stablecoin issuer counterparty appears on this register with a current licence number and effective date before onboarding it as a partner or accepting its stablecoin.

title: Beware of tokens purported to be associated with licensed stablecoin issuers
summary: The HKMA alerts the public to tokens with the tickers 'HKDAP' and 'HSBC' that falsely trade on the names of two licensed stablecoin issuers. Anchorpoint Financial Limited and The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited. Both licensees have confirmed they have not issued any regulated stablecoin so far. The HKMA tells the public to check the licensees' own official announcements and to acquire or use stablecoins only through regulated channels.

key_points.point: Tokens ticker 'HKDAP' and 'HSBC' have appeared in the market but are not issued by, or associated with, the named licensed stablecoin issuers.
Both licensed stablecoin issuers have confirmed they have not yet issued any regulated stablecoin.
Public should check the licensees' own official announcements if in doubt and use only regulated channels to acquire or use stablecoins.

title: Annex: Proposed Amendments to the Banking (Capital) Rules (Cap. 155L)
supersedes_or_amends: Banking (Capital) Rules (Cap. 155L), version effective 1 Jan 2026
summary: This annex sets out illustrative drafting for proposed BCR amendments. Most items concern CET1 capital-base deductions and Basel technical updates with no VA link. The stablecoin/crypto-relevant items would: define a new BCR category of 'other regulated financial institution' covering entities such as HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers. Generally exclude such subsidiaries from an AI's consolidated capital-ratio calculation (subject to HKMA override); confirm that carrying on a licensed stablecoin activity counts as an activity ancillary to banking. Add specific default-risk-exposure rules for hedged 'group 2b cryptoasset derivative contracts'; and remove cryptoassets from the BCR's list of assets treated as low-risk 'cash items'.

key_points.point: A new BCR term, 'other regulated financial institution', would be created to cover licensed entities such as HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers, distinct from banks, insurers and securities firms.

An AI's stablecoin-issuer or other-regulated-financial-institution subsidiary would generally be left out of the AI's consolidated capital-adequacy-ratio calculation. The exception is if HKMA decides on reasonable grounds it is prudent to include it.

In deciding whether to include such a subsidiary in consolidation, HKMA may weigh several things. These are the subsidiary's business and activities, its size and financial significance to the AI, the risks it poses to the AI, and any other relevant factor.

The BCR's 'financial sector entity' definition would be clarified to expressly cover activities ancillary to banking listed in the Banking Ordinance's Fourteenth Schedule. The drafters confirm carrying on a licensed stablecoin activity falls within this.

An AI's stablecoin-issuer or other-regulated-financial-institution subsidiary may have a capital shortfall it fails to fix in time. If so, HKMA could require that shortfall to be deducted from the AI's own CET1 capital.

A new rule would set out how to calculate default-risk exposure on 'group 2b cryptoasset derivative contracts' when an AI hedges the counterparty credit risk with a guarantee or credit derivative. Mirroring the general hedging-recognition mechanics proposed elsewhere in the annex.
Cryptoassets would be removed from the definition of 'cash item' in Part 6 of the BCR. This means they can no longer be treated as a low-risk cash-equivalent exposure for capital purposes.

title: Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and Amended Common Reporting Standard) Bill 2026 to be gazetted
summary: The government announced that a bill implementing the OECD's Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) and the updated Common Reporting Standard (CRS) would be gazetted 22 May 2026. It would be tabled for first reading in the Legislative Council on 3 June. CARF requires crypto-asset service providers with a Hong Kong reporting nexus to register with the Inland Revenue Department. They must comply with due diligence, filing and record-keeping duties, taking effect the year after passage. Sharing tax data automatically on crypto-asset dealings with partner jurisdictions, alongside the amended CRS, are both targeted to start in 2028.

key_points.point: The bill was to be gazetted on 22 May 2026 and introduced to the Legislative Council for first reading on 3 June 2026.

CARF will be implemented the year following the bill, from 2027. Crypto-asset service providers with a Hong Kong reporting nexus must register with the Inland Revenue Department and meet due diligence, return-filing and record-keeping duties.

Hong Kong aims to start swapping tax data on crypto-asset dealings with partner jurisdictions automatically, from 2028. It also aims to roll out the amended Common Reporting Standard from the same year, depending on those jurisdictions' own readiness.

A public consultation ran from December of the prior year to February of the Budget year. Stakeholders, including the financial and crypto-asset sectors, generally supported the proposals, and their feedback informed the bill's drafting.
The Inland Revenue Department will issue guidance and provide technical support to help industry adapt to the new requirements.

This applies wherever it, or an affiliate, qualifies as a crypto-asset service provider with a Hong Kong nexus. Compliance should start scoping which of the bank's digital-asset activities will trigger CARF registration ahead of the 2027 effective date.

Build due diligence, return-filing and record-keeping processes for crypto-asset transactions ahead of the regime taking effect the year after the bill passes (para 4).

title: Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and Amended Common Reporting Standard) Bill 2026
supersedes_or_amends: Inland Revenue Ordinance (Cap. 112)
summary: This bill amends the Inland Revenue Ordinance to insert a new Part 8B creating Hong Kong's CARF reporting regime and to update the Common Reporting Standard rules. It defines Hong Kong Reporting Crypto-Asset Service Providers (HKRCASPs), sets nexus, due-diligence, registration and reporting duties. Creates new offences and penalties, including a financial-penalty alternative to prosecution.

key_points.point: Part 2 of the Ordinance (the CARF rules) starts on 1 January 2027; Part 3 (amended CRS) starts on 1 January 2028. The rest starts on gazettal.
A new Part 8B (sections 50M-50Y) sets out interpretation, nexus rules, registration duty, due diligence, and reporting duties for HKRCASPs.
An HKRCASP that fails to register, carry out due diligence, or file a return without reasonable excuse commits an offence punishable by a fine at Level 3.
For registration, reporting, and certain notice failures, a continuing daily fine of $500 applies after conviction for each day the offence continues.
For a due-diligence breach, the court can instead fine $1,000 multiplied by the number of affected crypto-asset users and controlling persons, if that is higher than the standard fine.
A person who knowingly or recklessly gives a misleading, false or incorrect self-certification commits a separate offence with a Level 3 fine.
An administrative financial-penalty mechanism is created as an alternative to prosecution, with a right to make written representations and to appeal to the Board of Review.
Engaging a third-party service provider to carry out CARF duties does not by itself excuse an HKRCASP from an offence for failing to register, do due diligence, or report.

title: Consultation Conclusions: Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Advisory Service Providers and Virtual Asset Management Service Providers
summary: This paper finalises how Hong Kong will licence virtual asset (VA) advisory services (modelled on Type 4) and VA management/discretionary services (modelled on Type 9). Both regimes are activity-based and technology-neutral. They catch AI-generated advice, robo-advisers and copy-trading, and they capture the substance of an activity regardless of labels like 'education'. VA management has no de minimis threshold — any discretionary VA exposure triggers licensing. VA management firms may appoint SFC- or overseas-regulated custodians of their choice for private funds (no mandatory SFC-custodian-only rule). Though self-custody of hard-to-place tokens will be subject to new SFC-prescribed safeguards. No deeming/grandfathering will be offered when the regimes commence, though an expedited track exists for firms already vetted. A single bill covering dealing, custodian, advisory and management regimes is targeted for the Legislative Council in 2026.

key_points.point: VA advisory and VA management licensing look to the substance of the activity, not its label. Content marketed as 'education', 'research' or 'trading signals' is regulated if it in substance advises on acquiring or disposing of VAs.

Both regimes are technology-neutral. Providing an algorithm or AI language model that generates VA advice, or a robo-adviser that makes discretionary VA investment decisions, counts as providing the regulated service.

Advising on tokenised securities, or on derivatives or structured products referencing VAs, generally falls under existing SFO licences (Type 4/5/11) rather than the new VA advisory regime. This is because the statutory VA definition excludes securities and futures contracts.

Advising on a client's combined VA-and-securities portfolio is not treated as wholly incidental to a Type 4 securities licence. A separate VA advisory licence is still required for the VA component, even if delivered alongside securities advice.

The SFC is separately reviewing finfluencer activity across both the SFO and the new VA regimes, having observed undisclosed conflicts of interest and 'education'-labelled promotion of specific VAs. A dedicated consultation may follow.

VA advisory service providers get a tiered capital baseline. This is HK$100,000 minimum liquid capital if not holding client assets, otherwise HK$5 million paid-up capital plus HK$3 million liquid capital, matching Type 4 treatment. Dual Type 4/VA-advisory licensees are not subject to double capital requirements.
VA management has no de minimis threshold. Any portfolio with discretionary VA exposure, however small, requires a licence, matching the 'no de minimis' approach under Type 9.
A VA management licensee that deals in VAs solely to service its own fund management (for example, converting subscription proceeds to VAs) is exempt from also needing a separate VA dealing licence.

Private VA fund managers retain flexibility to appoint any qualified custodian globally (not restricted to SFC-regulated custodians) for the funds they manage, mirroring existing Type 9 treatment. The SFC will however prescribe specific safeguards where a manager self-custodies tokens lacking any supporting custodian.

No deeming or grandfathering arrangement will be offered. Both regimes take full effect on the commencement date, with an expedited approval track for firms already assessed by SFC or HKMA. Existing RA9 managers below the old VA de minimis threshold must either seek a licence or wind down their VA management activity in an orderly way by commencement.

The VA dealing, advisory and management regimes will operate as standalone AMLO licensing regimes. These replace the current practice of imposing VA-related terms and conditions on SFO licensees under the Joint Circular, whose existing requirements become the new regimes' baseline.
Both regimes prohibit actively marketing VA advisory or management services to the Hong Kong public from anywhere in the world without an SFC licence or registration.

VA advisory/management minimum liquid capital (holding client assets)
VA advisory/management minimum liquid capital (not holding client assets)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This settles the two remaining pieces of Hong Kong's VA-intermediary framework relevant to any bank providing digital-asset advice or discretionary management. The no-de-minimis rule means even a token amount of client VA exposure triggers licensing. The confirmation that private-fund custodians need not be SFC-regulated gives more counterparty flexibility than the parallel dealing-services regime.

flags: VA management private funds are NOT required to use only SFC-regulated custodians (unlike VA dealing service providers, which are) — an easy point to conflate between the two related consultation-conclusions papers.

Advising on a mixed VA-and-securities portfolio needs a separate VA advisory licence even when delivered concurrently with securities advice — no 'wholly incidental' carve-out applies here, unlike some other cross-regime exemptions.

obligations: If advising clients on VAs in any form (including AI-generated advice, robo-advice, or copy-trading signals), obtain a VA advisory licence/registration once the regime commences, regardless of how the service is labelled (paras 6-9, p.5).

If exercising discretionary investment power over any VA exposure in a managed portfolio, however small, obtain a VA management licence/registration — there is no de minimis exemption (para 32, p.9-10).

Maintain the applicable tiered capital baseline (HK$100,000 liquid capital if not holding client assets; otherwise HK$5m paid-up plus HK$3m liquid) for each licensed VA advisory/management activity (paras 25, 48, p.8, p.12).
Do not actively market VA advisory or management services to Hong Kong persons without the relevant licence, wherever the bank or its personnel are located (para 70, p.18).
controls_and_monitoring: Review staff competence standards for anyone giving VA advice, since the SFC intends to align these with existing investment-advice competence requirements (para 13, p.6).
Monitor any AI/algorithmic tools used in advisory or management workflows, since they trigger the same licensing duties as human-delivered advice or management (paras 9, 40, p.5-6, p.11-12).

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told VA advisory and VA management will each require separate licensing with no minimum threshold for management, that AI-driven advice tools are captured, and that private-fund VA custody rules differ from the dealing-services regime.

title: Consultation Conclusions on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Advisory Service Providers and Virtual Asset Management Service Providers
summary: FSTB and SFC conclude the further consultation (closed January 2026) on separate AMLO licensing regimes. These cover VA advisory services (modelled on SFO Type 4) and VA management services (modelled on SFO Type 9). The scope is technology-neutral, covering AI/algorithm-driven advice and discretionary robo-management, and excludes advice or management confined to tokenised securities (which stays under the SFO). No de minimis threshold applies to VA management. Private funds managing VAs will retain flexibility to appoint qualified custodians globally rather than being restricted to SFC-regulated VA custodians. Though the SFC plans to set strict rules for VA management firms that hold client tokens themselves because no qualified custodian is available. No deeming/grandfathering arrangement will be given; a bill is targeted for the Legislative Council in 2026.

key_points.point: VA advisory services scope covers giving advice, or issuing analyses or reports, on whether, which, when or on what terms VAs should be acquired or disposed of. The assessment turns on substance, not labels like 'educational content' or 'trading signals'.

Mirror/copy trading that provides trading signals for others to replicate constitutes VA advisory. If execution is also provided, that constitutes VA dealing, and if trades are executed on a discretionary basis, that also involves VA management.

Technology tools, such as algorithms or AI language models, that generate specific VA recommendations for others' use amount to VA advisory services. Tools that merely filter factual information for self-directed research do not.

Advice on a client's portfolio comprising both VAs and securities is not treated as 'wholly incidental' to RA4 (securities advisory). VA advice requires a separate VA advisory licence even when given concurrently with securities advice.

The SFC is separately reviewing finfluencer activity across both the SFO and the new VA regimes, citing concerns about undisclosed conflicts of interest and 'education'-labelled promotion of specific VAs.
No de minimis threshold will apply to VA management. Any entity managing a portfolio with any VA exposure needs a licence or registration, mirroring the VA dealing/custodian regimes' approach.

A VA management licensee can deal in VAs purely to support its VA management work, for example turning subscribed VAs into cash before investing. In that case it will not also need a VA dealing licence.

SFC-licensed or registered intermediaries dealing in 'Relevant Stablecoins' (specified stablecoins issued by HKMA-licensed issuers) will be exempt from needing separate VA service provider licences for those SFO activities.

Private funds retain flexibility to appoint qualified VA custodians globally (not restricted to SFC-regulated custodians) for VAs held by the funds, mirroring existing RA9 treatment. However, the SFC intends to impose strict conditions where a VA management service provider holds client tokens itself because no qualified custodian exists for them.

Financial resources requirements for VA advisory and VA management providers mirror RA4/RA9. This is HK$100,000 minimum liquid capital if not holding client assets, otherwise HK$5 million paid-up capital plus HK$3 million liquid capital. Dual RA4/RA9-and-VA licensees are not subject to double capital requirements but must meet the highest applicable requirement.

There will be no deeming or grandfathering for firms already providing VA advisory or VA management services. Both new regimes become fully effective on the statute's commencement date, though the timing of commencement will factor in transition needs.

The VA Dealing, VA Advisory and VA Management Regimes will run as standalone regimes under the AMLO. This takes over from today's approach of attaching terms and conditions to SFO licences for intermediaries under the Joint Circular, whose existing requirements will become the regimes' baseline.

The VASP Regimes will apply extraterritorially. Any person actively marketing VA advisory or VA management services to the Hong Kong public, from inside or outside Hong Kong, must be SFC-licensed or registered.

VA advisory/management minimum liquid capital (not holding client assets)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This finalises the scope, exemptions and custody flexibility for any bank-affiliated VA advisory or fund/portfolio management activity. Two carve-outs matter most: Relevant Stablecoins dealt in by SFC-licensed intermediaries don't need separate VA licences, and private VA funds are not forced into SFC-regulated custodians only.

title: FSTB and SFC conclude consultations on virtual asset advisory and management regimes
supersedes_or_amends: Further Public Consultation on Legislative Proposal to Regulate Virtual Asset Advisory Service Providers and Virtual Asset Management Service Providers (25CP12, 24 December 2025)
summary: The Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB), together with the SFC. Issued their conclusions on the plan to license providers of virtual asset (VA) advisory and VA management services, after getting broad support across 51 responses. Following the 'same business, same risks, same rules' principle, the new regimes will be aligned respectively with Type 4, which covers advising on securities. Type 9, which covers asset management, regulated activities under the SFO. The FSTB and SFC will finalise legislation under the AMLO, aiming to bring a bill to the Legislative Council (LegCo) in 2026. Together with the already-concluded VA dealing and custodian regimes, this completes the planned set of new VA intermediary licences envisioned in the FSTB's Policy Statement 2.0 (June 2025). That statement covers VA trading platforms, stablecoin issuers, dealing, custody, advisory and management.

key_points.point: 51 responses came in from a wide range of stakeholders on the further consultation for the VA advisory and management regimes, with broad market support.

The VA advisory regime will align with Type 4 (advising on securities), and the VA management regime with Type 9 (asset management). Both are regulated-activity categories under the SFO -- following the 'same business, same risks, same rules' principle.
The FSTB and SFC will finalise legislation under the AMLO (Cap. 615) for these new regimes, aiming to bring a bill to LegCo in 2026.

This wraps up the fourth and final piece of a set of new VA intermediary regimes (dealing, custody, advisory, management). Together with the existing VATP and stablecoin issuer licences, these are meant to cover the key parts of Hong Kong's digital asset ecosystem under Policy Statement 2.0 (June 2025).
Firms already offering, or planning to offer, VA advisory and management services are strongly urged to start talking with the SFC well before they apply.

title: Circular on provision of Relevant Stablecoin service by virtual asset trading platforms and licensed corporations
supersedes_or_amends: Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities (22 Dec 2023, as supplemented 30 Sep 2025)
Guidelines for Virtual Asset Trading Platform Operators
Appendix 6 and Appendix 7 to the Joint Circular (licensing/registration T&Cs)
summary: This SFC circular clarifies how the VATP Guidelines and the Joint Circular on intermediaries' virtual asset activities apply to 'Relevant Stablecoins' -- specified stablecoins under the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) issued by an HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuer and authorised under that licence. Because Relevant Stablecoins are already subject to HKMA reserve-backing and redemption oversight, the SFC removes or relaxes several VATP/intermediary requirements that otherwise apply to virtual assets generally. These are the liquidity/index requirements for retail-tradable tokens and the client virtual-asset-knowledge assessment (for Relevant-Stablecoin-only clients). They also cover the requirement to count Relevant Stablecoin holdings toward a client's virtual asset exposure limit. Suitability requirements still apply when a VATP or LC solicits or recommends a Relevant Stablecoin. The circular also permits licensed corporations to partner directly with HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers (not only VATPs) and to hold client Relevant Stablecoins in segregated accounts at the issuer itself. It removes the prior requirement that retail VA dealing go only through an omnibus account with a platform not subject to a professional-investor-only condition. Revised VATP licensing conditions and updated Appendix 6/7 terms and conditions (clean and tracked-changes versions) are attached.

key_points.point: Relevant Stablecoins are specified stablecoins under s.4 of the Stablecoins Ordinance issued by an HKMA-licensed issuer and authorised under that licence. The circular does not apply to other stablecoins.
The retail-tradability liquidity and index requirements (VATP Guidelines paras 7.7-7.8; Joint Circular paras 20(a)(iv) and 28) need not be applied to Relevant Stablecoins.
VATPs and LCs must disclose material information on a Relevant Stablecoin's stabilisation mechanism and redemption arrangements.

VA-knowledge assessment is not required for clients who are provided Relevant-Stablecoin-only services. Firms must still assess a non-Relevant-Stablecoin-only client's VA knowledge even if that client ends up trading only Relevant Stablecoins.
Client holdings of Relevant Stablecoins need not be counted toward the client's virtual asset exposure limit.

A Relevant Stablecoin is treated as a non-complex product. If a VATP/LC solicits or recommends one, ordinary suitability requirements apply and commission rebates must not be the primary basis for the recommendation.
Licensed corporations may now partner directly with an HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuer (not only a VATP) to provide dealing services in that issuer's Relevant Stablecoin.
Joint Circular paragraph 20(a)(iii), which required retail VA dealing via an omnibus account with a platform not subject to a professional-investor-only condition, is removed.

Licensed corporations may now hold clients' Relevant Stablecoins in segregated accounts maintained with the relevant HKMA-licensed issuer itself, which provides custody with client-asset segregation. This is not only with VATPs or authorized financial institutions.

VATPs and LCs don't need the SFC's prior written approval to admit a Relevant Stablecoin for trading. They must give the SFC written notice ahead of time whenever they plan to admit, suspend or remove one.
Firms must review and update internal policies, procedures and disclosures to comply with the circular.

Revised VATP licensing condition removes the 12-month track record requirement for Relevant Stablecoins and disapplies VATP Guidelines paras 7.7(b), 7.8 and 16.4 to them. Para 9.4 is disapplied where a licensee serves Relevant-Stablecoin-only clients.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This directly shapes how the bank, as a Registered Institution, can onboard, disclose, and distribute HKMA-licensed Relevant Stablecoins, including a new option to custody them directly at the issuer. Suitability rules still apply whenever the bank solicits or recommends one.

quote.text: holdings of Relevant Stablecoins are not required to be included

reading_guide: Read paras 1-13 (pages 1-4) for the substantive relaxations, and Appendix 1 for the exact revised VATP licensing condition text. The lengthy Appendices A1/A2/B1/B2 T&C attachments mainly restate the same Relevant Stablecoin carve-outs across Part I/II dealing and advisory clauses and the portfolio-management T&C. Skim for the definitions and the specific paragraphs flagged by the stablecoin cross-references, rather than reading the full boilerplate T&Cs end to end.
flags: Corrects an assumption that all virtual assets need a 12-month trading track record before retail admission on a VATP - HKMA-licensed Relevant Stablecoins are explicitly exempted.
Notable structural point: licensed corporations can now custody client Relevant Stablecoins directly at the issuing stablecoin issuer, not just via VATPs/banks - a new custody pathway.

Joint Circular para 20(a)(iii) is formally removed by this circular, so the omnibus-account-via-non-PIO-platform requirement for retail VA dealing no longer applies generally (not just for stablecoins) - worth flagging since it reads as a broader intermediary change embedded in a stablecoin-specific circular.

obligations: As a Registered Institution dealing in a Relevant Stablecoin, disclose material information on its stabilisation mechanism and redemption arrangements (para 5, p.2).
Still perform a VA-knowledge assessment for a client not otherwise Relevant-Stablecoin-only, even if that client ends up trading only Relevant Stablecoins (para 6, footnote 7, p.2).
Apply ordinary suitability requirements if soliciting or recommending a Relevant Stablecoin, and do not make commission rebates the primary basis for the recommendation (para 8, p.2).
controls_and_monitoring: Client holdings of Relevant Stablecoins need not be counted toward the client's virtual asset exposure limit (para 7, p.2) -- update exposure-monitoring logic accordingly.
notifications_reporting: Notify the SFC in writing in advance of any plan to admit, suspend or remove a Relevant Stablecoin, though no prior approval is required (para 12, p.3).
counterparty_due_diligence: The bank may now partner directly with an HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuer (not only a VATP) and hold client Relevant Stablecoins in segregated accounts at the issuer itself (paras 9, 11, p.3) -- confirm the issuer's segregation arrangements before relying on this route.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told this creates a lighter-touch distribution lane for HKMA-licensed stablecoins specifically, distinct from the bank's general VA-dealing conduct rules under the Joint Circular.

title: Relevant Stablecoin-related Activities
summary: Since the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656, the SO) took effect on 1 August 2025, banks have shown interest in services involving stablecoins issued under an SO licence ('Relevant Stablecoins'). This short letter to all AIs covers three services: dealing in, advising on, and managing portfolios involving such coins. When a bank does any of these, it should meet the same standards the HKMA set for registered institutions (RIs) in its companion circular of the same day. That includes the terms and conditions in Appendices A1 (dealing and advice) and A2 (portfolio management). The letter stresses it does not imply a Relevant Stablecoin is an investment product. Banks are reminded to discuss their plans with the HKMA before starting.

key_points.point: 'Relevant Stablecoins' are specified stablecoins whose issue is authorised under an SO licence.
The guidance covers three services: dealing, advisory and portfolio management involving those coins.
The letter should not be read as treating a Relevant Stablecoin as an investment product.
Banks should apply the same standards set for RIs in the companion 27 May 2026 circular.

key_points.point: Appendix A1 terms apply to dealing and advice; Appendix A2 terms apply to portfolio management.
key_points.locator: p.1, 'Dealing, advisory and portfolio management services'
