title: Licensing or registration conditions and terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions providing virtual asset dealing services and virtual asset advisory services
supersedes_or_amends: Appendix A to the Supplemental Joint Circular of 30 September 2025 (Appendix 6 to the Joint Circular of 22 December 2023)
summary: This May 2026 consolidated text sets the conditions the SFC imposes (in consultation with the HKMA for banks) on firms that broker or advise on VAs. Part I covers introducing clients and dealing through omnibus accounts, and Part II covers advice. The May 2026 edits add HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers alongside SFC-licensed platforms as permitted venues for licensed stablecoins. They also create lighter paths for 'stablecoin-only' clients: no VA knowledge test, no VA exposure limit, no generic VA risk warnings, and suitability based on the client's use case. It also embeds VA financing as defined in the SFC's 11 February 2026 circular, with statement, record and custody provisions for VA collateral. Other rules such as client identity, contract notes, custody through segregated accounts, staking, record keeping and reporting of material breaches continue.

key_points.point: Introducing agents may only introduce clients to SFC-licensed platforms, or (new) directly to an HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuer for that issuer's own coins. They must not relay orders or hold client assets.
key_points.locator: Part I, introducing agent conditions (a) and (c), pp.4-5

key_points.point: Omnibus dealing is allowed only through accounts with SFC-licensed platforms, or with the licensed issuer for its own stablecoin.
key_points.locator: Part I, omnibus conditions (a), p.6; T&C para 4.1, p.10

key_points.point: Clients normally must be the firm's Type 1 (securities dealing) clients, but an RI offering stablecoin-only dealing need not limit service to Type 1 clients.
Retail clients may trade only VAs the platform or issuer offers to retail investors.
Trades need pre-funding unless the firm does securities margin financing and these terms sit on its Type 1 registration (enabling VA financing).
No yield arrangements on client VAs other than the permitted staking under Part VIII.
Discretionary accounts may put under 10% of gross asset value into VAs.
Recommended VAs for retail should be large-cap (in two qualifying indices from independent providers) and retail-available, except that licensed stablecoins are exempt from the liquidity test.
Advice on licensed stablecoins to non-institutional clients should rest on analysis of the client's use case and avoid rebates as the main driver.
Firms should detect red flags of manipulation and notify the SFC, and also the HKMA if a licensed stablecoin was involved.

VA knowledge test, risk profiling and exposure limits apply to non-institutional clients. Clearly separated stablecoin-only accounts are exempt from the knowledge test and exposure limit, and licensed stablecoin holdings are excluded from exposure counts.
Firms should identify who originates each instruction and who benefits, and keep those records in Hong Kong before effecting trades.
Generic VA risk disclosures do not apply to stablecoin-only clients; information for licensed stablecoins should include the stabilisation and redemption set-up.
Contract notes by end of the second business day; statements for financial accommodation events; monthly statements within seven business days.

Client VAs should be held on trust in segregated accounts at an SFC-licensed platform, an AI meeting HKMA custody standards, or the licensed issuer. VA collateral is kept in a separate collateral account.
Client VAs may only be used for settlement or fees, as secured creditor for VA financing, or under one-off written directions.
Receipts and withdrawals go via client-owned addresses unless third-party payment controls meet the AML guideline requirements.
Staking only through an SFC-licensed platform or an AI, with client authority, risk disclosures and client acknowledgement for non-institutional clients.
Daily reconciliation with banks, platforms and stablecoin issuers; records kept at least seven years (some two years).
No market making on an execution venue used for client dealing.
Report actual or suspected material non-compliance to the SFC and, for RIs, the HKMA as soon as practicable.
Advisory services: similar knowledge-test, suitability and liquidity rules, with stablecoin-only carve-outs and a duty to disclose the coin's stabilisation and redemption set-up.

numbers_and_dates.value: End of 7th business day after month end
Minimum 2 acceptable indices from 2 independent providers
7 years; 2 years for contract notes, receipts, on-request statements, order records

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: These conditions are imposed on a bank's SFC registration and are what HKMA and SFC examiners test for VA brokerage and advice. Compliance should update onboarding, suitability, disclosure and custody procedures for stablecoin-only accounts and for VA financing.

quote.text: Generally, Relevant Stablecoins may be made available to clients across different risk profiles.

reading_guide: Start with the Part I conditions (pp.4-6), then paras 4.1-4.8, 6.1-6.11 and 7.1. Skip the contract-note mechanics (6.12) unless building statements.
flags: Para 4.3 does not itself grant VA financing; it ties financing to firms with securities margin financing and these terms on their Type 1 registration. HKMA's companion financing circular sets RI conditions.
Part III (financial soundness) is repealed.
Custody option (a)(ii) points RIs to AIs meeting HKMA custody standards, i.e. the May 2026 custody Annex.

obligations: Use only permitted venues: SFC-licensed platforms, or the licensed issuer for its own stablecoin (Part I (a), p.6; para 4.1).
Apply knowledge test, risk profiling and exposure limits except for demarcated stablecoin-only accounts (paras 6.1-6.4A).
Disclose stabilisation and redemption details for licensed stablecoins (fn 11; Part II para 3.3B).
Hold client VAs on trust in permitted segregated accounts (para 7.1(a)); keep VA collateral separate (fn 13).
No market making on the execution venue used for clients (para 11.1).
controls_and_monitoring: Surveillance for manipulative or abusive trading red flags (para 5.1).
Geo-blocking and VPN detection for jurisdictions banning VA trading (para 6.5(b)).
Daily reconciliation with platforms, banks and stablecoin issuers (para 9.2(a)(vi)).
Account flagging to keep stablecoin-only clients from other VAs (paras 6.2A, 6.4A, 6.10A).
notifications_reporting: Notify the SFC, and the HKMA if a licensed stablecoin was involved, of actual or potential manipulation as soon as practicable (para 5.2).
Report material non-compliance to the SFC and HKMA as soon as practicable (para 12.1); provide information on request (para 12.2).
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm the platform is SFC-licensed or the issuer is HKMA-licensed and the coin is issued under its licence (Part I (a)).
For staking, confirm the Staking Service Provider has SFC approval or has discussed with the HKMA (para 8.3).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should know that stablecoin-only accounts get lighter onboarding but must be ring-fenced, and that breaches must be self-reported to both regulators.

title: Terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions which manage portfolios that invest in virtual assets
supersedes_or_amends: Appendix 7 to the Joint Circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities
summary: These May 2026 terms apply to an LC or RI managing a fund or discretionary account that meets the VA 'de minimis threshold'. That threshold is a stated VA objective, or an intention to hold 10% or more of gross asset value in VAs. They cover custody of fund assets (independent custodian or self-custody, due diligence on custodians, custody agreements and disclosure), valuation and record keeping. They also cover audits, investor disclosures and reporting to the SFC and, for banks, the HKMA. Schedules add discretionary-account rules, counterparty and cyber risk controls and example risk disclosures. The May 2026 edits carve out licensed stablecoins. Where the VA portion is only such coins, generic VA risk examples and the knowledge test for discretionary clients fall away, and the retail liquidity test does not apply to them. The companion circular also says an RI whose portfolios hold licensed stablecoins but no other VAs does not need Type 9 registration.

key_points.point: The terms bite when a portfolio's stated objective is VA investment or it intends to put 10% or more of gross asset value (GAV) into VAs.
A mainly-securities fund that drifts over 10% only through price rises is not caught if it is taking steps to reduce. If the breach looks lasting, the SFC and (for banks) the HKMA should be alerted.
Fund assets go to a functionally independent custodian and are segregated; there should be controls for new platform/custodian accounts, IP and wallet whitelisting and asset transfers.
The manager should choose and document the custody arrangement, weighing access speed, security and the custodian's ability to compensate losses.
Self-custody requires independent custody staff, trust-style segregation and adequate insurance.

Custodian selection should consider track record, regulatory status, segregation through the chain, financial resources and insurance, cyber controls and sub-custodian oversight; prefer a regulated custodian and consider more than one.
A formal custody agreement should set the custodian's scope of responsibility and liability, and be monitored.
Disclose custody arrangements, including split across custodians where more than 10% of GAV sits with one custodian or in self-custody.
Keep records at least seven years (two years for order records) and appoint an auditor able to verify VA existence, ownership and valuation.
Generic VA risk examples in Schedule 4 do not apply where the VA portion consists solely of licensed stablecoins.
Report material non-compliance promptly and give at least 7 business days' notice of significant business changes to the SFC and, for banks, the HKMA.
Discretionary clients (non-institutional) need a VA knowledge check, except where the VA portion of the mandate is licensed stablecoins only.
Retail discretionary accounts may hold only large-cap, retail-available VAs, with licensed stablecoins exempt from the liquidity test.
Mandates with licensed stablecoin holdings should disclose the coin's stabilisation and redemption arrangements.
Assess the creditworthiness of trading platforms (licensing, governance, custody, surveillance, cyber, financial resources) and set counterparty limits.

numbers_and_dates.value: 10% or more of GAV in VAs, or stated VA objective

numbers_and_dates.item: LC liquid capital when holding VAs for funds
numbers_and_dates.value: Higher of HK$3 million and variable required liquid capital
More than 10% of fund GAV with one custodian or self-custody

flags: The Type 9 registration relief for licensed-stablecoin-only portfolios is in the companion RI circular (para (6)), not in this Appendix.

Appoint an independent custodian or meet self-custody safeguards and insurance (paras 4.1, 4.4-4.6).

Disclose stabilisation and redemption details where mandates hold licensed stablecoins (Sch 2 fn 8).
controls_and_monitoring: Controls over account creation, IP and wallet whitelisting and transfers at platforms and custodians (para 4.1(d)).
Custodian monitoring and counterparty exposure limits (paras 4.10; Sch 3 para 3).
Monitor VA share of GAV against the 10% threshold (p.3-4).
notifications_reporting: Alert the SFC and HKMA if an over-10% VA drift is expected to persist (p.4).
Report material non-compliance to the SFC and HKMA as soon as practicable (para 7.1).
Notify significant business changes at least 7 business days ahead (para 7.2).

Trading platform creditworthiness factors in Schedule 3 para 2(a)-(j).

title: Virtual asset-related activities in relation to relevant stablecoins issued by licensed stablecoin issuers
supersedes_or_amends: Joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities (22 Dec 2023)
Supplemental joint circular on intermediaries' virtual asset-related activities (30 Sep 2025)
summary: This is a 27 May 2026 HKMA letter to all registered institutions, formulated jointly with the SFC. It eases how the existing VA Joint Circular regime applies where the virtual asset is a 'Relevant Stablecoin' issued under a Stablecoins Ordinance licence. It removes several retail-protection frictions for Relevant-Stablecoin-only activity: the VA knowledge test, VA exposure-limit counting, high-liquidity and complex-product presumptions, and standard VA warning statements. It keeps core suitability, disclosure and conduct duties, and requires advance notice to HKMA and SFC before starting such activities.

key_points.point: The circular sets HKMA guidance for RIs' dealing, advisory, asset-management and product-distribution activities where the virtual asset is a Stablecoins-Ordinance-licensed 'Relevant Stablecoin'. It was issued jointly with SFC guidance to licensed corporations.

VA activities are currently governed by the Dec 2023 Joint Circular and the Sep 2025 supplemental circular. After the Stablecoins Ordinance commenced on 1 Aug 2025, HKMA and SFC reviewed how those circulars should apply to Relevant Stablecoins, given their different, currency-pegged payment-token risk profile.

The circular appends corresponding updates to the Joint Circular's Appendix 6 (dealing/advisory terms and conditions, now Appendix A1) and Appendix 7 (portfolio management terms and conditions, now Appendix A2).

None of this applies to stablecoins that are not Relevant Stablecoins, or to AIs that are not RIs. It also does not apply to an HKMA-licensed issuer's dealings in its own stablecoin, since issuers face separate HKMA standards.
RIs may now provide Relevant Stablecoin dealing services by partnering with either an SFC-licensed VATP or the HKMA-licensed issuer of that stablecoin.

RIs may partner with a VATP that carries a professional-investor-only licensing condition to serve retail clients indirectly. The RI must make sure retail clients trade only in tokens the VATP has cleared for retail use. As a result, paragraph 20(a)(iii) of the Joint Circular no longer applies.
RIs offering Relevant-Stablecoin-only dealing services no longer need Type 1 (dealing in securities) registration, and are not limited to Type 1 clients. The conduct terms in Appendix A1 still apply.

For clients whose accounts are clearly ring-fenced as Relevant-Stablecoin-only, RIs need not run the standard VA knowledge test. RIs should still consider why the client wants the stablecoin, that is, its use case.
A client's Relevant Stablecoin holdings need not be counted toward the VA exposure limit normally required for retail (non-institutional, non-qualified) clients.
RIs may deal in Relevant Stablecoins through the issuer itself, and the 'high liquidity' requirement that otherwise applies to VAs offered to retail clients does not apply to Relevant Stablecoins.
RIs may receive and process client withdrawals of Relevant Stablecoins via segregated client accounts held with the HKMA-licensed issuer, which itself keeps client assets segregated from its own.
RIs should disclose material information on a Relevant Stablecoin's stabilisation mechanism and redemption arrangements when providing dealing services.

An RI managing a portfolio holding only Relevant Stablecoins (no other VAs) does not need Type 9 (asset management) registration on that account. It remains subject to the conduct terms in Appendix A2.
Relevant-Stablecoin-only advisory services no longer have to be limited to Type 1 or Type 4 (advising on securities) clients, though Appendix A1 conduct terms still apply.

Advice on Relevant Stablecoins should still be diligent and grounded in real analysis of the client's use case and alternatives. Conflicts of interest, such as commission rebates, should not drive the recommendation.
The 'high liquidity' requirement does not apply to advisory services in Relevant Stablecoins, and RIs may advise on stablecoins the issuer itself makes available.

Products that invest in, derive value from, or track Relevant Stablecoins are not automatically presumed complex the way other VA-linked products are. Complexity should instead be assessed against the SFC's general product-complexity factors and published examples.

For non-complex Relevant-Stablecoin-related products, the professional-investor-only selling restriction, the VA knowledge test and the standard VA warning-statement requirement do not apply. A net-worth check is only required if the product is a derivative or the transaction is leveraged.

RIs should still watch for applicable selling restrictions in Hong Kong and elsewhere. This includes the ban in Part IV of the Securities and Futures Ordinance on offering unauthorised investments to the Hong Kong public.

RIs should have adequate policies, procedures, controls and staff training for Relevant-Stablecoin activities. They are reminded to give HKMA and SFC advance notice before starting such activities or materially changing previously-notified arrangements.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Gives the bank a materially lighter conduct regime for licensed HK stablecoins specifically, but conditions it on advance HKMA/SFC notification, ring-fenced client handling, and continued suitability/disclosure discipline.

quote.text: primarily blockchain-based payment tokens

reading_guide: Read the whole letter (9 pages); the Roman-numeral headings (I-IV) map to dealing, portfolio management, advisory and distribution respectively.
flags: Relief is conditional on accounts/services being clearly ring-fenced as Relevant-Stablecoin-only; mixing in other VAs pulls the client back under full standard VA requirements (footnote 4, p.4).
Relief does not extend to the stablecoin issuer's own dealings in its stablecoin, which are governed separately (footnote 3, p.2).

obligations: Give HKMA and SFC advance notice before starting, or materially changing, Relevant Stablecoin dealing/advisory/asset-management/distribution activities (Implementation, p.9).
Maintain adequate policies, procedures, controls and staff training for these activities (Implementation, p.9).
Disclose stabilisation-mechanism and redemption-arrangement information to clients before dealing/advising (paras (5) and (10), p.5, p.7).
Observe applicable HK and overseas selling restrictions, including SFO Part IV, for Relevant-Stablecoin-related products (para (15), p.8).
controls_and_monitoring: Ring-fence Relevant-Stablecoin-only client accounts distinctly, since mixing in other VAs removes the lighter-touch treatment (footnote 4, p.4).
Manage and minimise conflicts of interest in advice, e.g. do not let commission rebates drive Relevant Stablecoin recommendations (para (8), p.6).
notifications_reporting: Advance notification to HKMA and SFC required before engaging in, or materially changing, Relevant Stablecoin dealing, advisory, asset-management or distribution activities (Implementation, p.9).
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm the stablecoin issuer holds an HKMA licence under the Stablecoins Ordinance and segregates client assets from its own before relying on issuer custody or dealing arrangements (para (4), p.5).
Confirm a partner VATP's professional-investor-only condition status and that it has completed retail token admission review before routing retail clients through it (para (1), p.3).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should know that regulatory relief now lets the bank deal in, advise on and distribute licensed HK stablecoins under a lighter VA regime (no knowledge test, no VA exposure-limit counting, no automatic complex-product tag), conditional on prior HKMA/SFC notification and strict ring-fencing of Relevant-Stablecoin-only client handling.

supersedes_or_amends: Terms and Conditions for Licensed Corporations or Registered Institutions Providing Virtual Asset Dealing Services under an Omnibus Account Arrangement (para 4.3, relaxed)

It also attaches the SFC's 11 Feb 2026 circular itself and cross-references the companion 27 May 2026 stablecoin circular (553c7d718bec).

It sits alongside two related current circulars: the 20 Feb 2024 tokenised-products circular and the 22 Dec 2023 joint circular on intermediaries' VA activities.
The substantive standards are in the attached letter, registered separately as e64b7b0267b2.

reading_guide: Landing page only; read attachment e64b7b0267b2 in full for the operative standards.

key_points.point: The operative text is the attached PDF letter.
It is addressed to all AIs, not only RIs.
It cross-refers to the RI stablecoin circular and Appendices A1 and A2 of the same date.

title: Circular on SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets
supersedes_or_amends: Circular on SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets issued on 7 April 2025
summary: This revised SFC circular supersedes the 7 April 2025 version. It sets the requirements under which the SFC will authorise public investment funds with more than 10% NAV exposure to virtual assets (VA Funds). The SFC authorises these funds under sections 104-105 of the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO), including VA-related activities such as staking these funds may undertake. It does not apply to exposure to Relevant Stablecoins or tokenised deposits, which are instead covered by FAQs on the UT Code. Requirements cover eligible management companies and eligible underlying VA, which must be accessible to the Hong Kong public on SFC-licensed VATPs. They also cover investment strategy limits, such as no leverage and VA futures only on conventional regulated exchanges. Transaction and custody channels must be SFC-licensed VATPs or qualifying AIs, meeting custody standards for cold storage, segregation and key management. Requirements also cover valuation methodology and disclosure obligations. Funds seeking more than 10% VA exposure, or wishing to engage in staking or other VA-related activities, require prior SFC consultation and approval.

key_points.point: Circular governs SFC authorisation of public funds with VA exposure exceeding 10% of NAV under ss.104-105 SFO.
Requirements do not apply to fund exposure to Relevant Stablecoins (HKMA-licensed, SO-authorised) or tokenised deposits; see UT Code FAQs Q20G instead.
This is a revised circular, superseding the earlier Circular on SFC-authorised funds with exposure to virtual assets, which was issued on 7 April 2025.
VA Funds are limited to investing in VA tokens -- whether directly, or indirectly through exposure -- that Hong Kong residents can already trade on SFC-licensed VATPs.
At the fund level, VA Funds are not permitted to take on leveraged exposure to VA.
Spot VA transactions/acquisitions must be through SFC-licensed VATPs or qualifying authorized institutions (or subsidiaries of locally incorporated AIs).

Custody should be delegated only to an SFC-licensed VATP, a qualifying AI or subsidiary meeting HKMA VA custody standards, or another SFC-acceptable entity. Firms should mainly use cold-wallet storage and keep hot-wallet holdings to a minimum. Seeds and private keys should be kept in Hong Kong with restricted access, anti-collusion measures such as multi-signature or key sharding, and backups.
Valuation of spot VA should use an indexing approach based on trade volume across major VA trading platforms via a reputable benchmark index provider.
Offering documents/KFS should disclose VA exposure investment limits and key risks (price, custody, cybersecurity, fork risk for spot; roll cost/operational risk for futures).

Under the ASPIRe roadmap, the SFC may let VA Funds take part in staking and other VA-linked activities, through SFC-licensed VATPs or qualifying AIs. This is subject to guiding principles on investment consistency, internal controls, due diligence, disclosure, investor notice, and reporting of VA committed to such activities.
Funds seeking >10% VA exposure, existing funds moving to >10%, or funds wanting to engage in staking/other VA activities require prior SFC consultation and approval.
Recognised Jurisdiction Schemes (incl. UCITS) and mutual-recognition-of-funds arrangements are generally exempt from these requirements, except the prior consultation/approval requirement.

numbers_and_dates.item: VA exposure threshold triggering these requirements
SFC started accepting VA futures ETF applications

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: As the current, in-force circular, this directly governs the custody and transaction-channel standards a bank AI must meet to provide VA custody to an SFC-authorised fund. It confirms stablecoin and tokenised-deposit fund exposure is regulated separately from this over-10% NAV VA-fund framework.

quote.text: should not have leveraged exposure to VA at the fund level

reading_guide: Read paras 1-3 for scope and supersession, then paras 17-21 (custody and transactions) and para 28 (staking) as the most operationally significant sections for a bank. Paras 22-27 (valuation, disclosure, distribution) are more standard fund-governance detail.
flags: Explicitly carves Relevant Stablecoins and tokenised deposits OUT of the VA-fund regime - a common assumption that 'stablecoin fund exposure' follows the same >10% NAV VA-fund rules is incorrect; it is instead governed by UT Code FAQ Q20G.
Confirms SFC now permits VA funds to engage in staking under the ASPIRe roadmap - a notable liberalisation from a stance of prohibiting yield-generating activities in retail VA funds.

obligations: Ensure any bank AI/subsidiary providing custody to an SFC-authorised VA fund meets the cold-storage, Hong Kong-based key-storage, anti-collusion and segregation standards required for custody delegation (paras 20-21)
notifications_reporting: Prior SFC consultation/approval is required for VA exposure over 10% of NAV or for staking/other VA-related fund activities (para 31)
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm VA fund custody and transactions run only through SFC-licensed VATPs or qualifying AIs, not unregulated custodians (para 17)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told stablecoin and tokenised-deposit fund exposure sits OUTSIDE this VA-fund regime (governed instead by UT Code FAQ Q20G), and that staking by VA funds is now permitted under guiding principles (para 2, 28).

title: Updated Guidance on Expected Standards on Provision of Custodial Services for Digital Assets by Authorized Institutions
supersedes_or_amends: Annex: Guidance on Expected Standards on Provision of Custodial Services for Digital Assets by Authorized Institutions (HKMA, 20 February 2024)
summary: This Annex lists 26 expectations for banks and their local subsidiaries that hold digital assets for clients, grouped under governance, segregation, safeguarding, outsourcing, disclosure, records, ongoing monitoring and staking. Compared with the 2024 version, it adds detailed wallet-operation controls. These include cold-wallet whitelists with system checks on every transfer, no smart contracts in cold wallets on public chains, and dedicated signing devices. It also adds air-gapped integrity checks, anti-blind-signing, code-management segregation of duties and 24/7 security monitoring. The fixed 50%/100% insurance or compensation footnote is gone; instead the bank is liable for losses attributable to it and must hold adequate financial resources, which may include insurance. The 98% cold-storage rule for VAs and the Hong Kong key-location rule stay. A new carve-out lets an HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuer, with HKMA consent, hold keys for its own coins in Hong Kong or another accepted location. A licensed stablecoin issuer is added as a permitted custody delegate, and third-party transfers are allowed for payments and settlement where controls exist. The separate AML section of 2024 no longer appears.

key_points.point: Scope: client-held crypto-based assets (VAs, tokenised securities, other tokenised assets) at AIs and local AIs' subsidiaries; limited purpose tokens and proprietary holdings excluded. Banks that also deal in the VAs must also follow the dealing rules, for example, on third-party transfers.
Before launch, run a full risk assessment and set policies and controls; board and senior management oversee risk before and after launch.
Resource the business with skilled people; train staff at the outset and continuously, with in-depth training for transaction signers on verification and handling exceptions (signer training is new).
Set written roles, responsibilities and reporting lines, and manage conflicts of interest across the bank and affiliates.
Maintain contingency and disaster recovery plans and now also run drills for emergency and business continuity scenarios.
Keep client assets in segregated client accounts and wallet addresses, apart from the bank's own, so creditors cannot reach them in insolvency or resolution.
Do not transfer title to, lend, pledge or encumber client assets except for settlement or fees owed, with prior explicit written client consent, or where law requires.
Controls may be risk-based by network type; new text notes permissioned tokens with smart-contract access controls may allow recovery of lost assets.
Written procedures should cover access authorisation plus detection of intrusion into critical wallet infrastructure (cold vault, signing devices, databases, production binaries, code repositories).
New: system-enforced controls should block unauthorised cold-wallet transfers, using whitelists with tight oversight of changes and systematic verification of each transaction.
New: procedures for handling security alerts and incidents by severity level with matching response protocols.
For client VAs the para 11 controls are generally required; for other digital assets a risk-based approach is allowed, with extra caution for permissionless tokens on public permissionless chains.

Keys and seeds are generated and stored in tamper-resistant devices such as HSMs. New text says AIs should perform due diligence on the HSM vendor, including its patching and prompt re-certification after patches.

Seeds and keys are generated, stored and backed up in Hong Kong. Footnote 7 lets an HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuer, with HKMA consent, custody its own coins for the bank with keys in Hong Kong or another HKMA-accepted location.
New: cold wallets should not use smart contracts on public blockchains; any smart contract in the custody process should be free of known flaws to a high level of confidence.
New: assess attack vectors regularly and before material changes, with several independent layers of data-integrity checking from start to end of each transaction.

New: strict segregation of duties for wallet code (reviews, testing, supply-chain control, approvals, secure deployment, audit trails) and least-privilege admin access, whether code is in-house or bought.
New: cold-wallet approval devices should be dedicated and isolated; integrity checks on critical transaction data should run on air-gapped devices kept in a cold vault.
Avoid single points of failure (for example, key sharding, multiple wallets) and, newly, prevent blind signing by showing signers every transaction detail in readable form.
At least 98% of client VAs should sit in offline cold storage (unchanged from 2024).

Deposits and withdrawals go only via whitelisted client-owned addresses, but third-party transfers are now allowed for payment services or client settlement instructions if effective controls exist. 'Clients' now also includes clients of SFC-licensed trading platforms.

The bank is liable to clients for losses from incidents attributable to it and must hold adequate financial resources, which may include insurance. The 2024 fixed 50% cold / 100% hot cover footnote no longer appears.
VA custody may be outsourced only to another AI (or local AI subsidiary), an SFC-licensed trading platform, or (new) an HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuer with HKMA consent for its own coins.

Delegate due diligence now includes independent code review and understanding the vendor's release process; ongoing review should test the delegate's security, incident reporting and disaster recovery, plus periodic independent cyber assessments.

Monitoring should be 24/7 including holidays, test all system changes before deployment, cover dependencies (vendors, protocols, cryptography, common libraries) and track industry incidents and public vulnerabilities.

numbers_and_dates.value: Hong Kong; or, for a licensed issuer's own coins, Hong Kong or an HKMA-accepted location
50% of cold / 100% of hot and other storage (2024 Annex fn 8) - no longer in 2026 text
numbers_and_dates.locator: 2024 Annex footnote 8, p.6 vs 2026 para 11(n), p.7

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the paragraph list HKMA will test custody against. Compliance needs a line-by-line gap analysis, especially for the new wallet-operation controls in paras 10-11 and 23-25. This includes the move from a fixed insurance percentage to liability plus adequate financial resources, and any plan to use a licensed stablecoin issuer as custodian.

quote.text: an AI should store 98% of the client digital assets in cold storage

reading_guide: Read paras 10-11 (safeguarding controls, pp.3-7) and 14-17 (outsourcing, pp.8-9) first, then 23-25 (monitoring). Paras 1-7 and 20-22 largely repeat the 2024 text.
flags: CHANGE vs Feb 2024 Annex: 2024 para 11 bullet + footnote 8 required insurance/compensation covering 50% of client VAs in cold storage and 100% in hot/other storage. The 2026 para 11(n) drops the fixed percentages and instead makes the AI liable for losses attributable to it and requires adequate financial resources (may include insurance). The 50%/100% figure now belongs only to the SFC VATP regime.

UNCHANGED: 98% cold storage for client VAs (fn 8 in both versions); Hong Kong key generation/storage/backup (para 11(b)) - but new fn 7 carve-out for HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuers (Hong Kong or HKMA-accepted location).
NEW delegation route (para 14(iii)) and new third-party transfer exception (para 11(m)).

NEW controls closely track the SFC's August 2025 VATP custody circular (25EC44): no smart contracts in cold wallets, whitelist-enforced cold wallet transfers, air-gapped integrity checks, anti-blind-signing and human-readable details, code-management SoD, third-party wallet provider due diligence and independent code review, 24/7 monitoring including holidays.

REMOVED: the 2024 Annex's separate section (G) on AML/CFT (old para 23) has no equivalent section in the 2026 Annex; old '(H) Ongoing monitoring' para 24 is now (G) paras 23-25, and a new (H) para 26 on staking was added. AML/CFT obligations still flow from other HKMA instruments and the cover letter's general reminder to comply with all applicable requirements.
Para 11(f) is one of few places using 'must' rather than 'should'.

obligations: Complete a risk assessment and board-overseen control framework before launching custody (para 1).
Segregate client assets and wallet addresses; no use or encumbrance without the three permitted exceptions (paras 6-7).
Implement all para 11(a)-(n) controls for client VAs, including 98% cold storage (fn 8) and Hong Kong key location (11(b)).
Accept liability for losses attributable to the bank and hold adequate financial resources, possibly including insurance (para 11(n)).
Outsource VA custody only to the three permitted delegate types (para 14); retain ultimate responsibility (para 19).
Give full and fair custody disclosures, including insurance/compensation, commingling and fork/airdrop treatment (para 20).
Keep per-client records and reconcile on-chain and off-chain positions regularly (para 21); produce records to the HKMA on request (para 22).
When offering staking from custody, also have regard to the SFC's VATP staking terms (para 26).
controls_and_monitoring: Intrusion detection over cold vault, signing devices, databases, binaries and code repositories (para 10).
System-enforced cold wallet whitelists with controlled changes and per-transaction verification (para 10).
HSM vendor due diligence and patch/recertification monitoring (para 11(a)).
Code-management segregation of duties and least-privilege admin access (para 11(f)).
Dedicated signing devices; air-gapped integrity checks (para 11(g)); anti-blind-signing (para 11(i)); anti-collusion controls (para 11(j)).
Regular attack-vector assessment, especially before material changes (para 11(e)).
BCP drills and end-to-end rehearsals with delegates against recovery time objectives (paras 5, 17).
24/7 security monitoring including holidays; dependency and industry-incident monitoring; independent audit (paras 23-25).
notifications_reporting: Custody records must be provided to the HKMA promptly on request (para 22).
Using a licensed stablecoin issuer as custodian requires HKMA consent (para 11(b) fn 7; para 14(iii)).
counterparty_due_diligence: Before appointing a custody delegate, assess financial soundness, reputation, management, technical capability incl. independent code review and release process (para 15).
Understand the delegate's holding terms and insolvency effect on client rights; ensure segregation per paras 6-7 (para 16).
Assess delegate resilience and contingency plans (para 17); regularly evaluate its security, incident reporting and DR (para 15).
HSM providers: capability and commitment to patching and re-certification (para 11(a)).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should approve the custody risk assessment and see a gap analysis against the 2026 Annex, notably liability plus adequate financial resources replacing fixed insurance ratios (para 11(n)) and the new wallet-operation controls (paras 10-11, 23-25).

title: Guidance on Offering of Financing for Virtual Asset Dealing, Shared Order Book, and Client Virtual Asset Withdrawals
supersedes_or_amends: Terms and Conditions for Licensed Corporations or Registered Institutions Providing Virtual Asset Dealing Services under an Omnibus Account Arrangement (para 4.3, relaxed)
summary: This is a 27 May 2026 HKMA letter to all registered institutions (RIs). It sets the standards under which RIs may offer margin financing for VA dealing, give clients agency access to a VATP's shared order book, and permit client VA withdrawals. It largely extends to RIs the standards the SFC set for licensed VA brokers on 11 February 2026. Eligible VA financing collateral is capped to bitcoin, ether and HKMA-licensed stablecoins, with prudent haircuts. Such loans get no capital credit for the VA collateral itself under the Banking (Capital) Rules.

key_points.point: Before the SFC's 11 Feb 2026 circular, licensed corporations and RIs were barred from providing any financing for clients to buy VA. This ban was under paragraph 4.3 of the omnibus-account Terms and Conditions.

That SFC circular now lets VA brokers under omnibus-account arrangements with SFC-licensed VATPs offer margin financing for VA dealing to clients with strong credit profiles and sufficient collateral.
HKMA is letting RIs providing VA dealing services offer the same kind of VA financing, provided they meet standards equivalent to those the SFC set for VA brokers.
VA financing may only be extended to a margin client based on the client's financial capability and on securities and/or VA collateral the client has posted.
Only the RI's existing securities margin-financing clients are eligible for VA financing.
An RI is not expected to raise a client's credit limit just because VA financing is now offered. It should factor in the price volatility of non-fiat assets when assessing financial capability.

Where a client's VA holdings feed into that assessment, the RI should weigh VA quality, volatility and price-gap risk. It should also weigh valuation and liquidity sustainability, and digital-asset sector concentration, including operator or treasury-company shares. It should also weigh asset-specific risk such as infrastructure failure, correlation with equities in stress, and likely deterioration of repayment ability. For corporates, it should weigh related-party VA exposure too.

The circular notes VAs have a limited track record through systemic shocks, and can fall sharply within a day or across days. VAs tend to move together across the VA sector in stress, and leverage from margin lending or derivatives can amplify losses.
An RI should carefully consider whether relying on VA as loan collateral is prudent at all, given these risks.
Eligible VA collateral is limited to bitcoin, ether, and stablecoins issued by HKMA-licensed issuers under the Stablecoins Ordinance ('Relevant Stablecoins'), with a prudent haircut applied.
A minimum 60% haircut applies to the market value of bitcoin and ether collateral; HKMA can revise this haircut later, giving RIs prior notice.

An RI relying on VA collateral should document its risk-assessment methodology in its margin lending policy, and set and monitor acceptable credit exposure accordingly. It should also keep the operational capability to track VA collateral volatility in real time and act promptly.
An RI should generally value a client's VA collateral using the execution price at the VATP where the client's orders are filled, and should keep a contingency plan for VATP outages.

VA financing counts as part of the RI's margin loan book, and existing margin-financing rules extend to it, including collateral-concentration controls covering VA sector concentration. VA collateral may not be repledged, reused or encumbered except to enforce it on client default.

RIs should fix sensible thresholds for triggering margin calls. When the loan balance is more than the collateral's worth, the RI should stop further advances and VA purchases and re-examine that client's limits. The same applies when a client has a live margin call plus a weak record of paying past ones.

The Banking (Capital) Rules (BCR) do not give VA collateral any recognition for risk-based capital purposes. So loans backed only by VA must be treated as clean, unsecured loans in capital calculations.
The underlying Terms and Conditions for licensed VA dealing/advisory services have been revised to reflect this relaxation, via the companion 27 May 2026 stablecoin circular.
For agency trading on a VATP operator's cross-platform 'Shared Order Book', or giving retail clients access to it, RIs should follow the same SFC guidance given to VA brokers.
The SFC's client-VA-withdrawal safeguards also apply to RIs that let clients withdraw VA, on top of HKMA's existing e-banking and technology-risk rules.
Tokenised products are outside this circular's financing rules; RIs should instead follow the HKMA's 20 Feb 2024 circular on sale and distribution of tokenised products.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This sets the precise conditions, collateral list, haircuts and controls a bank must have in place to lawfully offer VA-backed margin lending. It confirms such exposures earn the bank no capital relief for the VA collateral itself.

quote.text: loans solely collateralised by VAs must be treated as clean loans

reading_guide: Read the whole letter; it is short (6 pages). Pay particular attention to paras (3)-(9) on the financing/collateral controls.
flags: Applies only to RIs, not to all AIs; a bank AI without RI registration is not directly bound.
Tokenised products are expressly carved out and remain governed by the separate 20 Feb 2024 circular, not the omnibus-account financing ban this circular relaxes.

obligations: Confine VA financing to existing securities margin-financing clients and base it on financial capability plus posted collateral (paras (1)-(2), p.2).
Cap eligible VA collateral to bitcoin, ether and HKMA-licensed stablecoins with a minimum 60% haircut on bitcoin/ether (para (4), p.3-4).
Set prudent margin-call triggers and suspend further advances/VA purchases when loan balance exceeds collateral value or a client has a poor margin-call history (para (8), p.5).
Book VA-collateral-only loans as clean loans for capital purposes (para (9), p.5).
controls_and_monitoring: Document VA risk-assessment methodology in the margin lending policy and monitor vulnerable VA exposures on an ongoing basis (para (5)(a), p.4).
Maintain real-time monitoring of VA collateral volatility and a VATP-outage contingency plan (paras (5)(b) and (6), p.4).
Apply collateral-concentration controls covering VA sector concentration and ban repledging/reuse of VA collateral except on default (para (7)(b)-(c), p.4-5).
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm any VATP relied on for pricing has adequate operational resilience, given the requirement to have an outage contingency plan (para (6), p.4).
Confirm any stablecoin collateral is issued by an HKMA-licensed issuer under the Stablecoins Ordinance before accepting it as collateral (para (4)(a), p.3).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told VA-backed margin lending is now permitted but tightly capped (BTC/ETH/licensed stablecoins only, ≥60% haircut), gets no capital credit as collateral, and requires real-time monitoring and documented risk methodology.

title: Updated Guidance on Provision of Custodial Services for Digital Assets
supersedes_or_amends: Provision of Custodial Services for Digital Assets (HKMA circular, 20 February 2024)
summary: The HKMA tells all authorized institutions (AIs, that is, banks) that it has refreshed its expectations for holding digital assets on behalf of clients. The review reflects market and technology change and the start of the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656). The refreshed standards sit in an Annex and allow arrangements proportionate to each asset's features and risks. They cover assets received as a virtual asset (VA) intermediary, through tokenised product distribution, or in a standalone custody business, and also reach subsidiaries of locally incorporated banks. Banks planning to start must discuss with the HKMA first; banks already active must review and upgrade their controls. The letter replaces the February 2024 circular.

key_points.point: 'Digital assets' covers crypto-based assets such as VAs, tokenised securities and other tokenised assets, and also the keys, seeds and backups used to access them.
Limited purpose digital tokens and the bank's or its group's own (proprietary) holdings are out of scope.
The standards apply whatever the route by which the bank came to hold the client assets: VA intermediary business, tokenised product distribution, or pure custody.
Meeting the Annex does not displace other applicable legal and regulatory requirements.
The circular covers AIs and the subsidiaries of locally incorporated AIs that do custody; the local parent should ensure those subsidiaries comply.
A bank (or local bank's subsidiary) that intends to offer custody should talk to the HKMA beforehand and show it meets the standards to the HKMA's satisfaction.
A bank already providing custody should review and revise its systems and controls to meet the latest Annex standards.
The 20 February 2024 custody circular is superseded.
The letter points to the joint HKMA-SFC VA circulars and the 27 May 2026 RI stablecoin circular as related guidance for VA intermediary activity.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Custody is now judged against the May 2026 Annex. Compliance should run a gap review of existing custody (including subsidiaries) and ensure any new custody line is pre-discussed with the HKMA before launch.

quote.text: This circular supersedes the HKMA's circular dated 20 February 2024

reading_guide: Read footnote 1 (scope) and the 'Implementation' section on p.2; the Annex carries the detail.
flags: Unlike the 2024 circular, the 2026 letter sets no six-month deadline to notify the HKMA and confirm compliance; existing providers are simply told to review and revise.
Signed by the Executive Director (Banking Conduct), copied to the SFC.

obligations: Apply the Annex standards to all client digital asset custody, however acquired (p.1-2).
Ensure custody subsidiaries of a locally incorporated bank comply with the circular and Annex (p.2).
Existing custody businesses: review and revise systems and controls against the latest Annex (Implementation, p.2).
controls_and_monitoring: Maintain a scoping record showing which holdings are client assets (in scope) versus proprietary (out of scope) (fn 1).
notifications_reporting: Before launching custody (bank or local subsidiary), discuss with the HKMA and demonstrate compliance to its satisfaction (Implementation, p.2).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should see a gap analysis of current custody controls against the May 2026 Annex and confirmation that any new custody plans go to the HKMA first.

title: Keynote Speech at Hong Kong Digital Finance Summit 2026
summary: In this policy-framing keynote, the HKMA distinguishes three categories of digital asset: speculative crypto-assets (SFC's remit), tokenised real-world assets, and 'tokenised money' (CBDCs, tokenised bank deposits, stablecoins). It also sets out three HKMA responsibilities: providing central bank money in new forms, setting guardrails for private-sector innovation, and building interoperable common infrastructure. It reviews a decade of HKMA digital-money work, including e-HKD, mBridge, tokenised green bonds, the Stablecoins Ordinance and the April 2026 first two stablecoin licences, and Project Ensemble/EnsembleTX. It previews an upcoming Ensemble Use Case Report and Ensemble Taxonomy. It states HKMA now prioritises wholesale e-HKD over retail, and flags 'digital twin' reconciliation burden and platform fragmentation as the two main remaining structural challenges to tokenisation.

key_points.point: HKMA distinguishes three categories of digital asset: (1) speculative crypto-assets like Bitcoin, regulated by the SFC for investor protection and market integrity. The second is tokenisation of real-world assets, such as bonds, funds and receivables, which is a market-infrastructure question. The third (3) is 'tokenised money' -- CBDCs, tokenised commercial bank deposits and stablecoins -- which are new means of payment, not investment instruments.

HKMA defines three responsibilities in digital finance: providing central bank money in new forms to anchor trust and singleness of money, and setting guardrails for responsible private-sector innovation. It also intends to build common, interoperable infrastructure as a public good.
key_points.locator: 'The Role for Central Banking Institution' section

key_points.point: Now that Phase 2 of the e-HKD Pilot Programme is done, HKMA judges that wholesale use cases matter more right now than retail ones for e-HKD. This is given how developed Hong Kong's retail payments already are.

The Government's third tokenised green bond issuance, in November 2025, raised roughly HK$10 billion in total across four currencies, drawing subscriptions above HK$130 billion. It was the world's first digital bond to use tokenised central bank money -- e-HKD and e-CNY -- for settlement.

HKMA confirms the April 2026 grant of stablecoin issuer licences to two entities, and states it expects regulated stablecoins to launch in Hong Kong within the next few months. It is keeping the licensing threshold high and the number of additional licences very limited.

In November 2025, Project Ensemble entered its pilot phase for real-value transactions, branded 'Ensemble TX'. This allows participating banks to settle tokenised assets against tokenised deposits on a delivery-versus-payment (DvP) basis.
HKMA will soon publish an Ensemble Use Case Report and an Ensemble Taxonomy -- a common set of terms built jointly with the Ensemble Architectural Community -- to support interoperability standards.

Most tokenised assets today follow a 'digital twin' model, where the off-chain register remains primary and the token is a mirrored claim. This delivers efficiency gains but relocates, rather than eliminates, reconciliation burden. The end-state goal is 'digitally native' issuance, where the token itself is the primary ownership record.
The immediate next step for Ensemble TX is to extend it to support settlement of tokenised deposits in central bank digital currency, enabling continuous 24/7 settlement.

Ensemble TX's initial infrastructure is built on the Ensemble Interoperability Layer, drawing on Hong Kong's existing RTGS system for interbank settlement. It is described as a pragmatic first step rather than the end-state architecture.

numbers_and_dates.item: third tokenised green bond issuance size
numbers_and_dates.value: approx. HK$10 billion equivalent across 4 currencies (HKD, RMB, USD, EUR)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is HKMA's clearest recent statement of its three-part regulatory philosophy for digital money, and its confirmation that wholesale e-HKD, not retail, is now the near-term priority. This should directly shape how a bank sequences its own tokenised-deposit, stablecoin and CBDC-interoperability roadmap and Project Ensemble engagement.

quote.text: trust in digital finance will not come from the technology alone

reading_guide: Read 'The Digital Finance Landscape' and 'The Role for Central Banking Institution' sections first for the policy taxonomy. Then read 'A Decade of Progress' for concrete milestones and 'The Road Ahead' for the digital-twin and fragmentation challenges; the speech has no page or paragraph numbering.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told HKMA has confirmed wholesale e-HKD is now prioritised over retail, that Ensemble TX is moving toward CBDC-based settlement of tokenised deposits next, and that the digital-twin reconciliation burden and platform fragmentation remain the two structural obstacles HKMA is targeting through the forthcoming Ensemble Taxonomy.

key_points.locator: 'List of applicants whose licence applications have been returned, refused or withdrawn' table, p.1

quote.text: NOT licensed by the SFC

numbers_and_dates.item: LegCo sitting date for First/Second Reading

title: Circular to licensed corporations, SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities Enhanced cybersecurity measures to address evolving risks arising from artificial intelligence-enabled cyberattacks
summary: This SFC circular alerts licensed corporations, licensed VATPs and associated entities (licensed firms) to heightened cyberattack risk from frontier AI models. Such models can identify and chain vulnerabilities, execute multi-step autonomous attacks, and lower the barrier for phishing, social engineering and deepfake impersonation. It reminds firms that senior leaders, including the Manager-in-Charge of IT, carry ultimate responsibility for cybersecurity risk. It sets out five areas firms should review and strengthen: patching and vulnerability management, access and privilege controls (zero-trust design), and detection and monitoring. The other two areas are third-party supply chain risk management, and incident response and recovery. Firms using AI language models must also apply the core principles from the SFC's November 2024 generative-AI circular. They must also comply with notification requirements for high-risk AI use cases under the Securities and Futures (Licensing and Registration) (Information) Rules. An Appendix gives non-exhaustive illustrative examples of controls for each of the five areas.

key_points.point: Senior management, including the MIC-IT, bears ultimate responsibility for handling the firm's cybersecurity risk. The MIC-IT should make sure changes to the cybersecurity framework get properly reviewed, approved and rolled out promptly.
Licensed firms should assess preparedness for AI-enabled cyberattacks and address vulnerabilities, seeking IT security expert advice as necessary.

Firms should maintain an accurate, up-to-date technology asset inventory identifying externally exposed and business-critical components, updated enough for same-day prioritisation when new vulnerabilities emerge.

Firms should enforce least-privilege/zero-trust access design, treat external/untrusted inputs (apps, emails, documents, webpages) as potentially adversarial, and require maker-checker sign-off before carrying out high-impact actions.

Firms using AI language models -- internal, group, third-party or open-source -- should ensure associated cyber risks are addressed per the November 2024 generative-AI circular. These risks include adversarial attacks, data leakage and system prompt override. Firms deploying such models for high-risk use cases must also meet the notification duties set out in the Securities and Futures (Licensing and Registration) (Information) Rules.
Firms should strengthen third-party supply-chain risk governance, including initial/ongoing assessment of third-party service providers for AI-enabled cyberattack risk.
Firms should establish escalation/reporting mechanisms and pre-planned containment/exploit-interruption strategies, since AI-enabled attacks may outpace traditional detection-and-response.
LCs engaged in electronic trading and VATPs must back up their business records along with client and transaction data at least once a day.
Firms are required to give the SFC prompt notice of any material cybersecurity incident or attack, per Code of Conduct para 12.5(e) and VATP Guidelines paras 16.7(b)-(c).
The circular's Appendix sets out illustrative, non-exhaustive control measures for the five areas; firms should scale measures to their nature, scale, complexity and risk exposure.
key_points.locator: para 3-19 framing; Appendix text not captured in the fetched source

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is addressed to LCs and SFC-licensed VASPs, not RIs, so it does not bind the bank directly. Its AI-enabled cyberattack guidance is still a useful benchmark for the bank's own cybersecurity framework, and a diligence reference when assessing a VATP counterparty's resilience.

quote.text: AI-enabled attacks may unfold faster than traditional detection‑and‑response processes

reading_guide: Read paras 1-8 (context and AI-model risk linkage) and para 18 (notification duty) first. The Appendix's five lettered sections are illustrative detail that can be skimmed for specific controls relevant to the firm's gaps.
flags: Explicitly extends the SFC's November 2024 generative-AI circular obligations to cybersecurity risk from a firm's own AI model use (data leakage, prompt override) - a cross-reference easy to miss if only the cyber circular is read.

Daily backup requirement (footnote 8) is stated as already mandatory for electronic-trading LCs and VATPs under the Code of Conduct, not a new obligation introduced here - this circular reiterates rather than creates it.

The Appendix referenced in the circular (illustrative control examples) was not captured in the fetched source text, so its detailed content, including any reference to 'Type 13 depositaries' or 'large retail brokers', could not be verified and has been removed/softened; footnote 8 (the only source basis for the daily-backup point) names only 'LCs engaged in electronic trading' and VATPs.

controls_and_monitoring: Use this circular's AI-enabled-cyberattack guidance (asset inventory, patching, zero-trust access controls, third-party supply-chain risk, incident response) as a reference standard when reviewing the bank's own cybersecurity framework, noting it is formally addressed to LCs and SFC-licensed VASPs, not RIs (paras 6-19)
counterparty_due_diligence: Where the bank relies on a VATP counterparty, confirm it has reviewed patching, access-control, detection and incident-response practices against this guidance given the SFC's stated expectation of prompt notification of material cybersecurity incidents (para 18)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee (via MIC-IT equivalent) should be briefed on the rising frequency of AI-enabled cyberattacks (15,877 incidents in 2025, up from 12,536 in 2024) and use this guidance to benchmark the bank's own cyber resilience, even though it does not formally bind RIs.

title: SPM CRP-1: update on cryptoassets classification conditions
supersedes_or_amends: SPM CRP-1 Classification of Cryptoassets, para 2.6.4
summary: BRDR catalogue page for the HKMA's 3 June 2026 letter clarifying one Group 1 condition in SPM module CRP-1. The letter is attached as PDF entry dca53ff0a62c and is filed under capital adequacy, linked to the November 2025 CRP-1 module.

title: SPM CRP-1: update on cryptoassets classification conditions
supersedes_or_amends: SPM CRP-1 Classification of Cryptoassets, para 2.6.4
summary: CRP-1 sets extra conditions before a cryptoasset on a permissionless blockchain can be treated as Group 1 for capital. One condition in para 2.6.4 requires that tokenised traditional assets on such chains have a financial market regulator's approval. The HKMA clarifies that this is also met where the business activities around the tokenised asset are supervised by a financial market regulator, even without explicit prior approval of the instrument. The change takes effect immediately and will be written into CRP-1 later. It widens, rather than tightens, the route to Group 1.

key_points.point: Para 2.6.4 is one of the added conditions for Group 1 treatment of cryptoassets on permissionless blockchains.
The existing wording requires regulator approval of a tokenised traditional asset on a permissionless chain.
That condition may now also be treated as met where a financial market regulator supervises the associated tokenisation business activities.
The rationale: some such assets need no explicit prior approval yet their tokenisation is still under regulatory oversight.
Effective immediately; CRP-1 text will be updated in due course.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Capital and product teams can reassess whether tokenised bonds or funds on public chains, issued under supervised activity but not individually approved, qualify for Group 1. Compliance should document which regulator supervises the activity when relying on this.

quote.text: may also be considered satisfied where the business activities

reading_guide: One page of substance; read in full with CRP-1 para 2.6.4.
flags: This is a clarification that loosens para 2.6.4, not a tightening.
Copied to HKAB, the DTC Association and FSTB.

obligations: When classifying tokenised traditional assets on permissionless chains as Group 1, the para 2.6.4 condition can be met by regulator approval or by regulator supervision of the related activities (p.1).
controls_and_monitoring: Keep evidence of the supervising financial market regulator in the classification file.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Risk committee should note that more tokenised traditional assets on public chains may now qualify for Group 1 capital treatment.

title: HKMA establishes Tokenised Bond Expert Group
summary: The HKMA announced the formation of a Tokenised Bond Expert Group (TBEG). It brings together industry representatives from financial institutions, legal advisers, financial infrastructure and technology providers, and industry associations. The purpose is to push forward the growth and scale-up of tokenised bonds in Hong Kong. The Expert Group held its first discussion session in May 2026, exchanging views on Hong Kong's legal and regulatory regime as applied to tokenised bond issuance and transactions. Feedback is feeding into HKMA's continuing collaboration with the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB) to explore potential regime enhancements, which will be announced separately. The release also recaps HKMA's tokenised bond track record since a 2021 BIS Innovation Hub proof-of-concept. This includes three landmark government tokenised bond issuances: the 2023 green bond, the 2024 multi-currency bond, and the 2025 digital bond integrating e-CNY and e-HKD. It also covers ongoing initiatives such as the Digital Bond Grant Scheme and EvergreenHub knowledge repository.

key_points.point: HKMA has convened a Tokenised Bond Expert Group (TBEG) bringing together industry representatives to explore policy measures, market practices and innovations for tokenised bond market development.
The Expert Group's first discussion session (May 2026) exchanged views on Hong Kong's current legal and regulatory regime as applied to tokenised bond issuance/transactions.

Feedback from the Expert Group is feeding into HKMA's ongoing work with the FSTB. They are reviewing potential enhancements to Hong Kong's legal and regulatory regime to facilitate broader tokenisation adoption in the fixed income market. Details are to be announced separately.
HKMA will continue engaging Expert Group members and will review/update its composition as needed.

Since a 2021 joint proof-of-concept with the BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre, HKMA has executed three landmark government tokenised bond issuances. These are the world's first tokenised government green bond (2023), the first multi-currency digital bond (2024), and a 2025 digital bond integrating tokenised central bank money (e-CNY and e-HKD).

numbers_and_dates.item: Digital bond integrating e-CNY and e-HKD

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is context for a compliance head: it signals Hong Kong's tokenised bond regime is under active, industry-consultative review. This review will eventually shape the bank's role as issuer, dealer or infrastructure provider, but no concrete rule change exists yet.

quote.text: drive further adoption and scalability of tokenised bonds in Hong Kong

reading_guide: Read the short body (paras 1-5); the Annex is simply a membership list of ~21 institutions/firms and can be skimmed.
flags: No concrete regime changes or timelines announced yet - this is a consultative/exploratory body, and 'details of the relevant exercise will be announced separately' signals substantive proposals are still pending.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No action needed yet; note that HKMA/FSTB are reviewing potential enhancements to the tokenised bond legal/regulatory regime via the Tokenised Bond Expert Group (para 3, p.1), with details to be announced separately -- worth periodic monitoring, not immediate escalation.

title: HKMA demonstrates potential of tokenisation to corporate treasury community
summary: HKMA ran its first seminar aimed specifically at corporate treasurers, called 'Corporate Treasury x Tokenisation: The Hong Kong Advantage in Action'. More than 150 people came, from roughly 50 companies, 30 financial firms, and treasury groups. Speakers showed how tokenisation is used in treasury work, including Project Ensemble tools for real-time treasury management and tokenisation for bond issuance and trade finance. The goal was to get more firms involved in HKMA's tokenisation work and thinking about issuing tokenised bonds. HKMA plans to follow up with interested corporate treasury centres (CTCs), in line with the government's Action Plan to Promote the Development of CTCs in Hong Kong, announced 9 June 2026.

key_points.point: More than 150 people from about 50 companies, 30 financial firms, and treasury groups attended HKMA's first seminar built for corporate treasurers.
The seminar's goal was to get more firms trying Project Ensemble and thinking about issuing tokenised bonds with HKMA's support.
Panel talks covered how Project Ensemble is used for real-time treasury management, plus tokenisation in bond issuance and trade finance.
HKMA will follow up with any corporate treasury centre that wants to explore tokenisation further, tying into the government's CTC development plan announced 9 June 2026.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This shows HKMA is actively pitching corporate treasury clients on Project Ensemble and tokenised bonds. A bank's digital-asset arm could position itself as an intermediary or infrastructure partner for that channel.

quote.text: Tokenisation holds the potential to enhance efficiency and reduce transaction cost

reading_guide: Short press release; read in full (4 short paragraphs), no sections to skip.

title: LCQ6: Development and regulation of stablecoins
summary: In this Legislative Council reply, the government confirmed the HKMA received 36 applications during the initial application window under the Stablecoins Ordinance. It granted licences to two entities in April 2026, with business launch of their regulated stablecoins expected around mid-2026. Officials stated the HKMA has begun engaging remaining applicants but has made no decision on further licence numbers or timing. They stressed the overall licensing threshold will stay high and that any additional licences will remain very limited in number. The two licensed issuers are already participating in HKMA's central bank digital currency and tokenised deposit pilots, including EnsembleTX. Their proposed use cases include enabling real-time on-chain tokenised-asset transactions.

key_points.point: 36 applications were received by the HKMA during the initial application window under the Stablecoins Ordinance, of which two entities were granted licences in April 2026.

The two licensed issuers must complete technology-platform testing, reserve-asset management and safekeeping arrangements, price-stabilisation mechanisms and redemption arrangements before commercial launch. Government expects launch as early as mid-2026, based on the issuers' own plans.

HKMA evaluates remaining stablecoin licence applicants against three criteria: practical and feasible use cases contributing to the ecosystem, and a robust and sustainable business model, including risk-management capability. The third criterion is compliance with Hong Kong and other relevant jurisdictions' laws.

The government states no decision has been made on the future number or timing of additional stablecoin licences. But it confirms the licensing threshold will remain high, and that any further licences granted will be very limited in number.

Both licensed issuers are already participating in HKMA's central bank digital currency and tokenised deposit pilot projects. Proposed use cases include real-time on-chain tokenised-asset transactions to enhance market liquidity.

numbers_and_dates.item: expected launch of Hong Kong-regulated stablecoins

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This confirms the licensed stablecoin market will stay extremely narrow: 2 of 36 applicants so far, officially described as staying 'very limited'. This matters directly for counterparty concentration risk if the bank plans to distribute, hold, or settle in a Hong Kong-regulated stablecoin.
reading_guide: Read the full reply; it is compact and entirely on-topic across all three question parts.
flags: Official confirmation that the stablecoin licensing threshold will stay high and future licence numbers will remain 'very limited' — a material data point for any bank assessing how many regulated stablecoin counterparties will realistically exist.

counterparty_due_diligence: Track the identity and pre-launch readiness of the two licensed stablecoin issuers before onboarding them as counterparties, given the government confirms very few further licences will be granted (Reply (2)).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should note that Hong Kong's regulated stablecoin market will remain very concentrated by policy design (2 licences from 36 applicants, threshold to stay high), shaping any strategic decision to partner with or hold exposure to a licensed issuer.

HKMA will follow up individually with corporate treasury centres that expressed interest in tokenisation, as part of its broader engagement under the Action Plan to Promote the Development of CTCs.
