title: HKMC's HK$12 billion inaugural public digital bond issuance
summary: Hong Kong Mortgage Corporation (HKMC) announced pricing of its first-ever digital bond issuance, worth about HK$12 billion in total. It was split into three tranches: a 2-year piece of HK$6 billion, a 5-year piece of HK$2.5 billion, and a 3-year CNH tranche of CNH 3 billion. It was issued under HKMC's US$30 billion Medium Term Note Programme and priced on 10 June 2026. It is called the largest digital bond deal in the world so far, and the first from a Hong Kong public-sector issuer. The five-year HKD tranche also stands as the longest-tenor HKD digital bond to date. The bonds are digitally created and settled on the Central Moneymarkets Unit's (CMU) distributed ledger technology (DLT) platform, linked to Euroclear and Clearstream, using the HSBC Orion digital-assets platform. The settlement cycle was shortened from 5 to 3 business days. The annex lists full deal terms, including ratings, yields, listing venue, and the 16 banks acting as Joint Global Coordinators, Bookrunners, or Lead Managers.

key_points.point: HKMC's first digital bond issuance totals around HK$12 billion equivalent, priced 10 June 2026, under HKMC's US$30 billion Medium Term Note Programme.

It is called the world's biggest digital bond deal to date, and HKMC is the first Hong Kong public-sector body to issue digital bonds. The 5-year HKD tranche is the longest-tenor HKD digital bond ever.

The deal comprised three tranches: a 2-year HK$6 billion piece, a 5-year HK$2.5 billion piece, and a 3-year CNH 3 billion piece. It drew an order book equivalent to roughly HK$24 billion at its peak, spread across over 100 accounts.
The bonds are digitally created on a DLT platform that the Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU) operates, and which also functions as their clearing and settlement system.
Settlement was cut from 5 business days to 3 (T+3), with investors accessing the deal through existing CMU links to Euroclear and Clearstream.

numbers_and_dates.value: from 5 business days to 3 business days

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is informational rather than a source of obligations. A compliance head should note the operating model it sets: CMU's DLT platform and the shortened T+3 cycle. It is relevant if the bank acts as arranger or dealer on future digital bond deals.

quote.text: largest-ever digital bond issuance globally to date

reading_guide: Read the press release body (paras 1-5) for the headline facts and quotes; the Annex is a standard deal-terms table useful mainly for exact figures/dates/bank names.
flags: The press release's Annex (deal terms table: exact issue/maturity dates, yields, credit ratings, listing venue, digital-assets platform name, legal advisers, and the 16-bank syndicate list) was not captured in the fetched source text -- only the body paragraphs (paras 1-6) could be verified. Claims that rested solely on the Annex (issue/maturity dates, yields, HSBC Orion as digital-assets platform, Clifford Chance/Linklaters as legal advisers) have been removed pending a verified capture of that Annex.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Tell the board about the operating model available here -- CMU DLT settlement and T+3 settlement -- for the bank's own digital bond arranging or dealing work (paras 4-5).

title: LCQ11: Management of stablecoins
summary: A Legislative Council written question-and-answer session where the Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury describes how the government sees stablecoin risk to banks and the public. He confirms two bank-linked groups now hold stablecoin issuer licences and expects launches around mid-to-late 2026. He explains reserve-asset placement rules, cross-border enforcement steps against unlicensed issuers, and plans for a bill covering virtual-asset dealing, custody, advisory and management services later in the year.

key_points.point: Two institutions with a banking background received HKMA stablecoin issuer licences, with market launch expected between mid and late 2026.
Licensed issuers must hold reserve assets such as bank deposits and high-quality liquid debt, placed with banks located in Hong Kong.
Only entities regulated under the Stablecoins Ordinance may lawfully offer stablecoins to the Hong Kong public; other acquisitions carry no statutory protection.
The HKMA has been sending letters to unregulated stablecoin-offering businesses explaining legal requirements and may refer persistent cases to police or prosecutors.
A bill to regulate virtual-asset dealing, custody, advisory and management providers, covering stablecoins among other tokens, is planned for introduction to the Legislative Council later this year.

numbers_and_dates.item: Stablecoin issuer licences granted to bank-linked groups

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Confirms which two licensed stablecoin issuers are entering the market and the government's reserve-asset and enforcement expectations. This is useful context for the bank's own due diligence on any issuer relationship, and for anticipating the incoming VA-services bill.

quote.text: same activity, same risks, same regulation

reading_guide: Read the Reply section in full (short, six paragraphs); skip the boilerplate Question preamble unless background on the LegCo member's concerns is needed.

counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm any stablecoin issuer the bank deals with or references is one of the HKMA-licensed entities named in this and related official releases, not an unregulated offshore issuer.
Check that a stablecoin partner's reserve assets are placed with a Hong Kong bank as required, before relying on the issuer's stability.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Note to the board that two bank-affiliated groups now hold stablecoin issuer licences and that a broader virtual-asset services bill is expected within the year.

title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - FSTB and HKMA to further unlock potential of distributed ledger technology in Hong Kong's fixed income market
summary: FSTB and HKMA announced conclusion of the first phase of a joint review on wider DLT adoption in Hong Kong's fixed income market. It found the existing legal and regulatory environment already flexible enough for tokenised bond issuances. The Companies Registry issued FAQs confirming a DLT-based register of debenture holders can satisfy Companies Ordinance record-keeping requirements. A second phase, starting in the second half of 2026, will examine legislative enhancements such as electronic execution of tokenised bond issuance documents. It will also look at concepts of possession and transfer for tokenised fixed income instruments.

key_points.point: The Companies Registry issued FAQs confirming that a register of debenture holders maintained using DLT can be deemed to fulfil the record-keeping requirements of the Companies Ordinance (Cap. 622).
key_points.locator: 'Issuing clarifications on DLT record keeping' section

key_points.point: The review's first-phase findings conclude that Hong Kong already has legal and regulatory settings flexible enough to support tokenised bond issuances. This is shown by three landmark Government issuances and a growing number of corporate tokenised bond deals.

A second phase of the review (second half of 2026) will examine legal enhancements including electronic execution of tokenised bond issuance documents (for example, recognising electronic signatures for trust creation) and concepts of possession/transfer for tokenised fixed income instruments.

The Government's tokenised bond issuance in November 2025 was, at that point, the largest digital bond anywhere in the world. It was also the first to weave in tokenised central bank money -- specifically e-HKD and e-CNY -- as part of the settlement.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Confirms a primary-source legal clarification -- DLT-based debenture registers satisfy Companies Ordinance record-keeping -- directly relevant to any bank acting as issuer, arranger or registrar for tokenised bonds. It also flags upcoming legislative changes on electronic execution and possession/transfer of tokenised instruments to track.

quote.text: keeping Hong Kong at the forefront of Web3 development

reading_guide: Short release; read in full.

title: FSTB and HKMA to further unlock potential of distributed ledger technology in Hong Kong's fixed income market
summary: FSTB and HKMA concluded the first phase of a review into using distributed ledger technology (DLT) more widely for Hong Kong's fixed-income market. They found the existing legal and regulatory setup is already flexible enough for tokenised bond issuances. As an immediate step, the Companies Registry issued FAQs confirming that a DLT-maintained register of debenture holders satisfies the Companies Ordinance's record-keeping requirements. A second-phase legislative review starting in the second half of 2026 will examine electronic execution of tokenised bond issuance documents and legal concepts of possession/transfer for tokenised fixed-income instruments.

key_points.point: The Companies Registry issued FAQs confirming that a register of debenture holders maintained using distributed ledger technology satisfies the record-keeping requirements of the Companies Ordinance (Cap. 622).
key_points.locator: section 'Issuing clarifications on DLT record keeping'

key_points.point: The review's first-phase finding is that Hong Kong already has legal and regulatory arrangements flexible enough to support tokenised bond issuances. This is shown by three government tokenised bond issuances and a rising volume of corporate issuance, including from Asian and Middle Eastern issuers.

A second-phase legislative review beginning in the second half of 2026 will examine electronic execution and signatures for tokenised bond and fund trust issuance documents. It will also examine legal concepts of possession and transfer for tokenised fixed-income instruments.

The most recent government tokenised bond issuance, in November 2025, was, back then, the largest digital bond in the world. It was also the first to weave in tokenised central bank money, in both e-HKD and e-CNY form.

numbers_and_dates.item: most recent landmark tokenised bond issuance
numbers_and_dates.value: November 2025 (described as world's largest digital bond at the time)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: If the bank arranges, invests in, or acts as trustee or registrar for tokenised bonds, this confirms DLT-based debenture registers are now officially recognised as compliant record-keeping. It also flags upcoming legal changes, such as electronic signatures and possession/transfer concepts, relevant to bond documentation and custody processes.
reading_guide: Read the whole release; it is short and entirely on-topic. The FAQ itself sits on the Companies Registry website (linked, not part of this text) and was not separately fetched.

controls_and_monitoring: If the bank services tokenised bond issuers/trustees, confirm registrar/record-keeping processes for DLT-based debenture registers align with the Companies Registry FAQ referenced here (section 'Issuing clarifications on DLT record keeping').
counterparty_due_diligence: Watch for the second-phase legislative outcomes on electronic execution and possession/transfer concepts for tokenised bonds before relying on these mechanics in documentation with counterparties (section 'Next phase').
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should note Hong Kong now formally recognises DLT-based debenture registers as Companies-Ordinance-compliant, and that further legal clarity on tokenised bond execution and transfer is coming in H2 2026 — relevant to any bond tokenisation the bank is involved in.

title: SFC mandates phishing-resistant authentication methods for internet brokers and VATPs to protect client accounts
summary: This SFC press release announces the same-day circular (26EC35). It requires internet brokers and VATPs to adopt phishing-resistant authentication, such as passkeys or bound devices, for client login and device binding. They must also cease using OTPs within 12 months of the circular, or immediately for large internet brokers. It quotes Dr Eric Yip, SFC Executive Director of Intermediaries, on the need for holistic prevention, detection, response and education measures. It reiterates that senior management is ultimately accountable, and that the SFC will hold firms accountable for client losses from control lapses. It also reminds investors to adopt safe practices and report suspected compromises immediately.

key_points.point: SFC circular requires internet brokers and VATPs to stop relying on OTPs when handling client login and device binding, because of the risks involved and the existence of sturdier alternatives.

Phishing-resistant login/device-binding authentication needs to go live promptly, and in any case within 12 months of when the circular was issued; large internet brokers are expected to move immediately.

Firms should also implement monitoring/surveillance for suspicious login, trading and withdrawal activity, notify clients of key account events, respond promptly to hacking incidents, and regularly alert clients to phishing risks.
SFC will hold senior management accountable for client losses arising from control lapses.
SFC first strongly encouraged (not mandated) LCs to stop using OTPs in its 6 February 2025 cybersecurity review circular; this July 2026 circular converts that into a mandatory requirement.

numbers_and_dates.item: Phishing share of reported HK cybersecurity incidents (2025)

numbers_and_dates.value: 12 months from circular issue date (9 July 2026)

numbers_and_dates.item: Prior encouragement to stop OTP use

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This formally binds internet brokers and VATPs, not RIs, to phase out OTP authentication in favour of phishing-resistant methods. The bank should treat it as a benchmark for its own client-authentication controls, and as a due-diligence checkpoint for any VATP or internet-broker counterparty's account-security posture.

quote.text: Licensed firms should strengthen their first line of defence with robust authentication solutions

reading_guide: Short press release (15 short paragraphs plus notes); read in full. It is a condensed public summary of circular 26EC35 (SFC ref 26EC35 / id 724f4d9f786e in this batch), which carries the full compliance detail.
flags: Confirms the OTP prohibition traces back to a 6 February 2025 circular that only 'strongly encouraged' (not required) stopping OTP use - this July 2026 circular is the point at which it becomes mandatory with a firm deadline.

controls_and_monitoring: Use this circular's shift away from OTP toward phishing-resistant authentication (passkeys, bound devices) as a benchmark for the bank's own internet/mobile banking authentication controls, noting it formally binds internet brokers (LCs) and VATPs, not banks (paras 2-4)
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm any VATP or internet-broker counterparty has implemented phishing-resistant login/device-binding authentication within the 12-month deadline (immediately for large brokers) before relying on their account-security posture (para on implementation deadline)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told the SFC now holds senior management of internet brokers/VATPs personally accountable for client losses from authentication control lapses -- a governance model worth benchmarking against the bank's own accountability structure for cyber incidents.

title: Circular to licensed corporations and SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers Implementing (i) robust authentication methods to reduce and mitigate hacking risks from phishing attacks and (ii) adequate monitoring and surveillance measures to identify suspicious activities
summary: The SFC expects internet brokers and SFC-licensed VASPs, currently meaning VATPs, to adopt phishing-resistant authentication, such as passkeys or robust device binding, for client login and device registration. It also expects them to implement effective monitoring and surveillance to detect suspicious account activity. This follows large-scale SMS phishing campaigns in 2025 that used man-in-the-middle attacks to intercept OTPs. OTP (email/SMS) is explicitly no longer considered phishing-resistant and should not be used for login/device-binding authentication. Firms are expected to implement robust authentication solutions no later than 8 July 2027, which is 12 months from the circular date, with large internet brokers expected to implement immediately. Other expected enhancements, such as monitoring and client awareness, should be made immediately or as soon as practicable. Clients generally may not bind more than three passkeys/devices without additional assessment. Senior management -- the Manager-in-Charge of Overall Management and Oversight, together with the MIC-IT -- is accountable. Firms failing to prevent large-scale unauthorised transactions after a hacking incident will be held accountable by the SFC for client losses. An Appendix gives detailed acceptable authentication examples including passkeys and device-binding verification methods.

key_points.point: The SFC expects internet brokers and SFC-licensed VASPs to adopt robust, phishing-resistant authentication for client login and device binding, and to implement effective monitoring/surveillance for suspicious activity.
The SFC regards OTP (whether by email or SMS) as falling short of a phishing-resistant authentication method, and says firms should not rely on it for login or device-binding steps.
Passkeys (FIDO-certified, public-key based) and robustly-verified device binding are the two acceptable authentication methods described; existing bound devices need not be re-registered.
Generally, firms shouldn't let clients register above three passkeys, or above three devices, unless they've done extra checks for the request.
Session idle timeout should generally be limited to within 30 minutes and clients should not be allowed to disable session timeout, absent justified and monitored exceptions.

Internet brokers and VASPs are expected to alert clients right away about successful logins and other high-risk account activity. This covers logins from new devices, device binding, or passkey creation or revocation, using more than one communication channel.
Internet brokers and VASPs should report hacking incidents to the SFC immediately and conduct root cause analysis with remedial action.

Internet brokers and VASPs are expected to implement robust authentication solutions as soon as practicable, and no later than 8 July 2027, which is 12 months from the circular. Large internet brokers are expected to implement immediately.
Firms unable to meet the 12-month implementation deadline should immediately notify their case officer-in-charge.

Senior management -- in particular the Manager-in-Charge of Overall Management and Oversight, together with the MIC-IT -- bears ultimate responsibility for overseeing these safeguards and keeping client accounts properly protected.

If a firm doesn't put in place sufficient controls to stop, catch and halt large-scale unauthorised transactions after a hacking incident, the SFC will hold that firm accountable. The firm will be held accountable for the resulting client losses.

numbers_and_dates.item: Phishing share of reported HK cybersecurity incidents (2025, HKCERT)
Maximum passkeys/devices per client without extra assessment

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is a direct, dated cyber-governance expectation for the bank's SFC-licensed corporation or VASP entity. Named senior managers are accountable, and OTP should be phased out as a login factor. The SFC has stated it will hold the firm liable for client losses from hacking if controls are inadequate.

quote.text: SFC does not consider OTP to be a phishing-resistant authentication solution

reading_guide: Read paras 1-3 (background and 2025 phishing incidents), and paras 21-25 (implementation timeline and management accountability), as most consequential. The Appendix's passkey and device-binding examples (paras 1-6) are useful implementation reference, but can be skimmed once the two acceptable methods are understood.
flags: Corrects a common assumption that SMS/email OTP is an adequate second factor - the SFC now explicitly disqualifies OTP as phishing-resistant and requires it be phased out for login/device-binding by 8 July 2027.

Firms face potential SFC-enforced liability for client losses from large-scale unauthorised transactions if they fail to implement adequate protective measures - a notable direct consequence tied to this circular's requirements.

obligations: If the bank's SFC-licensed corporation or VASP is an internet broker, implement phishing-resistant authentication (passkeys or robust device binding) for client login/device registration and stop using OTP for that purpose, no later than 8 July 2027, with large internet brokers expected to implement immediately (para 21(c), p.6).
controls_and_monitoring: Limit clients generally to three passkeys/devices without additional assessment (para 10, p.3) and cap idle session timeout at around 30 minutes absent justified exceptions (para 11).
Notify clients promptly of successful logins and high-risk account activity via multiple channels (para 13, p.4).
notifications_reporting: Report hacking incidents to the SFC immediately with root-cause analysis and remedial action (para 18, p.5); notify the case officer immediately if the 12-month deadline cannot be met (para 23, p.6).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told that the Manager-in-Charge of Overall Management and Oversight and MIC-IT are personally accountable (para 24, p.7), and the SFC will hold the firm accountable for client losses from unauthorised transactions if adequate measures are not implemented (para 25, p.7).

title: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Cybersecurity Webinar
summary: This is an administrative SFC circular inviting licensed corporations, SFC-licensed VASPs and associated entities to nominate staff to attend one of two free Cybersecurity Webinar sessions. Nominees could include management, compliance and IT staff, and system vendor representatives. The sessions, in English and Cantonese, ran on 30 July 2026 via Zoom, covering the cyber threat landscape and the SFC's expectations under its AI-enabled cyberattack circular. Enrolment (max three representatives per firm, one form per firm) was due by 24 July 2026 via a linked online form, allocated first-come-first-served.

key_points.point: SFC hosted two Cybersecurity Webinar sessions (English 15:00-16:15, Cantonese 16:30-17:45) on 30 July 2026 via Zoom.
Webinar objectives: raise awareness of AI-enabled cyberattack threats and share SFC expectations/guidance/practical measures under the related circular.
Each firm should submit only one enrolment form, with a maximum of three representatives, by 24 July 2026, allocated first-come-first-served.

Webinar covered the current/emerging cyber threat landscape, SFC's expectations under the AI-enabled cyberattack circular, and practical mitigation measures, with speakers from the SFC, PwC Hong Kong and NyxLab.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Purely a past training-event notice tied to the AI-enabled cyberattack circular (26EC32); no independent regulatory obligation, now historical since the event date has passed.

quote.text: raise awareness of the evolving threats posed by artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled cyberattacks

reading_guide: Short administrative circular; read in full (2 pages) - mainly logistics, now of historical interest only since the 30 July 2026 event date has passed.
flags: Event-logistics circular only, now historical (webinar date has passed as of 2026-09-25); no substantive new regulatory requirement beyond referencing the 2 June 2026 AI-cyberattack circular (26EC32).

title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - EvergreenHub: Navigating Bond Tokenisation  Digital Bond Knowledge Repository
summary: EvergreenHub is HKMA's reference repository on Project Evergreen and Hong Kong's tokenised bond market. It recounts three Government tokenised green bond issuances: the Feb 2023 proof-of-concept and the Feb 2024 first multi-currency digital bond. The third is the Nov 2025 record HK$10bn issuance integrating e-CNY/e-HKD settlement. It also lists ongoing HKMA efforts: consistent tokenised government bond supply, financial infrastructure interoperability, and the Tokenised Bond Expert Group. Other efforts include the DLT legal-framework review with FSTB, and the Digital Bond Grant Scheme, a subsidy of up to HK$2.5 million per eligible digital bond issuance.

key_points.point: The Government's first tokenised green bond, in February 2023, proved compatibility with Hong Kong's legal and regulatory framework, and completed a full bond lifecycle on DLT, from issuance to redemption. It also shortened primary settlement from typical T+5 to T+1.
The second issuance, in February 2024, broke new ground as the world's first digital bond spanning multiple currencies (HKD, RMB, USD, EUR), worth around HK$6 billion equivalent.

The third issuance, in November 2025, set a new record, raising more than HK$10 billion across four currency tranches, with over HK$130 billion in subscriptions. It stretched tenor out to five years, and became the first to settle via tokenised central bank money -- e-HKD and e-CNY -- for its HKD and RMB tranches.
The HKMA's Digital Bond Grant Scheme pays up to HK$2.5 million per qualifying digital bond issued in Hong Kong (see separate registry entry for the Guideline, id 5a0563de8142).
HKMA is exploring legal framework enhancements for DLT adoption in the fixed income market jointly with FSTB (see the related 29 June 2026 press release, id 279f10054c6e).

numbers_and_dates.value: over HK$10 billion equivalent, 4 currency tranches

numbers_and_dates.item: Digital Bond Grant Scheme maximum grant

numbers_and_dates.value: shortened from typical T+5 to T+1

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is a central reference hub for any bank considering acting as arranger, dealer or DLT platform provider on a tokenised bond in Hong Kong, including the DBGS subsidy scheme. It links to the underlying HKMA 'Bond Tokenisation in Hong Kong' report, separately registered as id a0b44be27c40, that sets out the legal deal-structuring analysis.
reading_guide: Read the three issuance summaries (2023/2024/2025) and the Digital Bond Grant Scheme paragraph; the page's substantial site-navigation boilerplate and long video/podcast list can be skipped.
flags: Three of this page's cited external attachments (BIS Project Genesis reports 1-3) failed to fetch (0 characters returned) and could not be reviewed; flagged as text_unavailable for those items.

counterparty_due_diligence: If engaging a DLT platform provider for a tokenised bond issuance, review the Tokenised Bond Expert Group and Digital Bond Grant Scheme eligibility criteria for Hong Kong-nexus requirements.

title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Regulatory Regime for Stablecoin Issuers
summary: This is the HKMA's standing web page for the stablecoin issuer licensing regime, which took effect on 1 August 2025 under the Stablecoins Ordinance. It links to the licensee register, the Explanatory Note on licensing, the Supervisory Guideline, the AML/CFT Guideline, and the full history of discussion papers, consultations and conclusions that preceded the regime. It also lists related press releases and speeches, including confirmation that the first licences were granted on 10 April 2026. The page is a navigation hub rather than a source of new obligations in itself.

key_points.point: Issuing a fiat-referenced stablecoin has been a licensable activity in Hong Kong since 1 August 2025, when the Stablecoins Ordinance regime started operating.
The page hosts the Register of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers, which the public can check for who currently holds a licence.
key_points.locator: 'Register of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers' section, p.1

key_points.point: Firms interested in applying are told to read the Explanatory Note and are invited to contact HKMA early for informal discussion before applying.
HKMA has published a general supervisory guideline and a dedicated AML/CFT guideline setting out its regulatory expectations for licensees.
key_points.locator: 'Supervision of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers' section, p.1

key_points.point: The first stablecoin issuer licences were announced as granted on 10 April 2026, roughly eight months after the regime began.
key_points.locator: press release list entry '10 Apr 2026', p.1

key_points.point: A sandbox for prospective stablecoin issuers was launched in March 2024 and its participants were announced in July 2024, well before the ordinance itself came into force.
key_points.locator: press release list entries 'Mar 2024' and 'Jul 2024', p.1

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This page is the fastest way for compliance to confirm who currently holds a Hong Kong stablecoin issuer licence, and to reach the current versions of the binding guidelines. This matters both for a bank's own potential issuance plans and for due diligence on any stablecoin issuer counterparty.
reading_guide: Read the whole page once; it is short. Use it mainly as an index to the Explanatory Note, the two guidelines and the register, rather than for substantive rules.

controls_and_monitoring: Periodically re-check the Register of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers before onboarding or continuing to deal with a stablecoin issuer counterparty.
counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm a stablecoin issuer counterparty appears on the HKMA Register of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers before treating its tokens as issued by a licensed entity.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told when the first licensees are granted or the register changes materially, as this affects which stablecoins the bank may safely deal in or distribute.

title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Complaints about Licensed Stablecoin Issuers
summary: This HKMA consumer-facing webpage explains how a customer can complain about a licensed stablecoin issuer. It states that the Stablecoins Ordinance obliges every licensed issuer to run a redress process that meets set quality standards. It also names a designated officer at each issuer to receive complaints, with a contact list attached. If an issuer does not resolve a complaint, or misconduct is suspected, the customer can escalate to HKMA, which logs, reviews and refers the case, and writes back with an outcome. HKMA is explicit that it stays out of the underlying commercial dispute and does not order compensation. A 7-business-day first-response target and minimal personal-data rules are also set out. The page was last revised 13 July 2026.

key_points.point: Under the Stablecoins Ordinance, each licensed stablecoin issuer must operate a complaints and redress process that is easy to reach, fairly run, timely and well-recorded.
key_points.locator: Section 'Lodging Complaint with Licensed Stablecoin Issuers', p.1

key_points.point: Every licensed issuer has a named officer or unit responsible for taking in customer complaints, with contact details on a companion list.
key_points.locator: Section 'Lodging Complaint with Licensed Stablecoin Issuers', p.1

key_points.point: A customer may bring a complaint to HKMA once the issuer has failed to fix it, or where the customer thinks staff or the issuer acted improperly.
key_points.locator: Section 'Lodging Complaint with the HKMA', p.1

key_points.point: HKMA's process for an escalated case is: acknowledge receipt, assess it, pass it to the issuer as needed, then write to the complainant once handling is finished.
key_points.locator: Section 'Lodging Complaint with the HKMA', p.1

key_points.point: HKMA will not second-guess an issuer's business choices, settle a dispute between issuer and customer, or direct an issuer to pay compensation.
key_points.locator: Section 'Lodging Complaint with the HKMA', p.1

key_points.point: Giving personal data beyond name and a way to be contacted is optional for a complainant.
key_points.locator: Section 'Lodging Complaint with the HKMA', p.1

key_points.point: HKMA targets a first substantive reply within 7 working days of validating a complaint or enquiry it receives.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: It sets the baseline consumer-redress standard a bank must meet if it, or an affiliate, becomes a licensed stablecoin issuer. It confirms HKMA will not compel compensation, so any redress promise to customers is the issuer's own commitment, not a regulator-backed guarantee.

quote.text: adequate, accessible, affordable, independent, fair, accountable, timely and efficient
quote.locator: Section 'Lodging Complaint with Licensed Stablecoin Issuers', p.1

reading_guide: Read the two short body sections ('Lodging Complaint with Licensed Stablecoin Issuers' and 'Lodging Complaint with the HKMA'); skip the site navigation menu text at the top, which is boilerplate.
flags: HKMA states plainly it will not order a licensed stablecoin issuer to pay compensation — worth correcting any assumption that regulator escalation guarantees a payout.

obligations: If the bank or a bank affiliate is a licensed stablecoin issuer, it must maintain a compliant complaints/redress process and a named complaint-handling contact (Section 'Lodging Complaint with Licensed Stablecoin Issuers', p.6).
controls_and_monitoring: Track complaint intake, resolution times and outcomes against the 7-working-day HKMA benchmark referenced on the page.
counterparty_due_diligence: When onboarding or relying on a third-party licensed stablecoin issuer, verify its published complaint-handling contact is current and its process meets the statutory standard.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should be told when a customer complaint against a bank-linked stablecoin issuer is escalated to HKMA, and that HKMA itself will not direct or guarantee compensation.

title: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities - Anti-Money Laundering / Counter-Financing of Terrorism (1) FATF Statement on High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action (2) FATF Statement on Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring (3) Outcomes from the FATF Plenary, 17-19 June 2026
supersedes_or_amends: SFC circular issued 13 March 2026 (ref 26EC13) on FATF High-Risk Jurisdictions
summary: This is a routine SFC anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing (AML/CFT) relay of the Financial Action Task Force's (FATF) 19 June 2026 statements. It covers the Call for Action list: countermeasures against North Korea and Iran, and extra due diligence for Myanmar. It also covers the Increased Monitoring list: Bosnia and Herzegovina and Iraq added; Algeria and Namibia removed. It also relays selected results from the FATF Plenary of 17-19 June 2026. These include a new report on public/private information-sharing partnerships, and a public consultation on cross-border payment transparency guidance under Recommendation 16, closing 21 August 2026. They also include a report on terrorist financing through social media, messaging, and streaming platforms, and a coming report on underground banking and hawala misuse. Further results are the seventh targeted update on how FATF's virtual asset and Virtual Asset Service Provider (VASP) standards are being applied. There is also a new targeted report on money-laundering, terrorist-financing, and proliferation-financing risk in decentralised finance (DeFi) platforms. Licensed corporations, VASPs, and associated entities are reminded to apply enhanced due diligence and the special high-risk-jurisdiction rules in the AML Guideline.

key_points.point: FATF calls for countermeasures against North Korea and Iran, and for due diligence proportionate to risk in Myanmar's case. This has been in place since October 2022, with countermeasures to be considered if there is no progress by October 2026.
FATF's Increased Monitoring list was updated: Bosnia and Herzegovina and Iraq were added; Algeria and Namibia were removed.

Firms are reminded to pay particular attention and take extra care with business relationships and transactions tied to higher-risk jurisdictions. They should apply the special high-risk rules under paragraphs 4.9 and 4.13 of the AML Guideline.

The FATF Plenary, held 17-19 June 2026, approved a seventh targeted update on how its virtual asset and VASP standards are being applied. It also approved a new targeted report on DeFi platforms' money-laundering, terrorist-financing, and proliferation-financing risk, both due to be published later.
A public consultation on new guidance for cross-border payment transparency under Recommendation 16 closes on 21 August 2026.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Most of this is a routine jurisdictional-risk update for AML/CFT screening. But the item on the coming FATF virtual asset and DeFi reports flags future SFC or HKMA guidance that a bank's digital-asset AML program should watch for.

quote.text: exercise extra care in respect of business relationships and transactions associated with jurisdictions

reading_guide: This is a routine FATF list relay. The jurisdiction lists (sections 1-2) can be skimmed for country names and changes. Section (3)(e), on the VA/VASP and DeFi FATF reports, is the only forward-looking item of note for digital-asset purposes.
flags: Routine FATF relay per usual convention, but contains a substantive forward-looking item: FATF's 7th targeted VA/VASP implementation update and a new DeFi-specific ML/TF/PF report were approved and are pending publication - worth tracking as a future source, not yet published as of this circular.

title: Digital Bond Grant Scheme
summary: This is a one-page HKMA summary flyer for the Digital Bond Grant Scheme (DBGS), a subsidy for issuing bonds on distributed ledger technology (DLT) in Hong Kong. It states it is for reference only, and points to a separate full Guideline for binding terms. A bond meeting only the basic conditions -- issued in Hong Kong, plus either genuine local DLT-team presence or issuance on the CMU's own DLT platform -- qualifies for a half grant. That half grant is up to HK$1.25 million, covering half of eligible costs. Meeting four extra conditions as well raises the cap to a full HK$2.5 million grant. Those conditions are an independent DLT platform provider, a minimum HK$1 billion issuance size, and at least five unrelated investors at issuance. The last condition is a listing on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong or an SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform (VATP). Eligible costs named are Hong Kong-based DLT platform, legal, listing, arranger and audit fees, plus CMU lodging and clearing fees.

key_points.point: The scheme reimburses half of eligible issuance costs, capped at HK$1.25 million, once only the basic conditions are met.
A higher cap of HK$2.5 million applies only if the basic conditions and all four additional conditions are satisfied.
One basic condition is that the bond is issued in Hong Kong.
The other basic condition, met either way, is that the DLT development/operations team has a real Hong Kong footprint, or the bond runs on the CMU's own DLT platform.
An additional condition requires the DLT platform provider to be unrelated to (not an associate of) the bond issuer.
Another additional condition sets a minimum issuance size of HK$1 billion equivalent.
A further additional condition requires at least five investors at issuance who are not connected to the issuer or the DLT platform provider.
The last additional condition requires listing either on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong or on an SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform.
Costs the grant can reimburse span Hong Kong-based DLT platform, legal, arranger and audit fees, exchange/VATP listing fees, and CMU fees for lodging and clearing the bond.

numbers_and_dates.value: HK$1.25 million (50% of eligible expenses, basic requirements only)

numbers_and_dates.item: minimum issuance size for full grant
minimum unrelated investors for full grant

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: A bank arranging, underwriting or issuing tokenised/digital bonds in Hong Kong can weigh this cost subsidy in DLT-platform and listing-venue choices. Compliance must still check the full Guideline, not captured in this text, for binding eligibility and application terms before relying on the flyer's figures.

quote.text: The summary below is for reference only

reading_guide: The whole one-page flyer is short enough to read in full; do not treat it as the authoritative source — the linked full Guideline (not in this text) governs actual applications.
flags: Only a summary flyer was captured; the full Guideline it references (accessed via a QR code) is not in the source text, so no paragraph-numbered locators exist — treat figures here as indicative pending the full Guideline.

controls_and_monitoring: If applying, track that all eligibility conditions actually used to claim the grant level (basic vs. full) remain true at issuance, since the higher cap depends on investor count, size and listing venue conditions being met together.
notifications_reporting: Application to HKMA is required to access the grant, per the enquiry/application contact given (dbgs@hkma.gov.hk), though the process itself is not detailed in this summary.
counterparty_due_diligence: Where a DLT platform provider or VATP is involved in a subsidised issuance, confirm it is not an associate of the issuer, as required for the full grant, and that any VATP relied on for listing is SFC-licensed.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board/risk committee should note this is a cost-incentive scheme, not a regulatory approval or safe harbour, and full terms sit in a separate Guideline not reviewed here.

title: Licensed Stablecoin Issuers’ Contact Persons for Handling Customer Complaints

HSBC's complaint contact is its Customer Relations Manager, reachable by phone, fax, email (feedback@hsbc.com.hk) or post.

title: Appointments to Task Force on Promoting Web3 Development
summary: The government named three new non-official members of the Task Force on Promoting Web3 Development; their term runs to 30 June 2027. title: Circular to licensed corporations, SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities Mitigating risks in receiving deposits through simplified eDDA arrangements
summary: The SFC highlights risks in licensed firms' use of simplified Electronic Direct Debit Authorisation (eDDA) arrangements for receiving client trading-account deposits. Under simplified eDDA, the firm, as payee, initiates a client's bank debit setup based on client-provided pre-authorisation, rather than the client initiating it via their own bank. Key risks are impersonation/unauthorised eDDA setup using stolen bank details, and financial exposure from indemnities the firm gives its bank against claims from fraudulent or erroneous setups. The circular requires firms to review their simplified-eDDA arrangements, assess risk, and implement mitigation measures before processing new setup requests, including verifying bank account ownership (for example, via a one-off small-value transfer) and verifying identification information consistency, declining/withholding processing on unresolved red flags (for example, deposits immediately converted to virtual assets and withdrawn), imposing transaction limits or withholding periods, and disclosing eDDA settings to clients with their consent. Where risks cannot be adequately mitigated, firms should switch to alternative deposit arrangements.

key_points.point: Under simplified eDDA, the licensed firm, as payee, initiates the setup request based on client-provided pre-authorisation and bank details, rather than the client initiating via their own bank (standard eDDA). Firms bear primary responsibility for ensuring proper authorisation where the payer bank does not require account-owner confirmation.
Firms may be required to indemnify their bank against losses from fraudulent or erroneous eDDA setup requests/deposits.

Before processing new simplified eDDA setup requests, firms should ascertain bank account ownership. This can be done by assessing the payer bank's authentication process, or via a one-off small-value transfer verified against the account holder's name. Firms should also verify identification information consistency with firm records.

Firms should decline or withhold processing where verification cannot be satisfied or red flags are detected. Red flags include repeated setup failures, frequent or large deposits without rationale, and deposits inconsistent with client profile. They also include a new eDDA setup followed by whitelisting a new VA wallet address, or vice versa, and deposits quickly converted to virtual assets and withdrawn.

Suspicious transactions must be promptly investigated and, where warranted, reported to the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit or Anti-Deception Coordination Centre (HKPF). They must also be notified to the SFC per Code of Conduct para 12.5 or VATP Guidelines para 16.7, where applicable.

Clients onboarded via 'online onboarding using a designated bank account in Hong Kong' should not have their initial deposit accepted via simplified eDDA. This is unless the firm can confirm the account owner has given their consent to that setup.
Firms should consider supplementary measures such as transaction amount/frequency limits, withholding periods after deposits, and step-up authentication.
Where risks cannot be adequately mitigated, firms should switch to other ways of taking deposits, such as standard eDDA or bank transfers.
Firms should disclose eDDA settings (limits, expiry) to clients, obtain consent, and remind clients to monitor their linked bank accounts for irregularities.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This circular binds SFC-licensed corporations and VASPs as eDDA payees, not the bank as the account-holding institution. A compliance head should treat its red-flag list -- especially rapid VA conversion after a new eDDA setup -- as a template for the bank's own deposit-fraud monitoring. This is because the bank's customer accounts are the ones being debited.

quote.text: new eDDA setup request followed by the whitelisting of a new wallet address

reading_guide: Read paras 1-6 for the mechanism and risk, then paras 9-13, the operative risk-assessment and mitigation requirements, as the core compliance content. Paras 14-17 are disclosure and administrative wrap-up.
flags: Explicitly links a bank-deposit fraud typology (eDDA) to virtual asset laundering by flagging 'eDDA deposit quickly converted to VA and withdrawn' as a named red flag - useful corrective for anyone assuming eDDA/deposit-fraud circulars are unrelated to VA/crypto risk.

controls_and_monitoring: If the bank's own securities/VA-dealing arm is an LC or VASP payee under simplified eDDA, verify bank account ownership (e.g. a one-off small-value transfer) and identification consistency before processing new setups (para 10)
Treat rapid VA conversion and withdrawal shortly after a new eDDA setup as a red flag requiring investigation (para 11)
notifications_reporting: Report suspicious eDDA-linked transactions to the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit / Anti-Deception Coordination Centre, and notify the SFC per Code of Conduct para 12.5 / VATP Guidelines para 16.7 where applicable (para 11, footnotes 7-8)
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be told that, as the payer bank whose customer accounts may be debited via a counterparty's simplified eDDA setup, the bank's own fraud-monitoring and customer-alert processes are a complementary control layer to the SFC's guidance directed at LC/VASP payees.

title: Circular to Licensed Corporations, SFC-licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers and Associated Entities Brokers' Forum
summary: This is an administrative SFC circular inviting licensed corporations, licensed VASPs and associated entities to nominate management and compliance personnel to attend a Cantonese-language Brokers' Forum. It takes place on 28 September 2026 at the SFC's office, focused on cybersecurity and anti-scam supervisory observations and regulatory updates for the securities industry. Attendance is free and offers 1.5 CPT hours. Enrolment, maximum two representatives per firm and one form per firm, was due by 10 September 2026 via a linked online form, allocated first-come-first-served.

key_points.point: SFC will host a Brokers' Forum on 28 September 2026, 16:30-18:15, at its office, conducted in Cantonese, focused on cybersecurity and anti-scam measures for the securities industry.
Attendance offers 1.5 Continuous Professional Training (CPT) hours for those attending the whole session.
Each firm should submit only one enrolment form, maximum two representatives, by 10 September 2026, allocated first-come-first-served.

Programme includes a keynote from a Legislative Council member, and a Hong Kong Police Force presentation on cyber resilience and scam prevention for brokers. It also includes a panel on collective action against financial scams with SFC, police and industry representatives.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is an administrative event notice; the enrolment window had already closed as of 25 Sept 2026, and the event itself is 3 days after this reading date. It is topically relevant as it signals continued SFC focus on cybersecurity and anti-scam supervisory themes echoed in the batch's other cybersecurity and eDDA-fraud circulars.

quote.text: Securing the Trade: Cyber Resilience and Scam Prevention for Brokers

reading_guide: Short administrative circular; read in full (1 page circular plus 1-page Appendix rundown) - mainly logistics and CPT/registration details.

title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC)
summary: This is the central bank's standing web page pulling together its whole central-bank digital currency workstream. It walks through the wholesale line of work, starting with an early proof of concept in 2017. This runs through joint cross-border trials with Thailand, a wider multi-country bridge project, and a tokenised-deposit initiative called Project Ensemble. It then covers a separate retail-facing strand, exploring a possible Hong Kong dollar digital currency for individuals and firms, including two rounds of public feedback and two pilot phases. The page states plainly that the authority has not yet decided whether or when to launch a retail digital currency. It will instead put its near-term effort into the wholesale, institutional side. It links out to the underlying reports, whitepapers and pilot summaries that give the detail behind each project name.

key_points.point: The authority is putting near-term priority on a digital currency built for banks and other institutions rather than one for consumers. It is keeping the option open to extend it to retail use later.

The wholesale work began in 2017 as a proof of concept with the three banknote-issuing banks, then extended cross-border with Thailand. It later added mainland China, the UAE and the BIS innovation arm, under the name mBridge.

A newer strand, Project Ensemble, launched in 2024 to build shared settlement rails for tokenised bank deposits and other tokenised assets. It moved from a sandbox into a live pilot called Ensemble TX, with named participating banks.

An architecture community of market participants was set up in 2024 to help agree common technical standards. This is so that tokenised deposits, tokenised assets and any future digital Hong Kong dollar can work together.

On the retail side, two rounds of market feedback and two pilot phases with industry were completed, with reports in 2023 and 2025. The authority then concluded that, for now, the bigger near-term value lies in the wholesale space rather than a retail digital Hong Kong dollar.
key_points.locator: e-HKD Pilot Programme Phase 1 / Phase 2 sections

key_points.point: No decision has been taken on whether, or when, a retail digital Hong Kong dollar would actually be launched. Preparatory legal, policy and technical groundwork is being completed instead, expected by the first half of 2026.

The authority also ran two earlier joint research projects on a possible retail digital currency with the Bank for International Settlements and other central banks. One project looked at a two-tier prototype, and the other at giving private firms direct access to a central-bank ledger.

numbers_and_dates.value: 20 banks in 4 jurisdictions, 160+ transactions, over HK$171 million

numbers_and_dates.item: e-HKD retail preparatory work target completion
numbers_and_dates.locator: 'HKMA's Policy Stance on e-HKD used in retail applications' section

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This page is the compliance head's map of every named HKMA digital-money initiative the bank may be asked to join or reference. It confirms there is still no live retail digital Hong Kong dollar and no firm launch date, so no new consumer-facing obligations arise from it yet. It does flag that tokenised deposits and cross-border wholesale settlement are the areas moving fastest, which is where the bank's treasury and payments teams are most likely to be approached next.

quote.text: has not yet reached a policy decision on whether or when

reading_guide: Read the wholesale and retail section headers and their opening paragraphs first. Skip the speech and press-release listings and the academic expert-group member table at the bottom, which are not substantive.

counterparty_due_diligence: Track which named banks and pioneers sit on Ensemble TX and the mBridge pilot, since those relationships signal where the authority expects institutional participation to grow first.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: No live retail digital Hong Kong dollar exists and none is imminent; the board should be told that current exposure is limited to voluntary participation in wholesale pilots such as Ensemble.

title: The Chief Executive's 2026 Policy Address
summary: This is the Chief Executive's annual policy speech to the legislature, setting government priorities across many areas. Within the finance chapter, it lists a cluster of digital-asset initiatives that regulators and market bodies are pursuing over the coming years. These include a test of putting Exchange Fund Bills on a distributed ledger, and a new digital-asset settlement platform at the clearing house CMU OmniClear. They also include wider bond tokenisation work, and a blockchain-based tokenisation platform at the exchange operator. It also flags planned moves to widen virtual-asset licensing coverage, let licensed trading venues offer regulated stablecoins, and expand tokenised bank deposits and a wholesale digital-currency settlement pilot. A separate customs-led programme will build systems to analyse digital-asset transactions for anti-money-laundering purposes by 2029.

key_points.point: The central bank will trial running Exchange Fund Bills on distributed-ledger technology by the end of the year, aimed at letting banks manage these instruments around the clock.
A cross-agency group will start a second round of legal review on how distributed-ledger technology can be used in capital markets, working with the finance bureau.
The clearing entity CMU OmniClear will stand up a new digital-asset platform this year to handle issuance and settlement of digital bonds in one place.
The stock exchange operator is building a blockchain platform covering several asset types, already used for carbon credits, and will add tokenised commodity warehouse receipts next year.
The securities regulator will widen virtual-asset licensing coverage and put out clearer rules so virtual-asset firms know what compliance is expected of them.
The securities regulator will update its rules for tokenised investment products so licensed venues can offer tokenised gold and similar real-world assets, plus new product types.
The securities regulator plans to let licensed virtual-asset trading venues offer regulated stablecoins, and let those tokens be used to settle tokenised money-market funds.
The central bank intends to add round-the-clock settlement using a wholesale digital-currency pilot (EnsembleTX) by roughly year-end, and keep looking for new uses of tokenised bank deposits.

The securities regulator will begin operating a system to watch over digital-asset custody arrangements sometime in the year's second half. It will also switch on a separate big-data surveillance tool for market abuse and money laundering in 2027.
The central bank will keep testing new uses for tokenised deposits, including a Mainland trade-finance pilot meant to finish transactions before year-end.

Customs authorities plan a second phase, targeted for 2029, of two new systems: one to analyse digital-asset transactions and one for anti-money-laundering analytics. These feed into a wider financial-crime data platform.

numbers_and_dates.value: tests by end of 2026; aim is round-the-clock use of more than $1.3 trillion of bills
transactions targeted to complete by end of 2026

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: None of this creates a binding rule yet -- it is a statement of government direction, so no immediate compliance action is required. It does flag several workstreams a compliance head should put on a watchlist. These include wider virtual-asset licensing and stablecoin trading permissions for licensed venues, and a new SFC custody surveillance system that will touch custodians the bank may rely on. It also flags the central bank's own tokenised-deposit and wholesale digital-currency pilots that the bank's treasury or product teams may be asked to join.

quote.text: raising Hong Kong's competitiveness as an international digital asset hub

reading_guide: Read paragraphs 34-52, pp.22-28, the fintech and capital-markets tokenisation measures, and Annex (I) New Indicators, item 209, p.112, the AML digital-asset analytics system. Skip the remaining roughly 370 paragraphs on national security, housing, healthcare and other non-financial topics.
flags: This is a speech-level policy statement, not legislation or a regulator's binding guidance -- it announces intentions and targets; the actual rules will come later in separate SFC/HKMA instruments.

The DATAS/AMLAS analytics systems sit inside a Customs & Excise Department anti-money-laundering programme, not an HKMA or SFC instrument, but they will ingest digital-asset transaction data by 2029 -- worth tracking even though it is outside the usual HKMA/SFC channel.

controls_and_monitoring: Track SFC's promised virtual-asset licensing framework update and its digital-asset custody surveillance system rollout (para 49(i), 51(iii), p.27) so internal controls stay aligned once detailed rules issue.
counterparty_due_diligence: Watch whether VATP counterparties gain permission to trade regulated stablecoins and settle tokenised money-market funds once the SFC's framework is updated (para 49(iii), p.27).
Note SFC's digital-asset custody surveillance system, due H2 2026, will add oversight of custody arrangements the bank's VATP or custodian counterparties use (para 51(iii), p.27).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Note for the board/risk committee that the central bank is piloting tokenised Exchange Fund Bills and CBDC-linked EnsembleTX settlement, and the securities regulator is preparing revised virtual-asset and stablecoin rules -- none binding yet, but relevant to any tokenisation roadmap the bank is developing.

title: Review of the Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners
summary: The HKMA reviewed the ECF, the bank staff qualification framework launched in 2014 with ten workstreams including Compliance, Fintech, AML/CFT and Cybersecurity. It proposes five changes: a single common Core Level for all practitioners, one consolidated Professional Level qualification per workstream, and shorter experience requirements. It also proposes letting practitioners keep certificates after changing roles if continuing training is met, and fewer overlapping qualifications. Industry feedback gathered through HKAB and HKIB committees was broadly supportive but stressed smooth transition. A three-phase roadmap runs from mid-2028 to 2030, with HKIB to set transition arrangements and courses and the HKMA to issue new ECF guidance. Specific competency standards will be revised in a later phase.

key_points.point: The review follows the August 2025 'Capacity Building for Future Banking, 2026-2030' study and its ASCEND action plan.
Core Level becomes one common, non-workstream module; completing it also gives HKIB Certified Banker Stage I.
Each of the ten workstreams (including Fintech and Compliance) will have one consolidated Professional Level qualification.
Experience: one year at an AI in Hong Kong for Core; three years for Professional, at least two in the workstream.
Holders may keep certificates after moving roles, provided they meet continuing professional development (CPD) requirements.
Direct entry to the Professional Level without first taking Core will be allowed.
Today the Fintech workstream alone has six separate qualifications, including one on distributed ledger technology.
Implementation is phased from mid-2028 to 2030: HKIB transition arrangements and new courses, and new HKMA ECF guidance.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Relevant to planning qualifications for digital asset compliance staff: the separate Fintech/DLT certificates will be merged and certificates will become portable. No near-term compliance obligation arises.

quote.text: specialisation will take place only at the Professional Level

reading_guide: Read the executive summary (pp.5-8) and roadmap (p.23); skip methodology.
flags: Roadmap text is garbled in extraction; the mapping of each action to mid-2028, mid-2029 or 2030 could not be confirmed.
Not digital-asset specific.

controls_and_monitoring: Track staff ECF certifications, including Fintech/Compliance, ahead of transition arrangements.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Informational: ECF restructuring from 2028 affects training plans, not current obligations.

title: Alert List — Suspicious virtual asset trading platforms category
summary: This is the SFC's running public register of entities it has flagged as suspicious, captured on the snapshot date. It groups names into categories such as suspicious virtual-asset trading platforms, fake regulators, unlicensed firms and phishing attempts. Rows are added and removed continuously, so the file is a point-in-time capture rather than a fixed publication. Most listed names have no formal enforcement outcome attached; inclusion just signals the SFC has received complaints or spotted impersonation activity. The virtual-asset sub-list is dominated by copycat sites impersonating licensed exchange brand names.

key_points.point: The register sorts flagged names into several buckets, including one specifically for suspicious virtual-asset trading platforms.
key_points.locator: Suspicious virtual asset trading platforms heading

key_points.point: Recent virtual-asset entries are dominated by look-alike domains copying a licensed platform's brand name, suggesting active phishing/impersonation campaigns rather than new unlicensed exchanges.
key_points.locator: Suspicious virtual asset trading platforms table, entries dated Jul-Sep 2026

title: HKIB Annual Banking Conference: Bank of Tomorrow: Transform to Excellence – Regulatory Update by HKMA
summary: This is Deputy Chief Executive Arthur Yuen's slide deck for a 25 September 2026 regulatory keynote. It is structured around four themes: governing agentic AI, engineering technology resilience, building trusted tokenisation, and fostering data excellence. On tokenisation, it presents the Supervisory Incubator for DLT as the launchpad for business-model transformation. It raises the open question of which roles banks can play as trusted intermediaries alongside smart contracts and AI agents. On resilience, it reports a first Quantum Preparedness Index score of 2.3 out of 10, with a target of full sectoral readiness by 2030. It also reports GenAI Sandbox++ growth to 36 use cases across 30 institutions and 27 tech partners.

key_points.point: The deck sets out an AI action spectrum from 'Assist', which retrieves information, through 'Recommend' and 'Decide', to 'Act', which carries out actions using approved tools. It makes clear that handing authority to AI systems doesn't hand off accountability too. The Board and senior management stay answerable throughout the whole action chain.

The GenAI Sandbox programme grew across three cohorts. The 2024 first cohort of GenAI Sandbox had 10 banks, 4 tech partners and 15 use cases. The 2025 second cohort of GenAI Sandbox had 20 banks, 14 tech partners and 27 use cases. The 2026 first cohort of the renamed GenAI Sandbox++ had 30 financial institutions, 27 tech partners and 36 use cases, reflecting a shift toward cross-sector agentic AI end-to-end processes.

HKMA's first Quantum Preparedness Index (QPI) score is 2.3 out of 10. Banks that have transition plans report an expected implementation time of 5.6 years, against an HKMA objective of full sectoral readiness by 2030.

Banks should secure their own and critical service providers' cyber fundamentals, and frontier AI-driven cyber risks should not be underestimated even as cyber risk management fundamentals remain the 'gold standard'.
The Supervisory Incubator for DLT is presented as a 'launchpad' enabling real-value, real-transaction business-model transformation trials for banks.

The deck poses an open question on 'who is authorised to move value' in a tokenised ecosystem involving smart contract guardrails, trusted transaction rails and AI agents. This frames potential bank roles as still under exploration.

Data Excellence is framed around a 'GRID' model: Granularity, Reliability, Ingenuity, Discoverability. Granular Data Reporting (GDR) 3.0 is aimed at moving from aggregated template-based reporting to data-point-centric submissions, described as 'report once, use multiple'.
95% fintech adoption was reported among surveyed banks, but 41% cited high-quality data as an adoption challenge.

numbers_and_dates.item: expected PQC implementation time among banks with plans

numbers_and_dates.value: 36 use cases, 30 financial institutions, 27 tech partners

numbers_and_dates.item: banks citing high-quality data as adoption challenge

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This signals HKMA's current supervisory priorities on AI governance, quantum-readiness timelines and tokenisation roles for banks, ahead of formal circulars. The accountability principle -- 'delegating authority does not delegate accountability' -- is directly relevant to any bank deploying agentic AI in digital-asset workflows.

quote.text: Delegating Authority Does Not Delegate Accountability

reading_guide: Slide deck with minimal running text; review slides 5-7 (AI governance and accountability), 10-11 (cyber and quantum) and 14-15 (tokenisation), which carry the substantive content. Slides 1-4 and 16-19 are largely agenda and branding.
