corpus-note: originally captured via the HKMA site "Latest Speeches" sidebar and wrongly linked to older speeches; relationship removed 2026-09-25

controls_and_monitoring: Board/senior management accountability must be retained and documented across the full AI action path (Assist/Recommend/Decide/Act), including for any agentic AI used in digital-asset operations (slide 7).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board should be briefed on HKMA's first published Quantum Preparedness Index score (2.3/10) and the 2030 full-readiness objective, and on the explicit accountability principle for agentic AI.

title: Fit and Proper Guidelines
supersedes_or_amends: Fit and Proper Criteria (December 2000)
summary: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) made these guidelines under section 399 of the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO). They list what the SFC normally looks at when deciding whether a person is fit and proper. They cover licensed firms and staff, and banks registered with the SFC as registered institutions (RIs). They also cover bank staff on the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) register and executive officers (EOs) of RIs. The four tests come from section 129(1) of the SFO: money and solvency, qualifications and experience, ability to act competently, honestly and fairly, and reputation and integrity. The guidelines are not law, and the SFC may still accept a person who misses an element that is not material. Firms and people must stay fit and proper after approval.

key_points.point: The guidelines name banks that apply for or hold SFC registration. They also cover staff on the HKMA register kept under section 20 of the Banking Ordinance (BO), and EOs of an RI given consent under BO section 71C.
For a bank, the four section 129(1) tests are applied to the institution and to its directors, chief executive, managers and EOs.
For a bank's registration application, the SFC must consider the HKMA's advice on fitness and may rely on it wholly or partly.
Where the guidelines refer to how recent a matter is, the SFC normally means within the last five years.
The SFC looks at substance and materiality, so missing one element does not by itself make a person unfit. The SFC invites applicants who are unsure to talk to its Licensing staff before applying.

The SFC expects individuals to show they can do the regulated activity well. It judges this on academic and industry qualifications plus relevant experience. The knowledge expected rises with the level of responsibility.
A firm or bank may fail the test if its non-executive directors, key staff, substantial shareholders or controllers fail any part of these guidelines other than the competence part.

A firm or bank is unlikely to be seen as competent if its structure and staff cannot meet regulatory requirements. The same applies if it lacks the controls to manage risk, avoid conflicts and keep an audit trail.

Past court findings of fraud, relevant convictions, regulatory discipline, director disqualification or market misconduct can count against an individual, weighted by seriousness, time elapsed and role.
Licensed and registered persons, relevant individuals and EOs must stay fit and proper after approval, and the SFC can discipline them under SFO sections 194 or 196.
Sanctions include suspending or revoking registration, barring someone from EO consent or from the HKMA register, reprimands and fines.

numbers_and_dates.item: Minimum age for representatives and HKMA-register staff
Creditor compromise threshold that triggers closer review

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: These are the standards an RI, its EOs and every person on the HKMA register must meet before and after taking up a digital-asset dealing, advisory or custody role. A compliance head uses them to design hiring checks and ongoing fitness reviews, and to judge their own eligibility as an EO.

quote.text: one who is financially sound, competent, honest, reputable and reliable

reading_guide: Read sections 2, 3 and 8 first for scope and the ongoing duty; sections 4 to 7 list the specific concerns and can be used as a checklist.
flags: Applies to banks through SFO registration and the HKMA register. For a bank's registration, the SFC must take into account the HKMA's advice on fitness and may rely on it wholly or partly (para 3.4).

obligations: Ensure the bank, its directors, chief executive, managers and EOs meet the four section 129(1) tests (para 3.1-3.2).
Ensure EOs and HKMA-registered staff remain fit and proper on an ongoing basis (para 8.1).
controls_and_monitoring: Pre-hire and periodic screening for bankruptcy, judgment debts, convictions, regulatory discipline and director disqualification (paras 4.1.1, 7.1.1).
Keep evidence of competence: qualifications, experience and product knowledge relevant to virtual asset (VA) activities (para 5.1.1(b) Note (ii)).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Fitness of executive officers and registered staff is a continuing condition of the bank's SFC registration (para 8.1).

title: Guidelines on Competence
summary: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) issued these guidelines under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO), section 399. They explain how the SFC judges whether a firm or a person is competent to carry on a regulated activity (RA). They apply to licensed firms and to banks registered as registered institutions (RIs). They also apply to a bank's executive officers (EOs) and its staff on the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) register. An EO must meet the same bar as a responsible officer (RO). A registered bank employee must meet the same bar as a licensed representative. For firms, the SFC looks at the business model, governance, staffing, controls, independent review, risk and compliance. For individuals, it looks at qualifications, industry and management experience, and a pass in a local regulatory paper.

key_points.point: An EO of an RI must clear the same competence bar as an RO, and a relevant individual (ReI) on the HKMA register faces the same as a licensed representative.
The RI itself must make sure an ReI meets the competence bar before submitting the name to the HKMA, and the HKMA considers these guidelines when deciding on EO consent.
For ReIs, the RI should keep records showing how each requirement was met and produce them if the HKMA asks.
A firm is judged on its business model, governance, people, controls, independent review, risk and compliance set-up, and on the combined ability of senior management and staff.
Supervisory staff in both front and back office should have at least three years of relevant experience plus suitable qualifications.
One element the SFC considers is an operational review function. The function is independent of the business, reports to a high-level independent authority, and assesses risk at least once a year.
Firms must stay competent, keep their people competent including on continuous professional training (CPT), and tell the SFC about material changes in business plans, structure or staff.
An RO or EO applicant must show they can properly manage and supervise the proposed activity.

Under the standard routes, an RO or EO applicant needs at least three years of relevant industry experience in the past six years. One route instead asks for five years in the past eight. The applicant also needs two years of management experience and a pass in the local regulatory framework paper (LRP).
Management experience means hands-on supervision of regulated functions or projects and staff; purely administrative supervision, such as HR or office staff, normally does not count.
Direct experience in a highly innovative technology can count as relevant industry experience. The person must have been key to building or running it, and it must be central to the new firm's RA.
Recognised industry qualifications and the LRP should normally be obtained within three years before the application.

numbers_and_dates.item: Minimum experience for front- and back-office supervisors

numbers_and_dates.value: at least 3 years in the past 6 years, or 5 in the past 8

numbers_and_dates.item: RO/EO route without the listed qualifications (only for people licensed before 1 January 2022)
numbers_and_dates.value: 8 years' experience in the past 11 years

numbers_and_dates.item: Validity window for qualification and LRP

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This sets the experience and exam bar for the bank's EOs and front-line staff in any SFO-regulated digital-asset business, including a compliance head who wants EO status. It also tells the RI what records the HKMA may ask for to prove staff competence.

quote.text: An EO and an ReI have to meet the same competence requirements as an RO

reading_guide: Read paras 2.1-2.6 on how the rules apply to banks, then 3.2 for firm-level expectations and 4.1-4.2 for EO requirements. Appendices A and B (sponsors, takeovers) can be skipped.

obligations: Confirm each ReI meets licensed-representative competence before registering them with the HKMA (para 2.2).
Keep supporting records of how each ReI meets the requirements, ready for HKMA inspection (para 2.5(b), 2.6(b)).
controls_and_monitoring: Track continuous professional training (CPT) completion and staff qualifications for registered staff (para 3.1.4, 3.2.1 Staff competencies (f)).
The SFC looks for an independent operational review with an at-least-annual risk assessment (para 3.2.1 Operational review).
notifications_reporting: Keep the SFC informed of material changes in business plans, structure and personnel (para 3.1.4).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Proposed EOs for any new regulated line need to meet the RO-level experience and exam bar, which the HKMA takes into account when deciding on EO consent (paras 2.2, 4.2.1.2).

title: Circular to Licensed Corporations Regarding Measures for Augmenting the Accountability of Senior Management
summary: This Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) circular created the Manager-In-Charge (MIC) regime for licensed corporations. It says senior management includes directors, responsible officers (ROs) and MICs. It names eight core functions, and each should have at least one MIC. All senior managers, licensed or not, can be disciplined as people involved in management. They may also be criminally liable for company offences under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO) that they consented to or caused by recklessness. The SFC generally expects the MICs for overall management oversight and key business lines to be ROs. It expects firms to file MIC details and an organisation chart, and to report changes within seven business days.

key_points.point: Senior management of a licensed corporation includes its directors, its ROs and its MICs; one person can hold all three roles.
The eight core functions are: overall oversight; key business lines; operations control and review; risk; finance; IT; compliance; and anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing (AML/CFT).
Each core function should have at least one MIC, though one person may cover several functions and several people may share one.

Whether someone is an MIC depends on their real or apparent authority over the function, such as decision rights, budget authority or representing the unit. The SFC generally expects MICs to report to the board or to the overall-oversight MIC.

MICs may sit overseas and need not be employees, but they are not outside service providers. The SFC does not approve MICs who are unlicensed, but it expects the firm to make sure they are fit and proper.
Every senior manager is a regulated person because they take part in management. The SFC can discipline them for the firm's misconduct that results from their consent, connivance or neglect.
Officers can also be criminally liable where a corporate offence under the SFO resulted from their consent, connivance or recklessness (SFO s.390(1)).
MICs of overall management oversight and key business lines are generally expected to be ROs; other MICs are not.
A long-serving head of a control function, such as compliance or risk, may be approved as an RO for the oversight role. The SFC usually adds a condition to work alongside a fully competent RO.
The board should approve a formal document setting out the management structure and each MIC's duties, and each MIC should acknowledge their appointment.
Changes in MIC appointments or particulars should be notified to the SFC within seven business days, with an updated organisation chart where relevant.

numbers_and_dates.item: Deadline for oversight and business-line MICs to apply as ROs

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: The MIC regime is addressed to licensed corporations, not banks. It applies to any SFC-licensed subsidiary the bank sets up, and it shapes how licensed brokers and managers the bank deals with are run. A compliance head who moves into an MIC role at such a firm takes on the personal regulatory exposure described here.

quote.text: The SFC also does not require every RO to be an MIC.

reading_guide: Read Parts C, E and F (paras 7-25) first, then Part G on the board and para 33 on notifications. Annex 1 describes each core function with example job titles.
flags: Addressed to licensed corporations only; registered institutions (banks) are not directly subject to the MIC regime, but the Guidelines on Competence cross-refer to it.
The separate MIC FAQs on the SFC website were not fetched in this batch.

counterparty_due_diligence: When onboarding an SFC-licensed broker, manager or VA trading platform, check that it has named MICs for compliance and AML/CFT and a board-approved management structure (para 7-8, 28-29).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: In an SFC-licensed subsidiary, the board is expected to approve the management structure, including MIC appointments, and each MIC carries personal disciplinary exposure (paras 17-18, 29).

title: Licensing Handbook
summary: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) Licensing Handbook is a practical guide to licensing under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO). It explains who needs a licence or registration, what approval criteria apply and what firms must do once approved. It has a chapter for registered institutions (RIs), meaning banks registered with the SFC. For a bank, it covers executive officer (EO) rules and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) register of bank staff. It also covers the fitness of shareholders and managers, and post-registration filings and fees. Other parts cover continuous professional training (CPT) and notice duties, including for virtual asset services. The virtual asset paragraphs describe the 2019 framework and do not mention the later platform licensing regime.

key_points.point: An RI is an authorized institution (a bank, restricted licence bank or deposit-taking company) registered under SFO s.119 for any regulated activity except Types 3 and 8.
A bank should appoint at least two EOs to supervise each regulated activity directly, with at least one available at all times.
EOs need HKMA consent under the Banking Ordinance, and the HKMA must refuse unless it is satisfied the person is fit and proper and has enough authority.

The SFC expects EOs to meet the responsible officer competence standard. Other bank staff doing regulated work are named on the HKMA register instead of being licensed by the SFC. They are expected to meet the licensed-representative standard, and their fitness is a statutory condition of registration.
The bank's substantial shareholders, directors, chief executive, managers and EOs must all be fit and proper.
The HKMA may ask a new or complex registration applicant for an Independent Assurance Report from an external firm it accepts.
Under the HKMA's management accountability circular and FAQs, a bank applying for registration should give the HKMA and SFC details of key managers for regulated business and an organisation chart.
RIs should send updates on that management information and chart to both regulators within 14 days of a change.
ROs and EOs must take two extra CPT hours each calendar year on regulatory compliance.
Firms and banks should keep CPT records for at least three years for SFC or HKMA inspection.
Intermediaries must notify the SFC before offering trading or asset management involving virtual assets, and are advised to discuss it with the SFC beforehand.
Adding a regulated activity to a bank's registration costs HK$23,500 per activity.

numbers_and_dates.item: Deadline for RI management accountability updates
RI fee for adding a regulated activity

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the one-stop guide to the bank's SFC registration mechanics: EO numbers, HKMA consent, register entries, notifications and training. It is the practical checklist for adding a digital-asset regulated activity or staffing a new desk.

quote.text: You should appoint not less than two executive officers

reading_guide: For a bank, read Chapter 6 (pp.38-39), paras 8.4 and 9.13-9.15, and the virtual asset paragraphs 1.4.3-1.4.7. Chapters on licensed corporations and representatives are background.
flags: The virtual asset paragraphs (1.4.3-1.4.7) still describe the 2019 framework and do not mention the AMLO VATP licensing regime or later joint circulars; check current SFC circulars.
Handbook page numbers differ from PDF page numbers by four; locators here give the printed paragraph, with PDF page in the page field.

obligations: Maintain at least two HKMA-consented EOs per regulated activity, one always available (para 6.1.2-6.1.3).
Ensure relevant individuals meet competence rules before HKMA registration and keep records (para 6.1.7, 6.2.1).
controls_and_monitoring: Track ROs'/EOs' extra compliance CPT hours and keep CPT records for three years (para 9.13.4, 9.13.9).
notifications_reporting: Notify the SFC of trading or asset management services involving virtual assets (para 9.14.1).
Update HKMA and SFC on management accountability information within 14 days of change (para 9.15.1).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: A new virtual asset dealing or advisory line needs executive officer coverage, an SFC notification and an updated management chart for both regulators (paras 6.1.2, 9.14.1, 9.15.1).

title: Management Accountability at Registered Institutions
summary: This Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) letter to all authorized institutions sets out its expectations on management accountability at banks registered with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC). Such banks are called registered institutions (RIs). For this purpose, management means chief executives and their alternates, directors approved by the HKMA under Banking Ordinance (BO) section 71, and managers notified under BO section 72B. It also covers executive officers (EOs) and anyone else who manages regulated-activity business. The detailed guidance sits in an attached set of frequently asked questions (FAQs). The HKMA expects RIs to send it and the SFC details of the senior people mainly responsible for regulated business, with an organisation chart. The letter adds no new approval steps or legal liabilities. It reminds banks that these managers are regulated persons under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO).

key_points.point: For this guidance, management covers CEs and ACEs, BO s.71 directors, s.72B managers, s.71C EOs and any other person involved in managing a regulated activity (RA) business of the RI.
The guidance should be read with SPM module SB-1, and CG-1 and CG-2 are also relevant; the SFC's December 2016 MIC circular is noted as useful reference.
The HKMA says the guidance neither duplicates BO governance rules nor changes approval or reporting rules for CEs, directors, managers or EOs.

The HKMA gave RIs six months to prepare and expected them to file the management information and organisation chart by 16 April 2018. From the same date, applicants for registration or for an added activity should file it too.
Anyone involved in managing a bank's RA business is a regulated person under SFO Part IX and can be disciplined by the SFC.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the bank-side counterpart to the SFC's Manager-In-Charge regime. It decides which senior bankers are on record as accountable for SFO-regulated digital-asset business, and it puts those people within reach of SFC discipline.
reading_guide: Two short pages; read in full, then go to the FAQs (Annex 1) for the operative detail.

obligations: Submit details of senior management principally responsible for RA business and an organisation chart to the HKMA and SFC (p.2, para 5).
notifications_reporting: Initial filing was due 16 April 2018; registration applicants file with their application (p.2, para 5).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The regulators hold named executives on record as accountable for each SFO-regulated business line (p.2, para 1).

flags: Still current: the HKMA's October 2025 consolidated registration circular lists this circular as existing applicable guidance (5313ebf35880, Annex 3) and does not list it among superseded circulars (Annex 5).

title: Management Accountability at Registered Institutions - Frequently asked questions
summary: These 15 frequently asked questions (FAQs) explain how a bank registered with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) should name the senior people accountable for its regulated-activity business. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) expects the bank to name at least one person for overall management, normally the chief executive (CE). It also expects one named person for each business or function in the Banking Ordinance (BO) Fourteenth Schedule, paragraphs 2 to 8, where it involves regulated activities. The HKMA expects these people to be CEs, alternate CEs, directors approved under BO section 71 or managers notified under BO section 72B. The FAQs also cover executive officer (EO) seniority, outsourced functions, temporary cover and updates within 14 days.

key_points.point: RIs should name at least one person principally responsible for the whole business, generally the CE, and for each Fourteenth Schedule business or function that involves regulated activities.
Non-executive and independent directors are not treated as management here, although the board remains ultimately responsible.
Not every CE, ACE, director or s.72B manager must be an EO, but those who directly supervise a regulated activity should be appointed EOs for it.
For each regulated activity, at least one EO should be a CE, alternate CE, director or section 72B manager. Any other EO should be no more than one rank below that level.

The HKMA treats control functions such as compliance, risk and internal audit as just as important as front-office roles. It expects the bank to name the senior person who covers compliance for regulated business.
A named person need not be an RI employee (for example a group employee), but an outside provider of an outsourced function cannot be named; bank management keeps accountability.
Fitness of named persons is already covered by HKMA approval under BO s.71 and the bank's own controls over s.72B managers.
The registered institution (RI), not the individual, files the information. The RI should make sure each named person has acknowledged their responsibilities.
Changes in named persons, their particulars, their responsibilities or reporting lines should be filed with the HKMA and SFC within 14 days, usually with a new organisation chart.
Banks applying for registration, or to add a regulated activity, should file the same information with their application from 16 April 2018.

numbers_and_dates.item: Maximum rank gap for EOs who are not senior management

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: If the bank adds a virtual asset dealing, advisory or custody-related regulated activity, the HKMA expects it to name who is principally responsible and to meet the EO seniority expectation. It also expects updated filings within 14 days of changes. The head of compliance may be the person named for the compliance function.

quote.text: RIs should also ensure that at least one of the EOs for a given RA

reading_guide: Read Q1, Q3, Q4, Q9 and Q14 first; Q5-Q8 and Q10 handle edge cases.

obligations: Name a principally responsible senior person for overall management and each relevant Fourteenth Schedule function (Q1/A1, Q4/A4).
Ensure at least one EO per RA is at CE/ACE/director/s.72B manager level and others are within one rank (Q3/A3).
controls_and_monitoring: Obtain written acknowledgement from each named individual (Q13/A13).
Keep outsourced functions under a named member of bank management (Q9/A9).
notifications_reporting: File changes with HKMA and SFC within 14 days, with an updated organisation chart (Q14/A14).
File the information with any application to add a regulated activity (Q15/A15).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The HKMA expects a named accountable senior person for each regulated business and control function, with filings updated within 14 days of change (Q1/A1, Q14/A14).

title: CG-2 Systems of Control for the Appointment of Managers
summary: This Supervisory Policy Manual (SPM) module is a statutory guideline issued under section 16(10) of the Banking Ordinance (BO). It tells every authorized institution (AI) how to make sure the managers it appoints are fit and proper. A manager is someone below director or chief executive (CE) level who is principally responsible for a business or function listed in the BO's Fourteenth Schedule. Examples are a business line, risk controls, anti-money laundering controls, IT, internal audit and compliance. The module lists fitness factors and the control systems an AI should run. It also covers notifying the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) of manager appointments and changes within 14 days under BO section 72B. The version read is version 1, dated 24 May 2002.

key_points.point: An AI must have adequate controls so that each manager is fit and proper; this is one of the BO's minimum criteria for authorization (Seventh Schedule, para 5A).
Functions needing a manager include business lines and any other material business, accounts, risk controls, anti-money laundering controls, IT systems, internal audit and compliance.
Materiality of an unlisted business can be judged by its share of income or profit, assets or capital, or operating costs.
Signs of being principally responsible include accountability for targets, a direct line to a director or CE, decision rights, budget authority and representing the unit.
The aim is to capture the layer of management just below the CE. The AI may need to go further down, for example where a broad division has separate retail and corporate heads.
A manager may be a group employee or an outside party, and managers can be personally accountable for many BO breaches.
Fitness rests on three pillars: honesty and good name; skills and track record; and sound finances free of conflicting ties. It applies at and after appointment.
Any doubt about a candidate or serving manager should be investigated, documented and cleared before they start or continue.
Performance appraisal of managers should not lean too heavily on financial results and should also weigh compliance with internal rules and regulation.
Internal audit should periodically review the AI's controls over appointing managers.

The module says AIs should notify the HKMA of new appointments, departures and changes of responsibility within 14 days, by a letter signed by the CE. AIs should also report removals for fraud, dishonesty or malpractice as soon as practicable.
Genuine temporary cover of up to a few months is exempt from notification, but becomes notifiable within 14 days if made permanent.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: The head of a digital-asset business line, and the head of compliance, may themselves be s.72B managers. This module sets how the bank vets, appraises and notifies such appointments, and the HKMA may test these controls on-site.

quote.text: What matters is the nature of the underlying activity or function

reading_guide: Read sections 2.3 (who is a manager), 3 (fitness factors), 4.1 (controls) and 6 (notification). Section 5 on HKMA powers is short background.
flags: Dated 24 May 2002 (version 1); references to section 72B coming into effect are historical. The fetched copy showed no later version.

obligations: Identify all s.72B manager positions, including any head of a material digital-asset business (para 2.2.3, 4.1.1).
Assess fitness before appointment and on a continuing basis, documenting any investigation (para 3.1.2-3.1.3).
controls_and_monitoring: Pre-appointment checks: declarations, certificate verification, public-record searches, conflicts, references (para 4.2.1).
Periodic internal audit of manager-appointment controls (para 4.1.12).
notifications_reporting: Notify the HKMA of manager appointments, cessations and responsibility changes within 14 days via CE-signed letter (para 6.1.3-6.1.4).
Report removals for fraud, dishonesty or malpractice as soon as practicable (para 6.1.5).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Any other business that is material to the bank, which could include a digital-asset unit, needs a manager identified, vetted and notified to the HKMA (paras 2.2.3, 6.1.3).

title: CG-6 Competence and Ethical Behaviour
supersedes_or_amends: CG-6 Competence and Ethical Behaviour V.1 (11.7.2011), V.2 (23.01.2013), V.3 (8.12.2017)
summary: This Supervisory Policy Manual (SPM) module is version 4, dated 23 May 2024. It is non-statutory guidance from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) on how authorized institutions keep all staff competent and ethical, not only those who need HKMA consent. It links staff competence to the Banking Ordinance (BO) criterion that a bank's business is run with integrity, prudence and professional competence. The board is ultimately responsible. The board should review manpower action plans, with measurable targets, at least once a year. Banks are strongly encouraged to use the Enhanced Competency Framework (ECF) as a benchmark. Banks should not launch new products until staff understand the products, markets and rules.

key_points.point: The expectations cover staff at every level, beyond directors, CEs, EOs, s.72B managers and SFO relevant individuals.
Banks that are RIs should ensure relevant individuals meet the SFC's initial competence requirements, as also noted in SB-1.
The board is ultimately responsible and should embed a culture of competence and ethics, with recruitment and appraisal weighing competence and integrity.
The board should set direction for manpower development; senior management should propose talent plans with measurable targets, which the board reviews at least once a year.
Banks are strongly encouraged to use the ECF as a benchmark for staff competence and to support staff to gain ECF certifications.
Staff who are not yet competent should not do the work without close supervision; reviewing output after the event is unlikely to be enough supervision on its own.
A bank should not launch new products or activities unless satisfied staff know the products, markets and applicable rules.
Competence should be monitored regularly and reflected in appraisal and variable pay, drawing on audit, compliance findings and complaints.
Where staff incompetence causes significant losses or likely serious reputational damage, the bank should tell the HKMA promptly and discuss remedial steps.
Banks should assess how technology changes job roles and keep a long-term reskilling plan with measurable targets approved by the board.
Where work is outsourced, the bank should check and keep monitoring the provider's competence using staff with the right expertise.

numbers_and_dates.item: Board review of manpower action plans

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Before a bank offers any digital-asset product, this module expects staff to understand the product and the rules, and the board to have a talent and reskilling plan. It gives the compliance head a basis to require training sign-off before launch and to escalate competence failures to the HKMA.

quote.text: Simple ex post review of work output is unlikely to amount, in itself

reading_guide: Read sections 2 and 3.7 (competence criteria including new products) and 4.1.3 (HKMA notification); section 5 covers ethics expectations.
flags: Non-statutory guidance note; the ECF is strongly encouraged, not mandatory. No digital-asset-specific ECF module is referenced in this version.

obligations: Do not launch new products or activities until staff knowledge of products, markets and rules is confirmed (para 3.7.4).
Ensure relevant individuals meet SFC initial competence rules (para 1.5, fn 2).
controls_and_monitoring: Documented job specifications and competence criteria per post (para 3.2).
Link competence to appraisal and variable pay (para 4.1.5).
Monitor outsourced providers' competence (para 2.9).
notifications_reporting: Notify the HKMA promptly of staff incompetence causing significant loss or reputational risk (para 4.1.3).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The HKMA expects the board to approve manpower and reskilling plans with measurable targets and to review manpower action plans at least yearly (paras 2.4, 4.2.2).

title: Guideline on Minimum Criteria for Authorization
supersedes_or_amends: Guideline on Minimum Criteria for Authorization (22 July 2022)
summary: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) issued this statutory guideline under Banking Ordinance (BO) section 16(10). It explains how the HKMA reads the Seventh Schedule criteria for becoming and staying an authorized institution. The criteria apply continuously, look forward and cover the whole institution. So a later failure can be a ground for revoking authorization. The guideline sets out how the HKMA judges the fitness of directors, chief executives (CEs), alternate CEs, executive officers (EOs) and controllers. It also says when the HKMA may meet candidates face to face. It states board-independence expectations and the seniority test for EOs of banks registered with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC). This version, dated 27 February 2026, replaces the version of 22 July 2022.

key_points.point: The authorization criteria keep applying after licensing, and failing them can lead to revocation at the HKMA's discretion.
Controllers include indirect controllers and anyone controlling 10% or more of voting power, with over 50% making a majority shareholder controller.
Directors, CEs and alternates of a Hong Kong-incorporated AI, and the Hong Kong CE of an overseas bank, need HKMA approval under BO s.71 and must be fit and proper.

The HKMA expects independent non-executive directors (INEDs) to make up one-third of the board or three members, whichever is higher. This applies to Hong Kong-incorporated licensed banks, and to restricted licence banks (RLBs) and deposit-taking companies (DTCs) designated as systemically important. At least two INEDs should have an accounting, banking or financial background.
Fitness depends on the role: a person may suit one position but not another with different duties, and time commitment is also weighed.
The HKMA may meet candidates for director, CE, alternate CE or EO face to face to test their knowledge of Hong Kong banking and key rules.
The level of probity expected is broadly the same whatever the position.
Each registered bank must appoint at least two EOs per regulated activity under BO s.71D; the HKMA is the front-line supervisor and gives consent under s.71C.
For EO fitness, the HKMA applies SFO s.129 and the SFC's Fit and Proper Guidelines, Guidelines on Competence and CPT requirements.
An EO should generally be the most senior person in the regulated activity and no more than one rank below a CE, alternate CE, director or s.72B manager.
The more influence a controller has, the higher the fitness bar; would-be majority controllers must present detailed plans for the bank.

numbers_and_dates.item: INEDs for licensed banks and systemic RLBs/DTCs
numbers_and_dates.value: higher of one-third of board or 3

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the HKMA's rulebook for approving the senior people a compliance head may one day become: CE, alternate CE, director or EO. It sets the EO seniority test that the HKMA expects any SFO-regulated bank desk, including a digital-asset desk, to meet, and the fitness factors the HKMA may probe in interview.

quote.text: a person could be fit and proper for one position, but not fit and proper

reading_guide: For career and approvals, read paras 10-33 (fitness of directors, CEs, EOs and controllers). Paras 1-6 explain how the criteria work; later paragraphs cover capital, liquidity and other criteria.
flags: Replaces the guideline issued on 22 July 2022 (para 1). Any registry entry for the 2022 version is superseded.

obligations: Keep at least two HKMA-consented EOs per regulated activity (para 23).
Ensure EOs meet the seniority test of no more than one rank below CE/ACE/director/s.72B manager (para 27).
Obtain HKMA approval before appointing directors, CEs or alternate CEs (para 12).
controls_and_monitoring: Assess candidates for time commitment, outside mandates and conflicts (para 15, 19(g)).
Track controllers at the 10% and 50% voting thresholds (para 9).
Prepare candidates for a possible HKMA face-to-face meeting (para 16).
notifications_reporting: Seek HKMA approval under BO section 71 for directors, CEs and alternate CEs, and HKMA consent under section 71C for EOs (paras 12, 24).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The authorization criteria are continuing, so a later failure can ground revocation; EO, CE and director appointments for any new line need HKMA consent or approval (paras 4(a), 12, 24).

title: Updated Guidance on Registration in Respect of Regulated Activities under the Securities and Futures Ordinance and Controls to Ensure Fitness and Properness of Staff
summary: This Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) circular to all authorized institutions (AIs) gathers the still-valid guidance on three topics in one place. These are registration with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), executive officer (EO) consent, and the HKMA register of bank securities staff. The HKMA says it adds no new standards. It replaces 14 older circulars listed in its Annex 5. It reminds banks that reference checks on new hires should ask about dismissals, forced resignations and internal conduct investigations. It also reminds banks to follow the Mandatory Reference Checking (MRC) Scheme. Banks should answer other banks' reference requests within a reasonable time. A separate annex covers due diligence on all potential employees, including past terminations and fraud or dishonesty convictions.

key_points.point: Under the securities law, anyone carrying on regulated activities has to be licensed by or registered with the SFC, unless an exemption applies. A bank that intends to do so should apply to become a registered institution (RI) and appoint at least two EOs for each activity.
The HKMA expects a bank to enter other staff doing regulated work on the HKMA register before they perform any regulated function.
The circular consolidates existing guidance and introduces no new regulatory standards; superseded circulars are listed in Annex 5.
Reference checks on a proposed registered employee should cover dismissals, requests to resign and internal investigations or discipline for conduct.
Banks should respond clearly and within a reasonable time to other banks' requests for information on former staff, using MRC timelines as a guide.

The HKMA reminds banks that they need to ensure all their employees are fit and proper, not just EOs and registered staff. This includes thorough due diligence on job candidates' past terminations and criminal convictions (Annex 4).

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the current HKMA playbook for staffing any SFO-regulated digital-asset activity at a bank: EO consent, register entries and hiring checks. It replaces older circulars, so policies citing them need updating.

quote.text: This consolidated guidance has not introduced any new regulatory standards.

reading_guide: The three-page letter is quick; the operative detail is in Annex 1 (registration, EOs, HKMA register), Annex 2 (fitness controls, unregistered dealing) and Annex 4 (pre-hire checks).
flags: The BRDR attachments numbered 20251027-3 and -4 are an unrelated climate-risk circular issued the same day; Annexes 1-5 of this circular are in one PDF (20251027-2-EN).

obligations: Register relevant individuals on the HKMA register before they perform regulated functions (p.1, para 2).
Run reference checks covering dismissals and conduct investigations and follow the MRC Scheme (p.2, para 2).
controls_and_monitoring: Review policies that cite superseded circulars listed in Annex 5 (p.3).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Hiring checks for staff in any SFO-regulated activity, including virtual asset sales and dealing, follow this consolidated HKMA guidance (p.2).

supersedes_or_amends: HKMA circular, 5 July 2002: Banking (Amendment) Ordinance 2002 and Securities and Futures Ordinance
HKMA circular, 12 September 2002: Register of relevant individuals to be maintained by the HKMA under the Banking (Amendment) Ordinance 2002

title: Annex 1 - Guidance on registration related matters (with Annexes 2 to 5)
summary: These annexes support the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) circular of 27 October 2025. They give the working detail for banks that are, or want to become, registered institutions (RIs) with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC). Annex 1 covers how to apply for registration and how the HKMA advises the SFC. It also covers consent for executive officers (EOs), provisional consent, and keeping the HKMA register of securities staff up to date. Annex 2 covers controls to keep registered staff fit and proper and to prevent unregistered dealing. Annex 4 sets pre-hire checks for all employees. These include the Banking Ordinance (BO) bar on hiring people with fraud or dishonesty convictions without HKMA consent. Annex 5 lists the older HKMA circulars that the package replaces.

key_points.point: A bank must apply to the HKMA for consent to at least two EOs per proposed activity no later than it applies to the SFC for registration.
key_points.locator: Annex 1, Part I, 'Application for registration as RIs'

key_points.point: The HKMA assesses registration applicants on experience, management, controls and resources, may ask for an Independent Assurance Report, and may recommend conditions such as limits on scope.
key_points.locator: Annex 1, Part I, 'Assessment of an application to become an RI'

key_points.point: Banks should tell the HKMA in advance of planned registration applications.
key_points.locator: Annex 1, Part I, 'Assessment of an application to become an RI'

key_points.point: No one may act as an EO before written HKMA consent; the applicant must show fitness and sufficient authority.
key_points.locator: Annex 1, Part II, 'Application to become an EO'

key_points.point: At least one EO per activity should be a CE, alternate CE, director or s.72B manager, and any other EO no more than one rank below that level.
key_points.locator: Annex 1, Part II, 'Assessment of an application to become an EO'

key_points.point: The HKMA may grant provisional EO consent under BO s.71E pending background checks, if depositors and investors are not prejudiced.
key_points.locator: Annex 1, Part II, 'Application for provisional consent'

key_points.point: An EO needs fresh consent before supervising an extra regulated activity.

The RI should tell the HKMA about changes to EO information, including an EO leaving, within seven business days. The RI is also required to tell the SFC and the HKMA whether it started an internal investigation into the person in the six months before the EO role ended.
Relevant individuals who stop being fit and proper, for example by failing to pass the local regulatory paper in time, should be promptly removed from the HKMA register.

The HKMA expects banks to have controls against unregistered dealing. Staff should report suspected cases to compliance at once. Where there are reasonable grounds to believe it happened, the bank should stop the practice at once and report in writing to the HKMA as soon as practicable.
Before hiring, banks should ask about past terminations and fraud or dishonesty convictions, including spent ones; such a person cannot be employed without written HKMA consent under BO s.73(1)(b).

Look-back for internal investigations on EO cessation

obligations: Apply for EO consent no later than the SFC registration application (Annex 1, Part I).
Do not let anyone act as EO before consent (Annex 1, Part II).
Screen new hires for fraud or dishonesty convictions, including spent ones, and require HKMA consent where relevant (Annex 4, item (2)).
controls_and_monitoring: Controls and training against unregistered dealing (Annex 2).
Prompt de-registration of staff who cease to be fit and proper (Annex 1, Part III).
notifications_reporting: Pre-notify the HKMA of intended registration applications (Annex 1, Part I).
Notify EO and register changes within 7 business days (Annex 1, Parts II-III).
Disclose internal investigations begun within 6 months before an EO ceases (Annex 1, Part II, item (d)).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Adding a regulated activity or changing EOs triggers HKMA consent and seven-business-day notices, so EO coverage and register accuracy are board-level items (Annex 1, Parts II-III).

title: Asset and Wealth Management Activities Survey 2025
summary: This is the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) annual survey of Hong Kong's asset and wealth management industry. It gives figures as at 31 December 2025 and was published in July 2026. Total assets under management (AUM) rose 20% to a record HK$42,202 billion. Net fund inflows rose 193% to HK$2,065 billion. Private banking and private wealth management, served by licensed corporations and by banks registered with the SFC, grew 24% to HK$12,945 billion. The report notes that SFC-authorised virtual asset (VA) funds may now stake, and that three VA spot exchange-traded funds (ETFs) were staking by December 2025. It also gives staff numbers, including 8,752 private banking and wealth staff reported by registered institutions (RIs).

key_points.point: Hong Kong's total assets under management rose 20% to HK$42,202 billion at end-2025, a record above the 2021 peak.
Net fund inflows rose 193% to HK$2,065 billion in 2025, the third straight year of growth.
Private banking and private wealth management assets, served by licensed corporations (LCs) and RIs, rose 24% to HK$12,945 billion, with net inflows up 79% to HK$686 billion.
After an April 2025 SFC update, authorised VA funds may stake. The SFC approved two VA spot ETFs for staking, and three were doing so by December 2025.
Hong Kong-listed ETFs and leveraged and inverse products reached HK$618.7 billion market value at end-2025, up 33.7%.
The report cites an InvestHK-commissioned study counting over 3,380 single-family offices at end-2025, with interest in digital assets among alternatives.
Firms licensed for asset management (Type 9) rose 7% to 2,358 and licensed individuals 5% to 15,747.
Industry headcount rose 5% to 56,557; about 51% of respondents plan to hire in the coming year.
47 RIs reported private banking or wealth business, and RIs reported 8,752 staff in that segment.
key_points.locator: Section VI, para 45 and fn 1, para 50

VA spot ETFs staking at Dec 2025
Staff in asset and wealth management

title: SFC-HKMA Joint Survey on the Sale of Non-exchange-traded Investment Products 2025
summary: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) run this survey each year. It measures sales of unlisted investment products by licensed corporations (LCs) and by banks registered as registered institutions (RIs) during 2025. It covers sales to non-professional investors, individual professional investors and some corporate professional investors. Total sales rose 63% to a record HK$9.9 trillion, and RIs made 62% of them. Funds and structured products drove the growth, and money market funds were the most popular fund type. Online channels reached 21% of sales. The survey excludes exchange-traded funds (ETFs), listed products and bank-issued currency and interest-rate linked instruments. It reports no virtual asset product category.

key_points.point: The survey covers 2025 sales by 2,611 surveyed firms (2,502 LCs and 109 RIs), with over 99% responding; 67 RIs reported selling investment products.
Exchange-traded funds, listed securities, insurance products and bank-issued currency and interest-rate linked instruments sold by RIs are outside the survey.
Total transaction value rose 63% to HK$9.9 trillion; RIs accounted for 62% and LCs 38%.
Collective investment schemes (CIS) rose 85% to HK$4.1 trillion and structured products 53% to HK$3.9 trillion, together over 80% of activity.
Clients completing at least one trade rose 33% to more than 1.6 million.
Online sales were 21% of the total, up from 17%, and 122 firms (including 36 RIs) sold through online platforms.
Sales staff reached a record 20,126, including 13,808 relevant individuals at RIs.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Registered institutions made 62% of unlisted investment product sales in 2025. This survey shows the scale and the online shift of the bank wealth channel. The regulators say they use the data to spot risks in intermediaries' selling (para 2).

quote.text: identify risks associated with the selling activities of intermediaries

reading_guide: Read Part III key findings (pp.4-5); Part IV has the detail and the appendix gives 2020-2025 series.
flags: No virtual asset or tokenised product category is reported; do not cite this survey for VA distribution volumes.

notifications_reporting: Large RIs (HK$30 billion or more in transactions) were asked for extra product detail in the survey (para 5).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Context for any board discussion on distributing VA or tokenised products through existing wealth channels.

title: Quarterly Report April-June 2026
summary: This Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) quarterly report covers 1 April to 30 June 2026, the first quarter of its 2026-27 financial year. On digital assets, it reports 13 licensed virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs), with six more applications under review. It reports 11 virtual asset (VA) spot exchange-traded funds (ETFs) with a combined value of US$451 million. Fifteen tokenised retail products held HK$10.3 billion in their tokenised classes. In May 2026, the SFC and the Government's Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB) published joint conclusions on regulating VA advisory and management services. The SFC says it aims to put a bill for the VA dealing, custody, advisory and management regimes into the Legislative Council (LegCo) in 2026. It also notes an April pilot that lets tokenised SFC-authorised funds trade on licensed VATPs.

key_points.point: The SFC and the FSTB published joint consultation conclusions in May 2026 on regulating VA advisory and management providers. They aim to put a bill covering VA dealing, custody, advisory and management into LegCo in 2026.
Thirteen VATPs were licensed at end-June 2026, with licence applications from six more under review.

The 11 VA spot ETFs had a combined market value of US$451 million at end-June, 55% above launch levels. Average daily turnover since launch was US$5.3 million. Three of them may stake through licensed VATPs.
In May 2026 the SFC issued guidance letting authorised funds use and hold tokenised deposits and HKMA-licensed fiat-referenced stablecoins.
A May 2026 circular set out conduct requirements for VATPs and licensed corporations offering services in HKMA-regulated stablecoins.
Since April 2026 a pilot lets tokenised units of SFC-authorised open-ended funds trade on licensed VATPs; the first batch is expected to be tokenised money market funds.
key_points.locator: p.32, 'Piloting secondary trading of tokenised products'

key_points.point: Licensees under AMLO (Hong Kong's anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing law) totalled 159 at 30 June 2026: 13 providers and 146 individuals. That is 30.3% more than a year earlier.
Fifteen tokenised retail products held HK$10.3 billion in tokenised classes, 5% lower than end-March but 280% higher year on year.
A report on lessons from the Project Ensemble sandbox was tentatively scheduled for August 2026.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This gives the latest official counts of licensed VATPs, VA ETFs and tokenised funds as at 30 June 2026. It also records the SFC's stated aim to bring a bill for new VA dealing, custody, advisory and management regimes to LegCo in 2026 (p.30).

quote.text: traditional finance structures remain sensible choices for the underlying vehicles

reading_guide: Read Highlights p.6 and the digital asset pages 30-33 (PDF pp.31-34); the rest covers listings, enforcement and financial statements.
flags: Locators use the printed page; PDF page is one higher.
The 2026 LegCo bill timing is the SFC's stated aim, not an enacted timetable.

controls_and_monitoring: Track the proposed AMLO regimes for VA dealing, custody, advisory and management; the SFC aims to introduce a bill in 2026 (p.30).
counterparty_due_diligence: Check a VATP's licence status against the SFC's list; 13 were licensed at end-June 2026 (p.30).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Board horizon-scan item: new VA dealing, custody, advisory and management regimes targeted for a 2026 bill.

title: SFC Annual Report 2025-26
summary: This Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) annual report covers the year to 31 March 2026. It reviews SFC work under its ASPIRe digital asset roadmap, which has five pillars: Access, Safeguards, Products, Infrastructure and Relationships. It records two joint consultations with the Government's Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB). The first was on licensing virtual asset (VA) dealing and custody providers. The second was on extending licensing to VA advisory and management, with a bill planned for 2026. New permissions include shared order books with overseas affiliates, affiliate market makers, staking and VA margin financing. With the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the SFC also issued guidance on off-platform trading. At year-end there were 12 licensed virtual asset trading platforms (VATPs), 11 VA spot exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and 13 tokenised retail products. Project Ensemble moved to its EnsembleTX pilot in November 2025.

key_points.point: The SFC and FSTB consulted in 2025 on licensing VA dealing and custody providers, then consulted in late 2025 on adding VA advisory and management, and plan a 2026 bill.
From November 2025 licensed VATPs may pool orders with overseas affiliates in a shared order book, and affiliates may act as market makers.
Twelve VATPs were licensed at 31 March 2026, with seven applications under review, four from deemed applicants.
The SFC clarified minimum custody requirements for VATPs, covering governance, cold wallet set-up, use of outside providers and live threat monitoring.
By 31 March 2026 there were 11 SFC-authorised VA spot ETFs, three permitted to stake through licensed VATPs, and two VATPs offering staking.
VA brokers may offer VA financing to securities margin clients with strong credit and collateral, subject to safeguards.
With the HKMA, the SFC issued guidance letting intermediaries use VATPs' off-platform trading services and clarifying subscriptions and redemptions paid in VAs.
VATPs may now list VAs for professional investors, and HKMA-licensed stablecoins, without a 12-month track record, and may distribute tokenised securities.
The Government confirmed that the stamp duty waiver for transfers of Hong Kong-listed ETFs extends to tokenised ETFs.

Project Ensemble moved to its EnsembleTX pilot in November 2025. The pilot lets real-value deals using tokenised deposits and digital assets run in a controlled setting. The report also says several banks have launched live tokenised deposits.
Thirteen tokenised retail products held HK$10.8 billion at 31 March 2026, up 594% year on year.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the SFC's own year-end record of which VA activities are now allowed and how big the market is. Some items involve intermediaries, including banks, directly: the joint HKMA-SFC guidance on off-platform VA trading and on client subscriptions and redemptions paid in VAs. It also records the planned VA dealing and custody regimes and the EnsembleTX pilot for tokenised deposits.

quote.text: several banks have launched live tokenised deposits

reading_guide: Read Highlights p.28 and the digital asset pages 64-66 (PDF 66-68), plus Strategic Priority 3 on p.12. Skip the financial statements.
flags: The annual report quotes VA spot ETF value as $4.3 billion at 31 March 2026, while the April-June 2026 Quarterly Report quotes US$451 million at 30 June 2026; the currencies and dates differ, so quote each with its own date.
Printed page numbers are two lower than PDF page numbers.

controls_and_monitoring: Track the proposed VA dealing, custody, advisory and management regimes; the SFC and FSTB plan a bill in 2026 (p.64).
counterparty_due_diligence: When using a VATP for off-platform trading or custody, check its licence and any affiliate arrangements (pp.64-65).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The SFC and FSTB plan a 2026 bill for four new VA regimes; the EnsembleTX pilot for real-value tokenised deposit transactions began in November 2025 (pp.64, 66).

title: HKMA Annual Report 2025 - International Financial Centre
summary: This is the International Financial Centre chapter of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) Annual Report 2025. It reviews the HKMA's fintech and market-development work in 2025. It records the launch of the Fintech 2030 strategy, whose four pillars are known as DART: data and payments, artificial intelligence (AI), resilience and tokenisation. It describes the November 2025 launch of EnsembleTX, for settling real-value deals with tokenised deposits. It records the end of Phase 2 of the e-HKD (Hong Kong's central bank digital currency) pilot, with a new focus on wholesale use by financial institutions. It also covers the Government's third tokenised bond and plans to issue tokenised bonds regularly. On stablecoins, it notes that the Stablecoins Ordinance took effect on 1 August 2025. The HKMA set a high bar for licences and announced the first two licensed issuers in April 2026.

key_points.point: The HKMA unveiled Fintech 2030 in November 2025 with four pillars (data and payments, AI, resilience, tokenisation) and more than 40 initiatives.

EnsembleTX, the pilot phase of Project Ensemble, launched in November 2025. It supports settling real-value deals in tokenised deposits. It starts with tokenised money market fund deals and real-time liquidity and treasury management.
After e-HKD Pilot Phase 2 ended in October 2025, the HKMA said it would prioritise e-HKD for financial institutions in wholesale settings while keeping retail readiness.
The Government's third tokenised bond, in November 2025, was described as the largest digital bond offering and the first to settle with tokenised central bank money (e-CNY and e-HKD).
The 2025-26 Budget announced regular tokenised government bond issuance, and the HKMA is reviewing the legal framework for tokenised bonds with the Government.

The Legislative Council (LegCo) passed the Stablecoins Bill in May 2025. The Ordinance took effect on 1 August 2025. The HKMA issued its supervisory guideline and its anti-money laundering guideline for issuers beforehand.
key_points.locator: p.138, 'New regulatory regime for stablecoin issuers'

key_points.point: The HKMA set a high bar for stablecoin licences: compliance, viable use cases and prudent operation. It began taking applications in August 2025 and announced the first two licensed issuers in April 2026.
The HKMA led the Financial Stability Board's thematic review of how jurisdictions implement the global crypto-asset framework.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the HKMA's own account of where tokenised deposits, e-HKD, tokenised bonds and stablecoin licensing stood at end-2025. It frames which bank digital-asset projects the HKMA is actively supporting.

quote.text: the HKMA has set a high bar for licensing

reading_guide: Read pp.133 (Fintech 2030), 137 (Ensemble, e-HKD) and 138 (stablecoins); p.125 covers tokenised bonds. The rest of the chapter covers payments, market infrastructure and research.
flags: Printed page numbers are 117 higher than the PDF page numbers of this chapter file.

counterparty_due_diligence: When dealing with a stablecoin issuer, check it is among HKMA-licensed issuers; only two were announced by April 2026 (p.138).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: HKMA priorities under Fintech 2030 include tokenised deposits (EnsembleTX), wholesale e-HKD and regular tokenised government bonds (pp.125, 133, 137).

title: HKMA Annual Report 2025 - Banking Stability
summary: This is the Banking Stability chapter of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) Annual Report 2025. It reviews bank supervision in 2025. For digital assets, it records April 2025 HKMA guidance on banks offering staking as part of custody. It records a September 2025 supplemental joint circular with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC). That circular lets intermediaries offer staking and use the off-platform trading services of SFC-licensed platforms. The HKMA, the Government and the SFC are also developing statutory regimes for virtual asset (VA) dealing and custody. The Basel crypto-asset capital and disclosure standards took effect in Hong Kong on 1 January 2026, through changes to the banking capital, disclosure and exposure-limit rules. The chapter also reports twice as many anti-money laundering on-site examinations, wider artificial intelligence (AI) use in transaction monitoring, and a longer engagement period for itinerant professionals.

key_points.point: In April 2025 the HKMA set out standards for banks offering VA staking as part of custody services.
A September 2025 supplemental joint HKMA-SFC circular let intermediaries offer staking and use SFC-licensed platforms' off-platform VA trading services.
The HKMA is working with the Government and SFC on statutory regimes for VA dealing and custody services.
The HKMA stepped up surveillance of crypto firms falsely claiming to be banks, in breach of the Banking Ordinance.
Thematic work in 2025 covered banks' digital asset-related activities among other conduct topics, within 24 on-site examinations and 509 thematic reviews.
The Basel crypto-asset exposure and disclosure standards took effect in Hong Kong on 1 January 2026 via changes to the Banking (Capital), (Disclosure) and (Exposure Limits) Rules.
key_points.locator: p.90, 'Prudential treatment of the cryptoasset exposures of banks'

key_points.point: HKMA on-site examinations of banks' anti-money laundering controls doubled from 14 in 2024 to 28 in 2025.

Banks' implementation plans show that more than 30% of banks with significant Hong Kong operations already use AI in transaction monitoring. The plans indicate this will rise above 80% over the next two years.
RIs may now engage itinerant professionals for up to 45 days a year, up from 30.
