title: Departmental Interpretation and Practice Notes No. 39 (Revised) - Profits Tax: Digital Economy, Electronic Commerce and Digital Assets
supersedes_or_amends: DIPN No. 39 (July 2001)
summary: This Inland Revenue Department (IRD) practice note explains how the IRD applies profits tax to e-commerce and, in paragraphs 41 to 52, to digital assets. It sorts tokens into payment, security and utility tokens. It says their tax treatment follows their nature and use, not their label. Profits from selling digital assets held as long-term investments are capital and outside profits tax. Hong Kong-sourced profits from crypto trading, exchange or mining are taxable. Tokens from airdrops or forks received in a crypto business count as business receipts, and crypto salaries are taxed at market value. The note states the IRD's view of the law as at March 2020, and taxpayers' rights to object and appeal are not affected. Its statement in paragraph 43 that Hong Kong has no specific digital-asset law is out of date.

key_points.point: The IRD treats payment tokens such as Bitcoin as virtual commodities, not legal tender in Hong Kong.
Tokens are grouped as payment, security or utility tokens, and profits tax treatment turns on the token's nature and use.

For an initial coin offering (ICO), the substance of the token's rights decides its treatment, not the issuer's stated intention. Proceeds from equity-like tokens are capital. Proceeds from utility tokens are prepayments for future goods or services.

Profits from selling digital assets bought as long-term investments are not taxable. Whether an asset is capital or trading stock depends on the facts, including the badges of trade and the intention at purchase.
Hong Kong-sourced profits from crypto trading, exchange or mining are chargeable, with source decided by where the profit-generating operations took place.
Whether crypto activity is a business depends on frequency, degree of organisation and profit motive.
New tokens from airdrops or forks received in a crypto business are treated as business receipts.
Crypto businesses are required to keep proper records of their crypto transactions under s.51C of the Inland Revenue Ordinance.
Payments made or received in crypto are valued at market value on the transaction date, and crypto salaries are taxed at market value when they accrue.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the IRD's published practice note on how profits tax applies to crypto activity. It matters when a bank's virtual asset dealing, custody or own-account line earns income, and when staff are paid in tokens. Its paragraph 43 description of the law dates from March 2020.

quote.text: Profits tax treatment of digital tokens would depend on their nature and use.

reading_guide: For digital assets, read paras 41-52 (PDF pp.29-33). Read para 43 as a March 2020 snapshot only. The earlier paragraphs cover e-commerce source and permanent establishment rules.
flags: Outdated statement: paragraph 43 says Hong Kong had no law or regulation made specifically for digital assets. That was the position in March 2020. Hong Kong has since legislated, for example the virtual asset trading platform licensing regime under the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance and the Stablecoins Ordinance (see their registry entries). The tax analysis in paras 41-42 and 44-52 is unaffected by that statement.

controls_and_monitoring: Keep full records of any crypto transactions for tax purposes (para 50).
Document holding intent (investment vs trading) when acquiring digital assets (para 46).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The IRD's tax treatment of virtual asset income turns on whether assets are held as capital or trading stock and on where profits arise (paras 46-47).

title: Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Preferential Tax Regimes for Funds, Family-owned Investment Holding Vehicles and Carried Interest) Bill 2026 gazetted
summary: This Government press release announces that a tax bill was published in the Gazette on 12 June 2026. The bill proposes wider tax breaks for privately offered funds, for family-owned investment holding vehicles (FIHVs) run by eligible single family offices, and for carried interest. It proposes a wider definition of fund, more qualifying investments, removal of the 5% cap on incidental transactions, and relaxed rules for special purpose entities. It also proposes better carried interest rules. The unified funds regime would gain a tax reporting mechanism and economic substance requirements. A Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB) spokesperson said the changes would complement Hong Kong's development in areas including digital assets. First reading in the Legislative Council (LegCo) was set for 24 June 2026.

key_points.point: The bill seeks better tax treatment for private funds, family-office FIHVs and fund managers' carried interest.
Proposed changes include a wider fund definition, more qualifying investments, dropping the 5% incidental-transaction threshold and relaxed rules for special purpose entities.
The unified funds regime would gain a tax reporting mechanism and economic substance requirements like those for FIHVs.
The FSTB said the measures would complement development in digital assets, precious metals and commodities, and attract private credit activity.
First reading in LegCo was scheduled for 24 June 2026.

numbers_and_dates.item: Incidental transaction threshold to be removed

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: The bill proposes tax changes for Hong Kong funds, family-office vehicles and carried interest, and the FSTB links them to Hong Kong's digital asset development. As of 25 September 2026 it is a bill, not law.

quote.text: complementing Hong Kong's development in areas such as digital assets

reading_guide: Short release; read in full. The bill text and LegCo Brief sit on the LegCo site.
flags: The release itself does not list digital assets as a qualifying investment; that detail is in the Government's earlier statements (see LCQ9, 30 July 2025) and the bill text, which was not fetched here (LegCo site not reachable).

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Tax concessions for funds, family offices and carried interest are proposed in a bill and depend on LegCo passage.

title: FSTB responds to media enquiries regarding preferential tax regime for carried interest
summary: This reply of 12 August 2026 from the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB) was republished on the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) website. It explains the carried interest part of the 2026 tax bill on funds, family offices and carried interest. The bill proposes that the concession cover other profits of eligible funds, not only private equity. A business trading with its own capital for its own account is not a fund, so pay from it would not qualify. Eligible carried interest must be linked to fund performance, set by the fund's governing agreement and non-discretionary. It must be earned for investment management services in Hong Kong. The Legislative Council (LegCo) Bills Committee had finished clause-by-clause scrutiny. The Government aimed to resume the second reading debate in the second half of 2026. If passed, the measures would apply from the 2025/26 year of assessment.

key_points.point: The carried interest concession would cover other profits of eligible funds, not just private equity.
A business trading or holding assets with its own capital for its own account is not a fund, so its staff pay would not qualify.
Eligible carried interest must depend on fund performance, follow the governing agreement and be non-discretionary, and be earned for investment management services provided in Hong Kong.
Clause-by-clause examination was complete, and the Government targeted resuming second reading in the second half of 2026.
If passed, the measures would apply from the 2025/26 year of assessment, and the IRD would issue administrative guidance where needed.

numbers_and_dates.item: Effective year of assessment if passed

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: It confirms the bill was still before LegCo in August 2026. It also shows the Government separates funds from own-account trading businesses for this tax concession.

quote.text: The Government does not have plans to further expand the scope of the preferential measures.

reading_guide: Read in full; paras 3-4 on scope and para 6 on timing.
flags: Status checked only to 12 August 2026; whether the bill passed by 25 September 2026 was not verified from an official source in this batch.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Track bill passage; effective from 2025/26 if enacted.

title: LCQ9: Promoting the establishment of family offices in Hong Kong
summary: This is the written answer from Hong Kong's Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury to a Legislative Council (LegCo) question on 30 July 2025. It describes the family office tax concession and plans to widen it. Family-owned investment holding vehicles (FIHVs) run by a single family office can get a profits tax exemption on qualifying transactions. They must meet a HK$240 million asset threshold and a substantial activities requirement. The reply restates the 2025-26 Budget proposal to add emission derivatives, insurance-linked securities, private credit and digital assets to qualifying transactions. It says the Government aimed to put legislation to LegCo in 2026, applying from 2025/26 if approved. It also cites about 2,700 single family offices at end-2023 and HK$1,551 billion of private banking assets linked to family offices and private trusts at end-2024.

key_points.point: FIHVs managed by single family offices that meet a HK$240 million asset threshold and substance test can get profits tax exemption on qualifying transactions, effective from 2022/23.
The Government proposed in the 2025-26 Budget to add digital assets, among other items, to the qualifying transactions for single family offices.
Industry consultation was complete, and the Government aimed to put legislation to LegCo in 2026, taking effect from 2025/26 if approved.
Multi-family offices are not covered by the FIHV regime, but vehicles meeting the fund definition with transactions arranged by an SFC-licensed corporation can use the unified funds exemption.

An InvestHK-commissioned consultant counted about 2,700 single family offices at end-2023; private banking and wealth assets of family office and private trust clients were HK$1,551 billion at end-2024.

numbers_and_dates.item: Private banking/wealth assets of FO and trust clients, end-2024

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: It is an official statement that the Government proposed adding digital assets to the qualifying transactions for family-office tax relief. The proposal was not law at the time. A bill on the family-office regime was gazetted in June 2026 (see fca785b80cff).

quote.text: insurance-linked securities, loans and private credit investments, and digital assets

reading_guide: Read the introduction and parts (1) and (4) of the reply; parts (2)-(3) are InvestHK statistics.
flags: The proposals described here were taken forward in the bill gazetted on 12 June 2026 (fca785b80cff); that bill's press release does not itself list digital assets. Use this reply as the record of the stated policy intent.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Context for private-bank VA offerings to family offices; the tax change is proposed, not enacted.

title: Digital Banks (list of digital banks, as at 31 August 2026)
summary: This Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) spreadsheet, linked from its Digital Banks webpage, lists the digital banks authorized in Hong Kong as at 31 August 2026. It names eight banks, all incorporated in Hong Kong, and gives a former company name for each. The webpage defines a digital bank as one that delivers banking services mainly or only through the internet or other electronic channels. It says digital banks follow the same supervisory requirements as conventional banks. Some requirements are adapted to their business models on a risk-based, technology-neutral basis. Digital banks were earlier called virtual banks, and the HKMA renamed its authorization guideline in October 2024.

key_points.point: The HKMA lists eight digital banks as at 31 August 2026: ANT BANK (HONG KONG) LIMITED, ELE BANK LIMITED, FUSION BANK LIMITED, LIVI BANK LIMITED, MOX BANK LIMITED, PING AN DIGITAL BANK (INTERNATIONAL) LIMITED, WELAB BANK LIMITED and ZA BANK LIMITED. Each has a former name shown in the list.
All eight listed digital banks are incorporated in Hong Kong.
The HKMA defines a digital bank by its delivery channel: services provided mainly or only online or through other electronic channels.
The HKMA says digital banks face the same supervisory requirements as conventional banks, adapted where needed on a risk-based and technology-neutral basis.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the official list to check before treating a firm as a Hong Kong digital bank, whether as a competitor, partner or counterparty for VA-related services. Names have changed, so use the list to match current and former names.
reading_guide: One-page list; check it against the HKMA Register of AIs for current licence status.
flags: Source is an .xls file converted to text for this registry. The list gives a former company name for each of the eight banks, for example AIRSTAR BANK LIMITED (now ELE BANK LIMITED) and PAO BANK LIMITED (now PING AN DIGITAL BANK (INTERNATIONAL) LIMITED).
Named entities are listed only as stated by the HKMA.

counterparty_due_diligence: Confirm a counterparty's status and current legal name against the HKMA list and Register of AIs.

title: Guideline on Authorization of Digital Banks
supersedes_or_amends: Guideline on Authorization of Virtual Banks (5 May 2000; updated 21 September 2012 and 30 May 2018)
summary: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) issued this guideline under Banking Ordinance section 16(10). It sets the principles the HKMA uses when deciding whether to authorize a digital bank. A digital bank is a bank that serves customers wholly or mainly through the internet or other electronic channels. The guideline replaces the Guideline on Authorization of Virtual Banks. Applicants must meet the usual minimum authorization criteria and must keep a physical office in Hong Kong. The HKMA expects them to be locally incorporated and to have committed, capable owners. The guideline stresses technology risk, a credible path to profit, an exit plan, fair treatment of customers and early discussion of material outsourcing. Digital banks are supervised on the same basis as other banks, with some rules adapted to their model.

key_points.point: A digital bank applicant must show real substance and a credible business plan, not just a concept riding on new technology.
Digital banks should not impose minimum balance requirements or low-balance fees.

The HKMA expects digital banks to be locally incorporated. A holder of more than 50% should normally be a supervised bank or financial institution. Otherwise, the HKMA expects a Hong Kong intermediate holding company with supervisory conditions.
Tech firms and other non-financial groups, as well as financial firms and existing banks, may seek to own a digital bank.
Digital banks face the same supervisory requirements as conventional banks, with some adapted on a risk-based, technology-neutral basis; boards need relevant technology knowledge.
Applicants must commission an independent expert review of planned IT governance and systems, and a fuller review before starting operations.
The HKMA would be concerned by aggressive market-share growth with heavy losses and no credible medium-term path to profit.
Applicants must provide an exit plan for an orderly wind-down if the business model fails.
The HKMA's view is that customers should not bear direct losses from unauthorized transactions unless they were fraudulent or grossly negligent.
Digital banks should discuss plans for material outsourcing with the HKMA in advance. They should show that the principles of the outsourcing module (SPM SA-2) will be met.

numbers_and_dates.locator: HKMA Digital Banks webpage; BRDR record

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: It sets the entry rules for a bank that operates mainly online. It also shows the HKMA's expectations on exit plans, independent IT assessments and outsourcing for technology-led banks. The guideline does not mention virtual or digital assets.

quote.text: it must have substance and cannot simply be a “concept”

reading_guide: Five pages; read in full. Pair with the Guideline on Minimum Criteria for Authorization.
flags: The guideline itself does not mention virtual or digital assets.

notifications_reporting: Discuss material outsourcing with the HKMA in advance (para 23).

title: Report on the Review of Virtual Banks
summary: This August 2024 Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) report reviews the eight virtual banks (now called digital banks) that launched from 2020. It finds they met the policy aims of promoting fintech, a new customer experience and financial inclusion. They had 2.2 million depositors by end-2023, but none was yet profitable. Six were registered with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) for securities business by July 2024. The HKMA saw no strong reason to license more virtual banks at that time. It said it would remove the rule that virtual banks must mainly serve retail customers, citing their growing dealings with businesses, including the digital asset sector. It says banks' digital-asset activities are supervised on a risk-based, 'same risk, same regulation' basis. The focus is prudential risk, anti-money laundering and financial crime risk, and investor protection.

key_points.point: By end-July 2024, six of the eight virtual banks were SFC registered institutions doing securities business and three were licensed insurance intermediaries.
Digital-asset activities of both incumbent and virtual banks are supervised on the same risk-based approach.
The HKMA will remove the requirement that a virtual bank mainly provides retail banking, noting their growing exposure to businesses including digital-asset and Web3 firms.
Some virtual banks want to expand into Web3 and digital assets, and the HKMA has guided them on regulatory expectations.
The HKMA's digital-asset supervision focuses on three areas: prudential risk, AML/CFT and financial crime, and investor protection.
Before any digital-asset activity, banks including virtual banks are expected to assess the risks and put in place mitigation that reflects applicable local and overseas rules.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: It records the HKMA's position that digital-asset activities at any bank, digital or incumbent, are supervised on the same risk-based footing, and that a risk assessment is expected before starting. It also explains why digital banks may now serve the digital-asset business sector.

quote.text: same risk, same regulation

reading_guide: Read the Executive Summary (pp.5-8) and paras 65-67 (pp.24-25) on digital assets.
flags: Virtual banks were renamed digital banks on 25 October 2024; this report uses the old term.

controls_and_monitoring: Complete a documented risk assessment before starting any digital-asset activity (para 67).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The HKMA expects banks, including digital banks, to assess the risks before any digital asset activity and to put mitigating measures in place (para 67).

title: Fraudulent websites and investment projects purporting to be related to HKMA
summary: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) warned the public about two scams that used its name. One fake site posed as the HKMA website. It used a made-up press release to push people to install a phone app carrying the "e-HKD" label and to buy so-called e-HKD bonds. The second scam claimed a recycling subsidy scheme was jointly overseen by the HKMA and a Mainland regulator. The HKMA said it has no link to either scheme and has referred both to the Police.

key_points.point: A fake website at gw.dgehkde[.]com posed as the HKMA site. It used a forged press release to get people to download an app named "e-HKD" and put money into "e-HKD bonds".
A second fake site claimed a Mainland state-owned firm ran a green recycling subsidy scheme overseen by the HKMA and a Mainland regulator. It asked people to join and deposit money.
The HKMA says it has no connection with these sites, the app or the schemes. It never contacts individuals or asks them to transfer funds about personal financial matters.
Firms taking part in the e-HKD Pilot Programme or other HKMA sandboxes do not raise money from the public or sell investment products linked to those programmes.
The HKMA has reported both cases to the Hong Kong Police Force. Victims are pointed to the Police Crime Wing Information Centre.

numbers_and_dates.item: Police Crime Wing Information Centre hotline

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: Scammers are using the e-HKD name to sell fake bonds and apps. Frontline and fraud teams can use this alert to explain to customers that no e-HKD investment product is offered to the public.

quote.text: will not solicit funding from the public or offer any investment products

reading_guide: Read the whole alert; it is six short paragraphs. The two bullets in para 2 describe the scams.

controls_and_monitoring: Fraud monitoring and customer-facing scam scripts can cover fake e-HKD bond offers and fake e-HKD apps (para 2, first bullet; para 4).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The e-HKD name is being used in public-facing investment scams; no action is required of banks by this alert.

flags: Paragraphs counted by us; the two bullets are treated as para 2.

title: HKEX and HKMA Launch Pilot Project to Enable Digital Payment Solution for Derivatives After-Hours Trading
summary: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and the exchange operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX) started a joint pilot. It tests paying advance margin for the derivatives after-hours trading session in e-HKD. Here e-HKD means a wholesale central bank digital currency (CBDC) that runs around the clock. Today, clearing participants must ask to deposit advance margin by 3 p.m. for it to count in the evening session. HKEX invited clearing participants of its futures clearing house to join real-value trial transactions on a voluntary basis. Both the trials and any wider use depend on regulatory approval and market readiness.

key_points.point: HKEX and the HKMA are testing e-HKD for advance margin payments in the derivatives after-hours trading (AHT) session. Here e-HKD is a wholesale CBDC that runs 24/7.

Under current practice, the futures clearing house, HKFE Clearing Corporation Limited (HKCC), must receive a clearing participant's advance margin request by 3 p.m. Only then do the funds count for that evening's AHT session.
HKEX invites HKCC clearing participants to join real-value trial transactions. Joining is optional.
The real-value trials, and any later wider rollout, depend on regulators approving them, the market being ready, and other factors.
An HKMA Deputy Chief Executive described the pilot as a wholesale CBDC use case in a live market setting.
The HKEX circular issued the same day says the pilot covers only advance margin payments, which are not a mandatory margin obligation. It set two participant briefings on 25 and 26 June 2026.

numbers_and_dates.item: Current cut-off for advance margin deposit requests
Derivatives record average daily volume in 2025
Average daily volume, first five months of 2026

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: It moves wholesale e-HKD into a live market setting with real-value trials. HKCC clearing participants were invited to join on an optional basis, for advance margin only.

quote.text: a wholesale central bank digital currency (CBDC) operating on a 24/7 basis

reading_guide: Read paras 2-4 for what is being tested and who may join. The HKEX circular (pp.1-2) adds scope and briefing dates; the quotes in paras 5-6 add little.

counterparty_due_diligence: Participation in the real-value trials is optional and subject to regulatory approval and market readiness (para 4); check whether any clearing-participant client or group entity has joined.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Wholesale e-HKD is being piloted for after-hours derivatives margin; it is a pilot, not a live service for all participants.

flags: The attached HKCC circular is issued by an HKEX subsidiary, not a government body; it is used only for scope and dates.

title: Beware of fraudulent document purported to be issued by HKMA
summary: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) warned about a forged HKMA document. It invites the public to join a "tender of Exchange Fund Bills" through a fake phone app, dressed up as an e-HKD business. The fake document says proceeds are paid in e-HKD and can then be withdrawn. The HKMA says the document and scheme are fake and have nothing to do with it. It has reported the matter to the Police.

key_points.point: Fraudsters posing as the HKMA spread a fake document about an Exchange Fund Bills tender. They presented it as linked to e-HKD.
The fake document tells people they can bid through a fake app, receive the proceeds in e-HKD, and then withdraw them.
The HKMA says the document and the investment scheme are fake. It never contacts individuals or asks them to transfer funds about personal financial matters.
Firms in the e-HKD Pilot Programme and other HKMA sandboxes do not raise money from the public or sell investment products tied to those programmes.
The HKMA has passed the case to the Police. People who shared details with the app are pointed to the Police Crime Wing Information Centre.

numbers_and_dates.item: Police Crime Wing Information Centre hotline

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: It follows a similar HKMA e-HKD scam alert of 3 June 2026. This one pairs the e-HKD name with a fake Exchange Fund Bills tender.

quote.text: under the guise of “e-HKD” related businesses

reading_guide: Read paras 1-3; the alert is short.

controls_and_monitoring: Fraud typologies can include fake Exchange Fund Bills tenders paying out in "e-HKD" via fake apps (para 1).
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: A further e-HKD-themed scam has been flagged by the HKMA; no action is required of banks by this alert.

title: Hong Kong maintains third place globally in Global Financial Centres Index
summary: This government press release reacts to the 40th edition of the Global Financial Centres Index (GFCI), in which Hong Kong kept third place overall. A government spokesman used it to restate financial policy priorities. On digital assets, the spokesman said Hong Kong's first regulated stablecoin went live in August 2026, after the first issuer licences in April. The release does not name the issuer or the stablecoin. The spokesman also gave a target date for a new bill. The government aims to put it into the Legislative Council within 2026. The bill would license virtual asset dealing, custody, advisory and management services.

key_points.point: The GFCI 40 report ranked Hong Kong third in the world and first in Asia Pacific. Hong Kong also stayed first globally for fintech offerings.
The spokesman stated that Hong Kong's first regulated stablecoin was launched in August 2026. The release names neither the issuer nor the coin.
The same paragraph recalls that the stablecoin issuer regime started in August 2025 and the first issuer licences were granted in April 2026.

The government is drafting legislative proposals for licensing virtual asset dealing, custody, advisory and management services. Its stated target is to introduce the bill into the Legislative Council within 2026.
The release links these moves to the First Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) and the 2026 Policy Address, both issued the same day.

numbers_and_dates.item: Target for virtual asset services bill
GFCI 40 overall rating for Hong Kong

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: This is the only official record found so far that a licensed stablecoin has actually launched in Hong Kong. It gives the month but not the issuer, so banks still need the HKMA register and issuer-level facts before relying on it. It also restates the 2026 target for the virtual asset services bill.

quote.text: the first regulated stablecoin in Hong Kong was already launched in August

reading_guide: Go straight to the digital assets paragraph (the second-last spokesman paragraph). The rest is general financial-centre messaging.

counterparty_due_diligence: The launch statement does not name the issuer (para 10); confirm any stablecoin counterparty against the HKMA Register of Licensed Stablecoin Issuers before treating it as licensed.
bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: Government states Hong Kong's first regulated stablecoin launched in August 2026, and targets a virtual asset services bill in LegCo within 2026.

flags: Paragraph numbers are counted by us; the release has no numbering.
Does not identify which licensed issuer launched; no HKMA press release on the launch was found for June-September 2026.

title: The First Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (2026-2030)
summary: This is Hong Kong's first five-year development plan, covering 2026 to 2030. The Chief Executive released it on 16 September 2026, the same day as the 2026 Policy Address. Its finance chapter sets broad aims rather than rules. On digital assets, it commits to a digital-asset licensing and supervision regime under a "same activity, same risks, same regulation" approach. It lists tokenisation as one of four fintech pillars. It names stablecoins, tokenised deposits, central bank digital currency, tokenised securities products and tokenised bonds as areas to develop carefully. It also plans regular digital government bond issues and more use of Project Ensemble.

key_points.point: The government plans a world-leading licensing and supervision regime for digital assets. Its guiding idea is "same activity, same risks, same regulation".
key_points.locator: Part 2, Chapter 6, Section 4, para 2.14, printed p.19 (PDF p.30)

key_points.point: Fintech work is to rest on four pillars: data and payment infrastructure, artificial intelligence (AI), resilience, and tokenisation of finance.
key_points.locator: Table 3 Finance+, item 1, printed p.20 (PDF p.31)

key_points.point: The plan supports wider practical use of tokenisation across asset classes through the HKMA's Project Ensemble.
key_points.locator: Table 3 Finance+, item 1, printed p.20 (PDF p.31)

key_points.point: It names stablecoins, tokenised deposits, central bank digital currency, tokenised securities products and tokenised bonds as digital assets to develop in a rigorous way.
key_points.locator: Table 3 Finance+, item 1, printed p.20 (PDF p.31)

key_points.point: The government will make digital government bond issues regular and improve the legal framework and market infrastructure for digital bonds.
key_points.locator: Part 2, Chapter 6, Section 2, para 2.8, printed p.16 (PDF p.27)

key_points.point: It will widen the use of supervisory sandboxes in financial services to balance innovation and regulation.
key_points.locator: Table 3 Finance+, item 1, printed p.20 (PDF p.31)

key_points.point: The risk section aims to strengthen fintech regulation and anti-money laundering capability as part of financial security.
key_points.locator: Part 2, Chapter 6, Section 5, para 2.15, printed p.21 (PDF p.32)

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: The plan is the top-level government direction for 2026-2030 and names stablecoins, tokenised deposits and CBDC as priorities. It creates no obligations. It sets out the government's direction for the period.

quote.text: same activity, same risks, same regulation

reading_guide: Read Part 2, Chapter 6 (printed pp.13-21), especially para 2.8, para 2.14 and Table 3. The rest of the plan covers non-financial areas.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The government's 2026-2030 plan names stablecoins, tokenised deposits, CBDC and tokenised bonds as priorities, and commits to a full digital-asset licensing regime.

flags: Printed page numbers differ from PDF page numbers by 11.
The PDF carries no issue date; 16 September 2026 comes from the GovHK press releases of that day.

title: Welcoming Remarks and Keynote Address at the Treasury Markets Summit 2026
summary: Eddie Yue, Chief Executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), spoke about the bond market at the Treasury Markets Summit. In the digital section, he said half of the world's digital bonds by volume in the first half of 2026 were issued in Hong Kong. He said the HKMA will keep supporting regular government digital bond issues. It also works with industry through its Tokenised Bond Expert Group. He described a digital-asset platform being built by CMU OmniClear for round-the-clock on-chain settlement. That platform will support settlement in central bank digital currencies and will explore links with tokenised deposits and regulated stablecoins. He also said the HKMA will test tokenised Exchange Fund Bills.

key_points.point: Hong Kong issued half of the world's digital bonds by volume in the first half of 2026.
The HKMA helped the government issue three digital bonds. They were a tokenised green bond (2023), a multi-currency digital bond (2024), and a bond using e-HKD and e-CNY (2025).
The HKMA will keep backing regular government digital bond issues and closer links with digital money. It works with industry through the Tokenised Bond Expert Group.
CMU OmniClear is building a digital-asset platform. It aims at 24-hour on-chain atomic settlement (both legs settle together or not at all).
The platform is designed to settle against central bank digital currencies (CBDCs). It will also explore links with tokenised deposits and regulated stablecoins.
The HKMA will test tokenised Exchange Fund Bills, to help banks look at new ways to manage assets and liabilities.

numbers_and_dates.item: Hong Kong share of global digital bond issuance by volume, first half of 2026
Government digital bond issues supported by the HKMA

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: The speech ties together the HKMA's current digital-bond plans in one place. The tokenised Exchange Fund Bills tests are aimed at banks' asset and liability management. The CMU OmniClear platform will explore settling bonds with tokenised deposits and regulated stablecoins.

quote.text: explore integration with tokenised deposits and regulated stablecoins

reading_guide: Read the 'Digital-native' section; the other sections cover bond market growth, RMB business and CMU links.
flags: Speaker (Eddie Yue, Chief Executive, HKMA) is taken from the web page header, which is not in the extracted text.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The HKMA plans to test tokenised Exchange Fund Bills with banks in mind, and CMU OmniClear's digital-asset platform will explore settlement with tokenised deposits and regulated stablecoins.

title: The SFC’s strategic action plan to implement the key initiatives under Hong Kong's first Five-Year Plan and the Chief Executive's 2026 Policy Address
summary: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) published a three-page table of short-term and medium-to-long-term actions. The table supports the First Five-Year Plan and the 2026 Policy Address. Most items cover renminbi business, stock and bond markets and commodities. Three items concern digital assets. In the short term, the SFC lists new digital-asset licensing regimes, plus tools to watch digital-asset custody, a "CrypTech" market surveillance function, and stronger anti-money laundering checks. In the medium to long term, it lists rules for tokenised investment products, such as tokenised gold and, where suitable, other real-world assets.

key_points.point: Short-term action under Finance+: bring in new licensing regimes for digital-asset activities.
key_points.locator: row 'Promoting Finance+', Short Term column, p.3

key_points.point: Medium-to-long-term action: set rules for tokenised investment products. These are to cover tokenised gold and, where suitable, other real-world assets.
key_points.locator: row 'Promoting Finance+', Medium to Long Term column, p.3

key_points.point: Short-term action under financial security: put in place surveillance of digital-asset custody, a 'CrypTech' market surveillance capability, and anti-money laundering capabilities.
key_points.locator: row 'Strengthening financial security', Short Term column, p.3

key_points.point: Medium-to-long-term action: use technology, including AI, in supervision, cybersecurity and anti-money laundering surveillance.
key_points.locator: row 'Strengthening financial security', Medium to Long Term column, p.3

key_points.point: The plan is a list of intended actions. It sets no dates for the digital-asset items and creates no new obligations.

why_it_matters_for_bank_HoDA: It confirms the SFC's near-term digital-asset agenda: new licensing regimes, custody and crypto market surveillance, and later tokenised product rules. Banks acting as registered institutions or distributing tokenised products can expect SFC work in these areas.

quote.text: Introduce new digital-asset licensing regimes

reading_guide: Only page 3 has digital-asset items (rows 'Promoting Finance+' and 'Strengthening financial security'). Pages 1-2 cover RMB, funds and market structure.

bank_compliance_angle.board_escalation: The SFC's action plan lists new digital-asset licensing regimes and custody/crypto surveillance as short-term items, and tokenised product frameworks as longer-term items.

flags: The document's own title is used; the press release calls it a strategic action plan.
